sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
From Newspaper Photography to Konstfack—Doubting the Appearance of Fact

Born in Gothenburg in 1967, von Hausswolff attended photography school before studying at Konstfack and the Royal Institute of Art, then began exhibiting internationally*16. She worked as a photographic printer and assistant and gained experience at the newspaper Göteborgs-Posten. She later recalled feeling uncomfortable in that role*2. Newspaper photographs are expected to communicate events clearly, yet they also produce familiar forms of fear, desire, and gender. That contradiction became a starting point for examining the appearance of fact from within photography.

Von Hausswolff moved to Stockholm in 1991 and studied at Konstfack. She has described the intense feminist debates of her student years as an important setting for her early series*2. Technical experience from the press, the histories of crime and war photography, and discomfort with the repeated image of the female victim all contributed to her continued use of photography. Bildmuseet mounted a major solo exhibition in 1998, indicating the early institutional reception of these concerns in Sweden*22.

Sweden in the 1990s—Critiques of Documentary and Feminist Debate

Social documentary photography held a strong position in Sweden during the 1970s, while subjective approaches became increasingly visible in the 1980s. By the early 1990s, younger artists were questioning both the appearance of photographic neutrality and the ways images repeat gender and power. The Hasselblad Foundation places von Hausswolff among the leading artists responding to these two earlier currents*4. She was strongly drawn to crime-scene photographs in the annual Nordisk Kriminalkrönika and studied their fixed details and compositions*2. Using friends and models allowed her to make anonymous scenes separated from the information of a specific case. Staging isolated the prone body, roadside setting, distant viewpoint, and cold light as recurring pictorial rules.

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
Back to Nature—Why Construct an Anonymous Scene?

Back to Nature (1993) shows women lying in natural settings at the distance and angle of crime-scene photographs. Magasin III holds early works and related pieces and publishes their physical specifications*6. The series began as a Konstfack assignment on “nature” and was shown in a student exhibition*2. Von Hausswolff used friends and models to construct scenes that recall crime photographs without identifying a person or event. The prone body, roadside location, remote viewpoint, and cool color are placed in the foreground. The title links the affirmative phrase “back to nature” with an image of an abandoned body. The visual grammar of crime photography meets a Nordic idea of landscape, revealing how representations that align women with nature can also invite fantasies of violence and disposal.

Hey Buster! What Do You Know About Desire—A Body That Returns the Question of Desire

Hey Buster! What Do You Know About Desire (1995) presents a prone body, a shoreline, and a dog standing nearby in a large-scale color photograph. Its title directs the question of desire back toward the scene. Moderna Museet describes the work as resembling a crime that will neither be investigated nor solved and compares the dog to a witness who sees but cannot speak*2.

The person’s name, the cause of the event, and what came before or after the image remain unknown. The photograph can therefore connect easily to plots repeated in crime reporting and film, yet the work confirms none of them. Its uncertainty reveals how conventions that read the female body as a sign of victimhood, desire, or death enter from outside the image.

Missing Causes and the Stories Viewers Supply

Magasin III describes von Hausswolff’s work as engaging social power, psychoanalysis, and violence at the border of reality and fiction*5. She specifies the orientation of a body, clothing, floor, furniture, and barriers while reducing the information that would identify cause or outcome. The image may suggest crime, sexual violence, accident, or performance, but it contains no evidence that settles on one narrative.

Different viewers may choose different stories and can reconsider whom they cast as a victim and which bodies they associate with danger or desire. A composition without a cause does more than create unease: it brings the conventions of gender and crime reporting used by the viewer into view.

Visible Details, Unknowable Events

Magasin III’s collection record for Hey Buster! What Do You Know About Desire publishes the 1995 C-print with an image of the work*3. Posture, skin, clothing, sand, and the dog’s coat are visible in detail. That abundance of information does not reveal the person’s condition, the preceding event, or the outcome. Von Hausswolff maintains the clarity of large-format color while separating material visibility from narrative understanding. Staging determines the body, clothing, and site precisely while removing clues that would identify the event.

Curtains, Blinds, and Foam—Moving Concealment Beyond the Image

Later works repeat curtains, blinds, cloth, foam, and furniture, moving concealment from the photographic surface into the exhibition space. A Moderna Museet curatorial text explains how foam that covers portions of an image and structures that obstruct sight regulate the viewer’s access*2. Andréhn-Schiptjenko’s artist material likewise connects series drawn from press and police archives to recent works combining UV printing, acrylic glass, oil paint, and metal prints*17. Concealment becomes a bodily experience of how close one may approach, what is reflected, and what remains stored away.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Large-Scale Color Photographs and the Cold Surface of Acrylic Glass

Many early photographs were produced as large-scale color prints and paired with smooth surfaces such as acrylic glass. The Hasselblad Foundation emphasizes the unity of staged photographs and spatial display*4. Glossy surfaces recall the visibility associated with medical, advertising, and police imagery while incorporating reflections of the viewer and gallery. As one approaches the body or object, one’s own image overlaps the surface of evidence. SFMOMA records Guided by Voices (1998) as a dye-destruction print mounted on aluminum, showing that the photograph was conceived as an object on the wall from an early stage*14.

Attempting to Deal with Time and Space—Measuring the Absence of the Body

In Attempting to Deal with Time and Space, measuring devices, furniture, and arrangement suggest traces of a body once present. SFMOMA’s artist page introduces holdings that move between photography and installation*7. Even in scenes without a visible person, the viewer may infer who touched, hid, was restrained, or departed. The room takes on the dual character of domestic shelter and forensic examination site.

Esoteric Forensic—Furniture That Stores an Invisible Content

Esoteric Forensic (2006) is a lockable cabinet whose interior is hidden by a curtain. Moderna Museet presented it in the retrospective as a work demonstrating continuity among photograph, object, and installation*1. “Forensic,” the public examination of evidence, meets “esoteric,” knowledge reserved for a limited group, within one piece of furniture. The certainty that something is stored remains, while the contents stay inaccessible.

Alternative Secrecy—A Retrospective as an “Incomplete Map”

The 2021–22 retrospective Alternative Secrecy placed more than three decades of work alongside roughly fifty objects selected by the artist from Moderna Museet’s collection. Von Hausswolff called the selected images an “incomplete map” of her own work*1. Other artists’ works, memories, and recurring motifs surround her practice without completing an authoritative self-explanation, echoing the unresolved structure of the photographs themselves. The Swedish-language exhibition text adds that the selected collection works and her own images were arranged to compare recurring subjects and methods*15.

Reducing Period Detail to Keep the Situation in the Present

In an email conversation published by Moderna Museet, von Hausswolff said that she does not experience her work as confined to a particular period or style*8. Clothing, hairstyles, and other dating devices are reduced so that posture, space, barriers, and emotional tension take precedence. The images move away from reenacting one particular event. Even when they cite older crime imagery, the viewer’s act of inference occurs in the present. Temporal ambiguity limits the possibility of treating violence and desire as safely completed events of the past.

sections.title: Criticism and Reception
sections.body_html:
From Staging to the Systems That Display and Store Images

The retrospective Alternative Secrecy used more than thirty years of work to connect concealment and access across photography, sculpture, and display, rather than gathering crime-like scenes for their shock value. Moderna Museet Malmö surveyed about seventy works, from the Konstfack period and the Venice Biennale to recent enamel and acrylic-glass pieces*18. The early staged photographs isolate the visual rules of crime imagery without reproducing a specific victim. Later appropriated-image works erase faces, alter context, and add acrylic glass or paint, making the reuse of archival images itself a subject. NOBA describes a continuous concern with concealment and secrecy from the early photographs to recent objects*9. The Göteborg Film Festival likewise presents her as an artist working across social and psychological tension and visual culture*10. The changes in medium progressively specify whose image is shown, in what state, and to whom.

Postmodern Photography and Feminist Debate in Sweden

Moderna Museet traces the emergence of photographic art in Sweden through the postmodern debates surrounding Implosion in 1987, a 1991 exhibition of contemporary Swedish photography, and a 1994 survey of contemporary Scandinavian photography*2. Working alongside figures such as Lotta Antonsson, Annika Karlsson Rixon, and Maria Miesenberger, von Hausswolff entered a field concerned with documentary authority, the body, and gender. In 1994 she participated in The Abject at the Oulu International Photography Triennial*2. Her photographs differ from self-performed role play by using crime-scene distance, prone bodies, empty rooms, and furniture to examine how forensic and news images produce the figure of the female victim. Casey Kaplan’s exhibition history records a sequence from The Abject to the 1996 São Paulo Biennial and the Nordic Pavilion exhibition End of Story in 1999*20.

Photographs, Furniture, and Barriers—The Right to Look in the Gallery

Acrylic glass placed before photographs, blinds, and cabinets introduced into the gallery make the viewer aware of reflection, position, and permissible distance as well as image content. In a 2005 conversation, von Hausswolff discussed both her concern over the disappearance of analog photography—darkrooms, light-sensitive materials, and chemicals—and the sense of release she found in making a large three-dimensional structure for the first time*21. The move into three dimensions transferred the darkroom and support’s functions of revealing and hiding an image into furniture and architecture. The University of Gothenburg reports that she regards photography as a medium with a distinct history and values independent photographic education*12. The museum’s white wall also appears as a structure that determines what is displayed, what is stored, and who may see it. An Artsy review similarly traces the extension of photography as a conceptual basis into sculpture, installation, and appropriated imagery*11.

Anonymous Bodies, Existing Images, and Locked Furniture

In Back to Nature and Hey Buster!, staged anonymous bodies lack names, causes, and outcomes. Oh Mother, What Have You Done uses an existing image of a restrained woman while erasing her face and changing the support and context. In Esoteric Forensic, the work becomes a cabinet with a curtain and lock that withholds its contents. Moderna Museet explains how von Hausswolff’s experience of treating large photographs as objects behind acrylic glass led toward curtains and furniture*2.

These methods regulate access at different points. Early works omit information about the event; works using existing images obstruct identification and original context; furniture physically closes the route to looking. An essay in Objektiv considers the movement from bodies to furniture, found images, and photographic materials through questions of desire and institutional vision*13. The Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago’s artist record indicates the reception of this work in collections beyond the Nordic region*19. Staging, alteration, and barriers allow von Hausswolff to address the displayed body and the right to look at the levels of image, support, and exhibition space.

anri-sala.html.lead_html: Anri Sala is an artist who addresses Albania’s political transition, lost language, cities, music, and architecture through disjunctions between image and sound. In Intervista (Finding the Words), Dammi i Colori, and No Barragán No Cry, recorded images survive even when their meanings and the memories attached to them do not remain intact. For photographic history, the central issue is how the evidentiary status of a recorded image changes through later testimony, translation, and reconstruction.
anri-sala.html.thesis_html: In Intervista, only the soundtrack was missing from a 16mm film showing his mother as a young woman under communism. Through lip-reading, testimony, and conversations with his mother, Sala made one problem central to the work: the survival of an image does not make history fully intelligible. He later connected sound to exhibition space, treating still images, moving images, and audio as elements whose meanings alter one another across time. The recorded image thus becomes less a container that preserves the past than an event that must be read again in the present.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Albania in Political Transition: From Painting to Moving Image

Sala was born in Tirana in 1974. After studying art there in the early 1990s, he studied moving image in Paris. Castello di Rivoli records his studies at the National Academy of Arts from 1992 to 1996, followed by training in film direction at the École Nationale Supérieure des Arts Décoratifs and Le Fresnoy*14. In a lecture at the Dallas Museum of Art, Sala described the rapid political changes in Albania and the excess of information and events around him. His sense that these could no longer be condensed into a single pictorial image formed part of his turn toward moving image*3.

Sala did not turn to moving image in order to produce a more accurate copy of reality. In an ENSAPC interview, he reflected on how his development as an artist and his choices of medium changed with his social and educational environment*10. Moving image gave him a way to work through duration with moments when time, language, and memory cease to align.

Discovering Intervista: Family Memory Meets the Language of the State

Intervista (Finding the Words) (1998) began when Sala found a 16mm film in an old box showing his mother, then a young activist in a communist youth organization, being interviewed. The film had lost its sound. Sala sought the help of lip-readers and reconstructed the speech in fragments*1. Werkleitz likewise describes the silent film as a kind of mirror of social change and traces the process by which Sala responds to it from the present*17.

When his mother hears the reconstructed words, she confronts the distance between herself and the political formulas she once spoke. Moderna Museet notes that the work moves between documentary and reconstruction, actuality and staging, leaving the image’s own authenticity unsettled*6. The Brooklyn Rail also identifies Intervista as a foundational early work linking political language, family history, and lost sound*2.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
An Image Can Survive While Its Meaning Does Not: Sound, Subtitles, and Photographic Evidence

At the core of Intervista is the fact that the physical survival of visual material does not automatically preserve its meaning. An ART iT interview examines how political history shapes the language within an image, while that language in turn structures how history can be read through the image*4. In a conversation with Barbara London, Sala himself explains that experiencing changes in syntax and vocabulary after the regime change contributed to his distrust of language*1.

From Distrust of Language to Music: Composing Time and Space Through Sound

After Intervista, music became increasingly central to Sala’s work. In a 2022 interview, he explains that Intervista made him conscious of the “opacity” of language. His inability to place complete trust in words as communication drew him toward music, which works more suggestively*25. He also describes music as a way of “composing time”: by breaking apart existing pieces and altering tempo and intervals, he can reconnect time and space and change the viewer’s relationship to the image*25. Through repetition, resonance, and duration, music creates a temporality in which the same past can sound different in the present. It gives multiple temporal experiences to meanings that words can otherwise appear to fix in place.

Sound in Sala’s work does more than explain a photograph or moving image. When sound is absent, meaning can collapse; when another voice fills the gap, an image from the past enters a present interpretation. Senses of Cinema discusses Sala’s work as one in which neither sound nor image takes precedence, and their disjunction becomes a way to experience place and history*12. This relation between sound and image bears directly on photographic evidence. The fact that something appears in an image does not settle its meaning; testimony, translation, and reenactment reopen the record over time.

Dammi i Colori: The Politics of Recoloring the City and the Limits of Its Image

Dammi i Colori (2003) combines a municipal program that repainted buildings in Tirana in vivid colors with narration by Edi Rama, then the city’s mayor. Kurimanzutto records the work as a 15-minute, 25-second color video with sound*7. Moderna Museet explains that its documentary-like images address Albania’s political situation while opening onto the utopian proposition of transforming a city through color*6.

Dammi i Colori does not settle whether the urban policy should be endorsed or rejected. The city’s surfaces actually change, while political speech describes that change and nighttime images of the city unfold alongside it. What is seen and what is said about the transformation do not fully coincide. A later ART iT interview traces Sala’s growing interest in exhibitions where works respond to one another in space and where the sound or timing of one work alters the experience of another*5.

No Barragán No Cry: Making a New Photograph from a Gap in the Archive

No Barragán No Cry (2002) began with a white wooden horse that appeared in an archival photograph of Luis Barragán’s house but was gone when Sala visited the site. Kurimanzutto’s archival text explains how Sala used this absence as a point of departure, placing a real white horse on a pedestal atop a high-rise building in Guadalajara and photographing it*8. Instituto Moreira Salles exhibited the work as a 2002 chromogenic print, confirming the continuing importance of still photography within Sala’s largely moving-image work*9.

The existing photograph functions as a trace of something once present and now absent. Sala physically reenacts that absence in a new setting, reconstructing a gap found in an archival photograph as another photograph. Like moving image, the still photograph becomes a point from which another time can be called back into the present.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Structuring Exhibition Space with Sound and Architecture

During the 2010s, Sala expanded his focus from individual videos to exhibitions combining multiple screens, speakers, musical performance, and architectural resonance. The New Museum’s guide to its 2016 exhibition includes works such as The Present Moment, Tlatelolco Clash, Long Sorrow, and Làk-kat, in which moving images and multichannel sound extend throughout the galleries*11. An interview in The Art Newspaper likewise discusses how music can bring different places and times into contact, and how an exhibition can be “performed” as a whole instead of treating each image as an isolated unit*13.

Sala’s stated interest in what listening can make visible is also central to the design of his exhibitions. He describes creating routes in which a distant sound announces an image before it can be seen and draws the viewer toward it, conceiving music as an “architecture of time” that unfolds time in space*25. The image therefore does not end at the screen. Sound anticipates images that remain out of sight and guides the viewer’s movement, making speaker placement and architectural reverberation part of the work itself.

Conversations published by Schaulager and Sala’s more recent work show that, even as he moves into other media including fresco and music, the problem of inscribing time into form remains*15. An exhibition at Ujazdowski likewise presents Sala’s installations as environments in which moving image, sound, and architecture continually alter one another*18.

Photography and Moving Image as a Continuum: Between Stillness and Duration

Sala’s photography and moving-image works form a continuum within the same sustained inquiry into memory and time. Kurimanzutto’s list of works places C-prints such as No Barragán No Cry and Untitled (cactus) alongside videos including Intervista, Dammi i Colori, and Answer Me*7. Sammlung Goetz has likewise presented his moving-image works from the early period onward as a sustained engagement with memory, sound, and political change*19.

In a still image, an absence left in a single moment comes to the fore; in moving image, the time spent searching that absence becomes visible. Moving between the two allows a recorded image to function both as something preserved and as material that a present viewer can reread at another pace.

In an interview with Time Out New York, Sala similarly discusses how sound changes the experience of place and the temporality of moving images*16.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Intervista: Post-Socialist Memory and Lost Language

Sala’s early works address the specific disjunction between official political language and private memory in post-socialist Albania. In Intervista, the state’s official language returns within a family memory and sounds estranged even to the person who once spoke it. ART iT notes that the work keeps its specific historical circumstances inseparable from broader questions of language and communication*4.

Benesse Art Site Naoshima introduces Sala as an artist who brings architecture and local history into contact with private experience, music, and moving image, linking a new work on Teshima to the island’s history of division and exchange*20. This reception shows how questions that began with the specific history of Tirana expanded into the problem of how a place is recorded and later heard again.

Dammi i Colori: Urban Renewal and the Debate over Propaganda

In a 2025 contribution to Frieze, Sala traces his relationship with Edi Rama back to childhood and writes that Rama taught him an approach centered on observing, selecting, and giving form to what cannot be seen, without treating the finished object as the sole aim*26. Writing about Dammi i Colori, he explains that he made the work to convey the “invisible magic of color and its political substance,” treating color as a force connecting urban perception and politics rather than as decoration*26.

Writing in Art Papers, critic Vincent W. J. van Gerven Oei approaches the work and Rama’s color policy from another angle. He argues that, after the social and economic crisis of 1997, repainting the city’s surfaces stimulated public debate while also risking the displacement of corruption and institutional problems behind aesthetic change. His essay asks how the boundary between “free art” and propaganda is produced when art and politics move into close proximity*27. Sala did not adopt the detached position of a reporter evaluating the policy from outside. By retaining the voice of Rama, both a friend and collaborator, within the work, he left later criticism to address the record of urban renewal and the politics of its image at the same time.

Recasting the Authority of the Recorded Image Through the Time of Re-Encounter

Sala made the time required for photographs and films to acquire evidentiary meaning into part of the work itself. The Brooklyn Rail treats Intervista as foundational because its delayed connection among an image from the past, a present investigation, and conversations with his mother anticipates the structure of his later work with sound and moving image*2. In his work, an image may show that something was there at a particular time while leaving the meaning of that presence unresolved.

Lip-reading, subtitles, sound, reenactment, exhibition space, and the duration of viewing connect the recorded image to present understanding. By treating records as material whose meaning continues to change in the present, Sala works across photography and moving image and sharpens a question central to documentary after the 1990s: what, exactly, can a record preserve?

Farocki and Ujică: From Public Archives to a Gap in Family Memory

Intervista (Finding the Words) is a work of family history, but it also belongs to a broader rereading of archival images in Eastern Europe after the Cold War. Research on the work places it alongside Péter Forgács, Ulrike Ottinger, Angela Ricci Lucchi and Yervant Gianikian, and Harun Farocki and Andrei Ujică’s Videograms of a Revolution, all of whom revisited Balkan and Eastern European histories after the Cold War. The study argues that these works foreground the difficulty of representing the past and the role of individual memory instead of reconstructing a single collective truth*21.

In Intervista, Sala works with a single reel of silent 16mm film in which his mother speaks under the communist regime. By reconstructing the missing soundtrack through lip-reading and returning those words to his mother in the present, he brings official political language and individual memory into the same image without allowing them to coincide. The ICP exhibition Archive Fever (2008) presented Sala alongside Farocki/Ujică, Tacita Dean, Walid Raad, Thomas Ruff, and others who reconsidered history, memory, and loss through photographic and film archives. Its inclusion of Sala shows how Intervista later came to be read within a broader archival turn*22.

From Moving-Image Works to Exhibited Time: Dean, Huyghe, and Parreno

Sala’s development after the 2000s can also be understood through exhibition form. Il Tempo del Postino (2007) conceived the exhibition as something that “occupies time” and brought Sala into a time-based program with Tacita Dean, Douglas Gordon, Pierre Huyghe, Philippe Parreno, and others*23. The participating artists did not share a single style. They incorporated duration, sequence, performance, and the viewer’s time on site into the structure of the work. Sala’s architectural installations belong to the same set of concerns through their synchronization and desynchronization of music and image and their attention to the viewer’s time in the exhibition.

MoMA PS1’s Reprocessing Reality (2006) likewise brought together Sala, Gianikian/Ricci Lucchi, Willie Doherty, and others in an exhibition examining the growing presence and importance of documentary film in contemporary art*24. Sala’s position cannot be reduced to a linear progression from still photography to moving image. He brings photographs, family film, subtitles, voices, cities, and music together as conditions through which something recorded can acquire meaning again at another time.

twitter.description: How Ansel Adams connected Group f/64’s straight photography with the Zone System’s control of exposure, development, and print. A source-based essay on Yosemite, print performance, conservation, and Manzanar.

ansel-adams.html.lead_html: Ansel Adams photographed Yosemite and the American West through precise judgments of exposure, development, and printing — converting natural landscapes into a language of light and tonal gradation. Through the Zone System, Group f/64, his relationship with Stieglitz, the idea of the print as musical performance, Bay Area photography history, environmental advocacy, and the Manzanar internment photographs, this page traces how photography separated itself from pictorialist painting and how Adams's approach has been both continued and contested by later landscape photographers.
ansel-adams.html.thesis_html: Adams did not rewrite the rules of the photographic medium — instead, he refined the straight photography methodology pioneered by Stieglitz and Strand into a unified system through the Zone System and the precision of the darkroom. His metaphor of the negative as score and the print as performance freed photography from mechanical reproduction, placing darkroom interpretation at the center of the work.

sections.title: How the Zone System relates to Group f/64
sections.body_html: Group f/64 gave Adams an aesthetic position: sharp focus, deep depth of field, straight printing, and a rejection of pictorialist blur.*5 The Zone System gave him a practical method for carrying that position through exposure, development, and printing.*20 They are not the same thing. In Adams's work, Group f/64 defined what photography could be as an autonomous medium, while the Zone System became the technical and expressive process that made that autonomy visible in the final print.

sections.title: Background & Era
sections.body_html: Ansel Adams was born in San Francisco. In 1916, during a family trip to Yosemite, he began photographing with a Kodak Brownie given to him by his parents. The National Park Service notes that after this first visit, Yosemite became central to his practice and his understanding of nature.*1 As a young man, Adams was deeply engaged not only with photography but with classical music, developing his sensibility toward nature and form through piano study. The NPS also notes that he lived for a time between two vocations — photography and concert piano.*1 His early work from the 1920s retained the soft tonalities of pictorialism, but his encounter with Paul Strand's photographs in 1930 became one of the key turning points that led him away from painterly soft-focus and toward a sharp, pure photographic image.*2 In 1932 he joined Group f/64 with Edward Weston, Imogen Cunningham, and others, and through the exhibition at the de Young Museum presented photography not as an imitation of painting but as an independent medium realized through the precision of camera and print.*5 This gathering showed that modern photography was not formed only around Stieglitz in New York — the Bay Area, including Oakland and San Francisco, was also a site of experimentation that pushed photography away from pictorialism toward its own specificity. SFMOMA identifies the 1932 Oakland meeting as the starting point of Group f.64 and a central event in Bay Area photography history.*22 In 1933 Adams showed work to Alfred Stieglitz at An American Place in New York, and in 1936 held a solo exhibition at the same gallery. The Art Institute of Chicago identifies this encounter and exhibition as a major turning point in Adams's career.*4 The Ansel Adams Gallery's biography also places his relationships with Strand, Weston, and Stieglitz within the arc of his move from pictorialism to straight photography and his institutional recognition as a photographer.*3 In the years that followed, Adams worked across Yosemite and Sierra Nevada landscapes, national park commissions, the documentary record of the Manzanar Japanese American internment camp, photography education, technical writing, and archive formation, co-founding the Center for Creative Photography at the University of Arizona in 1975.*2

sections.title: Work and method
sections.body_html:
Yosemite as a structure of light, not a scenic vista

Adams's landscape photographs are widely known as beautiful images of Yosemite and the American West. But the center of his expression is not only the preservation of nature as scenery. SFMOMA's notes explain that Adams aimed to establish a photographic style specific to the American West rather than imitating European art, using large-format cameras to capture the breadth and scale of natural space.*7 What matters here is that the large-format camera was not simply a tool for capturing more detail — it was a device for treating the density of rock faces, clouds, snow, trees, and sky as an ordered whole across the picture plane. In the press release for MoMA's 1979 exhibition, John Szarkowski saw the fundamental subject of Adams's photographs not as rocks, trees, and water themselves, but as the light that modulates them.*8 The Met's notes on Winter Yosemite Valley describe how his musical background and attachment to Western landscape came together in works that translate natural experience into graphic equivalents.*10 For Adams, Yosemite was at once a stage for displaying sublime nature and a laboratory in which light touches matter and transforms into tonal gradation from white to black. In Monolith, the Face of Half Dome, Yosemite National Park, California, the rock face is not a geographic description but a vertical composition in which dark sky, moon, rock surface, and foreground silhouette are held in tension. The Met records the work as a gelatin silver print made from a 1927 negative and printed in 1974.*11

Piano, Stieglitz, and the print as performance

Adams insisted on print precision because he did not regard photography as mechanical reproduction. He studied piano seriously in his youth and, after turning to photography, continued to use the feeling of musical performance as a metaphor for printmaking. In SFMOMA's audio guide, Adams himself says that when visualizing a photograph, it is important not only to see with the mind's eye but to "feel" the quality one wants in the final print, comparing the negative to a musical score and the print to its performance.*7 MoMA's press release makes the same point — that different prints from the same negative at different times embody the idea that the negative is the score and the print is its performance.*8 Seen through this metaphor, Adams's precision was not a rigid technique for fixing nature, but a condition for re-performing each negative — every time shaped by feeling, paper, chemistry, exposure, burning, and dodging. The University of Arizona's "Performing the Print" feature explains that comparing multiple prints from the same negative reveals Adams's decisions in cropping, dodging, burning, and overall contrast and brightness.*9 Phoenix Art Museum's notes on the same exhibition explain that multiple prints from one negative help viewers understand Adams's practice as "performance" rather than just "photography."*23 This attitude connects with Stieglitz's goal of establishing photography as fine art, but photographic autonomy did not mean making photographs look artistic by borrowing pictorialist blur or literary narrative. It meant generating emotion and composition from photography's own conditions — the clarity of the lens, the information held in the negative, the tonality of paper, and the interpretation in the darkroom. In a David Sheff interview, Adams explains that film lacks the tonal range of the eye, and that he works within those limits by choosing filters, exposure, development, and darkroom work to arrive at the values he wants in the print.*20 For Adams, composition was not the convenient arrangement of nature but the work of reconstructing the intensity of a moment of seeing as an order of black, white, and gray that a viewer could experience before the print. The Art Institute of Chicago notes that Stieglitz welcomed Adams as a young photographer and that the 1936 solo exhibition at An American Place was significant for him.*4 In an exhibition pamphlet described there, Adams himself states that perception, visualization, and execution are strictly linked and that technique alone becomes an empty shell — confirming that precision was the condition for arriving from an imagined vision to the print, not the goal itself.*4

Group f/64 and the autonomy of photography in the Bay Area

Group f/64 is an important entry point for understanding Adams's photography. The Met explains that the name f/64 came from the small aperture available on large-format view cameras and expressed the idea of celebrating — rather than hiding — the camera's capacity to present the world "as it is."*5 Adams himself, in a later interview, describes f/64 as a small aperture for deep depth of field and sharpness, and explains that it was a commitment to straight prints — not sentimental or allegorical images — on which the texture of the paper did not interfere with the texture of the photograph.*20 This "as it is" does not mean erasing the photographer's judgment. Deep depth of field, contact prints, glossy paper, and precise framing were methods of moving away from pictorialist blur, but they also demanded more strongly which forms to choose, where to cut the frame, and which tones to preserve. The significance of Group f/64 lies partly in the fact that West Coast photographers created a space to show land, plants, architecture, bodies, and industrial objects in sharp contour and density — separate from the modern photography centered on Stieglitz's galleries in New York. While Stieglitz's gallery "291" was the base of modern photography in New York, Willard Van Dyke's small gallery and residence at 683 Brockhurst Street in Oakland became a gathering place where West Coast photographers discussed photography after pictorialism. The name "683" comes from that address. The Met describes this "683" as the West Coast counterpart to Stieglitz's 291.*5 SFMOMA's recent exhibitions treat Group f.64 as one of the starting points of Bay Area photography history, presenting the shared move away from pictorialism, the participating photographers of the 1930s, connections to Langston Hughes, Tara Krajnak's responses to Weston and Adams, and San Francisco street photography from the 1970s onward as a continuous regional history.*22 SFMOMA's notes on the legacy of Group f.64 extend to women photographers, racial injustice, workers' rights, and photography education and urban culture after the San Francisco Art Institute.*6 Seen within this regional history, Adams's precise printing stands not as a cold objectivity for surveying nature, but as a practice demonstrating that photography — without borrowing pictorialist atmosphere — could hold the intensity of the picture plane through contour, density, and paper texture alone.

Nature as a concept in modern photography

Among this West Coast movement from pictorialism to straight photography, Adams's landscape work was modern not only because it depicted mountains and wilderness. Pictorialism sought to make photography artistic by bringing it closer to painting; straight photography, by contrast, did not hide the clarity of the camera or the materiality of the print — it placed them as the foundation of expression. The Art Institute of Chicago's Stieglitz materials locate Adams and subsequent straight photographers within the line of Strand's advocacy for photography that respects the limits and potential of the medium without relying on technical manipulation.*21 For Adams, that idea appeared through converting Yosemite's rock faces, sky, snow, clouds, and trees into the ordered tonality created by negative and print — rather than through urban fragments or social cross-sections. The Met's notes on Winter Yosemite Valley explain that his musical background and attachment to Western landscape connected to the work of converting natural experience into graphic composition.*10 That Szarkowski, in MoMA's 1979 exhibition materials, saw the subject of Adams's photographs as the light modulating rocks and trees rather than the objects themselves aligns with an understanding of nature as tonal relationship rather than a record of things.*8 Combining these two sources, when we say Adams converted nature into photographic language, this does not mean he simply preserved mountains and clouds. It means he reconstructed the experience of seeing as a relationship of light and density through the lens, negative, paper, darkroom, and exhibition space.

Adams reconsidered through later landscape photography

When Adams's landscapes are placed alongside later photography, his images open beyond beautiful mountain photographs toward the question of how the American West has been presented as a particular kind of land. MFA Boston's "Ansel Adams in Our Time" situates Adams's work between 19th-century government survey photographs and contemporary artists, showing how Adams — influenced by the precedent of survey photography — transformed Yosemite, Yellowstone, and Canyon de Chelly into the symbolic images of national parks.*26 The same exhibition connects Adams's legacy to "the environment, land rights, and the use and misuse of natural resources" not because contemporary artists imitate his compositions, but because they rephotograph the Western landscape Adams widely visualized — now to show the changes of deforestation, mining, drought, fire, development, urban expansion, and issues concerning Indigenous peoples and the Southwest.*26 SFMOMA describes the 1975 "New Topographics" as a fundamental turn away from sublime natural landscape toward industrial sites, suburbs, and everyday human-built environments.*25 Through this contrast, Adams's photographs become less a direct departure point for later artists and more a comparative reference for thinking about what has been shown as nature worth preserving — and what has been overlooked as the problem of development and ownership — when looking at the American West through photography.

The Zone System and Group f/64: control from exposure to print

The Zone System, at the center of Adams's technical thinking, was not merely a technique for calculating exposure but a way of thinking about how to bring the visual experience of taking a photograph through to the final print. The Center for Creative Photography shows that Adams's archive contains over 2,500 fine prints along with correspondence, interviews, unpublished manuscripts, equipment, commercial photographs, exhibition materials, and Sierra Club-related materials — demonstrating that his work was preserved not only as images but as an accumulation of methodology and education.*2 In a David Sheff interview, Adams explains that film has limits, and that within those limits he chooses filters, exposure, development, and darkroom work, thinking ahead about the values he wants in the print.*20 This "previsualization" meant holding a completed future image in mind — not simply receiving the subject's brightness as it was, but deciding which areas to drop into deep black, which whites to preserve, and which grays to allow to resonate richly. In Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico, the moon, clouds, white crosses in the cemetery, and distant mountains form — despite being an unexpected encounter — a strong arrangement of light and dark on the print. The National Gallery of Art holds the work as gelatin silver prints from 1941 and 1980, with a visual description of the moon, low hills, and church and cemetery placed under a dark sky.*12 In an interview Adams explains that by burning in the sky to darken it, he nearly eliminated the presence of clouds and brought the image closer to the dramatic visualization he first imagined.*20 What this example shows is that Adams's "precision" was not for preserving what was seen as it appeared, but for accurately transferring the relationship of light experienced in the moment of seeing to a different material — the print.

Conservation, national parks, and landscape as institution

Adams's landscape photography did not close within personal mountain experience. He maintained a long connection with the Sierra Club, and through national parks, publishing, museums, education, and archives, extended the places where landscape photography could hold social weight. The National Park Service notes that through the Sierra Club he was involved in the movement to establish Kings Canyon National Park, and that his photographs were used in Congressional debate.*1 The National Archives explains that in 1941, the National Park Service commissioned Adams to create photographic murals for the Department of the Interior building, and that although World War II interrupted the project, 226 photographs taken between 1941 and 1942 remain in the archives.*16 Here, landscape was at once a private aesthetic object and a subject the state protected, exhibited, educated, and publicized. The reason Adams's photographs worked powerfully as images of environmental protection was not that they simply described nature, but that they created pictures in which what should be preserved appeared to hold value that was visually as well as spiritually irreplaceable. MoMA's 1979 exhibition materials record that Adams's long relationship extended to the museum's photography department, and that he was involved in its founding in 1940.*8 Including this institutional scope, Adams's landscape photography can be read not as the claim that "nature is beautiful" but as the process by which photography came to show nature as a public value and became a cultural apparatus calling for its preservation.

Manzanar and the ethics of documentary photography

To avoid closing Adams's work with Yosemite's sublime landscapes, it is necessary to include the 1943 photographs of the Manzanar Japanese American internment camp. The Library of Congress introduces this series as a different kind of work from his representative landscape photographs, making both original negatives and prints available in parallel so that differences in cropping and darkroom processing can also be examined.*13 The collection includes portraits, daily life, farm work, sports, and leisure photographs, showing how Adams attempted to document the lives of Japanese Americans placed within the institution of forced internment. The Library of Congress's earlier special page introduces Born Free and Equal as a book of Manzanar internment camp photographs and Adams's text, published in 1944 by U.S. Camera.*14 The Japanese American National Museum's "Ansel Adams at Manzanar" gathered more than 50 vintage prints held at the Library of Congress, Center for Creative Photography, Honolulu Academy of Arts, and the museum itself to re-examine this work as an exhibition.*15 The Manzanar photographs show that Adams's "previsualization" and print control touched not only the sublimity of nature but the question of how to photograph human dignity and the contradictions of state institutions. However, his perspective did not foreground critique of internment policy, and tended instead to focus on the community formation and continued life of the internees — meaning that in later reception, the work needs to be read alongside the records of Dorothea Lange and the Japanese American photographer Toyo Miyatake.

sections.title: Reception and critical assessment
sections.body_html: Adams's reception has been strongly shaped by iconic images such as Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico and the Yosemite photographs. MoMA's artist page shows numerous works online and records his involvement with multiple exhibitions.*18 The National Gallery of Art also publishes 96 works on its artist page, showing how deeply Adams's photographs have been embedded in the major American museum collections of modern photography.*19 SFMOMA's "Ansel Adams at 100" pointed out the tendency to conflate his reputation as a beloved spokesman for conservation with his aesthetic achievement as a photographer, and was conceived as an exhibition intending his critical reassessment.*24 Recent exhibitions have moved beyond simply celebrating Adams as a "master of nature photography" to questioning the image of the American West his photographs created. The Portland Art Museum's "Ansel Adams in Our Time" traced his work from early pieces to mature national park photographs while placing contemporary artists including Jonathan Calm, Zig Jackson, and Will Wilson alongside, structuring an exhibition that reviewed Adams's national park images against current questions of land ownership, belonging, environmental crisis, and the representation of the American West.*17 SFMOMA's reconsideration of Group f.64 also re-reads the movement's legacy within Bay Area photography history, women photographers, racial and labor and political contexts, and responses by contemporary artists.*6 Historically, Adams's position is not simply that of a photographer who perfected high-resolution large-format landscape photography. He was a photographer who intersected precision for freeing photography from painting, print as musical performance, public images of conservation, photography education and museum institutions, and wartime documentation of a Japanese American internment camp. The essence of his photography is not that he made nature look beautiful, but that he attempted to control how nature, people, and places — passing through light, negatives, paper, institutions, and viewers' memories — become a particular kind of "object to be seen."

anthony-goicolea.html.lead_html: Anthony Goicolea is known for Multiple Portraits, in which he disguises his adult self as a uniformed boy and repeats the same body many times within a single image. Because every boy in scenes of school, play, eating, violence, and desire is the same person, peer relations also read as roles distributed within one self. Digital compositing becomes the structure that allows several social positions to coexist in one photographic space.
anthony-goicolea.html.thesis_html: Goicolea performs every member of a group of boys with a single body, placing exclusion from the group and belonging to it within the same frame. The bully and the pursued, the viewer and the viewed, the desiring subject and the object of desire are all made from him, so social roles appear as positions that can be exchanged. Growing up in the American South as Cuban American, gay, and Catholic gave him direct experience of being seen through several social categories. His adult body, disguised as a schoolboy and multiplied through digital compositing, gives those categories, desires, and power relations simultaneous photographic presence. Photoshop provides the condition for several affiliations and roles to inhabit one apparently coherent social world.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
The Late 1990s — Digital Compositing Meets Performed Photography

Goicolea was born in Atlanta as a first-generation Cuban American. Recent interviews and artist profiles describe his upbringing in the American South amid the Cuban refugee crisis, the AIDS crisis, and the rise of the religious right, and note the social stigma he experienced through being Cuban, gay, and Catholic*21. His awareness of social categories and identities that shift within politics provides a concrete background for the groups of boys, uniforms, conformity, and exclusion in his early photographs.

After moving to New York in the 1990s, Goicolea studied photography, sculpture, and film and began, toward the end of the decade, to composite multiple self-portraits into single images. By 2001, the International Center of Photography was presenting these early works as scenes in which boys on the threshold of adolescence enact fantasy, ritual, and social taboo*22. At a moment when large-scale staged photography and digital editing were gaining prominence in contemporary art, Goicolea concentrated those tools on the question of whom the self can perform.

Large-scale staged photography and digital editing were becoming increasingly common in contemporary art during this period. Goicolea chose to keep a surface that resembled an actual scene from school life instead of drawing attention to the composite through overtly cybernetic effects. The Museum of Contemporary Photography’s 2002 exhibition clearly described the structure at an early stage: the adult artist transforms himself into adolescent boys through makeup, wigs, and costume, then performs multiple roles within the photograph*1.

Photographing Queer Adolescence as an “In-Between State”

Uniforms, dormitories, games, competition, eating, violence, and sexual tension recur throughout Goicolea’s early work. He has said that he is especially drawn to “in-between states,” moments in which things are undergoing transformation*9. As the Museum of Contemporary Photography described the adult artist’s return to boyhood through makeup, wigs, and clothing as “adolescence in reverse”*1, the role of the boy functions as a mask for repeatedly performing a transitional state before body, desire, and belonging settle into fixed terms.

In Musée Magazine, Goicolea discusses his interest in chaos, loss, displacement, and change and says that Cindy Sherman was a natural reference during his period of self-portraiture*8. Building on the precedent of a single body assuming different guises, Goicolea places several roles within one frame and makes identical bodies perform social relations with one another.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Making a Crowd from One Body — What Digital Compositing Does

Repeating the same self many times within one image serves more than a technical effect. Goicolea himself connects his interest in identity to being socially positioned through several categories—Cuban, gay, and Catholic*21. Self-duplication allows the same person to occupy positions of conformity, deviation, aggression, and desire at the same time. Digital compositing makes those divergent roles coexist within one convincing social space.

This structure lets friendship and exclusion, domination and submission, and desiring and desired positions be performed simultaneously within the same body. In a statement published by Lenscratch, Goicolea likewise describes casting himself in multiple roles within staged self-portraits to create artificial and isolated worlds*12. Digital duplication turns contradictory roles within the self into relationships among figures who appear to exist at the same moment.

Seamless Realism Brings the Multiplied Self Close

Goicolea’s early photographs conceal the joins of the composite and first establish the realism of a school photograph or film still. In Musée Magazine, he emphasizes integrating visual manipulation into the image’s aesthetics and ideas instead of letting the manipulation draw attention to itself*8. The viewer can therefore accept the scene as a school photograph or film still before noticing the repeated face.

ASU Art Museum also identifies the digital multiplication of Goicolea’s own body as the mechanism that produces group scenes of boys*13. The stronger the photographic realism, the more psychologically immediate the impossible relationships become. Once the scene has been accepted as plausible, the repeated face is discovered and the initial realism turns into unease.

The “Boy” as Mask — Layering Age, Desire, and Power onto One Body

The Museum of Contemporary Photography describes the artist, then around thirty, performing adolescent boys through makeup and costume as an enactment of developmental transformation in reverse*1. Institutional settings such as uniforms, dormitories, and dining halls function as visual codes for age and belonging. Inserting an adult male body as a boy and then multiplying it into a group makes boyhood and the norms of male peer groups appear as roles repeatedly performed through clothing, posture, hierarchy, and desire.

Telfair Museums’ Alter-Ego exhibition page reproduces Morning Sleep (2004) and describes the early work as enigmatic, humorous, and unsettling scenes constructed through costume, wigs, makeup, and digital compositing*2. Queer desire emerges through the arrangement of who looks at whom and which positions the same body occupies.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Morning After — Constructing the “After” Through Self-Duplication

The Whitney Museum’s Morning After is a representative example of the early large-scale color photographs in a museum collection*3. Across these works, bodies, food, disorder, and exhaustion suggest events before and after the pictured moment. Cause and consequence remain outside the frame for the viewer to imagine.

Telfair Museums’ retrospective Alter-Ego organized roughly a decade of work to show the movement from early images of adolescence and ritual toward later concerns with solitude, displacement, aging, and environmental unease*2. Seen across the retrospective, the multiplied boys lead into sustained concerns with isolation, movement, aging, and environment.

From Photography to Drawing and Film — What Remains After the Multiplied Self

Ron Mandos describes Goicolea’s work across photography, film, drawing, and sculpture through memory, identity, and family history*10. After multiplying the self in his early digital photographs, the work expands toward faceless figures, forests and houses, and family memory. Across changing media, the question of who was there is distributed through several forms and layers of memory.

In Anonymous Self-Portraits, white painted forms cover the face, bringing gesture and clothing forward over facial recognition. Ron Mandos explains that hiding the face shifts the cues through which identity is read from expression toward posture and body language*11. From the early repetition of the same face to later works that cover the face, Goicolea continually unsettles the identification expected of portraiture.

Related — Building Family History from Photographs, Memory, and Narrative

In Related, the multiplicity once located within the same face expands into family time. The official biography identifies his family’s departure from Cuba in 1961 as part of the background to the work*7, and KADIST reads Related 3a through family history, migration, and memory*4. By building a past he did not personally experience from family photographs, resemblances, and narrated memory, Goicolea extends the earlier problem of a self that cannot be contained in one identifying image into questions of generation and migration.

KADIST likewise presents his work across several media through themes of family, migration, history, and inheritance*5. The later work on his official site makes clear that the recurring concern is the decomposition and reconstruction of the memories and social roles that form the self across several media*6.

sections.title: Reception of Staged Photography and Queer Imagery
sections.body_html:
Early Reception — Seduction and Unease in the Same Image

The Library of Congress catalogue describes Goicolea’s photographs as large-scale staged images concerned with adolescence, identity, and desire, and records how the monograph organized key early images*15. In the early 2000s, attention centered both on the technical finish of the digital manipulation and on the sexual and violent ambiguity of the boy figures.

Hyperallergic’s review of Alter-Ego traces a growing sense of apocalypse and solitude across photography, film, painting, and installation*14. This reading shows how treating the early crowds of duplicated selves as digital spectacle alone would obscure their continuity with the later work.

Photographing a Queer Self Through Exchangeable Roles

More Art describes a body of work, including public projects, concerned with migration, family, queer identity, and memory*16. In Goicolea’s photographs, the structure in which one person performs an entire group also contributes to the queer self-image. Positions of viewer and viewed, dominant and dominated, exchange places within the same body.

Aurel Scheibler similarly presents the digitally manipulated self-portraits, landscapes, films, and drawings as one multimedia body of work*17. The early use of Photoshop matters because it creates power relations and exchanges of desire among duplicated bodies. Staged photography becomes a psychological and social space in which several selves can occupy one image simultaneously.

Turning the Self-Portrait into a Group Portrait in 2000s Staged Photography

From the late 1990s into the 2000s, large-scale color staging and digital editing helped turn photography into a space for constructed scenarios. Goicolea’s early work is distinctive within this development because every figure returns to the artist himself, producing an invented “society” from one body. ICP’s 2001 description of the work as self-duplication performing the threshold of adolescence, fantasy, ritual, and social taboo shows*22, that digital manipulation was received early on as a structure for examining identity and group norms.

As Goicolea’s attraction to “in-between states” suggests, the work repeatedly focuses on identities in the process of changing*9. He multiplies the same face, turns it into a boy, and later conceals it. Across those operations, the self-portrait becomes a form for asking how many roles can make a person at once.

From Early Self-Duplication to Sheltered Life

The Brooklyn Museum’s Ice Storm belongs to the 2005 Sheltered Life series and marks a development from duplicated groups of boys toward allegorical scenes in which the environment itself overwhelms the figure*18.

The U.S. Department of State’s Art in Embassies profile likewise describes the group scenes of boys as large-scale self-portraits in which one artist performs every figure through costume, wigs, makeup, and Photoshop*19.

A contemporary Artforum review discusses Detention (2001–02) as a series of digitally arranged clones of the artist in uniform, showing that the mechanism of one person performing a group was already central to the work’s early reception*20.

anuschka-blommers-niels-schumm.html.lead_html: Anuschka Blommers and Niels Schumm build the lighting, models, clothing, and studio sets of fashion shoots with exacting control, then use the camera position alone to make objects look like faces, fixed structures appear airborne, or an upright image seem inverted. From their editorial work for Self Service to Anita and 124 Other Portraits, More, and Foam’s Mid-Air, they have redirected the studio techniques developed to make products legible toward images in which the viewer cannot easily determine what is being seen.
anuschka-blommers-niels-schumm.html.thesis_html: In the 1970s, Guy Bourdin and Helmut Newton brought narrative and sexual tension into fashion photographs that had once functioned primarily as descriptions of clothing. By the 1990s, independent fashion magazines and art photography were moving increasingly close to one another, and both snapshot-like everyday imagery and cinematic staging entered the fashion page. Blommers and Schumm physically construct objects, bodies, and backgrounds so that only when the scene is compressed into two dimensions from a single camera position does a face become an object, foreground and background collapse onto one plane, or a static set appear to be caught in mid-fall. They retain the lighting, focus, and set-building precision developed to make commodities clear, while turning that precision itself into the condition for misrecognition.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
From the Rietveld Academie to Self Service—Why Two Credits Became One Name

Niels Schumm graduated from the Gerrit Rietveld Academie in 1995, and Anuschka Blommers in 1996. According to an interview with Stof, Schumm first studied architecture before moving into photography, attracted by the camera’s ability to arrive directly at a result; Blommers came to photography through dressing and photographing friends and through her father’s darkroom*2. While they were students, Schumm, one year ahead, helped Blommers with technical questions and her graduation work; after graduation, each began assisting on the other’s shoots*2. At Self Service, Schumm initially handled still lifes and Blommers portraits under separate names. As “photography” and “lighting” credits began switching between them from one assignment to another, distinguishing whose photograph was whose became increasingly meaningless, and they adopted a single joint credit*2. Blommers’s interest in directing people and Schumm’s interest in constructing objects and space converged in the shared studio.

From Bourdin to Goldin and Teller—How Fashion Photography Changed in the 1990s

Fashion photography had been moving between commercial and artistic languages long before Blommers and Schumm. The V&A describes how figures such as Guy Bourdin and Helmut Newton foregrounded narrative, sexual tension, and character in the 1970s, beyond the straightforward presentation of clothing, while the style and youth magazines of the 1980s developed alternatives to polished advertising aesthetics*20. MoMA’s Fashioning Fiction in Photography since 1990 addresses a period in which interaction between art and commercial photography intensified, bringing both cinematically constructed scenes and the snapshot-like aesthetics associated with Nan Goldin and Juergen Teller into fashion magazines*19. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum similarly notes that the 1990s saw photographers and independent fashion and culture magazines exceed the conventional task of showing clothes attractively, allowing the photographic image itself to carry a broader sense of contemporary life*21. Blommers and Schumm entered precisely this editorial environment, where commissioned fashion work no longer had to function only as product description. Instead of adopting a rough snapshot style, they concentrated on sets, light, and the placement of objects, using the precision of commercial studio photography to produce perceptual error*2.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Physical Illusions That Exist Only from the Camera’s Viewpoint

Blommers and Schumm’s photographs can resemble digital composites, but Foam’s studio visit shows how often they physically arrange everyday objects, paper, glass, and bodies so that the scene becomes another image only from the camera’s position*3. In an interview with the Nieuwe Instituut, Schumm speaks about constructing physical illusions far enough to make clear that they are not Photoshop effects; the accompanying account describes a process in which light and sets are carefully prepared while the number of exposures is reduced*9. The reason photography is necessary is specific. Objects and bodies that remain separated in three-dimensional space can share contours and lose their depth relations when projected through a lens onto a single plane. Photography can fix a misreading that belongs to one viewpoint as a final two-dimensional image. Because the image is produced through a real set and the camera’s projection, everything depicted can have physically existed while its depth, scale, or function remains easy to misread.

“Fashion Is Something We Use”—Treating Clothing as Material, Not Subject Matter

In an interview with the Nieuwe Instituut, the artists explain that they are less interested in communicating fashion itself than in treating fashion as something they can “use”*9. This is not a rejection of commercial work; it describes their treatment of clothing as visual material. Clothes, models, styling, and magazine layouts carry established conventions for making bodies appear attractive, youthful, and desirable. Keeping those conventions in place while making a pose awkward, exchanging a face for an object, reversing orientation, or photographing a still life as if it were a portrait exposes how fashion images teach viewers to read bodies. Their interest in turning photographs upside down, discussed in the Stof interview, similarly tests what determines an image’s “correct” orientation rather than using inversion as novelty alone*2.

Why Beauty and Disorientation Remain in the Same Image

They refine lighting, skin, clothing, and backgrounds to a high degree, then introduce slight inconsistencies in contours, depth relations, or the apparent function of objects. Wallpaper* presents Mid-Air as a retrospective in which the seduction of fashion photography remains inseparable from unease*10. Duel Magazine likewise emphasizes images whose apparently perfect surfaces are held in suspension by small mismatches*17. Foam’s press material describes Mid-Air as the duo’s first major solo exhibition*5, while The Ravestijn Gallery traces a career spanning fashion magazines and art exhibitions through reproductions of their work*6. They do not abandon commercial finish in favor of an anti-advertising roughness. Instead, the polished image itself becomes difficult to resolve. The critical tension comes from the precision of fashion photography rather than from an external gesture of refusal.

How the Collaboration Works—Concept, Casting, and Technique in Constant Exchange

Their shared authorship grew from the practical work of assisting one another until roles began to overlap. In the Stof interview, they describe developing ideas together while Blommers often takes more responsibility for casting, models, hair, and makeup, and Schumm more often handles technical execution*2. The Agents Club likewise presents their work as a collaboration spanning concept development, set building, and photography*13. The exchangeability of still life and portrait, photography and lighting, that characterized their early working relationship remains visible in the images. Objects are treated like people and bodies arranged like still lifes; categories of subject matter and divisions of labor both resist becoming fixed.

sections.title: Key Works, Photobooks, and Media
sections.body_html:
Anita and 124 Other Portraits—Re-editing Magazine Portraits as a Photobook

Anita and 124 Other Portraits gathers 125 portraits made between 1997 and 2007. Valiz explains that the subjects are placed in alphabetical order, separating the photographs from their original editorial settings, while an appendix reproduces the magazine layouts in which they first appeared*7. ARTBOOK likewise presents the publication as a re-editing of ten years of fashion photography and other portrait work into a single volume*12. In magazines, the photographs were read in relation to clothing, personalities, articles, and advertisements. In the book, they become a sequence of portraits. The structure demonstrates how a change of editorial medium can change what a photograph means.

More—Turning More Than Twenty-Five Years of Editorial Photography into a Visual Archive

Roma Publications’ More condenses more than twenty-five years of work into 240 pages, placing fashion, portraiture, still life, and autonomous work in the same visual flow*8. A Japanese presentation by Book of Days likewise emphasizes the constructed nature of the images—all elements are captured in-camera—and the movement between commercial styling and independent work*18. The book re-edits editorial assignments themselves as a long-term body of work. As commissions made for different contexts meet across page spreads, the recurring method becomes visible: bodies treated as objects, objects treated as bodies.

Self Service and the Magazine Page—Photographs Whose Meaning Is Made in Sequence

The duo have worked continuously for fashion magazines, including Self Service. The archive of issue 8 confirms that their photographs circulated within editorial culture in the late 1990s*14; their continued participation in issue 9 shows the magazine functioning as a repeated site of experimentation*15. A project with the magazine presented by Et Caetera demonstrates how the work operates through sequences of pages, relations between figures and blank space, and the interaction of clothing and type, rather than through isolated prints alone*16. Libraryman’s A Day in the Life of... similarly shows their sustained use of the book as a medium organized by sequence*11. In magazines and photobooks, neighboring images, text, and page order can alter the meaning of the same photograph. Editing is part of the work’s structure, not merely a stage that follows the shoot.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Using Commercial Precision for Illusion—Disrupting Fashion Photography from Within

To place Blommers and Schumm in photographic history solely as fashion photographers whose work entered museums would fold them into a much broader crossing of fashion and art since the 1990s. The Brno Biennial describes their field as a “gray zone” where fashion, art, and photography overlap*1. Foam’s retrospective likewise refuses a firm separation between editorial commissions and autonomous work, showing how the same working methods have operated across both for more than twenty-five years*4. As MoMA’s account makes clear, fashion magazines had already absorbed both cinematic staging and snapshot realism by this period*19. What distinguishes Blommers and Schumm is their decision to keep the even lighting, exact sets, and smooth rendering of skin and objects cultivated by advertising photography, then use that clarity to generate illusion. An apparent face resolves into an object; something that seems to be falling turns out to be a fixed set. The commercial demand to make things legible and attractive begins to work in the opposite direction. Their specific place in photographic history lies less in a general collapse of the boundary between fashion and art than in redirecting studio techniques designed for clarity toward perceptual uncertainty.

Making the Image In-Camera in the Age of Digital Compositing

Once digital compositing became commonplace, the production of strange images ceased to be unusual in itself. Blommers and Schumm’s insistence on physical sets and a single camera viewpoint keeps a specifically photographic problem in play. Foam explains that the strangeness of the final image comes from the relation between the camera’s viewpoint and what was physically placed before it, rather than from post-production manipulation*3. The method does not use the absence of digital alteration as proof of truth. It demonstrates the opposite possibility: even an unmanipulated exposure can make reality appear radically different through arrangement and viewpoint alone. This is why photography, rather than image-making in general, remains necessary to their critique of bodies, commodities, and desire in fashion imagery.

araki.html.lead_html: Nobuyoshi Araki began with Satchin, photographs of children in Tokyo's old downtown districts, and expanded his subjects to life with his wife Yoko, Tokyo, sex, meals, flowers, the sky, illness, and death. He published an enormous body of first-person photography through self-published books, magazine serials, photographic diaries, and photobooks. In Sentimental Journey (1971), he turned his honeymoon into a privately published book; in the 1980s, Shashin Jidai carried his life, the city, and eroticism in serial form from issue to issue. In Araki's I-photography, photographing intimate experience and making it public proceed together. The force of the work and the questions surrounding the photographer's authority emerge from the same mode of production.
araki.html.thesis_html: At a time when social documentary photography and the urban imagery of PROVOKE held a strong presence in postwar Japan, Araki published marriage, sexual life, meals, illness, bereavement, and everyday Tokyo—situations in which he himself was a participant—as first-person photography*17. In the preface to Sentimental Journey (1971), he criticized the way magazine photography manufactured faces, nudity, private life, and landscape through shooting and editing, and presented photography made from his actual life with Yoko as his point of departure*19. In Araki's I-photography, whom he lived with, whom he desired, and whom he lost became the very relationships that determined where he stood with the camera and how the photographs could be edited. He published the honeymoon while the marriage was still unfolding in 1971, carried Yoko's illness and death into Winter Journey, and used magazine serials to release everyday Tokyo on a short cycle. The “I” thus remained in motion: he photographed life as it was happening, made that life public, and carried the published self back into the next phase of living and photographing. This work gave major momentum to I-photography in Japan while leaving a persistent question over who ultimately has the authority to select, publish, and reuse images of the bodies and lives of intimate others*18.
