sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Why Use Existing Photographs? — Because the Object of Critique Is the Image Itself

Based in London, Reid has worked across photography, collage, video, digital media, and text. Her official biography describes a body of work spanning printed and digital images and shows her repeated use of material taken from advertising and published media in different forms*1 A BOMB interview presents her as an artist who borrows images from advertising, publishing, television, and the internet and cuts, writes over, and pastes into them to address messages embedded in beauty, sexuality, and identity*23She uses already circulating photographs instead of making new nudes or advertising-style images because her subject is not the body in isolation. It is the advertising, pornography, and magazine photography through which bodies have been taught to be seen. An ICA exhibition in 2008 specifically documented her process of collecting images from tabloids, magazines, and the internet, then copying, altering, enlarging, and repeating them in large wall collages*5By retaining the source image within the work, Reid places the object of critique and her own intervention in direct comparison on the same surface.

From Advertising’s Suggestion to Explicit Online Self-Representation

ICA’s Nought to Sixty situated Reid as an artist working with found images across printed and digital environments*4 She later participated in the New Museum exhibition Free, which addressed how the internet was changing the circulation of information and interpersonal relations*24 In BOMB, Reid specifically observed that a vulgarity once couched in suggestion within advertising had become explicit in the language and imagery of online self-presentation and greeting cards*23Her concern is therefore more specific than the general claim that there are simply too many images. She follows the shift by which the language of commercial advertising, once delivered one-way from corporations to audiences, is repeated by individuals as a language for describing themselves and others.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Advertising, Pornography, and Celebrity Images — Making Their Implications Explicit

Reid works with advertising, magazines, television, pornography, celebrity photography, and other images in which the value of the body has already been edited and coded. In an artist statement preserved by Saatchi Gallery, she identifies the relationship between images of bodies and objects in advertising and the construction of our view of the world as a central concern*9 In BOMB, she describes her intervention as a way to “vulgarize” existing images. In Window “Smoke” Square, deliberately redundant labels are attached to elements within the image, making the act of looking conspicuous*23 Take No Photographs, Leave Only Ripples likewise fixes printed imagery, handwritten marks, text, and rephotography onto a single photographic surface*10By writing the commands and sexual implications of the source image in a more explicit form, Reid brings to the surface what the image had treated as self-evident.

Abandoning the Punk/DIY Look

Reid’s lines, tape, and stickers leave the joins of the collage visible, preserving the speed and roughness of the work. The Guardian noted that because the pieces are made quickly and mistakes are left in place, their surfaces appear as unstable as the media world they depict*15 Studio Voltaire similarly describes her work through punk, DIY, and bricolage, with celebrity, pornography, fashion, cartoons, and art theory brought together on the same surface*11 Yet in 2012 Reid explicitly stated that the resemblance to punk and DIY had become easy to read as a stylistic reference, and that détournement had limits when it could no longer generate ambiguity or contradiction*23Her change of method in 2012 makes clear that she did not equate a rough appearance with critical force. Once graffiti-like interventions on found imagery became easily recognizable as a “Clunie Reid style,” the method risked making the work predictable before it unsettled the advertising image. She chose to shift toward video and writing rather than preserve her best-known visual signature.

Rephotography — Turning the Critical Intervention into a Reproducible Image

In Take No Photographs, Leave Only Ripples, Reid intervenes directly in found photographs, then rephotographs and reprints them. UAL Research Online records the project as a major research output and describes a process in which photography and handwork are combined over several stages*6 The university’s research-output listings place photographs, video, and publications from this period together as works concerned with the reproduction of images*8 Fotomuseum Winterthur’s discussion of the work in its collection also indicates that it was understood in relation to photographic reproduction, not simply as paper collage*18Rephotography keeps the handwritten lines, tape, and stickers from remaining merely annotations added on top of a magazine photograph. Once photographed again, source image and intervention are fixed onto the same plane and become equally reproducible as one image. The critical mark itself can now circulate in the same way as the advertising photograph it addresses, preventing the work from settling into the position of judging advertising from the outside.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Your Higher Plane Awaits — Reflecting the Viewer in a Silver Surface

Your Higher Plane Awaits uses silver, reflective supports and glossy surfaces. UAL records the work as one of Reid’s research outputs and documents its combination of photographs, text, and reflective material*7 Images from Galerie Reinhard Hauff likewise show silver and black surfaces, handwriting, and photographic fragments combined on the same plane, with reflected light changing according to the viewer’s position*19As a result, light from the gallery and the viewer’s own body are reflected onto the same support as advertising and bodily imagery. The material reflection disrupts any position in which the viewer remains outside the work while judging media images at a distance. A photography-now record specifies the support of Your Higher Plane Awaits as “Digitaler Druck auf Silver MET”; the silver reflective surface is an actual material component of the work*21.

Faker Drinker Soldier Heiress — Making Images and Words Collide across the Page Sequence

Published by Book Works, Faker Drinker Soldier Heiress is a sixty-four-page artist book made from advertising, internet and magazine imagery, along with Reid’s own photographs and drawings. The publisher describes images, jokes, text, and drawings layered over blacked-out and mirrored pages*12 Its specifications—offset printing, two spot colors, and full UV varnish—transfer the gloss and reflection of Reid’s wall works to the pages of a book. Book Works’ artist page also shows that publication has remained an ongoing medium in her work alongside exhibitions*13The specific shift in this book is the conversion of operations previously carried out on large reflective prints into a sixty-four-page object that unfolds through the sequence of turning pages.

Toward Video and Language — Digitizing Still Images and Reediting Them in Time

Reid’s work expanded from still photography into online video and edited text. Free, preserved by Rhizome, survives as a work built from networked imagery and language*17 The New Museum exhibition Free was itself organized around the ways the web was altering access to information, artistic production, and interpersonal relationships*24 In BOMB, Reid explained that she had begun bringing digital versions of still images into video and combining them with more extreme images and text, treating video as another way of presenting images that are no longer still*23The earlier process of drawing over paper photographs and rephotographing them becomes, in video, a process of rearranging digitized still images along a timeline. A 2013 Frieze review of In Pursuit of the Liquid describes four screens repeating kittens and images of women while pink text scrolls over them, reediting phrases taken from porn pop-ups and chat rooms*16.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Beyond Quotation — What Reid Takes from the Pictures Generation Is Self-Implication

Reid can be related to appropriation after Cindy Sherman, Barbara Kruger, and Richard Prince, but in BOMB she emphasized something other than quotation as a technique. What drew her to the Pictures Generation was the move from simple negation toward a criticism that acknowledges the critic’s own implication in the system being criticized*23 Collage exhibitions at The Photographers’ Gallery and FOTOHOF’s Karaoke have situated her within a broader history of cutting, rearranging, and reenacting existing images*14For Reid, the aim is not to point at advertising photographs from outside and expose them as false. Her critique begins from the recognition that she too has learned meaning through the same advertising, pornography, and online imagery; she writes into those images and recirculates them. Her participation in FOTOHOF’s Karaoke: Bildformen des Zitats also placed the work within an international exhibition context devoted to quotation and reenactment of existing images*20.

From Rough Collage to Video and Text — Refusing a Fixed Method

Reid’s exhibition history includes ICA, Tate Britain, the New Museum, and Fotomuseum Winterthur, where her work has been presented across photography, video, and installation*2 Tate Britain’s Art Now likewise presented her alongside James Richards as an artist working with photographic collage and media imagery*22 Institutional recognition did not lead Reid to preserve the appearance of her earlier work. In the 2012 BOMB interview she acknowledged that punk/DIY references and détournement no longer felt sufficiently specific and described a concrete shift toward more extreme imagery, video, and writing*23Once the early appearance of a “defaced photograph” lost its specificity, Reid let go of that appearance itself. This decision gives a concrete reason for her move into video and writing. Her official website similarly brings photographs, videos, publications, and exhibition history together as one body of work, confirming a practice that has not remained tied to a single medium*3.

coburn.html.lead_html: British-American photographer who moved from pictorialist lyricism to urban aerial views and then to abstract photographs made with a vortoscope. The Vortograph series of 1916–17 stands as an early experiment in photographic abstraction.
coburn.html.thesis_html: Beginning in the lyrical surfaces of Pictorialism, Coburn pulled photography away from the reproduction of its subject through high overhead views of the city and a mirrored device. His 1916–17 Vortograph series is recorded as an early attempt at abstraction through photography, connecting the abstract movements in painting with the camera.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Alvin Langdon Coburn was born in Boston in 1882 and engaged with photography from an early age, later working also in London in the 1900s. *1 He participated in Stieglitz's Photo-Secession and was published in Camera Work, gaining recognition as one of pictorialism's most successful practitioners. *2 His early photographs of London fog, the Thames and atmospheric urban scenes, rendered in soft tonal registers, earned wide critical praise. *3

In the 1910s, Coburn began exploring aerial views of cities. Photographs taken from elevated vantage points in New York and London read streets as patterns and compositions rather than as spaces of figures and narrative. *4 Between 1916 and 1917, he attached a device called the vortoscope — three mirrors arranged in a triangle — to his camera lens, creating the Vortograph series in which subjects are fractured, reversed and multiplied into geometric forms. *5 In later life he turned toward mysticism and spiritual inquiry, reducing his photographic activity, though his experimental records are preserved in museum collections. *6

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
From pictorialism to urban geometry

Coburn's early photographs typify pictorialism: atmospheric conditions — fog, rain, dusk, harbours — combined with soft focus and tonal warmth. *7 But in the 1910s his interest shifted from the lyrical beautification of subjects toward the question of how elevated viewpoints transform what is seen. The Tate records document how in his aerial views of cities, streets are stripped of figures and narrative and converted into flat patterns. *8 This direction unsettled the premise that photography is a descriptive medium, demonstrating that the manipulation of viewpoint can change the character of an image fundamentally. *9

The Vortograph and mirror-based abstraction

The Vortograph series was produced during Coburn's engagement with the poet Ezra Pound and Vorticist ideas. *10 By placing the vortoscope — three mirrors in a triangle — in front of the lens, the subject is fractured, inverted and layered into geometric forms. MoMA's Object:Photo records Coburn's own claim to have made "the first purely abstract photographs," and whatever the historical validity of the claim, it documents how his experiment has been received within photographic history. *11 Unlike the cameraless experiments of Man Ray or Moholy-Nagy, the Vortograph method inserts a transforming device between the lens and the subject, pursuing abstraction through optical transformation rather than through the elimination of the camera. *12

Vorticism placed the energy, fragmentation and speed of the machine age at the centre of avant-garde art, and Coburn's photographic experiment is one of its visual manifestations. *13 The series did not become a sustained practice, and he later turned toward spiritual concerns, but within photographic history it remains a document of the intersection between photography and the avant-garde in the 1910s. *14

Photo books, portraiture and the Victoria and Albert Museum

Coburn also produced portrait albums and urban photo books; his collections of literary and artistic portraits represent a document of the intersection between London publishing culture and photography. *15 The Victoria and Albert Museum collection provides access to records of his wide photographic activity. *16

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Coburn stands at the boundary between pictorialism and modernism, and photographic history has positioned him in both periods simultaneously. *17 MoMA's Object:Photo project's engagement with the Vortograph indicates that his experiment has been re-evaluated as a point of intersection between European avant-garde and photographic modernism. *18 The George Eastman Museum and Getty Museum also hold collections, functioning as records of the transitional period from pictorialism to experimental photography. *19 Coburn's career stands as a rare example of a photographer whose style and direction shifted dramatically within a single lifetime, and he has been positioned in photographic history as a figure who contains both pictorialism and modernism simultaneously. The availability of both his early lyrical works and his experimental Vortographs in major collections makes him a useful case for examining the coexistence of multiple directions within the artistic development of photography.

collectif-fact.html.lead_html: collectif_fact is an artist duo that treats the city as a visual environment shaped by live-action photography, film dialogue, advertising, archival images, 3D scans, CGI, and sound. In Worldmaking, CITYmulation, and White Shadow, they connect the act of photographing real cities with the generation of other worlds from existing images, testing how strongly memories of cinema and digital imagery shape what viewers recognize as a “realistic” city.
collectif-fact.html.thesis_html: Urban photography developed in large part as a way of recording the city in front of the camera. collectif_fact begins from the premise that contemporary cities are already understood through cinema, advertising, surveillance imagery, CGI, and mapping platforms, and therefore uses live-action photographs, 3D models, found footage, and sound as materials within the same image of the city. From Worldmaking to White Shadow, photography serves both as an image that records the city and as data used by photogrammetry to generate new three-dimensional forms. Their work shifts the emphasis from photographing the city to examining how image technologies produce what a city looks like.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
collectif_fact is a Swiss duo formed by Annelore Schneider and Claude Piguet, active since the early 2000s. DDA Genève describes their current collaboration as centered on moving image and divided between London and Geneva*1. In an earlier phase they worked as a trio with Swann Thommen; support from the City of Geneva in 2010 and a Swiss Art Award in 2011 were among the steps that accompanied their expansion into international exhibitions*2. Wilde Gallery identifies the current duo as Schneider and Piguet and describes their work between London and Geneva *3. Goldsmiths records White Shadow and Dissonance as joint works by the two artists *4. Acme Studios documents their 2024 London residency and recent research into the production and consumption of digital images *5.

What connects collectif_fact’s early and recent work is an interest in the images used to know the city. Centre d’Art Contemporain Genève’s text on Worldmaking identifies urban planning and advertising on one side and Hollywood cinema on the other as two major fields informing the work*2.Their current official biography describes a method that has expanded into 3D scanning, film dialogue, archival images, and sound editing, with the alienation and environmental costs of mass-producing and consuming digital images now part of the subject. The early question of how cities are seen continues into a more recent concern with what kinds of burdens the data and images used to construct cities place on the world*6.

sections.title: Core Ideas and Methods
sections.body_html:
Treating the City as a Place Already Learned Through Images

The cities in Worldmaking can feel familiar even when the location itself is unknown. As Centre d’Art Contemporain Genève notes in citing urban planning, advertising, and Hollywood cinema, high-rise buildings, empty roads, elevated viewpoints, and particular kinds of lighting call up both lived urban experience and visual memories learned from film and advertising*2. They bring cinematic codes into urban imagery because the contemporary eye is already trained by an accumulation of such images.

Editing Memories of Film, Advertising, and 3D Images to Produce “Realism”

Tenderpixel describes collectif_fact’s moving-image work as a weave of film dialogue, quotations, fragments of music, and references to film history*7. Their official biography likewise describes a method of editing 3D scans, film dialogue, archival images, and sound into collages built from recognizable imagery*6. Editing here does more than combine different media. The order of fragments and the layering of sound blur the boundary between existing and generated places, while the viewer’s own memory supplies the feeling that the scene is plausible.

A “Near Future” Built by Extending Present-Day Image Habits

In an interview with DDA Genève, the duo describes its videos as staging a “near future”*8. They construct that near future by slightly exaggerating extensions of the present city, smartphone culture, servers, advertising, and CGI, which helps the images retain a sense of plausibility. HEAD Genève’s Narratives of a Near Future similarly framed the future across art and science in relation to present perception and action, sharing a set of concerns close to collectif_fact’s work*9.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Worldmaking — Joining the Acts of Photographing and Constructing the City

In Worldmaking (2011), visual vocabularies from cities, advertising, and cinema were incorporated into film and photography*2. The official project page records it as a major solo exhibition by collectif_fact*10. As the title suggests, a world is produced through decisions about which images to select, how to sequence them, and what sounds to layer over them. Photography functions both as evidence of a city and as material for assembling another one.

White Shadow — Imagining 3D-Scan “Data” as a Pile of Things

White Shadow is a 10-minute, 40-second video made from existing 3D scans and sounds downloaded from online libraries*11. The official text begins with the premise of what might happen if images of selfies, food, cars, and other subjects became physical objects that filled space. At the Swiss Art Awards, the video was shown with a series of twelve images, foregrounding photogrammetry and the materiality of digital images*12. The work gives image excess a physical form, presenting it as a buildup of objects that obstruct the city. Chronus Art Center describes the piece as transforming flat images into enormous 3D objects and making the material and ecological costs of digital production visible *13.

CITYmulation / At a Loss for Words — Putting Cities and Conversations into Simulation

CITYmulation moves between fragments of existing cities and modeled spaces, inviting the city itself to be experienced as a simulation*14. Documentation from Centre de la photographie Genève likewise places the project at the boundary between photography and moving image in its treatment of urban representation*15. In At a Loss for Words, the mismatch between cinematic dialogue and image produces uncertainty in communication*16. In Dissonance at Wilde Gallery, moving image, photography, silkscreen, and objects form a speculative scenario, extending their method of world-building through editing across the entire exhibition*17. Swiss Cultural Fund describes At a Loss for Words as a video in which two people discussing a breakup try several modes of communication while cinematic codes are dismantled*18.

Collaborative “Ping-Pong” Repeatedly Re-edits the Image of the World

In an interview with DDA Genève, the two describe their long collaboration as a form of “ping-pong”*8. One artist may add sound or a quotation to an image made by the other, prompting another round of editorial decisions. Their method allows a world to emerge from the exchange of multiple materials and judgments instead of fixing the city from a single authorial viewpoint. That collaborative structure resonates with their broader idea that realism itself is built from shared memories of cinema, advertising, and digital images as well as from individual perception.

Photography Becomes Both Final Image and Material for Building 3D Worlds

A key feature of White Shadow is that photographs appear as finished flat images while also serving as input data from which photogrammetry generates three-dimensional models. The Swiss Art Awards identifies this technique and the materiality of digital imagery as central to the work*12. The same body of work contains photographs that record a city from a chosen viewpoint and photographs made in large numbers around an object so that a calculable model can be built. Photography therefore extends from “an image of the city” to “material for calculating another image of the city,” turning the boundary of photography after the digital turn into part of the work.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Photography Circulates Through the Same Image Economy as Film, CGI, and 3D Data

In collectif_fact’s exhibitions, still photography, moving image, 3D models, sound, and text establish one another’s terms of viewing. Réseau Documents d’Artistes identifies the mass production of digital images and content, their ubiquity, their alienating effects, and their environmental impact as major concerns in the duo’s current work*19. In White Shadow, 3D data circulating online is downloaded and fed back into the work, so the image becomes both an object of viewing and a reusable resource. The chain of image capture, circulation, re-editing, and storage comes within the scope of the work. collectif_fact’s participation in the Maison Européenne de la Photographie exhibition L’objet photographique in 2011 also shows how this work has been received within discussions of photographic materiality, apparatus, and support*20.

Urban Reality Emerges from Edited Memory

Their urban images contain many recognizable elements—roads, buildings, signs, advertisements—while also producing a strong déjà vu reminiscent of film scenes or game environments. Kunsthaus Baselland described collectif_fact early on as a practice combining urban space with cinematic construction*21. The work begins by asking why a particular view reads as a “future city” or an “ominous city” in the first place.

Photogrammetry Turns the Camera into a Device for Sampling Surfaces

The 3D scans used in White Shadow are connected to photogrammetry, which reconstructs an object’s three-dimensional form from numerous photographs. The Swiss Art Awards explicitly identifies this technology as an important production method in the work*12. Instead of selecting one decisive viewpoint, the process samples many images around an object and constructs a model through computation. The camera becomes both a compositional tool and a sensor for generating 3D data.

Using Déjà Vu to Activate the Viewer’s Internal Image Archive

As Tenderpixel’s exhibition title Suspension of Disbelief suggests, the work actively uses the viewer’s learned willingness to enter fictional worlds*7. DDA Genève similarly identifies the viewer’s desire to be drawn in and slightly deceived by images as an important element*1. That feeling of being fooled depends on visual memories built through years of watching film, advertising, photography, and CGI.

daguerre.html.lead_html: Daguerre invented the daguerreotype and made it available worldwide on August 19, 1839, through the French state's announcement. Each image was a unique, non-reproducible object — a direction that democratized portraiture while diverging fundamentally from the negative-positive reproducibility Talbot would develop.
daguerre.html.thesis_html: Daguerre established the daguerreotype as a workable technology and, with the public release of the process in 1839, pushed the finely detailed image written by light into something society could actually own. Because each plate was a unique, unrepeatable object, the method advanced a democratization of the portrait — placing within reach of the middle class likenesses that had once required a painter — while taking a path distinct from Talbot's route of repeated prints from a single negative. The resolving power that one observer called a “mirror with a memory” raised early on both the wonder at a device that records reality directly and the question of whether photography was art or record; later overtaken by the reproducibility of the wet-collodion process, it nonetheless marked the point from which photography spread into society.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre was born in 1787 in Cormeilles-en-Parisis, Picardy. He trained as a stage designer and architect in Paris and in 1822 co-invented and opened the Diorama — a spectacle that transformed vast translucent canvases from day to night by switching between transmitted and reflected light, cultivating his obsession with fixing light and image*1.

After learning of Nicéphore Niépce's experiments, Daguerre entered a formal partnership with him in 1829. After Niépce's death in 1833, Daguerre continued refining a method that developed a latent image on a silvered plate by exposure to heated mercury vapor. The critical discovery — probably made around 1835 — was that mercury vapor could make a faint latent image visible with great speed and clarity, dramatically reducing exposure times*2.

On January 7, 1839, François Arago announced the daguerreotype at the French Academy of Sciences. On August 19 the French state released the process to the world — outside Britain — as "a gift to all." The technique spread rapidly, but each daguerreotype remained a unique, non-reproducible object*3. His Boulevard du Temple (c.1838) became famous for capturing what is often described as the first human figure in a photograph: a man standing still for a boot-shine while moving carriages and pedestrians disappeared in the long exposure*4.

A fire at his studio on March 8, 1839 destroyed much of his early work; fewer than twenty-five confirmed originals survive. Daguerre died in 1851*5.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The daguerreotype's defining qualities were its extraordinary resolution and its singularity. Recorded directly on a silver surface, the image achieved a fineness no contemporary painting or engraving could match. Oliver Wendell Holmes called it "a mirror with a memory" — an object close to a reflection of reality itself*6. Because no negative existed, no copy was possible; each plate was constitutionally unique.

The dramatic shortening of exposure times — from hours toward minutes outdoors, and eventually tens of seconds in studio conditions — made portrait photography practical for the first time. By the 1840s, New York, Paris, and London had studios where a likeness could be obtained at a price accessible to the middle class rather than reserved for oil painters*7. This democratizing force is the central paradox of the daguerreotype: a non-reproducible object that nevertheless transformed how societies represented themselves.

The rapid global spread of the process was facilitated by Daguerre's own publication of a detailed technical manual and public demonstrations, which enabled independent replication within weeks of the August 1839 announcement*8.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
The daguerreotype's cultural shock is registered most clearly in its critics. Baudelaire argued that photography could only serve as art's handmaid — never as art itself — but this very argument bears witness to how forcefully the new medium had entered cultural life*9.

Through the 1840s daguerreotype portrait studios multiplied rapidly in American cities; at the 1851 Great Exhibition in London, American daguerreotypists dominated their category*10. After the wet-collodion process was introduced in 1851, competition from reproducible paper photographs accelerated; by the 1860s the daguerreotype had largely given way to other forms.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art writes that the daguerreotype remains without rival "in its intricacy, detail, and luminous quality," and it is today valued not only as a historical origin but for its visual distinctiveness*11. The George Eastman Museum and the Smithsonian hold major daguerreotype collections, and ongoing conservation and digitization projects continue to recover damaged Civil War-era examples*12.

daisuke-yokota.html.lead_html: Daisuke Yokota struggled to find a subject he could follow over time. He continued working by returning existing images to cycles of rephotography, hot-water development, copying, bookmaking, and burning. A photograph fixes the scene at the moment of exposure, while memory changes through present experience. Yokota returns an image to production and leaves the subsequent choices, chance events, and material changes visible within it. Through Back Yard, Site / Cloud, Inversion, and MATTER / BURN OUT, this page traces why this method became necessary and how it allows the present to act on photographs of the past.
daisuke-yokota.html.thesis_html: Darkroom manipulation and damaged photographs have a long history. What distinguishes Yokota within that history is his method of treating the photograph as material that can be remade repeatedly from the present. Digital images, rephotographed negatives, emulsion, copies, photobooks, and installation materials all pass into subsequent stages of production; choices made after exposure and chemical reactions become part of the image’s history. Yokota’s work makes the photograph visible as both a record of the past and material through which the present can repeatedly remake it.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Why Yokota Chose Photography: The Darkroom Before the Subject

Yokota’s route into photography began with cameras and the darkroom, before he had found a subject he wanted to photograph. The memory of his father’s SLR as a special object led him to the Nippon Photography Institute, where he learned darkroom processing. He has connected the chemical transformations he encountered there to his childhood experience in a chemistry club*1. After graduating, he built a darkroom in his family home. For Yokota, photography first meant working directly on light, chemicals, film, and paper; selecting the external world through the camera came later.

The Crisis of Having No Subject and They: Making Photographs After Exposure

As Yokota tried to establish himself as a photographer, he confronted the question of what he could continue photographing. Unable to find a subject he could follow over time, he worried that “if photography cannot exist without a subject, then I cannot make photographs”*2. His snapshots included unintended figures and signs, leaving him uncertain about what he had actually chosen at the moment of exposure. To identify the elements to which he had responded, he erased faces and words in Photoshop, rephotographed the images on film, and developed them aggressively. They became an answer to his predicament: existing images could serve as material for continued work even without a stable subject*1.

Where Darkroom Work Met Sampling: Extending the Process into the Zine

Darkroom work and music production gave Yokota a way through this crisis. He had sampled cable hum and other noises, building music through the repetition of fragments. That experience of sampling led him to process existing photographs in search of another image*1. In photocopied booklets, scratches from the copier, variations in density, and show-through from the reverse side also generated new decisions. In Back Yard and Site, shooting, editing, copying, and page order formed a continuous process; each result guided the next treatment and sequence*5. The zine became part of the process through which photographs were repeated and altered.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Photography and Memory: Remaking the Past from the Present

Discussing Back Yard, Yokota has said that repeatedly recalling the same experience never produces the same memory twice; memory changes in relation to the present*6. A photograph fixes a scene, while recollection produces different meanings from each new vantage point. David Bate describes photography as a “device of recall” that produces memory within culture*24. Annette Kuhn argues that “memory work” with personal and family photographs reveals how the past is narrated anew from the present*25.

Yokota’s rephotography makes this reconstruction occur within the image as well as in the viewer’s account. Street photographs such as Untitled No. 421 (2012) developed into Site / Cloud*18. Yokota passes existing images through digital processing, printing, rephotography, high-temperature development, and scanning, transforming them while retaining traces of their earlier states*1. The photograph no longer remains a finished object fixed at the moment of exposure; it becomes material through which the present repeatedly acts on the past.

Why Rephotography and Chemicals Were Necessary

When an indistinct image is designed entirely through digital processing, its range of change tends to remain within operations selected in advance by the artist. Yokota has described a cycle in which he allows more chance into the shooting process, brings the image closer to an ideal during editing, and then introduces unforeseen changes again through development*5. He has also said that results that thwart expectation and detach the photographed subject from both its surroundings and himself provide clues for the next stage of work*22. Chemicals, heat, and peeling emulsion introduce changes that the artist cannot fully determine in advance. Yokota’s authorship emerges in his response to what occurs: he selects which images to retain and which to process again.

For Mortuary, Yokota developed enormous sheets of photographic paper with limited equipment, accepting scratches and uneven development as conditions of production*10. Ceidra Moon Murphy reads the disintegrating photographs of Yokota and Stephen Gill as works concerned with the process of recollection more than with the contents of memory, treating the decomposition of the image as a form of production that cannot be explained solely as loss*23. Caitlin DeSilvey’s study of cases in which decay and disassembly also generate meaning provides a related point of reference*28. Damage is not a decorative effect that makes an image resemble memory. It is the process through which an earlier image changes through contact with the body, apparatus, and materials of the present.

Inversion: Leaving the Subject to Examine How Photographs Arise

As Yokota continued rephotography and hot-water development, his attention shifted to the imaging apparatus itself. He came to believe that compact-camera design, exposure controls, and image processing define the range of what counts as a photographic image, and that his own snapshots could not escape those limits*20. In Inversion and Color Photographs, he developed unexposed film at high temperatures, producing images through peeling emulsion and the flow of chemicals*2. The Getty catalogs Inversion as a 2015 gelatin silver print with solarization*8. Yokota has explained that the everyday use of digital photography reduced the need to treat film as an efficient recording medium, allowing him to approach it as a chemical material*2.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Back Yard, Site, and VERTIGO: The Photobook as a Structure of Repetition

Yokota’s photobooks translate repeated processing into the time of turning pages. In Back Yard and Site, the dense blacks of photocopying, thin paper, and show-through connect images as figures and streets recur in altered states*5. Bibliographic information and page images for Site are available through shashasha*14. In VERTIGO, recurring bodies, darkness, and reflections call earlier photographs back into view as the sequence unfolds*22. The Seattle Art Museum likewise presents Immerse and Linger as works in which book design forms part of the artwork*12.

Inversion and Color Photographs: Abstract Photography and the Viewer’s Projection

In Inversion and Color Photographs, references to specific events recede, bringing the surfaces of developed film and photographic paper forward. In a Kominek Gallery exhibition text, Brad Feuerhelm places Yokota’s color chemigrams within a history of abstract photography based on chemical reaction, reading them as works that loosen the artist’s control over representation and open space for the viewer’s projection*17. Each page of the photobook INVERSION was screenprinted, leaving variations from copy to copy*15. Yokota has said that photographic material becomes a “phenomenon” when someone encounters it at a particular time and place*30. As reference weakens, the viewer’s role in finding forms within the emulsion becomes more apparent.

MATTER / BURN OUT and Matter / Vomit: The Weight and Waste of Image Overproduction

For MATTER / BURN OUT, Yokota burned a group of photographs previously exhibited in Xiamen, photographed the combustion in roughly 4,000 frames, and carried those images into a new work and photobook*9. The earlier installation disappeared, but its destruction returned to the present work as new photographs. Yokota neither preserved the previous work intact nor discarded it completely; the state of burning became material for the next image. In Matter / Vomit, he bound approximately 100,000 prints with wax and exhibited them as a mass that covered the floor*16. Images that circulate lightly as reproducible data became 100,000 sheets of paper, wax, occupied exhibition space, and post-combustion debris. The volume of images and the burden of preserving or discarding them became perceptible within the same space.

Room. Pt. 1 and Sediment: How Supports Alter Black, Transparency, and Viewing Distance

In Room. Pt. 1, the same images made in a love hotel appear on light-emitting monitors, light-reflecting photographic paper, transparent OPP sheets and PVC, and wall-mounted panels*4. Because one output serves as the negative for the next work, the depth of black, the degree of transparency, the relation between front and back, and the viewer’s distance all change even when the same data is used. Comparing the supports shows that an image is not identical information independent of its medium. It looks different under the conditions of emission, reflection, and transmission*20. In Sediment, multiple images and supports overlap like geological strata, making visible a history in which each output becomes a different photographic object, while the reconstruction of the original location recedes.

Plants, Tama River Midstream Area and Plants, Darkroom: Observation and Darkroom-Generated Images

In recent years, Yokota has described the plants of the middle reaches of the Tama River as “the first subject I have wanted to pursue”*2. In Plants, Tama River Midstream Area, he observes the forms of wild plants with a large-format camera; in Plants, Darkroom, he returns to the same region through images produced with his distinctive darkroom methods*3. This development also shows that memory cannot account for Yokota’s entire body of work. Even after finding a subject, the question remains: how closely should he observe forms in the external world, and how far should he accept forms that arise in the darkroom?

sections.title: Critical Reception and Position in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Zines and International Circulation: Post-Digital Photography in the 2010s

Yokota sent Back Yard and Site abroad, gaining recognition through photobook circulation before receiving broad institutional recognition in Japan*2. He has acknowledged that his black-and-white Xerox booklets acquired value overseas through their association with “Japanese photography”*5. Recognition followed through the Outset | Unseen Exhibition Fund in 2013, the John Kobal New Work Award in 2015, and the Foam Paul Huf Award in 2016*7. His works move among Photoshop, printers, scanners, photocopiers, rephotography, and emulsion. The central issue is the process of returning images altered by different apparatuses to the next stage of production, beyond a simple division between digital and analog.

Photographic Materiality: Bringing the Photograph’s Later History into Production

Elizabeth Edwards and Janice Hart describe photographs as both images and objects, arguing that physical properties, modes of handling, and cultural settings help shape their meanings*27. Ordinarily, scratches, fading, and traces of movement accumulate after a photograph has been made. Yokota produces stains, folds, peeling, wax, and burn marks during production, then rephotographs those states for use in subsequent images. Photographic materiality appears here as a mechanism through which present handling changes both the form and the interpretation of an earlier image, not simply as a surface effect.

José van Dijck argues that the manipulability of digital photography accommodates the continual remaking of personal images, while making it difficult to control how those images will be reused or placed in new settings in the future*26. Yokota extends this plasticity beyond the digital file, passing images among film, chemicals, paper, copies, and installation materials. What matters is how each present treatment changes the status of an earlier photograph—as record, material, copy, or remnant.

A History of Abstract Photography: A Process That Does Not End in a Single Finished Image

Cameraless photography and darkroom manipulation have histories extending throughout the twentieth century. The inclusion of Inversion in Tate Modern’s Shape of Light indicates Yokota’s reception within the history of abstract photography*19. His position becomes clearer when abstraction and damage are seen as stages in an ongoing chain—digital images, rephotographed negatives, emulsion, copies, photobooks, installation materials, and records of burning—rather than effects resolved in a single finished image. Each earlier output can become material through which present production makes contact with a photograph of the past again, instead of remaining fixed as either a failed image or a final work.

Studies of photography and memory have also applied Bergson’s ideas of duration, perception, and memory to photography and film, considering the relation between the isolated instant and time as lived continuity*29. This does not establish a direct influence on Yokota. It provides a broader intellectual context for considering the photograph as more than a fixed instant, and for understanding how earlier states persist within the present. The direct basis for interpreting Yokota remains his own statements and his repeated production processes.

A Contrast with Max Pinckers: Constructing Representation and Remaking Records

The 2016 Foto-Forum exhibition Floating Worlds paired Yokota’s Linger with Max Pinckers’s Two Kinds of Memory and Memory Itself*11. Pinckers approaches documentary as a “speculative process” that exceeds the reproduction of external reality, studying the structures surrounding its production and consumption*13. Colin Pantall distinguishes Pinckers’s questioning of representational frameworks from Yokota’s layering of present-day processes onto earlier images*21. Yokota’s work centers on returning the already photographed image itself to present conditions; the reenactment of a past narrative is not his primary concern.

david-octavius-hill.html.lead_html: Hill combined a painter's compositional knowledge with Adamson's technical expertise to produce around 3,000 calotypes between 1843 and 1848, the first sustained artistic photographic practice. The Newhaven fishermen series is the earliest major social documentary project in photography, and Stieglitz called Hill "the father of pictorial photography."
david-octavius-hill.html.thesis_html: Hill is regarded as the first substantial practitioner to use photography deliberately not as a means of record but as a field of pictorial composition. His tonal handling, drawing on Rembrandt's prints, together with his active reframing of the calotype's supposed “inferiority” as an artistic quality, opened in the early nineteenth century a way of rethinking the relationship between photography and art. His series of Newhaven fishermen, among the first organized records of a specific social group, is positioned as a forerunner of later documentary photography.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
David Octavius Hill was born in 1802 in Perth, Scotland. He trained as a painter in Edinburgh, worked as a landscape printmaker and oil painter, and became a founding member and long-serving secretary of the Royal Scottish Academy from 1830. A prominent figure in Edinburgh's intellectual life, his ease with people made him an exceptionally effective presence in photographic portraiture*1.

His involvement with photography began with the Disruption of May 18, 1843. On that day approximately 155 ministers left the Church of Scotland to found the Free Church of Scotland, protesting state interference in church appointments. Hill witnessed the event and resolved to paint a monumental commemorative canvas depicting all 470-plus signatories. Needing portrait references, he was introduced to the young photographer Robert Adamson by the physicist David Brewster*2.

Hill brought compositional knowledge from painting; Adamson handled all technical operations — sensitizing paper, exposing the camera, developing negatives, printing salt prints. Under this division of labor they produced an estimated 3,000 calotypes over roughly five years between 1843 and 1848. Their subjects ranged from Edinburgh intellectuals and clergy to the fishermen and fishwives of Newhaven, and architectural views of Edinburgh and its surroundings*3.

After Adamson died in 1848 at around 26 or 27, Hill set photography aside and returned to painting. The Disruption canvas was finally completed in 1866. Hill died in 1870*4.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Hill and Adamson chose the calotype over the daguerreotype. The calotype's optical resolution was inferior, but Hill framed this limitation as an artistic choice. His written remark is explicit: "The rough and unequal texture throughout the paper is the main cause of the calotype failing in details before the Daguerreotype — and this is the very life of it." This is a claim that the medium's limitation was also its defining visual quality*5.

The warm brown tonality and matte, light-absorbing surface of salt prints recalled Rembrandt to contemporaries immediately. The watercolorist John Harden wrote in November 1843, on first seeing their work: "The pictures produced are as Rembrandt's but improved, so like his style and the oldest and finest masters"*6. Hill consciously placed subjects with reference to Rembrandt and Dutch portraiture. This intentional pictorial reference is what distinguishes the Hill-Adamson practice from the work of photographers who were not trained in the visual traditions of painting.

The Newhaven series — about 130 photographs of fishermen and fishwives from the fishing community on the south shore of the Firth of Forth — is recognized as the first major social documentary project in photography. A systematic visual record of a specific occupational community, it anticipates the social documentary tradition that would define the medium's public function in the twentieth century*7.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
The decisive rehabilitation of Hill and Adamson's work in photographic history came through Stieglitz's advocacy. Stieglitz called Hill "the father of pictorial photography" and published photogravure reproductions of their calotypes in Camera Work in 1905, 1909, and 1912. For the pictorialists of the early twentieth century, Hill's practice offered a nineteenth-century precedent for the proposition that photography could be art*8.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art writes that their photographs "still rank among the highest achievements of photographic portraiture"*9. The Getty Museum identifies their partnership as one of "the most important" in the history of Western photography*10. The Scottish National Portrait Gallery (Edinburgh) holds the world's largest collection of Hill and Adamson calotypes — approximately 3,000 prints and related materials*11.

That Hill began photographing as a practical aid to painting, and then exceeded that purpose, is visible in both the volume of work and his own accounts. The question of whether to evaluate him as photographer or painter leads directly to the nineteenth-century debate about photography's status — a debate his practice helped shape from the inside*12.

david-seymour.html.lead_html: From the Spanish Civil War to postwar Europe's children, Chim shaped the humanitarian language of documentary photography with a gaze at once gentle and politically committed. One of the founding members of Magnum Photos in 1947.
david-seymour.html.thesis_html: Through a trajectory from the Spanish Civil War to the refugees and children of postwar Europe, he shifted the focus of war photography from soldiers and combat toward the lives and dignity of civilians. By participating in the founding of Magnum Photos, he helped establish a framework in which photographers organize their work autonomously outside institutional control. A gaze that questions the relationship with the subject rather than the weapon was inherited by subsequent photographers as the methodology of humanitarian documentary.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
David Seymour was born in 1911 near Warsaw in a Jewish publishing family. After studying printing and photography in Germany and France, he began working as a photojournalist from Paris in the early 1930s under the name "Chim." When the Spanish Civil War broke out in 1936, he was among the first photographers to travel to Spain, recording not only the front lines but also the daily lives of civilians and refugees*1. During World War II he obtained US citizenship and served in US Army Intelligence; returning to postwar Europe, in 1947 he co-founded Magnum Photos with Robert Capa, Henri Cartier-Bresson, and George Rodger*2.

Immediately after the war Seymour undertook a UNESCO-commissioned project photographing children across war-devastated Europe, published as Children of Europe in 1948*3. After Capa was killed by a landmine in 1954, Seymour briefly led Magnum as president. He was killed by Egyptian machine-gun fire while covering the Suez Crisis in 1956, aged 45*4.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The gaze of the Spanish Civil War

Seymour's Spanish Civil War photographs focused more often on civilians behind the lines than on dangerous front-line action. Rather than heroicizing militias or political rallies, he recorded family separation, children's anxiety, and rural hardship at close range—anchoring the work in concrete human experience rather than political symbolism. ICP's CHIM archive, which spans the Civil War through postwar Europe, serves as a primary research reference for the intersection of photojournalism and humanitarian documentary*5. Whereas Robert Capa is known for proximity to the edge of survival, Seymour's work reads as a quieter witness to how war dismantles the fabric of everyday life. ICP's Death in the Making exhibition revisited the context in which Capa, Gerda Taro, and Seymour jointly covered the Civil War, making it a key reference for evaluating this period of Seymour's output*6.

Postwar children and the humanitarian visual language

The work that most widely conveyed Seymour's name was his photographs of children across postwar Europe. Carried out under the auspices of Magnum and UNESCO, the project focused on institutionalized children, orphans, and children of refugee families, with a basic stance of recording resilience and human dignity rather than sensationalizing trauma*7. Magnum Photos' documentation on Children of Europe functions as primary material for cross-referencing the institutional context of the UNESCO commission with the on-the-ground decisions Seymour made. The work is regularly cited as an early model for the relationship between postwar international organizations' humanitarian communications and photographic media*8. ICP's 2014 exhibition We Went Back: Photographs from Europe 1933–1956 by Chim presented Seymour's output as a continuous record from prewar Spain to postwar reconstruction, demonstrating the historical scope of his project*9.

The Mexican Suitcase and archival rediscovery

In 2007, three boxes known as the Mexican Suitcase, containing approximately 4,500 negatives from the Spanish Civil War, were discovered in Mexico City. The boxes held negatives shot by Capa, Taro, and Seymour, portions of which had long been considered lost*10. ICP responded by organizing The Mexican Suitcase exhibition, presenting the historical circumstances of the photographs' distribution, preservation, and disappearance. This rediscovery is repeatedly cited in photographic history research as a demonstration of how political and geographic circumstances can fragment and disperse journalistic archives.

Designing the Magnum institution

In founding Magnum Photos, Seymour was involved in designing a cooperative structure in which photographers retained their copyrights and could negotiate the terms of supply to media themselves*2. The 1947 founding was an attempt to change the wartime situation in which photojournalism was subordinated to the logic of states, militaries, and magazine publishers. Magnum's historical resources reveal the commercial and ethical tensions the institution carried internally, and show how central Seymour's involvement was to Magnum's early formation*11.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: After Seymour's death, his work remained less well-known than that of Capa or Cartier-Bresson for several decades. From the 1990s onward, however, reassessment of his Spanish Civil War photographs and postwar children's work advanced through ICP's CHIM exhibition, the establishment of the David Seymour Archive, and the We Went Back exhibition*9. His background as a Jewish Polish migrant who lived through both world wars has been reexamined from the perspective of displacement and testimony, as in the Jewish Cultural Quarter's Chim: Legendary Photojournalist exhibition*13. TIME's "A Second Look: Chim's Children of War" discussed what Seymour's child photographs can still communicate to readers more than half a century later, demonstrating the photographic testimony's trans-temporal reach*14. Seymour's work is positioned as evidence of an era in which photography functioned not merely as a carrier of information but as an apparatus forming the humanitarian language of the postwar world*15.

demachy.html.lead_html: Robert Demachy was a Paris-based photographer who championed the gum bichromate process as the defining technique of Pictorialist photography. Working as a wealthy amateur, he contributed to the international art photography movement through his connections with Stieglitz and Camera Work, arguing that manual intervention in the photographic image was the basis of its artistic legitimacy.
demachy.html.thesis_html: Through his exploration and theoretical advocacy of alternative processes — gum bichromate, oil print, photogravure-aquatint — Demachy introduced into photographic debate the proposition that the photographer's manual intervention is what makes photography art. His systematic argument for a manipulative approach in opposition to photographic realism is still cited as an early articulation of the tension between photography's indexical character and its claims to artistic expression. Working as a wealthy amateur unconstrained by commercial pressures, he contributed to Camera Work and international art-photography networks, helping to form the intellectual connections between Paris and New York.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Robert Demachy was born in 1859 into a wealthy Parisian banking family. He worked throughout his life as a wealthy amateur rather than a professional photographer. As a leading member of the Photo-Club de Paris, he helped connect France's art photography movement with the broader international network.*1

Through his relationship with Alfred Stieglitz he built ties with the Photo-Secession and contributed both photographs and theoretical essays to Camera Work, making him a prominent defender of art photography's theoretical foundations as well as a practitioner.*3

One notable fact is that Demachy abruptly stopped photographing in 1914. The reason remains unclear. The sudden abandonment of nearly three decades of sustained practice stands as an unexplained episode in photographic history. He died in Paris in 1936.*5

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Gum bichromate and manual intervention — the logic of manipulation

Demachy devoted the greatest part of his energy to exploring and theorizing the gum bichromate process. In this process, paper coated with a light-sensitive gum solution is exposed and then the emulsion partially removed or manipulated during development using a brush or water. The photographic image moves away from realistic record and toward a painterly surface that retains brushwork and texture.*1

Demachy argued that this manual intervention was precisely what gave photography its artistic legitimacy. Straight photography advocates — particularly Peter Henry Emerson — held that photography's value lay in the camera's objective record of the subject and considered darkroom manipulation a form of dishonesty. Demachy countered that the camera produces only a mechanical image, and artistic value lies in the photographer's judgment and handwork that transforms it. This debate is now a foundational reference point in discussions of photography's relationship to truth and manipulation.*4

French Pictorialism developed in proximity to Symbolism and Impressionism in painting. Demachy's practice was a conscious attempt to bring photography into contact with these pictorial traditions — not simply to pursue beauty for its own sake but to apply the critical standards of contemporary painting to the photographic image as a strategic argument for the medium's legitimacy.*21

Oil printing and photographic aquatint — multiple technical experiments

Beyond gum bichromate, Demachy worked with several alternative processes. Oil printing attaches oil-based ink selectively to a dried bichromate emulsion, lending prints a printmaking quality and tonal depth. Photographic aquatint (photographic aquatinte) combines etching technique with photography, enabling a linear, engraving-like expression. These technical choices reflect a consistent orientation toward transforming the photographic image into a handcrafted surface.*5

The Cleveland Museum of Art's Demachy work displays the distinctive granularity and soft chiaroscuro of the gum bichromate process, demonstrating how the photographic surface could be transformed into a painterly texture. The Getty Museum also holds several Demachy works, situating them within an international Pictorialist collection.*20

Key works — Speed, In Brittany, A Street in Normandy, Behind the Scenes

Struggle is among Demachy's best-known works, translating the movement of a ballet dancer through the gum bichromate process into an ambiguous, dynamic image in which contours are deliberately blurred and the human form appears as pictorial energy. The Metropolitan Museum holds the work, where it continues to be cited as an important example of Pictorialist photography.*6

Speed, In Brittany, A Street in Normandy, and Behind the Scenes demonstrate that Demachy consistently pursued painterly transformation across urban, regional, and theatrical subjects alike. Pont des Arts, Paris at the National Gallery of Art dissolves figures on a Paris bridge into hazy light and blur, positioning photography not as urban record but as a poem of atmosphere and light.*8

Camera Work and participation in international debate

Demachy contributed theoretical essays as well as photographs to Camera Work, actively engaging in the debate between straight photography and art photography. Camera Work Number 5, held at the Princeton University Art Museum, includes his work and illustrates the journal's role as an international art photography forum.*3

His exchanges with Stieglitz demonstrate that the New York and Paris art photography movements functioned as a single international network. MoMA holds Demachy's works in its collection, and the George Eastman Museum holds pieces including photographic aquatints. Such holdings in major North American institutions indicate that Demachy's practice has been understood within the context of the international Pictorialist movement.*22

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
In his own time Demachy was known as the "apostle of the gum bichromate process," and his theoretical arguments occupied a central position in the art photography debates of the era. His sudden cessation of photography in 1914 complicated his legacy; questions about photographic manipulation recur throughout the twentieth century, and Demachy's position has been cited as an early precedent in those recurring discussions.*1

The Musée d'Orsay includes Demachy as a significant figure in French art photography of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, indicating his established place in France's photographic history. The Paris Musées collection also makes works available online, increasing his accessibility within French visual culture history.*11

In contemporary photographic history scholarship, Demachy's gum bichromate experiments are positioned as a practice that made visible the tension between photography's indexical quality (faithful recording of reality) and its artistic dimension (the photographer's intent and manual transformation). As straight photography rose to dominance, his manipulative approach receded; yet in recent debates around digital manipulation, the questions he argued have returned in new form. The Yale University Art Gallery and the Philadelphia Museum of Art hold works, providing a broad institutional research base for scholars approaching his practice.*13

The Amon Carter Museum of American Art and SFMOMA also hold Demachy's work, where they continue to serve as reference points for the Pictorialist collection. Gallica (BnF) digitized documents and the Paris Musées catalogue records function as source material demonstrating his place within France's cultural heritage. The ongoing presence of his practice in these institutional collections indicates that Pictorialism — photography's so-called lost era — continues to pose questions that art history has not fully resolved.*12

denjiro-hasegawa.html.lead_html: A photographer who produced travel and expedition photobooks across Manchuria, the Himalayas, and India, positioning himself at the intersection of colonial visual culture and publishing photography in 1930s–40s Japan. After the war he turned to temple and Buddhist sculpture photography within Japan.
denjiro-hasegawa.html.thesis_html: By successively publishing photobooks of Manchuria, the Himalayas, and India, Hasegawa pioneered the format of the travel photobook that connected geographic imagination and commercial publishing within Japanese photography culture. His work, which functioned as visual language synchronized with Imperial Japan's geographic expansion, is now evaluated as a resource for examining the relationship between photography and geopolitical and cultural imagination — including his postwar turn to Buddhist sculpture photography.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Denjiro Hasegawa was born in 1894 and developed a photographic practice centered on travel and expedition through the 1920s–40s, working primarily in Manchuria, the Himalayas, and India*1. For Manchuria he published the photobook Manshū Gensō (Manchurian Phantom, held in the Shōwakan Digital Archive) and the travel-narrative Manshū Kikō, linking travel photography to commercial publishing*2. The NDL bibliographic record for Manshū Gensō shows the book carried the subtitle "Legendary Photographer Denjiro Hasegawa" and encompassed landscapes, people, and cities*3. The Tokyo Metropolitan Museum of Photography holds works by Hasegawa as part of its collection of colonial and travel photography from the 1930s–40s*4.

Hasegawa also participated in Himalayan expeditions, publishing those records as photobooks and travel narratives. The Shōwakan Digital Archive holds Himalaya no Tabi (limited edition, with plates, maps)*5. The Kotobank biographical dictionary records that he also photographed Buddhist sites in India, extending his range into religious heritage*6. The CiNii bibliographic record for the postwar sculptural photobook Yomigaeru Yamato no Butsuzō shows his turn toward domestic temple and Buddhist sculpture photography after the war*7. Died 1976.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Travel photography and publishing media

Reducing Hasegawa to "travel photographer" obscures the specificity of his role. In 1930s Japan, travel photography was not simply a personal pursuit but a form of visual culture received through magazines, photobooks, lectures, and exhibitions. As JCII Camera Museum's framing of 1930s–40s "outer territories" photography demonstrates, Hasegawa's Manchurian and Himalayan work overlaps with the circulation routes of colonial visual representation in his era*8. The NDL-catalogued Manshū Gensō can be read as a publication that, in entering commercial distribution, took on meanings associated with touristic imagination, geographic curiosity, and colonial gaze*3.

Manchuria as representational space

The Manchuria in which Hasegawa worked in the 1930s was a politically charged space following the establishment of "Manchukuo," and the visual language of photographs and travel writing carried imperial Japanese imagery of foreign territories. The subtitle "Legendary Photographer" on Shōwakan's copy of Manshū Gensō suggests the work was already received as exceptional by contemporaries*2. Hasegawa's photobooks were produced at the intersection of imperial expansion and the growth of the tourism industry, and the landscape, human, and urban images they contain remain as material for considering how modern Japan saw and circulated images of foreign territories.

Expedition photography and the Himalayas

Beyond Manchuria, Hasegawa joined Himalayan expeditions and published the records. Expedition photography differs from general travel photography in its stronger character as an apparatus visualizing the spatial imagination of the unknown; the "discovery" narrative strongly shaped the meaning of images in publication. The Shōwakan's bibliographic record for Himalaya no Tabi shows the limited-edition format combined photographs with maps and plates as exploration documentation*5. His extension into Indian Buddhist sites shows travel photography connecting to religious-cultural inquiry as well as tourism*6.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Hasegawa's name appears infrequently in postwar photographic histories dominated by expressive or documentary photography. Yet as research into colonial visual representation and travel publishing in 1930s–40s Japan has advanced, his work has attracted renewed attention as material for imperial Japanese visual culture*8. The Tokyo Metropolitan Museum of Photography's collection situates his works among those produced in colonial and expedition contexts, making them a reference point for tracing the lineage of travel and colonial photography in modern Japanese photographic history*4.

diana-scheunemann.html.lead_html: Diana Scheunemann is a Swiss/German photographer who has worked in fashion, advertising, and celebrity portraiture while maintaining personal projects centered on herself and her friends. Ambisexual, the self-portrait diary Behind My Face begun in 1999, Freedom in Flashes, and the book-and-film project Love American Skin move among friends, self-portraits, professional models, and people encountered while traveling under different working conditions. Her career has kept commercial photography and diaristic image-making within the same broader activity.
diana-scheunemann.html.thesis_html: Scheunemann carried the same close, conversational way of photographing across fashion work and records of private life. In Ambisexual she photographed friends as an extension of everyday life; in Behind My Face she has photographed herself with dates since 1999; in Freedom in Flashes she worked at close range with professional models using a 50mm lens and a small amount of flash.She brought the conversation and physical proximity of photographing friends into sessions with models and private clients while retaining the lighting and staging of commercial photography. In the current YOU BY DIANA project, wardrobe, pose, and lighting are discussed with the sitter before the session. Across personal and commercial work, the final image is shaped through exchange with the subject rather than determined solely by the photographer or commissioning client.
