george-rodger.html.lead_html: Rodger covered the European theater throughout World War II, leaving an indelible mark on photographic history with his images of the liberation of Bergen-Belsen. That experience forced a fundamental rethinking of how close to photograph human beings, leading him toward Africa and a founding role in Magnum Photos.
george-rodger.html.thesis_html: Through his documentation of the liberation of Bergen-Belsen, he inscribed in photographic history the recognition of composing corpses as visual elements, raising the question of what it means for photographers to be present at scenes of violence — what "seeing" and "recording" do to the one behind the camera. That experience led to his subsequent refusal to cover war and his turn toward Africa, and connected to the co-founding of Magnum Photos as an autonomous institutional design for photographers.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
George Rodger was born in 1908 in Cheshire, England, and came to photography after working as a merchant sailor and farm laborer*1. When World War II began he became a LIFE correspondent, covering the North African front, Ethiopia, Burma, India, and the Middle East. LIFE Photo Archives' holdings of Rodger's work demonstrate the breadth of his field coverage across multiple theaters of war*2. In April 1945, at the liberation of Bergen-Belsen, Rodger recorded the massed bodies and the condition of survivors. As the biography material at George Rodger Photographs recounts, Rodger later described being shocked to discover he had been looking for compositions among the bodies — an awareness that led him to refuse thereafter to photograph battlefields*3.

In 1947 Rodger co-founded Magnum Photos with Robert Capa, Henri Cartier-Bresson, and David Seymour*4. The axis of his postwar work was long-form reportage in Africa, with extended projects recording the peoples and cultures of Sudan's Nuba Mountains, the Sahara, and other regions. Magnum Photos' documentation of his Sahara work shows the shift from wartime immediacy to a different temporal scale of practice*5. Died 1995.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Bergen-Belsen and the question of looking

One of the most important turning points in Rodger's career was recording the liberation of Bergen-Belsen in April 1945. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum holds Rodger's Belsen photographs as part of its collections, showing how this record has been referenced historically as visual testimony to the concentration camp*6. The Bergen-Belsen Memorial site recounts Rodger's reported statement that he felt nauseous when he realized he was using bodies as compositional elements — an experience said to have forced him to rethink, at a fundamental level, the distance at which human beings may be photographed*7. This episode is repeatedly cited in photographic history as a case in which "the act of seeing and recording" was shown to exact a cost from the photographer. The Photographers' Gallery archive PDF also addresses this transformation, providing a reference for the postwar ethical reorientation of his practice*8.

The turn toward Africa and the method of long-form reportage

After Belsen, Rodger avoided the battlefield and turned toward Africa. His photographs of the Nuba Mountains in Sudan and of Saharan peoples are characterized not as single-issue news reportage but as long-term documentation of specific regions and peoples. Magnum's Sahara materials demonstrate that this work was carried out on a time scale fundamentally different from wartime immediacy*5. ICP's profile of Rodger serves as evidence that the postwar African direction substantially redefined his self-understanding as a photographer*9. At the same time, Rodger's African photographs are critically subject to questions about the colonial gaze of Western photographers depicting Africa; the boundary between anthropological curiosity and humanitarian concern must be read critically.

Magnum Photos and institutional autonomy

As a Magnum co-founder, Rodger was involved in designing a cooperative structure in which photographers owned their copyrights and controlled the terms of their work's publication*4. The interpretation that his years photographing war under the logic of a major publisher — LIFE — generated a conviction about the need for an autonomous institution is repeatedly cited in histories of Magnum. Magnum's historical resources discuss how each founder's wartime experience crystallized into the organization's founding principles; Rodger's role can be understood as part of the institution's ethical foundation*10. The official George Rodger Photographs chronology provides a systematic record of his career from prewar years to his death as a foundational research resource*11.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: George Rodger's critical standing has long been framed by the Belsen record and the context of war photography. More recently, however, reassessment has engaged both the meaning of his long-form African work — including the critical problem of the colonial gaze — and his institutional role as a Magnum founder. The monograph Humanity and Inhumanity: the photographic journey of George Rodger, bibliographically accessible through Internet Archive, is positioned as the primary research resource for reading his war documentation and African reportage as a continuous career*13. Rodger's work continues to be referenced in current debates about the ethics of war photography, as a case study in questions about what testimony means and what it costs a photographer to be present at scenes of violence*7.

gerard-byrne.html.lead_html: Gerard Byrne brings magazine conversations, debates from art history, and displays in natural-history museums into the present through actors, photography, film, and multi-screen installation. In New Sexual Lifestyles, 1984 and Beyond, and A thing is a hole in a thing it is not, he overlays texts from the past with voices, bodies, architecture, and filming styles from another time. The works examine how the meaning of a historical document is shaped by its medium and mode of presentation as well as by its content.
gerard-byrne.html.thesis_html: Magazine articles and interviews from the past are usually encountered as printed documents, accompanied by the photographs of their time. Byrne has actors reenact those texts and layers present-day voices, bodies, architecture, and filming styles onto words from an earlier era. A 1963 forecast of the future or a 1973 discussion of sexuality then becomes evidence of past ideas while also revealing how a sense of period was produced through magazine editing, photography, clothing, and performance. Byrne’s method makes the archive’s content and the forms that make it look “historical” available for examination at the same time.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Byrne was born in Dublin in 1969. Working with film, photography, and performance, he brings twentieth-century literature, magazines, and exhibition history into contemporary production. IMMA identifies the reenactment of historical situations with professional actors and theatrical methods as a central part of his work*1. Lisson Gallery likewise presents his revisiting of historical conversations and cultural technologies alongside photographic series whose images remain fixed while their interpretation shifts over time*2.

Byrne himself cautions against reducing his motivations to a single theory. In an interview with The White Review, however, he describes the use of texts tied to a specific period—and the confrontation of the recent past with the present—as a major artistic gesture*3. His sources include a 1963 forecast of the future, a 1973 roundtable on sexuality, and debates around Minimal art from the 1950s and 1960s. These moments retain especially clear traces of the language and media through which modern society organized ideas about the future, sexuality, and art.

In 2007, Byrne represented Ireland at the Venice Biennale, followed by major presentations at institutions including Tate, Whitechapel Gallery, and the Renaissance Society*4. This institutional reach reflects the way his work has been understood across the histories of film, photography, exhibition making, publishing, and the archive.

sections.title: Core Ideas and Methods
sections.body_html:
Returning Magazine Conversations to Actors’ Voices and Bodies

New Sexual Lifestyles is a three-channel work in which actors perform a 1973 Playboy roundtable on sexuality. Artforum noted how the restaging of a decades-old conversation by amateur actors brings the historical character of the statements into the same space as the contemporary performance*5. According to IMMA, the conversation is dispersed across three monitors, introducing chance into the combination of sound and image*6. A conversation once stabilized through print acquires an unstable duration in the gallery. Frieze likewise draws attention to the temporal mismatch between 1970s-style interiors and contemporary clothing, describing how reenactment unsettles the document’s sense of period*7.

Reenactment Gives Old Words Bodies from Another Time

In 1984 and Beyond, science-fiction writers’ 1963 Playboy discussion of life “beyond 1984” is spoken by actors in the 2000s. By the time Byrne made the work, the future they had imagined already belonged to the past. CAC Vilnius describes the piece as a “future past” in which document, reenactment, photography, and film overlap*4. Reenactment lets Byrne reconstruct tone of voice, pauses, gestures, clothing, and interior design as present-day choices—elements that a quotation alone would leave largely implicit. The content of the words and their period character begin to move independently, so the 1960s image of the future also reflects a question back onto the 2000s: what kind of future can the present imagine?

Still Photographs Present the Past at a Different Speed from Film

Although Byrne’s major works are often discussed primarily as moving-image installations, 1984 and Beyond includes twenty black-and-white photographs*8. Separated from the continuous time of film, the photographs acquire a distinct sense of age. A Guardian review of the Whitechapel exhibition observed that Byrne’s silvery-gray photographs provide few clues from which to date them, creating the impression that the past has entered the present*9. The coexistence of fixed photographs and moving images gives viewers two different speeds through which to experience temporal dislocation.

The “Modern Ruin” — Photographing Modernity That Still Persists

At a Tate Britain artist talk, Byrne’s interest in the “modern ruin” was discussed alongside 1984 and Beyond*10. The term includes more than ruined buildings. It can also describe visual systems that carry another period into the present: the future imagined in the 1960s, conventions for displaying Minimal art, or a natural-history diorama. The Biologiska Museet discussed in The White Review is a key example, preserving a nineteenth-century image of nature as a three-dimensional apparatus*3.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
New Sexual Lifestyles — Undoing the Sequence of Magazine Editing

The Playboy roundtable was edited in print into a sequence that readers could follow. Byrne disperses the conversation across three screens and transfers the same statements into the voices of contemporary actors*6. Aesthetica’s review of a retrospective treats the work as an early formulation of the method later developed in 1984 and Beyond, noting how performance unsettles the distance between historical fact and fiction*11. Byrne’s editing reintroduces, in altered form, pauses, vocal tempo, and exchanges of glances that disappeared in the original printed transcription.

1984 and Beyond — A Later Generation Performs the Future Imagined by the Past

In 1984 and Beyond, forecasts by Arthur C. Clarke, Isaac Asimov, and other science-fiction writers are reenacted within modernist architecture*12. The White Review describes the actors as speaking the 1963 text with a quality of “ventriloquism,” producing an atmosphere in which time and authorship seem unmoored*3. The work moves beyond checking whether the predictions came true. It asks how words about the future become legible as a “record of their time” when joined to particular photographs, architecture, and voices.

A thing is a hole in a thing it is not — Refilming the History of Minimal Art

A thing is a hole in a thing it is not (2010–11) addresses the historical reception of Minimal art through multiple films. The Renaissance Society connects the work to its own history of presenting early Minimal artists*13. e-flux describes four films running in parallel, preserving historical works and events from several perspectives*14. Exhibition history is repeatedly edited through texts, installation photographs, the placement of works, criticism, and later restagings. Byrne reconstructs that process as a moving-image installation.

Biologiska Museet — Filming the Diorama as a Prehistory of Photography

Jielemeguvvie guvvie sjisjnjeli — Film inside an image centers on Stockholm’s Biologiska Museet. The White Review describes how the late-nineteenth-century diorama fixes Nordic nature within a single field of vision through painted backdrops, modeled terrain, and taxidermy*3. In a photography-history program at Moderna Museet, Byrne similarly reads the museum as a visual apparatus akin to a camera, linking it to the photographic history of preserving nature*15. At the center of the work is a nineteenth-century technology for turning nature into a single view. Moderna Museet exhibited the work in 2017 as part of a photography-history program, explaining Byrne’s view of the large-scale diorama, built in 1893, as a “camera” that makes an image with light from a skylight*16.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Recovering Forms of Speech Alongside Facts from the Archive

What Byrne retrieves from magazines and records includes the statements themselves and the editing, photography, page design, architecture, and exhibition formats that turned those words into cultural events. In its retrospective covering 2003–12, Whitechapel Gallery brought together discourses preserved in different institutions, from sexual politics to the production and display of artworks*17. Once source material is given to actors, voices and bodies absent from the printed document are produced anew; in the gallery, screen placement and projection order become another act of editing. Byrne’s use of archives combines the recovery of past information with an inquiry into the forms through which information is preserved as history. Simon Fraser University’s introduction to an artist talk likewise identifies the “transposition” of text into image as a central concern*18.

Reading Evidentiary Appearance and Period Feeling from the Same Photograph

In Case Study Loch Ness, photographs and 16 mm film related to Loch Ness are connected to the cultural desire to determine whether the monster is real*19. The work asks what was photographed and why particular image qualities and compositions feel like evidence. Lytle Shaw’s essay “The Utopian Past” similarly analyzes the connection to the past in 1984 and Beyond as an operation conducted through multiple mediations*20. Byrne’s still photographs both fix events and produce the visual atmosphere through which a period is perceived.

Exhibition Sequence Rewrites the Order of History Each Time

In multi-screen works, viewers miss material on one screen while concentrating on another. Photographs remain still amid that shifting attention. An artist talk at the Renaissance Society records Byrne discussing this exhibition structure as part of his method*21. Circa’s discussion of the later In Our Time likewise notes Byrne’s continuing interest in releasing viewers from fixed screening times and reconfiguring the relation among broadcast, exhibition, and time*22. Reenacting documents and editing an exhibition can be understood as two aspects of the same operation: assigning a new order to the past.

germaine-krull.html.lead_html: German-born photographer known for the photobook Métal, which edits industrial structures through fragmentation and diagonals. She moved across avant-garde practice, photobooks, reportage and commercial media, supporting the popular circulation of modernist photography across multiple countries.
germaine-krull.html.thesis_html: As exemplified by the photobook Métal, which edited industrial structures into fragments and diagonals, Krull connected avant-garde visual experiment to the photobook, reportage and commercial media. Developed while moving across several countries, her work carried modernist photography outside the exhibition and opened routes for its popular circulation through print.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Germaine Krull was born in Germany in 1897 and pursued photography while moving through Munich, the Netherlands and Paris. *1 She established her base of operations in Paris in the 1920s, working in parallel on magazine reportage, fashion and avant-garde photographic experiment. *2 Her 1928 photobook Métal — compositions of the Eiffel Tower's iron structures, machines and urban infrastructure made with extreme angles and fragmentation — occupies an important place in the history of the photobook. *3

Her career is characterised by a mobility that resists fixing to a single country or movement. Her connections include French Surrealism, journalism, and travel photography in Southeast Asia and India. *4 Centre Pompidou and MoMA both position her at the intersection of the avant-garde and popular reportage and publishing. *5 She died in Germany in 1985. *6

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Métal and the structure of the photobook

Krull's Métal is not a photobook that documents machinery: it is a book that edits the skeleton of the modern city as fragments, diagonals, repetitions and the rhythm of print. *7 Iron towers and bridges may be massive structures, but on the pages of the photobook they become abstract compositional elements. What matters here is that the photobook as a medium creates a sequential visual experience rather than a collection of individual photographs. MoMA's Object:Photo project includes Métal as a significant case in photobook history, analysing the aesthetics of sequencing and printing. *8

Where Rodchenko used extreme angles within post-revolutionary Soviet public vision and Sheeler saw American industry as precise order, Krull grasped urban infrastructure as a moving gaze. *9 Her photographs have an industrial beauty while also connecting to reportage, travel, commercial publishing and political migration, resisting fixing to a single country or style. Comparing her with Rodchenko, Moholy-Nagy and Sheeler reveals the multiple directions taken by industrial modernism. *10

Reportage, mobility and the position of the woman photographer

Krull worked as a press photographer covering political events across Europe while continuing her avant-garde photographic experiments in parallel. *11 The evaluation of her as a woman photographer with a mobility and cross-media range that resists a national artist image has been one of the frameworks in which she is discussed at Jeu de Paume, MoMA and elsewhere. *12 Centre Pompidou's collection holds Krull's photographs and archives, forming the basis for research that re-evaluates her at the intersection of avant-garde vision and reportage and publishing. *13

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: MoMA, Centre Pompidou, Jeu de Paume, the Getty and Tate all provide access to works and materials, and re-evaluation continues both of her position at the intersection of avant-garde vision and reportage/publishing and of her mobility as a woman photographer. *14 ICP, the Metropolitan Museum, the AIC and the MFA Boston also hold related works. *15 In later photobook studies, Métal is repeatedly cited as an early example of the photobook functioning as a medium that creates a distinctive visual experience through editing, printing and design rather than simply collecting photographs. *16 Krull's mobility and cross-media range have been discussed as a case for reconsidering the position of women photographers within photographic history, given how difficult her practice is to contain within a national artist image. Her practice — spanning avant-garde, reportage and commercial work in equal measure — demonstrates a diversity in early twentieth-century photographic practice that resists single-genre framing.

twitter.description: Nan Goldin began photographing friends and lovers in 35mm color, shaped by her unease with how her family retold her sister’s death. This essay reads The Ballad of Sexual Dependency through New Documents, Larry Clark, New Color, underground film, the AIDS crisis, and the history of intimate-life photography.

goldin.html.lead_html: Nan Goldin began photographing as a way to preserve, in concrete detail, the time she shared with people she loved after watching her family’s account of her sister’s death change over time. In Boston and New York during the 1970s, she photographed friends, lovers, drag queens, and herself in 35mm color, developing the work into The Ballad of Sexual Dependency, a slideshow of roughly 700 images set to music. This essay examines her recurring portrayal of the same people as they love, suffer, fall ill, and die, locating the form at the intersection of subjective documentary, the domestic slide show, and underground film.
goldin.html.thesis_html: Goldin developed photographs that resembled domestic color slides into a musical projection in which the same people return across years. She included her own relationships, experiences of violence, and addiction, showing friends as people whose lives change within relationships instead of fixing them as lovers, addicts, or AIDS patients. In doing so, she extended photography from evidence of an instant into a film made of still images, a form for revisiting shared time.

sections.title: Why Photography Became Necessary
sections.body_html:
Barbara’s Death: Resisting the Revision of Memory

Goldin’s point of departure was the memory of her sister Barbara, who died by suicide in 1965. As she watched her sister’s life and death recast within the family into a more acceptable account, Goldin began using photography to preserve the details of people and places*23. In the introduction to The Ballad of Sexual Dependency, she describes photography as a way to preserve her world*2. She later said that the work grew less from a plan to become an artist than from a “need to record everything”*23.

Family albums often select birthdays, trips, weddings, and other events a family wants to remember. Goldin also photographed sex, arguments, drug use, injury, and illness as parts of the same life. She chose to preserve shared time with all its contradictions instead of constructing a portrait from happy occasions alone.

Photography as a “Mirror”: The Relationship Comes First

In her mid-teens, Goldin was given a Polaroid at an alternative school; the first person she photographed was her close friend David Armstrong. She has explained that the relationship usually came first and that the photograph became a “mirror” that could show people a beauty they did not recognize in themselves*1. She continued photographing the same people for twenty or thirty years, so that changes in those relationships unfolded across the work itself.

In the early 1970s, she frequented the Boston drag bar The Other Side and photographed while living among her friends who performed in drag. Goldin has described the work as a tribute to their beauty*9. Her loose circle at the School of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston—including David Armstrong, Mark Morrisroe, and Jack Pierson—later became known as the Boston School. The ICA Boston describes these artists as focusing on the queer underground in and around Boston from the late 1970s through the 1980s and using photography to preserve a record during the AIDS crisis*29.

New Documents and Tulsa: Taking Subjective Documentary Further

Before Goldin, documentary photography was already moving away from the idea of social reform and toward openly personal ways of seeing. MoMA’s 1967 exhibition New Documents presented Diane Arbus, Lee Friedlander, and Garry Winogrand as a generation less concerned with reforming society through photographs than with understanding the world they inhabited*30. Larry Clark’s Tulsa (1971) made the lives and deaths of his friends into a black-and-white photobook from the position of someone who was both participant in and observer of the drug culture*28.

Goldin encountered Clark’s and Arbus’s photographs around age nineteen, finding precedents for photographing from inside a community*3. She expanded this approach through color, music, long-term recurrence, and a projected sequence that included self-portraits. Women, men, drag queens, and Goldin herself appear in the same work, including her own face after an assault. Clark followed his friends through the fixed order of a book; Goldin built a live projection in which the same people returned across years.

sections.title: Where Did the Form of The Ballad of Sexual Dependency Come From?
sections.body_html:
New Color and the Family Slide Show: Using Color as Information for Memory

In the 1970s, William Eggleston photographed familiar places in the American South in color; MoMA presented the work in a 1976 solo exhibition and the book William Eggleston’s Guide*21. Stephen Shore’s American Surfaces similarly recorded meals, motels, roads, and people as a color diary during a 1972–73 journey*22. In Goldin’s work, color does more than organize a single frame. Skin, lipstick, bar lighting, wallpaper, and sheets become cues to whose room she was in, with whom, and when. Color helps connect appearances of the same person across different days.

Her compact 35mm camera could move easily through bars, clubs, and bedrooms, while direct flash recorded people and the surrounding objects in dark interiors. Goldin has said that she framed furniture and possessions along with the people so she could remember the environments in which they lived*3. She projected sex, violence, drug use, and illness in the same format used for family slides of vacations and birthdays. The audience therefore encountered the work at the intimate distance of being shown an acquaintance’s album.

Warhol, Jack Smith, and Vivienne Dick: Giving Photographs the Time of Film

Underground film was as important as photography to Goldin’s early visual education. She has named the films of Andy Warhol and Jack Smith as major influences from before she studied photography, and thought of the recurring cast she photographed for decades—David, Cookie, Sharon, and others—in terms of Warhol’s “superstars”*1. As film characters change from scene to scene, her friends do not end with a single portrait; they return years later.

The slide projections began because her art school had no darkroom and she showed color slides in place of prints*23. Her interest in film and music helped turn that practical accident into a sustained form. Goldin has said that Vivienne Dick’s films taught her how to start and stop music and move into another scene*23. The Ballad of Sexual Dependency is a sequence of color snapshots and, at the same time, a film of still images combining photography, popular music, and live performance in clubs.

One Picture Cannot Preserve a Person: Repetition, Music, and Live Editing

Goldin did not believe that one photograph could encompass an entire person, and she has worked with multiple images, grids, and triptychs*23. In The Ballad, Nan and Brian, Cookie and Vittorio, and others reappear through embraces, arguments, sleep, care, illness, and death. A person who might be read in one image as “the happy lover,” “the violent man,” or “the AIDS patient” returns in different roles and expressions, making it difficult to treat any single photograph as the final account of that life.

The early projections took place in bars, parties, and underground cinemas. Goldin manually advanced hundreds of slides and revised the sequence during the performance*7. Friends depicted in the work sat in the audience, and she removed photographs when they objected. Subjects also retained editorial input in private screenings during the 1990s*23. Princeton University Art Museum describes the current version as a forty-two-minute work of approximately 700 images*5. The shape of memory depended on more than taking photographs: Goldin chose which person would return and which songs would surround each appearance.

Why Private Life Was Read Politically: Gender, Violence, and Editorial Control

While Goldin worked at the Times Square bar Tin Pan Alley, co-owner Maggie Smith read The Ballad as a political work about gender, sex work, and male violence. Goldin has said that Smith’s observation enabled her to understand her work politically*23. When love, domestic violence, queer life, and dependency recur within the same relationships, gendered disparities of power and violence left unspoken by others appear as specific events.

MoMA’s program on The Ballad asks viewers to consider photography, memory, and the diary as “critical documentary”*27. The museum’s account emphasizes that the photographs grew from ongoing relationships rather than external observation*12. The photographer appears as a lover, friend, and survivor of violence, making her position visible. Goldin nevertheless retained authority over shooting, selection, and projection. The work records violence within intimate life while raising questions about who selects, owns, and circulates the images. Liz Kotz has argued that insider status does not in itself eliminate voyeurism or disparities of power*20.

sections.title: From Recording Life to Mourning
sections.body_html:
The Ballad of Sexual Dependency: Live Projection, Photobook, Museum

The Ballad of Sexual Dependency developed from live projections in bars and underground cinemas in the late 1970s*7. After its presentation in the 1985 Whitney Biennial, Aperture published the photobook in 1986, fixing 127 images selected from the projected version into a page sequence*8. Marvin Heiferman, who worked on the edit, has described how a presentation that changed each time became a single edition in book form*6.

MoMA exhibited the work as manually advanced 35mm slides with music, tracing its development from live performance*4. The recent retrospective This Will Not End Well was organized around six slideshows and reconsidered Goldin’s work as a combination of still images, sound, and duration*17. Live projection, photobook, and museum installation establish different relationships to the audience. They also show how a work whose subjects could once intervene from the seats became an artwork preserved and shown repeatedly.

Nan One Month After Being Battered: A Self-Portrait Against Forgetting

Nan One Month After Being Battered (1984) is a self-portrait made one month after Goldin was assaulted by her partner Brian*11. A swollen eye, wounds, carefully arranged hair, and red lipstick occupy the same frame; victim, photographer, and the person deciding to preserve the image are one and the same. MoMA places the self-portrait at the end of her relationship with Brian*12. The photograph keeps love and violence within the history of the same relationship, leaving their consequences on Goldin’s face instead of dividing them into separate narratives.

AIDS and Witnesses: Preserving Names as a Community Disappeared

By the late 1980s, many of the friends Goldin had photographed had died of AIDS. Images of Cookie and Vittorio move from marriage to illness and death, turning a record of romance into a record of care and loss*5. Goldin has said that during current projections she sits at the back, counts how many people have died, and speaks to them through the slides*23. The purpose of the work shifted: from recording the desires and relationships of a living community to maintaining contact with the dead and preserving the lives they had led before they could be collapsed into anonymous “victims.”

In 1989, Goldin organized Witnesses: Against Our Vanishing at Artists Space, gathering art and writing by friends affected by AIDS*13. She has explained that the exhibition began when she tried to return to her community and found that many friends were already dead or dying*14. The NEA’s withdrawal of funding over an essay by David Wojnarowicz made the government’s response to AIDS, religious conservatism, and arts censorship matters of public dispute*15.

Sisters, Saints, Sibyls: Reexamining Her Sister’s Death Through Documents

The three-channel video Sisters, Saints, Sibyls (2004–22) brings together the legend of Saint Barbara, the life and death of Goldin’s sister Barbara, and Goldin’s own hospitalization*18. Using family photographs, psychiatric reports, images of the psychiatric ward, voices, and moving images, the work examines how her family and psychiatric institutions treated her sister*19. Religion, family, medicine, and autobiography appear simultaneously across three screens, with no single account treated as definitive. The method that repeated her friends’ lives in The Ballad returns here as a way of comparing documents left about her sister and questioning the memory constructed by the family.

sections.title: Intimate Life in Photographic History: What Remains Unresolved
sections.body_html:
What Passed to Tillmans, Billingham, and Fashion Photography

“Intimate Life” provides a way to compare contemporary photography of family, lovers, and friends in which the photographer also appears as a participant in the life being recorded. ICP places Goldin, Emmet Gowin, Sally Mann, Carrie Mae Weems, and others in a lineage extending from the family album, diary, and self-portrait*25. MEP’s Love Songs likewise built a multigenerational history of photographs of lovers around Goldin and Nobuyoshi Araki*26.

Wolfgang Tillmans expanded from photographs of friends and club culture into abstraction and social activism, constructing installations that included slide projection*10. Richard Billingham’s Ray’s a Laugh organized photographs of his family home, marked by alcoholism and poverty, into a color photobook*16. In 1990s fashion photography, direct flash, disordered interiors, and unguarded bodies were used to suggest everyday life in place of the idealized model*24. Subsequent artists inherited more than the look of direct flash or snapshot informality. They also inherited questions about whom one photographs over time, how multiple images are sequenced, and how images made within close relationships should be handled after they enter public circulation.

Photography, Projection, Publication, Recirculation: Four Stages of Consent

At early projections, friends depicted in the work asked for photographs to be removed, and Goldin complied*23. The Ballad of Sexual Dependency later became a photobook, a museum work, and a set of reproduced images that continues to circulate decades after the photographs were made. Permission to take a photograph, agreement to show it among friends, consent to publication in a book, and posthumous display in museums and markets each have a different scope.

Kotz argued that belonging to the same community does not erase differences in authority over editing, exhibition, and sale, while viewers can observe intimate lives from a protected distance*20. The difference between early projections, where subjects could ask for an image to be removed, and museum displays that repeat a fixed sequence reveals both the strength and the limit of Goldin’s method. Because personal relationships provided the basis for the photographs, the question remains: who decides what may be shown after those relationships change?

From Witnesses to P.A.I.N.: Connecting Memory to Institutional Responsibility

Founded in 2017, P.A.I.N. grew out of Goldin’s own opioid dependency and targeted both the Sackler family’s pharmaceutical profits and the museums that accepted their donations*23. Goldin has cited ACT UP as an organizational model and described choosing museum lobbies and galleries as sites of protest*14.

P.A.I.N., like her earlier work, asked who controls the account of personal experience and who bears responsibility. With her sister’s death, Goldin opposed the explanation constructed by the family. In The Ballad, she preserved the contradictory lives of lovers and friends. Witnesses documented a community disappearing through AIDS and the censorship surrounding it. P.A.I.N. redirected attention from narratives that treated addiction as individual failure to pharmaceutical marketing, museum donations, and social shame. Across Goldin’s work and activism is a consistent effort to preserve the people she loves and expose the power of families, governments, corporations, and art institutions to determine what their memories mean.

Goldin’s place in photographic history lies in bringing together the subjective documentary that emerged after the 1960s, 1970s color photography, Larry Clark’s insider documentary, the family album, and the editing of underground film in one projection set to music. The Ballad of Sexual Dependency developed a form that refuses to explain a person through a single image and repeatedly revisits shared time. It also left later artists and museums with a question: who may select images of intimate subjects, and for how long may those images remain public?

gonzalo-puch.html.lead_html: Gonzalo Puch is a Spanish artist who assembles foam-board architecture, plants, maps, equations, household objects, and figures in studios, homes, and classrooms, then preserves scenes that disappear after the shoot as large-scale photographs. In works such as Homenaje a Vermeer, Incidentes, and Le Corbusier con piña, he draws on photography’s appearance of factual evidence while making no attempt to conceal that the “reality” before the camera was constructed for the photograph.
gonzalo-puch.html.thesis_html: Puch physically builds fragile sets inside real rooms and records them as conventional photographs. He preserves photography’s factual claim that “this was actually there” within constructed scenes containing traces of sculpture, theater, laboratories, and everyday life. This overlap is the core of his method. Photography no longer serves to determine whether something is real or fictional; it becomes a form of “document-fiction” in which both conditions coexist.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
From Painting to Sculpture to Photography: Recording Temporary Scenes

Puch was born in Seville in 1950. He began with painting and gradually moved toward work combining sculpture and photography. Banco de España describes this transition as the development of scenes in which figures temporarily “inhabit” fragile foam-board architecture and objects that exist only for the moment of the photograph*1. A UCLM biography likewise identifies the construction of situations he calls “incidentes” in neutral spaces such as classrooms and homes, later presented as large photographic prints, as a basic feature of his work*4.

A long 2018 interview gives a more specific account of this transition in Puch’s own terms. Around 1986, when he began teaching at the University of Cuenca, he found himself unable to stop attaching objects to paintings. He felt a growing mismatch between his intuition and the act of “making painting,” and bought a camera almost on impulse*26. Over the next four years, the canvas disappeared. Iron, wood, and painted structures appeared on floors and walls, while photographs entered the same environment. In his 1991 solo exhibition at Galería Buades, illuminated structures and photographs occupied a shared, unstable space*26. The camera did not simply replace painting with another flat medium. In Puch’s words, “the studio became portable.” It became a tool for bringing together, as an image, temporary configurations of sculpture, action, fire, water, and bodily movement that could be assembled and carried to another place*26.

During the 1990s, staged photography—constructing a scene before exposure—became an important method in contemporary art. Puch’s sets retain unstable, visibly provisional constructions made from foam, paper, plants, and household objects. A CA2M collection catalog describes these scenes as laboratory-like environments and notes the presence of his interests in light, mathematics, science, and education throughout the work of the 1990s*11.

Why Photography? Turning Temporary Sculpture into “Evidence”

In a 2002 interview with El País, Puch himself emphasized the manual construction of an actual scene before exposure over the production of illusion through digital manipulation*5. Because the set physically existed in front of the camera, a fictional scene retains photography’s documentary trace that “this place existed.” Banco de España explains that this undermines ideas of the snapshot and photographic “truth,” producing what José Lebrero Stals calls “documento-ficción”*2.

Photography for Doubt: Refusing a Settled Genre

In the same interview, Puch places his work in the realm of “doubt” rather than “certainty,” saying that what interests him is the movement toward a place he does not already know*26. His wish to mix photography, video, drawing, collage, and photomontage without sorting them into separate categories—creating a “hybrid document” that crosses the boundaries of the photographic image and resists fixed definition—is another key to his form*26. Staged photography becomes an experimental site in which physically made objects and events are fixed into images that retain an evidentiary charge. Drawings, scientific signs, actions, and everyday objects collide within scenes that do not fit easily into established photographic genres.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Homenaje a Vermeer: Light, Science, and a Disordered Classroom as One Experiment

Homenaje a Vermeer (1994) uses window light, maps, books, paper, and a laboratory-like interior to overlap the visual language of Vermeer’s studio scenes with that of scientific experiment. A Comunidad de Madrid catalog connects the work to Puch’s concentrated interest in light, painting, and science during the 1990s, describing how actual objects and inexplicable events coexist within the same scene*12. The photograph contains both a reference to painting and spaces—classrooms and laboratories—where knowledge is supposed to be ordered, fixing a state in which scattered objects prevent meaning from settling.

UCLM also lists mathematics, science, music, biology, and environmental studies among his subjects. Diagrams and models recur as signs of his interest in the institutional processes that make knowledge visible*4. The scenes do not provide a solution to a puzzle; they are structured so that relations become less stable as information accumulates.

Incidentes: Theater, Sculpture, and Domestic Space Compressed into the Instant of a Photograph

The CAAC solo exhibition Incidentes (2003–04) presented Puch’s method in concentrated form. The CAAC publication archive records the exhibition catalog as a standalone publication*13. ABC Sevilla described the work of this period as a practice that questions photographic truth and constructs scenes as “documentos-ficciones,” reporting Puch’s comments on laboratories, art and science, and staging*6.

The construction of the set itself carries the work’s thinking. Banco de España describes white architectural forms, household objects, and figures coexisting only during the shoot, producing a state difficult to classify as theater, performance, photography, or moving image*1. The photograph ultimately compresses multiple temporalities and media onto a single surface, and that surface alone extends the life of the scene.

Le Corbusier con piña: Modernist Utopia Contaminated by Refrigerators and Fruit

In Le Corbusier con piña (2005), a white high-rise and model roads coexist with an open refrigerator, potted plants, and an enormous pineapple on a shelf. Banco de España’s exhibition text reads the image as a collision between the utopian ideals of Le Corbusier’s urban planning and the memory of perishable matter associated with Baroque still life*3. As the pristine modernist model is invaded by the disorder of everyday life, the distance between the order of the plan and the space that is actually lived becomes visible.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Large-Scale Prints: Returning Constructed Objects to the Viewer as a Scene

Puch has presented his constructed “incidents” as large-scale color photographs. UCLM identifies large-format prints as a basic form of his work*4. Museo Reina Sofía lists a 2004 Sin título as a 160 × 225 cm digital chromogenic print, indicating the physical scale at which the final image confronts the viewer*10.

Around 2007, the exhibitions themselves became more explicitly installation-based. A CA2M catalog records how Puch retained photography as a principal support while incorporating moving image, with exhibitions after 2007 expanding into installation*11. A 2007 review in El País likewise discusses the work as a practice in which photographs, lightboxes, and exhibition space extend beyond the frame*7.

Science and Nature: Uncertain Landscapes in the Guise of Research

At PHotoEspaña 2006, Puch had a solo exhibition at the Real Jardín Botánico; Photography Now also records the exhibition in his history*19. CAAC’s 2008 exhibition Untamed Paradises included Puch among artists addressing relations between science and nature and presented a project in which the artist’s studio became something like a “hospital” for plants*17. The exhibition press material placed him in a section reconsidering relations between nature and knowledge through art’s borrowing of scientific methods and instruments*18.

Puch’s “experiments” do not seek to reproduce scientific correctness. Measurement, models, classification, and the laboratory are shown as devices that simplify reality in order to make it intelligible, while chance, jokes, and everyday clutter enter those systems. The photograph fixes these unstable arrangements. It resembles a record of experimental results while refusing to settle what the results mean.

Una jornada sin nubes: Extending the Studio Experiment into the Environment

Writing on the 2011 CAB de Burgos exhibition Una jornada sin nubes (literally, “a day without clouds”), Sema D’Acosta notes that Puch moved away from his earlier theatrical tableaux vivants populated by figures and expanded toward unstable structures made from discarded materials, still lifes of cut vegetables, drawings, and installation. The continuing subject was the relation between humans and nature; his unease with scientific interpretation detaching nature from its surroundings turned toward environmental degradation and artificial landscapes*27.

Puch’s “laboratory” is not fixed to a particular interior set. In the 1990s, scientific diagrams, models, and everyday objects collided indoors; by the 2010s, his field had expanded to waste materials, plants, and exhibition space. Moving among photography, drawing, sculpture, and installation, he repeatedly constructs situations in which the bond between knowledge and matter comes apart. The early method of composing a scene for the camera remains, but as the environment itself becomes a subject, space outside the photograph also becomes part of the work.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Physically Constructed Fiction Behind a Surreal Appearance

Puch’s images can appear surreal at first, but that appearance comes from physically constructed sets and actions. Los Claveles presents Buscando en la zona as a continuation of the “incidentes,” where installation, moving image, and laboratory logic intersect*20. e-flux likewise featured him in an exhibition of artists who addressed psychological and social realities through constructed scenes*21.

A consistent principle is that fiction is made physically in front of the camera rather than hidden inside invisible computer processing. His emphasis in El País on photography as handwork reveals the central paradox: he questions photographic truth while retaining physical contact with reality*5. This physical construction produces photographs that are fictional and, at the same time, records of events that actually existed.

Spanish Photography After the 1990s: Between Photography and Installation

The artist’s official exhibition history includes solo shows at CAAC, PHotoEspaña, CAB de Burgos, and Julie Saul Gallery in New York, among others, documenting his reception in both photography-specific and contemporary-art venues*8. His public collections include Reina Sofía, MUSAC, CAAC, the Blanton Museum, and Banco de España, among others*9. The Junta de Andalucía also recorded the acquisition of his work by CAAC in an official 2004 document*16.

Lessons from Pina Bausch and Robert Wilson: Scenes That Do Not Stand Still

The sense that Puch’s figures and objects have been caught in the middle of an action reflects theatrical influences as well as photographic precedents. He has said that seeing productions by Pina Bausch and Robert Wilson taught him to think of light, color, installation, performance, energy, and movement as inseparable, with the image continually “happening”*26. He consequently came to feel that figures in a photograph did not need to stand still and pose; they could be in the middle of doing something*26. The theatrical sensibility Puch drew from Bausch and Wilson allows his photographs to compress the duration of sculpture and action into a single frame. Photography is necessary because it stops the action, leaving enough within the arrested instant to suggest what came before and after without supplying an ending.

Puch’s place in photographic history lies in loosening the binary between photographing reality and making fiction. Building objects, positioning figures, and determining light before exposure are unmistakably acts of staging, yet the finished photograph also records the real existence of that staging. His constructed photography retains photography’s factual charge while making the fact itself something produced for the camera.

CAAC collection materials have continued to present Puch as an artist in the collection of contemporary Andalusian art*14. A 2006 collection exhibition likewise presented his work in a context crossing photography and installation*15.

Alongside Casebere and Demand: Returning the “Constructed Image” to Spanish Everyday Space

A 2005 exhibition of the Telefónica contemporary photography collection at MARCO was organized around a shift from photography as “document” toward “narrative/representation” at the end of the twentieth and beginning of the twenty-first century, when artists increasingly worked consciously with the medium’s own codes. It included Puch and James Casebere in the same exhibition*22. The exhibition traced this history through the Düsseldorf School, artists around John Baldessari, and the cinematic or pictorial photography of Jeff Wall, situating Puch at a moment when the distinction between “photographer” and “artist using photography” was becoming less rigid.

The connection to Casebere and Thomas Demand lies in a shared method of constructing the scene before exposure, not in a claim of direct influence. Guggenheim Bilbao places both within a history of the “constructed image,” in which models or full-scale environments are built in order to be photographed*25. In Puch’s interiors, constructions, scientific diagrams, furniture, plants, and bodily traces are not concealed within a seamless stage set; the disorder of work in progress remains visible. CAAC calls this method “documento-ficción,” describing a practice that gives fiction the appearance of reality while favoring accumulation over classification*24. For Puch, the trace of real objects, fabrication, knowledge, and play colliding within one frame matters more than the seamless perfection of an illusion.

New Uses of Photography in the Late 1990s: The Interior as a Device for Producing Fiction

Fundación Telefónica included Puch in Interiores, an exhibition of works made from the late 1990s to the early 2000s. It described a period in which fragments of interiors, streets, churches, and faces acquired new meanings through manipulation, fiction, and desire*23. The cluttered studio in Incidentes does more than provide a backdrop for strange events. The interior temporarily connects sculpture, drawing, scientific signs, and everyday objects; photography alone fixes that connection onto a single surface that carries the appearance of fact.

guadalupe-ruiz.html.lead_html: Guadalupe Ruiz is a Colombian-born photographer and artist who draws on a life divided between Bogotá and Switzerland, photographing familiar subjects such as family, interiors, cities, food, and her child’s constructions, then editing them into photobooks and exhibitions. Bogotá D.C., Kleine Fotoenzyklopädie, and Petit Suisse connect migration, close observation of everyday life, classification, and printing as one continuous process.
guadalupe-ruiz.html.thesis_html: In Bogotá D.C., Ruiz addresses Bogotá’s social stratification through 120 photographs of homes without their residents, arranged by social class and subject instead of using portraits to stand for each group. Beds, living rooms, exteriors, gardens, and diplomas become comparable details, presenting the city as a sequence of domestic interiors. Kleine Fotoenzyklopädie later organizes 645 travel photographs into a personal taxonomy, while NY Apples and Pears reprints and cuts fruit photographs from one section into new still-life arrangements. Each book establishes a different rule: comparison across housing classes, private taxonomy, or physical reworking of the printed image.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
From Bogotá to Switzerland—Distance Makes the Everyday Newly Visible

Ruiz was born in Bogotá in 1978, moved to Switzerland in 1996, and studied photography at institutions including ECAL in Lausanne. She is now based in Biel/Bienne and connects her work to the experience of moving between Colombia and Switzerland*1.

In an interview, Ruiz explains that physical distance from her family and the need to describe her background in another language prompted her to look again at people close to her and to train her eye*2. Migration enters the work less as an abstract theme than as a practical condition of photographing: whom she looks at from what distance, and what must be explained before an experience can be shared.

Choosing Photography to Look Precisely

Ruiz has said that she chose photography because she wants to show what she sees as precisely and concretely as possible. She gives priority to looking closely at the people and things in front of her and retaining their differences in the photograph, rather than transforming reality through special effects or elaborate staging*2.

In an interview with FotoTazo, Ruiz likewise recalls that everyday life in Bogotá suddenly looked new after she moved to Switzerland, leading her to photograph family, friends, and interiors*3. Distance from home made her attentive to furniture, colors, clothing, and food that she might previously have passed over.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Bogotá D.C.—Reading Urban Class Through Domestic Interiors

In Bogotá D.C., Ruiz photographed the interiors and exteriors of homes without their residents, avoiding portraits as stand-ins for Bogotá’s social classes. She explains that she used natural light and a medium-format camera and organized 120 images—beds, living rooms, façades, front and back gardens, diplomas—into a grid by social stratum and subject*2. The photobook Bogotá D.C., published by Scheidegger & Spiess, turns differences among homes into a structure for comparison*5.

The distance involved in returning from Switzerland to photograph Bogotá did not lead Ruiz to consolidate home into a nostalgic image. She has said that she is more interested in the present than the past, while recognizing that photographing places that are disappearing may give the images documentary value later*2. The housing photographs in Bogotá D.C. are therefore organized around the furniture, decoration, and architecture of a particular moment instead of one symbolic image of belonging.

In a 2011 essay, Santiago Rueda Fajardo notes that Ruiz’s work can at times display a deliberately constructed banality, while praising Bogotá D.C. for its curious observation of the urban environment and its ability to find strangeness in ordinary life. His observation that the publishing environment for photobooks in Colombia was itself limited at the time also helps clarify the significance of organizing domestic interiors as a comparative sequence in a book. *21

Kleine Fotoenzyklopädie—A Book of Personal Classification

Kleine Fotoenzyklopädie gathers photographs of architecture, art, society, food, and nature made while traveling and edits 645 images into a private system of classification. Flowers, domestic decoration, potatoes, corn, and sweets become entries within the same body of knowledge*7.

Ruiz has said that she carried out as much of the process as possible herself, from shooting and layout to offset printing, in order to give digital photographs a more tactile material presence*8. The encyclopedic form does not claim comprehensive authority; it becomes a small editorial device that openly shows what the artist chooses to place together.

WorldCat records Kleine Fotoenzyklopädie as a 2015 publication containing 645 photographs. The large number of images is not used to claim completeness. It creates enough repetition to test how personal categories such as “fruit,” “furniture,” and “travel” differ from the supposedly objective knowledge system of an encyclopedia. *23

Cutting and Reprinting—NY Apples and Pears

NY Apples and Pears is a publication made by reprinting photographs of apples and pears shot in New York State, cutting them out, and rearranging them into new still-life compositions. Ruiz describes the process of reprinting the photographs, cutting out their forms, and recombining them*2. Published by Kodoji Press in 2017, the book contains eleven black-and-white images across twenty pages*9.

Perimeter notes that the repetition of fruit creates a classificatory, pop-like surface and also connects to the verbal association between New York and the “Big Apple”*10. Ruiz does not leave the apples and pears as straightforward catalog images. She prints them, cuts around their outlines, and places them onto new pages. Fruit that had been one category within Kleine Fotoenzyklopädie becomes the material for a new still life made from printed photographs.

Making Family Time into a Book for Her Child

In Lupita, je garde un abricot…, Ruiz edited photographs and writing about her native Bogotá into a book addressed to her son, who is growing up in Switzerland*11. Because he did not experience the same Bogotá in the same period, the book avoids the continuity of a conventional family album and instead passes on fragments of streets, objects, and memory through words and photographs. The book brings a mother’s memory and a child’s unexperienced place onto the same pages.

In the 2025 project El Libro ilustrado / The Picture Book and the exhibition Consuelo, Ruiz combined staged images made at home, analog photographs of her son accumulated over many years, and various collected images in a single book*12. The home appears as a place of making where knowledge passes between generations through photography, embroidery, reading, and workshops.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Petit Suisse—Typologizing a Child’s Constructions

Petit Suisse records small sculptures made by Ruiz’s son from materials close at hand, using a consistent photographic procedure. Images Vevey describes the constructions as metaphors for contemporary Swiss society and reads the child’s ability to combine several origins more naturally than the artist herself*13.

The constructions are temporary objects made at home, but in Petit Suisse each is photographed individually in the studio and becomes part of a comparable series. Images Vevey describes the project as Ruiz photographing her son’s constructions “like real artworks,” recording the creativity of early childhood*13.

ECAL also presented Petit Suisse at Festival Images Vevey as a series born from Ruiz’s relationship with her son. Together with the fact that she graduated from ECAL in 2002, this establishes a path from her photographic education in Switzerland to the typological treatment of objects produced daily within the home. *22

Photojournalism and the Documentary Value Images Acquire Later

As a student, Ruiz photographed daily life around the FARC in the demilitarized zone for San Vicente del Caguán. She has said that questions of permission and withdrawal, danger, and uncertainty about her position as a reporter led her to leave the material unedited for years and later self-publish it as a historical document*15.

Nada Es Eterno (Oodee, 2014) is a limited twenty-eight-page publication concerned with family representation. Oodee describes Ruiz photographing members of her family in everyday situations while addressing identity, social representation, and stereotypes surrounding family*6. The subject differs from the reporting context of San Vicente del Caguán, yet both works show how the moment and form of publication shape the meaning of photographic material.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Recent Work on Reproduction and Cultural Translation

In the 2025 exhibition Consuelo, photographs appeared alongside furniture, household objects, and collected material. Art Viewer’s installation documentation shows that Ruiz’s recent work has expanded beyond the photobook into installations that include reproduced objects and items from domestic life*17.

Ruiz was selected as a winner of the 2025 Swiss Art Awards*14. FHNW published the jury’s account, describing her sustained engagement with exchange, imitation, translation, appropriation, and reproduction, and relating those concerns to her experience of migration*18. From Bogotá D.C. to her recent work, the recurring question is concrete: what happens to the use and reading of a photograph or object when it passes into another country, page, or generation.

Using Photobooks to Compare Distant Places and Generations

Recent exhibition records also trace a movement from a photobook-centered practice toward installation. Contemporary Art Library documents a 2019 group exhibition and the 2025 exhibition Consuelo*16. AICA Switzerland discussed the 2025 presentation as a small retrospective linking early and recent works and highlighted questions of migration, reproduction, and collecting*19.

Photography Now records Bogotá D.C. as a solo exhibition at Centre de la Photographie Genève in 2004, followed by I feel it all at the same institution in 2007. The circulation of Ruiz’s work across photography centers, publishers, and festivals corresponds to a practice in which the photobook has remained a major form of presentation. *4

As ArtNexus’s feature on Colombian photobooks suggests, Ruiz’s work belongs to both Latin American photobook culture and the contemporary-art and publishing environment of Switzerland*20. Bogotá D.C. uses a sequence of different domestic interiors to show class distinctions within a city; Kleine Fotoenzyklopädie divides 645 images into private categories; NY Apples and Pears isolates fruit from that system and physically recuts the printed images. The three books do different jobs: comparing housing, constructing a private encyclopedia, and reworking the printed photograph.

Placed chronologically, the three books also show a change in what publication does. Bogotá D.C. compares 120 photographs across a grid of social strata and subjects. Kleine Fotoenzyklopädie divides 645 travel photographs into personal categories. In NY Apples and Pears, one category already printed in a book is reprinted and cut apart to become material for another work. Publication becomes the place where each project establishes its own rules of comparison, classification, or reworking.

gursky.html.lead_html: Andreas Gursky moved from early photographs of people at ski resorts and riverbanks to ports, stock exchanges, discount stores, apartment blocks, and factories. From distant viewpoints and through digital editing, he assembled arrangements of people, commodities, architecture, and information that no single position could encompass, presenting them as prints several meters wide. Salerno, 99 Cent, and Rhein II show how the descriptive precision he learned from Bernd and Hilla Becher became a means of addressing globalized space, the relationship between photography and painting, the contemporary sublime, and the risk that capitalism itself may be transformed into spectacle.
gursky.html.thesis_html: Gursky made spaces that could not be surveyed from one position or exposure legible within a single photograph, using multiple exposures, stitching, deletion, and adjusted perspective. His prints of ports, exchanges, discount stores, and apartment blocks reveal, from a distance, the structures that move people and objects; at close range, they disclose differences among individual figures and commodities. He retained photography’s descriptive detail while making large quantities of information about contemporary society comparable within one image.
