sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
From Engineering to Photography

Hiromi Tsuchida graduated from the Faculty of Engineering at Fukui University, then studied in the evening program at the Tokyo College of Photography while working at a Pola Cosmetics research laboratory. He left the company in 1971 to become a full-time photographer.*12 He has recalled candidly that photography initially seemed easier to enter than painting because pressing the shutter at least produced an image.*11 What kept him with photography, however, was the opposite experience. Photographs did not come back as he had imagined or as he thought he had seen; the discrepancy made him realize “how little I actually see,” and that discovery interested him.*11 Comparing what he believed he had seen with what the photograph actually contained became a reason to keep working with the medium.

High-Speed Growth and Zokushin

Tsuchida came into his own as a photographer in the 1970s, a period he describes both as “political” and as one of intense economic change, when Japanese society as a whole was moving toward “discarding the past.”*1 As urban capital and ways of life spread into regional Japan during the years of high-speed growth, the differences between city and countryside narrowed quickly. Tsuchida deliberately moved against that current, turning to local festivals and communities in order to reconsider the culture and environment that had formed him. SFMOMA likewise places Zokushin within a search for ways of life not yet fully homogenized by capital flowing out from the cities, while noting that the photographs also register signs of tourism beginning to flatten the difference between urban and rural Japan.*13 Tsuchida did not point his camera toward an “old Japan” simply to preserve vanishing customs. He wanted to see what was being discarded as Japan changed rapidly, through bodies, clothing, festivals, and gestures that still remained.

Autistic Space and the “Failed” Photograph

In Autistic Space, which received the Taiyo Award in 1971, Tsuchida says that among the many negatives he made in Asakusa he deliberately selected photographs he considered “failures.” Frustrated by the straightforward documentary quality of pictures that were properly exposed and focused, he wanted his own interpretation to remain visible in the image.*11 The approach continued into Zokushin, but Tsuchida later recalled that as he intensified missed focus and blur, he cast a “net” of his own image over the subject until the subject’s reality itself began to disappear.*11 In the Hiroshima work that began alongside this impasse, he made what he called a “180-degree” turn: he subdued his own taste and gave greater priority to the camera’s capacity to record.*11 The frontal clarity of his later photographs of people and objects in Hiroshima did not grow from an original faith in “objective photography.” It was a method he chose after deciding that an overemphasis on his own style through blur and missed focus had made the subject itself harder to see.

Koen Shigemori and PROVOKE

At the Tokyo College of Photography, Tsuchida studied under the critic Koen Shigemori. He recalls that because Shigemori explicitly criticized PROVOKE, the students felt that they had already “gone beyond” it.*11 At the same time, Tsuchida acknowledges that the 1960s and 1970s were years in which established forms and institutions were being challenged in both politics and photography, and that he worked on “the same kind of ground” as the circle around PROVOKE.*11 MoMA’s 1974 exhibition New Japanese Photography included Tsuchida alongside Daido Moriyama, Shomei Tomatsu, Kikuji Kawada, Masatoshi Naito, and others.*15 Tsuchida’s later direction, however, was not to intensify the force of a rough photographic surface. After using blur and missed focus in Autistic Space and Zokushin to inscribe his own way of seeing, he concluded that his manner could instead obscure the subject. In Hiroshima he reversed course, photographing the subject frontally and clearly and supplying the necessary past through text. The visual manner he had intensified in Autistic Space and Zokushin became something he deliberately suppressed in Hiroshima.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Zokushin

Tsuchida began photographing Zokushin around Japan in 1968, but the series is not an ethnographic catalog of festivals and folk beliefs.*10 He has explained that although he initially intended to photograph rituals, his interest gradually shifted toward the participants themselves.*1 When the camera is raised, people smile, pose, and sometimes perform more emphatically. Tsuchida kept those reactions in the picture. The photograph therefore contains not just an inherited form of festival but also a person in the present who smiles, braces, or performs because a camera is there. In the Smithsonian’s Entertainer, Asakusa, from Zokushin, the figure’s gesture does not remain still as an ethnographic specimen; it comes forward as a response to being photographed.*4

Counting Grains of Sand

In Zokushin, Tsuchida kept people who performed back to the camera. In Counting Grains of Sand, he did almost the opposite: he kept photographing until no one in the crowd was looking at him. He has described using a wide-angle lens, refusing to fix attention on a single face or event, seeing the whole frame as a “plane” rather than a collection of “points,” and allowing the camera to record things he had not consciously noticed.*7 He continued releasing the shutter until the group broke apart, then chose photographs in which the photographer’s presence had been ignored. The aim was to let the camera register arrangements of people that his own field of vision could not apprehend at once. SFMOMA describes the book as moving from a few scattered figures toward crowds that fill the frame, culminating in people gathered in front of the Imperial Palace after the death of Emperor Hirohito in 1989.*2 The method of photographing reactions to the camera in Zokushin and the method of waiting until the camera has been forgotten in Counting Grains of Sand are nearly opposite approaches within the work of the same photographer.

Turning toward Hiroshima

By the time Tsuchida turned toward Hiroshima, Japanese photography already included Ken Domon’s records centered on hibakusha, the personal and symbolic imagery Shomei Tomatsu developed in 11:02 Nagasaki, and Kenji Ishiguro’s Hiroshima Now, which approached the past from the present. A research bulletin from the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum notes that Tsuchida was deeply affected by Tomatsu’s work as a student, yet by the time he approached Hiroshima he had decided that foregrounding self-expression was inappropriate there; Ishiguro also provided a concrete methodological cue.*20 Tsuchida himself has said that the atomic bombing was an event without precedent in human history and that, as a documentarian working in Japan, he could not accept simply turning away from it.*25 His answer was not to search for faces more tragic or scars more severe than those photographed by earlier artists. He photographed hibakusha as they wished to appear in the present, returned to the same places, and photographed surviving objects one by one from the front with their histories attached. People, places, and objects were not forced into a single style; each received a different method of record.

Photographing Hibakusha

For Hiroshima 1945–1979, Tsuchida photographed 107 hibakusha without concentrating the tragedy of the bombing in their faces. In an Art21 interview, he explains that he accepted, as far as possible, the places and activities his subjects requested—at work, in a garden, dancing—and photographed them as people living in the present.*25 When someone refused to be photographed, he did not force a portrait. In some cases he photographed the surrounding landscape or objects instead and reported the fact that permission had been refused.*11 Tsuchida did not conceal the “person he could not photograph” as a missing number. The refusal itself entered the record, undermining the assumption that a photographer is entitled to photograph anyone he chooses.

Hiroshima Collection

In discussing Hiroshima Collection, Tsuchida states his premise plainly: “photography can only photograph the present.”*21 In 1982, a camera could record the form a scorched dress or melted bottle had at that moment. The surface of the object could not reveal who held it on August 6, 1945, or what happened afterward. Tsuchida therefore gave equal weight within the work to the photograph of the surviving object and a written account of its owner’s experience.*25 The viewer looks at the object, reads the text, then returns to the object. Tsuchida has also said that he felt a need to photograph these things “beautifully,” so that they would first attract attention as everyday objects instead of being staged solely as images of horror.*25 He did not make the photograph reenact 1945. The photograph carries the object as it exists in the present; the text carries what that object passed through in 1945.

The text is not simply a transcription of the museum’s existing caption. Tsuchida reads donation interviews and archival material, then edits lengthy records into a form that can be read alongside the photograph, deciding what to retain, what to remove, and in what order.*21 When the donor and date of donation are included, the reader can also see whether an object remained with a bereaved family for decades or when the owner eventually entrusted it to the museum. The photograph presents the surviving object in the present; the written account presents the event of 1945; the donation information records the time the object passed through before entering the museum.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Zokushin, 1968–75

In Zokushin, Tsuchida photographed festivals, banquets, and entertainment districts while preserving the gestures and expressions people directed toward the camera. He later recalled that being photographed made his subjects more expressive, and that those responses mattered to him.*1 Ethnographic photography often minimizes the photographer’s presence in order to classify its subject from outside. Zokushin instead allows the act of photographing to alter what happens in front of the camera. The person holding the camera changes the other person’s gesture, and that change enters the photograph. This differs sharply from the later Hiroshima work, where Tsuchida tried to suppress his own stylistic habits as much as possible.

Counting Grains of Sand, 1975–89

Counting Grains of Sand gathers crowds from different cities and events into a single book, sequencing them from sparsely populated frames toward mass gatherings. The Smithsonian’s Tokyo, 1981, from Counting Grains of Sand is meant to be seen in relation to the other crowd photographs rather than isolated as a single “great moment.”*5 The book ultimately arrives at the enormous crowd outside the Imperial Palace after Emperor Hirohito’s death in 1989; individual faces that can still be followed near the beginning become increasingly difficult to distinguish by the end.*2 In the later New Counting Grains of Sand, Tsuchida went further by digitally inserting himself—the person who had stood behind the camera—into photographs of crowds. He described the contradiction as a way to expose how readily viewers treat whatever appears in a photograph as “a fact that was there at the scene.”*7

Hiroshima and Monument

Within the Hiroshima Trilogy, the people-centered Hiroshima 1945–1979 was extended in 2005 when Tsuchida revisited hibakusha he had photographed in the 1970s, making new portraits of the same people roughly thirty years later. The Yokohama Museum of Art holds Declined, from Hiroshima 1945–1979/2005, which records a refusal to be photographed, as a work in the series.*22 In Hiroshima Monument, he returned at intervals of roughly a decade to buildings, trees, and other sites that remained in the city, photographing the same places again. Aging appears in faces; buildings undergo preservation and repair; the city around them is rebuilt. People, structures, and the city do not change at the same rate even though all trace back to the same bombing. Tsuchida places earlier and later photographs together, allowing the difference between the two images to show the change.

Hiroshima Collection, 1982–

Hiroshima Collection began in 1982 with photographs of atomic-bomb materials in the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and has grown over more than forty years to roughly four hundred objects.*8 The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum holds a photograph of Dress*16 and also publishes images of Fountain Pen*17 and Melted Sake Bottles, all photographed frontally as individual everyday objects within the same series.*18 The texts Tsuchida adds are not copied from the museum’s short labels. He reads donation interviews and supporting material, then edits them himself into a length that can be read together with the photograph. He has said that he spends about as much time on the writing as on the photography.*21 When new objects enter the collection, he photographs them; when he learns more about an owner or the circumstances of a donation, he revises the text. Across more than four decades, choosing which part of the past to preserve in words has become part of the work alongside the act of photographing.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photo History
sections.body_html:
International Reassessment of Hiroshima

Tsuchida’s Hiroshima Trilogy does not photograph the instant of the atomic bombing or its immediate aftermath. It photographs people roughly thirty years after the bombing, places from 1979 onward, and surviving objects from 1982 onward. The 2014–15 international exhibition Conflict, Time, Photography organized war photography not by nation or conflict but by the interval between an event and the making of the photograph—minutes, years, decades—and placed Ken Domon, Shomei Tomatsu, Kikuji Kawada, and Tsuchida on the same temporal axis as Don McCullin, Susan Meiselas, Sophie Ristelhueber, Taryn Simon, and others.*23 Tsuchida was thus positioned not as a photographer who witnessed 1945, but as one who photographed the people, places, and objects that remained decades later. His work entered the exhibition as photography of what survives long after war, not photography of the instant of war itself. An earlier milestone in this reassessment was the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s 2007–08 retrospective, which brought together Zokushin, Counting Grains of Sand, and the Hiroshima Trilogy, tracing both “self-expression” and “thorough documentation” across his work.*3

From MoMA in 1974 to ICP in 1979

Yoshiaki Kai’s study of the reception of MoMA’s 1974 New Japanese Photography notes that Tsuchida and Masatoshi Naito were positioned within a group associated with regional folk customs and traditional religion.*24 Zokushin grew from a question about high-speed economic growth homogenizing regional culture, yet abroad it could also be read as evidence of a “traditional Japan” that still survived. Five years later, in ICP’s Japan: A Self-Portrait, Tsuchida appeared through Children of Hiroshima: 33 Years Later, which combined photographs and interviews with hibakusha.*9 The same photographer was presented at MoMA in 1974 as a photographer of Japanese festivals and folk culture and at ICP in 1979 as a photographer of hibakusha thirty-three years after the atomic bombing. The two exhibitions framed different versions of “Japan” through the same photographer.

A 1987 U.S. Review

Tsuchida’s restrained approach did not always persuade critics. Reviewing a 1987 U.S. exhibition titled Hiroshima, the Los Angeles Times argued that graphic film footage of atomic-bomb injuries shown in the gallery overwhelmed Tsuchida’s quiet photographs and split the exhibition’s message.*14 The same review, however, singled out the frontal, precise photographs of objects from the museum and the written histories attached to them as among the exhibition’s strongest sections.*14 The same refusal to dramatize suffering could appear weak beside moving images yet work forcefully when viewers spent time with one object and one person’s history. Both sides of that problem were already visible in U.S. criticism at the time.

The Difference from Miyako Ishiuchi

Getty exhibition materials note that Miyako Ishiuchi, who began photographing clothing and objects belonging to hibakusha after 2007, knew the earlier work of Shomei Tomatsu and Tsuchida and deliberately chose a different method.*19 Shuichi Tsukada’s research contrasts the two approaches to time. He describes Tsuchida’s Hiroshima Collection as a method of resisting the erosion of memory by recording objects together with their histories as people and the city change, whereas in hiroshima, Ishiuchi photographs aging garments as objects that exist “now” and greatly reduces the amount of detailed information attached to them.*6 Even when photographing objects from the same museum, Tsuchida preserves in writing “whose object it was and what happened in 1945.” Ishiuchi, by contrast, shows the discolored and damaged clothing itself as it exists in the present.

The Carnegie International

At the 58th Carnegie International in 2022, twenty-nine works from Hiroshima Collection were shown, the largest presentation of the series in a U.S. museum to that point. A research bulletin from the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum records that the series played an important role in the exhibition and was repeatedly identified as a highlight in press reviews.*20 With twenty-nine photographs and accompanying texts shown together, international audiences encountered the project through the accumulated quantity of images and records made by the same method, not through a single representative photograph.

related_annotations./en/photographers/keizo-kitajima.html: A contemporary who also worked with Japanese society after the 1970s. Kitajima published photographs in the month he made them and used close-range flash on the street; Tsuchida returned to the same people and places years later.
related_annotations./en/movements/documentary.html: Tsuchida expanded the time of documentation beyond a single encounter by rephotographing hibakusha and places and by joining photographs of surviving objects to written records.

hiroshi-sugimoto.html.lead_html: Hiroshi Sugimoto (1948–) was born in Tokyo. He moved to the United States in 1970 and began making photographs from a New York base in 1974. In series including Dioramas, Theaters, Seascapes, Portraits, Architecture, and Lightning Fields, he has subjected museum displays, movie theaters, the sea, wax figures, architecture, and electricity to different photographic conditions, examining how photography constructs time and the appearance of reality. He employs a large-format camera, long exposures, deliberate manipulation of focus, and camera-less techniques according to the demands of each series.
hiroshi-sugimoto.html.thesis_html: Photography is often understood as a medium that faithfully preserves reality. Hiroshi Sugimoto, however, photographs subjects whose appearance has already been designed—museum dioramas, movie theaters, the sea, wax figures, and architecture—and makes the conditions under which an image appears real the substance of his work. His specific shift was from photography as a record of its subject to photography that examines how time, systems of display, light, and memory produce a sense of reality. In Theaters, he accumulates the duration of an entire film in a single image; in Architecture, he deliberately defocuses the 8 × 10 camera ordinarily used for precise description; and in Lightning Fields, he removes the camera and allows electricity to act directly on film. This practice matters because it does not separate conceptual inquiry from the accomplished craft of gelatin silver photography. It brought a central question into contemporary art: not what a photograph depicts, but under what conditions it becomes an image.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Hiroshi Sugimoto’s Career and Move to New York

Hiroshi Sugimoto was born in Tokyo in 1948. He moved to the United States in 1970 and began working between New York and Japan in 1974. A key point in understanding his early work is that he treated photography as a mode of production encompassing exposure, development, and printing. An exhibition at the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, identifies gelatin silver photography as the origin of Sugimoto’s art and includes production notes dating from the late 1970s as materials documenting his shooting and developing procedures*1. His major early series include Dioramas, photographs of displays in natural history museums; Theaters, which condenses the running time of a film onto a single screen; and Seascapes, with its repeated horizons between sea and sky. The National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, groups these three series in a chapter titled “Time, Light and Memory,” showing that these themes entered Sugimoto’s work at an early stage*1. Polar Bear (1976), the first work in Dioramas, is listed on MoMA’s official collection page as an acquired work, object number 287.1977*2. Sugimoto presented Movie Theaters at Sonnabend Gallery in New York in 1981. In 1988, Dioramas, Theatres, and Seascapes traveled in New York and Tokyo, followed by an exhibition of the same name at the National Museum of Art, Osaka, in 1989*3. Since the 2000s, exhibitions including End of Time at Mori Art Museum, Étant donné: Le Grand Verre at Fondation Cartier, Black Box, organized by Fundación MAPFRE and Foam, and Time Machine, which traveled to Hayward Gallery, UCCA, and MCA Australia, have presented him as an artist whose work crosses photography, scientific models, architecture, antiquities, and the performing arts*3.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Dioramas and Photographic Verisimilitude

Dioramas, Sugimoto’s point of departure, is a series depicting displays in natural history museums. It makes the artificial nature constructed from taxidermied animals, painted backdrops, and exhibition lighting appear real within the photograph. The series arose from Sugimoto’s visit to the American Museum of Natural History in 1974, when he discovered that a display of taxidermied animals against a painted background suddenly looked real when seen with one eye*4. Photography here acts as an apparatus that makes an artificial object appear real. Taxidermy, painted scenery, display lighting, the museum’s taxonomic presentation, monocular perspective, and the detailed rendering of a large-format camera converge on the photographic surface to create a lifelike image of animals that were never present in the depicted scene. MoMA lists Polar Bear as a 1976 gelatin silver print, providing an official collection record for a defining work from Dioramas*2. In this series, the photograph turns the museum’s model of nature into a still more convincing scene. Sugimoto photographs the mechanism by which nature is made to look real more than nature itself.

Theaters and Long Exposure

In Theaters, an entire film projected on a movie screen is transformed through a single long exposure into a luminous white plane. Sugimoto has said that while photographing in natural history museums, he asked himself what would happen if he photographed a whole movie in one frame. He opened the shutter as the film began and closed it two hours later, producing a glowing white screen*5. The light illuminates the theater interior, usually submerged in darkness, bringing the screen, seats, ceiling, and wall ornament into a single photograph. The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s account of Avalon Theatre, Catalina Island likewise explains that the light of the projected film makes the theater interior visible*6. The series centers on how the duration of a screening remains on the photographic surface, rather than on plot or characters. MoMA lists U.A. Walker, New York as a gelatin silver print dated February 23, 1978*7. The work departs from the idea of photography as the capture of a decisive moment: it accumulates the duration of a screening as a quantity of light, which in turn records the architectural space.

Stefano Baschiera discusses Theaters as photographic work that makes visible the cinematic apparatus itself—screen, projection, architecture, seating, and running time—not simply as photographs made by exposing a whole film. When a film is compressed into a single image as the average of roughly 170,000 frames, narrative and actors disappear, leaving only the light and theatrical space that make cinema possible*38. Theaters thus uses the photograph’s long exposure to demonstrate in reverse that cinema is an apparatus through which time unfolds.

Seascapes and the Horizon

Seascapes repeats a composition divided almost equally between sea and sky at locations around the world, presenting both geographical difference and the nearly unchanging experience of the horizon. Sugimoto regards water and air as conditions of life and has said that whenever he sees the sea, he feels the reassurance of visiting his ancestral home and embarks on a “journey of seeing”*8. In light of this statement, what matters in Seascapes is the sustained observation, under consistent conditions, of the horizon where water, air, and light meet, more than the landscape information of each site. The seascapes presented as Time Exposed were made between 1980 and 1991. Addressing changes at the point where sky and sea meet, they were exhibited concurrently at the Carnegie Museum of Art and IBM Courtyard in Japan in 1991*9. By photographing seas around the world in the same horizon format, place names, dates, weather, and gradations of light remain as comparable differences within a single pictorial structure. Although its title identifies a particular sea, the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Ligurian Sea, Saviore foregrounds the horizon, tonal gradation, and quality of light over geographical information*10. The repetition in Seascapes shows that even when the sea is reduced to horizon, tone, and light, viewers still recognize it as sea. Each image superimposes a record of place and an abstract composition.

Portraits and Historical Portraiture

In Portraits, Sugimoto turns the self-evident impossibility of directly photographing historical figures into a photographic problem by photographing wax figures. The series layers Holbein’s portrait of Henry VIII, the wax figure at Madame Tussauds, Sugimoto’s own study of Renaissance lighting, and photography as a surrogate means of record. Sugimoto explains that if the depicted figure appears alive, we should reconsider what it means to be alive*11. The Guggenheim Museum Bilbao’s exhibition page explains that the series began with a commission from Deutsche Guggenheim and presented historical figures against black backgrounds with dramatic lighting in near-life-size black-and-white portraits*12. Their appearance of authenticity arises from the combination of royal portraiture, the wax museum’s reconstruction, black backgrounds and dramatic lighting, and the precision of gelatin silver prints. As the figure passes from painting to waxwork and from waxwork to photograph, the historical face emerges as an image constructed through several media.

Conceptual Forms, Opticks, and Lightning Fields

In Sugimoto’s later series, photography extends to mathematics, the history of science, and optics. Conceptual Forms depicts German mathematical and mechanical models from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries preserved at the University of Tokyo, treating mathematical lines, zero, and infinity as human inventions rather than discoveries*13. The photographs record visible objects while addressing the equations and conceptual forms behind them. In Fondation Cartier’s exhibition Étant donné: Le Grand Verre, the series was divided into mathematical and mechanical forms and presented in a spatial arrangement relating it to Duchamp’s The Large Glass*14. For Opticks, Sugimoto drew on Newton’s prism experiments and Goethe’s theory of color. He explains that he used nearly obsolete Polaroid film to photograph color not only as the seven colors into which natural science divided it, but also as the difficult-to-name hues between them*15. In Lightning Fields, his interest in Franklin, Faraday, and Talbot led him to apply electrical discharges to photographic plates, reenacting discoveries from the history of science in the darkroom so that he could verify them with his own eyes*16. Photography here renders as images not just the surfaces of objects, but ordinarily invisible conditions such as mathematical hypotheses, the division of light, and traces of electricity.

Why Sugimoto Chose Photography

Each of Sugimoto’s series begins with a predetermined photographic procedure. Methods such as photographing an entire film in one image, repeatedly photographing the boundary between sea and sky in the same composition, or portraying wax figures as historical people become visible images through exposure time, the large-format camera, darkroom work, the tonal range of gelatin silver prints, and the scale of the exhibition space. The National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, identifies the increasingly endangered medium of gelatin silver photography as the origin of Sugimoto’s art because the procedures from shooting through developing and printing cannot be separated from the appearance of the work*1. Sugimoto’s own remarks also show how closely this method is bound to his interest in time. In an interview with Time Sensitive, he describes fossils as records of time from millions of years ago and speaks of his interest in how his personal history, human history, and the history of life began*17. He further connects the acquisition of a sense of time to the beginning of human consciousness and explains that he uses the camera to investigate this curiosity*17. In the same conversation, he says that handling fossils and stone tools evokes a sense of tracing the memory of human existence, rather than personal memory*17. His interest in time can therefore be understood as a question about tracing the beginnings of life, human toolmaking, and consciousness through present bodily experience, rather than as nostalgic recollection. It directly shapes the form of each series. In the same interview, Sugimoto says that the camera works as a time machine for examining the past; that the duration of a film returns to white light in Theaters; and that in Seascapes, he sometimes stops time and at other times lets it flow to see what appears on the film*17. He also explains that his experience of an artificial display appearing real when seen with one eye and stripped of depth led to the monocular camera and the use of a large-format camera in Dioramas*17. In Art21, Sugimoto similarly treats fossils as records of time and history and describes photography as the “fossilization of time”*18. For Sugimoto, photography is thus a means of addressing how time remains in matter, how light becomes an image, and under what conditions memory and history return on a present surface. In Theaters, screening time and projected light accumulate on a white screen; in Seascapes, the horizon where water, air, and light meet is repeated; and in Dioramas and Portraits, display, wax, lighting, and the camera’s descriptive power make constructed things appear real. UCCA explains that Sugimoto’s work raises questions about time and memory, the medium’s ambiguity between record and creation, and the nature of photography itself*19. Fraenkel Gallery likewise describes his work as addressing time, empiricism, and metaphysics, and as using classical photographic techniques to explore how photography can record traces of invisible forces*20. This work overlaps with artistic developments since the 1960s in which photography began to examine its own conditions. The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Photography on Photography: Reflections on the Medium since 1960 explains that photography—mechanically reproduced and distributed throughout culture in printed matter, passports, and photo booths—became a means for artists to consider the medium itself after the 1960s*21. The Met attributes the attention given to Sugimoto and James Welling amid the rise of digital imaging to their early combination of an interest in conceptualism with close attention to the material basis of analog photography*21. In Sugimoto’s case, the effort to make time, memory, and light into works of art brings exposure, film, the darkroom, the print, and the exhibition space itself to the fore, revealing photography’s ability to accumulate time, create verisimilitude, and leave images of what cannot ordinarily be seen.

sections.title: Major works, method, and medium
sections.body_html:
Starting Dates and Photographic Methods of the Major Series

Dioramas began in 1976, transforming natural history museum displays into photographs with a large-format camera and long exposures*4. Theaters began in 1978; Sugimoto kept the shutter open throughout an entire film, accumulating the image on the screen as white light*5. Beginning in 1980, Seascapes repeated a composition bisected by the horizon into sea and sky*32. From 1997, Architecture employed deliberate defocusing, while from 2006, Lightning Fields subjected photosensitive material directly to high voltage*33. Sugimoto’s methods should therefore not all be grouped under “long exposure”; the distinct conditions of camera, exposure, focus, and camera-less production must be considered series by series*35.

FIG. 01 — Polar Bear, 1976 (Dioramas)

The first work in Dioramas, made in 1976, depicts a diorama at the American Museum of Natural History. MoMA holds it as a gelatin silver print, object number 287.1977*2. It arose from Sugimoto’s experience of seeing a display of taxidermied animals against a painted background suddenly appear real when viewed with one eye*4. The work first embodied the method of Dioramas, in which photography turns a museum’s model of reconstructed nature into a still more convincing scene.

FIG. 02 — U.A. Walker, New York, 1978 / Avalon Theatre, Catalina Island (Theaters)

These are two defining works from Theaters. MoMA holds U.A. Walker, New York as a gelatin silver print dated February 23, 1978*7. A single long exposure transforms the full running time of a film into a luminous white plane, whose light brings the theater’s seats, ceiling, and wall ornament into a single image. The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s account of Avalon Theatre, Catalina Island likewise confirms that the light of the projected film makes the theater interior visible*6.

FIG. 03 — Ligurian Sea, Saviore (Seascapes)

The Metropolitan Museum of Art holds this photograph as one of the representative works of Seascapes*10. Although its title names a specific sea, the image foregrounds the horizon, tonal gradation, and quality of light over geographical information. It embodies the series’ repetition of the same horizon composition across seas around the world, layering a record of place and an abstract composition within one image.

FIG. 04 — Portraits—Re-Portraying Historical Figures

This series portrays wax figures of historical people. It began with a commission from Deutsche Guggenheim and presents a wax figure based on Holbein’s portrait of Henry VIII against a black background with dramatic lighting, in a near-life-size black-and-white portrait*12. Sugimoto’s statement that if the depicted person looks alive, we should reconsider what it means to be alive clarifies the series’ premise*11. By passing the figure from painting to waxwork and from waxwork to photograph, the work makes visible how a historical face emerges through multiple images and media.

Architecture, 1997—Defocusing the 8 × 10 View Camera

In Architecture, Sugimoto photographs modern architecture with an 8 × 10-inch view camera but shifts the focus—described as “twice-infinity”—deliberately blurring the outlines with a large-format camera ordinarily used for exact description. His official website places 1997 examples including World Trade Center and Church of the Light among the series’ earliest works*33. MW Editions likewise describes the series as beginning in 1997 and employing deliberate manipulation of focus with an 8 × 10 view camera, confirming a method that removes details to test whether architecture can persist as a “form” in memory*34.

Lightning Fields, 2006—Recording Electricity Directly on Film

Lightning Fields began in 2006. Sugimoto applies high voltage from a Van de Graaff generator directly to film, turning traces of electric current into images. His official website identifies Lightning Fields 001 as a work from 2006*35. Fraenkel Gallery describes the group as made with electrical charges of 400,000 volts. This is a camera-less process in which electricity acts directly on photosensitive material, rather than an exposure that records the outside world through a lens*36.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Assessments of Photography, Time, and Reality

Critical responses to Sugimoto have emphasized more than the stillness of his black-and-white images and their minimal compositions. They have also addressed his treatment of photographic truth, time, systems of display, and historical memory. His photographs have been read as works that make visible the procedures through which photography produces time and an appearance of reality. The Met places Sugimoto in this context because his photographs neither merely present concepts nor merely preserve classical techniques; they bring both into operation within the same image*21. The white screens of Theaters and the wax figures of Portraits possess a strong sense of reality because the clarity of their ideas cannot be separated from the precision of exposure, development, and printing. This quality kept Sugimoto’s analog photography relevant to contemporary questions as digital images proliferated. His place in the broader field of contemporary art also reflects how often his work has appeared beyond specialist photographic contexts—in museums of contemporary art and in settings concerned with the history of science, architecture, the performing arts, antiquities, and site-specific spatial production. Fraenkel Gallery’s biography describes a career centered on photography since the 1970s that has expanded into architecture, sculpture, performance, and installation while exploring history, temporal existence, empiricism, and metaphysics*20. Museum Brandhorst’s Revolution rotates nocturnal seascapes ninety degrees, turning the horizon into a vertical line. The museum presents the series as a vertical composition recalling Barnett Newman*22. Once a nocturnal seascape is rotated, its horizon becomes a line running vertically through the image, and information about sea and sky appears as a dark plane, a layer of light, and a vertical tension. Through this operation, Sugimoto’s seascapes can be read simultaneously as landscape photographs indicating a site and as abstract images showing relations between line and plane. Benesse Art Site Naoshima relates his work to themes of time, human perception, and the origins of consciousness, as well as to spatial works extending to Go’o Shrine on Naoshima and the Enoura Observatory*23. UCCA presents Time Machine as a retrospective of 127 works in eleven series spanning the previous fifty years, including Seascapes, Theaters, Lightning Fields, and Portraits, and identifies it as an exhibition organized by Hayward Gallery in London*19. The artist profile for Aichi Triennale 2025 names Dioramas, Seascapes, Theaters, Architecture, Portraits, and Conceptual Forms, describing themes that include the compression of time through long exposure and reversals between life and death, reality and fiction, and nature and artifice*24. On the basis of this reception, Sugimoto can be situated beyond the categories of conceptual photography and minimalism as an artist who has moved among museums, cinemas, seas, wax museums, scientific models, optical experiments, and architectural spaces to examine the conditions under which photographs are trusted as records.

Against the conventional idea of photography as a technology for preserving an instant, Susana Santoyo reconsiders photographic time and technique through the examples of Sugimoto and Wolfgang Tillmans. She situates Sugimoto’s work as producing different concepts of time through exposure length and the operation of the apparatus, instead of freezing a single past instant*39. When several hours are compressed into a white screen in Theaters, and seas from different times and places are placed within the same horizon format in Seascapes, time becomes part of the photographic procedure itself, not a theme outside the photograph.

Critical and International Reception in the 1980s and 1990s

The reception of Sugimoto’s work from the late 1980s through the 1990s can be traced not simply through the growing number of solo exhibitions, but through the language critics used to describe it. Sugimoto presented Movie Theaters at Sonnabend Gallery in 1981. In 1988, he showed Dioramas, Theatres, and Seascapes at Sonnabend Gallery in New York and at Sagacho Exhibit Space and Zeit-Foto Salon in Tokyo*3. The National Museum of Art, Osaka’s 1989 exhibition Recent Works 5: Hiroshi Sugimoto introduced thirty-five works from Dioramas, Theaters, and Seascapes to the Kansai region for the first time. Its record notes the attention given to Sugimoto’s precise rendering of space with a large-format camera and his capture of “silent time”*25. Criticism from the period addressed the void beneath appearances, traces of time, and the instability of verisimilitude alongside the beauty of the still images. An Artforum review from 1988 treats Sugimoto’s photographs of the sea, museum dioramas, and theaters as highly specific images with a pronounced stillness*27. The summary of another Artforum review reads the “trace of time” as an instrument for exposing the void beneath appearances*28. These responses show that Sugimoto’s work was received not simply as beautiful black-and-white photography, but as photography that unsettled the certainty of what could be seen. During the 1990s, solo exhibitions at Sonnabend Gallery, Fraenkel Gallery, the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art were accompanied by reviews in the New York Times, Artforum, the Village Voice, the New Yorker, and the Los Angeles Times. Seascapes, Motion Picture, and Still Life became recurring subjects in critical columns as well as the gallery market*26. Later criticism has extended these readings in several directions. Memo Review writes that Dioramas passes as wildlife photography from a distance, while the unnatural painted backgrounds and composite materials become visible at close range and the illusion fractures. It reads Sugimoto’s photographs as folding and stretching time and testing the limits of the medium, as well as “stopping time”*29. While responding favorably to Opticks, The Arts Desk argues that in comparison with abstract painting, the work risks appearing like a scientific experiment because the traces of the hand and emotional density evident on a painted surface are difficult to see*30. Writing in REALKYOTO against the background of photographic materials disappearing with digitization, Akira Asada presents a reading of Sugimoto as the “last photographer.” He frames this less as simple praise than as the position of an artist standing at a point where the material conditions of the photographic medium are approaching their end*31. Sugimoto’s reception has thus developed through critical debates over the construction of verisimilitude, the treatment of time, the boundaries among photography, cinema, museums, wax figures, and scientific experiments, and the end of gelatin silver photography, alongside praise for stillness and technical accomplishment.

At the same time, affirming the quiet of Seascapes solely in terms of universality or spirituality captures only one aspect of its critical history. Joshua Petitto argues that Sugimoto’s “oceanic vision,” while seeking an alternative to modernity and the recovery of religious feeling, also comes into contact with politically regressive ideas in Japanese cultural production of the 1930s and with an aesthetics of death and stasis*37. This argument does not directly identify Sugimoto’s own work with a particular political ideology. It reexamines the meanings that a vocabulary of the horizon, eternity, and a return to the premodern has carried within twentieth-century Japanese intellectual history. This perspective keeps assessments of Sugimoto from ending with praise of his work as “serene and universal.”

iosif-kiraly.html.lead_html: Iosif Király is known for Reconstructions, in which photographs of the same place made on different dates and from different angles are joined while their seams remain visible. This page traces mail art under late socialism, subREAL, Bucharest after 1989, and his architectural education to examine how return and assembly continually alter photographic memory.
iosif-kiraly.html.thesis_html: Reconstructions expands photographic time from one exposure to the extended duration of return and editing. Király revisits the same place, combines film and digital images, mixes focal lengths and date stamps, and leaves overlapping prints and cut edges visible. Architectural alteration, tree growth, changes of political regime, and the photographer’s movement appear within one image, destabilizing unified perspective and a single present. He treats the recorded place and time of each photograph as an “objective fragment,” while making visible how selection and connection construct subjective memory. The political transformation of Romania is not reduced to one emblematic image; it is read through a photographic form in which personal and social memory are repeatedly updated by omission, repetition, and rearrangement.

sections.title: Background and Context
sections.body_html:
Experimental Education and Architecture in Timișoara

In the 1970s, Király studied at a Bauhaus-oriented art school in Timișoara, where he encountered the educational environment of the Sigma group, which connected art, new technologies, and Neo-Constructivism. He later graduated from the architecture institute in Bucharest, worked in architectural practice, and returned to contemporary art through installation, performance, and photography, as he has described in interviews.*1 The spatial awareness and interest in multiple viewpoints developed through architecture became a basis for joining different positions and moments in Reconstructions.

Photography as a Medium for Preserving and Circulating an Action

In Romania during the 1980s, routes for presenting experimental actions publicly and reaching audiences abroad were limited. Király photographed bodily performances and sent the images across borders by mail. In this method, which he calls “performance photography,” the photograph preserves the trace of an action and becomes the work that travels across time and national boundaries.*1 He later said that photographs help him understand more fully what he has experienced.*2 Portability, reproducibility, and the capacity to reread experience later made photography an appropriate medium under conditions of restriction. *3

subREAL and Photography Education after 1989

After the political change of 1989, Király formed subREAL with Călin Dan and took possession of the photographic archive of the discontinued art magazine Arta. By rearranging artwork photographs, installation records, and portraits, the group examined what the socialist art system preserved and what image of the artist it produced.*4 In 1995, Király helped establish the Department of Photography and Dynamic Image at the National University of Arts in Bucharest, participating in the institutional formation of photography as an independent artistic field for studying time, space, and memory.*5

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
Reconstructions: Leaving Different Moments of Exposure Visible at the Seam

The early Reconstructions were assembled by hand from film snapshots. By the late 1990s, Király introduced cameras that recorded date and time within the frame and later added digital processing.*1 Technological change does not serve to erase the seam. It preserves a state in which fragments from different dates assert competing versions of the same space. Overlap, jump, and error remain visible as components of memory.

Assembling Experience and Memory from “Objective Fragments”

Each exposure records a particular place, moment, and focal length. Király calls these “objective fragments,” although the choice of fragments and their points of overlap belong to the photographer. In a conversation published by ARTMargins, the contradiction through which a subjective reality is built from objective photographic pieces is discussed as central to the work.*1 Buildings in Reconstructions break at the seams, a person may appear twice, and shadows cast in different directions cross the same road. The image retains a memory revised through return, selection, and assembly; no single exposure contains the experience intact.

Király’s architectural training appears in the construction of urban space from several parts. Roads, apartment blocks, squares, railways, advertising, and building sites become surfaces affected by shifts in political system and economy. Anca Poterașu Gallery describes Reconstructions as photographic assemblages investigating perception, time, synchronization, and memory.*6 Architecture becomes a historical site altered with every return.

In Eastern Europe during the 1980s, mail art provided an important circuit for sending small works, instructions, and photographs beyond national borders. Király photographed actions because the event could be reproduced and delivered to audiences in another place and time. In the ARTMargins conversation, he also discusses how photography transforms a live experience even as it carries that experience to another audience.*1 Portability and preservation became formal responses to censorship and institutional limitation.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Repeated Photography of the City and Change after 1989

After the transition to a market economy, advertising, construction, demolition, and privatization rapidly changed the streets of Bucharest. Király also participated in research projects such as D-Platform and RO-Archive with architects, artists, and anthropologists, following urban change through several disciplines.*7 The returns of Reconstructions do more than compare a before and an after. They include what the photographer forgot between visits and where he chose to stand when he came back.

The work includes family photographs, the artist’s shadow, and people close to him alongside large-scale urban change. A presentation with Aurora Király at Paris Photo used their two archives to trace the recognition of photography as art during the limited resources and heightened expectations of the 1980s and 1990s.*8 Personal material is not reduced to evidence for national history; it forms points where one person’s memory meets public history.

Continuities among Photography, Collage, and Panorama

Király works with black-and-white and color photography, Polaroids, video, and digital processing without treating older and newer media as a hierarchy of progress. He consistently places different moments beside one another and leaves missing time between images. A photographic collage made between 1986 and 1990 in MoMA’s collection already contains the continuity of viewpoint and breaks in time that later characterize Reconstructions.*9 Even after introducing digital processing, he kept the seams visible and retained the manual boundary as a trace of edited memory.

Layering Several Moments onto the Continuous View of the Panorama

An image joined from several photographs resembles a panorama, but the camera positions and dates differ, and overlap and absence remain. In images reproduced by Anca Poterașu Gallery, lines of buildings break at a boundary, the same person repeats, and the direction of shadows changes midway across the scene.*6 A conventional panorama extends a continuous field from one position. In Reconstructions, the wider the image becomes, the more visible the disagreement among viewpoints and the fact that the whole was made from several visits.

Király’s shadow and traces of the position from which he holds the camera sometimes remain in the photographs. Anca Poterașu Gallery’s account of Letting the Days Go By describes slightly altered angles, fragments carried into the next image, and the artist’s shadow in the background as details through which memory forms.*10 The person who walked, selected, and joined the site is inscribed in the geometry and repetition of the image.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Memory Rewritten with Every Return

For Király, a photograph is an anchor driven into the past and a fragment whose meaning changes as experiences accumulate in the present. Fotofestiwal made the transformation of personal and collective memory through accumulated experience a central theme of a retrospective.*7 Repeated buildings, cars that disappear midway, and people who appear twice across a seam register the entry of present perception into a past scene.

Photography after socialism is often read as evidence of the scars of the former regime or the disorder of market transition. Király’s images contain advertising, construction, demolition, and privatization, but the seams and repetitions prevent the city from dividing cleanly into “before” and “after.” The date of the photographer’s return, the position from which he stood, and the fragments he did not select remain as indications of the partial viewpoint through which history is understood. *7

In the history of photography, the “decisive moment” has provided a powerful norm for the single exposure that captures the essence of an event. Reconstructions brings return, waiting, technological change, and urban alteration into one image, extending photographic time across years. An exhibition at H401 likewise presented this sustained investigation as layers of memory.*11 Later visits continue to enter earlier photographs instead of allowing one instant to remain definitive.

Distinguishing subREAL’s Institutional Critique from Király’s Individual Work

With subREAL, Király and his collaborators jointly critiqued an existing art-photography archive, institutions, and the image of the artist. In the individually authored Reconstructions, the emphasis falls on fragments he photographed and accumulated over time. The two share an interest in archives, but subREAL rearranges a body of images already produced by an art system, while Reconstructions joins a body of images that grows with every return to a place. Reading MNAC’s retrospective material separately from records of Király’s solo exhibitions clarifies the methodological difference between collective institutional critique and individual work on memory.*4

Materials from Art Encounters and Jecza Gallery situate Király’s work across experimental photography under socialism, subREAL, and the urban and mnemonic transformations after 1989.*12*13 In What About Y[Our] Memory, Borrowed Memories, and Constructed Geometries, personal photographs, family memory, urban space, and different moments of exposure overlap, clarifying an understanding of memory as an act of editing inherited material in the present.*14*16*17

Works presented at Paris Photo and on international photography platforms likewise identify seams, repetition, and multiple viewpoints as central to Király’s method.*15*18*19 The recent Ecology of the After Life combines materials marked by demolition or abandonment with photographic archives, expanding memory after political transition from the urban landscape to cycles of remains and disposal.*20

irving-penn.html.lead_html: Irving Penn was a photographer who extended the design intelligence he developed at Vogue into white backgrounds, worn theater curtains, natural light, still lifes, occupational portraits, and platinum-palladium prints. He transformed the clarity required by fashion and advertising into a form attentive to the contours of people and objects, silence, surface, and the texture of photographic paper, quietly rearranging the boundary between commercial and fine-art photography.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Irving Penn was born in 1917 in Plainfield, New Jersey, and studied at the Philadelphia Museum School of Industrial Art from 1934 to 1938. There he worked under Alexey Brodovitch, a Russian-born designer who had moved through Parisian culture of the 1920s and taught modern art and design across magazines, exhibitions, architecture, and photography *1. After assisting Brodovitch and working as an art director, Penn traveled to Mexico in 1941 hoping to become a painter, but grew disappointed with his own canvases, destroyed them, and returned to New York *1. In 1943, Alexander Liberman — also Russian-born and steeped in Parisian publishing culture — hired Penn as the new art director of Vogue, assigning him to develop layouts and cover ideas *1. Liberman saw in Penn's contact sheets from travels an eye that already knew what to look for, and encouraged him to take photographs himself *1. From that point, Penn worked for Vogue for more than sixty years, channeling magazine work, advertising, portraiture, still life, travel portraits, and printmaking into the conditions of the studio: compressed composition, observation of surface, and the gradations available on photographic paper. To call him simply a "refined fashion photographer" obscures the work of binding multiple domains into a single photographic form. The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes Penn's nearly seventy-year career as a spare studio aesthetic defined by composition, nuance, and attention to detail *3. The Smithsonian American Art Museum treats him as an artist who moved across fashion, portraiture, still life, and private studio work — one of the photographers who narrowed the distance between magazine photography and fine-art photography *4.

sections.title: Vogue, Studio Portraits, Still Life, and the Print
sections.body_html:
Not eliminating the background, but creating the conditions of looking

When Penn chose white paper, worn theater curtains, north-facing natural light, and portable tent studios, the purpose was not simply to remove backgrounds — it was to take responsibility himself for how a subject would be seen. In drafts preserved in the Art Institute of Chicago archives, Penn notes that he was often disappointed by photographs that tried to show people in "natural situations." His reasoning is quite specific: he acknowledged that he could not sufficiently accomplish the kind of photography that entered a person's living space and captured the entire environment around them. Instead, he chose a more limited method — separating a person dressed in clothes and accessories from the accidents of daily life, the explanatory background, the story of a place — and facing only "the person themselves" *15. Penn's white backgrounds and makeshift studios were not blank spaces for simplifying the world; they were devices for reducing excess explanation so that posture, the texture of clothing, hands, face, tools, and the concentration of a gaze could remain. The north-facing natural light studio rented in Cusco in 1948, the later tent studios, the warehouses and barns converted into shooting spaces — these were realizations of that idea in actual places *15. Penn believed that when a subject crossed the threshold of the studio, they stepped slightly away from the community's everyday behavior, concentrated on the experience of being seen by a stranger, and took on a dignity and focus difficult to achieve outdoors *15. He described the tent studio as a place belonging neither to the subject nor to himself — a middle space — and said it was precisely in this space that neither party fully belonged that contact could occur *15. At MoMA's 1950 symposium "What is Modern Photography?," Penn stated that modern photographers were conscious of their work being seen in brief time, and had acquired an "economy of means" like graphic artists *16. Penn's sparseness of background connects to this "economy of means" — placing people, clothing, tools, skin, and paper tones in the same light and at the same distance, so the image communicates instantly on the magazine page and bears extended looking as a print.

Seeing fashion as line and plane, not as movement

When considering postwar fashion photography, Penn is often placed alongside Richard Avedon, but their methods differ substantially. Where Avedon frequently transformed clothing into a contemporary event through bodily movement, the tension of encounter, and the performativity of models, Penn stills clothing as line, plane, fold, weight, and silhouette. His continued use of worn Paris theater curtains found in 1950 as a backdrop was not a way to place garments in a grand setting — it was a way to show how a garment stands as form *1. Collaboration with models like Lisa Fonssagrives, who understood the shape and posture of the body, reinforced this direction *1. Here models do not become characters in a narrative; instead clothing, body, background, and the tonal range of the print become a single composition. Fashion is simultaneously an image stimulating desire and possession, and an object showing how fabric stands, how sleeves and folds create planes, how the body supports the frame. Penn's photographs do not only make a product look appealing — they pull images consumed at the speed of magazines back into time spent looking at composition and surface.

Small Trades and the type of occupation

Small Trades is a series that constructs occupation as a relationship among clothing, tools, posture, and background. The J. Paul Getty Museum notes that Penn photographed craftsmen and workers in Paris, London, and New York in the early 1950s — dressed in work clothes, holding their tools — under neutral backgrounds and natural light *5. The Art Institute of Chicago archives note that the series was inspired by the tradition of old prints depicting London street vendors and small Parisian trades, and connects to the occupational portraits of Eugène Atget and August Sander *15. Workplace noise, street movement, and economic context are excluded from the frame. Instead, figures stand on a quiet studio stage while carrying the signs of their occupation. Penn's later decision to remake the series as large platinum-palladium prints was not simple preservation or embellishment. The Chicago archives explain that the 1970s platinum-palladium versions draw out with clarity the wrinkles of an apron and the veins of a forearm — making manual work visible as a trace on the body *15. The archives also note that Penn was strongly aware of how postwar corporatization and the growth of chain stores were causing these trades to disappear *15. The reprinting of Small Trades was therefore not an act of decorating old negatives with a luxury technique, but a process of making the physicality of disappearing work readable again through the weight of paper, gradation, and density of detail.

Still life, waste, and the intelligence of surface

Penn's still life photography is not a sideline removed from fashion and portraiture. The same approach used to place people against white backgrounds and curtains was turned toward flowers, bones, cigarette butts, food, cosmetics, gloves, and insects. The Art Institute archives note that Penn's magazine still lifes were often given narrative or anthropomorphic character — traveling bags and small objects spoke of journeys in place of people — while other still lifes mixed sharply uncomfortable elements into luxury goods, disturbing readers turning the page *16. When Penn described an "acidic, unsettling tone" in his notes, it was because simply arranging products beautifully would be absorbed into the magazine's economy of desire; introducing insects, tears, decay, and the atmosphere of waste was a way to briefly stop the viewer's ease *16. In Summer Sleep, New York, for instance, what reads most sharply is not the sleeping woman but the torn window screen and fly in the foreground, while the interior behind blurs like damp heat *16. The viewer encounters not a beautiful summer scene but screen, insect, heat, and stagnant air. In his flower series, Penn often chose blooms past their peak, beginning to show spots, browning, and twisting *16. Works like Cigarette No. 37, New York — held in the Pace Gallery collection — approach waste not as moral accusation but as an object where form, stain, ash, and the texture of paper are concentrated *14. Penn's still lifes show goods and household objects while mixing damage, death, and post-consumption residue into their surfaces, lightly roughening the smooth pleasure of magazine photography.

The print is not the final step

For Penn, the print was not a finishing touch after the shoot but the central process by which the meaning of a photograph was determined. The Smithsonian identifies Penn's revival of platinum printing in the 1960s and 1970s as a major achievement *4. What matters is not simply the fact of using an old technique. At MoMA's 1950 symposium Penn had stated that for the modern photographer the final product was not the photographic print but the printed page *16. But at Brodovitch's 1964 workshop, he said he was wounded with disappointment whenever he saw his photographs in magazines — that a beautiful print was not a provisional state on the way to the page but something complete in itself *16. Gagosian Quarterly explains that behind this lay dissatisfaction with editorial work in the early 1960s, declining magazine print quality, and a shock at seeing old photographers' prints at George Eastman House *18. Penn was thus making images that communicate instantly in magazines while trying to recover through the print what reproduction loses: gradation, paper weight, the depth of surface, the time of handwork. The Art Institute's description of his platinum printing notes that photosensitive platinum salts were hand-coated onto paper, exposed by direct contact with the negative, and the process of coating and exposure repeated multiple times as needed *6. Penn also mounted paper onto aluminum supports to prevent warping and managed precise registration across multiple process steps *6. Gagosian Quarterly adds that Penn treated a negative not as a single determined image but as a source generating prints that differed in texture, scale, and tonality *18. The importance of platinum-palladium prints was therefore that they moved photography from "illustration to be published in a magazine" to an object remade repeatedly through choices of paper, metal, gradation, size, and version. The fact that the Metropolitan Museum has collected and exhibited Penn's Small Trades platinum prints and nudes demonstrates how this obsession with printing has supported the examination of Penn's photographs as works in museum contexts *24.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Penn's photographs first circulated in the pages of Vogue and were seen in the context of advertising and fashion. Later, in museums and catalogs, individual photographs came to be examined not only for what they were images made to sell, but for the composition, background, light, and printing through which they were made. MoMA records collecting and exhibiting Penn's work since 1943, and held a retrospective organized by John Szarkowski in 1984 *7. The Metropolitan Museum's Irving Penn: Centennial catalog contains approximately 300 photographs, treating Penn as a whole — encompassing early documentary work, portraiture, fashion, nudes, people of Peru, Dahomey, New Guinea, and Morocco, still lifes, advertising photography, and printing processes *8. What is meant by "a photographic form readable in museums" is a form that can be analyzed as work through its composition, recurring backgrounds, the relationship between models and clothing, the texture of prints, and comparisons within series — even when detached from the advertising purpose or the date of magazine publication. The same fashion photograph functions in the magazine as an image conveying clothing, but in the gallery one can see which background the model stands before, how the lines of the garment transform the body, and how tone and texture shifted in later platinum prints. The fact that the Metropolitan retrospective treated fashion, still life, Cusco, urban workers, nudes, New Guinea portraits, flowers, and cultural figure portraits in the same exhibition indicates that Penn's photographs are examined not as work in separate genres but as a shared studio grammar *3. In Japan, the Tokyo Metropolitan Museum of Photography held "Irving Penn: All Work" from 1999 to 2000 *12. At KYOTOGRAPHIE 2022, "Irving Penn: Works 1939–2007" from the MEP collection was presented in Kyoto *2. The Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art describes Penn's work as highly regarded in silver gelatin prints, platinum-palladium prints, and color prints alike *13.

Penn's influence beyond his death is not simply the spread of white backgrounds and minimal composition, but his treatment of fashion, portraiture, and still life through the same studio grammar — making it possible to revisit commercial photography as a matter of composition, series, printing method, reprinting, and exhibition space. The Met explains that Penn's retrospective was structured to show the difference between the original Vogue publication and the later reuse and reprinting *24. MEP describes Penn as an important figure in twentieth-century photography who exerted deep influence on fashion photography, portraiture, and still life since the 1950s *17. The most visible instance of that influence is his long collaboration with Issey Miyake. The Met notes that from the 1980s, Miyake sent garments each year to Penn in New York, and Penn responded photographically, stimulated by their structural inventiveness *19. 21_21 DESIGN SIGHT's exhibition notes describe how Miyake's absence from the shoot gave Penn freedom, and how the photographs showed Miyake the garments as a new world even for him *20. Museum für Gestaltung Zürich also frames this collaboration not as conventional fashion photography but as a practice that foregrounds form, gesture, and abstraction *21. In relation to later portraiture, it is more useful to ask what was carried forward and what changed than simply to place Penn as the "originator of the white background." Thomas Ruff's Porträts, for instance, shares Penn's use of frontality, neutral background, and repeated form, but the Met situates Ruff's large portraits in connection with the Bechers' typological method, minimalism, identity photography, and the gaze of surveillance society *25. David Zwirner's artist text also describes Ruff's portraits as placing expressionless figures before neutral backgrounds, aiming at sharply objective rather than sentimental photography from a position of doubt toward the polished imagery of advertising *26. Where Penn condenses person, clothing, gesture, and the texture of paper into a single quiet form, Ruff enlarges faces while presenting psychology as unreadable. The two can therefore be situated not in direct influence but as a comparative axis along which white backgrounds, repetition, and frontality moved from the concentrated focus of commercial pages toward questions of surveillance, identification, and anonymity in contemporary photography. More recently, Hank Willis Thomas curated "Kinship" at Pace Gallery, revisiting the structure in which Penn's photographs were made and the position from which they are seen *22. Pace's description notes Thomas as an artist concerned with how images are made and consumed, and how the position and perception of the viewer changes the photographic experience *22. The exhibition placed photographs within spaces evoking the structures Penn used for portraiture, inviting viewers to experience with their own bodies the intimate, enclosed space that subjects once entered *22. This rereading treats Penn's photographs not only as questions of what is depicted, but of the space in which a person is seen and where the viewer stands to look at that image. Penn's form has been reinterpreted repeatedly from different vantage points — less as a style to imitate than as a method for rearranging the relationships among commercial pages, clothing, bodies, objects, prints, and exhibition space.

To summarize Penn's photographs as "commercialism elevated to art" is to obscure his method again. Penn converted the clarity demanded by commercial photography — the conditions of magazine printing, the legibility required by advertising — into stripped-down space, compressed composition, the surface of objects, and the density of prints. The National Portrait Gallery's "Irving Penn Portraits" gave a retrospective view of Penn's portraits centered on cultural figures across nearly seventy years of career *9. The Guardian's review of that exhibition argues that Penn's portraits — simple settings, restrained lighting, subtly choreographed poses and gestures — did not expose the inner life of subjects directly but revealed it within the range of what appeared on the exterior *10. This touches on both the limits and the strength of Penn's photography. His studio was less a place for subjects to speak freely than a place to bring people, clothing, tools, paper, and light into the same rigorous form. Penn's photographs therefore do not speak the psychology of the subject directly; it emerges slowly before the viewer through posture, silence, surface, and the weight of the print. Despite being a commercial photographer, his importance in the history of photography lies in having extended the clear imagery made for magazines into the question of how photography can "re-place" people and objects.

issei-suda.html.lead_html: Issei Suda photographed Tokyo alleyways, regional festivals, passersby, signs, and plants with a Rolleiflex in the 6×6 format. Around 1968, Provoke challenged the clarity of press and advertising photography through are-bure-boke—grainy, blurry, out-of-focus images—while Compora photography shifted attention from events to everyday life. Suda rejected any affinity with either tendency, saying they had “absolutely nothing to do” with him. Fushikaden, Waga Tokyo 100, and Human Memory show why he placed his response at the moment of exposure ahead of the ideas of a movement. They also reveal how precise square frames turned ordinary scenes into images whose circumstances remain unresolved.
issei-suda.html.thesis_html: Suda established a mode of street photography in which everything is sharply rendered, yet what is happening cannot be determined. The 6×6 negative records faces, clothing, lettering, and plants in detail, while the square frame cuts away the before and after of an event and gives people and objects equal visual weight. Provoke disrupted photographic transparency with grain, blur, and harsh contrast. Suda kept the surface clear while leaving the clues needed to explain the situation outside the frame.
