sections.title: Background and Context
sections.body_html:
From Research into News Images to Staged Photography

Hondius’s turn toward migration and citizenship can be traced to a period of study at FAMU in Prague in 1997. He visited Roma families who had been denied Czech citizenship and recognized how existing reporting confined Roma people to types associated with wandering, poverty, and crime. For The Tolerance Campaign, he reduced the explanatory background of the domestic environment and displayed the faces and postures of his subjects as posters in public space.*1 He later researched images of the Kosovo conflict, Palestine, Afghanistan, and European migration policy, constructing scenes from interviews that resembled news photographs without serving as evidence of a particular event.

Building “Possible Scenes” from Testimony and Field Research

Production begins with research into migration policy, ethnic conflict, border control, and military institutions. Hondius gathers personal testimony alongside press photographs and constructs a “reality that could have happened” with actors and collaborators from several experiences. His official description of Photographic Works calls the combination of media imagery and personal testimony “fiction based on fact.”*2 Around 2010, he conducted many interviews with young Afghan migrants in Paris and Calais. He later wrote that an encounter at sea in 2025 with people traveling toward the United Kingdom made their vulnerability register as a reality different from familiar news images.*3 Staging measures the difference between visual types and face-to-face experience; it does not simply substitute imagination for a distant event.

News photographs are commonly read as evidence of situations witnessed on location. Hondius makes the constructed nature of his scenes clear through the exhibition setting and assigns the works a task separate from verifying facts. Even without a place name or event caption, viewers rapidly supply narratives such as “refugees,” “conflict,” and “forced migration.” That response makes it possible to examine the roles of repeated press imagery, advertising polish, and captions in the public understanding of political events. *2

Experiences gathered through several interviews are not consolidated into a script that reenacts one person’s testimony. They are divided into luggage, posture, distance inside a vehicle, and buildings in the background. The absence of a direct correspondence between a finished photograph and one witness can protect personal information, while also weakening the specificity of experience. The ethical question of staging lies less in a binary between fact and fiction than in the point at which testimony becomes an anonymous visual sign.

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
Leaving Unexplained Details within the Finish of Press Photography

Hondius’s large color photographs render clothing, luggage, and vehicle color with controlled clarity. Their finish, close to advertising photography, attracts the eye first. Continued looking reveals that a cart is unnaturally clean, that several gazes align too perfectly, or that it is difficult to decide who is guarding whom. The beauty of the frame can make political suffering easy to consume, while these discrepancies interrupt the first interpretation and send the viewer back into the image. *2

The Visual Types Used to Explain Migration and Conflict

In The Tolerance Project, Hondius photographed Roma people in the Czech Republic and avoided using their living environment as an explanatory background, seeking to weaken the established stereotype of a wandering group.*1 Reducing the background can obscure social conditions, yet it also creates distance from a journalistic convention in which poverty or itinerant life stands in for the whole person. What the frame excludes, and how much the title explains, shapes whether a subject is seen as an individual or as the sign of a social problem.

Bus windows, stacked luggage, waiting crowds, and border fences have become rapid signs for “migration,” “flight,” and “deportation” in news imagery. Hondius designs scenes from field research and testimony, repeating the same signs in arrangements that are slightly too emphatic. His official account of Photographic Works places the tension between the seduction of commercial photography and sociopolitical content at the center of the method.*2 As more figures appear with similar postures and belongings, individual histories recede and the image approaches a generalized picture of “the migrant.”

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The Bus Photographs: How the Vehicle Turns Individuals into a Group

In the best-known bus images, window frames separate faces one by one, while the direction of the seats and the structure of the vehicle submit everyone to the same movement. The bus crosses borders, but it also regulates boarding, waiting, and surveillance, presenting different people as a “group in transit.” Collection records at Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen include Bus and UN Defender, situating them within a continuing body of work on mobility and institutions.*4

Titles suppress place names and event names, making it difficult to determine country, ethnicity, or reason for movement from the image alone. The same window, luggage, and exhausted posture can be assigned different histories and agents of responsibility when labeled “evacuation,” “deportation,” or “migrant labor.” The Stedelijk Museum’s paradocs program presented the works as deliberate disturbances of the boundary between reality and staging.*5 The viewer’s change of story before and after reading a title or exhibition text becomes part of the work.

To Unveil a Star: The Time through Which an Institution Stages Itself

The 2021 film To Unveil a Star follows, in a partly fictionalized form, the artist’s long relationship with a star-shaped sculpture symbolizing NATO. The official project page describes it as an essay film about his relation to a work of art that gives form to a global political ideal.*6 Moved when NATO facilities relocated, the sculpture changes site, unveiling ceremony, and publicity footage while continuing to provide the abstract idea of alliance unity with a material appearance. Labyrint Film likewise presents the film as an intersection of political symbolism and the artist’s personal fixation.*7

The still photographs make it difficult to decide within one frame whether a scene is found or staged. In the film, the sculpture’s transport, negotiations, archival footage, and narration unfold in sequence, revealing the process by which an institution prepares its visible form. Stroom Den Haag’s Alliance and Allegiance presented the work through a discussion of NATO’s visual politics and geopolitical imagery.*8 Hondius’s subject expands from a single event to the long duration through which sculpture, architecture, ceremony, and publicity repeat a political idea.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
The Risk That Staging Dilutes Real Suffering

Reenacting refugees or ethnic conflict with actors and collaborators risks converting lived experience into polished fiction and obscuring specific agents of responsibility. Suppressing the place and event can expose a viewer’s assumptions, but it can also erase differences among political situations. In light of the official description of the relation among press images, testimony, and constructed photography, evaluation must consider which sources were used, who participated, and at what stage testimony became an anonymous visual sign, beyond the disclosure that a scene was staged. *2

Controlled color and composition can make images of refugees and conflict comfortable to consume in a museum. Hondius does not use rough image quality as a guarantee of truth. He attracts the viewer through the finish of art photography, then delays interpretation through objects that are too clean, gazes that align too precisely, and ambiguous titles. At times this pause resists immediate consumption; at others the beauty of the image can remain dominant. The conditions of production and the exhibition text therefore matter to the assessment of each work. *2

Separating Political Photography as Evidence from Political Photography as a Model of Understanding

Hondius’s photographs do not aim to replace the evidentiary function of press images. Field research and testimony support their production, while the finished frame exposes which composition, background, gesture, and remembered news image the viewer used to understand the situation. Criticism on the official site identifies the tension between commercial photographic aesthetics and sociopolitical information as the work’s method.*2 Where reporting seeks to verify what happened, his constructed photographs return the question of what kind of human figure the viewer believed they were seeing.

The star-shaped sculpture followed in To Unveil a Star was made to visualize unity among NATO members and moved when the institution relocated. Stroom Den Haag’s Alliance and Allegiance presented the film as a project about sculpture, NATO publicity, and political allegiance after the Cold War.*8 An abstract ideal reaches bodies and memory through a sculpture outside a building, an unveiling ceremony, archival footage, and the time the artist spends following it, as well as through conference documents. The problem of political imagery expands from photographs of events to the performances through which institutions maintain their own appearance.

Taken together, materials from the artist’s official site, CNAP, and AKINCI describe a sustained “almost documentary” approach combining press imagery, advertising lighting, testimony, and reenactment, beyond a single project on refugees.*9*10*15*18*19 Archives at the Van Abbemuseum and de Appel, together with exhibition records at Photography Now, document the sustained reception of his constructed photographs within Dutch photography and contemporary art, particularly in debates over the truth claims of news imagery.*12*14*17

Production materials and interviews for To Unveil a Star present the pursuit of NATO’s star-shaped sculpture as a long-term relation that includes the artist’s own fixation and participation, not simply an external critique of an institutional symbol.*13*20 More recent projects with climate activists and exhibitions centered on local faces extend the question developed through migration and military institutions—who is represented in public space—into climate politics and regional portraiture.*16*11

kajima-seibei.html.lead_html: Kajima Seibei (1866–1924) was born in Osaka. The second son of the Osaka sake wholesaler Kajimaya, he became the eighth Kajima Seibei through his marriage to Nofu, heiress to the main Kajimaya house in Shinkawa, Tokyo. He was known as the "photographic magnate" for investing the family fortune in photography on a grand scale. He supported the Tsukiji Dry Plate Manufacturing Company, the Photographic Society of Japan, the Greater Japan Photography Exhibition, the Genrokukan studio in Kobikicho, the Japan Magic Lantern Society, and demonstrations of new lighting technologies, while also producing his own portraits and Twenty-Four Views of Mount Fuji. In later life, he left the Kajima family, operated photography studios, and eventually became a Noh flutist.
kajima-seibei.html.thesis_html: Photography in mid-Meiji Japan depended on imported materials, individual studios, and the limited activities of a few organizations. Kajima Seibei did more than make photographs himself. By financing the Tsukiji Dry Plate Manufacturing Company, participating in and supporting the Photographic Society of Japan and the Greater Japan Photography Exhibition, establishing the Genrokukan, and conducting public experiments with magic lanterns, X-rays, and artificial lighting, he simultaneously developed the materials for making photographs, places to learn techniques, forums for evaluating work, and venues for presenting it to audiences. His distinctive contribution to photographic history was to move photography from the realm of individual skill and luxurious recreation toward a cultural system of sustained production, evaluation, and public display. His importance does not rest on the invention of a new style. Kajima's activities demonstrate concretely that the establishment of modern photography required patrons who could connect funding, materials, facilities, organizations, and public presentation technologies, as well as photographers.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Kajima Seibei's Life and the "Photographic Magnate"

Kajima Seibei was born in 1866 as Masanosuke, the second son of Kajima Seiemon, head of the Osaka sake wholesaler Kajimaya.*1 After marrying Nofu, heiress to the main Kajimaya house in Shinkawa, Tokyo, he took the name Kajima Seibei VIII. Beginning in 1885, he invited the Asakusa photographer Imazu Shojiro to his home to teach him photography. In 1888, he established the Tsukiji Dry Plate Manufacturing Company with Ogawa Kazumasa and William K. Burton. The following year, he joined the Photographic Society of Japan, and in 1893 he became vice president of the Greater Japan Photography Exhibition.*7

The name "photographic magnate" arose from his lavish use of a wealthy merchant family's resources for expensive equipment, large-format photographs, the administration of photographic organizations, and experiments with new technologies. He should be understood as more than an extravagant hobbyist. At a time when photography in Japan still depended heavily on imports and individual expertise, he devoted his private wealth to developing it into a culture encompassing materials, organizations, exhibitions, publishing, and public demonstrations. A FUJIFILM exhibition likewise presents the Tsukiji Dry Plate Manufacturing Company, the Photographic Society of Japan, the Greater Japan Photography Exhibition, and the Genrokukan as a connected series of achievements.*2

The relationship between the Kajima family fortune and his spending on photography should not be reduced to a simple causal account. Research by Wako University observes that although the main Kajima house had amassed immense wealth since the closing years of the Tokugawa shogunate, the liquor trade itself was changing during the Meiji period. The dissolution of merchant guilds, changes in sake transportation routes, the shift from barrels to bottles, and direct sales by Nada brewers had already begun to erode the family business.*22 Seibei's extravagant lifestyle and massive investment in photography coincided with these developments. The evidence therefore supports an account in which changes in distribution structures and his personal spending and investments proceeded simultaneously, rather than one that attributes the wholesaler's decline to his expenditure on photography alone.

Dry Plates and Reproductive Technologies in the Meiji Period

The 1880s and 1890s, when Kajima invested heavily in photography, also saw changes in how photographs were made and circulated. Gelatin dry plates eliminated the wet-plate requirement that chemicals be applied at the shooting location and the plate developed before it dried. Photographers could instead carry factory-made light-sensitive plates and develop them later. A technical account by the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum explains that this change reduced the burden of carrying a portable darkroom and a full set of chemicals for outdoor work, allowing photographers to concentrate on making pictures.*16

During the same period, Ogawa Kazumasa expanded beyond dry plates into photomechanical reproduction, printing, and publishing, transforming photography from a medium of single prints into one capable of mass reproduction. Research by the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum notes that Ogawa created the foundations that allowed photography to function in society through dry-plate production, printing, and publishing.*17 Kajima's distinctive contribution went beyond financing this technological transition. Through the Tsukiji Dry Plate Manufacturing Company, the Genrokukan, exhibitions, and magazine frontispieces, he supported material production, photography, display, and reproduction as interconnected aspects of photographic culture.

The spread of dry plates also changed the social composition of those able to make photographs. Research on photographic history by the International Research Center for Japanese Studies explains that simpler techniques and lighter equipment increased the number of amateur photographers in the mid-Meiji period. Equipment remained expensive, however, and early users were largely drawn from affluent groups such as the aristocracy, senior officials, wealthy merchants, physicians, and university professors.*21 Kajima was an extreme example of this early amateur class. By connecting his personal enthusiasm to organizations and systems of evaluation such as the Photographic Society of Japan and the Greater Japan Photography Exhibition, he also shows how an elite pastime contributed to the organization of photographic culture.

The Genrokukan's Facilities and Photographic Culture

Established in 1895 in Kobikicho, near present-day Ginza, the Genrokukan was a large photographic facility with an art gallery, a revolving stage, and powerful arc lamps. A contemporary advertisement at the end of Shashin Shinsho stated that the studio offered night photography and enlargements up to eight shaku square. By incorporating large-format photography, artificial lighting, and exhibition space into a facility whose functions extended beyond portraiture, the Genrokukan reveals that Seibei regarded photography as a means of presentation to an audience as well as a technique for making pictures.*10

In the same year, he founded the Japan Magic Lantern Society with Toda Ujikyo and others. He conducted a public experiment in X-ray photography in 1896, followed in 1897 by outdoor night photography using magnesium flash at the funeral of Empress Dowager Eisho. His simultaneous engagement with photography, magic lanterns, X-rays, and artificial lighting as technologies for showing new kinds of images in public further clarifies the character of the Genrokukan.*7

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The Tsukiji Dry Plate Manufacturing Company and Domestic Dry Plates

In 1888, Seibei established the Tsukiji Dry Plate Manufacturing Company with Ogawa Kazumasa and William K. Burton. Japan then relied on imports for many photographic materials, including dry plates, and the attempt to manufacture them domestically was itself an effort to build an industrial foundation distinct from the photographer's craft. Seibei's role was less that of an inventor than that of a financial backer who made the experiments of engineers and photographers possible.*7

The Photographic Society of Japan and the Greater Japan Photography Exhibition

He joined the Photographic Society of Japan in 1889 and served as vice president of the Greater Japan Photography Exhibition, founded in 1893. His provision of funding and organizational support for places where photographers could gather, compare their work, and have it evaluated—not simply make pictures—was important to the institutionalization of photography in Meiji Japan. Technical information and standards of judgment that were difficult for individual studios to accumulate could now be shared through organizations and exhibitions.*2

The Photographic Society of Japan was formed in Tokyo in May 1889. Its membership included university professors, engineers, merchants, and foreign residents of Japan as well as professional photographers, and it helped disseminate photographic knowledge by introducing overseas techniques and presenting work. Art Platform Japan's record of the organization also confirms Kajima's participation.*24 This cross-disciplinary membership shows photography moving beyond the specialized work of the studio and becoming a field of collaborative inquiry linking science, commerce, recreation, and art.

Dividing the Work with Ogawa Kazumasa—Photography, Reproduction, and Circulation

Although Kajima Seibei and Ogawa Kazumasa both participated in the Meiji photographic world, they played different roles. Ogawa worked as a photographer and developed techniques for printing images in quantity through his photomechanical printing business and publishing activities. Kajima joined Ogawa and Burton in experimenting with dry-plate production, invested in exhibitions and the Genrokukan, and created places where engineers, photographers, and audiences could meet. A landscape published in the magazine Taiyo in 1895 and credited both "Photographed by Genrokukan" and "Photographic engraving, plate-making, and printing by Ogawa Kazumasa" demonstrates how photography and reproduction were linked as distinct forms of expertise.*14

X-Ray Photography and Night Photography

Seibei was also active in presenting new photographic technologies to the public. In 1896, he successfully conducted a public experiment in X-ray photography at the Greater Japan Photography Exhibition. The following year, he photographed the funeral of Empress Dowager Eisho outdoors at night using magnesium flash. FUJIFILM's chronology identifies the latter as Japan's first use of magnesium flash for outdoor night photography.*7 Together with the Genrokukan's arc lamps, these activities show his effort to use artificial light to expand the times and places in which photography, previously dependent on natural light, could be undertaken.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The Genrokukan and Theatrical Photography

The Genrokukan was both a photographic studio that showcased the latest equipment and a place where kabuki and its actors were translated into photographic media. A Meiji University study of theatrical photography devotes a separate chapter to "Kajima Seibei and the Genrokukan" in its account of how theatrical photographs circulated to broad audiences through magazines, postcards, and photobooks from the late 1880s onward.*8 By turning actors' appearances from singular events onstage into reproducible printed matter, the Genrokukan became more than a portrait studio: it was a production center linking theater and modern media.

Murashima Ayaka's study Omokage of the Stage: Theatrical Photography, Actors, and Photographers includes a chapter titled "Kajima Seibei and Kabuki Shinpo," examining Kajima within the modern visual culture that developed from actor prints through theatrical photography to print and publishing media.*15 The Genrokukan's importance lies less in preserving the stage exactly as it appeared than in photographing actors and making their images reproducible beyond the theater through magazines and other publications. Theatrical photography connected the commercial work of the studio with modern entertainment media, which is one reason Kajima's activities cannot be explained simply as a wealthy man's fascination with technology.

The setting for theatrical photography also shifted during the Meiji period from the studio toward the theater. A research bulletin from the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, traces a progression from a time when kabuki actors visited studios such as the Genrokukan for costumed portraits to the establishment, as photographic techniques improved, of an outdoor shooting area with a hanging backdrop behind the Kabukiza dressing rooms. Photography thus moved closer to the space of performance.*23 Kajima's theatrical work stands at the threshold between the early system that brought actors into the studio and the next phase, when photographic equipment moved toward the theater. Murashima Ayaka's decision to devote a chapter to Kajima and Kabuki Shinpo likewise reflects photography's role in circulating stage imagery to magazine readers, beyond merely preserving actors' likenesses.*15

The Japan Magic Lantern Society and Projection Culture

The Japan Magic Lantern Society, which Seibei founded in 1895, shows his involvement in a culture that used light to project images for an audience as well as in the production of photographic prints. FUJIFILM's detailed chronology places the opening of the Genrokukan and the founding of the Society in the same year, followed by the public X-ray experiment in 1896.*7 Viewed as a continuum, his work with studios, exhibitions, magic lanterns, and X-rays makes clear that his central concern was how new images could be produced and presented in public, beyond the skillful making of a single photograph.

Mount Fuji Photographs and Meiji Landscape Media

Kajima's photographs of Mount Fuji extend beyond the works presented to the Imperial family. In a JCII Photo Salon exhibition of photographs of Mount Fuji from the final years of the Tokugawa shogunate and the Meiji period, Kajima's View of Mount Fuji from Tagonoura appeared alongside works by Beato, Stillfried, and others. The exhibition situated it within the transition from an era in which foreign photographers shaped a touristic image of Japan to one in which Japanese photographers themselves incorporated Mount Fuji into modern photographic representation.*13

Volume 1, no. 9 of Hakubunkan's Taiyo, published in 1895, also featured a landscape photograph as a frontispiece in its "Twelve Views of Japan" series, credited to "Genrokukan, photographer" and "Ogawa Kazumasa, photographic engraving, plate-making, and printing." The image made at the Genrokukan was transferred to mass magazine printing through Ogawa's photomechanical process. This example shows how Kajima's work reached beyond the studio to the formation of shared images of the Japanese landscape in modern publishing.*14

Photographic Record of the Sino-Japanese War—War and Modern Media

The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum holds a substantial group of works attributed to Kajima under the title Photographic Record of the Sino-Japanese War, No. 1. In addition to harbor views such as View of the Japanese Settlement from the Busan Harbor Anchorage, the group includes laborers assembled before the Japanese consulate, the training of military horses, captured ships, fortifications, and camps.*18 Its documentary value lies in recording logistics, personnel, ports, and military facilities as a series, instead of concentrating exclusively on dramatic moments of battle.

The Captured Ship Hanyang takes the seized vessel itself as its subject, while another plate records soldiers camped near Pyongyang.*19 Seen alongside his photographs of Mount Fuji and actors, these images show that Kajima's production extended beyond aesthetic landscapes and commercial portraiture to encompass images of national events, war, and the records required by publishers.*20 At a time when Meiji photography was expanding simultaneously into art, entertainment, news, and state documentation, Kajima supported these varied uses through the same network of facilities and financing.

Twenty-Four Views of Mount Fuji and the Imperial Family

Seibei produced Twenty-Four Views of Mount Fuji, photographing the mountain from multiple directions. An album dating from around 1895 is held by the Museum of the Imperial Collections, Sannomaru Shozokan. The Genrokukan name remains in the work's record, confirming that he fashioned his photographs of Mount Fuji into a cohesive series presenting a national symbol through modern photography, instead of treating them as a private travel record.*4 Exhibition materials from the Sannomaru Shozokan list both Photograph of Snow-Capped Mount Fuji from 1894 and Twenty-Four Views of Mount Fuji from around 1895, confirming the presence of several Mount Fuji works by Kajima in the Imperial collection.*12

The "Photographic Magnate" as a Patron of Photography

The name "photographic magnate" can overemphasize anecdotes of extravagance, but Seibei's funds were distributed across dry-plate production, photographic organizations, exhibitions, studios, publishing, and public presentations of new technologies. Works from the Sino-Japanese War period held by the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum also show that he photographed contemporary events in addition to Mount Fuji and portraits.*11 The convergence of patron and photographer in one person makes Kajima significant to the formation of photographic institutions in Meiji Japan.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Kajima Seibei and Ogawa Kazumasa—Institutions, Technology, and Circulation

Kajima Seibei's place in photographic history becomes clearer when compared with that of Ogawa Kazumasa. Ogawa circulated photography through society as a reproducible print medium by means of photography, photomechanical reproduction, and publishing. Kajima funded dry-plate production and supported photographic organizations, exhibitions, the Genrokukan, magic lanterns, and artificial lighting, taking responsibility for the institutional structures that sustained production and public presentation. Research on Ogawa by the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum shows that dry-plate manufacture, printing, and publishing were essential conditions in transforming photography into a social medium.*17 Kajima's significance lies in investing his private wealth in several mechanisms that linked photographers, engineers, funding, facilities, and audiences, rather than consolidating these conditions in a single enterprise.

Later Years after Leaving the Kajima Family

After investing large sums in expensive equipment, large-format photographs, dry-plate production, photographic organizations, and the Genrokukan, Seibei left the Kajima family and closed the Genrokukan in 1897. Research examining contemporary sources notes both the studio's extensive equipment and services as described in its advertisements and the circumstances of his departure from his adoptive family that year.*10 No confirmed evidence establishes his spending on photography as the sole cause of the sake wholesaler's decline. It is therefore more appropriate to distinguish his large-scale investment of family resources in photography from his departure than to reduce the story to the claim that photography ruined the family business.

After leaving the family, he bought Ponta out of her geisha contract and opened a photography studio in Kyoto, but the business did not succeed. He later opened the Harukikan studio across from the Hongoza theater in Tokyo. After losing his right thumb in a magnesium explosion, he closed the studio and subsequently became a flutist of the Morita school of Noh under the name Miki Kisaragi. Art Platform Japan records his death on August 6, 1924.*9 His later years allow the "photographic magnate" to be understood through both the splendor of his privately financed support for photographic institutions and the personal history that made it impossible for him to sustain those activities.

Surviving Works and Current Reassessment

Treating Kajima solely as an institutional supporter obscures his own photographic activity. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum holds his Taedong Gate and the Walls of Pyongyang, made during the Sino-Japanese War in 1894–95, confirming that contemporary wartime landscapes joined Mount Fuji, portraiture, and theater among his subjects.*11 Considered together with Twenty-Four Views of Mount Fuji at the Museum of the Imperial Collections, Sannomaru Shozokan, the Genrokukan's activities encompassed a mode of production that circulated photographs of landscapes, public events, and theater, in addition to investment in the photographic industry.

Recent research and exhibitions have also moved Kajima beyond the anecdotal image of a man who spent his fortune on a hobby and returned him to the history of photography's institutional formation. In a lecture at the SieboldHuis, Sebastian Dobson discussed Kajima within the international setting of Meiji photography.*3 A program at the Maison de la culture du Japon à Paris also presented Kajima as a figure through whom to consider Japanese photography after Yokohama shashin.*5 The 2019 exhibition at FUJIFILM SQUARE offered a comprehensive account of the "photographic magnate's" life and achievements, and an exhibition record also remains on Tokyo Art Beat.*6 This reassessment corresponds to a broader approach that considers not only individual photographers' masterpieces but also those who supported materials, facilities, exhibitions, and publishing as subjects of photographic history.

twitter.title: Izima Kaoru | Landscapes with a Corpse and Fashion Photography | Photo Coordinates
twitter.description: A study of Izima Kaoru through Landscapes with a Corpse, Saigo ni Mita Fūkei, and One Sun, examining fashion photography, staged death, photographic sequences, and collaborative production.

kaoru-izima.html.lead_html: Izima Kaoru photographed the “desired deaths” imagined by actresses and models, staging them in designer clothing and carefully chosen locations and arranging the images in sequences that move from long shot to close-up. Through Landscapes with a Corpse, zyappu, Saigo ni Mita Fūkei (The Last Landscape Seen), and One Sun, this page traces his experience in fashion photography, his fear of death, the gaze directed at the dead, and critical debates around his images of women.
kaoru-izima.html.thesis_html: Izima inserted a future death imagined by the sitter, and the time required to discover the body as pages turn, into the machinery through which fashion magazines circulate clothes, models, and brands as objects of desire. A body that nearly disappears into the landscape in the opening view becomes an identifiable person in the middle distance and close-up, while the brand name ties the dead figure to the consumer culture of the moment in which the photograph was made. After established magazines declined the project, he continued it in his independently published zyappu, combining photographs, fictional news reports, styling, and page design into a single form. He redirected portraiture from the preservation of present beauty toward a future absence chosen by the sitter, shaped through negotiation with the production team and through the viewer’s approach to—and voyeuristic inspection of—the body. The series makes a structural contradiction visible: the beauty of fashion photography turns death into an alluring image even as it keeps the viewer’s fear at a distance.

sections.title: Background and Context
sections.body_html:
From the Fashion Magazine zyappu to Landscapes with a Corpse

Izima worked in advertising, music, and fashion magazines from the 1980s, learning to bring clothes, models, locations, and the sequence of a spread into a single image system. In the early 1990s, while looking for a project distinct from existing Japanese fashion photography, he arrived at the idea that “it would be interesting if the model were a corpse.” Established magazines did not take the project to publication, so in 1994 he founded the quarterly magazine zyappu. Published through 1999, the magazine allowed him to move among the roles of editor in chief, photographer, and the fictional persona “Arizona Gorō,” creating a medium in which he could sustain the project at a distance from existing editorial policies and advertisers’ decisions.*1*2

In zyappu, Landscapes with a Corpse did not end with a small group of photographs. The images appeared alongside fictional reports of the incident, the model’s name, and fashion-brand credits.*3 A reader opened the magazine expecting a fashion story, found a tiny body in the landscape, and turned the page to identify the clothing and face. Izima brought commercial lighting and styling into an art project, while also using the magazine’s editorial capacity to assign images a sequence, text, and information about prices and brands. What began as a surprising premise became a long-term form because each issue could reconstruct the reader’s movement through discovery, approach, and identification, rather than relying on the image of a corpse alone. *4

Fear of Death Emerges through the Long-Running Series

Izima later wrote that he had no clearly defined intention to make death his subject when he began Landscapes with a Corpse. Over fifteen years of work, he recognized the intensity of his own fear of death and began to think about religion and prayer as ways of gaining distance from that fear.*5 Asking sitters how they wished to die also became a form of portraiture that elicited how they wanted to live and how they wished to be remembered, rather than a collection of outlandish deaths. Izima’s statement similarly links the consideration of an ideal death to the consideration of an ideal life, and explains how the techniques of fashion photography gave visual credibility to extraordinary scenes.*6 His ability to translate his fear of death and the values articulated by his sitters into clothing, place, body, and light allowed the initial idea to develop into a sustained body of work.

The viewpoint of the series changed as the work continued. The early sequences largely approached a body in the landscape from the position of the photographer or discoverer. Later works introduced the idea that the dead person’s soul had left the body and was looking down on the last landscape it would see; the Japanese photobook title became Saigo ni Mita Fūkei (The Last Landscape Seen).*1 This shift from looking at death from outside to imagining the dead taking leave of the world deepened the project from an unusual fashion feature into a prolonged reflection on fear, separation, and mortality.

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
From Long Shot to Close-up: The Viewpoints of the Discoverer and the Dead

A scene usually unfolds across three to five photographs. In the first image, a mountain, road, beach, or interior fills most of the frame, while the body is small enough to be overlooked. The next photograph moves closer, and the final image reveals details such as clothing, face, wounds, or flowers. The Hatje Cantz photobook likewise identifies the repeated movement from long shot to close-up as the series’ basic structure.*4 In the early work, this movement resembles the viewer’s discovery of a corpse. The later sequences also carry a movement in the opposite direction, as the soul leaves the body while looking at the landscape for the last time.*1

How Magazines, Brands, and Exhibitions Structure the Time of Looking at Death

Titles name the model and identify brands through phrases such as “wears Prada” and “wears Alexander McQueen.” Clothing does more than decorate the scene: it attaches the person to the fashion industry, consumer culture, and a specific social image at the moment of production. Viewers who already know the actress or model bring memories of her face, profession, and clothes to the image before they encounter the body as an anonymous dead figure. Celebrity recognition and the value of luxury brands remain attached to the corpse. Death appears as a common endpoint, yet the figure never fully escapes the hierarchies and commodity values of life. *7

Because the series appeared in zyappu alongside advertising and fashion features, the act of identifying a brand flowed directly into the act of searching for a body. In a photobook, turning the pages produces the movement from long shot to close-up; in a large exhibition, the viewer’s walk toward the wall performs the same approach. Death arrives through a process in which the viewer discovers the figure, moves closer, and registers beauty and unease at the same time, rather than through the shock of a single image. *4

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Landscapes with a Corpse: Translating the Sitter’s Idea into a Long-Term Production

The series began in 1993 and expanded to actors and models in Japan and Europe. Each production started with the sitter imagining a desired death, clothing, and location. Izima, stylist Tomoko Yasuno, and the production team then spent several months translating those ideas into a site, season, and bodily pose.*1 The sitter’s answer was not simply reenacted on the day of the shoot. It had to be reconciled with accessible locations, loans of clothing, and the practical conditions under which a body could safely lie in place. The final image therefore brings together the sitter’s fantasy, the brand’s contribution, the production team’s decisions, and the camera distance chosen by Izima. Any account of the work must distinguish this collaborative dimension from the photographer’s authority over the final image.

In Tominaga Ai Wears Prada No. 405, the title binds together Ai Tominaga, Prada, the work number, and the series. The photograph retains the conventions of fashion imagery, in which who a person is and what she wears circulate with equal force, while depriving the body of movement. Exact styling and the pose of the corpse complete the image. Beauty softens the fear of death while creating the further problem of turning the dead into an alluring object.*7

One Sun: From Fear of Death to a Prayer Directed at the Sun

As he continued to think about death and religion, Izima wrote that a stay in Weimar, in the former East Germany, made him acutely aware that the same sun shines regardless of political borders. Over several years, he developed the idea of photographing the sun as an object of prayer, using a fisheye lens and long exposure to record its path from sunrise to sunset in a single image.*5 One Sun changes the form established by the staged death scenes while carrying forward their concerns with finite life, fear of death, and a form of prayer outside organized religion.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Post-Mortem Photography and Landscapes with a Corpse: Mourning and a Future Death

Nineteenth-century post-mortem photographs were made to mourn and remember family members who had actually died.*8 In Landscapes with a Corpse, a living sitter imagines a future death and performs the role of her own corpse. Both forms leave a photographic image of the dead, but the earlier photographs preserve the memory of someone already lost, while Izima’s series stages a death that has not yet occurred. The comparison clarifies that his work reorients portraiture toward a future absence; it does not reenact the conventions of post-mortem photography.

Beautifying Death: Critiques of the Voyeuristic Gaze

Mudam explains that the works’ aesthetic construction tempers the fear of death while exposing the voyeuristic desire of both viewer and photographer to look at the dead.*9 Japanese criticism has also argued that the low viewpoint, the approach toward a woman lying on the ground, the luxury clothing, and the carefully arranged body beautify the dead woman and reinforce a structure in which the recurrent figure of the “sleeping woman” in painting and photography is offered to a male gaze.*10 The work unsettles fashion photography’s standards of beauty while deriving its appeal from those same standards. *11

The Sitter’s Participation and the Photographer’s Final Authority

The sitter participates in imagining the desired death, clothing, and location, so her conception remains visible in the photograph. Izima determines the final composition, the order of distances, the printing, the title, and the circulation of the series. Calling the work “collaborative” does not by itself account for the unequal authority of sitter and photographer, the female body idealized by the fashion industry, or the viewer’s gaze. Each work requires attention to whose fantasy survives in the image and who turns the beauty of death into a commodity or artwork. These tensions make Landscapes with a Corpse both a device for imagining death gently and a series continually challenged by questions about images of women and the institutions of beauty. As a magazine project moved into photobooks and museum exhibitions, the intimacy of reading a sitter’s wishes and the distance involved in treating a dead woman as an object of display assumed different forms in each medium.

Art Platform Japan records the artist as Izima Kaoru and situates his trajectory from fashion photography through Landscapes with a Corpse and later still-life works within Japanese museum collections and exhibition histories.*21*13*22 Records from Kunsthalle Wien, Studio la Città, Von Lintel Gallery, and the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston show the international circulation of the series through exhibitions on the boundary between fashion and art, solo exhibitions, and photography collections.*12*14*20*19

The outdoor installation at Echigo-Tsumari and a 2009 exhibition offer examples of how the movement from long shot to close-up, originally structured by the sequence of a photobook, was reread through a regional landscape and exhibition space.*16*17*18 Recent exhibition texts and conversations with the artist have returned to the project’s development over time: the initial idea that “a corpse would be interesting,” the discussions with models, magazine editing, his fear of death, and the emergence of a portraiture concerned with how a person wishes to live.*15*23*24

twitter.title: Gertrude Käsebier | Pictorialism and Photo-Secession | Photo Coordinates
twitter.description: Using museum, archive, and specialist sources, this page examines Gertrude Käsebier through Pictorialism, Photo-Secession, and Portrait.

kasebier.html.lead_html: Gertrude Käsebier trained as a painter before turning to photography, bringing pictorialist light and composition to portraiture. Co-founder of the Photo-Secession with Stieglitz, she demonstrated through works such as Blessed Art Thou Among Women that photography could pursue artistic and spiritual aims distinct from the technical competition of commercial studios.
kasebier.html.thesis_html: Drawing on a training in painting, Käsebier transplanted a developed sense of light and composition into portrait photography, demonstrating from a position that straddled commercial studio practice and the artistic photography movement that the medium could carry deliberate aesthetic intent. As a co-founder of the Photo-Secession with Stieglitz, and through participation in Camera Work, she helped build the institutional structures of early twentieth-century art photography from the inside. Work centered on maternity, faith, and individual character was undervalued until feminist art-historical scholarship recovered it; it is now held in major collections as a pioneering practice in the possibilities of portrait photography.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Gertrude Käsebier was born in 1852 in Fort Des Moines, now Des Moines, Iowa. She spent her early years in the frontier territory of Colorado, then moved to New York, married Eduard Käsebier in 1874, and raised three children. In 1888, at thirty-six, she enrolled at the Pratt Institute in Brooklyn to study painting. She turned to photography seriously after that training, opening a studio on Fifth Avenue in 1897.*1

By the turn of the century Käsebier had become one of the most commercially successful portrait photographers in New York. Alfred Stieglitz called her "the leading portrait photographer in America," an assessment that spread widely through the profession and shaped her public reputation.*5

In 1902 Käsebier co-founded the Photo-Secession with Stieglitz and Edward Steichen. The organization aimed to win institutional recognition for photography as a fine art, and through Camera Work it exerted a lasting influence on photographic history.*1

Her studio continued to thrive commercially while she maintained her involvement in the Photo-Secession. Her relationship with Stieglitz grew strained in the 1910s, partly over aesthetic differences as the movement shifted toward straight photography. She also photographed Native Americans connected with Buffalo Bill's Wild West show, pursuing the documentary and artistic dimensions of her practice simultaneously. She continued to work until her death in New York in 1934.*8

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
From painting training to photographic light and composition

The defining characteristic of Käsebier's photography is the direct transfer of her Pratt Institute painting training into the way she handled composition and light. Her portraits use soft-focus lenses, back-lighting, and diffused white light, giving priority to the overall quality of light and atmosphere in the frame over precise facial detail. This was a central method of Pictorialism — the practical argument that photography could achieve artistic parity with painting.*8

Käsebier favored platinum and palladium printing, which produces rich mid-tones, deep blacks, and a velvety surface quality. Compared to silver gelatin, these processes offered superior archival stability and a tonal depth associated with printmaking. The choice was not only visual but strategic — positioning the photograph as a singular, precious object close to painting or etching rather than a mass-reproducible image.*15

Käsebier believed that a portrait should function as "biography" — drawing out the essential temperament, spirit, and humanity of the subject in a single image. Where New York's commercial studios competed on technical accuracy, she used print texture and lighting to fix an interior quality on the picture surface.*1

Blessed Art Thou Among Women — motherhood and religious iconography

Made in 1899, Blessed Art Thou Among Women is both her signature work and one of the most discussed images in Pictorialist photography. A mother stands in a doorway while her small daughter stands before her. The composition references the iconography of the Annunciation, and bright back-lighting with white dress amplifies the devotional mood. According to the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, the title quotes a Biblical verse and frames the mother-and-child relationship as a religious scene within everyday life.*2

The work resonates with the same subjects — motherhood, femininity, and religious feeling — that Julia Margaret Cameron pursued in Britain, though Käsebier came to her practice not from aristocratic leisure but as a working studio owner with family responsibilities. The Metropolitan Museum holds the gelatin silver print, where the soft contours and tonal contrast remain fully visible. The Brooklyn Museum also holds a version, situating the image within the visual history of the theme of motherhood.*16

Native American portraits and resistance to typological photography

Käsebier chose Native American sitters as subjects alongside her wealthy commercial clients. Unlike many contemporaries who photographed indigenous people as "ethnic types" for scientific classification, her portraits sought individual expression and interiority — a direct application of her consistent belief that the portrait should function as biography rather than documentation of a category.*5

The Metropolitan Museum's collection includes The Sketch, which shows the same attention to individual presence that characterizes her best portrait work. The National Gallery of Art also holds multiple Käsebier prints as part of its American modern photography holdings.*18

Camera Work and her position within the Photo-Secession

Käsebier's work appeared in Camera Work from its first issue and in several subsequent numbers, including Number 10, a copy held at the Princeton University Art Museum. Inclusion in Camera Work was not merely magazine publication but a strategic move in the institutionalization of photography as art, and Käsebier was one of its central figures.*20

Her position within the Photo-Secession was complex. As Stieglitz steered the movement toward straight photography and his own aesthetic preferences increasingly dominated the selection for Camera Work and 291, Käsebier's Pictorialist approach gradually moved toward the margins of the organization she had helped to found. The George Eastman Museum holds an extensive collection of her work and situates her as a central figure in Pictorialist photography's institutional history.*12

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
During her lifetime Käsebier was recognized by Stieglitz as the leading portrait photographer in America and occupied a central position in the fine-art photography movement. When the Photo-Secession dissolved and Stieglitz shifted toward straight photography, her Pictorialist style came to be associated with a superseded aesthetic moment by some critics.*1

From the late twentieth century onward, feminist art-historical scholarship systematically reappraised women photographers of the Pictorialist era and substantially reframed Käsebier's place in history. MoMA's 1992 exhibition examined her work in depth, re-establishing her as a pioneer who pursued the artistic possibilities of portraiture from a position of both commercial necessity and genuine artistic ambition — a combination that distinguished her from many male contemporaries of the period.*19

Today the National Museum of Women in the Arts identifies Käsebier as a founding member of the Photo-Secession and situates her practice at the intersection of women's perspectives and artistic ambition in photographic history.*1 Major works are held at the Amon Carter Museum, Metropolitan Museum, Cleveland Museum, Getty Museum, George Eastman Museum, and Smithsonian Institution — collectively positioning her as one of the defining figures of American Pictorialist photography.*14

kate-steciw.html.lead_html: Kate Steciw builds photographic objects by cutting, rotating, and compositing JPEGs sourced from stock-photo libraries and search results, then outputting them onto Plexiglas, irregular frames, Dibond, fabric, and other supports. Drawing on roughly a decade of commercial retouching, she places less emphasis on the original image made by a photographer than on the chain through which an image passes: search terms, licensing, compression, editing, printing, exhibition, and rephotography. Her work approaches 2010s post-internet photography through the conditions of image production—who selects, alters, materializes, and recirculates existing images. A generic “internet” look is secondary to those procedures.
kate-steciw.html.thesis_html: Traditional photographic authorship has often centered on the photographer making an original image with a camera and producing prints from its negative or data. In advertising and e-commerce, however, photographs continue moving after exposure through retouchers, stock agencies, search engines, and clients, repeatedly cropped, compressed, and resaved for new uses. After spending roughly a decade working inside that commercial system, Steciw removed taking the original photograph from the list of requirements for her own work and began using stock images purchased through searches. JPEG compression, Photoshop layers, long strings of search terms, Plexiglas, and irregular frames become parts of one continuous process, making it impossible to locate the work's origin only in “the moment the shutter was released.” Artie Vierkant unsettles the distinction between digital file and exhibited object; Lucas Blalock leaves Photoshop interventions visible on the image. Steciw instead converts anonymous commodity imagery and the systems of search, retouching, and licensing behind it into physical objects. Her work is distinctive for treating networked photography through the procedures of circulation and transformation, with image content only one part of that process.

sections.title: Background and Era
sections.body_html:
Steciw studied sociology at Smith College before earning an MFA in photography from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 2003. Her official CV and Higher Pictures trace a path from photographic training into work spanning photography, sculpture, collage, and video.*18

After graduate school she spent roughly a decade working in commercial photographic retouching, devoting much of each day to cutting products out of other people's images, correcting skin and backgrounds, and compositing photographs for advertising.*7 In that environment, the finished photograph was never determined by the photographer alone. It passed through retouchers, art directors, advertisers, stock agencies, and other systems. Steciw's later emphasis on who finds, selects, alters, and remakes an image therefore grew from direct experience of photographic production as divided labor, not from an abstract critique imposed afterward.

Around 2010, Web 2.0, stock photography, search engines, and social media had become places for obtaining visual material as well as viewing images. Rhizome's account of Steciw's early work likewise assumes an environment of mass online circulation and interchangeable commodity images.*7 The internet was not merely a subject in her work; gathering materials through a search box became part of studio work itself.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Using Stock Images as Material

For her 2014 Higher Pictures exhibition, Steciw collected online images through chains of search terms and repeatedly rotated, layered, and distorted them. Long strings of keywords survive in the titles, making the route through a database part of the structure of the work.*1

Stock photographs are designed for general reuse in advertising, largely detached from the particular life or location of the photographer who made them. For Steciw, images of tires, food, furniture, and plants can therefore function less as meaningful subjects than as reusable fragments of color, contour, and surface.*12

Working With JPEG Compression

In an interview with Tasweer, Steciw said that at a certain point the JPEG began to appear distinct from what had traditionally been called a “photograph.” A negative is a fixed record of a chemical interaction; a JPEG is compressed data that can change through copying and repeated saving.*5

Under this view, degraded resolution and compression artifacts are not mistakes to be eliminated but traces of an image moving through a network. Steciw describes resolution and compression as formal conditions comparable to the way a painter might work with viscosity or transparency.*5

Plexiglas and Irregular Frames

The digitally composited image does not necessarily end as a conventional rectangular print. Higher Pictures describes works in which tinted Plexiglas, geometric cutouts, chains, stickers, and wooden frames conceal some areas and expose others.*1 The layer structure of a JPEG is translated into physical fronts and backs, frame depth, holes, and cuts, aligning on-screen editing with the fabrication of an object.

As The New Yorker wrote of the 2014 exhibition, Steciw turns images taken from the internet into layered constructions; the JPEG visible behind the surface competes with supports that actually project into the viewer's space.*8

The materiality in Steciw's photography is different from a return to the tactile character of silver-gelatin paper. Images that circulated online as data are output onto boards that can be cut, transparent sheets, and frames with weight, physically reorganizing the relation between foreground and background.*20

Snapshots and Stock Images

In a 2016 exhibition, Steciw brought her own snapshots back into the work alongside stock photography. Higher Pictures explains that she refused to establish a hierarchy between the two types, sending both through the same editing process as images that might otherwise be forgotten.*2

This approach declines to privilege the photograph made by the artist. On a network, personal and commercial photographs can appear as equivalent files, each searchable, savable, and editable. Authorship therefore shifts from the instant of exposure toward the ways images are selected, transformed, and materialized.*6

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Boundless Hyper

Boundless Hyper (2012) was critically discussed as an early development in Steciw's use of stock photography and digital processing. Hyperallergic noted the role of internet databanks and existing systems of commercial imagery, emphasizing her treatment of pictures as products of information systems whose commercial origins remain active in the work.*12

The work addresses more than what advertisements depict. It incorporates the systems through which images are tagged on search sites, made interchangeable with similar images, and cropped for different uses into the composition itself.*7

The 2014 Higher Pictures Exhibition

In the 2014 exhibition, a small group of online images reappeared across multiple works while layers, Plexiglas, and frame shapes changed. Collector Daily described the exhibition as a set of variations in which shared image fragments were placed into different physical situations.*13

A work with a long search-term title shown in ICP's What Is a Photograph? likewise challenged the idea that a photograph proceeds from a single original. The exhibition situated Steciw among artists reconsidering photographic objecthood and production processes.*9

Fabric Works After 2016

At Higher Pictures in 2016, Steciw introduced machine-cut Dibond elements and long printed lengths of sateen fabric that were knotted or draped. Collector Daily observed that the curves and bodily fall of fabric added another physical behavior to the hardness of anonymous digital imagery.*14

The artist's official site traces a continuing change of support, from the 2015 Construction works using aluminum and chains to collages on canvas in the 2020s, continuing her move away from flat photographic printing.*16

Higher Pictures' archive likewise presents a continuous development from early stock-image works into fabric and three-dimensional formats, confirming the sustained movement between reused digital imagery and physical supports.*3

These changes show an ongoing test of what kinds of objects networked images can become, instead of fixing a recognizable “post-internet” look.*15

sections.title: Reception and Historical Position
sections.body_html:
The Production Conditions of Post-Internet Photography

Steciw herself has described “post-internet” less as the name of a stable style than as a term for a generation that knew life before the internet and then moved its entire working environment into networked conditions.*6 Focusing only on brightly colored collage or Plexiglas therefore misses the production conditions that matter to the work: search, compression, licensing, Photoshop, and output.

An earlier example is The Hole's 2011 exhibition Attachments, which brought together Steciw and other artists around a viewing environment in which announcements and artwork images circulated first as email attachments.*10 The New Yorker likewise described the exhibition as addressing the digital images encountered before and after a viewer sees the physical show.*11

ICP's 2014 exhibition What Is a Photograph? brought experiments from the 1970s into relation with the digital revolution, placing Steciw alongside Artie Vierkant, James Welling, Christopher Williams, Liz Deschenes, and other artists. ICP focused on practices that refused to confine photography to flat prints or camera capture, treating light, color, support, and mixtures of digital and analog processes as part of the work.*9 Steciw's inclusion therefore depended less on her status as a young artist “using the internet” than on her return of existing data to physical form and her reexamination of photographic support and authorship.

Aperture's review of the same exhibition connected the 2010s digital/material experiments to the history through which Conceptual art in the 1970s helped bring photography into the exhibition spaces of painting and sculpture. Steciw was presented at a point where the history of appropriation met the practical conditions of online search and digital manipulation.*4

Differences from Vierkant and Blalock

Using preexisting images did not begin with the internet. In the 1970s and 1980s, Pictures Generation artists such as Sherrie Levine, Richard Prince, and Louise Lawler rephotographed and repositioned magazine advertisements, art reproductions, and existing works in order to question authorship and the codes of representation. The Met identifies this generation as a major turn in appropriation: borrowing already existing images and changing their context became a central artistic operation.*25

Steciw shares with that history the refusal to make shooting the original image a requirement of authorship. The environment in which she searches for material, however, differs from the one in which Levine rephotographed reproductions of Walker Evans or Prince rephotographed magazine advertising. Prince began using advertisements left behind after his job clipping magazine articles at Time-Life, cropping, enlarging, and rephotographing them to disrupt the apparent naturalness of mass-media imagery.*26 For Steciw, the image is already tagged on a stock site and searchable as a JPEG carrying a price and license. The problem of authorship therefore expands from “whose photograph was borrowed?” to the infrastructure that moves images as commodities through keywords, licensing, compression, retouching, and output.

Artie Vierkant's Image Objects are produced as sculptural UV prints from digital files, then officially documented in photographs that are further altered before circulating online. This makes it difficult to decide whether the physical object or its JPEG is the “real” work.*22 Steciw also moves between data and object, but places greater weight on the anonymity of stock images, keywords, commercial retouching, and decorative commodity surfaces.

Lucas Blalock deliberately leaves Photoshop cloning, warping, and fills awkwardly visible, bringing onto the image surface digital operations that commercial photography normally hides. MoMA describes this as a practice that makes the relation between photography and editing software legible.*23 Steciw comes out of the same retouching culture but moves beyond leaving editing marks on a flat picture: she converts software “layers” into actual thickness through Plexiglas, cutting, chains, and fabric.

All three artists share a networked image environment, but the location of the problem differs. Vierkant focuses on the distinction between work and reproduction; Blalock on conventions that conceal digital processing; Steciw on the economy and division of labor through which commodity imagery is searched, purchased, and altered. The differences become clearer when “post-internet photography” names a question about which systems an image passes through before becoming an artwork, instead of a shared style.

ICP and FOAM in 2014

Also in 2014, FOAM's Under Construction placed Steciw alongside Jessica Eaton, Sara VanDerBeek, Lucas Blalock, Daniel Gordon, and others as a North American generation reconsidering the value and meaning of photography during digitization.*24 The artists did not share a single look; they shared an attention to collecting, constructing, and manipulating images across analog and digital methods and across flat and three-dimensional forms.

The comparison helps specify Steciw's method. Eaton uses analog multiple exposure to generate color inside the camera from gray three-dimensional objects, while VanDerBeek builds temporary sculptures for the camera and then dismantles them. Steciw can omit the act of photographing altogether and begin with JPEGs already circulating as commodities. Their responses to digitization therefore operate at different points: inside the camera, in the object built before exposure, and in the circulation of existing images.*24

During What Is a Photograph?, ICP also organized a lecture devoted to Steciw, treating her methods as a subject for education and theory as well as exhibition. The relation between online imagery and physical objecthood had entered a specialist photography institution as a problem of technique and medium.*19

Writing about the 2026 OSMOS Address exhibition, Collector Daily described works from 2023–26 that extend into inkjet on canvas, collage, and three-dimensional form, continuing Steciw's experiments with support and objecthood from her 2010s digital photocollages. OSMOS's archive likewise records Kate Steciw: Pictures, confirming the continuation of this work in current exhibitions.*17 Even after “post-internet” lost some of its usefulness as a period label, questions of image excess, reproduction, and materialization remained active in the work.*21

Steciw's distinction lies less in the fact that she used internet images than in her treatment of retouching, search, licensing, compression, printing, display, and rephotography as one photographic production process. Roughly a decade of commercial retouching connects that process to labor she actually performed and grounds the critique in firsthand experience of image industries. ICP and FOAM's decision to place such work at the center of major photography exhibitions in 2014 indicates that photography institutions themselves could no longer explain contemporary production solely by asking what an artist had photographed.*9

kazuyoshi-nomachi.html.lead_html: Kazuyoshi Nomachi spent years photographing the Sahara, the Nile, Ethiopia, Tibet, and Mecca, recording terrain, labor, pilgrimage, and praying bodies in color. The clear composition of advertising photography and the international color magazines of the 1970s shaped his visual language. A boy’s prayer witnessed in the Sahara, wide-ranging travel by car and aircraft, and repeated returns to the same places shaped his subjects and working duration. In Sahara, Bahar, Tibet, and Mecca Pilgrimage, he moved away from the instant of an event to report on the time of river basins and pilgrimage routes. The same books also raise a question: how does cross-cultural photography organize other cultures into a story of “land and prayer”?
kazuyoshi-nomachi.html.thesis_html: Nomachi shifted the unit of photojournalistic inquiry from events to deserts, river systems, and pilgrimage routes. Aerial views and long shots show the terrain and the movement of people; close views record individuals engaged in prayer and labor. His photobooks bring together the dry and rainy seasons, river source and mouth, and the departure and arrival of pilgrims across several years. He joined the communicative force of advertising photography and color magazines to long-term reporting. At the same time, his use of an “archetype of prayer” to connect different religions and societies risks reducing their historical and political differences.
