sections.title: Advertising, International Color Magazines, and the Sahara: The Formation of Nomachi’s Method
sections.body_html:
Bringing the Compositional Force of Advertising into Overseas Documentary Photography

Kazuyoshi Nomachi was born in Kochi Prefecture in 1946. After studying with photographer Takashi Kijima, he became independent in 1971*1. Before independence, he worked in advertising photography, learning how composition could communicate a product’s subject quickly, how to organize areas of color, and how light could attract attention in print. Nippon.com explains that Nomachi consciously carried the clear messages and vivid color of advertising into his later documentary work*7. He retained these skills after moving into reportage, using them to convey the relation among terrain, people, and ritual in a single image to international readers who did not share the language or historical background of his subjects.

The Sahara in 1972: From the Horizon to Water and Daily Life

The turning point came in 1972, when Nomachi visited the Sahara at the age of twenty-five. He has written that he traveled to North Africa out of a fascination with the horizon, then shifted his attention from photographing sand and rock to people searching for water, tending livestock, and moving across the desert*3. His interest in terrain moved from uninhabited spectacle to the ways water sources, pasture, trade routes, and differences between daytime and nighttime temperatures shaped daily life. Placing figures within the expanse of the desert allowed him to show the distances people walked and the places where they found water and shade, as well as the scale of the environment.

A Boy at Prayer and the Working Hypothesis of an “Archetype of Prayer”

Nomachi’s interest in religion was decisively shaped by the prayer of a sixteen-year-old boy who traveled with him in North Africa. He later described how the boy, who had been joking moments earlier, stood beyond a dune, bent, knelt, and repeatedly pressed his forehead to the ground*10. Photography cannot directly record an inner state of faith. It can register the body’s orientation, contact with the ground, repeated movement, distance traveled, and the flow of a crowd. From this encounter came a method that placed the desert, plateau, religious architecture, and pilgrimage route surrounding the body within the same body of work as close portraits.

Nomachi understood deserts and plateaus as “religious spaces” in which individuals confront a scale beyond themselves. After witnessing full-body prostration in Tibet, he began to seek an “archetype of prayer” across Islam, Christianity, and Buddhism*8. For the 2005 exhibition A Photographer’s Pilgrimage, he wrote that globalization was standardizing places around shared values of efficiency and convenience, while a renewed attachment to one’s own culture was intensifying through religious revival*16. The “archetype of prayer” became a working structure for considering what sustained local cultures amid increasing uniformity, as well as a search for bodily actions held in common. He linked standing, kneeling, touching the forehead to the ground, circling a sacred site, and walking great distances across the Sahara, Tibet, Mecca, the Ganges, and the Andes. This emphasis on commonality can also reduce differences of state, ethnicity, class, and religious institution.

Overseas Travel and Color Magazines as a Publishing Network in the 1970s

Nomachi’s long-term work abroad depended on more than individual resolve. During the 1970s, overseas travel from Japan became less costly and logistically easier. A travel boom and growing interest in other cultures helped international color magazines such as National Geographic and GEO reach large audiences*7. Sahara (1978) began as a dummy book submitted to Heibonsha and developed into a collaborative project that included the Italian publisher Mondadori, leading to editions in several countries*7. Color printing and international co-publication helped sustain hundreds of days of fieldwork as a profession. They also created pressure to condense complicated regions into forceful single images that could be understood at once.

sections.title: Cars, Aerial Photography, and Return Visits: Photographing Broad Geography Over Extended Time
sections.body_html:
Combining Wide-Ranging Travel with Long-Term Stays

Nomachi returned to the Sahara ten times through 1993, spending more than eight hundred days there in total. For his work on the Nile from 1980 to 1982, he used a Land Cruiser shipped from Japan as well as aircraft. Across five trips, he spent roughly four hundred days traveling through the basins of the White and Blue Nile*7. A short visit tends to center unfamiliar scenery; a stay in one place cannot account for the routes connecting source and mouth, dry and rainy seasons, or pastoral and agricultural life. Cars and aircraft allowed him to understand the terrain as a whole. Repeated visits then allowed him to photograph seasons, festivals, labor, and family time, presenting a region as a connected field of movement and daily life instead of a collection of isolated points.

Long Shots and Close Views: Geography as a Whole and the Individual Body

Luminous Landscape identifies Nomachi’s movement between long shots that place figures within vast terrain and close views of faces and bodies as a defining feature of his work*10. The long shots make water sources, grazing land, pilgrimage routes, rock-hewn churches, and the paths circling the Kaaba legible. The close views record fatigue, age, hands and feet, clothing, meals, and proximity to livestock. In Nomachi’s photobooks, elevated or aerial photographs of terrain and crowds are followed by close views of individuals made at ground level. The first describes routes of movement and collective structure; the second shows the bodies that travel those routes.

Color and Dramatic Light: The Selectivity of Immediate Legibility

Nomachi’s color photographs organize sand, rock, water, clothing, and religious architecture through firm contours and areas of color. White pilgrimage garments, red earth, blue shadows, golden sand, and the darkness inside rock-hewn churches allow readers across languages to distinguish climate, time of day, material, and ritual function quickly*7. Sunrise, reflected light on dunes, and beams entering a church also shape contemporary lives into epic and monumental scenes. This direct communicative force underlies international comparisons with Sebastião Salgado and Steve McCurry*10. The same form selects terrain, clothing, ritual, and light as the elements most likely to be remembered, while roads, urbanization, commodity circulation, and political institutions receive less attention.

sections.title: Major Works: The Sahara, the Nile, Tibet, Mecca, and Siberia
sections.body_html:
Sahara: From Desert Scenery to Lives in Motion

Sahara brought oases, nomadism, trade, gathering, and prayer into a regional sequence alongside the geometry of sand and sky. On the official Sahara Horizon page, Nomachi’s text and photographs trace his movement from uninhabited mineral landscapes toward the lives of people bound to the desert*3. Compositions pairing the horizon with a small figure show distances of travel and water. They can also condense a life into the emblem of a person enduring the land.

Bahar: Photographing the Nile as a Basin Across Borders

Bahar: Africa Flows was published in 1983, structuring the sources and mouth of the White and Blue Nile as a continuity of peoples, pastoral life, religion, and terrain*2. Views of the river, floodwater, cattle, settlements, rituals, and close portraits alternate, bringing several countries and ways of life connected to the water system into one book. Bahar and Sahara Everlasting earned Nomachi the third Domon Ken Award in 1984*1. The river itself, instead of a single event, became the unit of reportage.

Tibet: Altitude, Distance, and Full-Body Prostration

Nomachi’s coverage of China’s Long March, begun in 1988, led him to the Tibetan Plateau and was published in 1994 as Tibet: The Heavenly Land*2. The official Tibetan Plateau page brings Mount Kailash, Lake Manasarovar, grazing land, monasteries, and pilgrimage routes into the same album*4. Distant views of the plateau establish the length of the pilgrimage. Worn clothing, gloves, foreheads, and marks on the ground record what full-body prostration leaves on the body. The sacred site appears as an itinerary of altitude, cold, walking, and lodging, as well as a work of architecture.

Mecca Pilgrimage: Permission, Conversion, and a View of the Crowd

In 1994, a Saudi publisher commissioned Nomachi to photograph Medina. That year he recited the shahada and converted to Islam. Nippon.com records both his long-standing interest in Islam, beginning with the Sahara, and the practical conditions that made work in the holy cities possible*7. From 1995 to 2000, he photographed Mecca and Medina, recording the pilgrimage through tawaf, Arafat, Mina, and Muzdalifah from aerial views of crowds and ground-level views of individuals*6. The official Mecca page shows the circular movement around the Kaaba, prayer, travel, and rest as a continuous sequence*5.

The English-language book Mecca, the Blessed, Medina, the Radiant combines Nomachi’s photographs with texts by the Islamic scholar Seyyed Hossein Nasr and historical materials*11. A Photographer’s Pilgrimage brings the Sahara, Tibet, Mecca, and the Andes together as a “path of prayer”*12. The combination of photographs and explanatory texts situates religious ritual through architecture, history, and routes of pilgrimage; it also integrates different faiths into a single spiritual history.

Siberian Prison Camp 1992: State and History Beyond Prayer

Reducing Nomachi’s work to prayer and pilgrimage omits another axis of his career as a photojournalist. In March 1992, immediately after the collapse of the Soviet Union, he photographed a corrective labor camp near Khabarovsk in the Russian Far East. Exhibition materials from the Japan Professional Photographers Society describe the series as a record of two connected subjects: a system that used prisoners as labor, and the uneventful daily routines that continued inside it. The work was made during a brief period when state control had loosened*19. Here the expansive land does not serve as a setting for religious transcendence. It is the place where the state isolated and managed people, and the prisoners’ repetitive lives register institutional time instead of faith. The series shows that Nomachi’s long-term fieldwork and his placement of figures within an environment could record political systems and history as well as sacred places.

sections.title: Access to Sacred Places, Cross-Cultural Imagery, and Nomachi’s Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Becoming a Participant Does Not Remove the Conditions of Access

Non-Muslims are not permitted to enter Mecca. Nomachi’s photographs depended on a Saudi commission, special permissions, conversion, and participation in the pilgrimage on several occasions. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum situates his work from 1995 to 2000 as a long-term record of Mecca and the pilgrimage*6. Conversion allowed him to enter the ritual route, but did not make the photographer a complete insider to the community. The places he could photograph, the aerial viewpoints available to him, and the scenes that could be published were structured by religious institutions and state authorization. The exceptional perspectives of the work cannot be separated from these conditions of access.

The Risk That Long-Term Documentation Produces an “Unchanging Tradition”

The ethnographic impulse to preserve a culture in a supposedly pure form before it disappears has been criticized as a “salvage paradigm”*13. When roads, state institutions, tourists, communications technology, and urban labor appear infrequently in Nomachi’s frames while ritual and the natural environment dominate, the people photographed can be read as bearers of a culture unchanged since antiquity. A 2015 FUJIFILM SQUARE exhibition described the work as “a documentary of land and people,” while also presenting the living environment and spiritual cultures of the photographed regions as “almost unchanged”*15. This reception shows both the photographs’ ability to connect land and life and the risk of interpreting a changing society as an enduring tradition. National Geographic has itself acknowledged a history of depicting non-Western people as exotic and close to nature while giving insufficient attention to race, power, and politics*14. Nomachi’s “archetype of prayer” can likewise push local institutions and histories into the background when it gathers bodily actions from different sects and societies into a single universality.

Nomachi’s fieldwork, however, was not a succession of one-time journeys. He returned to the Sahara, the Nile, Ethiopia, and Tibet, photographing different seasons and decades. The Setagaya Art Museum’s 2025 exhibition placed early photographs beside later returns and took political instability, urbanization, mobile phones, and other changes in the photographed regions as part of its premise*9. Reading these recorded changes alongside the monumental scenes of prayer allows the work to be assessed as more than the preservation of a “vanishing tradition.”

From Events to River Basins and Pilgrimage Routes: Nomachi’s Place in Color Documentary Photography

When Nomachi began working abroad in the 1970s, the weekly edition of LIFE had ended. Monthly magazines such as National Geographic and GEO were gaining influence by presenting distant lands and cultures in large-format color*7. Nomachi retained photography’s reportorial ability to communicate distant circumstances, but he did not use the time of a war or political event as the basic unit of inquiry. Over several years, he photographed lives crossing deserts, the Nile basin, routes taken by pilgrims, and seasonal festivals, assembling aerial photographs, long shots, and close views in photobooks.

The compositional discipline of advertising, the expansion of overseas travel, international color magazines and co-publication, and movement by car and aircraft gave Nomachi’s form its visual and material conditions. Repeated visits totaling hundreds of days and his hypothesis that an “archetype of prayer” could be sought through terrain and the body shaped its duration and subject. Its historical distinction lies in retaining the communicative force of photojournalism while shifting the subject from the event to the river basin and pilgrimage route, and the duration from an instant to several years. The same clear color and monumental composition organize different societies into a universal account of “land and prayer.” The strength of the long record and the limitations of cross-cultural imagery made for international magazines must be examined within the same photographs.

International reception has valued both the reportorial and formal qualities of Nomachi’s work. Le vie del sacro, held at MACRO/La Pelanda in Rome from 2013 to 2014, was his first European retrospective. It divided roughly two hundred photographs into seven sections; the official materials praised pictorial compositions in which figures and landscape merge, and light that remains descriptive while carrying a sense of transcendence*17. In 2014, the Photographic Society of Japan presented Nomachi with its International Award for contributions to international photographic culture*20. Alongside the duration of his fieldwork, this reception depended on images whose strong color, horizons, and crowds could be grasped across national borders.

Later retrospectives have moved beyond defining Nomachi solely as a photographer of sacred places. A 2023 exhibition at the Museum of Art, Kochi assembled 215 photographs in three parts: “A Documentary of Land and People,” World Heritage sites, and Siberian Prison Camp 1992. It placed work made in religious spaces and within state institutions in the same career*18. Understanding Nomachi’s form requires both the photographs that place praying bodies against the scale of the land and those that record bodies confined by the state. The method of organizing broad geography and extended time within a single image and across a photobook remains consistent, while the forces it describes differ among religion, nature, and the state.

keizo-kitajima.html.lead_html: Keizo Kitajima began in the 1970s at CAMP in Shinjuku, where he exhibited and published Photo Express: Tokyo every month. In NEW YORK (1981–82), he photographed people on the street at close range with flash, often shooting without fully looking through the viewfinder. After working in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, he turned in the 1990s to PORTRAITS, photographing the same sitters against a white background year after year, and from the 2000s to UNTITLED RECORDS, a long-term study of anonymous places. Moving from Leica snapshots to repeated 8×10 portraits and serial landscape records, Kitajima repeatedly questioned methods that had already worked for him.
keizo-kitajima.html.thesis_html: Kitajima took up the post-PROVOKE problem of the photographer’s subjectivity from a different direction: instead of repeating the look of are-bure-boke, he asked how far his own intention could be reduced. When he entered the WORKSHOP photography school in 1975, are-bure-boke had, in his own account, shifted from “resistance” to an imitable style, while roughening an image in the darkroom only brought the photographer’s hand back into it. He responded with the even light of flash, shooting without a viewfinder, and methods that compressed the interval from exposure to exhibition and booklet publication, trying to accept images produced through chance rather than make them conform to a prior intention. In Koza, however, he confronted the fact that even mechanical shooting could not erase the political position of “someone from mainland Japan photographing people in Okinawa.” In NEW YORK, PORTRAITS, and UNTITLED RECORDS, he went on to reconsider, by different means, the decisive moment, the supposedly “characteristic” portrait, unusual subject matter, and places whose meaning can be explained at a glance. As a photographer of the generation that sought an “actual” photography after the era of political movements and saw are-bure-boke shift from a form of resistance into an imitable style, he continued to ask how much of the image the photographer should control and where the camera should take over. That sustained question defines Kitajima’s position in photographic history.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
The “Actual” after the Political Movements

Kitajima entered photography not in the midst of the student and antiwar movements around 1968, but in the mid-1970s, when their charge still lingered in photography and magazines. In an SFMOMA interview, he recalled that after the worldwide political movements and protests of 1968, photography in 1970s Japan appeared to him as an “actual” and forceful medium—more radical than fine art.*2 PROVOKE likewise emerged at the end of the 1960s, amid the Anpo protests, anti–Vietnam War demonstrations, and university conflicts, from a sense that established press and commercial photography could not answer the changes taking place in society.*9 Research on the period also shows that the equation “photograph a protest and the result is a political photograph” had reached an impasse; around PROVOKE, photographers increasingly recognized that conventional protest photography could not itself change society.*20 Nobuyoshi Araki’s Satchin and Daido Moriyama’s Accident, which Kitajima encountered in high school, and the Moriyama class at WORKSHOP that he joined after leaving university, were part of the photographic urgency that remained after that “season of politics.”*25 For Kitajima, photography was compelling less as a vehicle for political slogans than as a medium that could take him into the street and respond on the spot to the people and cities of his time.

The Mechanical Image after PROVOKE

To describe PROVOKE simply as photography that aggressively asserted the photographer’s subjectivity captures only part of its connection to Kitajima. SFMOMA summarizes its legacy through are-bure-boke—grainy, blurry, out-of-focus images—together with ideas of subjectivity and anti-commercialism.*3 Philip Charrier’s study of Koji Taki’s photographic theory, however, argues that PROVOKE also sought to question the “truths” produced by established knowledge and relations of power, using photography’s automatic character to expose them.*10 Another study of urban photography in the 1960s notes that Taki and Takuma Nakahira treated the camera’s nonhuman, automatic, and mechanical properties as a way to escape artistic intention and preexisting meaning.*19 PROVOKE therefore held two impulses at once: the force of the photographer’s body and subjectivity, and a desire for moments when the world registered as an image beyond the photographer’s intention. By 1975, when Kitajima entered WORKSHOP, the look of are-bure-boke had itself become a reproducible style. He later recalled that “handmade” are-bure-boke—scratching film and roughening the image in the darkroom—only brought the author’s intention back into the picture. He pointed instead to Nakahira sending color reversal film directly to the lab, and to Moriyama’s interest in the flash photography of Weegee and Katsumi Watanabe as a form of “machinism” based on even artificial light; Kitajima said he had no intention of continuing are-bure-boke himself.*25 What he carried forward was less the rough surface than the unresolved question of what the camera might record before the photographer has decided what it means.

From Koza to New York

Koza, Okinawa, not long after reversion to Japan, was where Kitajima learned that the idea “let the machine decide and the author’s intention disappears” was not enough. In a later interview, he called it a mistake to believe that, as someone from mainland Japan, he could stand outside history as a “pure” presence and that accidents produced by the camera could likewise be pure. The act of photographing still contained the asymmetry of mainland/Okinawa and photographer/photographed.*18 The problem extended to publication. As “Okinawa” became a larger issue the more he photographed in Koza, he found himself unable to show the work fully; afterward, he decided to photograph only in places where he was prepared to make the results public.*1 Explaining why he chose New York in 1981, Kitajima said he imagined that a city where high-rise wealth and cultural power coexisted with poverty at street level might make the positions of photographer and photographed less fixed than they had been in Okinawa.*25 The move from Koza to NEW YORK was therefore partly a search for a place where that relationship might not remain predetermined. In Okinawa he had been “the person from the mainland who came to photograph”; in New York he entered the same streets as a poor foreigner himself and tried to work in a situation that was not simply one of observing others from outside.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Photo Express: Tokyo

In Photo Express: Tokyo, Kitajima changed the exhibition at CAMP every month from January through December 1979 and simultaneously issued twelve sixteen-page booklets.*8 In his own recollection, he sometimes turned the exhibition room into a darkroom, projected images directly onto sheets of photographic paper covering the walls, applied developer and fixer with sponges, and displayed the results in that state.*22 Kitajima instead sought to compress the interval among shooting, developing, exhibiting, publishing, and circulation, allowing chance that escaped a prior intention to enter the work itself.*23 At CAMP, photographs made in a given month appeared on the wall and in a sixteen-page booklet that same month instead of being culled for years before being shown as “finished works.” Keeping shooting and publication almost simultaneous was itself the method of Photo Express: Tokyo.

Direct Flash and Shooting without a Viewfinder

In Kitajima’s early photographs, close-range flash cuts faces and clothing sharply out of the night street, while shooting from waist level without fully looking through the viewfinder produces cropped bodies and tilted frames. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum identifies this as a defining feature of the New York period, where the method produced unpredictable compositions and hard outlines.*4 Writing about CAMP 1979, Kitajima said that he wanted to make images through a “mechanical” method beyond his own control, using chance as a way to experience the world instead of realizing a preconceived intention in the photograph.*23 He lit dark alleys with the same flash output and did not compose each person carefully in the viewfinder. The camera and light were expected to make an image before the photographer’s judgment of “how I want this to look.” Koza exposed the limit of that idea. Even if the image was handed over to the machine, Kitajima’s position as a mainland photographer pointing a camera at people in Okinawa remained embedded in the historical asymmetry of mainland/Okinawa and photographer/photographed.*18 Reducing the photographer’s feelings did not erase the photographer’s social position. That gap became unavoidable in Koza.

NEW YORK

After moving to New York, Kitajima said he walked the city as a poor foreign photographer himself and felt less able to draw a clear boundary between his own position and the people on the street.*25 Clubgoers, passersby, people living on the street, celebrities, and figures in advertisements all entered the same flow of shooting; clothing, faces, signage, and artificial light collided in the frame before biography or psychology could explain the subject. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum records roughly nine hundred rolls of film and some 35,000 exposures from this period, making the city itself a field of intensive photographing and selection.*4 In Koza, the position of “a person from mainland Japan photographing people in Okinawa” had remained in place. In New York, Kitajima entered the same streets as a foreigner struggling with rent and living expenses, trying to keep the role of “an outsider observing the city’s people” from becoming equally fixed.

Eastern Europe and USSR 1991

In Eastern Europe in 1983–84, Kitajima gradually moved away from the hard flash of the New York period and began to photograph faces and upper bodies in natural light. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum describes this shift as a move from the stimulation of the street toward a stronger interest in individual faces.*4 When he repeatedly visited the Soviet Union from late 1990 through 1991, he was struck by the rapid collapse of a Cold War structure that had existed since before he was born.*2 Even so, he did not immediately gather those photographs into a book. He later said he intended to wait at least ten years so the faces would not be read only through the label “Soviet citizens just before the collapse.”*4 The photographer who had shown pictures in the same month he made them in 1979 now waited more than a decade. He wanted the faces to escape the news headline “people just before the fall of the Soviet Union.”

PORTRAITS

Around 1991, after roughly fifteen years of street snapshots, Kitajima felt he had reached their limit and moved toward PORTRAITS, separating the face from the street.*25 What troubled him was the mechanism by which portrait photography chooses one “most characteristic” face and fixes a person’s identity through that image. He called the convention of selecting a single flattering funeral portrait a “terrifying enemy” of portraiture.*25 He therefore established a set of rules: an 8×10 camera, landscape orientation, a white background, a white shirt, and the same sitter photographed again each year. He avoided vertical framing because it could too easily turn the person into a symbol, and he removed the photographer’s freedom to decide that “the first year’s photograph is better.”*25 Both pictures show the same person, yet neither can be singled out as the “true” person. Creating that condition was central to PORTRAITS.

sections.title: Major Works, Photobooks, and Exhibitions
sections.body_html:
Photo Express: Tokyo, 1979

Photo Express: Tokyo was made very differently from a photobook that retrospectively collects a photographer’s finished masterpieces. Twelve exhibitions and twelve sixteen-page booklets proceeded on the same monthly cycle in 1979, with the selection and printing of each issue leading directly into the next round of shooting.*8 The Steidl/LE BAL facsimile preserves the original twelve-booklet format and emphasizes that the monthly exhibitions and publications were produced together.*7 The close-up figure in the work held by the MFAH functions less as an isolated representative image than as one face among many arriving in sequence across the pages.*6 Research on PROVOKE has stressed photography as a medium that encounters the city through paper, printing, and successive pages, not only through the formal perfection of a single print.*19 In Photo Express: Tokyo, that media logic took the concrete form of producing CAMP’s monthly exhibition and sixteen-page booklet at the same time. Photographs made in Shinjuku only weeks earlier were returned immediately to the city on CAMP’s walls and through inexpensive printed booklets, before the photographer could later redefine a few of them as “representative works.”

NEW YORK, 1981–82

NEW YORK combines black-and-white and color photographs, placing clubs and streets, anonymous passersby and famous figures, within the same flow of shooting. In the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s NEW YORK Club STUDIO 54, direct flash cuts clubgoers and lighting fixtures with the same hard illumination.*16 In East Village, the close crop does not fully isolate the figure from the setting; clothing and signage remain attached to the surface of the city.*15 The photobook NEW YORK received the Kimura Ihei Award in 1983 and established Kitajima as a major figure in Japanese street photography. He later lost faith, however, in a method built around selecting the instant that happened to be cut most effectively, and he abandoned the approach that had first brought him recognition.

USSR 1991 and PORTRAITS

USSR 1991 was not published in a consolidated form immediately after it was photographed. After a 2007 exhibition and a 2012 photobook, the 2025 edition brought together ninety-five color photographs from the former Soviet Union with fifty-seven black-and-white photographs made in Eastern Europe in 1983–84.*17 SFMOMA’s 12/10/1991 Moscow, Russian SFSR, USSR carries the date of the state’s collapse in its title, yet Kitajima avoided immediately circulating the work as news photographs of “citizens just before the fall of the Soviet Union.”*21 PORTRAITS avoids another kind of headline: “this face is this person.” The same sitter returns a year later under the same conditions, and the images are given equal weight. USSR 1991 steps back from the label of a historical event; PORTRAITS steps back from the label that reduces a person to one representative face.

UNTITLED RECORDS, 2014–21

UNTITLED RECORDS is a serial photobook project of twenty volumes and 320 photographs published from 2014 to 2021, made in hard-to-name places across Japan from Hokkaido to Okinawa, including disaster areas in Sanriku and Fukushima.*13 The publisher, photographers’ gallery / KULA, describes the project as emerging after the earthquake, nuclear disaster, and globalization had unsettled the distinction between the reality before one’s eyes and images arriving from elsewhere.*14 Kitajima has said more recently that he became tired of making “interesting photographs” out of unusual people in back alleys or conspicuous clothing, and wanted to avoid a situation in which a photograph’s interest depended only on the novelty or attributes of its subject.*25 In landscapes as well, he has emphasized seemingly “meaningless places”—a white wall whose subject is not immediately clear—or elements that make the viewer stumble over an easy reading of the frame.*25 UNTITLED RECORDS therefore does not search only for symbolic places that instantly explain tsunami destruction or nuclear disaster. It deliberately keeps its distance from pictures that immediately answer, “this is a disaster zone” or “this is a ruin.”

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photo History
sections.body_html:
Criticism of the Close-Range Flash

Kitajima’s early photographs were not immediately accepted as canonical examples of what is now called Japanese street photography. Materials for his retrospective at the Nagano Prefectural Art Museum cite Daido Moriyama’s description of him as a “mugger in broad daylight” and criticism of his flash by Kazuo Nishii, then editor of Camera Mainichi.*5 Blasting a person with artificial light at close range and taking the image before consent or psychological explanation could enter the encounter gave the same method that Kitajima valued for its chance effects an unmistakable aggression. In Koza, Kitajima himself recognized that “the person taking the photograph is stronger.” Moriyama’s and Nishii’s criticisms therefore concerned the act of firing a flash directly in front of another person, not simply a preference for rough or polished images.

Comparisons in International Criticism

When Kitajima has been presented abroad, his early and late works have often been connected to very different photographic histories. Reviewing a New York exhibition in 2009, The New Yorker wrote that his dark, uneasy street photographs brought Brassaï, Leon Levinstein, and Daido Moriyama to mind.*11 Conscientious Photography Magazine, by contrast, compared the white background and frontal structure of PORTRAITS with Thomas Ruff while stressing a major difference: Kitajima photographs the same person repeatedly at yearly intervals.*26 Kitajima has explained that this repetition was intended to produce the problem that “both photographs are you, and yet neither is you.”*25 These are not claims of direct influence from Brassaï or Ruff. They show that international criticism has tended to place the early work in a lineage of close engagement with the nocturnal street and the later work in a lineage that tests the conventions of photographic portraiture.

The Rules of PORTRAITS

The move to the large-format camera was not welcomed without reservation. Reviewing the 2009 retrospective, Kotaro Iizawa read the path from shooting without a viewfinder and using flash to PORTRAITS as a continuing effort at “self-erasure,” reducing the photographer’s taste and compositional preferences; in the later work, he argued, that erasure was built into the procedure in advance.*24 At the same time, Iizawa asked whether the logically ordered rules had diminished the contingency and danger of the early snapshots.*24 PORTRAITS makes comparison possible under the same conditions each year, but the abrupt cuts and street-level collisions of the earlier work disappear. Iizawa’s criticism asks what may have been lost when the rules became more rigorous.

“There Are No Old Photographs”

In interviews around his 2025–26 retrospective, Kitajima has said that older photographs can be placed in new combinations through editing in the present and that “there are no old photographs.”*25 The curator at the Nagano Prefectural Art Museum followed that idea by avoiding a simple chronology and allowing early and recent photographs to move back and forth across the exhibition.*25 Kitajima received the Ina Nobuo Award for USSR 1991 in 2007*12 and the Domon Ken Award for UNTITLED RECORDS in 2022.*13 The works recognized by major awards thus extend far beyond his early flash photographs, encompassing the Soviet and landscape projects of later decades. As in the 2025 publication that recombined Soviet photographs from 1991 with images from Eastern Europe, the date of exposure is not allowed to dictate the single “correct” way a photograph must be read.

kelli-connell.html.lead_html: Kelli Connell is a photographer known for Double Life, a series in which a single model performs two roles and separate negatives or image files are seamlessly composited. By making two figures who appear to be lovers turn out to be the same person, Connell brings gender, sexuality, self-image, and photography’s status as evidence into the same frame. In the more recent Pictures for Charis, she revisits the story of Edward Weston and Charis Wilson through a queer, collaborative practice.
kelli-connell.html.thesis_html: In Double Life, Connell kept digital compositing visually unobtrusive and used it to make a single model appear as a couple, allowing posture and clothing to suggest two distinct roles. The same body appears in a single frame as lover, double, and opposing self. By placing fiction inside an image that retains photographic realism, the series unsettles both documentary credibility and the habit of reading gender and intimacy as fixed roles.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Connell was born in Oklahoma City and earned a BFA from the University of North Texas and an MFA from Texas Woman’s University. From early on, she was interested in how viewers infer personality and even the nature of a relationship from the direction of a body, clothing, and physical distance in a photograph. The Museum of Contemporary Photography situates her work around questions of identity and social constructions that are activated in the viewer. *5 In an interview with Strange Fire Collective, Connell explains that her first high-school photography class led her toward the medium and that Double Life developed into a long-term project through which she examined self-understanding and the roles people assume in relationships. *4

Double Life began in the early 2000s, as Photoshop-based image manipulation was becoming part of photography’s everyday vocabulary. In a 2004 exhibition, Lawndale Art Center placed Connell within the “Photoshop Generation” while emphasizing doubling, gender, and role-playing over technical trickery itself. *2 Alice Austen House likewise describes the twenty-year series as an autobiographical inquiry into sexuality and gender roles. *3

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Why Double Life Turns One Person into Two

The decision to make one model appear as two people gives multiple, shifting roles within a relationship the same body. In an interview with Strange Fire Collective, Connell says that Double Life began after the end of a long-term relationship, when she started reconsidering her sexuality and the roles she had performed within relationships*4. Different clothing, postures, lines of sight, and degrees of physical distance make masculine/feminine, active/passive, supporting/supported positions appear as roles that can exchange places within one person. The Met describes The Valley as a work made by photographing one model multiple times and digitally joining the images so that they appear to depict a relationship between two women*1.

In an interview with Time Out Chicago, Connell explains that she watched body language and clothing in places such as supermarkets and gay bars, thinking about how quickly people infer gender and the roles of a couple from those cues*15. In Double Life, gestures move back and forth within the same body without settling neatly into conventional butch/femme roles. Because the scenes resemble ordinary photographs of couples, the viewer’s own act of assigning roles from posture, distance, and clothing becomes part of how the image works.

Seamless Compositing and Doubt about Photographic “Evidence”

The concealment of the composite is essential. Connell photographs the model in separate roles with a medium-format camera while keeping location and light consistent, then joins the images. MoCP’s account emphasizes how body language, clothing, and lighting establish the emotional distance between the two figures and allow the scene to register first as an everyday moment. *5 Catherine Edelman Gallery’s 2011 exhibition similarly identifies the seamless combination of a single model performing two roles as central to the work’s appearance as an ordinary relationship photograph. *20 In an interview with The Advocate, Connell also explains that she was drawn to photography not because it could certify “truth,” but because it could generate questions for the viewer. *6 The fiction in Double Life therefore does not announce the failure of photographic truth. It first earns belief, then makes the basis of that belief uncertain.

Model, Performance, and Self-Timer: The Roles of Photographer and Subject

Connell’s long collaboration with model Kiba Jacobson does not follow a portrait structure in which the photographer alone determines the subject’s image. According to an interview with BLOW Photo, Connell used the self-timer to test positions herself, working out bodily orientation and points of contact as she constructed a scene. *7 A conversation published by Yoffy Press discusses the self-timer as a way to reduce the fixed power difference between photographer and “muse.” *8

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Twenty Years Change the Bodies of the “Two” Women

Works including Picnic, The Valley, Carnival, Reflection, and Head to Head carry the pleasures of romantic attachment alongside silence, fatigue, arguments, consolation, and solitude, as if they belonged to the history of the same two people. Alice Austen House’s Double Life, 20 Years made the duration of the series central to the exhibition, tracing the model’s body from early scenes that perform a relationship between young women into middle age*3.

Twenty years also introduced aging into a project already concerned with gender and sexuality. A 2021 Musée Magazine review reads the model’s movement from youth into middle age as bringing female aging—still underrepresented in visual culture—into the frame*16. Here digital compositing does not function as retouching that fixes the body at a younger age. Across the doubled images, it records how the same person changes over two decades.

Pictures for Charis and a Reconsideration of the Weston/Wilson Story

In the more recent Pictures for Charis, Connell studied Edward Weston’s photographs and Charis Wilson’s writings, then traveled with her partner Betsy Odom through parts of the American West where Weston and Wilson had lived and worked. The Cleveland Museum of Art presents the series as a reconsideration of Wilson’s life, which has often been simplified in the shadow of Weston’s canonical reputation, through several overlapping positions: photographer/subject, man/woman, heterosexual/queer. *9 The High Museum explains that nearly a decade of research and repeated travel also raised the problem of how a photographer might avoid flattening another person’s life. *10 Aperture likewise describes the book as visual research that combines photographs and writing. *11

Pictures for Charis also changes Connell’s method. Aperture’s publication materials describe it as her first project to combine photography and writing as methods of visual research and storytelling*17. Double Life creates fiction within the boundaries of a single photograph. Pictures for Charis instead brings together archival research, travel photographs, Wilson’s writing, Weston’s photographs, and Connell’s own experience with her partner, using that sequence to investigate and revise a received photographic history.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photo History
sections.body_html:
Comparing Cindy Sherman and Francesca Woodman: From Role-Playing to Intimate Collaboration

Connell’s work is frequently compared with Cindy Sherman, although Connell does not identify Sherman as a primary early influence. She says that she was drawn to photography immediately after her first high-school class and names Francesca Woodman, Larry Sultan, and Roni Horn among the artists who strongly affected her early development; Sherman, she explains, was not one of the principal influences at that stage. *14 The comparison between Connell and Sherman rests more on formal proximity: one body performing multiple roles and scenes with a cinematic charge. Because Connell assigns two roles to the same model instead of staging herself, the question shifts from “Who do I appear to be?” toward the possibility that what looks like a relationship between two people may also describe multiplicity within one person.

While developing Pictures for Charis, Connell researched photographic histories built around the long-term photographing of intimate partners. She has said that she studied Alfred Stieglitz and Georgia O’Keeffe, Seiichi Furuya and Christine Gössler, and Edward Weston and Charis Wilson*4. The positions of viewer/viewed and lover/self that one model performed in Double Life became, in Pictures for Charis, a question of how to make portraits collaboratively with an actual partner. The Cleveland Museum of Art likewise describes the act of lovers photographing one another as an intimate form of collaboration*19. Connell’s work sits where two histories meet: performed identity and the sustained relationship between photographer and partner.

In Pictures for Charis, the question already present in Double Life—who performs whom, and who looks at whom—is redirected toward the historical photographer/model relationship of Weston and Wilson. An exhibition at the Center for Creative Photography foregrounds portraiture as a record of the relationship between photographer and sitter, while Cleveland’s related programming places Connell’s work within her continuing inquiry into gender, sexuality, and identity. *12 Columbia College Chicago’s profile also shows that she has continued to make work while teaching photography since Double Life. *13 Connell’s distinctive strategy is to keep Photoshop from becoming the visual event: she first lets an image pass as an ordinary photograph of a couple, then returns the question to the viewer—why did you assume there were two people? She repeated that structure for more than two decades.

Digital Compositing in the Early 2000s: The Critical Force of Hiding the Technique

Double Life began at a moment when digital compositing had itself become part of the debate over photographic truth. Lawndale Art Center’s 2004 exhibition connected Connell to the “Photoshop Generation,” discussing digital technology alongside Surrealist doubling and gender roles. *2 Connell, however, does not place Photoshop itself at the center of the work. She develops the film, tests possible pairings by hand from contact sheets, scans the negatives, and finally joins them seamlessly so that viewers can, at least initially, believe that both figures occupied the same moment. *14

Writing on digital photography has examined this compositing in relation to photography and reality. Yi-Hui Huang analyzes Double Life as an example of digital compositing that joins images that never existed in a single exposure and gives photographic form to a “reality” unavailable to direct vision*18. The two women in Connell’s frame were never simultaneously present, yet the project begins from the experience of contradictory roles, desires, and self-images coexisting within one person. The composite therefore gives two bodies to a psychological and social multiplicity that a single exposure cannot show simultaneously in one body.

For Connell, digitization is not a competition to display the traces of manipulation. It is necessary to establish the premise that two people shared the same place, then undo that premise afterward. Connell has said that creating emotional weight and tension matters more than the Photoshop process itself. *14 Within queer self-representation in the 2000s, her work also avoids presenting sexual identity as a single label. Instead, it embeds a person’s movement between active/passive, masculine/feminine, supporting/supported positions within a relationship in a form that looks as ordinary as possible: the couple photograph. Hiding the technique creates the conditions for questioning fixed gender roles and photography’s evidentiary authority at the same time.

Why Double Life Looks Like a Real Couple Photograph: The Viewer’s Misreading

Double Life changes once the composite is recognized. At first, viewers may read the image as an ordinary photograph of lovers and infer a relationship from the angle of a shoulder or the direction of a gaze. Once they learn that both figures are the same person, the body language they had treated as “evidence” of a relationship becomes multiple roles performed by one individual. MoCP addresses both the technical construction and the psychological dimension because this two-stage reading is built into the work*5. If the composite were conspicuous, the viewer could distance the image as fabricated from the outset. Connell instead matches lighting, focus, and domestic details closely enough to create the time of an ordinary snapshot. The central issue is not whether the viewer can detect Photoshop, but how quickly a single photograph is used to infer lovers, gender, and personality. Connell’s account of the self as fluid takes concrete form in this act of misreading*4.

kikuji-kawada.html.lead_html: Kikuji Kawada joined close views of the Atomic Bomb Dome, war relics, flags, and fragments around American bases through dense contrast in the photobook The Map, turning postwar memory into a material experience of the book. Kohei Sugiura’s design, double-page spreads, foldouts, and recurring darkness made photography less an explanation of place than a structure for encountering history when it cannot be read easily.
kikuji-kawada.html.thesis_html: In The Map, Kawada arranged walls inside the Atomic Bomb Dome, war relics, flags, and fragments of occupation culture across dense spreads and foldouts, tracing postwar memory through material residue. Through close-up, dark printing, and Kohei Sugiura’s book design, he transferred the survival of history as fragments in the present into the structure of the book He expanded the photobook from a container for images into a medium that requires readers to open, return, and test relations among photographs.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
VIVO and Postwar Japanese Photography: Making Photobooks Beyond Reportage

Kawada worked in the photography department at Shinchosha before forming VIVO in 1959 with Shomei Tomatsu, Eikoh Hosoe, Ikko Narahara, Akira Sato, and Akira Tanno. Although the collective dissolved after a short period, it provided a setting in which photographers could publish self-directed work outside magazine assignments and determine both subject and editing*1. For Kawada, photographing the postwar period came to mean combining material remnants and fragments of memory in a photobook rather than explaining events chronologically.

Twenty Years After Defeat: The Historical Distance of The Map

The first edition of The Map appeared in 1965, twenty years after Japan’s defeat and the atomic bombings. Reconstruction and rapid economic growth were advancing, while the bomb, occupation, military bases, and war responsibility remained unresolved. The Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art presents the book as an allegorical response to the political and social conditions of postwar Japan*2. Kawada did not photograph from the position of immediate aftermath; he approached memory through traces that had persisted and eroded over time.

Shinchosha and VIVO: From Press Photography to an Independent Series

At Shinchosha, Kawada photographed gravure features for Shukan Shincho and learned how photographs were joined to articles, headlines, and print. When he left in 1959 and joined VIVO, he entered an environment in which the subject and mode of presentation of a series could be self-determined*1. This publishing experience became a foundation for The Map, whose meaning depends on multiple images and book design rather than on an isolated photograph.

From Magazine Editing to The Map: Turning Information into Page-Bound Memory

At Shinchosha, Kawada observed the process by which news photographs were organized into the meaning of an article. After joining VIVO, he photographed walls in the Atomic Bomb Dome, war relics, flags, and fragments around American bases, colliding distant images across spreads. He later described coming to see stains on walls and surviving objects as images capable of symbolizing memories of war*4. The form of The Map replaced the sequential explanation of reportage with a bodily encounter in which defeat’s remaining signs are approached by opening pages, returning to earlier images, and unfolding inserts.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
The Map: Why Did Kawada Photograph the Walls of the Atomic Bomb Dome at Close Range?

At the center of The Map are close photographs of dark stains and peeling surfaces on walls inside the Atomic Bomb Dome. Removed from architectural overview and explanatory evidence, the wall becomes an abstract field resembling ground, skin, or astronomical imagery. The Met’s copy of the book shows these images joined on spreads with war relics, flags, advertisements, and photographs from areas around American bases*3. Close-up gives priority to material alteration inscribed on the surface over the name of the object. It is the distance at which history appears sedimented in matter.

Close-Up and Darkness: Making Difficulty of Reading a Historical Condition

Extreme proximity to the Dome walls removes the building’s overall form and location from the frame, leaving stains, cracks, and peeling surfaces. Kawada narrows information through proximity and concentrates historical duration in damage and residue. For a later photographer unable to record the instant of destruction, the limit of approaching history through material traces appears as difficulty of reading the image. The archive of negatives, contact sheets, notes, and books acquired by the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, shows that these abstract pictures were selected through on-site work and careful editing*18.

What Place Does The Map Show? From Geography to the Structure of Memory

The title The Map does not function like an ordinary map that locates Hiroshima or Japan with precision. As the book proceeds, stains, soldiers’ belongings, signs of occupation, the Japanese flag, and Coca-Cola advertisements recur, placing different times and places within one dark terrain. An Aperture interview discusses The Map as a work that established the photobook as an artistic object and made political and social criticism through abstract, experimental form*4. Information does not move in a single explanatory direction; relations among fragments are tested through movement back and forth across pages.

Kohei Sugiura’s Book Design: How Material Form Carries Historical Meaning

Kohei Sugiura’s design for the 1965 edition incorporated a double slipcase, a folded cover, and heavy black printing, making the acts of opening and turning pages part of the work. Photographs emerge from dark pages, apart from isolated display on a white wall, and acquire different meanings through neighboring images*3. Design becomes a medium for the difficulty of approaching history and the bodily time of excavating memory, not an exterior decoration applied to photographs.

Published on August 6, 1965: Presenting War Memory Twenty Years Later

The Map was published on August 6, 1965, exactly twenty years after the atomic bombing of Hiroshima*7. At a time when memories of defeat were being organized through official commemoration and narratives of reconstruction, Kawada fragmented maps, flags, relics, occupation culture, and walls into a book that withheld a clear conclusion. Sugiura’s gate-like case, folded pages, and dark printing impede linear progress and create a sense of the past repeatedly entering the present. Book design thus resists fixing war memory into a concise lesson.

What Do Symbols Communicate, and What Do They Leave Unclear?

Kawada arranged clocks, medals, flags, soldiers’ belongings, and signs of American culture with restrained captions. Symbolic editing can hold defeat, sacrifice, the state, occupation, and consumer society in view at once without closing the postwar period into one claim. Images that do not identify whose experience they show also risk abstracting the specific voices of atomic-bomb survivors. The book’s critical force does not rest on ambiguity as an end in itself. It preserves the gap between explainable history and material memory that exceeds explanation.

Reeditions and The Last Cosmology: Editing the Past Without Fixing It

The Map has been reissued several times, with changes in paper, printing, format, and contents. Kawada later edited photographs of the cosmos, politics, cities, and signs of disaster in works including The Last Cosmology, Los Caprichos, and World’s End*2. Rather than repeating the early book, he connected the photographic archive to contemporary crisis. “The map” expanded from a completed volume into an ongoing method of giving the world new arrangements.

The Double-Page Spread: Producing a Third Meaning Between Images

The Map sets unlike photographs against one another across spreads: stains on a wall and a flag, a damaged object and an advertisement. The images do not simply add information. Their adjacency produces tension between things without a stated causal relation and generates a third meaning. Each return to a page places the same image in another chain and alters what comes before and after. The book’s criticism lies in the unexplained distance between images as well as in the symbolic strength of individual photographs.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The Chizu Print and the Photobook: Is the Same Photograph the Same Work?

MoMA holds a print titled Chizu as an individual object, presenting the formal qualities of one image removed from the book*5. The Met preserves the 1965 edition of The Map as a complete work, including print, sequence, and support*3. The same photograph produces different viewing time and context when encountered as a single print or as a page within the photobook.

Darkness, Grain, and Close-Up: Techniques That Complicate Documentary Reading

Kawada’s early work often gives black a broad presence, makes grain conspicuous, and withholds an easily identifiable whole. Fragmentary evidence changes meaning through relation to other images and words. Darkness and grain sustain the difficulty of reading historical traces. As stains on a wall begin to resemble maps or skin, close-up and high contrast open the subject to several associations. The photograph remains evidence while resisting confinement to one verbal explanation.

Long-Term Production and the Date: Editing the Present as a Sign of Catastrophe

Kawada continued photographing into old age and reedited images from different decades into new series. A 2024 exhibition at the Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art presented the artist, born in 1933, as an active photographer who has pursued social and historical signs that are difficult to grasp with the naked eye*2. In this method, the meaning produced when a photograph later meets another image matters more than its immediate news value. The archive serves as material for editing the present rather than as a fixed storehouse of the past.

Los Caprichos: Bringing Goya’s Title into the Present

In Los Caprichos, Kawada borrowed the title of Goya’s print series and combined fragments of cities, politicians, crowds, television, and strange objects. The quotation brings an older language for questioning social reason and madness through fragmentary images into contemporary urban photography. Postwar Japan meets Goya’s era as the anxieties of different times correspond through photographic sequence.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photo History
sections.body_html:
Kawada and Shomei Tomatsu: At What Distance Should Postwar Matter Be Seen?

Tomatsu also photographed the persistence of war in objects and bodies, including a melted bottle, a stopped watch, and scarred skin in Nagasaki. Tomatsu retained the encounter with individual people and things, while Kawada collided heterogeneous fragments across photobook spreads. From the same VIVO milieu emerged both an approach grounded in material encounter and one that linked symbols through book design. Their difference shows that postwar memory did not settle into one dark style; it changed with distance and medium.

Beyond the Canonical Photobook: The Political Tension of The Map

The Map is now internationally valued as a rare photobook, a landmark of book design, and a canonical work of postwar Japanese photography. When market value and design innovation dominate discussion, its political tension around the atomic bomb, occupation, and national symbols can become decorative. A PGI exhibition emphasized Kawada’s continuing attention to the signs of his time after The Map, resisting the isolation of one book as a self-contained masterpiece*6. Its formal intensity remains tied to a postwar history that is difficult to read.

A Critique of Postwar Realism: Keeping Evidence While Showing Its Limits

The VIVO photographers inherited the ethical demand of postwar realism to confront actual conditions while moving away from confidence that one picture could stand for society. The images in The Map are grounded in concrete subjects such as the Atomic Bomb Dome and surviving objects, preserving historical places within abstract surfaces. Knowing the object’s name, however, does not complete the meaning of war. Recent scholarship has analyzed this tension between visibility and invisibility as a problem of representation in the atomic age*20. Kawada’s criticism made the limits of documentary explanation explicit through photobook form.

An Artist Still Working: Not Ending Kawada’s Career in 1965

Kawada continued to publish new work and reedit earlier photographs in the 2020s, remaining an active photographer as well as a historical figure born in 1933*2. After The Map, his subjects expanded to celestial phenomena, disaster, politics, and digitally recorded dates. The early concern with postwar memory differs from his later apocalyptic register, but the method persists: selecting fragments of an era and giving them relations through books and exhibitions.

kishin-shinoyama.html.lead_html: Kishin Shinoyama worked through advertising, magazines, photobooks, and museum exhibitions, photographing celebrities, nudes, architecture, Tokyo, and traces left after disaster as public images of his time. Through Hareta Hi, Ie, TOKYO NUDE, ATOKATA, and Shinorama, he showed how photographing, editing, printing, circulation, and exhibition shape public images of people and the memory of places.
kishin-shinoyama.html.thesis_html: Shinoyama’s contribution to postwar Japanese photography was to place the production conditions of advertising and magazines at the center of photographic expression. Hareta Hi edited the people and events of 1974 into the duration of a book; Ie recorded traces of life in buildings across Japan; Shinorama and TOKYO NUDE used multiple cameras and large-scale staging to construct a changing Tokyo. His historical position is most clearly seen in the way he designed who would encounter a photograph, through which medium, and at what scale.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Light Publicity and Photography Magazines: Making Images for a Mass Audience

Kishin Shinoyama’s approach took shape in the 1960s, when advertising production, photography magazines, and museums were closely connected. While studying photography at Nihon University College of Art, he received the APA Award at the Japan Advertising Photographers’ Association exhibition in 1961 and gained experience at the advertising production company Light Publicity. His graduation work appeared in Camera Mainichi in 1963; in 1966 he was the youngest participant in Ten Photographers of Contemporary Photography at the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo; and in 1968 he began working independently*1. In advertising, commissions, planning, models, lighting, art direction, design, printing, and placement all contribute to the finished image. Shinoyama used this collaborative process as the means by which an image reached society. The pace of advertising and magazine serials taught him to photograph contemporary people, buildings, commodities, and events continuously, then deliver their reproduced images to a large readership. He saw photography as a way to take part in the transformation of present-day people and places into public images, preserving the surface of an era through mass-produced print.

“Reproducing the Times” and Kettō Shashinron: Locating Photography in the Present

Shinoyama stated that “a photographer can photograph only the era in which he lives,” and described his own work as “a reproduction of the times”*1. This idea included events in the world, the pose of a star, advertising light, a magazine spread, the order of a photobook, and the scale of an exhibition. Each revealed how an era shared images of people and places. In 1977 he published Kettō Shashinron with Takuma Nakahira, presenting their dialogue on photography and reality, the photographer’s position, and contemporary expression*12. In Shinoyama’s view, documentation and staging, artwork and commodity, individual expression and mass media belonged to the same production process. He entered the places where society manufactured images of stars and bodies, and made their desires, technologies, speed, and circulation both the subject and the conditions of his photographs. His critical concern lay in working from the center of the present, making images that would later become historical documents.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Hareta Hi: Editing 1974 at the Speed of a Magazine

The photobook Hareta Hi grew from a six-month series in Asahi Graph that began in May 1974, supplemented with other photographs made that year. Art, entertainment, politics, professional and amateur sports, and everyday life appear in the same volume; figures such as Shigeo Nagashima, Kōichi Wajima, and Yoko Ono share the chronology of 1974 with public events*1. The book foregrounds the editorial fact that images of different subjects and scales existed at the same time, without imposing a single visual style. Shinoyama spoke of the mass character inherent in photography, and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum has described the book as a critique of the Shōwa era*1. The reporting cycle of a magazine created speed and proximity to the present, while the page sequence of the photobook created time for looking back over a year. He approached people and events before their historical importance had been settled, then edited heterogeneous images into the memory of a single year. The method positioned the photographer as both a selector of events and an editor of public imagery.

Ie and Kaikan no Yakata: Photographing Time in Architecture

Ie was serialized in the monthly magazine Ushio from January 1972 through December 1975. Shinoyama photographed sites from Hokkaido to Okinawa, including the State Guest House, former Imperial General Headquarters ruins, rural homes, an abandoned coal-mining settlement, Tokyo apartments, and a Kyoto teahouse*1. In Ie, held by the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum, furniture, walls, light, wear, and empty rooms reveal the life that once occupied the building as clearly as its exterior form. The museum’s object page presents the image and identifies it as a 1975 silver dye-bleach print*3. As housing and communities changed rapidly during Japan’s high-growth period, Shinoyama photographed marks of use, the tastes of occupants, regional differences, and time held within a space. For the 2016 Hara Museum exhibition Kaikan no Yakata, he photographed thirty-three models inside the museum and installed seventy-seven works in spaces corresponding to where they had been made*6. Ie records time accumulated in a place; Kaikan no Yakata layers the photographed building with the building occupied by viewers, turning the exhibition into a new event. Architecture determines the positions of bodies, light, memory, and the spectator.

Shinorama and TOKYO NUDE: Constructing Tokyo with Multiple Cameras

Developed from 1983, Shinorama joined multiple cameras for simultaneous exposures and assembled adjacent frames into a wide image. In TOKYO NUDE, postmodern buildings, roads, artificial light, and bodies arranged as groups form a city image with visible seams. Materials from the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum document a large production process that included scouting locations, numerous models, makeup, and lighting*1. Small differences in viewpoint and time remain between adjoining frames, and Tokyo appears as a stage where several scenes unfold at once. Nude bodies are organized as urban elements alongside architecture, roads, and advertising light. Shinoyama applied the collaboration, lighting, and direction of advertising photography at the scale of the city, presenting a changing Tokyo across joined frames. Shinorama offered more than an expanded angle of view. It divided the unified viewpoint of a single photograph and transferred the city’s excess of information and artificiality into the structure of the image.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
From Myōjō to Monumental Exhibitions: Circulating Public Images of People

Beginning in 1971, Shinoyama photographed covers for Myōjō and participated in the process through which singers and actors became the shared mass-cultural image of the “idol”*1. In Carmen Maki, in the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum collection, pose, background, and lighting shape an image that can be recognized immediately in print*4. Kobayashi Akira shows a similar clarity in the force with which the sitter occupies the frame*7. In celebrity portraits and nudes, clothing, body, gaze, lighting, and background determined how a person appeared as a social image. These portraits moved from magazine covers to photobooks, advertisements, and exhibitions, acquiring a different scale in each medium. The touring exhibition The People by KISHIN, launched in 2012, presented photographs of celebrities and public events as monumental prints and traveled to thirty-two venues across Japan through 2019. Gallery AaMo records works more than eight meters wide and a cumulative attendance of about 990,000*5. Shinoyama treated print run, image size, and viewing distance as parts of production, designing the conditions under which a public image of a person reached an audience.

ATOKATA: Recording Objects and Places After the Disaster

Made after the Great East Japan Earthquake, ATOKATA redirected Shinoyama’s long-standing concern with recording an era toward places marked by loss. Between May and autumn 2011, he made four visits to the disaster area, photographing trees felled by the tsunami, stranded boats, collapsed buildings, quiet landscapes, and traces of domestic life left in houses*1. TIME described the photobook, published that year, as a record of damaged wood, metal, and stone in the immediate aftermath of the disaster*18. Ie photographed time accumulated in dwellings; ATOKATA records, through objects and space, places where that accumulation was severed at once. The large-scale lighting and direction used in celebrity photography and Shinorama recede, leaving the position and surface of objects and their surrounding landscape to register directly. Shinoyama described photography as “a record made as things are dying,” connecting glamorous public images and post-disaster traces through a commitment to carry the present into the future*1. His form changes with the subjects and media demanded by each period, but the impulse to reproduce the present before it disappears remains.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
From Commercial Photography to a Record of an Era: What Shinoyama Changed

Advertising, magazines, photobooks, the Venice Biennale, and museum exhibitions ran concurrently throughout Shinoyama’s career. Circulation, celebrity, production crews, printing technology, and exhibition scale all entered into the making of an image, joining commercial photography and museum work within a single history of production. In 1976 he presented work based on Ie in the Japan Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, moving a magazine series into an international exhibition space*6. His contemporary Daidō Moriyama used a small camera, chance encounters in the street, and coarse grain to record the unstable experience of the city. Shinoyama organized concepts, lighting, models, architecture, printing, and large-scale displays to produce the shared public images of people and cities. Both used magazines as a primary medium, yet they approached reproduction and urban life through different methods. Hareta Hi gathered the events of 1974 into a book; Ie recorded living environments through architecture; TOKYO NUDE constructed bubble-era Tokyo across multiple frames; and ATOKATA followed post-disaster loss through objects and places. Shinoyama incorporated the production conditions of advertising and magazines into photography, designing image-making, editing, printing, distribution, and display as a continuous expression. He changed form for stars, nudes, houses, cities, and disasters, recording how an era presented itself, what it lost, and what it remembered. His distinct place in postwar Japanese photography lies in treating photography’s mass circulation as a condition of historical critique.
