twitter.title: Daido Moriyama | Provoke, Are-Bure-Boke, and Japanese Street Photography | Photo Coordinates
twitter.description: Daido Moriyama is explained through Provoke, are-bure-boke, photobooks, Tokyo street photography, rephotography, and postwar Japanese image culture.

moriyama.html.lead_html: Daido Moriyama (1938–) was born in Ikeda, Osaka Prefecture, now Ikeda City. After working in commercial design, he turned to photography, moved to Tokyo in 1961, became Eikoh Hosoe’s assistant, and began working independently in 1964. Through Japan: A Photo Theater, PROVOKE, Farewell Photography, and Record, he has transformed the streets of Tokyo and other parts of Japan, along with advertisements, television, and printed matter, into grainy, blurred, high-contrast images made with a small camera. His treatment of shooting, movement, magazines, photobooks, and reproduction as one continuous practice has had a major influence on both postwar Japanese street photography and photobook culture.
moriyama.html.thesis_html: In 1960s Japan, photojournalism and commercial photography placed a strong premium on clarity, reproducibility, and explanatory force. After PROVOKE, Moriyama continued to use coarse grain, camera shake, lack of focus, tilted compositions, and degradation in print as elements that conveyed a body moving through the city and the instability of perception, not as failures to be eliminated. His specific intervention was to reconfigure the very criteria of photographic value, centered on an image being “well taken,” by introducing the uncertainty of the image, the photographer’s movement, and even the reproduction of existing images. By repeating and reediting images in magazines and photobooks, he also made page sequence and print quality part of a work’s meaning, extending it beyond a single finished picture. This shift matters because it left later street photography and photobooks a strong precedent for understanding the city through processes of perception, editing, and reproduction instead of technical finish.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Daido Moriyama’s Career and Tokyo in the 1960s

Daido Moriyama was born in 1938 in Ikeda, Osaka Prefecture, now Ikeda City. After studying commercial design, he encountered photography at the studio of Takeji Iwamiya and moved to Tokyo in 1961. By the time he sought to join the photography collective VIVO, it was already moving toward dissolution. He instead became Eikoh Hosoe’s assistant and witnessed the production of Ordeal by Roses. He began working independently in 1964, photographing areas around U.S. military bases, theaters, and streets for photography magazines. The chronology of the Daido Moriyama Photo Foundation also notes that his association with Takuma Nakahira began during this period.*3

In 1968, Moriyama published his first photobook, Japan: A Photo Theater, pairing his photographs with text by Shūji Terayama, and joined PROVOKE with its second issue that same year. In 1970, he published “First, Abandon the World of Pseudo-Certainty”; in 1972, he released Farewell Photography and A Hunter. That July, he launched the self-published magazine Record, producing five issues through 1973. His method took shape through magazines, photobooks, photography made while traveling, rephotography, and printing before it did through exhibitions. This is crucial to understanding Moriyama as more than a photographer of the street: he is an artist who has worked with the very forms through which photographs circulate.*22

Moriyama’s early visual formation drew on Iwamiya and Hosoe, as well as Shomei Tomatsu through VIVO, Takuma Nakahira, and the photobooks of William Klein and Robert Frank. Fondation Cartier describes how Moriyama developed a way of photographing while moving through the city, using a small camera as though it were an extension of his body. Seen within this lineage, are-bure-boke did not emerge suddenly from a single fashionable style. It developed across postwar documentary photography, the photobook, and street snapshots.*24

Reading Moriyama’s work of the late 1960s backward from the “Daido Moriyama look” established later can obscure the trial and error of his early years. Philip Charrier examines the formative period from 1966 to 1972 through Moriyama’s collaboration with Shūji Terayama, magazine series such as Accident and A Journey to Something, and the making of his early photobooks. He argues that Moriyama’s photographs contained a tension between photography as a cold, authentic record and the image as an emotional re-creation of contact with the external world.*27 From this perspective, grain and blur were not a fully formed signature from the outset. They took shape as Moriyama sought to retain both journalistic “fact” and embodied experience within the photograph.

Jan-Frederik Rust’s doctoral dissertation analyzes Moriyama’s photobooks and magazine work from 1965 to 1978 through editing, page sequence, printing, collaboration, and the reuse of previously published photographs, as well as through individual images.*26 By treating Japan: A Photo Theater, Farewell Photography, and A Hunter as works with distinct editorial logics instead of containers for exhibition prints, the study confirms that the photobook was not a secondary mode of presentation for Moriyama, but a site of production where the meaning of photographs was reconfigured.

sections.title: Provoke, Are-Bure-Boke, and Street Photography
sections.body_html:
PROVOKE and a Language Specific to Photography

Daido Moriyama is closely associated with Provoke, but that association alone narrows the scope of work that extends across magazines, photobooks, the street, and reproductive media. PROVOKE was an experimental photography magazine founded in 1968 by Takuma Nakahira, Yutaka Takanashi, Kōji Taki, Takahiko Okada, and others. Subtitled “Provocative Materials for Thought,” it included Moriyama beginning with its second issue.*4 The “language specific to photography” sought by PROVOKE was less an abstruse concept than an attempt to make the sensations of an era that words could not fully explain legible through photography’s material elements. Grain grows coarse, the frame tilts, focus slips, adjacent photographs collide on the page, and the image deteriorates in reproduction. When such phenomena carry meaning, the photograph ceases to be an illustration for a text and becomes a medium for thinking photographically. In an Aperture interview, Simon Baker describes PROVOKE photography as a subjective, expressive medium conveying lived experience in Tokyo from the late 1960s to the early 1970s, rather than a medium of objective explanation.*5 In a text on Accident, Moriyama likewise writes that photography records truth yet is also a lie, and that, while holding this contradiction, it becomes “a language” beyond verbal language.*6

The theoretical background of PROVOKE cannot be reduced to a simple anti-establishment movement. Philip Charrier analyzes Kōji Taki’s arguments of 1967–68 as an attempt, informed by structuralism and semiotics, to use photographs resistant to established linguistic codes to expose relations of power and knowledge embedded in the urban environment.*29 The method contained a paradox. Are-bure-boke, which deliberately “misused” the camera to disrupt legible codes, became recognizable as a new style as it spread. Understanding Moriyama therefore requires seeing it as a movement in conflict with stylization itself, beyond assessing its appearance as a style that could be imitated.

Gyewon Kim examines avant-garde photography in 1960s Japan through the material conditions of paper, printing, and the magazine page, as well as through the cities photographed. She argues that PROVOKE rejected conventional photojournalism and naive realism while seeking to connect avant-garde experimentation and documentary photography as a method of social critique.*30 Grain, blocked-up shadows, and sequences extending across pages matter in Moriyama’s photographs because they reconstruct the city’s speed and fragmentation in the material form of print, in addition to depicting the city as their subject.

Visual Culture During the High-Growth Era and PROVOKE

PROVOKE’s provocation was necessary because, as Japan moved from postwar reconstruction into rapid economic growth, photography was increasingly absorbed into the clarity of news reporting and the consumer imagery of advertising. MoMA explains that PROVOKE’s roughness, blur, and lack of focus stood in sharp contrast to the public imagery of the time and sought to unsettle a Japanese photographic culture inclined toward sober European-style photojournalism and straightforward commercial photography.*4 Coarse grain and unstable compositions were therefore more than the results of careless shooting. They provided a way to return the anxiety, desire, chance, and political tension felt on the street to the orderly, easily understood consumer images made by advertising and magazines. The Photographers’ Gallery similarly presents Moriyama’s career of more than sixty years as work that has challenged how photographs are seen and reconsidered the nature of photography itself.*7

Moriyama’s own recollections are also important in keeping this historical setting from being reduced to political slogans. In an SFMOMA interview, he recalls that from Yokosuka during the Vietnam War until around 1970, young artists in Japan shared a sense of rebellion against and criticism of their genres, their worlds, and politics. He says, however, that he was moved by feelings of rebellion and criticism arising from everyday life rather than by the expression of a direct political message.*31 His rough images are therefore better understood as unstable perceptions formed by physically moving through a politicized society than as illustrations of political circumstances, an interpretation closer to his own account.

Are-Bure-Boke and Urban Perception

Moriyama’s coarse grain, strong contrast, tilted compositions, camera shake, and lack of focus do not organize the city into a clean view. They preserve the photographer’s close proximity to subjects encountered in the street and his movement at the moment of exposure. Fondation Cartier explains that Moriyama, with a small camera in hand, photographed while running or from a moving car, using grainy, blurred, tilted images to reveal unsettling aspects of the streets and alleys of Japan’s major cities.*8 The idea that Moriyama’s photographs touch reality is more than an abstract metaphor. When he photographs the city, signs, television screens, posters, movie screens, and car windshields become elements of the same frame as buildings and people. In an SFMOMA interview, Moriyama says that he approaches cities, cars, people, television screens, posters, and movie screens from the same point of view.*9 In Moriyama’s city, reality appears both as an unmediated landscape and as existing images in print, video, posters, and screens. To draw these subjects into a single frame, his compositions become close, fragmentary, and strongly contrasted.

On the Road and the Snapshot in Motion

What Moriyama took from Jack Kerouac’s On the Road was more than the freedom of travel. It was a responsiveness to fragments of roads, people, cities, and time encountered en route, with the destination taking second place. Penguin Random House introduces the book as a story about the search for meaning and “authentic experience” through cross-country journeys.*10 In Moriyama’s own text published by C/O Berlin, he recalls reading On the Road when he was young, becoming fascinated by Sal Paradise’s “eyes for the road,” acquiring a friend’s old Toyota, and beginning to travel roads throughout Japan.*11 SFMOMA also records that Moriyama hitchhiked around Japan, traveled highways day and night, stopped at run-down cafés, and photographed through car windows, and that these images were serialized in Camera Mainichi beginning in 1968.*2 Moriyama says that the dog in Stray Dog, Misawa appeared walking toward him as he moved through the city of Misawa, and that he photographed it in an instant.*9 Moriyama’s snapshots do not record planned subjects in sequence. He rides, walks, turns, looks through a window, and glances back. Along the way, signs, dogs, passersby, light, roadways, and storefronts suddenly enter his view, and the shutter is released before deliberation. This is a gaze through which the body responds to fragments of the city, not a perspective that organizes the city from above.

Photobooks, Magazines, and Reproductive Media

Moriyama’s importance lies not only in individual masterpieces but in his sustained inquiry into how photographs are arranged, reproduced, degraded, and given different meanings in magazines and photobooks. His effort to weaken authorship and style in Farewell Photography was not an abrupt act of self-negation, but a response to an era when photographs already circulated as copies. Aperture describes the book as a photobook that includes photographs, cut-up negatives, and even works by other artists, revealing a process intended to negate authorship and style.*12 Moriyama kept a photograph from resolving into “a single picture I took beautifully.” By mixing failed negatives, other people’s images, rough printing, and page sequences, he destabilized the questions of who owns a photograph and at what point it becomes a work. This idea also connects with Warhol’s reproductive images, which strongly attracted Moriyama at the time. SFMOMA describes Accident as a Warhol-like series that remade existing images through newspaper and magazine clippings and rephotography.*2 What mattered to Moriyama about Warhol was less the Pop surface than the way existing photographs of accidents and other events acquired an intensity distinct from the events themselves as they were copied repeatedly across newspapers, magazines, and television. In an SFMOMA interview, Moriyama says that he sees the essence of photography in copying and reproduction and strongly identified with Warhol’s method.*9

The privately published Record, which Moriyama began in 1972, differed from a photobook selecting only finished signature works. It was a form through which he continually released photographs taken at a given moment in small booklets. The first five issues appeared from 1972 to 1973, during the same period as Farewell Photography and A Hunter, creating another circuit that repeatedly brought photography and publication close together without containing the work’s completion within a single volume. The official publication chronology lists Record as an independent publishing activity, further confirming that how images were printed, sequenced, and distributed mattered as much to Moriyama’s work as how they were photographed.*22

Moriyama later called Record his “personal medium,” distinguishing it from a conventional photobook organized around a theme. He also specifically attributed the suspension of its initial run in 1973 to the sharp rise in printing costs caused by the oil crisis.*32 This shows that his photographic work was shaped by the material conditions of printing costs, publication scale, and distribution as well as by aesthetics. In bringing “taking photographs” close to “printing them and passing them on to others,” Record became one of the media that most directly expressed Moriyama’s refusal to think of photography solely as an exhibition object.

sections.title: Key Works, Photobooks, and Media
sections.body_html:
Key Works and Composition

In Japan: A Photo Theater, theater, spectacle, street figures, and popular culture intermingle, presenting the city in postwar Japan as a theatrical space. SFMOMA’s account of Japan Theater reads its figures as actual performers who also become metaphorical presences marked by the uncertain modernity of the 1960s.*2 ON THE ROAD is identified in SFMOMA’s collection records as a gelatin silver print from 1969.*13 Its title also points to Moriyama’s extension of the experience of photographing in motion into sequences in photobooks and magazines. Discussing Grand Level, Yubari, The Met explains that Moriyama documented life in postwar Japan and was influenced by avant-garde Japanese photography and the tilted documentary approach of William Klein.*14 Moriyama’s approach is close to documentary photography in its engagement with society and the street. Yet he transformed documentary form: instead of an objective report aligned along horizontal and vertical axes, images made from excessive proximity, tilted frames, stark blacks and whites, and moments of movement convey urban disorder as a bodily sensation.

The Meaning and Translation of Are-Bure-Boke

The phrase is romanized as are-bure-boke, which MoMA describes as “grainy, blurry, and out-of-focus.” Are refers to coarse grain or a rough printed surface, bure to image blur caused by movement of the camera or subject, and boke to a lack of focus. The three terms are not synonyms for the same indistinctness; they disrupt photographic clarity at the separate levels of grain, movement, and focus.*4 The Art Institute of Chicago likewise identifies coarse grain, blur, and lack of focus as elements characterizing the photographic language of PROVOKE.*18

MoMA treats the term as an expression that gained currency around PROVOKE in the late 1960s.*4 The Art Institute of Chicago’s material also does not identify a single person who coined it. The sources trace its origin to the words are, bure, and boke, but do not establish a sole originator.*18

Differences from Takuma Nakahira

Takuma Nakahira was one of PROVOKE’s theoretical centers, but by the early 1970s he had begun criticizing the consolidation of are-bure-boke into an artist-specific style and moved toward a more literal mode of recording. SFMOMA’s chronology situates his subsequent activities, including this abrupt change in direction.*19 Moriyama, by contrast, continued to link coarse grain, strong contrast, blur, and lack of focus to the perception of the street after PROVOKE ended. Read alongside MoMA’s discussion of Nakahira, their difference becomes clearer when they are not grouped as photographers sharing the same look: Nakahira sought to leave behind its stylization, while Moriyama continued to embrace the indeterminate image as a bodily experience of the street.*20

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Beyond a Fixed Reading of Are-Bure-Boke

As Moriyama’s international profile grew, are-bure-boke also became a convenient label for explaining his entire body of work. A 2022 Aperture essay argues that reading his dark, rough photographs solely as a mirror of the social conditions of postwar Japan reaches only the surface of Moriyama’s concerns; at their core is a question directed at the medium itself: what is photography?*12 Given his attempt to dismantle authorship and a finished style in Farewell Photography, fixing are-bure-boke as Moriyama’s definitive style contradicts his own act of self-negation in the early 1970s. His continuity lies in his sustained inquiry into where an image becomes a photograph as he moved across the street, rephotography, magazines, photobooks, color, and digital media, rather than in the repetition of a single look.

Within photographic history, Moriyama’s shift becomes still more specific. Masafumi Fukagawa argues that Moriyama challenged the realism and the “photo essay” (kumi shashin) that held a strong position in postwar Japan, the conceptions of photography represented by Yōnosuke Natori and Ken Domon, and the very norms of modern photography.*28 The crucial point is not that he changed “beautiful photographs into rough photographs,” but that he unsettled the assumption that photographers could grasp the world correctly and explain it to viewers in an orderly way. The self-destructive editing of Farewell Photography made this conflict within photographic history visible in its most extreme form.

International Reception and Place in Photographic History

A major turning point in Moriyama’s international reception was New Japanese Photography, held at MoMA in 1974. The Daido Moriyama Photo Foundation’s chronology records that the exhibition traveled from MoMA to SFMOMA and other venues.*3 SFMOMA’s Daido Moriyama: Stray Dog, which toured beginning in 1999, used approximately two hundred black-and-white works and large Polaroid works to examine the relationship between postwar Japanese society and Western influence, particularly that of the United States.*15 At issue here is neither simple admiration for American culture nor simple rejection of it. U.S. military bases, jazz, bars, imported goods, and the desire for American-style affluence had entered the postwar urban landscape in ways inseparable from the security-treaty system, memories of the occupation, and unease at the rapid development of consumer society. SFMOMA’s publication text likewise explains that Moriyama’s photographs reveal deep ambivalence toward the embrace of American ideals and embody the cultural dilemma of postwar Japan’s rapid change from an isolationist, fascist society into an international, capitalist one.*16 The “transformation” of Japanese photography did not simply mean that rough photographs became fashionable. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum explains that Moriyama’s high-contrast, grainy work of the 1960s and 1970s brought about a transformation in Japanese photography, although it was initially criticized as rough, blurred, and out of focus.*17 More specifically, the criteria of judgment shifted from a view centered on clear photojournalism and commercial photography toward an inquiry into photography’s truth, reproducibility, and embodied nature through photobooks, magazines, rephotography, and subjective snapshots.*5 In its citation for the 2019 award, the Hasselblad Foundation assesses Provoke as a movement that liberated photography from tradition and reexamined the medium itself, positioning Moriyama as one of the most important artists to emerge from it.*1 Moriyama’s photographs are records of reality and, at the same time, copies drawn from magazines, television, and advertising. This movement between original and reproduction, document and expression, and street experience and mass-media imagery has been repeatedly addressed in recent retrospectives and collection texts.*7

Influence on Photobook Culture

In accounts of Moriyama’s international standing, the photobooks themselves have been cited repeatedly alongside his prints. The International Center of Photography positions Moriyama’s photobooks as landmarks of postwar photography, valuing rapid shooting on the street together with editing in print.*23 Materials from the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum retrospective also show that Farewell Photography, A Hunter, and issues 1–5 of Record were concentrated in the PROVOKE period from 1968 to 1972, when photography, publishing, and criticism operated in close succession over a short span.*21 Moriyama’s influence consequently extends beyond the visual look of are-bure-boke to Japan’s photobook culture, in which photographs are edited as books, magazines, and series and delivered to viewers as reproductions.

Works by Moriyama are also held in the National Gallery of Art’s collection, giving him an enduring place in international collections of photographic history beyond the limited context of avant-garde photography within Japan.*25

multiplicity.html.lead_html: Multiplicity is a Milan-based research network involving architects, urban researchers, photographers, geographers, and other specialists. Combining photography, video, maps, testimony, travel times, and related material, projects including USE, Solid Sea, and The Road Map investigated European cities, the Mediterranean, and the Israel/Palestine border as systems that organize the movement of people and information.
multiplicity.html.thesis_html: A photograph of a city or border can record visible buildings, seas, roads, and walls, but a single image has difficulty showing who is allowed to pass through them or why the same distance takes radically different amounts of time for different people. Multiplicity treated photography as one component of an investigation, checking it against maps, testimony, video, timetables, and institutional information instead of presenting the photograph as a conclusion. In Solid Sea and The Road Map, the emphasis moves from the appearance of landscape to the mechanisms that permit, delay, or block movement, extending documentary photography into a method for reading territory through multiple forms of evidence.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Multiple Viewpoints Emerging from 1990s Urban Research

Multiplicity is a Milan-based research network formed to read urban change across architecture, planning, geography, photography, and social research. Fondazione Antonio Ratti describes its method as directing multiple voices and viewpoints toward a single subject and investigating the same place from different angles*1.

In an oral history for the Canadian Centre for Architecture, Stefano Boeri recalls the 1990s urban research that led toward Multiplicity. Photography was used to break apart the “single viewpoint” through which planning maps and aerial photographs organize territory from above, replacing it with multiple ways of seeing that included people moving through a place and the imaginations of its residents*21.

The method responded to a European urban condition after the 1990s in which change could no longer be understood simply through completed buildings. In a text republished by documenta, Stefano Boeri and Multiplicity describe leaving behind the conventional architectural magazine and the city center as privileged viewpoints, gathering case studies of migration, informal economies, cross-border lives, and the reuse of industrial land at urban margins*3.

Photography thus became an observational tool for connecting changes on the ground to other evidence, not a medium for producing a representative image of the city. In a recent interview, Boeri compares the method to a “local biopsy”: examining a small site closely in order to read the condition of a larger whole and making the less visible processes shaping space legible through phenomena changing in real time*4.

The need for “multiple viewpoints” was built into Multiplicity’s approach to urban research from the outset. Multiplicity—Mappe at Viafarini in 1995 raised the problem that conventional architectural and planning methods were failing to register changes in both the form of cities and the ways they were inhabited*26 From the beginning, photography was treated as a kind of map for reading flows, routes, continuities between places, and memory, rather than as a record of architectural exteriors alone.

USE: Refusing a Single Overview of the City

USE: Uncertain States of Europe involved seventy researchers from fifteen countries, each describing urban transformations across Europe through different forms. A Boeri/Multiplicity text republished in documenta’s Platform 6 records the use of photographs, video, diagrams, and other media according to the needs of each case, with multiple forms presented together in the final exhibition*3.

Kunstinstituut Melly likewise describes USE as a “survey-installation” in which a large research network brought the research itself into exhibition space, documenting presentations in Bordeaux, Brussels, Tokyo, Perth, and Milan*7.

The multiplication of media was not an end in itself. Urban change appeared through labor, movement, legal systems, informal use, and differences in time as well as through buildings, so each subject required a different combination of photographs, maps, testimony, and video.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Solid Sea: Reading the Sea as Routes and Selection, Not Empty Space

Solid Sea investigated the Mediterranean as a political space through which people, goods, information, and capital move under different rules. The project turns from familiar images of open water and cultural exchange toward the institutions that regulate passage. Generali Foundation explains that Multiplicity treated the Mediterranean as a “solid mass,” examining it from several directions through maps, photographs, and video*5.

An e-flux announcement likewise describes Solid Sea as an ongoing investigation of the flows of people, goods, information, and capital across the Mediterranean and the unequal conditions of mobility experienced by those who live there*6.

A photograph of a point at sea does not directly show who may pass through it, which routes are classified as legal or illegal, or how many hours the same distance takes for different people. By connecting photographs to maps, interviews, video, and documents, the project makes the institutions behind the landscape readable.

The Ghost Ship: Reconstructing an Event through a Chain of Evidence

Solid Sea 01: The Ghost Ship investigated a maritime disaster off Sicily at Christmas 1996 in which many migrants died. IFFR presents the work as a reconstruction of the event and describes Multiplicity as a collective investigating “recent, hidden transformations” of cities and territories*8.

A 2002 Nettime post by Boeri on Solid Sea records both the 1996 sinking and the long period during which the event itself was denied*24 Photographs and testimony were gathered to reach the fact that the disaster occurred through multiple routes of evidence, not to stage a dramatic reenactment of an unseen tragedy.

Xing presents The Ghost Ship as the first in a sequence of case studies on transformations of the Mediterranean and records the limited recovery and identification of bodies after the disaster*17.

Domus describes The Ghost Ship as a two-room video installation built from underwater footage by Giovanni Maria Bellu and testimony from people involved, addressing the long denial of the 1996 Mediterranean sinking*18 Here, photographs and video become part of political evidence through comparison with testimony and spatial information rather than through any claim to prove the event on their own.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The Road Map: The Same Start and Destination Do Not Mean the Same Distance

The Road Map recorded two taxi journeys near Jerusalem between nearby starting points and destinations, one taken by a person with Israeli identification and the other by a Palestinian traveler. Pratt Institute notes that one trip took about an hour while the other took more than five, demonstrating how checkpoints and territorial divisions alter movement*10.

The 2003 exhibition Territories at KW Institute presented Multiplicity through research comparing “border devices”—checkpoints, roads, identity documents, legal categories, and other mechanisms that filter human movement*22 The Road Map was therefore more than a one-time demonstration of unequal travel time. It measured how architecture and legal systems split everyday routes.

Boeri himself later described the experiment as an example of border devices altering bodily travel time, using the two routes to measure the territorial structure of the West Bank*4.

The work layers maps, time, travel records, and photographs to show how institutions turn the same geographic space into different realities. Photographs give specificity to the map, while the map reveals differences in route that the photographs cannot contain; each medium makes the limits of the other visible.

Photography, Video, Maps, Exhibition: Documentary without a Fixed Medium

TBA21 lists Solid Sea as a documenta 11 commission and records it as a collaborative work by Stefano Boeri, Maddalena Bregani, Francisca Insulza, Francesco Jodice, Giovanni La Varra, John Palmesino, and others*9.

CAMERA Torino’s retrospective materials confirm that photographer Francesco Jodice was one of Multiplicity’s founding members and describe his individual work as moving across photography, video, and installation*14.

Stefano Boeri Architetti lists Solid Sea, The Road Map, and USE among Multiplicity’s principal projects, linking them respectively to migration, borders in the West Bank, and the self-organization of European cities*11.

A Landscape Biennial profile likewise traces Boeri’s study of urban and territorial change in the 1990s and his use of Multiplicity to analyze social phenomena beyond the boundaries of architecture*15 The medium changes because each subject requires a different mode of presentation.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
After documenta 11: From the Photographic Work to the Structure of Research

Multiplicity’s presence in the official archive of documenta 11—the eleventh edition of the international contemporary art exhibition held every five years in Kassel—shows that Solid Sea entered the 2002 exhibition as part of broader debates on migration and globalization*2.

Current documenta retrospective materials describe documenta 11 as a project built from five “Platforms,” including discussions across four continents, that addressed intersections between culture and complex global systems of knowledge*25 This structure closely matched Multiplicity’s emphasis on research, discussion, and knowledge production over the presentation of a self-contained finished object.

A Studio International review of documenta 11 argues that the exhibition foregrounded works addressing politics, history, and global inequality instead of promoting a single artistic style, a setting in which Solid Sea was also read*12.

A Generali Foundation publication describes several international collectives of the period as examining migration, labor, and information systems in search of new geographies that conventional geographic divisions could no longer adequately describe*16.

Later criticism around Manifesta 12 also cites Solid Sea as an earlier point of reference for thinking about contemporary art in relation to Palermo and the Mediterranean*13 From the perspective of photographic history, Multiplicity shifts documentary emphasis away from the search for a decisive single image and toward who gathers the material, how it is cross-checked, and in what sequence it is made public.

Allan Sekula addressed related questions during the same period through a different method. The Getty Research Institute situates Sekula after Conceptual art as an artist who moved documentary beyond isolated decisive moments into long-term sequences and writing in order to critique globalization*27 Fish Story likewise follows port labor and the global economy through photographs, text, and slides, reading the sea as a space of logistics and work*28 There is no confirmed direct line of influence, but their shared participation in documenta 11 shows that around 2000, multiple practices were using several forms of material to describe systems that could not be seen in a single photograph.

Evidence Is Not Neutral: Editing and Diagramming as Objects of Critique

A 2003 article in il manifesto describes The Ghost Ship as a work that traced a Mediterranean disaster and institutional silence through multiple screens and documents*19.

A contemporary Frieze review discusses the Ghost Ship component of Solid Sea as a story where the deaths of migrants from Sri Lanka intersected with prolonged administrative silence, noting how multiple screens of underwater footage and testimony functioned as an assembly of voices*23.

AlbumArte’s profile of Francesco Jodice likewise confirms that he cofounded Multiplicity and continued to work across photography, video, and social research*20.

More material does not automatically produce greater objectivity. The scale of a map, the selection of testimony, the editing of video, and the order of an exhibition all involve interpretation. Multiplicity does not conceal those choices; it places photographs in structures where they can be compared with other forms of evidence.

Photography is not fixed as an art object, a press record, or an urban-planning document. It enters the same investigative process as collecting materials, interviewing people, and conducting fieldwork. In that sense, Multiplicity provides an important point of contact between research-based art and expanded documentary practices since the 1990s.

muybridge.html.lead_html: Eadweard Muybridge (1830–1904) was born in Kingston upon Thames, England. After gaining recognition for his landscape photographs of the American West, he used multiple cameras to make sequential photographs of horses in motion in the 1870s, and in the 1880s he produced Animal Locomotion at the University of Pennsylvania. With the zoopraxiscope, he projected sequences of still images back into motion, developing a body of work that connected photography, motion studies, visual education, and the prehistory of cinema.
muybridge.html.thesis_html: At a time when photography was understood as a medium that fixed a single instant, Muybridge synchronized multiple cameras to break motion into still images at equal intervals. His decisive transformation was to turn movement that appears continuous to the naked eye into a sequence of frames that could be compared and measured. As his work progressed from the sequential photographs of a horse made in 1878 to Animal Locomotion at the University of Pennsylvania, walking, athletic activities, everyday actions, and animal movement were recorded according to the same visual standard, extending photography’s use into science, medicine, and art education. The zoopraxiscope then projected those separated images back into motion. His importance lies less in any claim that he invented cinema single-handedly than in his connection of “photography that breaks down motion” with “a device that reconstructs and displays motion,” establishing a concrete technological route from photography toward the study of time and moving-image culture.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Muybridge’s Career and Sequential Photographs of Horses

Eadweard Muybridge was born in Kingston upon Thames, England, in 1830 and moved to the United States in the 1850s.*1 After working as a bookseller and in other occupations in California, he turned to photography. From the late 1860s, he gained recognition for his large-format landscape photographs of Yosemite and San Francisco. Through landscape photography, he mastered the technique of organizing a broad expanse of space into still images from a single vantage point.*2

In 1872, the businessman Leland Stanford commissioned him to use photography to investigate a horse’s gait. By 1878, Muybridge had successfully photographed motion in sequence by arranging multiple cameras along a track. The importance of this work extends beyond confirming that all four of a horse’s hooves leave the ground. Its methodological shift lay in triggering multiple devices in temporal order, turning motion itself into a sequence of frames instead of using one camera to capture a decisive instant.*3

Following a lecture in Philadelphia in 1883, a purpose-built outdoor studio was constructed in 1884 on the grounds of the University of Pennsylvania’s veterinary hospital, expanding the project into Animal Locomotion. The university advanced $5,000 and provided a setting with three black walls, a white measuring grid, and banks of cameras. The defining change of the 1880s was the transformation of a private experiment into an institutional study of motion supported by university funding, facilities, subjects, and publishing.*4

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Breaking Down Time with Multiple Cameras

Muybridge’s motion photographs are historically important for more than proving the positions of a horse’s body. By placing multiple cameras at equal intervals and triggering their shutters in sequence, he converted a single movement into a series of still images arranged along a timeline.*6 As the Library of Congress notes, this apparatus made visible instants that the naked eye could not isolate, replacing ordinary vision with a mechanical division of time.*7 While Marey compressed time into a single image through multiple exposures on one dry plate, Muybridge unfolded time across independent frames.*29

sections.title: Key Works, Apparatus, and Media
sections.body_html:
Animal Locomotion at the University of Pennsylvania

For the study begun in 1884, Muybridge used three banks of twelve cameras, thirty-six in total, with electrically activated shutters and dry plates in place of wet plates. A white grid covered the walls of the black outdoor studio, allowing the distance traveled and the subject’s posture to be compared across frames. By standardizing the apparatus, background, and time intervals, he made motion into repeatable observational material instead of a moment skillfully captured by a photographer.*4

Published in 1887, Animal Locomotion comprised 781 plates. It presented walking, running, jumping, sports, everyday activities such as domestic work and manual labor, and a variety of zoo animals in the same sequential format. Patients from Philadelphia Hospital also served as subjects. From a contemporary perspective, a study that classified human bodies as specimens of motion raises ethical questions alongside its scientific utility, including whose bodies were subjected to observation and classification.*4 The publication was used by artists, anatomists, physiologists, and athletes, setting a precedent for photographs to circulate simultaneously as works of art and scientific documents.*13

Three-Directional Photography and the Classification of Bodies

The University of Pennsylvania apparatus did more than photograph a movement in sequence from one side. Its multiple banks of cameras made it possible to compare the same action from the side, front, and an oblique angle. Walking and jumping could thus be treated as data encompassing different directions instead of as a single beautiful pose. The photographic equipment and materials in the university archives offer concrete evidence of this research environment.*5 Publication records for Animal Locomotion show that the plates were organized by action, subject, camera angle, and time interval; the publication itself was designed as a searchable catalog of motion.*12

Placing bodies against the same background and recording them at the same intervals and angles may appear to describe universal human movement, but the selection of particular bodies as ideals or standards was not neutral. Elspeth H. Brown analyzes the male bodies in Animal Locomotion through the racialized “virile body” and gender norms that took shape in late nineteenth-century America.*32 Sequential photographs could suppress individual differences to make bodies comparable, while that very comparison could also make norms of health, masculinity, race, and ability visible. Muybridge’s innovation in photographic history must therefore be understood as both a way of showing motion and a means of reinforcing the visual forms through which modern society compared and classified bodies.

Circulation in Art, Medicine, and Sports

The sequential photographs circulated beyond the photographer’s studio as references for artists depicting the human body, observational material for physiology and anatomy, and aids for comparing athletic movements. PhotoAnthology emphasizes that the study has been repeatedly cited in both science and art.*14 The Met’s holdings from Animal Locomotion likewise demonstrate the plates’ dual status: made as scientific records, they are now preserved as works in the histories of photography and art.*8

The Zoopraxiscope’s Design and Public Projection

Muybridge devised the zoopraxiscope in 1879 and gave public projection lectures in San Francisco in 1880. It is therefore more accurate to distinguish the year of invention from the year of public projection than to say it was publicly presented in 1879.*27 For the device, figures of people and animals based on sequential photographs were redrawn around the circumference of a glass disc. As the disc rotated, a shutter briefly projected each image onto a screen. The surviving disc and shutter in the Science Museum Group collection demonstrate this construction.*26

The device differed from later motion-picture projectors, which transported photographic negatives on a strip of film. Yet it marked an important stage in the history of moving images by connecting two operations: breaking motion down photographically and reassembling the sequence before an audience as a moving image. Describing Muybridge as a pioneer who established a practical link between sequential photography and projection clarifies how his work differed from later film technology without presenting him as the sole inventor of cinema. The Science Museum Group likewise explains his work as an intersection of motion photography and early moving-image technology.*28

Glass Discs and the Lecture as Media

The zoopraxiscope did not project the sequential photographs directly; their contours were refined and the figures redrawn on glass discs. Muybridge Image & Context presents this “zoopraxography” as a process of remaking situated between photography and projection.*15 The discs and apparatus preserved at Kingston Museum provide physical evidence of how photographed motion was transformed into visual teaching material for lectures.*16 Published in 1893, Descriptive Zoopraxography was Muybridge’s own account of his motion studies and projection device, articulating photography, analysis, and public presentation as a unified method.*9

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Muybridge as Scientific Photographer and Precursor to Cinema

Animal Locomotion did more than create a transparent window onto the “truth” of motion. Its black background, white grid, fixed direction of travel, nude bodies and prescribed actions, and multiple camera angles transformed bodies into material designed for comparison. Scientific objectivity arose from the studio, directions given to subjects, time intervals, classification, and publication format as well as from the camera. The photographic apparatus, cropping masks, and even a retouching desk preserved in the University of Pennsylvania archives show that these photographs belonged to a system that included post-exposure selection and production.*4

Placing bodies within the same grid and time intervals enabled comparison while turning subjects into specimens for classification. The inclusion of Philadelphia Hospital patients shows that the production of medical knowledge cannot be separated from the power relations that determined whose bodies were placed under observation. The continuing preservation of Muybridge materials for study in NYU Special Collections reflects questions that reach beyond technological history into the representation of bodies, medical history, and gender studies.*22

Patients with Neurological Disorders and Medical Observation

Animal Locomotion included patients from Philadelphia Hospital as well as members of the public and athletes. Recently rediscovered clinical records confirm that Muybridge collaborated with the neurologist Francis Dercum to photographically study how neurological disorders, including ataxia, altered gait.*30 This offers a concrete example of sequential photography’s contribution to medical knowledge while also showing how bodies affected by illness became objects of comparison and classification before a university research apparatus. Its scientific utility must be considered together with the asymmetry between observer and observed.

A broader view of the relationship with pathology shows that Muybridge’s work was not an isolated undertaking. Marta Braun and Elizabeth Whitcombe compare photographs of pathological gait by Muybridge, Marey, and Albert Londe, examining how late nineteenth-century neurology used sequential photography to record and classify abnormalities of movement visible on the body’s surface.*34 The capacity of sequential photography to make phenomena visible expanded medical knowledge while abstracting patients’ bodies into cases. The scientific character of motion photography must be assessed in terms of both its observational achievements and the institutions that rendered those observed into classifiable objects.

Publications and Museum Collections

Animal Locomotion circulated as a large-format publication in eleven volumes and appears in the Library of Congress catalog as an 1887 publication.*24 The Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History holds an individual plate as an artifact in the history of science and technology.*18 The Seattle Art Museum holds a work from the same series as art, crossing the boundary between scientific documentation and fine-art photography.*20 An individual plate also entered the collection of the Detroit Institute of Arts, demonstrating how museums in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries have reframed a nineteenth-century research publication as “art.”*25

The Collaborative Structure Preserved in the Archive

Muybridge’s research cannot be reduced to the invention of a lone genius. Contracts with the university, equipment, correspondence, and publications preserved at the University of Pennsylvania make it possible to trace a collaborative project involving funders, university personnel, technicians, and subjects.*5 Selected materials published by the university archives include documents and plates that trace the research process, revealing an institutional background to production and study that the finished sequential photographs alone cannot show.*10 Penn Libraries also organizes Muybridge materials as a major collection in its own right, allowing photographs, publications, and research materials to be consulted together.*11 The Smithsonian Archives of American Art preserves another body of documents concerning the University of Pennsylvania and Muybridge’s motion studies, providing resources that span photographic and institutional history.*17 The inclusion of Animal Locomotion in an exhibition at the FUJIFILM SQUARE Photo History Museum shows that the study now circulates beyond the history of American science in international education on photographic history.*23

Continuity from Landscape Photography to Motion Studies

Before turning to motion photography, Muybridge organized views of Yosemite and San Francisco through multiple viewpoints, panoramas, and large-format photographs. SFMOMA’s artist materials document a long career that includes landscape photography and resists limiting his identity to motion studies alone.*19 The National Gallery of Art likewise treats his Western landscapes and motion studies as parts of a single photographer’s career.*21 Although their subjects differ, the landscapes and motion photographs share a process of mechanically dividing vision and subsequently rearranging it to produce forms of seeing unlike those of the human eye.

Reconstructing Time, Not Inventing Cinema

The zoopraxiscope did not operate like later motion-picture film, but Muybridge’s public lectures demonstrated that still images are perceived as motion when sequential photographs are shown in temporal order. The Kingston collections preserve the apparatus, discs, and lecture materials together, making it possible to trace the transformation of photographic results into an audience’s experience of time.*16 At the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago, Muybridge operated the “Zoopraxographical Hall,” turning motion studies into projected entertainment for a large audience.*4 His place in the prehistory of cinema lies in his concrete articulation, through photography, publication, and projection, of photography’s transition from preserving an instant to breaking down and reconstructing time.

Current Assessments and Reconsiderations

Scholarship has moved beyond celebrating Muybridge’s technical innovations to examine how faithfully he captured natural movement and how selection and retouching affected claims to scientific objectivity. Penn Today presents the motion studies as a transformation in science and visual culture while describing Muybridge’s relationships with contemporary researchers and artists.*13 PhotoAnthology’s account similarly surveys the work’s lasting role as a reference in both art and science.*14 Attending to this dual character places Muybridge beyond the simple heroic image of the “father of cinema” and identifies him as a complicated figure who incorporated modern time measurement and bodily classification into photography.

Recent scholarship has also been cautious about reading Animal Locomotion solely as a success story in which machines produced objective truth. A study in History of Photography focuses on sequences ill-suited to physiological analysis: actions unrelated to productivity, such as dancing, reclining, and posing; inconsistent time intervals; and rearranged plates. It notes that photographs exceeding the logic of mechanization and standardization exist within the same atlas.*31 Animal Locomotion was therefore a scientific apparatus that standardized bodies while also preserving movements and photographic failures that did not fully conform to that standard. Contemporary critical assessment reads beyond a binary between science and art to consider the gap between the order intended by the apparatus and the images it actually produced.

Marta Braun has further reconsidered Muybridge’s authority as a scientific photographer through his post-exposure retouching, cropping, and rearrangement of images, as well as his relationship with the University of Pennsylvania’s Muybridge Committee.*33 This does not mean that the work was “fake.” It shows that scientific objectivity was not automatically guaranteed by the camera but was constructed through human decisions about which images to select and alter and how to sequence them for publication. Muybridge’s significance in photographic history also lies in exposing how objectivity itself is designed, beyond the myth that the mechanical eye eliminated human subjectivity.

nadar.html.lead_html: Nadar (1820–1910) was born in Paris as Gaspard-Félix Tournachon. After working as a journalist and caricaturist, he turned to photography in the 1850s, portraying such contemporary cultural figures as Baudelaire, Hugo, and Sand with spare backgrounds and carefully directed light. He expanded the technical scope of the medium through experiments with aerial photography in 1858, a patent for photography by electric light in 1861, photographs of the catacombs in 1862, and photographs of the sewers in 1865. His studio at 35 Boulevard des Capucines also became a meeting point for commerce, culture, and avant-garde art.
nadar.html.thesis_html: In mid-nineteenth-century portrait studios, backdrops, props, and costumes served as important signs of social standing. Nadar subdued these elements and sought to draw out an “intimate likeness” through light, posture, expression, and dialogue between photographer and sitter. His first major shift was to move portrait photography away from the performance of status and toward a modern representation of the individual that invited viewers to read intellect and character. At the same time, through aerial photography, underground photography by electric light, and a vast commercial studio, he reconfigured the technical and social conditions governing where, under what light, and whom photography could depict. His importance lies in more than the distinguished portraits he left behind. He established the photographer as image maker, technical experimenter, entrepreneur, and intermediary within a network of cultural figures, demonstrating that photography could become a medium for organizing information and character in urban society.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Nadar’s Career and Nineteenth-Century Paris

Gaspard-Félix Tournachon, known as Nadar, was born in Paris on April 6, 1820. The BnF authority record also documents his death in Paris on March 20, 1910.*18 Before becoming a photographer, he worked as a journalist, writer, and caricaturist in the Parisian press and literary worlds. His large 1854 lithograph Panthéon Nadar assembled such contemporary cultural figures as George Sand, Victor Hugo, Balzac, and Alexandre Dumas. Even before he photographed people, he was already mapping those who shaped the culture of his time as a network of faces.*15

Around 1854, he established a commercial photography studio at 113 Rue Saint-Lazare and produced portraits primarily of his friends among writers, artists, and actors. The BnF emphasizes how Nadar’s bohemian circle converged with portraiture as a commodity, distinguishing his operation from the large commercial studios of the period.*19 In 1860, he moved to a large studio at 35 Boulevard des Capucines, developing an enterprise that The Met describes as one of the foremost portrait studios in Paris.*14

“Nadar,” however, was never a name fixed exclusively to Félix’s signature. A BnF retrospective examines three Nadars—including his brother Adrien and his son Paul—and shows how the studio name developed into both a family-based production system and a commercial brand.*2 Distinguishing later works credited to “Atelier Nadar” from photographs made by Félix himself is therefore important when assessing dates and authorship.

Nadar also took photographic technology beyond the studio. He began experimenting with aerial photography in 1858, patented a photographic process using electric light in 1861, photographed the catacombs in 1862, and photographed the sewers in 1865. He did not use the giant balloon Le Géant for the experiments of 1858; Le Géant belonged to a separate aeronautical venture of the 1860s. By photographing from the opposite extremes of the air and the underground, he sought to free the photographic viewpoint from ground level and natural light at a time when transportation, sanitation, and urban reconstruction were transforming Paris under the Second Empire.*21

In April 1874, Nadar’s former studio at 35 Boulevard des Capucines hosted the first Impressionist exhibition, featuring Monet, Degas, Pissarro, Renoir, and others. The fact that a portrait studio, aeronautical experiments, records of the urban underground, and a venue for avant-garde art all intersect in one life makes Nadar more than a celebrated portrait photographer.*4

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Portrait Photography—Light and Psychological Likeness

In his portraits, Nadar kept the background spare and directed attention toward the face, posture, hands, clothing, and the angle of the light, instead of explaining social status through layers of opulent furniture and painted scenery. In Nadar’s own words, preserved by the BnF, photographic technique can be learned, but a feeling for light and the ability to understand the sitter’s “psychological side” cannot easily be taught.*19 Portraiture thus shifted from a setting filled with signs of rank to a question of how the photographer sees and forms a relationship with the subject.

The Portrait Industry under the Second Empire

Portrait photography was itself becoming rapidly accessible to a mass public in the 1850s and 1860s, as Nadar developed his studio. In 1854, André-Adolphe-Eugène Disdéri patented the châssis multiplicateur, which made it possible to take several small portraits on a single glass plate and thereby lowered production costs and retail prices. The BnF explains that this invention brought the carte-de-visite portrait within reach of a broader clientele.*23 Nadar’s portraits emerged within a market in which photographs of faces were beginning to circulate widely as commodities, after the era when studios served only a small number of privileged clients.

35 Boulevard des Capucines—Commercial Studio and Cultural Circle

The large studio that opened in 1860 was a commercial portrait business visited by ordinary bourgeois clients as well as a private setting where Nadar photographed his artist friends. The Met describes it as one of the leading portrait enterprises in Paris and notes that Nadar’s own photography coexisted with a high volume of commercial work made by his staff.*14 The aesthetic of the “natural portrait” took shape within the studio system that produced photographs as repeatable commodities. This conjunction was central to the modernity of nineteenth-century portrait photography.

Disdéri and Nadar—Mass Portraiture and Psychological Portraiture

Disdéri’s carte-de-visite process efficiently placed multiple poses on a single plate and reduced the price of a portrait. Nadar, while embracing the commercial studio system, foregrounded the adjustment of light, posture, expression, and conversation for each sitter as the source of a portrait’s value. The distinction cannot be reduced to “mass production versus art.” Musée Carnavalet holds a carte-de-visite portrait by Atelier Nadar, confirming that Nadar’s own studio participated in the commercial circulation of small-format portraits.*24 The difference lay in changing how a person was presented within the same commercial market, not in rejecting the format.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Aerial Photography—The Experiments of 1858 and Paris in 1868

In 1858, Nadar experimented with making wet-plate photographs from a balloon. The BnF reports that he achieved his first success over Petit-Bicêtre in the autumn of that year, although no print survives.*12 The Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum identifies a photograph taken over Boston by James Wallace Black in 1860 as the oldest surviving aerial photograph.*13 The 2026 exhibition at the Catacombs of Paris further presents Nadar’s 1868 aerial view of Paris as one of the earliest surviving urban aerial photographs, showing how a viewpoint from the sky changed representations of the modern city.*21

The wet-plate collodion process required the photographer to expose and develop a sensitized glass plate before it dried. Aerial photography therefore required bringing not just the camera but also darkroom work into the balloon. The innovation consisted of moving the entire photographic process, previously bound to a ground-based working environment, into the air and detaching the photographer’s viewpoint from the earth, as well as photographing from a great height.*13

Artificial Light—Photographing the Catacombs in 1862

Nadar began experimenting with photography by artificial light around 1859 and obtained a patent in 1861. The BnF describes his photographs of the catacombs in 1862 and the sewers in 1865 as later developments of this work.*17 The Met’s Catacombs, Paris, made in April 1862, is held as an example produced with an early arc lamp designed by Nadar himself.*16 Underground photography became more than a novel technical experiment: it also documented urban infrastructure hidden from street level during Haussmann’s reconstruction of Paris. The exhibition at the Catacombs of Paris treats aerial and underground photography as two vertical perspectives on a city being remade.*21

A technical history focused only on the ability to illuminate darkness cannot fully account for the photographs of the catacombs and sewers. Shao-Chien Tseng interprets Nadar’s images of subterranean Paris made by electric light as a map of the “urban body,” showing how the Haussmann-era city isolated, sanitized, and managed corpses, sewage, and waste.*25 Beneath the modern order taking shape above ground lay the infrastructure of death and excretion that sustained it. Nadar’s artificial light made hidden sites photographable and brought before the public an urban interior that modernization had rendered invisible.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Nadar’s Place in Photographic History

Nadar’s portraits hold an important place in photographic history for more than the visual spareness of their backgrounds. He combined the observational experience of a journalist and caricaturist, direct ties to a bohemian cultural circle, and the mass-production setting of a commercial studio. In doing so, he moved portraiture away from images that defined a sitter through social signs and toward photographs that sought to read individual character and intellect. The BnF distinguishes Nadar’s work from that of the large studios of his day by describing his portraits as lively, sympathetic to their subjects, and artistic.*19

From Panthéon Nadar through his studio portraits, Nadar did more than photograph nineteenth-century Parisian cultural figures one by one: he visualized a human network spanning literature, art, theater, and journalism. At the same time, 35 Boulevard des Capucines was a commercial establishment serving the general public, where artistic portraiture and the photographic industry operated in the same place. The BnF chronology documents the development of the business, including the move to a large studio and its high operating costs.*20

Aerial and underground photography were not sidelines unrelated to Nadar’s portraits. Just as he removed extraneous staging from the sitter in his portraiture, his technical experiments removed the assumptions that photography depended on the ground, natural light, and the studio. The paired directions—from above to survey the city and from below to examine its internal structure—helped turn photography into a means of visualizing the modern city. The current exhibition at the Catacombs of Paris likewise reassesses this work in relation to the urban transformation of the Haussmann era.*21

The use of his former studio for the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874 also shows that photography and painting cannot be understood solely in terms of simple competition. Moving among the roles of photographer, entrepreneur, aeronautical experimenter, and friend to cultural figures, Nadar embodied the ways photography was produced, commercialized, and shared within nineteenth-century urban culture.*4

Stephen Bann examines Nadar as more than a hero who achieved a succession of technical “firsts.” He presents him as a figure who continued to reflect through both photography and writing on the historical experience of a nineteenth century shaped by the intersections of revolution, war, and social and economic progress.*26 Viewed as a continuous body of work, the aerial photographs, underground images, portraits, and memoirs share more than a curiosity about new technology. Across these different endeavors runs the question of how photography records a rapidly changing society and how people come to understand that change as history.

From Portrait as Commodity to the Representation of the Individual

Within the portrait market of the Second Empire, Nadar’s spare backgrounds did not signify an escape from commercial photography. At a time when the carte de visite had turned the face into a commodity that could be exchanged and collected in large numbers, Nadar placed greater value on subtle differences in faces and bodies than on backdrops and props, while working within the same studio economy.*23 His shift did not rescue portraiture from mass circulation. It demonstrated that even after mass circulation had been established, the relationship between photographer and sitter could itself become the content of a photograph.

Nadar’s Portraits and Celebrity Culture

Nadar’s portraits were also bound up with the expanding nineteenth-century culture of possessing and viewing the faces of celebrities. His portrait of Théophile Gautier in MoMA’s collection dates to 1855, while the portrait of Honoré Daumier in the National Gallery of Art was made in 1856–58. Private relationships with writers and artists were thus transferred into a commercial network of portraiture.*6 The NGA describes the Daumier portrait as an expression of esteem for a fellow artist and notes that Nadar may have charged less than his usual fee.*8 These works clearly demonstrate Nadar’s method of constructing a persona through a spare background, clothing, posture, and gaze, without using props to explain the sitter’s celebrity.

Nadar’s studio, however, was a business that mass-produced portraits as commodities, as well as a salon for friends. The 1857 Portrait de femme in the Musée d’Orsay bears the stamp “NADAR & Cie, SOCIETE DE PHOTOGRAPHIE ARTISTIQUE, 113 R. St LAZARE,” showing that the ideal of artistic portraiture operated within a corporate organization and the mechanisms of commercial photography.*9 The many portraits held by MoMA also make it possible to trace, work by work, the breadth of his portrait photography from the 1850s onward.*7

Nadar himself was not an observer standing outside this culture of celebrity. Jillian Lerner analyzes how, during his transition from caricature to photography, he repeatedly used signatures, self-portraits, images combining photographs and illustrations, and advertising to establish “Nadar” as a recognizable brand across multiple media.*27 Artistic portraiture and commercial publicity were compatible here. Photographing cultural figures, performing as a cultural figure himself, and making the studio a recognized urban landmark together created a single photography business.

His conception of portraiture was not limited to the face. Emily Eastgate Brink discusses La main du banquier D. as a modern “portrait in pieces” that attempts to read character and identity from a banker’s hand alone.*28 Nadar’s portraiture matters for more than his use of simplified backgrounds to photograph faces: it connected photography to the nineteenth-century problem of representing character itself, asking whether a person could also be read through fragments such as handwriting, a hand, or posture.

Documentary Photography and Scientific Vision

The photographic activity of the Nadar family extended beyond portraiture and aerial photography. The BnF details the family’s involvement in photographic applications connected with the observational sciences, including medicine, anthropometry, anthropology, agriculture, cartography, and military strategy.*10 Unlike portraits constructed as psychological character studies, these applications called for seemingly objective forms such as frontal views, clarity, and the recording of detail. Read as extensions of documentary photography, Nadar’s aerial and underground images show that he did not repeat a single style but reconfigured the appearance of photographs according to their purpose.

Artificial light was not introduced suddenly for underground photography. The photographic records of the French Ministry of Culture include the 1861 Effet de lumière sur une main, an experiment in lighting a hand with artificial light.*11 This experiment, which led to the catacomb photographs of the following year, mattered both as the technical achievement of photographing in darkness and as a change to the spatial and temporal constraints of photography, made possible by the photographer’s active design of light.

Collections and Scholarship on Nadar

The Met, George Eastman Museum, and Getty Museum hold substantial groups of Nadar’s portraits and technical experiments, allowing the date and process of individual works to be compared.*1 The Eastman Museum presents materials on Nadar as a major figure in the history of photographic technology, while the Getty organizes groups of portraits by maker.*3 The Met’s monograph Nadar spans portraiture, technical experimentation, and cultural history, showing that his current reputation extends beyond that of a portraitist of celebrities.*22 The Getty’s object records likewise provide a basis for examining the studio’s long activity work by work.*5

nakaji-yasui.html.lead_html: Photographer who worked within Kansai photographic culture — the Naniwa and Tampei photography clubs — developing wide-ranging experiments from pictorialism to constructive photography and composite negatives. He is increasingly recognised internationally as a representative figure of pre-war Japanese photographic experimentation.
nakaji-yasui.html.thesis_html: Based in the camera clubs of the Kansai region, Yasui experimented across a wide range of techniques, from Pictorialism to constructive photography and composite negatives. Refusing to settle into any single style, his work shows the breadth of experimental possibility in prewar Japanese photography, and has recently been reassessed both in Japan and abroad.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Nakaji Yasui was born in Osaka in 1903 and became familiar with photography in his teens. *1 He participated in the Naniwa Photography Club and subsequently developed his activities across several Kansai photography groups including the Tampei Photography Club and Ginrei-sha. *2 Kansai photographic culture provided a rich environment for experimentation for amateur photographers of the time, with magazines and exhibitions creating space for testing new expressions. *3

Records held in the Art Commons of the National Art Center Tokyo document his activities within his short life of 1903 to 1942. *4 Entering the 1930s, he actively incorporated experimental techniques such as composite negatives and cropping during printing, making his departure from simple realism explicit. The Aichi Prefectural Museum of Art retrospective analysed these techniques empirically. *5 He died in 1942 at the age of 39. His influence continued after his death, with statements of appreciation left by later photographers including Domon Ken and Daido Moriyama. *6

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The range of experiment that resists fixing to a single style

Yasui's expression cannot be fixed to a single style. Early on he used soft focus and pictorialist compositions; gradually this expanded to still life, urban scenes, portraiture, constructive photography, composites and cropping. *7 His importance lies not in incorporating diverse techniques as fashion but in his continuous search for methods of creating symbolic images from fragments of reality. The Tokyo Station Gallery checklist PDF systematically organises Yasui's works, allowing the breadth of his experiments to be confirmed. *8

Kansai photographic culture is an indispensable context for Yasui. The Naniwa and Tampei photography clubs were environments where amateur photographers competed in technique and experimented with new expressions through magazines and exhibitions. *9 Within these settings, rather than directly imitating the reception of the European avant-garde, Yasui converted fragments of the everyday, urban anxiety, bodies and object arrangements into a distinctive tension. The British Museum holds photobook materials on Yasui, providing one international point of reference. *10

Composite negative experiments and cropping

Composite negatives and cropping convert photography from simple documentation to a medium for reconstituting fragments of reality. *11 Through these techniques, Yasui conducted experiments of decomposing the reality captured by the camera and reassembling it as a different order. The Aichi Prefectural Museum of Art retrospective analysed these techniques empirically, and per-work technique records continue to function as research materials. *12 The National Art Center Tokyo's records document this retrospective as an important node in Yasui's re-evaluation. *13

The Tokyo Art Beat exhibition report provides detailed evaluation of the 2023–24 retrospective, allowing Yasui's contemporary positioning to be confirmed. *14 These technical experiments have become an important prehistory for thinking about subjectivity, urban sensibility and experimentality in later Japanese photography. *15

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Recent exhibitions at the Aichi Prefectural Museum of Art, the Tokyo Station Gallery and the Hyogo Prefectural Museum of Art have reconsidered Yasui as an outstanding figure in pre-war Japanese photography. *16 The British Museum functions as an international point of reference for photobooks, reprints and bilingual commentary. *17 CiNii Research and NDL Search hold numerous research articles and bibliographic materials, and scholarly re-evaluation is advancing. *18 As the statements by later photographers demonstrate, Yasui's experiments are received not as the inheritance of a particular style but as a question about how photography reorganises reality and subjectivity. *19 In the re-evaluation of pre-war Japanese photography, Yasui's work is centrally cited as evidence that original experiments were conducted within the institutions of domestic amateur culture — clubs, magazines and exhibitions — going beyond the framework of simply receiving Western avant-garde influences.

naoya-hatakeyama.html.lead_html: After the compositional approach he had developed as a student ceased to work for him in Tokyo, Naoya Hatakeyama returned to the cement plant and limestone quarries of his hometown. He began to understand the city by tracing its materials back from the visible surface to the resources extracted elsewhere and the cavities left underground. Lime Hills and Lime Works connect extraction, processing, and construction through large-format color photography; Blast, made with the knowledge of blasting engineers and remote equipment, records the instant rock becomes an urban resource. Extending his research to aerial views, rivers, subterranean spaces, and post-disaster Rikuzentakata, Hatakeyama added material circulation, industrial labor, and the duration after catastrophe to the human-altered landscapes established by New Topographics.
naoya-hatakeyama.html.thesis_html: After New Topographics made the surfaces of human-altered landscapes a subject of photographic history, Hatakeyama used interconnected series to show limestone moving from mountain to factory and city while leaving cavities underground. He chose large-format color for the detail of quarry faces, a small motor-driven camera for the seconds of an explosion, aerial photography to compare mines and cities, and repeated photography for post-disaster change. By changing apparatus and timescale with each subject, he repositioned landscape photography from the description of a finished view to a long-term investigation of the processes, labor, consumer responsibility, and post-disaster change that produce a place.
