sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
The Rikuzentakata Cement Plant and Kiyoji Otsuji—Thinking About the External World and the Medium Together

Naoya Hatakeyama was born in Rikuzentakata, Iwate Prefecture, and developed an early interest in the hardness of rock and metal*4. The first subject he painted on canvas in high school was the cement plant on his route to school. In 1979 he entered the School of Art and Design at the University of Tsukuba and turned toward photography in Kiyoji Otsuji’s classes. In an SFMOMA talk, Hatakeyama identified his interest in the plant and his encounter with Otsuji as starting points for his work*1.

Otsuji’s teaching joined composition and printing technique to questions of twentieth-century art, reproduction, the readymade, matter, and language. In the critical climate of the 1980s, modernism’s inquiry into photography’s specific properties carried considerable authority, while “literary” or “painterly” photography could be rejected for lacking self-criticism of the medium*6. This environment encouraged Hatakeyama to construct images clearly while examining how photography transforms the external world. He later argued that after formalism reached its limits, photographers including Nobuyoshi Araki, Nan Goldin, and Larry Clark returned the direct force of the subject to photography*6. His work developed toward series that held together scrutiny of the medium and attention to socially situated places.

Friedlander, New Landscape, and New Color—Permission to Photograph the Everyday

When Hatakeyama studied photography, Japanese audiences were encountering Lee Friedlander, American documentary work of the 1970s, New Landscape, New Color, and new photographic criticism. Friedlander appeared in Otsuji’s first lecture, and Hatakeyama has recalled the stimulus of an approach that photographed ordinary surroundings with conviction instead of searching for landmarks or events*1. These imports showed that everyday built landscapes could be analyzed and that ordinary places could command a different kind of attention through photography.

As a student, Hatakeyama made pictures that placed buildings or trees as simple forms within broad spaces. After graduation, Tokyo’s signs, buildings, traffic, and wires divided his field of vision so densely that his previous compositions no longer worked. He returned home in search of open space and revisited the cement plant instead of immediately devising a new urban photography in Tokyo*1. This impasse directed him beyond the city’s visible appearance toward the materials from which Tokyo was made.

When Photographing Tokyo Failed, the Quarry Became a Study of the City

A cement-plant employee took Hatakeyama to a limestone quarry, an encounter that directly led to Lime Hills. With support from the Japan Limestone Association, he visited mines and factories from Hokkaido to Okinawa for roughly eight years and learned large-format architectural photography in the process*1. Instead of seeking a composition capable of ordering Tokyo’s complicated streets, he investigated extraction, processing, and transport at the distant sites that generated the city’s form.

Seen from an airplane, Tokyo’s densely built surface resembled the exposed rock of a quarry. Limestone becomes cement and concrete, accumulating in roads, housing, dams, and office districts. Hatakeyama linked the mountain’s missing volume to the city’s mass as movements of the same material, bringing what might appear as separate subjects—a regional industrial landscape and a metropolitan center of consumption—into a single process of urbanization*1. The idea situated postwar concrete construction and redevelopment after the 1980s within a geography that included extraction sites beyond the city.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Miners’ Distrust—Questioning the Visual Formula of Environmental Accusation

While photographing mines, Hatakeyama heard workers express distrust toward news photographs that presented quarries as symbols of environmental destruction. A cut mountain can form a forceful image of accusation, while the urban life that consumes limestone as roads and buildings disappears outside the frame. Hatakeyama declined to place responsibility solely on extraction companies and returned attention to the chain of consumption that included himself as a city resident*1.

The experience also changed his understanding of nature. Hatakeyama distinguishes nature as the environment in which people live from nature consumed as a beautiful view, and argues that the sense of beauty is itself shaped by histories of literature and art*1. A quarry shown as a single wound permits viewers to feel outrage while forgetting its relation to urban life. He therefore connected mines, factories, cities, and underground spaces across long-term series, bringing the position of resource users into the meaning of the images.

Large-Format Color and Nationwide Research—Returning a Single Wound to an Industrial System

Large-format color could register geological strata, heavy machinery, work roads, and the contours of cut rock at once. During nearly eight years of nationwide research, Hatakeyama acquired the techniques of architectural photography and photographed mines as working spaces in which extraction continued*1. The clarity of the image preserved equipment, labor, geology, and scale beyond an immediate verdict of environmental damage.

Repeatedly photographing mines across Japan also corrects the tendency to treat a single quarry as an exceptional tragedy. Topography, machinery, extraction methods, and surrounding vegetation vary from site to site, while a common industrial system sends limestone from each region into urban construction. The long-term series was chosen to hold local specificity and nationwide structure within the same work.

Blast—Remote Operation and the Collapse of a Safe Observer’s Position

Photographing quarry blasts from a distance with a telephoto lens preserves the divide between a safe observer and a dangerous site. Hatakeyama wanted to examine more closely how rock fractured and fell. A large-format camera could neither use the required shutter speed nor produce a sequence, and a single blast yielded only one frame. He therefore chose a small camera, motor drive, and FM radio remote control*1.

The camera position was chosen with advice from blasting engineers who understood the rock face, explosives, and direction of falling stone. They predicted how two thousand tons of rock would collapse and indicated positions where the equipment was less likely to be destroyed*1. Blast is an image made jointly by site knowledge, radio signals, a motorized camera, explosives, and rock. Landscape photography moves here from a distant view to the contact zone where matter changes state.

Aerial Views, Rivers, and Underground Spaces—Changing Viewpoint With the Movement of Matter

Hatakeyama does not preserve one viewpoint as a personal style; he changes position as the research requires. Aerial photography compares quarry faces and urban density at a common scale. Photographs along rivers vertically connect buildings to the water beneath them. Sewers and underground quarries reveal the cavities to which the city sends wastewater or leaves behind after extracting building material*13. Movement among distant views, ground surfaces, water, and subterranean spaces follows the routes taken by matter.

For exhibitions, Hatakeyama constructs models to test print sizes, spacing on the walls, and movement between series*5. Viewers walk among ground level, underground spaces, distant prospects, and explosions, understanding separated sites as one social process. Exhibition design turns bodily movement into a means of tracing an urban cross-section.

Light and Photosensitive Material—Nature Within the Photographic Medium

Referring to William Henry Fox Talbot’s “pencil of nature,” Hatakeyama extends nature from mountains and plants before the lens to the light, photosensitive material, chemical reactions, and chance operating within photography itself*1. In A Bird / Blast, a bird enters the frame at the instant of detonation, introducing an unplanned living presence into the engineered movement of explosives and rock.

This account revises the idea of photographic technology as an instrument of control standing outside nature. The photographer determines composition, exposure, and placement, yet light, emulsion, birds, dust, and the pattern of falling rock add their own results. Hatakeyama’s clear images observe traces of contact between human planning and material response.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Lime Hills, Lime Works, and Blast—Limestone Across Three Timescales

Begun in 1986, Lime Hills photographs limestone quarries across Japan in large-format color, recording terraced quarry faces, work roads, heavy machinery, and surrounding mountains. White rock forms broad planes across the image, while machinery and roads provide measures of scale. The quarry does not become a single symbolic wound; geology, working processes, and vegetation remain within the same field of vision.

Lime Works moves into the factory and photographs the equipment that crushes, transports, and processes limestone into cement*8. Connecting mines and factories through books and exhibitions makes the white section of rock and the concrete wall of a city appear as different states of the same material. The stillness of the large-format image presents a finished landscape while inviting attention to the daily extraction and processing continuing behind it.

Blast, begun in 1995, divides the rock face before detonation, expansion, dust, and falling stone into sequential frames. A scene that a single photograph might turn into spectacular explosion becomes, across several frames, the process by which rock turns into an urban resource*11. Lime Hills holds strata and quarry faces within a still image; Lime Works registers the repetitive time of conveyors and kilns; the sequences of Blast break down several seconds of fragmentation. Together, the three series place the same limestone within geological, industrial, and explosive durations.

River Series, Underground, and Ciel Tombé—The City’s Substructure

River Series aligns buildings with the water flowing beneath them along a vertical axis, adding waterways to the city’s visible surface. Underground brings artificial light into sewers and records pipes, walls, water, and reflections in square color images. In SFMOMA’s Underground #7109, a dark conduit extending into the distance and light on the water render the city’s interior as an architectural space*2.

Ciel Tombé photographs underground quarries and reinforcement structures in Paris. The stone city above was built from material cut below, leaving cavities produced by that movement*13. The three series present the city’s lower levels as physical conditions of surface life—drainage, extraction, and structural support—rather than as a mysterious separate world.

Natural Stories, Rikuzentakata, and Tsunami Trees—Time After Disaster

The 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami devastated Hatakeyama’s hometown of Rikuzentakata and brought profound personal loss, including the death of his mother. He began photographing before receiving commissions from newspapers, museums, or galleries and continued without deciding where the images would be shown. Hatakeyama has said that he accepted photographs capable of producing silence or discomfort without waiting for them to be validated as art*16.

The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s Natural Stories brought limestone, coal, factories, mines, and Rikuzentakata together as works on the long interaction of human beings and nature*17. When the exhibition traveled to SFMOMA, the pre-disaster quarry and city series were reread within a career concerned with human powers of construction and changes in nature*3.

Rikuzentakata presents a large body of photographs as a chronological slideshow, linking the different rates at which debris, embankments, roads, plants, and houses change. Tsunami Trees photographs trees that continue growing after damage by the tsunami, shifting attention from the instant of disaster to years in which plants, construction, and memory proceed at different speeds*12. Repeated photography preserves several simultaneous times within the land instead of consolidating reconstruction into a linear story of recovery.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
After New Topographics—From the Landscape’s Surface to the Material Before and After

The 1975 exhibition “New Topographics” replaced sublime natural scenery with restrained views of industrial zones, cleared land, suburban housing, and other human-altered places*18. Hatakeyama learned from New Landscape and New Color the confidence to photograph ordinary built environments*1. Their influence appears in the clarity of his large-format color, while his series move beyond description of the visible surface toward the resources and processes that produce a landscape.

Bernd and Hilla Becher compared industrial structures as types, while Lewis Baltz analyzed the flat surfaces of developed land. Hatakeyama connects mines, factories, aerial cities, rivers, underground spaces, and explosions, following the same material before extraction, during processing, after construction, and in the underground absences left behind. Large-format cameras, remote sequences, aerial views, and subterranean photography provide distances and durations suited to each stage. His position lies in adding material movement, industrial labor, and the choice of photographic technology to analytical landscape photography after New Topographics.

Capitalist Production of Space and “Creative Destruction”

Hatakeyama avoids presenting mining as a simple environmental evil and emphasizes a chain of resource consumption that includes urban residents. Recent criticism has asked how fully the work makes capitalist urban formation visible. Piekalkiewicz reads limestone extraction, concrete production, and high-rise construction as a continuous production of space, and sees in Blast the destructive force on which building depends*14.

This interpretation may appear to add politics to the formal beauty of large-format photography, but the tension already exists within the work. Precisely rendered quarry faces may be received in museums as beautiful abstractions, while they also possess a use as urban building material. Hatakeyama places mine and city within the same exhibition instead of writing a conclusion into the image, allowing viewers to locate the distance between their own lives and extraction sites.

2011 and After—Words Enter Landscape Photography

The post-disaster work adds private record to Hatakeyama’s earlier landscape research and alters the assumptions carried by the word “landscape.” In an SFMOMA talk, he describes how the same photograph changes once viewers are told that his home once stood beneath a rainbow in the image, and argues that the decision to exclude memory and language in order to see a “pure” landscape is itself ideological*15.

The question also concerns the public life of disaster photography. Images of Rikuzentakata contain the artist’s personal history, yet in museums they are shared as images of a disaster area, reconstruction policy, land use, and mourning*9. Hatakeyama accumulated photographs with dates and places while leaving their eventual audience open*16. Personal memory and public record meet on the same land within the work*10.

Turning Landscape Into Time Moved by Resources, Technology, and Memory

Hatakeyama treats mountains, factories, cities, underground spaces, and post-disaster land as a continuity of matter and time moving through places. Different apparatuses record the years in which limestone travels from mountain to city, the seconds in which rock collapses during a blast, and the decade-plus transformation of Rikuzentakata through reconstruction and plant growth. The time of landscape photography expands from a moment of exposure to the long processes by which industry and disaster remake land.

After New Topographics made human-altered landscapes visible and the Bechers organized industrial structures typologically, Hatakeyama introduced a landscape’s material prehistory and afterlife into interconnected series. What Jun Tanaka called “mineral urban photography” extends the city beyond its geographic surface into an order formed by geology, extraction, chemistry, and construction*7. Hatakeyama’s conviction that a photograph records the external world while changing meaning through a viewer’s knowledge and time supports his long-term series, exhibition models, and chronological slideshows*1.

After Hatakeyama—Landscape Photography as Research Into Architecture, Resources, and Memory

Hatakeyama’s historical “after” appears in his use of landscape photography as sustained research. The look of large-format color is one component of that method. Across several decades he has investigated mines, factories, cities, rivers, underground spaces, and post-disaster land, combining photographic apparatuses, photobooks, exhibition models, slideshows, and lectures to bring distant places and times into a single question. The New Yorker has likewise described the work—from quarries to cities and post-disaster Rikuzentakata—as a study of how cities are built and destroyed*20.

In the 2023 exhibition The Lives of Documents—Photography as Project, the Canadian Centre for Architecture placed Hatakeyama among artists working since the 1970s who treated photography as a medium among artwork, research tool, and document. The exhibition examined how photography helps shape the built environment and interprets the institutions and processes that produce the visible world*19. This placement shows that Hatakeyama’s series on mines, cities, and underground spaces have been received as photographic projects for investigating architecture and infrastructure as well as for viewing landscape.

Criticism since Natural Stories has situated the work in relation to the Anthropocene, capitalist production of space, creative destruction, and disaster memory*14. Sources establishing direct influence on particular later photographers remain limited. What can be established is that Hatakeyama’s work continues to serve as a reference point when photography investigates architecture, infrastructure, resource politics, and post-disaster land beyond the conventional boundaries of landscape photography.

natalie-czech.html.lead_html: Natalie Czech makes Hidden Poems by finding sequences of words in magazines, newspapers, record covers, and product packaging that match existing poems, marking them with highlighter or drawn lines, and photographing the results. She connects photography’s reproducibility, as developed in her Düsseldorf training, with concrete poetry, appropriation, and print culture, organizing within a single photograph several ways of looking and reading: seeing the page, following the poem, and returning to the source article.
natalie-czech.html.thesis_html: Conceptual photography after Ed Ruscha made classification, instruction, repetition, and the structure of printed matter into artistic material. Appropriation art of the 1970s and 1980s used rephotography to examine the authority of authorship and the original. Natalie Czech marks words from poems hidden within existing magazine pages and enlarges the entire layout, including article, advertisement, photograph, and margin. Viewers shift among reading the source text across the page, following the marked words in sequence, and seeing the page as color and form. The camera records a private discovery in reading and gives it a scale, distance, and order that allow others to perform the same reading. The poet, the author of the source article, editors and designers, Czech’s markings, and the viewer’s reading remain as distinct layers within one image. By making a new poem without erasing its source and designing reading order and viewing distance as photographic form, Czech brings concrete poetry, appropriation, and photographic conceptualism into direct contact.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Photographic Education in Düsseldorf and Printed Matter Already in Circulation

From 2000 to 2005, Czech studied photography with Thomas Ruff at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf.*20 Düsseldorf photographers, including Ruff, had shown how photographic meaning changes through reproduction, enlargement, printing, and display, using large-scale prints, typologies, existing images, and digital processing. From this educational setting, Czech chose pages that had already been edited, printed, and circulated as her subjects.*7

During the 2000s, newspaper and magazine articles moved online, and search, copying, and pasting made it easy to extract parts of a text. Czech’s magazine pages retain headlines, body text, photographs, advertisements, margins, folds, and halftone dots at once. Unlike a search result that displays only the requested phrase, the entire source page remains visible as a physical object.

Around 2010, when Hidden Poems began, Czech shifted the emphasis of her work from observing and waiting for events in streets or among people to prolonged searches through existing materials. Reading the language of articles, advertisements, product names, and record covers—and deciding which poem to seek and which page to use—became the principal work performed before the shutter was released.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Hidden Poems: Joining Search, Marking, and Photography in a Single Procedure

Czech first selects a short poem, then searches for a page in which its constituent words appear in the same sequence within another article or advertisement. She indicates the words with highlighter, pencil, lines, or erasure and photographs the entire page at high resolution. Poems by Robert Creeley, Rolf Dieter Brinkmann, E. E. Cummings, Jack Kerouac, and others emerge from magazine articles on unrelated subjects.*2 *10

Chance moves from an unexpected encounter in the street to the discovery of a required sequence of words within a text. Czech can choose the poem and the body of source material, but she cannot determine in advance when or on which page the words will appear in the necessary order. Once the page is found, marking establishes the sequence, while photographic scale and framing create the conditions for the viewer’s eye to follow the same route.

A scan can transmit text in a readily legible form. Czech’s large photographs also show paper fibers, printing dots, overlapping highlighter, and traces of erasure. The handheld reading distance of a magazine becomes a wall-based encounter, and a private discovery becomes a visual procedure repeated by multiple viewers.

Bringing Concrete Poetry and Appropriation Together on One Page

Concrete poetry developed internationally during the 1950s in Europe, Brazil, Japan, and elsewhere. It treats spacing, repetition, typeface, and position on the page as part of poetic composition, working with the visual and material form of language as well as the meanings of words. Appropriation refers to artistic methods that quote or reuse existing images and texts in order to examine authorship, ownership, and originality. MAMCO places Czech’s work where these two lineages meet.*3

Czech does not present an existing poem as her own language. She retains the poet’s name in the title and keeps the source article readable. Highlighter brings the poem’s words forward, while the article, photographs, and advertisements remain in the frame. The same word functions as part of news or product description in the source text and as part of another poem when followed in the marked order.

MAMCO uses “intertextuality” to describe the idea that a text does not arise from a single author alone but is formed through its relation to earlier language, quotations, idioms, and other texts.*3 In Hidden Poems, this relation appears on the page as words belonging simultaneously to the source article and the quoted poem. Czech develops appropriation’s questions of authorship and origin through a method that keeps the source visible and allows two texts to be read against each other on the same page.

Switching Between the Eye That Looks at a Page and the Eye That Reads

In front of the work, viewers first register the color, photographs, margins, and typography of the page as a whole. Once they locate the marked words, the eye begins to read them in sequence, and attention to the overall composition recedes. Exhibition material from Ludlow 38 describes this movement of vision back and forth between looking at an image and reading a text.*8 *17

After finishing the poem and returning to the source article, viewers encounter the same words under a different grammar and subject. From farther away, handwritten lines, dirt on the paper, and printing misregistration appear before verbal meaning. The work is not structured as a puzzle completed by finding a single answer. Its appearance changes according to whether attention falls on poem, prose, image, or page.

Large prints move the intimate reading distance of a magazine onto the wall. Up close, letters and paper surfaces become visible; at a distance, color fields and composition take over. The photograph reproduces the text while also regulating reading speed, standing position, and the path of the eye.*6

Dividing Authorship Among Poet, Editor, Photographer, and Viewer

A single work involves the poet whose text is quoted, the writer of the source article, the magazine’s editors and designers, Czech as selector and modifier of the page, and the viewer who follows the words. e-flux describes Hidden Poems as engaging authorship, subjectivity, documentation, and contextualization.*4 Their roles divide into distinct actions: writing a poem, editing an article, finding a quotation, and reproducing the sequence through vision.*9

The viewer follows the markings and performs Czech’s reading again. The markings also prescribe the order and place clear limits on interpretation. Authorship does not pass completely to the viewer; it is shared within constraints produced by several contributors.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Hidden Poems: Turning Discovery into a Shareable Photograph

In Hidden Poems, Czech selects words in sequence from existing prose and makes an already written short poem emerge from another setting. She has distanced the work from the mystique of discovering a secret message, emphasizing instead a different way of reading in which poetic structures arise from everyday prose.*2 The fact that the same words belong to several texts provides the starting point.*1

Fluorescent color, underlining, and erasure act as editorial signs distinguishing source text and poem. The intensity of the marking alters the balance between their legibility. Czech calibrates photographic magnification and print size as well, allowing both texts to remain traceable.

In photobooks and artist talks, Czech presents the work through pages that are turned and read as well as through large prints on gallery walls. In exhibitions, movement of the body creates the order of reading; in books, page sequence and the hand perform a comparable role.*13

From Poems by Repetition to Response / Response

Poems by Repetition matches the repetition of words within a poem to repeated photographs and markings. Voyelles addresses vowels and the arrangement of letters, moving reading toward questions of sound and shape. The 2013 exhibition I Cannot Repeat What I Hear showed how poetry, journalism, lyrics, and letters produce different rhythms within photographs.*14 *5

In to icon and Poet’s Questions, Czech extended her sources to commands and icons from digital environments, consumer products, and records. By selecting questions from existing poems and combining objects that contain their letters, she allows language to function differently as an on-screen command, a product name, and a poetic question.*15 *11

For Response / Response (2024), Czech invited poets and writers to make texts responding to other poems and photographed pages bearing pencil, erasure, and reply.*16 Earlier works found poetry within texts already in circulation; here, she establishes the conditions under which others produce new writing. The photographer’s role expands from finder to commissioner and editor, making the work’s multiple authors explicit.*12

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
In Relation to Ed Ruscha and Shannon Ebner: From Letterforms to Procedures of Reading

Ed Ruscha arranged buildings and gas stations according to fixed rules in inexpensive offset-printed books, treating photographs as conceptual lists.*19 Shannon Ebner fabricates letters and photographs them among streets and objects, bringing the shape, material, and political use of language into photography. MoMA presents her work as a meeting of poetry, experimental writing, political language, and photographic conceptualism.*18

In Ruscha’s work, the sequence of photographs creates the concept; in Ebner’s, constructed letters and their locations alter meaning. Czech’s single image retains both the source article and the quoted poem, and the order of attention changes according to which is read. Her subject therefore includes the action of reading the same page in several ways, as much as the letters themselves.

This distinction separates Czech’s photographs from illustrations of literary works or reproductions of visual poetry. They show the form of letters while moving viewers between a distance for reading meaning and a distance for seeing the page as an image. Time spent in front of the photograph is structured as carefully as the page being photographed.

Appropriation That Retains the Source Page

Digital search and copying can remove only the needed phrase from a source page. Czech also extracts parts of a text, but she leaves the article, advertisement, photographs, margins, and paper surface in the frame. After reading the poem, viewers can return to the source subject and compare the role of the same words in another text.

Fluorescent color and orderly typography can turn a lengthy search and the politics of the original article into an attractive composition. When viewers follow only the poem, the discourse produced by advertising, news, and commodities recedes. Retaining the whole page preserves the material needed to move between poem and source and to identify which text has been brought forward.

After the poem has been read, Czech’s work sends the eye back to source article, photograph, advertisement, and paper surface. The labor of poet, article writer, designer, and photographer is not consolidated under a single author’s name; each leaves a trace on the same page. Reading appears as an action composed of meaning, distance, order, enlargement, material surface, and verification of the source.

nate-lowman.html.lead_html: Nate Lowman is an American artist who works with images already in circulation—newspapers, tabloids, advertisements, online images, and road signs—transforming them through painting, silkscreen, shaped canvases cut to the contours of their motifs, and installation. Works including Untitled (History of the SUV—No Blond Jokes), Autocide, and Maps examine how images of crime, celebrity, and national symbols acquire new meanings through reproduction and reediting.
nate-lowman.html.thesis_html: Photographs have often been read in terms of what the photographer saw and what the original image recorded. From the 1980s onward, appropriation art made the reuse of existing photographs a subject in itself. Lowman pushed the question toward what happens after an image enters circulation: it passes through news media, photocopies, the internet, and commercial printing, losing resolution and context as it settles into public memory. By retaining halftone dots, low resolution, cropped edges, and the degradation of reprinting in the painted surface, he makes visible how a photograph’s meaning can be rewritten each time it is circulated and reused.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
2000s New York and an Already-Photographed Reality

Born in Las Vegas in 1979 and based in New York, Nate Lowman has long begun with images already reproduced in public life: newspapers, tabloids, advertisements, the internet, crime reporting, and road signs. An Aspen Art Museum exhibition situated his paintings and installations within an American visual culture structured by mass-reproduced images*1.

MoMA’s artist record notes Lowman’s participation in Greater New York in 2005 and Defamation of Character in 2006–07, showing that his work had entered institutional discussions in New York by the middle of the decade*21.

MASSIMODECARLO likewise describes Lowman as working across painting, sculpture, and installation while repeatedly incorporating circulated images and tracking how their meanings change when they enter new settings*2.

For Lowman in the early 2000s, photography was less a privileged medium for capturing new reality than a substrate of visual information worn down by newsprint, photocopying, web circulation, and commercial reproduction. In Stay in School at NYU’s 80WSE, he transferred images of youth, pop stars, and violence from magazines and newspapers onto the walls, making the construction and destruction of the installation part of the work itself*3.

What Remained After Appropriation

Lowman inherits the appropriation strategies of the 1980s, when artists quoted and reused preexisting images to question authorship and the value of the original. His work, however, cannot be reduced to a rejection of artistic originality. The Met describes Autocide as incorporating an online image of a snowman and reproducing in paint the degradation caused by repeated copying, linking post-Warhol Pop with conceptual forms of quotation*4.

MoMA PS1’s Defamation of Character took détournement—the redirection of existing media toward different meanings—as one of its organizing ideas and presented Lowman’s “hijacked landscape” in relation to a culture in which pollution, racist language, and damaged reputations circulate*22.

Astrup Fearnley Museet identifies news, popular media, and art-historical images as Lowman’s raw material, while emphasizing his interest in making new narratives from them. Installations that gather multiple images on a wall without a fixed hierarchy generate meaning through proximity. They function less as attempts to expose an image’s source than as ways to test how public memory changes when one image is joined to another*5.

To place Lowman within photographic history, it is useful to consider his distance from the Pictures Generation, whose artists in late-1970s and 1980s New York rephotographed and reedited mass-media imagery. The Met notes that Sherrie Levine, Richard Prince, Sarah Charlesworth, and others cropped, rephotographed, and decontextualized magazine photographs, advertisements, and logos in order to question authorship and originality*25 Lowman belongs to a later generation. His starting point is less the act of quotation itself than the fact that the quoted material has already been copied repeatedly and has moved across news media, commodities, and the web.

The distinction becomes especially clear in the New Museum’s 2010 exhibition The Last Newspaper. During the run of the show, Lowman added paintings responding to weekly news stories, folding the speed at which newspapers update into the time of production itself*26 The question here is not simply who owns the source image, but how events become news, are displaced by newer images, and are filtered so that only certain images persist.

An early 2003 text already described Lowman as a “second-, third-, or perhaps fourth-generation” appropriation artist after Warhol and Prince, documenting his collection of media images of madness, rebellion, politics, and violence and their incorporation into collage, painting, photography, and wall arrangements*27 For that reason, there was little need for him to photograph an event anew. The object of critique already appeared as an existing image circulating through society before he approached it.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Turning Copy Degradation into Painterly Surface

Lowman translates low-resolution photographs, newspaper halftones, and the fading of photocopies into screenprinting, resin-based alkyd paint, and stippled brushwork. Gagosian’s text for Never Remember emphasizes how printing technologies and mass-media images acquire on the painted surface an immediacy akin to skin or a wound*6.

Recurring motifs from early in his career—bullet holes, smiley faces, air fresheners, hand-drawn hearts—also become shaped canvases whose supports follow the contours of the images themselves. According to Gagosian, the bullet holes are treated as trompe-l’oeil decals, placing photography’s appearance of being a trace on the same plane as the sign-value of a commodity*7.

The Whitney’s Reverse Escalade uses screenprinting and acrylic on an irregularly shaped canvas, allowing a fragment from printed media to determine the very shape of the painting*8 The photograph is not concealed as a preparatory image beneath the painting. Halftone dots, cropped contours, and losses produced through reproduction remain part of the finished work’s form.

What Do We See When We Look at Images of Events?

Lowman’s use of crime and accident photographs is not simply a way to introduce shocking subject matter. In a work such as the Whitney’s The Last Marilyn, familiar figures and press images are joined to painted and sprayed marks, so viewers encounter the event together with the imagery through which they already know it*9.

MoMA’s Untitled (History of the SUV—No Blond Jokes) (2003) layers an image of a famous woman repeatedly circulated in tabloids through copying and distorted silkscreen transfer, turning the media’s reshaping of the event’s memory into the structure of the work*23 What matters here is circulation after the photograph has been made. As an image moves through newspapers, photocopies, television and the internet, and commercial printing, each repetition gives it a new level of resolution, a new explanation, and a new set of value judgments.

At the Whitney in 2013, Lowman performed a public copy of a work by Jay DeFeo. By deliberately reenacting the longstanding museum practice of copying, he shifted appropriation away from anonymous data extraction and back toward the acts of looking, copying, and repeating as forms of making*10.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Autocide and the Materialization of an Internet Image

Autocide (2012) enlarges an online image of a snowman onto a monumental canvas in oil and alkyd. As Lowman’s official biography makes clear, his work extends beyond painting into publishing, exhibition making, and collaborative projects, but these activities share an editorial approach to selecting existing images anew*11.

That editorial impulse also appears in his curatorial projects. The projects gathered on his official site show that creating situations in which images and works are read through juxtaposition, rather than in isolation, extends across both his making and exhibition activity*12.

David Zwirner similarly describes Lowman’s recent work as bringing signs and reproduced images from everyday American life into painting, moving between visual familiarity and the material presence of paint*13.

From Maps to Parking: National Territory and Everyday Signs

In the Maps series from Never Remember, Lowman cut the outlines of U.S. states from studio drop cloths, layering stains, splashes, and associations of stitching onto the shapes of political maps. Gagosian describes the series as unsettling the sense of the nation as a single fixed diagram and treating borders as accumulations of history and contingency*6.

In Parking (2024), parking lots, road surfaces, signs, and peripheral urban forms observed in Los Angeles became a new painterly vocabulary. David Zwirner presented the exhibition as part of Lowman’s ongoing attention to the density of forms and signs in everyday surroundings, rather than as a detached sociological survey*14.

The exhibition checklist includes works such as Tunnel Kiss, Howl, and Shade in the Made in media ranging from oil, enamel, and latex to monotype and bronze. Keeping photographic source imagery from being tied to a single technique is part of what allows Lowman to treat the image itself as material*15.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Working Without Taking the Photograph: Making Image Circulation into Art

A 2025 exhibition at Gallery COMMON in Tokyo presented Lowman’s method as a continuum of appropriation, repetition, and reframing. When an image moves into another cultural setting, its prior meaning is not preserved intact; that instability is one of the conditions under which his work operates*16.

In an Interview Magazine conversation, Lowman describes how images in progress become connected to news, personal memory, and accidents in the studio, indicating that the finished work is not intended as an illustration of a single source of information*17.

An earlier Interview Magazine feature likewise describes his habit of picking up existing visual material encountered in the city and in the media and moving it into painting*18 This shifts the historical question from who pressed the shutter to what an image accumulates as it circulates through society after it has been made.

The Limits and Force of Media Critique

The New Museum archive places Lowman in the context of “neo-appropriation,” in which earlier appropriation strategies were reactivated within a 2000s image environment of news media, graffiti, bumper stickers, and related forms*19 Its force lies in leaving intact the contradiction that Lowman does not claim a position outside the media from which to expose the truth; he selects, reproduces, and commodifies images from within the same circuits he examines.

The e-flux announcement for The Natriot Act situates Lowman’s use of quotation in relation to Duchamp, Warhol, Richard Prince, and Kenneth Noland, while emphasizing his selection, editing, and manipulation of existing images into nonlinear narratives*24.

The Brant Foundation describes tabloid clippings, bumper stickers, bullet-hole decals, and other found images as materials through which Lowman reconnects public history and personal memory*20 In Lowman’s work, painting and exhibition making center on how press photographs, online images, and printed matter continue to persist after they have separated from the events they once described.

nicephore-niepce.html.lead_html: Niépce invented héliographie and made what is now recognized as the oldest surviving photograph, the View from the Window at Le Gras (c. 1826–27). Suppressed in the 1839 announcement, he was reassessed by twentieth-century scholarship as the first person to permanently fix a camera image by chemistry.
nicephore-niepce.html.thesis_html: Niépce was the first to demonstrate the principle of fixing the fleeting image projected by the camera obscura permanently onto a material support through a photochemical reaction. “View from the Window at Le Gras” (about 1826–27) is positioned as the first instance of a real scene inscribed directly by light without the intervention of the hand, at the conceptual origin of photography. Largely overlooked at the official announcement of 1839, he has been reassessed — through Gernsheim's rediscovery of the plate in 1952 and subsequent scholarship — as the first to achieve the photochemical fixing of an image that lies at the core of the medium. As his research partnership with Daguerre suggests, his method also formed a technical bridge toward the daguerreotype, placing the origin of photography's invention where several contributors overlap.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Joseph Nicéphore Niépce was born in 1765 in Chalon-sur-Saône, Burgundy, into a well-to-do legal family with strong interests in science and craft. After brief military service under Napoleon, he returned to the family estate at Saint-Loup-de-Varennes, where he and his brother Claude worked on a series of inventions. In 1807 they co-invented the pyréolophore, a boat-propulsion engine often described as one of the first internal combustion engines*1.

Around 1816 Niépce began trying to fix the image projected by a camera obscura. The process he called héliographie coated a pewter plate with bitumen of Judea — an asphalt derivative — dissolved in oil of lavender. A long camera-obscura exposure hardened the bitumen where light struck; unexposed areas were washed away with lavender oil, leaving a permanent record. This was the first time light had been used to chemically and durably fix a camera image in a physical material*2.

The View from the Window at Le Gras (c. 1826–27), taken from an upper-storey window of his estate, is now recognized as the oldest surviving photograph. The exposure is estimated at many hours or perhaps several days. The sun's movement across the sky during that time caused buildings on both sides of the courtyard to appear lit simultaneously — the visible evidence of the long exposure duration*3.

In 1827 Niépce visited England hoping to present his process to the Royal Society, but was refused because he would not disclose his method. He signed a ten-year partnership agreement with Daguerre in 1829, sharing heliography's details. Together they developed the physautotype in 1832, but Niépce died in 1833 before a commercially viable process was realized. Daguerre continued alone and announced the daguerreotype in January 1839. The official announcement barely mentioned Niépce; his son Isidore published a pamphlet in 1841 contesting this omission*4.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The View from the Window at Le Gras has the character of scientific proof more than artistic intention. The image is faint and tonally compressed, lacking the sharpness the daguerreotype would later achieve. Its significance lies not in optical quality but in the fact that a real scene was directly and permanently registered by light acting on chemistry*5.

Niépce's bitumen-on-pewter process operated on a different chemical principle than the silver salts later adopted by photography. But the core concept — that a camera's convergent light could be registered chemically without human drawing — was demonstrated by Niépce in 1826–27, before anyone else succeeded*6. The long exposure was a direct consequence of bitumen's low photosensitivity. Daguerre's contribution was to find a much faster silver-based process, reducing exposure times to practical lengths.

The secrecy Niépce maintained about his method — from the Royal Society refusal to the careful management of the Daguerre partnership — reflects a clear awareness of the competitive stakes of invention in early industrial Europe*7.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
In the French government's 1839 announcement of the daguerreotype as "a gift to the world," Niépce's role was reduced to a brief historical footnote. The positioning of Daguerre as the sole named inventor remains the first major dispute over photographic priority and is analyzed in those terms today*8.

The decisive reassessment came in 1952, when photographic historians Helmut and Alison Gernsheim rediscovered the Le Gras heliograph, which had been missing for decades*9. In 1963 the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin acquired it*10. In 2002–03 the Getty Conservation Institute carried out X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy, scientifically confirming the plate as bitumen on a tin-lead alloy*11.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art writes that Niépce "had achieved primitive but real results as early as 1826," explicitly recognizing his founding role*12. The National Science and Media Museum (Bradford) positions Niépce as the inventor of photography and states that Daguerre could not have succeeded without him*13.

The estate at Saint-Loup-de-Varennes where Niépce worked is preserved today and opened as a museum in 1974. International programs marking the bicentennial of photography have centered Niépce's role as the point of origin*14.

nikki-s-lee.html.lead_html: Nikki S. Lee is an artist who made self-portraits within real social groups while using herself as the subject. In Projects, she spent weeks or months with punks, Latino communities, white Ohioans, skateboarders, and other groups, adopting their clothing and behavior before asking friends or passersby to take dated snapshots of her. By combining self-portraiture with vernacular photography, she showed that a self-image is shaped by the artist's performance, a group's acceptance, the photographer's viewpoint, and the viewer's classifications of race, class, and gender.
nikki-s-lee.html.thesis_html: Self-portraiture long centered on a model in which artists controlled both camera and image while staging their own bodies. From the 1970s onward, Cindy Sherman, Adrian Piper, Eleanor Antin, and others used costume, personas, and actions in public space to examine how social roles shape a self-image. Lee's Projects added sustained time inside actual communities to that history. She entered a group for weeks or months, learned its clothing and behavior, and ultimately handed the shutter to a member of the group or a passerby. Because she relied on the everyday evidentiary quality of a dated snapshot—the sense that “this person was here with these people”—the self-portrait did not end with the artist's disguise. A group's willingness to accept her, another person's decision about the frame, and a viewer's judgment of social belonging from appearance all became part of the photograph. Projects can therefore be situated as a practice that connected self-portraiture, once centered on the presentation of an individual's face or role, to the social approval and classification embedded in the group snapshot.

sections.title: Background and Era
sections.body_html:
Lee grew up in South Korea and was surrounded by photographs through her father, who was a photographer, but she did not decide early on that she would become one herself. She studied photography at Chung-Ang University, moved to New York in 1994, encountered fashion at the Fashion Institute of Technology, and worked as an assistant to photographer David LaChapelle. In a 2025 Aperture interview, she recalled that she initially wanted to become a fashion photographer and that graduate study at NYU gave her distance from commercial production as she searched for her own form of work.*22

Guggenheim teaching materials trace Lee's move from photographic study in Korea to New York and the emergence of Projects in 1997 while she was at NYU.*21 The work centered less on technical polish than on the procedure of entering a real group and reaching the point at which she could be photographed as one of its members.

Lee later said that she was more interested in photographs that testify to a person's presence over time—funeral portraits, snapshots, and family albums—than in technical virtuosity or the production of a “beautiful image.” For Lee, who had initially wanted to work in film, photography was not a substitute for a long continuous narrative. A single photograph could preserve the relation between a person and a place, then later be received as something that looked like fact.*11

By the late 1990s in New York, photography, performance, appropriation, and multiculturalism had opened broad challenges to fixed ideas of the self. Projects emerged in that environment, but its method extended beyond individual masquerade: Lee entered specific communities and incorporated the time of actually living alongside them into the production of the work.*7

The Fukuoka Asian Art Museum's account of The Young Japanese Project (6) likewise describes recognition by the group and the act of being photographed within it as conditions of the work itself.*6

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Self-Portraits Made Within Social Groups

Western traditions of self-portraiture long assumed that artists presented their own appearance as a primary subject and largely defined the resulting image themselves. In contemporary photographic self-portraiture, that simple model of “photographing oneself” becomes less stable when another person operates the shutter or when the artist performs a role. Scholarship on Lee places Projects within this shift while emphasizing how she extends the relation between author and subject outward to the group and the viewer.*9

Lee observed each group, learned its clothing, posture, speech, and behavior, joined its daily life for several weeks, and then appeared in photographs with actual members. U.S. Department of State material likewise describes this sequence of observation, participation, and photography as her working method.*5 The work therefore depended on more than the accuracy of a disguise. It included whom she stood beside, how close she stood, and which situations allowed her to be treated as part of the group. Studies of Lee similarly discuss this extension of self-portraiture beyond the artist's body through the positions of artist, group, photographer, and viewer.*9

The Evidentiary Look of the Snapshot

The ordinary snapshot format of Projects served a purpose beyond reducing technical complexity. Consistent with Lee's interest in photography as testimony, she asked friends, group members, and sometimes passersby to use automatic cameras, bringing the images close to family photographs and casual pictures among friends.*11

Date stamps at the edge of the frame, slightly rough color, and off-center figures make the pictures look more like photographs made by someone who happened to be present than carefully composed art photographs. That ordinary appearance allowed Lee to use the unspoken credibility of vernacular photography—the assumption that if people appear together in a snapshot, they probably belong together—as material for the work.*1

From Projects to Parts

Across The Ohio Project, The Hispanic Project, The Punk Project, and The Exotic Dancers Project, the same body looks different from group to group. Seen across the series, one person occupies several social roles. Zabludowicz Collection describes the snapshots as traces that blur the boundary between fact and fiction.*8

Beginning in 2002, Parts cropped male partners out of the frame, leaving only an arm, leg, or other fragment of the body. An interview in Cahier de Séoul shows that Lee's concern with a self-image that changes with one's counterpart continued into these intimate relationships, where appearance and behavior were likewise responsive to another person.*11

The National Museum of Women in the Arts also presents the movement from Projects to Parts as an inquiry into female self-image formed through relations with other people as much as clothing or the body. The self-portrait is therefore less concerned with revealing a “true face” than with the way the same person appears differently as partners or groups change.*2

This development makes it difficult to treat Projects simply as a celebration of self-transformation or the freedom to become anyone one chooses. The photographed self takes shape through what surrounding people, intimate partners, and viewers perceive, and therefore cannot be fully possessed or controlled by the artist.*10

The Ethics of Performing Race and Class

Lee's work has also drawn criticism for incorporating racial and ethnic signs into her own body. X-TRA's criticism addresses the appeal of the work while also asking who has the power to enter another group temporarily and then leave it.*4

The historical significance of Projects therefore cannot be reduced to a celebration of fluid identity. Because the work depends on habits of classifying race, class, gender, and age through appearance, it retains both the capacity to expose those classifications and the risk of repeating them.*20

The Yuppie Project was discussed early on as a work that reverses the habit of treating only ethnic minorities as “racialized groups,” showing that affluent white professionals also possess social codes legible through clothing, location, and bodily behavior. In a 2001 Art Journal essay, Maurice Berger treated the work through the problem of making “whiteness” visible and argued that Projects could not be explained solely as transformation into other cultures.*24

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The Ohio Project

In The Ohio Project (8), blond hair, clothing, posture, and even the physical distance between bodies indoors are adjusted to the snapshot conventions of a white Midwestern community. The work depends on Lee entering the photographic grammar shared by actual people; a generic “white appearance” alone would not produce the same social evidence. The Met likewise identifies the process of learning each group's style and behavior before being photographed as central to the series.*1

A single image can look like an ordinary commemorative photograph. Placed beside other Projects, however, the same face repeatedly enters different versions of what looks “normal.” Clothing, posture, and distance within the group, which first seem natural, emerge as photographic forms learned within specific communities.*19

The Hispanic Project and The Hip Hop Project

Princeton teaching materials use The Hispanic Project (1) to examine how ethnicity and social codes are recognized within photographs.*3

Guggenheim's The Hip Hop Project (1) shows that the appearance of belonging is produced by more than clothing and pose; where a person stands within the group also matters.*13

In The Yuppie Project, by contrast, some photographs do not look like fully successful assimilation. The individual Projects therefore form a comparative sequence that tests where social classification appears to work and where it begins to fray. They are not a catalog of successful transformations.*14

a.k.a. Nikki S. Lee

In the 2006 video a.k.a. Nikki S. Lee, Lee performs different versions of “Nikki,” introducing fiction into a documentary format that would ordinarily promise access to the artist's authentic self. An e-flux screening record confirms that after moving from photography to video, the work continued to address the boundary between self-image and fiction.*12

The method of asking others to press the shutter in Projects and the performance of “the artist herself” as another role in this video belong to the same inquiry. Both unsettle, through their form, the expectation that photography or film automatically guarantees the truth of a person.*12

sections.title: Reception and Historical Position
sections.body_html:
Comparing Sherman, Piper, and Antin

In Cindy Sherman's self-portraits, the artist transforms herself into figures that evoke film stills or art-historical types, placing established images of femininity and their conventions at the center of the frame. Lee also uses disguise, but in Projects the self-image is produced by entering real groups and appearing in group photographs made by other people. Performing an existing image alone would not account for this social dimension. Korean scholarship on self-portraiture likewise identifies this expanded structure—from artist alone to artist, group, and viewer—as an important difference between Lee and figures such as Sherman and Yasumasa Morimura.*9

Adrian Piper's The Mythic Being placed her body in 1970s public space wearing a masculine Afro, mustache, and sunglasses, exposing the mechanisms through which strangers rapidly read race, gender, and class. Lee also works with classification through appearance, but she does not primarily create direct tension with viewers in public space. She participates in a community over time and leaves snapshots in which her belonging appears ordinary. Cherise Smith compares the two artists within the same study as practices of embodying the position of another.*23

Eleanor Antin used works such as The King and The Ballerina to sustain fictional personae over time, testing from the 1970s onward how the self could resist fixation as a single identity. Lee's personae are not wholly fictional: they are assembled from the existing codes of punk, hip-hop, yuppie, and other communities. Her performance therefore carries the ethical problem of temporarily borrowing another culture. Smith places Antin, Piper, and Lee within the same history of “performing the other” in order to historicize both this shared method and its tensions.*23

The particular force of Projects as self-portraiture therefore lies in more than Lee's ability to “become anyone.” Sherman worked through existing representations, Piper through social readings in public space, and Antin through sustained personae. Lee made participation in real groups and a third party's shutter conditions of the work. The image depends both on how the artist presents herself and on how other people treat her as a member of a particular group.*9

Snapshots Enter the Museum

When Projects enters a museum as art, the snapshot's resemblance to a family photograph cannot be separated from the long procedure required to produce that resemblance. Lee joins a group, adjusts her appearance and behavior, asks a third party to take the picture, and finally selects the photographs. What institutions such as SFMOMA collect is therefore an image in which the structure of an “ordinary commemorative photograph” has been deliberately produced through this entire procedure, not merely a snapshot technique.*16

Hundred Heroines Museum lists Lee's work in collections including MOCA Los Angeles, the Museum of Contemporary Photography, the Hirshhorn Museum, ICP, Guggenheim, and the Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, indicating the extent to which Projects has circulated across regions and institutions.*15

Reception and Criticism

Liverpool Biennial presented Lee as an artist who challenges fixed ideas of national and cultural identity.*7

A French exhibition archive from 2003 preserves images from The Lesbian Project and The Ohio Project and discusses clothing, attitude, and behavior as signs of social belonging. It shows that Projects, begun in New York, was already being received outside the United States as work concerned with the visual codes that make a person appear to belong to a group.*18

A 2000 Frieze review observed that the repeated appearance of the same person in photographs that initially look like ordinary snapshots exposes apparently natural scenes as constructed.*17 The same mechanism also reveals how quickly viewers classify people through hairstyle, clothing, skin color, and place. Current assessments therefore need to address more than the skill of Lee's transformations: they also have to consider her ability to enter another culture temporarily and leave it after the photograph, as well as the contradiction that the work must mobilize stereotypes in order to make them visible.

norihiko-matsumoto.html.lead_html: Norihiko Matsumoto photographed stage performers including Fubuki Koshiji and Yaeko Mizutani over long periods, building an ongoing record of performances, roles, costumes, and gesture. Alongside stage photographs such as Fubuki Koshiji, Long Recital and Yaeko Mizutani, Meiji Ichidai Onna, he also made urban color works such as Venice. This page traces the full range of his activity across image-making and photographic historiography, including his participation in a major 1968 survey of Japanese photographic history, research on museum photography collections, and writing and editorial work.
norihiko-matsumoto.html.thesis_html: By the time Norihiko Matsumoto began working after the war, stage photography in Japan already had important precedents. Masao Horino photographed theater and dance at Tsukiji Shōgekijō in the 1920s and later moved into modernist photography and graphic montage.*27 Ihei Kimura photographed kabuki from the 1930s onward, using a small camera to catch fleeting changes in expression during performance.*26 Matsumoto’s contribution took shape inside a different postwar system: he produced large quantities of professional photographs of Nissay Theatre productions for newspapers and magazines while following performers such as Fubuki Koshiji and Yaeko Mizutani across many productions and roles. In doing so, publicity photographs made for immediate use accumulated into sequences through which the changing stage lives of individual performers could be compared.*21 His role in the 1968 survey of a century of Japanese photography extended this activity into chronology-building and source research; later he also investigated museum collections and the preservation of photographic originals.*12 His place in photography history lies in the continuity between professional stage photography, historical editing, and the preservation of source materials.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Photography and the Mass Media

Matsumoto first became interested in photography around his second year of junior high school. In a 2024 interview, he recalled borrowing a twin-lens Ricohflex for a week from a boy who had been evacuated to his area, and using it to photograph Onomichi, a shipyard, and a launching ceremony.*21 In the same interview, he said that he read science magazines avidly, was curious about everyday topics, and was considering a career in “mass media.”*21 Photography gradually came to him as a medium linked to that work: a way to go out toward unfamiliar subjects and communicate people and events to a broad public. He later entered the Department of Photography at Nihon University College of Art and began photographing stage artists from Japan and abroad while still a student.*2 His own desire to “see and touch anything,” together with his interest in mass media, became a common starting point for activities that later ranged across theater, magazines, and research into photographic history. Art Platform Japan likewise lists Matsumoto as both a photographer and a writer on photography, reflecting the long coexistence of image-making and writing in his career.*1

Fourteen Years with Fubuki Koshiji

Stage photography at Nissay Theatre had a clearly defined practical use. Matsumoto recalled preparing roughly 500 photographs from a single production for distribution to newspaper reporters, while also photographing rehearsals; stage photography functioned as part of the publicity and news infrastructure linking the theater to newspapers and magazines.*21 He also said that although he had photographed Fubuki Koshiji earlier, his sustained work with her began at Nissay Theatre.*21 The Kyushu Sangyo University Museum notes that Matsumoto photographed Koshiji both onstage and at home over fourteen years.*2 In Fubuki Koshiji, Long Recital, lighting, costume, and gesture are tied to a specific performance, unlike a portrait reconstructed in the studio.*5 The immediate purpose was press distribution, but following the same performer over years produced an accumulation of changing repertory, bodies, costumes, and stage direction. Ephemeral publicity use and the later value of the negatives as a comparative cultural record occupy the same body of work.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
The Body on Stage

Yaeko Mizutani, Meiji Ichidai Onna is cataloged as a National Theatre performance of June 24, 1975.*7 Tsukiyo Garasu is recorded as a November 7, 1974 performance at Shinbashi Enbujō.*4 Matsumoto’s work at Nissay Theatre was closely tied to the practical task of photographing rehearsals and performances for distribution to newspapers and magazines.*21 Under those conditions, the photograph had to preserve enough of the lighting, costume, posture, and relation to other performers to identify the role and production. A self-contained psychological portrait was not the primary task. Repeatedly photographing the same actor over long periods produced a sequence in which the body changes according to role and staging. The result differs structurally from a conventional portrait album of one person. The 1979 National Theatre catalogue devoted to Yaeko Mizutani shows one way in which photographs first made for theatrical publicity later became material for the history of performance.*8

Venice and Color

Collection records show that Matsumoto’s work also includes urban color photographs such as Venice and Venice at Night. Tokyo Museum Collection catalogs Venice as a silver dye-bleach color print.*9 In the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s Venice at Night, artificial urban light, signage, and nighttime color organize the image differently from a theatrical spotlight.*10 These works show that his photography extended beyond records of stage performers into observations of the city using color processes from the 1960s through the 1980s. What they share with the stage photographs is an attention to temporary scenes formed by people and architecture under artificial light; color becomes a means of registering differences among light sources and places.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The 1968 Survey of Japanese Photography

The 1968 exhibition surveying a century of photographic expression in Japan was a large-scale attempt by photographers themselves to investigate and select from the country’s photographic past. Matsumoto recalled that his writing experience led to his being assigned the chronology, which involved extensive reading and searching for photographs around the country.*21 The committee, which included Shōmei Tōmatsu, gathered photographs and reproductions on the scale of hundreds of thousands and classified commercial photography, accidents, advertising, state propaganda, Manchuria, and wartime material alongside art photography, bringing the involvement of Japanese photographers in colonial rule and wartime propaganda into the exhibition’s historical field.*12 Takuma Nakahira and Kōji Taki carried this research into the critique of established systems of representation that fed into Provoke.*24 Matsumoto did not move toward Provoke’s visual language. His role was to collect past photographs as a professional photographer and participate in the decisions—through chronology and classification—about what would count as Japanese photographic history. The project marks an institutional shift in the late 1960s, when production and historical writing were being undertaken within the same community of photographers. In a 1968 roundtable held during preparations, Tōmatsu remarked that photographers themselves had previously done little with history, and described beginning with chronology-building and the study of prewar magazines.*11 Recent scholarship has examined the exhibition as an effort in which photographers surveyed roughly 500,000 items, selected 1,640, and compiled a national history comparatively, a form of “photographers as historians” that also anticipated later thinking about the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.*15 The exhibition catalogue and chronology are now held by the National Diet Library, making the exhibition itself a historical research object.*14 The NDL record gives the exhibition dates as June 1–12, 1968, identifies the Japan Professional Photographers Society as organizer, and notes the appended chronology of Japanese photography.*6

Preserving Photographic Originals

Matsumoto’s institutional work moved beyond surveys of museum holdings to the preservation of photographic originals themselves. Nihon no Bijutsukan to Shashin Korekushon is cataloged as a foundational survey of photography collecting in museums across Japan.*13 The Japan Professional Photographers Society’s Photo Archive explicitly identifies the dispersal or disposal of film after a photographer’s death and image loss caused by deterioration in Japan’s hot, humid climate as reasons for its establishment.*22 The same page includes Matsumoto’s own reports on film deterioration and the archive’s activities, as well as on securing a storage facility for photographic originals, confirming his direct involvement in both preservation science and collection logistics.*22 The Photo Archive gathers and organizes negatives and film that would not survive through museum collecting of finished prints alone. Matsumoto worked on both the survey of museum collections and the preservation of originals, participating from within the professional photographic community in two related decisions: what should enter a museum as a work, and which source materials should survive as evidence for photographic history. Preservation here was an active part of determining the archive available to future historical research. In 2007, Matsumoto also took part in a hearing of the Copyright Subdivision of Japan’s Council for Cultural Affairs as a working professional representing the Japan Photographic Copyright Association and the Japan Professional Photographers Society.*19 This shows a parallel involvement in the institutional questions of photographic use and rights. The JPS now lists him as an honorary member.*18 A 2026 exhibition by the Japan Photographic Copyright Association likewise included his work, identifying him as a former executive director.*20

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Before Matsumoto: Stage Photography in Japan

Before Matsumoto, Japanese photography already had an important history of the stage as subject. Masao Horino photographed theater, dance, and actors around Tsukiji Shōgekijō in the 1920s, later connecting bodily performance to modernist photography and graphic montage in the 1930s.*27 Ihei Kimura photographed kabuki alongside his advertising and snapshot work; in images such as Sixth-generation Onoe Kikugorō, Kagamijishi (1934), the small camera catches a fleeting expression or gesture within performance.*26 Matsumoto’s difference lay in working inside the repetitive professional system of postwar theater publicity, photographing many productions while following the same actors and singers over years. The 1995 JCII Photo Salon catalogue on Nissay Theatre performances from 1964 to 1971 brings productions with Tatsuya Nakadai, Chieko Higashiyama, Mikijirō Hira, Kyōko Kishida, Haruko Sugimura, and others into a single sequence.*28 Images distributed immediately to newspapers and magazines could later be compared across years as records of performers’ bodies, costumes, lighting, and stage direction. The inclusion of Matsumoto’s photographs of Fubuki Koshiji in the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s broad survey of postwar Shōwa photography also reflects this shift in use.*16 The 2019 exhibition on world stage artists photographed from 1955 to 1986 similarly presented decades of stage portraits as a sequence extending across postwar international performance culture, beyond their original publicity function for separate productions.*25 Nissay Theatre, which opened in 1963, continued to produce and present drama, musicals, and opera; Matsumoto’s work of the 1960s and 1970s developed alongside the establishment of this large-scale postwar theater culture.*3

Roku no Kai and VIVO

Matsumoto formed Roku no Kai (Group of Six) with classmates from Nihon University College of Art—Tadashi Takamura, Keisuke Kumakiri, Tōru Nogami, Keiichi Kimura, and Kōichi Saitō—and the six continued exhibitions and small-format photobooks for decades while maintaining different professional specialties.*23 In the late 1950s, Kazutaka Narahara, Eikoh Hosoe, Kikuji Kawada, Shōmei Tōmatsu, and others formed VIVO, a short-lived platform that pushed self-directed work and highly individualized visual languages beyond the demands of news and advertising.*24 No direct line of influence between the two groups has been established, but their organizational models were markedly different. VIVO condensed strong individual authorship into an independent presentation platform over a short period; Roku no Kai brought together photographers working in theater, portraiture, reportage, architecture, and other fields, who sustained collective exhibitions alongside their professional careers for more than half a century. Matsumoto’s stage photography belongs to this second model. It shows how postwar photographers working outside avant-garde movements also used exhibitions and publishing to separate their own work from its immediate professional function and place it within critical circulation.

Matsumoto in Postwar Photography History

Matsumoto’s career repeatedly changes the institutional setting in which the same photographs operate. First, stage photographs made at Nissay Theatre were immediate professional images distributed to newspapers and magazines.*21 Second, exhibitions, portfolios, and museum collections reorganized those photographs as works and historical records through which postwar stardom and stage direction could be studied.*16 Third, Matsumoto himself participated in chronology-building for the 1968 exhibition, surveys of museum collections, and the preservation of photographic originals through the JPS Photo Archive, taking part in the selection of what would remain available as primary material for photographic history.*22 Unlike a photographer whose historical position centers on a new formal language, Matsumoto linked production, editing, and preservation through the continuity of professional photographic work. His career therefore contains the process by which images made for short-term theatrical use later became sources for the histories of photography and performance. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum Library’s holding Norihiko Matsumoto photographs: portfolio III also shows stage photographs preserved as a portfolio selected and edited by the photographer, giving press images a second life as an authored group.*17
