sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
The History of Black Portraiture and Photographic Education in Chicago

In nineteenth-century America, images of Black bodies were used in the classifications of slavery and racial science. Frederick Douglass, by contrast, sat repeatedly for portraits and presented himself to the public as a thinking, acting citizen. The National Portrait Gallery notes that Douglass became the most photographed American of the nineteenth century and consciously used photography’s social power to shape his public image.*3 Black portraiture has therefore carried both the image imposed by others and the public construction of dignity by Black subjects themselves.

For the 1900 Paris Exposition, W. E. B. Du Bois and Thomas J. Calloway assembled roughly five hundred photographs for the “American Negro Exhibit,” presenting African American life and progress through education, work, family, and organizations. The Library of Congress makes available portraits and scenes of daily life originating in that exhibition.*1 Johnson’s early photographs were made within a history in which Black people had been classified by the camera and had also used photography for self-representation.

Johnson studied photography at Columbia College Chicago with Dawoud Bey, known for sustained work with communities. According to Shelley Rice, photographic education at the time treated the power relations involved in photographing people in poverty as a central issue and drew on critiques of social documentary by Martha Rosler, Allan Sekula, John Tagg, and others.*14 The danger that photographers might use other people’s lives to explain a social problem formed part of the environment in which the young Johnson worked.*16

The subjects of Seeing in the Dark were unhoused Black men Johnson met near his studio on South Michigan Avenue. Johnson was himself a Black man and shared aspects of racial experience with them, while his photographic education, studio, and access to art institutions placed him differently in class terms. Because racial proximity and class difference coexisted, reducing each person to a representative of “Blackness” or “homelessness” would have erased the relation’s complexity. Rice identifies the varying degrees of trust, resistance, and self-disclosure from one sitter to another as central to the series.*14

In 2001, the work was selected for Freestyle at the Studio Museum in Harlem. The term “post-black,” used by Thelma Golden for the exhibition, described a situation in which Black artists addressed racial history while moving beyond the demand to represent a single, stable idea of Blackness.*9 Johnson’s photographs likewise avoid defining one affirmative Black image, altering the relation among subject, photographer, process, class, and institution from picture to picture.

Seeing in the Dark: A Slow Encounter Shaped by a Historical Printing Process

Van Dyke brown printing is a nineteenth-century process in which sensitizer is brushed onto paper, a large negative is contact printed, and exposure is made with ultraviolet light or sunlight. Johnson used an 8 × 10 Deardorff camera to make close studio portraits.*14 Because preparation and exposure take time, the sitter is not captured in a passing street instant. He has time to sit, face the camera, close his eyes, or raise a hand between himself and the lens.*5

The years 1998–99 coincided with the rapid spread of digital photography and images made quickly and in volume. Johnson chose an older chemical process and made each brown-toned print individually.*14 Coating the paper and making a contact print gave the portrait a temporality different from the immediate record of news photography or identification. By directing a format associated with historical museum portraiture toward named unhoused Black men, Seeing in the Dark brought the description of poverty into the same frame as the formal bearing of a portrait intended to endure.*6

The dark tonal range has also been linked to Roy DeCarava.*14 Details of face and clothing do not appear all at once, and the viewer must spend time reading the image. In Jonathan, a large hand interrupts the approach to the face; in Eugene, the hat and lowered eyes limit access. The men are not fully opened to view as evidence explaining poverty. Each retains a particular way of responding to the camera.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Staging Du Bois’s Double Consciousness as an Imaginary Social Club

The New Negro Escapist Social and Athletic Club (2008–) imagines a secret club of Black intellectuals and photographs formally dressed men in the format of membership portraits. In the National Gallery of Art’s Emmett, the figure appears twice; the chair, dark background, historically indeterminate clothing, and brown print create the look of an old archival photograph.*7

Johnson connects the series to W. E. B. Du Bois’s “double consciousness,” the condition of seeing oneself through one’s own experience while also seeing oneself through the judgments of white society. The doubled figure, historical clothing, and formal pose translate these two viewpoints into the photograph’s structure.*4 The club offers temporary distance from external racism while also establishing its own standards of education, class, and masculinity.

Contemporary friends and models perform as imaginary members, and the photographs are made as records of an organization that never existed. Title, costume, printing process, and exhibition give Black history an invented social space. At the same time, the old brown print, formal pose, and museum collection status reveal the conditions through which a photograph comes to resemble a credible historical document.

Dispersing Self-Image from the Face Across Soap, Books, Music, and Plants

As Johnson moved into sculpture and installation, he spread Black self-image beyond the face across black soap, shea butter, wax, mirrors, tiles, houseplants, books, and records. These materials connect to barbering, self-care, the home, study, music, and life across the African diaspora. MCA Chicago describes this incorporation of domestic materials into art structures as “hijacking the domestic.”*2

Writing about Wifredo Lam, Johnson considers the way African diasporic religion, Cubism, and modern art meet within a single painting. His interest in allowing different cultural references and art histories to coexist without reducing a figure to one racial sign continues in later works that gather books, records, plants, and household objects.*11

The materials carry symbolic associations and physical effects. Shea butter changes shape with temperature, black soap leaves gloss and residue on the wall, and mirrors reflect the viewer. Books and records show how knowledge and taste are selected, owned, and presented to others. Gridded shelving organizes a personal cultural history like furniture and also recalls museum systems of classification and display.*18 *10

Portrait photography encourages viewers to read race, class, education, and psychology together from a single body. Johnson’s shelves and spatial works treat books read, music heard, substances applied to the body, plants tended, room arrangements, and the viewer’s movement as elements of self-image alongside the face. Blackness appears through multiple acts of selecting, possessing, and presenting culture, rather than as a single appearance.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Jonathan’s Hands, Calvin, and Emmett: Changes in Naming and Historical Appearance

Jonathan’s Hands (1998) places the hands prominently before the face, stopping an approaching gaze. In Calvin (1999), face and clothing emerge gradually from the dark print. Personal names bring each sitter into the work as an individual before the social category of “homeless person.”*8 *15

The name Emmett (2008) evokes Emmett Till, although the model is a different contemporary person. The present-day sitter, the appearance of an old membership photograph, and the doubled image bring several periods together. In the early work, names resist anonymity; in the later series, a name connects one model to another figure or narrative in Black history.

Seen together, the three works trace a shift from making dignified portraits to examining the forms through which dignity becomes visible. Formal dress, historical printing, and learned titles present Black men as historical subjects. The same elements can also confine dignity within codes of education, class, and masculinity.*16

Shelving and Architectural Space: Extending Self-Image into Possessions and the Viewer’s Experience

MCA Chicago’s 2012 exhibition Message to Our Folks brought together fourteen years of work, from early photographs to sculpture, film, and installation.*2 Gridded shelves support books, plants, records, ceramics, incense, and monitors, recalling domestic storage, modernist architecture, and the order of museum display at once.

Choosing what to place on a shelf resembles choosing clothing and background in a portrait. After viewing an image from the front, visitors walk around the structure, see themselves in mirrors, and encounter sound and smell. In the Whitney’s New Poetry, the structure extended from the museum interior into outdoor space, connecting the act of looking with movement through a public setting.*12

At an architectural scale, viewers can follow the books, music, domestic materials, plants, furniture, and institutions through which a person shapes a self. Selection and arrangement once contained within the photographic frame become an experience of walking, reflection, scent, and sound.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Black Portraiture After Lorna Simpson and Carrie Mae Weems

Since the 1980s, Lorna Simpson has combined Black women turned away from the camera, bodies without visible faces, and text to question the habit of reading race, gender, and psychology directly from a portrait.*19 Carrie Mae Weems reused historical materials that photographed Black people as scientific types, exposing photography’s and the museum’s participation in racial classification.*20

Working after these interventions, Johnson used historical processes to make new photographs. Simpson limits information about the figure; Weems rereads an existing archive; Johnson produces fictional portraits that look like historical materials. New Negro Escapist imagines a social club absent from Black history while showing how costume, title, printing process, and museum collection create the appearance of historical truth.

The method also contains an affirmative image. Formally dressed Black men, personal names, and learned titles clearly express aspirations toward dignity and self-formation. Class selection, male-centered membership, and awareness of white social judgment accompany that image, revealing the rules that structure an ideal self.

From the Appearance of Historical Portraiture to the Objects and Institutions That Support Self-Image

In Seeing in the Dark, the slow Van Dyke brown process and its brown surface extend the encounter between photographer and sitter and present unhoused Black men as historical portraits with personal names. In New Negro Escapist, the same appearance gives documentary credibility to imaginary members and an invented institution. The historical process gives real people the temporal weight of portraits made to be preserved; it can also make a history that never existed look like a trustworthy record.

In the installations, the elements that form self-image expand from expression, clothing, and background to books, music, bodily materials, plants, furniture, and museum display structures. The portrait’s task of describing a person continues as the problem of exhibiting how an individual selects culture, arranges a life, and becomes visible within institutions.

In the early photographs, the sitter’s gesture, distance from the photographer, and the surface of the historical print build an image of one person. In the spatial work, possessions, architecture, sound, scent, and the viewer’s reflection divide that work among themselves. Johnson’s movement from photography into multiple media forms a continuous expansion: Black self-image is no longer assigned to a single face but extended to the objects and institutions through which a life is made.

Museum collections including SFMOMA hold the early photographs and later mixed-media works as parts of the same artistic development. The Guggenheim’s 2025 retrospective likewise traced Black self-image, domestic materials, anxiety, and escape across photography, sculpture, film, and painting.*17

This retrospective reception allows Johnson’s move from photography into three-dimensional work to be read as a widening of the elements that make a portrait—from the face to objects, architecture, and the viewer’s experience—rather than as a break between media.*13

renger.html.lead_html: Renger-Patzsch made the photographed object itself central, rejecting both pictorialist beautification and Bauhaus-style visual experiment in favor of precise structural description.
renger.html.thesis_html: From a position distinct from both Pictorialist beautification and Bauhaus visual experiment, Renger-Patzsch observed the structure of things themselves with precision and pulled the subject of photography back to the matter-of-fact form of the object. His approach became central to New Objectivity photography and proposed a way of describing the world objectively.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Albert Renger-Patzsch was born in 1897 in Wurzburg and learned photography early through his father*1. After serving in the First World War, he worked in the early 1920s above all on plant photography and images made for printed publications, then gradually widened his field to industrial products, machine parts, and architectural detail*2. In 1928 he published Die Welt ist schon (The World Is Beautiful), a photobook that was quickly received as a defining statement of New Objectivity photography*3. In 1929 he moved to Essen, where he maintained a studio and office at Museum Folkwang while photographing mines, steelworks, and limestone landscapes across the Ruhr over long periods*4. After losing much of his early archive in wartime bombing in 1944, he shifted his base to the Wamel / Mohnesee area, continued photographing the Ruhr industrial region and trees after the war, and died in Wamel in 1966*5.

sections.title: New Objectivity and Neues Sehen: The Photography of Things
sections.body_html:
Neither pictorialism nor the Bauhaus, but a third path

In 1920s Germany, photography was being pulled toward two dominant directions. One was the lingering pictorialist tradition, which used soft focus and artisanal print processes to align photography with the established language of fine art*1. The other was the Bauhaus and the New Vision, where steep angles, aerial views, montage, and optical experiment treated photography as a medium for reorganizing perception itself*6. Renger-Patzsch chose neither route. He rejected pictorialist embellishment and also kept his distance from the dramatic perceptual shocks associated with figures such as Laszlo Moholy-Nagy and Aleksandr Rodchenko. Instead, he committed himself to rendering the form, surface, repetition, and material texture of things with maximum technical clarity*2.

The World Is Beautiful and the parallel display of things

Die Welt ist schon, published in 1928, assembled one hundred photographs of factory chimneys, railway bridges, plant structures, ceramic reflections, cast-metal tools, and other subjects. What unifies the book is not romantic atmosphere but a single insistence that things already possess their own structural beauty, and that photography can disclose it without beautifying it further*3. Plants, industrial objects, animals, architecture, and human figures are deliberately interwoven so that natural and manufactured forms can be compared across the book as a visual table of correspondences*10. Renger-Patzsch is said to have preferred the plain title Things, while the publisher chose Die Welt ist schon for commercial reasons, which makes the point even clearer: his interest lay less in lyrical world-view than in the factual presentation of things themselves*3. His experience with botanical close-ups carried directly into industrial subjects. Close proximity, even light, deep focus, fine tonal control, and stripped-down composition let surface grain, reflection, and repeating modules become the real subject of the image*2. The procedure does not simply make objects look beautiful; it pulls their latent order into the picture plane.

New Objectivity, editing, and the myth of neutrality

This approach developed alongside August Sander's typological archive of people and Karl Blossfeldt's enlarged studies of plants, and the three are repeatedly placed at the center of New Objectivity photography*11. Where Sander organized social types and Blossfeldt treated plants as formal morphologies, Renger-Patzsch applied the same cool scrutiny to industrial objects, everyday manufactured things, architecture, and natural detail*8. Yet this supposed objectivity was never a neutral recording of the world. Distance, angle, cropping, light, and tonal control all actively shape the object's formal legibility*10. The photographs look as if things reveal themselves, but that appearance is achieved through a series of decisions that isolate structure, regularize the frame, and suppress everything that would distract from material and form*10.

Toward the Bechers and the argument for a specifically photographic method

The pattern of judgment established here would later echo through the Bechers' typological documentation of industrial architecture and, further on, through Dusseldorf School and typological photography*11. German advertising photography, product catalogues, and architectural magazines of the late 1920s and 1930s also drew on this style, and when read alongside Germaine Krull's photographs of metal structures they show how a modern vocabulary for seeing industrial things was assembled across several practices at once*7*16. Shared devices included severe low angles, close-ups of mechanical parts, frontal views of factory facades, cropped views of trusses as abstract pattern, serial repetition, and attention to matte metallic surfaces*7. These methods took shape under very different political and theoretical commitments. Rodchenko treated radical camera angles as part of a revolutionary visual language of labor and machinery*14. Moholy-Nagy developed photography at the Bauhaus as a program for re-educating perception under the name of the New Vision*15. Krull moved between photojournalism and abstraction, especially in Metal, where bridges and cranes became dynamic constructions of line and repetition*16. Renger-Patzsch, by contrast, remained more narrowly committed to the exact presentation of structure*10. What later gets inherited is therefore not a single unified method but the proof that a stance of objectivity can become a compelling photographic practice. In that sense, he is less the sole origin of later typological work than an early and durable baseline to which later photographers kept returning*11. The posthumous translation and publication of his writings in The Absolute Realist also made it easier to read his photographs together with his theoretical insistence that photography should not imitate painting but discover its own proper way of presenting the structure of things*9*10.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: The decisive contemporary criticism remains Walter Benjamin's objection in A Short History of Photography. Benjamin suggested that the very attitude summarized by The World Is Beautiful risked absorbing historical contradiction into aesthetic order, turning structural beauty into a way of not seeing the social conditions around it*4. That criticism has remained central because it challenges not only Renger-Patzsch but the political limits of New Objectivity itself*11. Postwar museum reception, meanwhile, has been sustained by major holdings at Museum Folkwang, the Pinakothek der Moderne, Tate, MoMA, the National Gallery of Art, George Eastman Museum, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art*7*8*12*13. With the Getty Research Institute's archival work and the English publication of his writings, Renger-Patzsch is now read both through the history of works and through the history of ideas, as one of the key starting points for arguments about photographic objectivity in modern art*9*10.

ricarda-roggan.html.lead_html: Ricarda Roggan seeks out disused furniture, cars, machines, and empty rooms, alters the physical setting, and photographs it with a large-format analog camera. Her use of photography grew from an interest in literature and space and developed through works such as Garage, Attika, Apokryphen, and 1971. Although the objects and places are real, her images make it difficult to separate what she found from what she constructed, bringing documentation and staging into the same photograph.
ricarda-roggan.html.thesis_html: Staged photography has often approached the boundary between fiction and reality through reenacted events or constructed models. Roggan begins instead with rooms and objects that already exist and have already been used. She removes dust, moves furniture, and at times rebuilds floors or walls, yet the final result still resembles a precise documentary photograph.She does not exhibit the altered rooms or objects themselves; what remains is a single photograph. The photograph alone does not reveal where discovery ends and staging begins. By shaping reality before photographing it, Roggan made documentation and mise-en-scène part of the same pictorial problem.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
From Literature and Space to Photography: Building a Room for a Single Image

Ricarda Roggan was born in Dresden. From 1996 she studied photography with Timm Rautert at the Academy of Fine Arts Leipzig, receiving her diploma in 2002 and completing her Meisterschüler studies in 2004. She also studied at the Royal College of Art in London from 2003 to 2005, establishing the basis of her work in the late 1990s and early 2000s.*1

In Roggan’s account, her path to photography began with literature and space, not with a fascination for cameras. As a child she was drawn to literature and enjoyed making rooms and thinking about spaces; photography initially served as a practical tool for those interests. She gradually recognized photography’s particular ability to fix the relationship between space and objects in a single image. In a 2021 conversation, she explained that once she reached a territory language could no longer fully describe, this process of turning a dialogue with objects into an image could, for her, happen only through photography.*24 This helps explain why, in her work, “making the room” comes before taking the photograph: altering the set or space prepares it for the way it will appear on the photographic plane.

Kino, 1994–99: Photographing the Movie Screen as Another Reality

The early series Kino, made from 1994 to 1999, used high-speed 35mm film to photograph screens showing American movies in cinemas, then grouped the images into categories such as landscapes, cars, roads, disasters, and hotels. Spector Books situates the project within a pre-digital desire for the analog images produced by the movie theater.*9 Roggan has also spoken about working as a projectionist; those memories later led to APPARATE, a series centered on projection equipment.*2 Before her later photographs of furniture and abandoned interiors, Kino was already treating reality and “reality that has already become an image” as part of the same photographic question.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Seeking Objects After Use and Slowing Down Their Time

Roggan repeatedly turns to chairs, tables, beds, damaged cars, projectors, game machines, and empty rooms that have outlived their original function. She has described being drawn to objects that remain after losing their practical value.*2 In a 2021 interview, she recalled that decades of use seemed to settle into the tears, corners, and surfaces of old furniture, and that she felt a need to preserve those objects once more as images before they were discarded.*24 Old objects matter in her work because their surfaces retain the time of human use at the moment when that use is about to end. The Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation similarly describes her as a “photo-archaeologist” in search of traces, emphasizing her search for abandoned buildings and furniture and the strict procedures she uses to reduce chance.*3 The Zabludowicz Collection connects her early furniture photographs to the material culture and memory of the former East Germany.*15

8×10 Analog: Using a Slow Process to Decide Before Exposure

Roggan says she continues to use an 8×10-inch analog view camera because it lets her define a portion of reality with particular clarity and because the process is slow and labor-intensive.*2 In another conversation, she noted that seeing a smartphone snapshot too early can determine the image too quickly and weaken the process of constructing the space mentally. With a large-format camera, she instead values the time spent thinking of the space in three dimensions, waiting, and searching for an image that is not yet visible.*24 Large-format photography requires decisions about camera position, light, the placement of objects, and even small traces in the background before exposure. The essay “Von den Dingen,” published on Roggan’s website, emphasizes that she works directly on reality before the photograph is made, preparing the final image instead of substantially remaking the negative afterward.*20 For Roggan, the slowness of large-format photography provides time to observe a space in three dimensions, decide where objects and the camera should be placed, and organize physical reality into a single image before exposure.*24

Stuhl, Tisch und Bett and Schacht: Rebuilding the Room Before Photographing It

In her early furniture works, Roggan removed discarded chairs, tables, and beds from the places where she found them and repositioned them in sparse photographic settings. KW Institute for Contemporary Art notes that the objects can appear naturally placed at first glance, while the precision of the image reveals the staging; small interventions in the physical space detach them from their former meanings and uses.*4 In Schacht and Attika, the interventions extend to the entire room. A 2008 Frieze review notes that the floor in Schacht was recast, windows and doors were sealed with plasterboard, and the spaces in Attika were thoroughly cleaned, challenging a simple reading of the work as photographs of East German ruins.*8 FOTOHOF’s book Schacht/Attika/Stall likewise connects the nearly empty interiors and the detail of Roggan’s large-format photographs with memories of a disappearing East Germany.*12

Garage, Baumstücke, and RESET: Applying the Same Rules to Cars, Forests, and Machines

Roggan applies the same process beyond interiors. In Garage, wrecked cars are placed in strongly frontal settings, making their damaged bodies resemble either advertising photographs or specimens. Galerie EIGEN + ART publishes images from Garage, Baumstück, SET, RESET, and other series, showing how Roggan continues to isolate her subjects, reduce their backgrounds, and create images that invite close scrutiny of detail even as the subjects change.*6 “Von den Dingen” records that Roggan prunes branches and leaves when photographing forests and removes stickers and cleans surfaces in RESET, demonstrating that she does not preserve things exactly as she finds them.*20 Sammlung Philara’s exhibition Ex Machina brought together such obsolete machines and devices, detached from their functions and presented as a kind of typology within carefully arranged spaces.*16

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
SET / RESET: Reducing Obsolete Machines to the Photographic Plane

In SET / RESET, disused game machines and other equipment appear without the noise or users that once surrounded them, reduced to combinations of rectangles, apertures, screens, and fields of color. The book SET RESET EXITS SEDIMENTS brings together several series made around 2008–11, including work photographed in Cyprus, and sequences them around the time embedded in spaces and objects.*7 The sequencing of the book is central. It places similarly quiet, structured images in succession, allowing objects that have lost their function to enter a different visual order without explaining the provenance of each one.

Apokryphen: Separating Personal Effects from Their Owners’ Stories

Apokryphen is a series of small gelatin silver prints depicting personal effects and relics associated with figures including Bach, Beethoven, Heidegger, Schnitzler, and Bloch under closely comparable conditions. The artist’s website lists works from 2013–15 and the specific objects they depict, including shells, eyeglasses, pocket watches, and hearing aids.*11 In 2016, PIN. Freunde der Pinakothek der Moderne acquired five works from the series and described Roggan’s method of removing commemorative objects associated with well-known figures from their original display contexts and placing them in a uniform, neutral setting.*19 Spector Books published Apokryphen as a standalone volume devoted to the series.*10 By leaving fingerprints, wear, and unusual forms visible instead of illustrating the owners’ biographies, the series creates a gap between knowing whose object it was and seeing what it looks like in the photograph.

1971: Restaging Timm Rautert’s Photograph Fifty Years Later

Presented in the 2022 MdbK Leipzig exhibition, 1971 (2021) reconstructs, roughly fifty years later in a former Leipzig spinning mill, Timm Rautert’s 1971 photograph of Walter De Maria’s New York studio. MdbK surveyed Roggan’s process of finding, transforming, and restaging places and objects before photographing them on analog film, placing this series between her earlier work and new production.*5 Here, Rautert’s 1971 photograph becomes the reference for a restaging that is itself photographed again. The earlier photograph and the present-day space move back and forth within a single process of reconstruction and image-making.*5

Offerte: Advertising Scale Without a Product Name

Offerte, made in 2016, enlarges photographs of two hands holding everyday objects; in 2021 the images were shown on outdoor billboards in Bremerhaven. Kunsthalle/Kunstmuseum Bremerhaven identifies the project’s central device as using the scale of advertising while withholding prices, product names, and promotional copy.*14 When Roggan’s method of isolating small objects against nearly blank backgrounds is transferred to the scale of urban advertising, viewers instinctively look for what is being sold and receive no answer. The isolation created during photography and the choice of display medium produce the same uncertainty.

sections.title: Criticism, Reception, and Connections to Other Photography
sections.body_html:
Rautert, Demand, and Wall: Comparing Documentation and Staging

Roggan studied with Timm Rautert, who had trained under Otto Steinert and worked both in social documentary and in Bildanalytische Fotografie (“image-analytical photography”), an inquiry into the mechanisms of photography itself. Rautert taught at the Academy of Fine Arts Leipzig from 1993 to 2008. Museum Folkwang lists Roggan among his students alongside Viktoria Binschtok and Tobias Zielony.*23 The Zabludowicz Collection exhibition Recent Photography from Leipzig likewise brought together HGB graduates including Roggan, Binschtok, and Falk Haberkorn, describing their shared ground in careful objectivity, conceptual rigor, and sustained questioning of the photographic medium.*22

Martin Hochleitner discusses Roggan’s spaces in relation to staged photography and distinguishes them from the “model worlds” of artists such as Thomas Demand: in Roggan’s photographs, an existing place and a constructed state remain present at the same time.*21 The same essay refers to Jeff Wall’s “near documentary.” Roggan takes a different route, reducing traces of events in existing objects and places and arranging them into quiet images.*21 Her staging can therefore be understood as a way of testing how far a real object or place can be transformed within a photograph while remaining materially itself.

East German Ruins and the Role of Staging in the Documentary Look

Roggan’s early work has often been discussed in relation to memories of East Germany because of her birthplace and the locations she photographed. The Zabludowicz Collection reads furniture and empty rooms as carriers of social memory, while FOTOHOF places the disappearance of East Germany among the work’s important backgrounds.*15 A 2008 Frieze review cautioned that limiting the work to a romanticism of ruins overlooks Roggan’s process of rebuilding floors, sealing walls, and moving objects.*8 Reading the early work solely as a record of a vanished East Germany leaves out a crucial part of how the images are made.The Zabludowicz Collection also notes that in Leipzig, in the former East Germany, inexpensive post-industrial spaces existed alongside active art schools and galleries, providing an important environment for younger photographers*22. This does not reduce Roggan’s subjects to urban history, but it helps clarify the working environment in which HGB’s photographic education existed in close proximity to former industrial spaces. Because Roggan photographs real objects that carry historical traces only after reducing or rearranging those traces, documentation and staging remain visible in the same image.

Suspending the Time of Objects: Critical Readings of an Afterlife

In Roggan’s work, objects separated from their original locations or owners do not lose their histories completely. Writing on Apokryphen, Hubertus von Amelunxen argues that photography temporarily detaches an object from the time of its setting, allowing its history of use and its present appearance to be considered together. Drawing on Rilke, Heidegger, George Kubler, and Walter Benjamin, he reads Roggan’s objects as things in which past events seem to have stopped yet continue to appear in the present.*25 This is a critic’s interpretation, not Roggan’s own philosophical declaration, but it offers one way to understand why she repeatedly photographs real objects that have lost a function or an owner instead of new ones.In Apokryphen, knowing an owner’s name and looking at wear, shape, and material in a small photograph happen simultaneously. The series depends on the fact that an object’s provenance never fully coincides with the surface presented by the photograph.

Japanese reception has likewise emphasized this act of looking at objects again.In 2005, Roggan participated in German Contemporary Photography at the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, where her work was presented within German photography shaped by social change after reunification and the development of digital technology.*18 In an essay published by ANDO GALLERY, Futoshi Hoshino emphasizes Roggan’s active interventions over objective classification and reads the photographs as giving objects that have lost their function another “afterlife.”*17 Set against Roggan’s working process, this interpretation suggests that cleaning and repositioning create a degree of distance from an object’s former use and establish the conditions for seeing it again in a photograph.

From APPARATE to REVISION: Continuities Revealed by Retrospective Exhibitions

Since 2013, Roggan has taught photography at the State Academy of Fine Arts Stuttgart, while her subjects have expanded from interiors to machines, cinema, and reenactment.*1 A 2022 exhibition at the Leonhardi Museum brought together ATTIKA, BAUMSTÜCKE, APOKRYPHEN, the newer REVISION, and moving-image work, surveying her production since 2005.*13 Across these changing subjects, the procedure persists: Roggan seeks objects and places that have lost their use or context, intervenes in physical reality, and fixes the result in analog photographs. The work repeatedly tests whether a photograph can still look like a record after the photographer has altered something that already carries a history.

richard-avedon.html.lead_html: Richard Avedon (1923–2004) was a New York–born photographer who, after taking identification photographs for the U.S. Merchant Marine during World War II, studied with Alexey Brodovitch at the New School’s Design Laboratory. He worked for Harper's Bazaar from the mid-1940s, for Vogue from 1965, and for The New Yorker from 1992, moving among fashion photography, portraiture, and reportage.
richard-avedon.html.thesis_html: Avedon took models into streets and circuses in his postwar fashion photography, presenting clothes not as static commodities but as events involving bodies that walked, jumped, and turned within urban space. In his later portraits, by contrast, he reduced the conditions to a white seamless background, a fixed 8 × 10-inch large-format camera, even light, and close shooting distance, turning faces, clothing, skin, posture, and the response to being photographed into the image’s information. The method that set bodies in motion in his fashion work and the method that left bodies almost unable to move in his portraits may seem opposed, but both place the subject’s behavior before the camera at the center of the photograph. In In the American West, he brought this white-background form into the field, eliminating the landscape while concentrating the traces of labor and life on the surface of the body.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Richard Avedon was born in New York, encountered photography as a boy, and took identification photographs for the U.S. Merchant Marine during World War II. The Richard Avedon Foundation records his recollection that photographing so many faces through this work made him realize he was becoming a photographer *1. This experience alone cannot explain his later portraiture. Yet the repeated act of photographing faces and treating slight differences in expression and posture as photographic information was already present at the beginning of his career. After leaving the service, Avedon studied with Alexey Brodovitch at the New School’s Design Laboratory and became a leading photographer for Harper's Bazaar *1. His starting point was not studio photography in isolation, but the magazine, where page design, editing, typography, the model’s movement, and the reader’s gaze came together. The International Center of Photography likewise notes that Avedon worked for Junior Bazaar, Harper's Bazaar, Vogue, and The New Yorker while also gaining significant recognition from museums *2. His career can therefore be understood less as a “conversion” from commercial to fine-art photography than as a process in which ways of presenting people developed on commercial pages moved into books and exhibitions at a different scale. SFMOMA’s retrospective similarly brought his early street photography, 1950s Paris fashion work, and celebrity portraits together within a single career, describing an oeuvre that crossed the boundaries of photojournalism, fashion photography, and fine-art photography *3.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Postwar Fashion

Avedon entered fashion photography as clothing culture shifted from wartime austerity to postwar glamour. The V&A situates Dior’s 1947 “New Look” as a symbol of the turn from wartime economy toward glamour and femininity, while the Getty explains that postwar fashion photography offered readers aspirations for a new way of life as well as the clothes themselves *7*32. On a personal level, Avedon grew up with a father who owned a women’s clothing store; after leaving the service, he studied with Brodovitch and joined Junior Bazaar at the age of twenty-one *4. Magazine work allowed him to place within one image both the form of a garment and a vision of life in which its wearer walked, laughed, and played in the city. For Avedon, fashion photography thus extended beyond photographing merchandise. Through bodily behavior and urban life, it created a new image of postwar womanhood on the printed page.

Magazine Portraiture

Avedon’s photographs operated in many settings: magazine spreads, covers, features, advertisements, photobooks, exhibition walls, and the presentation of individual masterpieces. The Richard Avedon Foundation’s magazine archive shows that his photographs continued to appear in Harper's Bazaar, Life, Vogue, Rolling Stone, The New Yorker, Egoïste, and other publications, and notes that in 1992 he became The New Yorker’s first staff photographer *5. Within a magazine, a photograph is neither merely an illustration decorating a text nor a product image explaining a garment. At the pace of turning pages, it becomes a device that instantly reconnects a person, clothing, the atmosphere of an era, and a social role. Avedon’s portraits derive their force not from extracting a subject’s inner self intact, but from leaving pose, hairstyle, clothing, accessories, light, blank space, and the printed surface in the image as clues from which a persona is made. Avedon himself said that photographs do not go beneath the surface, expressing his belief that surfaces are filled with clues *6. Here, surface does not mean superficial appearance. It encompasses everything photography can actually address: face, clothing, posture, blank space, the printed surface, and the medium of publication. Avedon’s portraits do not “reveal the true personality.” They ask readers and viewers to judge a person solely through the arrangement of surfaces, while exposing the precariousness of that judgment.

Politics, War, and Family

Avedon did not abruptly turn from fashion to social issues. The Richard Avedon Foundation explains that success in advertising and the commercial studio gave him the freedom to pursue cultural, political, and personal concerns as long-term projects, citing his work on the civil rights movement, the Vietnam War, and the series portraying his father, Jacob Israel Avedon *1. In 1963, he photographed members of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. The image appeared near the end of Nothing Personal, published with James Baldwin the following year, as part of a sequence addressing American race relations, violence, and political division *38*39. In Saigon in 1971, he photographed a victim of napalm, recording directly the damage war had left on a civilian body *40. Fashion, politics, and war were distinct bodies of work, yet they were continuous in asking viewers to read in a person’s clothing, posture, and expression the social and historical circumstances to which that person belonged.

The series in which he repeatedly photographed his father from 1969 until his death in 1973 brought this concern into its most private setting. The Met explains that the series grew from Avedon’s anger toward and distance from his father since childhood, as well as his adult desire to rebuild their relationship *24. Shown in just eight photographs at MoMA in 1974, the series did not treat aging and death as abstractions; it enacted the photographer’s attempt to photograph someone he was about to lose *19. More important than the differences among politicians, activists, victims of war, and his father is the continuity with his later portraiture: an effort to record, through face and body, the social and personal circumstances in which each person was situated.

Fashion Photography in Motion

Avedon renewed fashion photography by creating moments in which clothing joined human movement and urban space, instead of simply presenting garments at rest. According to the Foundation, Avedon was initially denied use of the studio at Harper's Bazaar, so he photographed models and clothes in streets, nightclubs, circuses, and at the beach *1. A Harper's Bazaar retrospective also recounts how Brodovitch recognized the experimental portraits Avedon had made in the Merchant Marine and urged him to carry that experimentation into fashion photography *33. The International Center of Photography similarly credits Avedon with breaking the conventions of static fashion imagery and bringing a strong sense of movement to postwar fashion photography *31. The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, explains that models laughing, jumping, dancing, and roller-skating conveyed a new postwar way of life along with the clothes *4. The Getty likewise cites his mid-1950s Paris shoots of Suzy Parker on roller skates and Carmen Dell’Orefice leaping over a puddle as examples of movement incorporated into the image *36.

The V&A presents the 1957 photograph Carmen (Homage to Munkácsi), coat by Cardin, Place Francois-Premier, Paris as a reference to Martin Munkácsi, who had moved models outdoors *7. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s Renee The New Look of Dior Place de la Concorde, Paris belongs to a 1947 Paris fashion portfolio, while SFMOMA features the 1955 Dovima with Elephants, Evening Dress by Dior, Cirque d'Hiver, Paris as a representative example *8*3. The content of these photographs includes more than information about clothing: it encompasses the image of women walking through postwar Paris and the gestures of a new way of life that magazines offered their readers.

Staging and Strobe Light

The “movement” of Avedon’s fashion period did not arise solely from snapshots awaiting chance. A 1958 report in The New Yorker describes sets and props being assembled and complex lighting equipment arranged in Avedon’s studio *35. The magazine’s account of a 1967 shoot with Twiggy records the use of a white paper background that curved onto the floor to eliminate the seam. Continuous modeling lights were used to check the lighting, while the strobe fired for the exposure *34. The same account describes Avedon giving precise directions about the model’s position and posture, showing that even seemingly buoyant images were staged through control of body, clothing, and light *34.

Differences from Irving Penn

Placed beside his contemporary Penn, Avedon’s particular qualities become clearer. The Getty notes that in postwar fashion photography Penn centered his work on the studio, while Avedon excelled at moving models on location *32. The Art Institute of Chicago’s Irving Penn Archives explains that as 1960s fashion photography shifted from elegance toward spontaneity, Avedon supplied dynamic poses evoking everyday urban life, while Penn continued to immerse himself in detail, form, and composition *9. The Metropolitan Museum of Art likewise describes Penn’s studio photography as a pared-down aesthetic built on meticulous attention to composition, nuance, and detail *10. The Penn Archives’ discussion of his portraits further shows how the “corner portraits” restricted the subject’s movement, closed off narrative readings, and turned toward subtle explorations of gesture and expression *11. Avedon, by contrast, released bodies into the city and circus in his early fashion work. In his later white-background pictures, he held the figure in place while bringing reactions, fatigue, resistance, and performance arising during the sitting to the fore. Both photographers carried magazine photography into forms examined through museum exhibitions and collections. Yet where Penn submerged clothing and faces in the density of composition and print, Avedon pursued bodily response, the pressure of the encounter, and immediacy on page and wall.

White-Background Portraits

The white background that recurs in Avedon’s mature portraiture is often described as a device for showing “only the person.” Treating it as a neutral ground or a guarantee of truth, however, oversimplifies his method. The white background removes landscape, interiors, workplaces, and props that explain class, bringing the subject’s body, clothing, skin, gaze, fatigue, tension, and resistance to being photographed to the front of the image. Discussing the 1955 Marian Anderson, the Met explains that the white ground and tight framing strengthen the figure’s presence *25. Viewers are consequently asked to determine “who this person is,” while also confronting the degree to which such a reading depends on surfaces. The Amon Carter Museum explains that in In the American West, subjects were placed before a seamless white background and stripped of references to place *12. SFMOMA’s press material likewise states that the figures appear against a white background without shadows or references to location, conveying ordinary human vulnerability instead of the stereotype of “rugged grandeur” commonly associated with the West *13. The white background does not make a person transparent; by erasing the setting, it makes what remains appear in excess. What remains is not the depth of personality itself, but a plane on which face, body, clothing, occupational title, circumstances of the sitting, and the viewer’s interpretation collide.

The 8 × 10 Camera and a Fixed Position

In Avedon’s mature portraits, the camera’s immobility became a method in itself. In 1969, he began working seriously with an 8 × 10-inch Deardorff mounted on a tripod, leaving behind the approach of holding a Rolleiflex at waist level and moving with his subject *24. The arrangement in which he stood beside the large-format camera and looked directly at the sitter continued in In the American West, where the 8 × 10 was placed close to the subject *28*30.

The 8 × 10 increased detail while narrowing the body’s freedom during the sitting. With slow shutter speeds and shallow depth of field, substantial movement could easily fall out of focus. Because Avedon used the entire negative, including its black border, the subject also had little room to shift position within the frame *24. In contrast to the walking and jumping of the early fashion work, the gaze, mouth, shoulders, hands, and wrinkles in clothing of a person standing in nearly the same position emerge as the differences from one mature portrait to the next.

Lighting and Shooting Distance

Avedon’s white backgrounds cannot be reduced to a single technique in which a powerful strobe blows the background out to white. The Met explains that his white-background portraits made with an 8 × 10 used diffused daylight that cast almost no shadows, or comparably flat studio illumination *24. Strobe use in the studio is documented, and Phillips identifies the combination of an 8 × 10, white background, and strobe as a typical method in his representative later studio portraits *34*37. In In the American West, however, white background paper was set up in the shade of a building, and the figures were photographed in natural light away from direct sun *26*28. What these different light sources share is an emphasis on making face, skin, fabric, and dirt legible across the image, rather than on dramatic light itself.

Avedon explained that for In the American West he stood a few inches to the left of the lens, rather than behind the camera, and photographed from about four feet away *30. At this distance, photographer and subject could read each other’s expressions and gestures directly. The combination of close range, large-format camera, and white background made the encounter itself a condition of the photograph, in place of observing a person from afar.

Encounter and Performance

Avedon’s form could move among fashion, celebrities, politicians, family members, and workers because it centered on the bodily response of a person placed before the camera, more than an explanation supplied by setting or story. Reducing place, evening out the light, and intensifying frontality left face, clothing, posture, hands, skin, and tension in sharp relief. In Harper's Bazaar and Vogue, this appeared as the freedom and refinement performed by models; in Rolling Stone’s The Family, as a roster of people who held political power; and in In the American West, as the bodies of workers and itinerants accompanied by occupational titles and shooting locations. The Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson explains that Avedon rarely idealized his sitters and presented the face with the clarity of a landscape *14. Frieze also argues that the “performance” involved in Avedon’s portraiture included the photographer’s conduct as well as the subject’s *15. The white background did not give every person the same meaning. It made visible, as conditions of the image, the relations among the role a person carried before the camera, the response the photographer selected, and what viewers read from the surface.

Differences from August Sander

A comparison with August Sander clarifies the distinction of Avedon’s method. Sander’s People of the Twentieth Century was a project that classified German society into social types and occupations—farmers, craftspeople, merchants, artists, and others—and incorporated individual portraits into a broad social archive *16. The Walther Collection, meanwhile, describes Avedon’s The Family as a series that echoes a Sander-like structure while bringing into view how political power is displayed and manipulated within a communal identity *17. Avedon, too, had a sense of classification and seriality, but instead of systematizing society through occupational types, he made the photographer’s proximity, the choice of subjects, and the viewer’s judgments based on expression and clothing part of the conditions of portraiture.

The Conditions of Photographing In the American West

In the American West brought Avedon’s white-background method out of fashion and celebrity culture and into conflict with the mythology of the American West. According to the Amon Carter Museum, its director Mitchell A. Wilder commissioned the project in 1979. Between 1979 and 1984, Avedon traveled through 189 towns in seventeen states and exposed 17,000 sheets of film in 752 sittings *12. His assistant Laura Wilson researched gatherings such as festivals and rodeos and studied the economic circumstances of the oil, mining, and agricultural industries while looking for potential subjects; choosing the figures for the series involved sustained research *27. The museum’s collection pages include A. L. Bean, cotton farmer, Sweetwater, Texas, 3/10/79 and Alton Terry, oil field worker, Frenstat, Texas, 9/28/80, recording both as part of the Amon Carter Museum commission exhibited in 1985 *18. For its 2025 exhibition, the Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson presented the series as portraiture that ran counter to traditional depictions and mythologizations of the American West *14.

The photography itself did not become location-based snapshot work. The Amon Carter Museum’s account of the shoots describes assistants setting white background paper on the shaded side of a building and placing prospective subjects before it *26. Gagosian likewise states that Avedon placed an 8 × 10 Deardorff close to the subject and used natural light and a seamless white background *28. A Sotheby’s catalogue note also records the procedure of placing the subject before white paper and using available light in the shade *29. The sky, roads, mines, and ranches of the West disappear, while mud, oil, sweat, wrinkles, scars, and work clothes remain in fine detail on the large-format negative. Showing the traces an environment left on bodies and clothes, instead of explaining that environment as a backdrop, joined the series’ technique to its subject.

Print size also shaped this effect. The Amon Carter Museum explains that some exhibition prints from In the American West reached approximately four feet high and eleven feet wide *12. By greatly enlarging the details of skin, hair, fabric, and dirt held by the 8 × 10 negative, figures isolated against white acquired a scale close to the viewer’s body on the museum wall. The roughly four-foot proximity of the sitting became an encounter with monumental figures in the exhibition *30.

Criticism of In the American West

From the time of its release, In the American West was criticized both for its forceful form and for whom Avedon had chosen to represent “the West.” Photography historian Mick Gidley examined the series through several biographical, historical, geographical, and aesthetic contexts, arguing that the white background’s separation of people from specific Western places itself made the work’s referent ambiguous *41. In 1985, The Christian Science Monitor also presented the criticism that the subjects did not offer a cross-sectional representation of Western society and that Avedon’s selection leaned toward struggling workers and itinerants *42. The following year, The Spectator went further, questioning the photographer’s power of selection on the grounds that real people had been incorporated into a preconceived framework of “the West” *43.

Avedon himself did not claim that the series was an objective cross section of the West. In a 1985 interview, he distinguished himself from a photojournalist and the title In the American West from The American West, explaining his position that photographs become the photographer’s opinions, not facts themselves *42. At the same time, he acknowledged the serious ethical questions involved in using other people to make art *42. Taken together, these criticisms and Avedon’s account indicate that In the American West must be read through whom he selected, which contexts he erased, and at what scale he presented the figures, not as an objective record of the West.

Selection and Ethics

Avedon’s portraits give their subjects a strong presence while also bringing to the surface the photographer’s role in constructing how they appear. Through decisions about who is selected, how completely the setting is removed, which expression is chosen, and how large the print becomes, the subject is presented in a particular form rather than simply “captured.” The National Portrait Gallery of Australia cites production testimony that for In the American West Avedon searched for what he “wanted to see” and that his choice of subjects was entirely subjective *6. The same article records that printer Rudi Hofmann received directions from Avedon such as “more gentle” and “make him look more nervous”—instructions concerning emotional states rather than technical values *6. The white background did not erase the traces of staging. It also made it easier to see that a subject’s appearance was produced through photographing, selecting, printing, and exhibiting.

The series portraying his father, Jacob Israel Avedon, placed this issue in its most private form. The Richard Avedon Foundation’s exhibition history records that the 1974 MoMA presentation consisted of eight images of his dying father, a small but thoroughly personal exhibition that drew both praise and criticism *19. Through portraits made from 1951 to 2004, The Image Centre also treats as an exhibition theme Avedon’s distance from the convention of idealizing famous people and his sustained attention to the traces of aging inscribed on faces *20. Avedon’s portraits cannot be resolved by labeling them either “merciless” or “empathetic.” The more forcefully a figure appears, the more the photographer’s instructions, the camera’s position, print size, exhibition space, and the viewer’s judgment contribute to the work’s meaning. In his work, making someone visible through photography cannot be separated from fixing that person as an image chosen by the photographer.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Magazine Editing and Society

Avedon’s reputation formed between magazine culture and the museum system. In mid-twentieth-century America, magazines were a primary medium for circulating photographs on a mass scale, and Avedon continually placed portraits of politicians, activists, and writers, as well as fashion images, on their pages *21*38. In Nothing Personal (1964), made with James Baldwin, the editing itself became a critique of American society by setting different kinds of people against one another across spreads and successive pages, beyond the meaning of any single photograph *21*39. From the time of publication, however, the book also drew severe criticism for its approach to social critique through celebrities. Frieze looks back on how that response affected Avedon’s subsequent portraiture *15. The magazine page was both a means of showing work widely and a place for expressing a social position through the arrangement and sequence of photographs.

Museums and Fashion Photography

Museum recognition came early. According to the Richard Avedon Foundation’s exhibition history, his work appeared in MoMA’s The Family of Man in 1955; he received his first retrospective at the Smithsonian Institution in 1962; and in 1978 he became the first living photographer to have an exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art *19. The same history explains that the 1978 exhibition was a retrospective of Avedon’s fashion photography and an event bearing on the legitimacy of photography as a medium and fashion photography as a genre *19. MoMA has continued to situate Avedon within numerous exhibitions and its collection *22. In 2013, the National Portrait Gallery of Australia organized the country’s first Avedon exhibition around his work in portraiture *6. In Japan, the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum included Avedon in Visions of America, placing him within a context for considering twentieth-century American photographic expression *23. What matters in this reception is not simply that commercial photography was “elevated” to art. Avedon moved the series, the spread, and the instantly legible arrangement of a figure from magazines to museum walls, unsettling the framework that treated fashion and fine-art photography as separate fields *15*19.

richard-billingham.html.lead_html: Richard Billingham photographed life with his father Ray, his mother Liz, and his brother Jason in a council flat in the Black Country, using 35mm color film, and assembled the images in Ray’s a Laugh. The same medium ordinary families used for everyday life and special occasions records an interior world shaped by repeated drinking, arguments, boredom, care, and laughter. The photographs began as references for paintings of his father and continued as a private attempt to understand his family. Once published and exhibited, they were also read as images of class marked by council housing, unemployment, and alcohol. The gap between Billingham’s purpose and those social readings became central to the work’s ethics.
richard-billingham.html.thesis_html: British social documentary often made working-class life public from an external viewpoint, while family color snapshots usually remained within the family as private memory. To paint a father who could not hold a pose for long, Billingham photographed their shared home with a cheap camera and direct flash, then edited scenes of turmoil, silence, care, and empty rooms into a photobook. He showed how private snapshots become representations of class once they circulate publicly, making intimacy and the social gaze inseparable problems within the same images.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
The Black Country in the West Midlands, where Billingham grew up, was shaped by manufacturing and heavy industry. Factory closures, long-term unemployment, and changes to council-housing policy in the 1980s reached deeply into domestic life. Billingham has recalled growing up in a high-rise estate and described how his father Ray spent long periods out of work and at home drinking*8.This social history helps explain why the work centers on repeated interior actions—waiting, drinking, sleeping, and caring—instead of workplaces or streets. Studies of class representation likewise discuss the work as one in which domestic interiors carry the traces of social structure in postindustrial Britain*18.

The work began with painting. While studying art, Billingham took photographs as references for portraits of his father. Because Ray had difficulty holding a pose, he used a cheap compact camera to catch brief moments. To reduce processing costs, he chose the least expensive film and development, and used direct flash in the dim interior. In an interview with The Observer, he describes beginning with photographs for paintings and working with a basic camera, built-in flash, and sometimes expired film*5. Blur, red-eye, and color casts arose from movement, interior lighting, limited funds, and the original purpose of the pictures. They became formal qualities through which unstable domestic time was conveyed. MoMA presented the photographs as a new photographic practice in the 1996 exhibition “New Photography 12”*17.

When the photographs entered the art world in the mid-1990s, exhibitions, the market, and the popular press surrounding young British artists consumed class and private life as compelling narratives. Ray’s a Laugh was included in “Sensation” in 1997, and Billingham himself was presented through a story of talent discovered in poverty.*13. As a body of work that began inside the home moved through books, exhibitions, and criticism, Ray and Liz’s lives also came to stand for working-class experience. A gap opened between the original effort to understand a family and the social meanings assigned by art institutions. That gap added an ethical question: who gets to look at, explain, and possess a family’s life?

sections.title: Family Photography and Class Representation
sections.body_html:
The Time Preserved by Family Photographs

Here, family photography means ordinary snapshots made at home, on trips, at birthdays, graduations, and other occasions, then kept in albums. Because 35mm color film was inexpensive and easy to use, it became a common medium for recording family life. Scholarship on family photography explains how such images select commemorative moments and create an ongoing domestic narrative*19. Alongside events such as birthdays, Billingham used the same medium to preserve Ray waiting in a chair, Liz working on a puzzle, animals crossing the room, and the silence after an argument.

A conventional family album is an edited object that selects events a family wants to preserve and share across generations. Repeated smiles, trips, birthdays, and rituals create a story of continuity. Ray’s a Laugh uses the familiarity of the same color snapshot while treating dependency, boredom, decoration, care, and loneliness as equally formative elements of family time.*19. Through the book’s sequence, repetitive everyday life—usually left outside commemorative photographs—enters the family’s memory.

When Private Memory Becomes Class Evidence

The photographs began as references for paintings of his father and as a private effort to understand family life. Once they circulated beyond the family, cramped rooms, peeling wallpaper, inexpensive furniture, homemade alcohol, animals, and injuries became social signs through which viewers read council housing, unemployment, welfare, and drinking. A reassessment in Nonsite argues that the book preserves the family’s specificity while also risking an institutional framing of Ray and Liz as examples of “working-class ruin.”*14. Family photography becomes class representation when the same interior picture is read as memory by relatives and as social evidence by museum viewers. Studies of family photography understand the album both as a container for private memory and as a convention through which a household presents itself socially.*20

How the Photobook Constructs Domestic Time

Among the images widely circulated from the first edition are Ray collapsing, Liz appearing to throw a cat, and rooms crowded with dishes and animals—scenes that prompt immediate judgments. In the book, Billingham emphasized relations between adjacent photographs: silence follows laughter, an empty room follows an argument, and windows and animals interrupt sequences of human figures. In an interview with Photoworks, he explains that the photographs needed to connect before and after one another like scenes in a film*1. A conversation with Redbrick likewise confirms his interest in editing individual images into the flow of a book*4. Through sequencing, a violent photograph becomes one episode within family life instead of an explanation of the family as a whole.

The 2024 “director’s cut” restores a longer sequence closer to an early dummy, increasing the presence of quiet interiors, solitude, and repetition. The Guardian notes that the new edition includes unpublished photographs and presents domestic time as quieter and more extended than in the 1996 version*3. Without resolving the ethical questions, the new edition restores the photographer’s long duration within the family home to a reception previously dominated by sensational individual images.

The Right to Photograph One’s Family

As a son, Billingham participated in family life and spent years in those rooms, with an access unavailable to a reporter arriving to make photographs. That proximity made it possible to photograph the moments before and after an argument, periods of waiting, and gestures of care. Yet decisions about photographing, editing, publishing, and selling remained concentrated with the son and his editors. A Financial Times review of the reissue observes that Billingham’s account of photographing in order to understand continues to coexist with doubts about making intimate hardship public*12. The difference between the access granted by family relations and the authority an author holds over publication produces the work’s ethical tension.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Medium
sections.body_html:
Ray

The photographs of Ray encompass scenes of falling, shouting, drinking, waiting, and repose. In works such as “Untitled, 1995,” a body standing against a wall and the colors of the room are compressed onto the same plane; the figure is central to the household and absorbed by it at once. MoMA holds the work as an example of the tension between body and interior produced by direct flash and close-range color*16. Across the book, Ray moves among several roles: tragic victim, comic drunk, father, and willing subject. The sequence keeps these roles in tension.

Liz

Liz’s floral clothes, tattoos, puzzles, ornaments, and vivid wallpaper reveal a strong visual instinct for remaking the interior according to her own taste. She composes clothing and body through emphatic color and sometimes meets the camera directly. The New Yorker argues that the hard flash reveals domestic damage, Liz’s visual imagination, and the family’s theatricality at the same time*11. Billingham’s training in painting brings the strong contrasts among red, yellow, blue, floral patterns, skin, and furniture into view as structural elements of the photographs.

Empty Rooms and Animals

Photographs of empty rooms, windows, birds, dogs, and cats, which gain greater importance in the new edition, create pauses between scenes of people.The National Science and Media Museum presents Billingham’s snapshots within a duration that continues before and after each action *2. Animals create cycles of care, noise, escape, and contact; empty rooms retain the afterimage of the family’s presence. These pictures add care, rhythm, and absence to the social reading of the interior.

Ray & Liz

In the film Ray & Liz, Billingham reconstructs three events from his childhood through actors, sets, and carefully reproduced details. He has said that he wanted to recreate the duration and atmosphere of situations he could not understand as a child*13. The photographs record the family in brief moments at the time of exposure; the film rebuilds scenes later from memory. Comparing the two media makes the construction of Ray’s a Laugh through camera position and editing more apparent. An interview in The Quietus describes how sets and actors were used to reconstruct parts of childhood that were never photographed*6. In an interview with The Seventh Art, reenactment is described as a means of examining how an event felt*9.

sections.title: Criticism, Reception, and Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Differences from Goldin and Clark

Billingham is often compared with Nan Goldin and Larry Clark within a lineage of photographers working from inside their communities. Goldin’s photographs created forms of self-representation for friends, lovers, and queer communities, along with a shared space in the slide show. Clark centered participation in youth culture and transgression. Billingham’s family bond existed before the camera and could not be freely entered or left. The work’s particular pressure comes from editing affection and disgust within that preexisting bond. MoMA exhibited these family photographs as a new contemporary practice in “New Photography 12” in 1996*17. The museum’s artist page brings together collection holdings and exhibition records, tracing how photographs known through the book entered museum collections and displays*7.

Admiration and Disgust

Early responses praised the photographs as frank and affectionate, while also criticizing them for turning poverty, obesity, and drinking into an art-world spectacle. A long article in The Observer records how the media joined Billingham’s story of upward mobility to his family’s life*5. Private memory, formal color, social signs of class, and market value overlap within the same images, so praise and criticism continue. A reassessment by M Creates shows that, three decades later, class voyeurism and familial affection remain competing readings*10.

Editing Family Time

British social documentary often made working-class life public through a photographer’s reporting and explanation, while family photographs were generally kept as memory within the household.Photographers had already worked from within lives they shared with their subjects. Billingham’s distinct contribution lies in the fact that images retaining the distance and color of the ordinary snapshots he made to paint his father became public representations of class as they passed through the photobook, the museum, and criticism—and that transformation remained visible within the work*14*17. Viewed alone, a collapsing father or chaotic room can easily become an explanation of the entire family. The book’s sequence restores the waiting, care, decoration, animals, and empty rooms that surround moments of turmoil. Separating Billingham’s attempt to understand his family at the time of shooting from the class representation produced through circulation reveals both the explanatory power and the violence involved when private intimacy becomes public social evidence*3*15.
