sherman.html.lead_html: Cindy Sherman transformed photography from a medium associated with evidence, likeness, and authorial self-expression into a way of testing how cinema, advertising, magazines, and art history produce recognizable roles. Working alongside the Pictures Generation in late-1970s New York, she used her own body, costume, makeup, setting, and camera position to unsettle the idea that a single image can reveal a stable person.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Cindy Sherman was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, in 1954, studied art at Buffalo State College in the early 1970s, and began working from New York soon afterward*1. In Buffalo, the artistic environment around her did not treat photography only as a finished, self-contained image. It also moved through bodies, disguise, serial images, video, performance, and exhibition. MoMA curator Eva Respini notes that Sherman shifted from painting toward photography as a student and encountered artists who were using the camera within conceptual art and performance*14. The work of artists such as Eleanor Antin, Hannah Wilke, and Adrian Piper, who used bodies, disguise, sequence, and recorded action to perform or dismantle identity, formed a nearby context for what would later become the Film Stills*14. Hallwalls, the alternative space Sherman helped found with Robert Longo, Charles Clough, and others, also began in Buffalo as a place for new work across visual art, media, performance, and literature; it encouraged a sense of photography as something that could move between image, body, documentation, and display rather than remain a purified genre*18. That tendency is already visible in Cover Girl from 1976. Apollo describes the work as a sequence built from actual women's magazine covers, versions in which Sherman replaced the model's face with her own while mimicking pose and makeup, and further images in which the cover's norm begins to break down*16. Made between 1977 and 1980, Untitled Film Stills is a series of sixty-nine black-and-white photographs that MoMA acquired in full in 1995 and exhibited as Cindy Sherman: The Complete Untitled Film Stills in 1997*2. The series evokes publicity stills from 1950s and 1960s Hollywood film, film noir, and European art cinema, but its importance lies less in the reconstruction of any actual movie than in the making of scenes that seem familiar yet cannot be identified. Through that uncertainty, the work shows how female figures are produced through repeated codes from cinema and advertising. Sherman used herself not because she wanted to reveal her private interior life. Using her own body allowed makeup, clothing, expression, pose, gaze, and the timing of the shutter to be built as one process. When she moved to New York, she was not responding only to films seen in theaters. In a New York Magazine interview, Sherman recalled seeing large numbers of women's images for photo-novels at the magazine company where David Salle worked*15. A photo-novel is a popular printed form in which photographs of actors or models are arranged like comic panels, with speech balloons or short captions carrying a romance, crime, or melodramatic story*19. Emerging from postwar Italian women's magazine culture, the form linked cinema, comics, and melodrama, using the photograph as a single scene that asks the reader to imagine what came before and after it*20. What mattered to Sherman was not simply the cheapness of those printed images, but the way a viewer could see one isolated picture and immediately invent a relationship, an incident, and a narrative around it*15. Her early method, then, was not costume as self-introduction. It was a way of rebuilding already circulating types of persona—drawn from film, women's magazines, advertising, television, and photographic story magazines—through her own body, clothing, hair, expression, interior spaces, streets, and camera position. The logic is closer to testing how easily the same body can be read as another person than to showing "herself." Change the costume or hairstyle, move from a room to a street, alter the height or distance of the camera, and one figure can become an actress, a woman on the run, a working woman, a lonely housewife, or a young woman approaching danger. Sherman has said that, at the time, she was not beginning from an articulated theory of the male gaze or objectification; she was reacting to the tension between her own attraction to makeup and old-fashioned clothing and a contemporary climate in which women were expected to appear natural*15.

sections.title: Untitled Film Stills, Staged Photography, and the Pictures Generation
sections.body_html:
The force of Untitled Film Stills comes from using photography's appearance of recording a real moment as the very material of fiction. In Untitled Film Still #21 , for example, The Met explains that Sherman performs a scene associated with mid-century Hollywood tropes while foregrounding production elements that usually disappear from view: camera angle, lighting, clothing, and setting*3. The Broad likewise describes the Film Stills as works that do not quote recognizable films directly but suggest genres, generating figures that feel less like individual actresses than types of personality or role*4. Sherman seems to photograph one woman, but she is also photographing signs that cinema has trained viewers to read: schoolgirl, secretary, housewife, fugitive, urban career woman. Because the image contains no clear before or after, and because the titles refuse explanation, viewers complete each scene from their own memories of movies, advertising, television, and magazines. The photograph activates narrative reflexes stored in the viewer before it reveals anything stable about the subject. In this sense, Sherman's image is not a decisive moment that captures an event; it is a device that summons the viewer's already learned ways of reading cinematic and magazine images. Respini writes that the Film Stills are not illustrations of a single theory, yet they belong to a moment when photography's truth claims were under pressure and they exploit the medium's capacity to lie, mask, and seduce*14. Sherman's historical update was not that she "invented staged photography." Performance and fiction had been present in photography from early on, and Respini places her in a longer line that includes Hippolyte Bayard, the Countess of Castiglione, Claude Cahun, and Marcel Duchamp's Rrose Sélavy*14. What Sherman expanded was the target of that performance. Disguise was no longer only an eccentric self-portrait or theatrical masquerade by an individual artist. It became a way to expose the systems through which film, advertising, magazines, and art history produce women as recognizable images. Photography thus moved from "accurately showing the person in front of the camera" toward exposing the visual codes that make that person legible as star, victim, seductress, worker, or upper-class portrait.

The Pictures Generation and feminist photography: performing the role of an image rather than making a self-portrait

Sherman is often discussed in relation to the Pictures Generation. The term comes from Douglas Crimp's 1977 exhibition Pictures at Artists Space in New York and refers to a loose group of artists who used photography, film, video, and performance to examine how images in mass consumer culture shape perception and desire*6. The Met's 2009 exhibition The Pictures Generation, 1974–1984 presents these artists as inheriting the self-reflexive logic of Minimalism and Conceptual Art while returning to recognizable imagery in order to ask how images shape the way we perceive ourselves and the world*5. The same essay describes a generation for whom television, film, magazines, and music were almost a weather system, and for whom translations of Foucault, Barthes, and Kristeva helped make identity readable not as a natural interior but as a social construction around gender, class, sexuality, and citizenship*6. Behind this was the overlap between a postwar consumer society saturated by images and the atmosphere after the civil rights and women's movements, in which artists were asking who had represented whom, and from what position. The Met places these younger artists in a period marked by the Vietnam War, Watergate, the sexual revolution, racial unrest, and assassinations, while also noting the force of the image culture that surrounded them*6. At the same time, the feminist avant-garde of the 1970s saw women artists move away from passive roles as muse or model and use their own bodies, photography, video, performance, and disguise to rework traditional images of women*25. The question of the period was therefore not simply how to find an authentic "true self." What became urgent was the speed with which "selfhood" or "femininity" could be produced inside the viewer by circulating poses, clothes, facial expressions, gazes, rooms, streets, printed images, and film fragments. Within that setting, Sherman and Laurie Simmons have been understood as artists who dug into visual cultures—B-movies, dollhouses, and other forms between private and collective memory—that seemed fictional yet already felt remembered*6. In Sherman's case, the question becomes sharply concrete: what is an individual if a single photograph can make the viewer assign profession, class, desire, danger, and past to a body almost immediately? She did not fix one person inside one image. She repeated the way the same body, slightly altered by composition, costume, expression, and setting, could be made to carry another occupation, another social class, another desire, another story. What becomes unstable in her work is not only the image of woman. It is the viewer's confidence that a single image can disclose someone's character, situation, history, or wish. MoMA describes Sherman as an artist who uses herself as model while drawing from images supplied by film, television, magazines, the internet, and art history to investigate the construction of contemporary identity and representation*10. In this context, "self-portrait" is too narrow a name for the work. The Broad's 2016 exhibition Cindy Sherman: Imitation of Life describes her as working alone in the studio as director, photographer, makeup artist, hairstylist, and subject, performing media-influenced stereotypes of women through varied personas, environments, and costumes*7. The self appears not as an inner core but as an accumulation of roles attached from the outside. Yokohama Museum of Art's entry for Untitled Film Still #23 notes that the series can be read as questioning images of women as objects of the male gaze, while also emphasizing the ambiguity that prevents Sherman's figures from being reduced to a single emotion or story*8. Her work is therefore not only "a critique of female representation." It first allows the image being criticized to become convincing and attractive, then lets the viewer recognize, often belatedly, how that attraction was built. Sherman's own comments clarify this distance. In a 2008 interview she said she was not working from a fully formulated theory of the male gaze or the objectification of women; she was responding to the contradiction between her interest in makeup and old-fashioned looks and a cultural expectation that women appear natural*15. That is where feminist photography, staged photography, and postmodern photography meet in her work.

After Centerfolds: gaze, body, aging, and the grotesque

In the 1981 Centerfolds, Sherman moved into a horizontal format close to magazine spreads and created uneasy relations in which the figure often seems to be looked down upon. The Met's entry for Untitled #87 explains that the series can place the viewer in a vicariously predatory male gaze and that it prompted criticism for not fully distancing itself from objectification*9. Objectification here means turning a person into a body or image to be viewed for desire, consumption, or control before encountering them as a distinct individual. In the Centerfolds, the horizontal frame, reclining body, and averted gaze recall familiar compositions from men's magazines and film. Even if a viewer knows the work is critical, the image first draws that viewer into the position of looking. The criticism, then, was not simply that Sherman exposed the objectification of women, but that the work might also reactivate the desire to see such an objectified image. That tension shows why Sherman's photographs do not judge stereotypes from a safe distance. They leave inside the work the very force by which stereotypes attract viewers. From the 1980s onward, she extended her method beyond the cinematic memory of the Film Stills into fashion, fairy tales, myth, historical portraiture, bodily damage, clowns, and upper-class portraits. MoMA's 2012 retrospective names major series including Untitled Film Stills , the Old Master-like History Portraits , and the Society Portraits , organizing the exhibition around artifice and fiction, cinema and performance, horror and the grotesque, myth and carnival, and identities of gender and class*10. SFMOMA likewise lists the Film Stills, the 1981 Centerfolds, the 1985 fairy-tale and mythological images, the 1988–90 History Portraits, the 1992 Sex Pictures, the 2000 Headshots, the 2002–04 Clowns, several fashion series, and the 2008 Society Portraits as key bodies of work*11. Across this expansion, the procedure remains consistent. Sherman takes on the visual roles of each period with her own body, makes them concrete enough to be believed, and then cracks the surface of that believability.

Turning to art history: Old Masters displaced by photographic artifice

In the later History Portraits / Old Masters , Sherman turns not only to images of women produced by film and advertising but also to the portrait types made by art history itself. NGV explains that in this series she moved from early tableaux with a B-movie charge toward art history, working with imagery that evokes Raphael, Caravaggio, Ingres, and others*22. She borrows composition, costume, pose, and ornament, but she does not close the image as faithful reconstruction. Clothing, prostheses, heavy makeup, artificial bodies, and props that seem gathered from flea markets roughly displace the authority of classical portraiture*22. Sammlung Goetz places the series as an inquiry into the representation of power and social status in Old Master painting, explaining that the photographs, while dressed as paintings, reveal the artificiality of depiction and self-fashioning*23. Sherman is not showing virtuosity in reproducing painting through photography. She is showing how the signs long carried by portraiture—authority, beauty, class, gender, and religious value—have been staged through clothing, pose, body, gaze, and material surface*22. MoMA's audio commentary on Untitled #224 also points to the layered structure in which Sherman takes on Caravaggio's Sick Bacchus : a woman artist performs a male painter, and that male painter is himself performing a god*24.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: What matters in Sherman's reception is that her work has been read not only as a model of postmodern photography, but also within the question that shaped feminist photography after the 1970s: how can the female body be represented? In a 1991 essay, Laura Mulvey argued that Sherman was not a didactic theorist, yet her work joined questions of feminist aesthetics, the body, representation, and popular culture, and she placed the early works as re-representations of femininity*12. This reception did not settle into the simple statement that Sherman was important because she criticized images of women. Respini notes that Untitled Film Stills has attracted several readings that sometimes pull against one another: postmodernism, feminism, psychoanalytic accounts of the male gaze, and the culture of spectacle*14. Craig Owens read Sherman's figures as models of femininity produced by media, while Mulvey emphasized the way gaze and framing draw the viewer into a voyeuristic structure*14. At the same time, the response to the Centerfolds shows that the danger of reactivating the desire being criticized became part of the work's reception early on*9. Sherman's photographs do not simply reject stereotypes from outside. They allow viewers to be attracted, to invent stories, and at times to enter the position of an aggressive gaze; because of that, admiration and unease have remained intertwined. Her work has therefore been received as something that passes through the image of femininity and destabilizes it from within, rather than merely denying it. The Broad's entry for Untitled #122 , from a 1983 fashion series, explains that the work registers 1980s high fashion, the dramatization of Hollywood fame, and the pathologizing of powerful female behavior at once*13. In such works, Sherman uses clothing and makeup not to make a figure beautiful, but to expose the class, desire, fear, age, and aggression that society reads into a woman's appearance. Institutional reception has also not reduced this complexity to the success story of a photographer. MoMA acquired the complete Untitled Film Stills in 1995, exhibited the entire series in 1997, and in its 2012 retrospective presented more than 170 works across artifice and fiction, cinema and performance, horror and the grotesque, and identities of gender and class*10. The Broad's 2016 exhibition, drawing on a collection of 127 Sherman works, situated her practice around personas shaped by cinema, advertising, media, and celebrity culture*7. The National Portrait Gallery's 2019 retrospective presented around 150 works and emphasized how Sherman uses sources from film, advertising, and fashion, together with the manipulation of her own appearance, to explore the tension between appearance and identity*17. As Studio International's review suggests, one strength of her photographs is that they leave room for viewers to construct a character's background or story rather than receiving an explained answer*21. This reception goes beyond the general claim that Sherman is an important artist. Her photographs touch questions that art after the 1970s repeatedly returned to: where is originality located if existing images are reused; how do gender, class, and age become readable as appearance; and is the viewer ever a neutral observer? In an era when photography's evidentiary promise was weakening and television, film, magazines, and advertising were shaping everyday gestures and desires, Sherman photographed less the fact that "someone is there" than the mechanism by which someone comes to look like a particular kind of person. In that sense, she expanded photography from the record of a person into an apparatus of representation that also includes the viewer's memory, desire, and media experience.

sherrie-levine.html.lead_html: Sherrie Levine is known for After Walker Evans and After Edward Weston, in which she rephotographed works by Walker Evans and Edward Weston from exhibition catalogs and exhibited them as gelatin silver prints under her own name. She left the existing images almost unchanged to show how the same image becomes a catalog illustration, an artist’s work, a saleable print, and a museum object. A single act of rephotography brought the reproducibility of photography into conflict with a history of modern photography organized around male masters.
sherrie-levine.html.thesis_html: Levine photographed Evans images printed in an exhibition catalog, made new negatives and prints, and exhibited them as her own under the title After Walker Evans. The image remained nearly unchanged while acquiring a Levine title, signature, sales record, and collection history. The work therefore shows that appearance alone does not establish a photographic original: its status depends on the history of who made, signed, and circulated the negative and print. By placing a woman’s authorial name over a male master’s work, After Walker Evans used the copy itself to ask who is recognized as an inheritor of modern photography.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
The 1970s: Distrust of the Avant-Garde Demand for Original Style

Levine studied painting and printmaking at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. After moving to New York, she made collages from magazine advertisements and found images. In 1977 she took part in Pictures, organized by Douglas Crimp at Artists Space*1. During the same period, Conceptual art challenged assumptions about the artist’s hand and the unique art object, while artists began using existing images from film, television, advertising, and magazines as material*26. The avant-garde ideal of continually renewing an original personal style also came under criticism. Levine’s subject became the authority and desire carried by images already in circulation.

“Where Could a Woman Artist Position Herself?”: Why Levine Used Images by Male Masters

Levine’s doubt about originality grew from her experience that anything she made in art school seemed derivative, and from her recognition that the center of modern art was occupied by male artists and male desire. She later recalled that copying released her from the frustration of trying to demonstrate originality*5. In 1986 she also said that, while the art system as a whole celebrated work expressing male desire, she could not see where a woman artist could position herself*25. Levine therefore did not add a new iconography intended to represent a woman’s point of view. She took up images by male masters whose work she herself valued and remade them under her own name. The same print could retain respect for its precedent and resistance to the history that had transmitted those works under the category of the “master.”

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Why Rephotography? Removing Visible Difference and Changing Attribution

A negative can yield multiple prints, and a photograph can spread through printed reproduction, yet the art system treats an individual print with a signature, provenance, and edition as a unique work. The Hammer Museum describes the After series as questioning the contradiction between reproducible photography and a culture that privileges the singular art object*12. Rephotography allowed Levine to produce another negative and print from a nearly identical image without redrawing its forms as she would in a painted copy. She did not return to Evans’s locations or subjects; she pointed her camera at printed reproductions in an exhibition catalog. The result was a different object with a new negative, paper, dimensions, frame, title, signature, seller, and owner. Photography’s reproducibility was essential because it allowed her to demonstrate materially how the same image becomes a work by another author*25.

After Walker Evans: How a Catalog Reproduction Became a Levine

In After Walker Evans (1981), Levine did not use Walker Evans’s negatives or his own prints. She photographed reproductions printed in an exhibition catalog. The catalog had already translated the original size, paper, and tonal range into a different printed object. Levine rephotographed those reproductions, made new negatives, and installed twenty-two small gelatin silver prints in a solo exhibition*8. The Whitney Museum’s collection record registers After Walker Evans: 4 as a 1981 work by Levine*10. The image remains nearly identical to Evans’s photograph, while the title, author, and collection record are distinct. The series also shows that Evans’s photographs were never neutral windows. He photographed tenant farmers during the Great Depression, turning their lives into canonical works of modern photography. Craig Owens argued that by taking again photographs of “the dispossessed,” Levine made visible how the first act of photography had already appropriated the subject’s life as art*25.

“After”: A Title of Regard, Inheritance, and Belatedness

After can indicate temporal succession, imitation, or work made in the wake of a predecessor. The Centre Pompidou explains that the term acknowledges a debt to a predecessor while also marking the position of an artist working after the major inventions of modern art have already been made*7. Levine keeps the reputations of Evans and Weston inside her titles. The citation does not erase the original, and it does not follow the conventional model of influence that produces a visibly different work. Placing After before the same image holds together attachment to the predecessor, unavoidable belatedness, and the act of taking that authority under her own name.

Respect for and Critique of Male Masters: Levine’s Feminism

Evans, Edward Weston, Edgar Degas, and Marcel Duchamp—the artists Levine rephotographed—have occupied central positions in modern art and photographic history. Once a woman’s name is attached to their work, questions arise about how the same image is read as a woman’s production and how women can enter an existing art history. The Centre Pompidou identifies After Walker Evans as a work that addresses the underrepresentation of women in art history alongside authorship and authenticity*7. This is not a simple substitution of a woman artist for a male master. Levine’s work depends on the fame of those masters, and her own authorial name becomes a new authority that guarantees the copy as an artwork. As AWARE’s account of the contemporary debate explains, the method was praised as a sophisticated critique of male-centered modern art and criticized for repeating the forms and authority it targeted*25. Because that dependence remains inside the work, the critique does not resolve into a clean transfer of authority.

Existing Photographs as Subjects: A Double Distance from People and Bodies

Levine did not point her camera directly at tenant farmers, nudes, women, or nature. She photographed images in which Evans, Weston, advertising, and art-historical reproductions had already rendered them as “poverty,” the “ideal body,” or “nature.” Discussing the later After Edward Curtis, the Hammer Museum describes a project that revisits the aims and biases of photographers and recorders, and asks whether a photograph can convey the complete truth about its subject*12. The photograph appears here as the result of selecting a subject, taking and printing an image, then assigning it a title and an author’s name. It cannot function as a direct window onto the world. Rephotography made the photographer’s viewpoint before the subject, and the circulation history of the reproduction, into the work’s subject.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
After Edward Weston: Reusing a Photograph That Turned the Artist’s Son into Abstract Form

In After Edward Weston, Levine rephotographed a reproduction of Weston’s Six Nudes of Neil, 1925*27. Fotomuseum Winterthur holds Levine’s work as a 1981 gelatin silver print*11. In the original, the nude body of Weston’s son Neil occupies the frame as a form whose contours and sheen recall shells or plants. Leaving the image nearly unchanged, Levine re-presented under her own name both Weston’s transformation of a family member’s body into abstract form and the history through which the photograph became a canonical modernist work. The work asks about ownership of the body and about how a photograph of an intimate nude came to be sanctioned as a master’s universal “form.”

After Edgar Degas: Adding Generations of Reproduction Between Photograph and Print

The 1987 work Untitled, from After Edgar Degas is a set of five photolithographs based on a reproduction of a work by Degas*15. The original first becomes a printed reproduction; that reproduction is photographed and then printed again as a lithograph. Each passage changes the paper, density, dimensions, and owner, while the form recognized as a “Degas image” persists. By adding stages of reproduction, Levine separates the possible bases of originality: material identity, repeated contour, and the artist’s name.

From Photography to Bronze and Glass: Testing the Value of the Original Through Material

From the late 1980s onward, Levine expanded into painting, wood, glass, and bronze. In Melt Down, she extracted average colors from paintings by Kirchner, Mondrian, Monet, and others, transforming them into fields of color in which the original compositions could no longer be identified*14. Fountain (Madonna) remade Duchamp’s industrial urinal as a polished bronze sculpture*8. In Newborn, she remade a Brancusi sculpture in clear crystal*16. The photographs examine how an existing image becomes another author’s work; the sculptures examine how an existing form is treated as a new original through material, fabrication, and the display plinth. Across media, the work addresses a system in which value is determined by who fabricates, signs, and exhibits a form, and in what material. Chronological priority is only one part of that system.

Mayhem: Photography, Sculpture, and Painting Across Periods

The Whitney Museum’s 2011–12 exhibition Sherrie Levine: Mayhem brought After Walker Evans, bronze and glass sculptures, and abstract paintings from different periods and media into the same exhibition*17. The accompanying guide explained the sources and production methods of works across photography, sculpture, and painting*8. Placing the early rephotographs beside later sculptures reveals the consistency of Levine’s operations: the form of an existing work is retained while the author’s name, material, fabrication process, and method of display change. The Whitney’s audio introduction likewise explains that Levine takes forms from art history and brings back into the work information usually treated as external to the image, including the artist’s gender and the material*18.

sections.title: Criticism and Place in Photo History
sections.body_html:
How After Walker Evans Separated the “Photographer” from the “Author”

Before After Walker Evans, Duchamp’s readymades, Pop art, and Conceptual art had already made existing objects and images into art. Levine’s distinct intervention was to reproduce canonical photographs with almost no change to their content or photographic technique, materializing under another author’s name the process by which a reproducible image becomes institutionalized as the rare “original” of a male master. The Met situates Levine within the Pictures Generation’s reuse of found imagery to analyze desires and social roles produced by mass media, describing her as photographing from behind the “fathers” of photographic history*26. Her work brought to the center of 1980s photography and contemporary art the possibility that photographic authorship could consist of selecting, remaking, titling, and exhibiting existing images, as well as choosing a subject and operating a camera.

The Paradox of the Copy as a Rare Art Object

Whether Levine’s rephotography dismantled the authority of the original became a subject of debate early on. After Walker Evans and After Edward Weston were made as gelatin silver prints and treated by museums and the market as works by Levine*10. A review in Frieze noted that the copy might create a new aura and price for Levine’s own work instead of erasing aura*20. The contradiction belongs to the work itself. Levine’s photographs reenact the mechanisms—signature, edition, provenance, and museum collection—that make a reproducible image singular. Her work cannot stand outside the art system; critique and commodification proceed together.

The Limits of Critique That Depends on Art-Historical Knowledge

Without knowledge of Evans or Weston, the images in the After series may appear to be straightforward reproductions of classic photographs. AWARE notes that understanding Levine’s feminism and critical argument requires knowledge of early twentieth-century photographic history, the source images, and the method of rephotography, and that the work has been criticized as not universally legible and as dependent on specialized codes*25. Martha Rosler warned that repeating an oppressive form could also repeat its oppression, while Abigail Solomon-Godeau argued that the reach of the critique was limited to the art world*25. The knowledge demanded by the work shows how the history of male masters is shared through education and museums, while potentially excluding viewers without access to that education.

Levine’s Place: Defining the Photographic Original as a History, Not an Image

In Levine’s photographs, the same image accumulates multiple material and institutional histories. Evans’s negative, the prints made from it, a printed reproduction in an exhibition catalog, Levine’s rephotography negative, her gelatin silver print, its gallery sale, and its museum accession are not the same work despite their visual similarity. The Whitney Museum connects this project to a present in which the copying and circulation of digital images have become ordinary*6. Levine showed that the status of a photograph as an original includes more than the chronological order of images; it includes the history of who made, signed, owned, and exhibited the negative and print. Placing a nearly identical image under two artists’ names offers a concrete point of comparison for authorship and ownership in reenactment, citation, and digital reproduction.

shigene-kanamaru.html.lead_html: Shigene Kanamaru shaped the institutional foundations of Japanese modernist photography through commercial practice, education, and criticism rather than primarily through individual image-making. His role in transplanting European New Photography into Japan and codifying advertising photography through teaching defines his distinct place in photographic history.
shigene-kanamaru.html.thesis_html: By systematically organizing and introducing European New Photography (Neue Sachlichkeit and Bauhaus-inflected vision) and connecting it to advertising photography practice through his studio Kinreisha, Kanamaru linked the institutional foundations of advertising photography and photographic education in Japan through his 1932 book "How to Make New Photography" and his central role in founding the photography department at Nihon University. As the founding president of the Advertising Photographers Association of Japan, he shaped the professional body of postwar commercial photographers, leaving an influence that extended through reception, translation, and education rather than through individual works.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Shigene Kanamaru was born in 1900. From the late 1920s he was involved in shaping the institutional foundations of Japanese photographic culture as photographer, critic, and educator, introducing European New Photography — including Neue Sachlichkeit and Bauhaus-inflected vision — into Japan*1. In 1932 he published Shinkō shashin no tsukurikata (How to Make New Photography), a technical and theoretical text that functioned as a manual for practitioners of New Photography in Japan*4. The work is held by the British Museum as a photographically significant publication*13. Through his commercial photography studio Kinrinsha he practiced advertising and publicity photography and covered the 1936 Berlin Olympics*5. He was involved in establishing the photography department at Nihon University College of Art, playing a central role in institutionalizing photographic education*2. In 1958 he became the first president of the Japan Advertising Photographers' Association (APA), leading the establishment of a postwar professional organization for advertising photographers*10. He died in 1977.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Reception and theorization of European New Photography

Kanamaru's significance in photographic history lies less in individual masterworks than in his systematic reception and theorization of European New Photography. Toriumi Saki's doctoral dissertation at Nihon University provides detailed scholarly argumentation for Kanamaru's central role in New Photography practice and early photographic education*2. The 2017 memorial retrospective at Nihon University College of Art Photography Department, organized forty years after his death, presented the full range of his practice including advertising photography, snapshots, Berlin Olympics coverage, wartime publicity photography, and previously unpublished materials*5. The Tokyo Art Beat English exhibition text introduces Kanamaru as "the founder of the photography department at Nihon University, pioneer of advertising photography, and leader of New Photography" — concentrating three roles in a single figure*6.

Commercial photography, advertising, and Kinrinsha

Kanamaru's commercial practice was based at the Kinrinsha studio. The Bijutsu Techō article organizes his achievement around the three axes of Kinrinsha, reception of European New Photography, and photographic education at Nihon University, demonstrating how commercial and educational roles combined in his practice*7. The TCDC Library bibliographic resource references the Kanamaru Shigene Archive / Nihon University Collection in the context of 1930s Japanese publicity and modernism, providing a complementary angle on advertising photography, propaganda, and modern design history*14. The KAKEN research grant "A Research on Shigene Kanamaru as a Pioneer of Advertising Photography in Japan" connects him to design history and extends his significance beyond art photography*9.

Photographic education and postwar institutional connections

The Artscape exhibition review by Iizawa Kōtarō documents the characteristic pattern of Kanamaru's reception — considerable influence during his lifetime followed by long postwar neglect — and discusses the scale of his 1920s–40s influence critically*8. The British Museum's holdings of both an artist authority record and a copy of Shinkō shashin no tsukurikata confirm that Kanamaru is referenced in overseas art and photography research institutions*12. The SFMOMA essay "Exhibiting 'The End of Modern Photography'" identifies Kanamaru's involvement in the "subjective/objective" classification framework used in 1970s Japanese photography exhibitions, extending the scope of his influence from prewar New Photography into postwar institutional criticism*11.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Reappraisal as institution-builder

Kanamaru's position in photographic history is defined more by his contribution to institution-building than by critical evaluation of individual works. As the Artscape review notes, he was widely recognized during his lifetime as a leading practitioner of Japanese advertising and New Photography, but was largely overlooked after his death; the 2017 retrospective marked the first systematic retrospective evaluation*8. The Kokusho Kankōkai monograph received the Japan Society for Photographic Arts Academic Award, confirming the scholarly importance of Kanamaru research*1. The SFMOMA essay demonstrates the continuity of Kanamaru's role into postwar photographic criticism and exhibition practice*11. The Mutual Images Journal article "Photography magazines and cross-cultural encounters in postwar Japan" positions Kanamaru as a continuing mediator of photographic language formation — not only a prewar New Photography practitioner but a bridge between prewar and postwar reception of foreign photography*15.

shinzo-fukuhara.html.lead_html: First president of Shiseido who, while shaping corporate culture, established the photographic institution of Japan through founding the Sha-shin Geijutsu-sha and Shiseido Gallery. He supported modern Japanese photography from both institution-building and expressive practice.
shinzo-fukuhara.html.thesis_html: Beyond making his own art photographs, Fukuhara — through founding the Shashin Geijutsu-sha and establishing the Shiseido Gallery — built institutional spaces in Japan where photography could be received as art. Engaging from both expression and institution, his activity prepared the ground for Japanese modern photography to circulate as fine art.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Shinzo Fukuhara was born in Tokyo in 1883, studied in Europe and America as the son of Shiseido's founder, and took over the management of Shiseido after his father. *1 During his time abroad he deepened his interest in the relationship between photography and art, and after returning to Japan he pursued management and photographic/cultural activity in parallel. *2 In 1921 he organised the Sha-shin Geijutsu-sha (Photographic Art Society) with the purpose of promoting and researching photographic art, working to build the institutional basis for positioning photography as a modern artistic culture. *3

In 1919 he established the Shiseido Gallery, which, while a commercial enterprise space, functioned as a cultural space connecting art, design, photography and advertising. *4 In 1923 he published "Light and Its Tone," an important photographic theory text setting out an aesthetic theory of photography based on light and tone. The Grey Art Museum (NYU) materials provide an important point of reference organising these activities. *5 He died in 1948. *6

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
As an institution builder

To think about Fukuhara's expression, it is necessary to address both the soft tonal quality of his photographic works and his role as an institution builder simultaneously. *7 Drawing on his time in Europe and America and the corporate culture of Shiseido, he worked to elevate photography from mere documentation or hobby to a medium bearing modern aesthetic values. The art photography he envisioned was not limited to imitation of pictorialism but a conception of comprehensive visual culture encompassing light, tone, printing, exhibition space and magazine culture. An exhibition marking the Shiseido Gallery's centenary reconsidered Fukuhara as an artist of social creation beyond corporate management. *8

Fukuhara's importance lies not only in the individual works he made but in the fact that he built the institutions through which photography could be received. The Shiseido Gallery, while a commercial enterprise space, functioned as a cultural apparatus for modern Japan connecting art, design, photography and advertising. The activities of the Sha-shin Geijutsu-sha and his theoretical writings also connect to the environment in which Yasuzo Nojima, Iwata Nakayama and Nakaji Yasui worked. *9

The aesthetics of light and "Light and Its Tone"

"Light and Its Tone," published in 1923, is a text exploring theoretically the relationship between light and tone in photography and occupies an important position in the formation of Japanese photographic theory. *10 The soft light and gentle tones in Fukuhara's works can be read not as mere personal preference but as an aesthetic produced between modern urban consumer culture and art photography. The Shiseido press release PDF can be consulted as materials organising the relationship between this theory and his works. *11

Art Platform Japan's Fukuhara Shinzo page functions as a database for confirming his position in Japan's art institutions. *12 ToMuCo (the Tokyo National Museum of Modern Art collection-linked database) also registers related works by Fukuhara. *13

Shiseido Gallery and the connection of corporate culture

The establishment of the Shiseido Gallery represents a uniquely modern Japanese model of a commercial corporation creating cultural space. *14 The connection between the business of cosmetics and fragrance and the values of light, beauty and art both shaped Shiseido's brand identity and created a cultural base in which commerce and art coexisted within modern Japanese visual culture. The bibliographic reference route via French-language sources on the Société photographique japonaise indicates the international referenceability of Japanese modern photography. *15

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Shiseido Gallery exhibitions and research materials remain the main venue for the re-evaluation of Fukuhara Shinzo. *16 CiNii Research holds numerous research articles. *17 NDL Search holds extensive related bibliographic materials. *18 Fragmentary material references are also possible at the British Museum and ICP Library. *19 The Art Platform Japan database allows his position in Japan's art institutions to be confirmed. Within photographic history, the distinctive character of his contribution becomes visible when institution-building — the creation of the very spaces that support photographic culture — is treated as a critical achievement alongside the evaluation of individual works. *20 The fact that Fukuhara worked simultaneously through the multiple channels of a corporation, a gallery, publishing and photographic theory makes his case an important reference point in the institutional history of modern Japanese culture for thinking about the relationship between individuals and organisations.

shirana-shahbazi.html.lead_html: Shirana Shahbazi is an Iranian-born, Zurich-based photographer whose work has expanded from the everyday scenes of Tehran in Goftare Nik / Good Words to portraiture, still life, landscape, and geometric abstraction. She translates analog photographs into signboard paintings, carpets, lithographs, wallpaper, and more recently 16mm film, continually recomposing images through photobooks and exhibition space.
shirana-shahbazi.html.thesis_html: Shahbazi grew up in a highly politicized environment and initially wanted to become a photojournalist. Migration and photographic education led her to question the assumption that a single photograph can simply represent an external reality. She kept documentary photography in play while testing that assumption from within the medium. Images made in Tehran were translated into signboard paintings and carpets; later, she photographed painted three-dimensional constructions with analog cameras to produce abstract images.She made post-shoot reproduction and display part of the work by placing these translated images and abstract photographs alongside documentary pictures. The production process itself demonstrates that a photograph is not determined solely by what it depicts.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
From Photojournalism — Can a Single Photograph Represent Reality?

Shahbazi was born in Tehran in 1974, moved with her family to Germany in the 1980s, and studied photography in Dortmund and Zurich. Fondation Vincent van Gogh Arles describes her work as moving across classifications while drawing on art-historical genres such as still life, portraiture, and landscape*24 Mirabaud similarly describes a body of work in which photographs made across different regions resist becoming simple representations of a nation or period*25 In a 2023 interview, Shahbazi explained that growing up in a politicized family and social environment initially led her toward photojournalism, but that migration to Germany and photographic education made her increasingly aware of contradictions in the relationship between a photograph and external reality*26 In the same interview, she said migration made belonging to a single place less self-evident and heightened her awareness of the ways viewpoint, language, and translation shape meaning*26Her move away from photojournalism was therefore not a retreat from reality into abstraction. She retained photography’s capacity to convey the world while making the viewpoint from which an image is produced, and the language or culture within which it is read, part of the work’s problem.

Goftare Nik / Good Words — Everyday Photographs beyond an Exoticized Iran

The early major work Goftare Nik / Good Words is a color series of streets, people, landscapes, and everyday scenes in Tehran. In 2002, The Guardian noted how its accumulation of ordinary fragments countered the simplified image of Iran produced by news and tourist imagery*10 Coverage of the Citibank Photography Prize that same year likewise emphasized the work’s documentary clarity alongside its refusal to reduce a nation or culture to a single narrative*11 The Museum of Contemporary Photography describes the series as an examination of how culture, religion, and identity in contemporary Iran are produced through images, and notes that its mixture of incidental scenes and staged photographs disrupts a simple East/West binary*27The aim is not to correct an external stereotype with one photograph of the “real Iran.” The work instead shows the process by which individual images align with, or depart from, expectations already held by viewers outside the country.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Analog Abstraction — Photographing Three-Dimensional Constructions to Make Nonfigurative Images

Shahbazi’s geometric color works can appear digitally generated, but they are made by arranging painted three-dimensional objects in the studio and photographing them with analog cameras, sometimes through multiple exposures. MoMA’s page for Composition-30-2011 confirms that forms which appear to be flat fields of color originate in photographed objects*4 Composition-40-2011 uses the same method, producing abstract fields of color from objects and light placed before the camera*5 An Untitled work in MoMA’s collection provides another example of the abstract photographs from this period*8The abstract forms could have been produced through painting or computer graphics, yet Shahbazi routes them through physical objects, light, lens, and film. She does not discard the link between photography and reality that had troubled her in photojournalism. Instead, she stretches that link toward nonfiguration by changing what is placed in front of the camera and how many exposures are made. MoMA’s New Photography 2012 similarly describes these works as photographs made through assembly and in-camera manipulation*2 MoMA’s artist page lists Composition-40-2011, Klausen Pass-03-2011, Untitled, and other works together, making abstraction, landscape, and still life visible as parts of the same photographic practice*9.

Placing Still Life, Landscape, and Abstraction Side by Side

In MoMA’s New Photography 2012, Shahbazi combined still lifes, landscapes, abstractions, and wallpaper-scale images within the same exhibition space*1 MoMA Inside/Out describes an installation in which photographs from different genres are placed next to one another so that repetitions of color, shape, and scale become as prominent as differences in subject matter*6 MoMA’s audio guide likewise explains how photographs of abstract studio constructions, black-and-white photographs made outdoors, and wallpaper were combined into a single installation*7This approach to display did not begin suddenly with the Hammer Museum in 2008, but that project made one of its operations especially clear: an Iranian sign painter translated one of Shahbazi’s new Los Angeles photographs into a wall-size painting, placing the photograph and its transformation into another medium within the same architectural space*3 The Hammer’s residency record confirms that making the new photographs and collaborating with the artisan were part of the residency itself*14 A public lecture was also organized for Shahbazi to discuss the production of the work*13When the colors of a flower photograph continue into a neighboring geometric image, the flower can no longer be read only as a still life, while the abstract photograph can be reconsidered as an image of physical objects. Shahbazi uses post-shoot arrangement and translation into other media to prevent the subject of any single photograph from fixing the meaning of the work.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Then Again — Holding Authenticity, Construction, and Selection Together

In the book and exhibition Then Again, photographs from different periods and genres are reedited across the boundaries of their original series. Galerie Peter Kilchmann’s publication information identifies this reediting as a defining feature of the project*19 Galerie Rudolfinum likewise centered the exhibition on the way photographic authenticity, construction, and selection operate together rather than excluding one another*20Street photographs and studio constructions are both recombined after the fact with works from other years. The fact of how an image was made is therefore not enough to determine the meaning of the series; what it is later placed beside becomes part of the production process as well.

Group Show — Rebuilding the Exhibition Each Time

In Group Show, an exhibition devoted to a single artist is installed as though different bodies of photographs belonged to a group exhibition. Camera Austria documents large color and black-and-white works, abstractions, and representational photographs creating a strong rhythm across the walls, with the arrangement of the room taking precedence over continuity within any one series*15 The institution’s press material similarly describes the exhibition as creating relationships through wall color, scale, and sequence rather than fixing photographs to a single meaning*17The same photograph may have different neighbors and a different scale in another exhibition. In Group Show, the images actually placed beside one another and their sizes determine how the work is encountered as much as the name of any series.

First Things First — Editing by Visual Affinity Rather than Chronology

First Things First is not a photobook that preserves years of work in chronological order or by series. Sternberg Press describes it as a publication in which still lifes, portraits, landscapes, and abstractions are arranged without being separated by series*12 The MIT Press record likewise notes that works from different periods are reedited through changes of scale and sequence*21As the pages turn, colors, contours, and recurring motifs link photographs from different moments before continuity within a single series takes hold. The operation Shahbazi uses in exhibitions—placing different photographic genres beside one another—is translated in the book into the relation between one page and the next.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Why Analog? — Delaying Results and Limiting Options

In an interview with Mutina, Shahbazi gives concrete reasons for using analog cameras: because the result cannot be checked immediately, she looks more carefully while photographing; fewer parameters can be manipulated in printing than in a digital workflow; and selections are made from contact sheets*16 In a 2023 interview, she again avoids treating analog as an absolute value, describing it as a way to create time for thought and experimentation while noting that she also uses digital images in lithography*26For Shahbazi, the value of analog photography lies in these working conditions: no immediate review during exposure, a restricted range of corrections, and selection from contact sheets. Avoiding an environment of virtually unlimited adjustment concentrates attention on observation at the moment of photographing and on a finite set of later interventions.

The Curve — Refusing the Divides of Iran/West and Document/Construction

Reality Show likewise placed photographs of existing subjects alongside constructed still lifes and abstractions, preventing the work from being organized simply according to whether or not it records an external reality*22 Writing on The Curve, Adair Rounthwaite argues that documentary photography, Northern European still-life painting, and religious murals in Tehran enter the same body of work, making it impossible to contain the photographs neatly within either “Western art history” or “contemporary Iranian art”*28That is more precise than simply calling the work multicultural. Shahbazi returns images made in Iran to Iranian sign-painting techniques, combines them with photographic forms learned in Europe, and places them in exhibitions alongside abstract studio photographs. Because Iranian sign painting, European photographic conventions, and studio abstraction occupy the same installations, no single cultural sphere can adequately organize the work. A 2017 retrospective at KINDL brought together about sixty works, showing black-and-white landscapes, still lifes, geometric abstractions, and documentary photographs without reducing them to chronology or one consistent style*18 Galerie Peter Kilchmann’s artist page also records holdings at institutions including MoMA, Tate Modern, and Centre Pompidou, as well as an exhibition and photographic practice continuing into recent years*23.

shoji-ueda.html.lead_html: Shoji Ueda staged everyday scenes on the sand dunes of Tottori, presenting family members and acquaintances as figures within carefully arranged compositions. His style, known as Ueda-chō, opened a distinct lineage within Japanese photographic modernism by treating ordinary life as theatrical arrangement rather than documentary record.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Shoji Ueda was born in March 1913 in Sakaiminato, Tottori Prefecture. In 1930 he moved to Tokyo to study at the Oriental School of Photography, graduating in 1932 and returning to his hometown*6. Starting from the realist regional photography of his mentor Shiotani Teiko, he developed an original staged method through study of Man Ray, André Kertész, and Jacques-Henri Lartigue*6. In 1937 he co-founded the Chugoku Photographers Group with local photographers, forming a nucleus of modernist photography practice in the San'in region*19.

During World War II he suspended his activities to avoid military photography assignments, resuming his staged work on the Tottori sand dunes after the war ended in 1945*6. In 1947 he joined Ginryusha, a Tokyo-based photographers' collective, building connections with avant-garde practitioners in the capital*19. His family series, including Papa and Mama and Children (1949), established the visual idiom known as Ueda-chō*3. He won the Nika Prize in 1954*19, and in 1958 Edward Steichen selected his work for an exhibition at MoMA, opening the way for international recognition*19. MoMA's holding of the gelatin silver print Snow Surface can be confirmed in the collection*4. From 1974 he contributed the "A Piece of Life" series to Camera Mainichi magazine, and from 1975 to 1994 he taught photography at Kyushu Sangyo University*19. He participated in the Rencontres d'Arles in 1978 and again in 1987, and in the Photokina exhibition in Germany in 1982*19. The Shoji Ueda Museum of Photography (Hōki-chō, Tottori) opened in 1995 holding approximately 12,000 works*7. In 1996 the French government awarded him the Chevalier des Arts et des Lettres*19. He died in July 2000.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Formation of the staged method and stylistic influences

Ueda's style draws from multiple sources. Where his mentor Shiotani Teiko documented the nature and rural life of San'in in a realist mode, Ueda absorbed Man Ray's surrealist manipulation and André Kertész's poetic construction, recasting them into a visual logic of staging*6. Composition (1937), documented on Art Platform Japan, is an early work showing that formalist experimentation preceded the sand dune and family series*14. The Tokyo Metropolitan Museum of Photography's 2013 exhibition "Ueda and Lartigue" juxtaposed Ueda with Jacques-Henri Lartigue under the shared axis of "the essential joy of amateur photography," showing how both photographers treated photography as play*16.

Theatricality of sand dunes and family

Ueda's characteristic method is to arrange family members and acquaintances in expansive, flat spaces such as sand dunes and build compositions that combine frontality, sparse spacing, and precise placement to create a coexistence of quiet absurdity and poetic feeling*1. Four Girls, Four Positions (1939) in the MOMAT collection shows the early staged method that preceded the family series and retains traces of formal experimentation before the mature style converged*2. Papa and Mama and Children (1949) is the canonical example of Ueda-chō — a family seen from behind on the sand dunes — and the MOMAT curator's text discusses it as a combination of modernist composition and the subject matter of family and everyday life*15. The Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art holds Boku to Neko (The Cat and Me, ca. 1950) and My Wife on the Dunes (ca. 1950), showing the variety of Ueda's staged approach during this period*6. SFMOMA also holds works by Ueda, confirming his presence in American museum collections*5.

Locality and the freedom of amateur photography

The fact that Ueda's photographic modernism was based in Tottori rather than Tokyo is an important supplementary lineage in Japanese photographic history. Ueda-chō is not merely a stylistic label but a marker that locality, non-professionalism, and proximity to family made that style possible. The Tottori sand dunes functioned as a fixed stage, and the accumulation and variation of compositions arising from repeated visits to the same site was a condition difficult to replicate in a commercial urban studio. The Fujifilm Square exhibition text documents connections to late works and photobooks, recording that the Ueda-chō idiom was maintained into his final years*8. The Shoji Ueda Museum of Photography, designed by Shin Takamatsu Architects, was conceived as "a facility for the permanent preservation and exhibition of a single photographer," reflecting the relationship between the works and their exhibition space from an architectural perspective*17.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Ueda-chō and its place in Japanese photographic modernism

Ueda's reception has been consistently strong at home and abroad, and since the 1995 museum opening systematic reappraisal has placed him in a distinct lineage separate from Ken Domon's realism and Kimura Ihei's snapshot work. MOMAT holds a wide range of works spanning his career and stages continuous exhibitions*2. The SFMOMA essay "Distant Relations: Japanese Photography in American Exhibitions in the 1970s" analyzes Japanese photography's reception in 1970s American exhibitions and documents Ueda's participation in the ICP exhibition Japan: A Self-Portrait (New York, April 27–June 3, 1979)*12. The large-scale 141-work retrospective at Three Shadows Photography Art Centre in China demonstrates reception extending beyond Japan and the West*18.

International recognition and after Arles

His participation in the Rencontres d'Arles in 1978 was the first occasion on which Ueda's work was assessed seriously within the context of European photography criticism*19. His presence continued throughout the 1980s with the Photokina exhibition in Germany (1982) and a second invitation to Arles (1987)*19. The French government's award of the Chevalier des Arts et des Lettres in 1996 represented institutional recognition that the Ueda-chō aesthetic had been evaluated within French art and cultural criticism beyond the frame of Japanese photography*19. Holdings at MoMA, SFMOMA, the Getty, and the Smithsonian confirm Ueda's standing as the internationally recognized representative of Japanese staged photography*13.

simon-norfolk.html.lead_html: Through For Most of It I Have No Words, Afghanistan: Chronotopia, and Burke + Norfolk, Simon Norfolk shifts war photography away from the instant of gunfire or bodily injury toward landscapes marked by ruins, communications facilities, missile test sites, archaeological remains, and imperial logistics. Using the detail of large-format color photography and the beauty of history painting, he treats land as evidence in which successive wars accumulate. His work reconsiders what war photography has overlooked through the form of landscape.
simon-norfolk.html.thesis_html: War photography contains several histories: Roger Fenton’s unpeopled battlefields, the human-centered photojournalism of the twentieth century, and the “slow photography” of damaged places that developed toward the century’s end. Norfolk brings these histories together and incorporates ruins, communications bases, weapons research facilities, border infrastructure, photographs from the age of empire, and glaciers into the same extended idea of the “battlefield.” His subject includes the technologies that plan violence before combat, images that repeat earlier conquests, and institutions that remain embedded in the land after war has formally ended. Through the precision of landscape photography and the sequence of the photobook, he made a representative contemporary method of reading war as a long-running system of empire, information, logistics, and environment rather than an event confined to one place.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Leaving Photojournalism and Extending the Meaning of “Battlefield”

Simon Norfolk was born in Lagos, Nigeria, and educated in Britain. Early in his career he worked within reportage and documentary photography on the far right, refugees, and war. He gradually came to feel that the structures of conflict had to be addressed across longer periods than the immediate news cycle allows. In his official CV, Norfolk describes more than two decades of work as an effort to probe and stretch the meaning of the word “battlefield” in all its forms*1. His subjects extend from war zones and refugee crises to supercomputers used in weapons design, nuclear missile tests, border facilities, and communications bases.

This shift took place during the 1990s, when conflicts in the Gulf, the former Yugoslavia, Rwanda, and Afghanistan circulated globally through satellite television and digital communication, increasing the apparent visibility of war. At the same time, military-supplied footage, embedded reporting, and images from remote weapons revealed the vast systems behind visible combat. Norfolk turned toward landscape in order to bring the military institutions and infrastructures that produce human suffering into the photograph. World Press Photo describes him as a landscape photographer who works across war zones and military technologies*2.

History Painting, Nineteenth-Century War Photography, and the Contemporary Aftermath

Photography of places after battle has a long history. The long exposures and cumbersome equipment used by Roger Fenton during the Crimean War led him to photograph roads, positions, cannonballs, and arranged soldiers more often than combat itself. John Burke, a nineteenth-century colonial photographer, accompanied the Second Anglo-Afghan War and recorded battlefields, cities, people, and ruins on glass plates. Norfolk rereads these precedents as a way of seeing present conflict in historical layers. The official introduction to Burke + Norfolk explains how the 2010 project began from Burke’s photographs and rephotographed contemporary Afghanistan*3.

Aftermath photography can aestheticize violence when it renders the traces of catastrophe as quiet landscapes. Norfolk deliberately uses the authority and duration of beautiful landscape photography while accepting this risk within the work. In an interview with BLDGBLOG, he acknowledges the attraction of damaged places and military sites as a form of the “military sublime,” arguing that their beauty can contain both awe before power and criticism of it*4. Securing enough attention for viewers to remain with the image and read its details becomes a condition for thinking about distant wars as long histories.

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Afghanistan: Chronotopia — Reading the Land as a “Museum of the Archaeology of War”

Afghanistan: Chronotopia (2002) was photographed after the 2001 U.S.-led attack and brings the Soviet invasion, civil war, Taliban rule, and American bombing into contact with the remains of ancient civilizations and earlier empires. On the project’s official page, Norfolk compares walking the streets of Afghanistan to moving through a “museum of the archaeology of war,” where different periods of destruction have accumulated*5. “Chronotopia” here names the binding of time and place within one image. A ruined building can retain several histories through cycles of repair, reuse, and renewed destruction.

The resolution of the large-format camera records distant mountains, rubble, bullet marks, roads, signs, and traces of daily life with equal density. The photographs minimize explanatory accounts of “what happened” and ask viewers to read layers. Belfast Exposed presents the series as a landscape in which different moments of war accumulate across the streets of Kabul*6. Halsey Institute likewise describes Norfolk’s connection of archaeological remains and present devastation as a way of addressing long-term suffering suppressed by mainstream media*7. For Norfolk, landscape remains a political document after the event has passed.

Large-Format Color and the Tension of “War Photography That Is Too Beautiful”

Norfolk’s photographs use evening skies, precise perspective, saturated color, and classical composition, often making ruins appear sublime. That beauty can seem disproportionate to the devastation of war. His method sustains the ethical tension within the picture. Military power attracts through monumental architecture, light, technology, and speed, and that attraction helps support state authority. Norfolk retains this appeal in the image so that the allure of military spectacle can itself be examined. The Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation holds his work as a precise color-photographic inquiry into the landscapes of war, empire, and technology*8.

The danger remains that aesthetic distance may push victims outside the frame. For Most of It I Have No Words (1998) photographs sites of twentieth-century genocide, creating a large gap between apparently ordinary landscapes and their histories. The Hyman Collection connects the series to both the return of massacre sites to everyday use and photography’s inability to show past violence directly*9. The title names the limit faced by words and images when they represent catastrophe. Norfolk’s beautiful landscapes make the invisibility of violence part of the subject.

Photographing Military Infrastructure — Expanding War from the Front Line to Networks and Borders

Information, surveillance, research, and weapons testing are crucial to Norfolk’s expansion of the battlefield. In Full Spectrum Dominance, he photographs communications facilities, radar, and space and missile technologies that sustain warfare, shifting the battlefield from the front line to a network. The official project page situates the series within a military doctrine that seeks dominance across land, sea, air, and the information sphere*10. Such facilities organize the geography of violence before remote strikes, explosions, or deaths become visible.

Fantasma en la Ciudad, Nogales, Arizona/Nogales, Sonora, Mexico (2006) pictures the boundary and urban lights separating the paired cities in the United States and Mexico. The Amon Carter Museum publishes the image and collection information, allowing the border landscape to be seen as a contemporary militarized space*11. By extending war from interstate combat to walls, surveillance systems, communications networks, and resource management that sort migrants, Norfolk reexamines the distinction between wartime and peace.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Burke + Norfolk — Photographing the Same Place and Repeating the Same History

Burke + Norfolk (2011) brought photographs made by John Burke during the Second Anglo-Afghan War back to Afghanistan as Norfolk rephotographed the country in the present. Past and contemporary images enter into dialogue, revealing continuities and differences in military intervention, roads, cities, and representations of people. The official introduction records that production began from Burke’s photographs in 2010 and included a workshop and exhibition with Afghan photographers in Kabul*3. Including local photographers gave the project a way to address, from within, the colonial problem of a British photographer once again representing Afghanistan.

LensCulture describes the series as a dialogue in which historical photographs frame the present while new images reconsider an imperial gaze from the past*12. Burke’s wet-plate photographs and Norfolk’s color works differ in technology and period, yet both share large equipment, extended preparation, and an interest in landscape and architecture. Photographing the same places reveals how Afghanistan has repeatedly been pictured by outside powers as a strategic landscape.

How the Photobook Turns Distant Places into a Historical Argument

Norfolk’s work gains force through series and photobooks more than through isolated master images. For Most of It I Have No Words places sites of several genocides in sequence, while Afghanistan: Chronotopia builds historical layers from cities, ruins, military sites, and traces of daily life. His official CV records the books, exhibitions, and awards through which these long-term projects circulated*1. Turning the pages links geographically distant places and transforms individual landscapes into a sustained argument.

Photofusion’s Afghanistan: Chronotopia exhibition presented the photobook and installation as a structure for reading Afghanistan’s long history of destruction*13. On the museum wall, large prints occupy the viewer’s field of vision and create bodily time for searching out small traces. In the book, captions and sequence supply historical relations. Norfolk combines images with text, place names, dates, maps, and earlier photographs, establishing the terms for reading landscape as evidence.

Time Taken — Glacial Time and the Long Duration of War and Climate

In Time Taken, Norfolk photographed Afghanistan’s glaciers and mountain ranges over an extended period, connecting the history of war and climate change on the same temporal axis. Michael Hoppen Gallery presents the glacier as an instrument that records time, linking geological duration far longer than human conflict to present environmental change*14. Here the “battlefield” expands further to include resources, climate, and the vulnerability of states.

The glacier photographs approach diminishing water supplies, agriculture, migration, and conditions for conflict from geological time. Norfolk’s understanding of landscape extends from an archive of past violence to a place where future crisis is taking shape. The official Time Taken page presents the series through photographs, scientific observation, and representations of time*15.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Moving Beyond the Human-Centered War Photograph—and the Cost of Doing So

War photography has conveyed urgency through the bodies of victims, soldiers, and protesters. Norfolk’s move toward landscapes where people are small or absent carries the risk of abstracting individual suffering. A Teesside University review of a symposium on war photography places him within debate about how contemporary images respond to situations in which “nothing can be seen,” including remote warfare, aftermath, and institutional limits*16. His photographs take on a different task from testimony by showing the durations and infrastructures that escape images centered on the body.

Human absence becomes an occasion to examine the limits of landscape photography. Burke + Norfolk crosses earlier colonial photographs with the perspectives of local photographers, while the title For Most of It I Have No Words names photography’s insufficiency. Both signal that landscape images contain the photographer’s position and historical gaze. Tate’s Burke + Norfolk exhibition juxtaposed John Burke’s nineteenth-century photographs with Norfolk’s new work, presenting Afghanistan as a land repeatedly imaged by empires*17.

From Roger Fenton to “Late Photography” — Reading the Absent Battlefield as a System

Fenton’s The Valley of the Shadow of Death shows a road scattered with cannonballs and signals war through the absence of bodies and combat. Since the late twentieth century, “late photography” has developed as an approach that records material traces after an event with quiet, high-resolution images, and a number of photographers have addressed military sites and post-conflict landscapes. An essay in Open Arts Journal discusses Norfolk alongside Angus Boulton, Gilad Ophir, and Roi Kuper within this history of late photography concerned with military landscape and memory*19.

Norfolk’s importance therefore lies in connecting the history of the unpeopled battlefield to contemporary military systems, not in inventing it. He links the quiet of aftermath photography to ancient ruins, colonial photographs, computers, satellites, border control, and climate change, editing apparently separate places into one military system. Works in SFMOMA’s collection range from training by the Afghan police to a BBC relay station on Ascension Island, placing bodies at the front and the communications networks of remote war within the same expanded battlefield*18. The evidentiary claim of photography shifts from being present at the decisive moment toward making visible the conditions that allow war to occur.

Place in Photographic History — Connecting Aftermath, Imperial Photography, and Military Infrastructure

A broad current of “late photography” was already addressing conflict through devastated land, military sites, and surveillance space. Within it, Norfolk moved from traces on the surface of the land toward links among present landscapes, nineteenth-century imperial photographs, military research, communications networks, borders, and future environmental crisis. His distinction lies in turning landscape from a container of memory into evidence of mechanisms through which war is designed, repeated, and deferred.

The beauty of large-format color draws sustained attention to ruins and military sites while retaining the danger of transforming violence into sublime scenery. Norfolk holds this contradiction in place and uses captions, historical materials, rephotography, and collaboration with local photographers to ask whose history a beautiful landscape has been made to tell. His contribution to photographic history is less the invention of a new subject called the “battlefield” than a method for integrating aftermath photography, historical images, military infrastructure, and environmental photography into one long argument. War photography could thereby examine the period before violence becomes visible and the duration after its end is declared, alongside its established role in recording explosions and injured bodies.
