sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Travel, Daido Moriyama, and Geography

Traveling to places and looking closely at the land preceded Matsue’s decision to become a photographer. In an interview published with Hashima, he recalled traveling throughout Japan from about age ten; by the summer he was fourteen, he had visited nearly the entire country and was drawn to old towns, industrial districts, canals, mines, and abandoned mines. His photographs of Hashima in 1983 began when he found an opportunity to reach the island while traveling through Kyushu. Matsue later described Hashima as “a document of a journey.” Moving through unfamiliar places on foot and bringing back what he encountered as photographs was already fundamental to his early work.*31

The immediate impetus to consider photography as a profession came at nineteen, when Matsue was strongly affected by Daido Moriyama’s photobook Light and Shadow. He later showed Moriyama his own photographs and recalled that Moriyama rejected them outright, leaving him with the sense that he had to find something of his own.*1 The encounter forced him to move beyond imitation and ask what his photography could be grounded in. Minoru Shimizu argues that Matsue transformed an interest in the tactile visual quality of Moriyama’s coarse printed images into photographs that compel close inspection of high-resolution detail.*19

At the same time, Matsue studied geography in the Faculty of Science at the University of Tokyo and worked with computer image processing. He had been interested in electronics since childhood and has recalled using mainframe computers in the 1980s to turn Landsat earth-observation data into images, writing his own programs for procedures such as edge enhancement.*1 This gave him experience of the earth’s surface as coordinate-based data converted into an image from which terrain and physical states could be read—a mode of seeing distinct from ordinary scenic vision. Encountering land through travel and reading information about the earth’s surface recorded by machines developed side by side during his early formation as a photographer.

By the mid-1980s Matsue was photographing Hashima, pavement, walls, manhole covers, and other surfaces; TRANSIT was presented in 1987. artscape Japan traces the series back several years before that presentation and situates it within the trajectory from Matsue’s early work to his retrospective.*5 Later exhibition materials identify his experience of walking and photographing the low-shadow streets of Andalusia in 1988 as a turning point from TRANSIT toward gazetteer.*4 Materials for the 2012 Higashikawa Awards state that a 1991 trip to Yemen helped establish his method of recording the earth’s surface precisely and evenly under frontal light.*38 The Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art retrospective likewise organized the development from TRANSIT through gazetteer, CC, and JP around a sustained interest in the earth’s surface and continuing changes in photographic and printing technology.*6

Urban and Landscape Photography in the 1980s

When Matsue began working in the late 1980s, several Japanese photographers were also reconsidering the city and the land as subjects in their own right, separate from their use as famous views or backdrops for personal feeling. Ryuji Miyamoto published Architectural Apocalypse in 1986, photographing buildings in the process of demolition and recording destruction and urban change themselves.*29 Around the same time, Naoya Hatakeyama began photographing limestone quarries in Lime Hills; his later work connected extraction sites, factories, and concrete cities through chains of material movement and production.*30

Matsue likewise photographed cities, extraction sites, roads, and buildings, but his work developed along a different line. Miyamoto connected the disappearance of architecture to urban history, while Hatakeyama traced causal chains from raw material to city. Matsue placed natural terrain, residential districts, and cemeteries under the same photographic conditions, developing a method for recording the earth’s surface before assigning a different narrative to each place. The comparison clarifies how Miyamoto, Hatakeyama, and Matsue chose different units and methods in response to a shared question in Japanese photography from the late 1980s onward: what, exactly, should a city or a landscape be treated as?

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Across Matsue’s statements and work, one question repeatedly emerges: should the content of a photograph be limited to what the photographer judged important at the moment of exposure? Human vision divides a scene into center and background and selects what it wants to see. A lens records pavement, windows, distant figures, and vegetation at the same time, including details the photographer may not have noticed on site. To retain as much of that mechanical record as possible, Matsue tightly controls the horizon, shadows, focus, camera height, and the extent of the frame. He has described enlarging a road photograph and discovering traces of past construction that he had not noticed when taking it; he also describes his method in terms of using the camera as a “machine” as close to the limits of its performance as possible.*1

The Camera’s Record and Human Vision

In the Landsat imagery Matsue handled at university, the earth’s surface was processed as an image from which information about particular locations could be read. Satellite images and Matsue’s photographs are not equivalent, but both involve reading information from an image that exceeds what the naked eye can register at once. Matsue himself has said that human vision does not perceive everything at a site accurately, whereas the lens retains information from the scene.*1

His decisions therefore concentrate on the conditions of recording. Before making the exposure, he determines what light, angle, height, focus, and field of view will preserve a broad range of information across the surface. In another conversation, he described his approach as a straightforward method faithful to the camera’s principles, emphasizing the effort to draw out the machine’s capabilities as fully as possible.*2 His break from imitating Moriyama, his training in geography and image processing, and his insistence on using the camera as a machine each support, from a different direction, a photography that does not rest solely on subjective emphasis.*1

Horizon, Frontal Light, and Shadow

Excluding the horizon and sky and working in clear frontal light helps Matsue limit the eye’s movement toward a distant vanishing point while preserving detail throughout the frame. In a conversation with Midori Matsui at the National Art Center, Tokyo, the reduced scale difference between foreground and distance was linked to treating the image as a single surface, while the chosen light preserves a large quantity of information.*3 The Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art likewise notes that these rules weaken the distinction between center and edge, allowing elements across the image to retain a comparable degree of clarity.*6

Minoru Shimizu analyzes Matsue’s usual format as one that closes off a composition leading the eye “beyond” the horizon and redirects attention from spatial depth to high-resolution information.*32 Flattening does not mean reducing detail. An oblique aerial view that leads the eye into the distance establishes an order from foreground to background; a view from directly overhead can turn variations in elevation into pattern. Matsue typically looks diagonally downward while keeping the surface nearly frontal, retaining relief while making it difficult for any single point to dominate the image.*32 Zoltán Somhegyi similarly links Matsue’s removal of the horizon and minimization of shadows to a flattened treatment of the earth’s surface that does not establish a privileged center or a hierarchy between natural and artificial elements.*24

“Absolute Focus” and High Resolution

This construction required high resolution. Shimizu calls Matsue’s method “absolute focus,” distinguishing it from conventional deep focus, in which the human eye accepts a certain range as sufficiently sharp. He describes it as an optical condition grounded in the principle of a lens focused at infinity rather than in what appears sharp enough to human vision.*32 “Absolute” here is not a judgment of perfection; it marks a refusal to use naked-eye perception as the standard.

Shimizu further argues that a high-resolution image develops a “depth of information”: when one area is enlarged, another image can be extracted from within it.*20 Because roads, windows, distant figures, rock faces, and trees remain legible, differences in density and form persist even when conventional depth and compositional emphasis are reduced. Shimizu’s essay in gazetteerCC likewise identifies this accumulation of high-resolution information, in place of conventional spatial depth, as central to Matsue’s form.*27 High resolution therefore does more than display technical precision. It keeps areas that were not primary subjects at the moment of exposure available for later examination.

This requirement also shaped Matsue’s move into color. He photographed in color earlier, but analog color printing could not preserve the focus and quantity of information he wanted. He began presenting color work in earnest only when digital scanning and printing reached sufficient quality. The commentary for gazetteerCC likewise identifies digital technology as a turning point because it allowed “absolute focus” and an excessive density of information to be sustained in color.*27 For Matsue, digital technology became a means of preserving a recording density he had already been pursuing, rather than a way to introduce a new visual effect.

Place Codes in gazetteer and CC

Gazetteer means a geographical dictionary; CC uses city codes, while JP uses codes for Japanese prefectures. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum identifies the city code attached to each title as a basic organizing principle of CC, a series begun in 2001.*7 The photobook jp0205 likewise organizes aerial views of Aomori and Akita through geographic codes, allowing multiple locations to be compared in sequence.*15

These naming systems do more than turn places into anonymous patterns. They remove descriptive judgments such as “beautiful mountain” or “vast city” from the title while retaining the shooting location as a name or code. Somhegyi notes Matsue’s encyclopedic accumulation of places without establishing hierarchies such as famous versus unknown or natural versus artificial.*24 At high resolution, concrete differences among roads, buildings, vegetation, and terrain remain visible; names and codes connect those differences back to specific locations. The combination of visual information and geographic indexing makes individual places comparable even when the photographic rules remain constant.

A Photographic Design Without a Dominant Subject

Matsue’s images contain few dramatic shadows or central figures, but this does not mean that the photographer makes fewer decisions. Midori Matsui describes his vision as “impersonal”: it avoids a dominant center and accepts details with a relatively even visual force, producing a structure unlike conventional landscape photographs in which one viewing subject integrates foreground, middle distance, and background.*3 Matsue, meanwhile, has spoken about his preference for strong midday light and the pleasure he finds in an abundance of information.*3

For aerial photography he plans the flight path, time, direction of the sun, and altitude; on the ground he also selects viewpoints and light with care.*2 artscape Japan notes that many works in gazetteer and CC were not made from aircraft. Matsue traveled in search of usable elevated positions—hills, cliffs, towers, and tall buildings.*5 The relative invisibility of the author in the finished image is therefore an effect of where judgment is concentrated. Instead of selecting an expressive face or dramatic contrast, Matsue chooses place, time, light, and focus so that detail can remain legible across a broad field.

sections.title: Major Works and Series
sections.body_html:
Hashima / TRANSIT / gazetteer

The photographs Matsue made on Hashima in 1983 precede the evenly structured elevated views for which he later became known. Hashima is a record of roughly twenty-four hours, arranged in near chronological order from the day before he reached the island through his departure. Matsue himself described it as “a document of a journey.”*31 The standardized rules of gazetteer are not yet present, but an early form of his later method can already be seen in the continuous gathering of surfaces while walking through a place.

In TRANSIT, pavement, walls, manhole covers, rubble, and other surfaces appear at a distance close to the body. The Museum of Fine Arts, Houston holds Kumamoto, Japan (1985) as part of this series.*12 Gazetteer later expanded the field to mountains, deserts, forests, and cities around the world, developing into a long-term accumulation of photographs paired with place names. The Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art retrospective gazetteer presented this development as a continuous trajectory from the early work through CC, JP, LIM, moving images, and makieta.*6

CC / JP

CC photographs cities from elevated positions on the ground and related viewpoints, assigning city codes to the titles. JP records Japanese prefectures from low altitude and uses prefectural codes based on ISO 3166-2. SFMOMA holds the 2005 work JP-22 08.*11 SYD 20119 (2012), from CC, is held by the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.*13 For aerial shoots, Matsue plans flight positions, time, direction of sunlight, and altitude in advance, making numerous exposures during a single flight.*2

In the photobook jp0205, each turn of the page shifts between locations in Aomori and Akita. Repetition of the same photographic rules brings differences in terrain, roads, vegetation, and settlements into sequence.*15 JP-34 similarly brings Hiroshima City, Miyajima, Kure, and Etajima into one book, creating a duration of comparison distinct from that of a single large print.*16

JP-01 SPK / JP-34

JP-01 SPK (2014) includes photographs that deliberately exceed rules Matsue had already established. Shimizu first summarizes his usual conditions—clear weather, frontal light, frontal orientation, no horizon, low altitude, and “absolute focus”—then draws attention to the arrival of clouds, oblique light, shadows, diagonal compositions, and views from ground level in this book.*32 Its sixty-four photographs move from forest through quarry and golf course to cemetery, suburb, and city, carrying several kinds of surface from nature to urban space within a single sequence.*32

In the continuation of his essay, Shimizu places the cemetery between nature and city, past and present, and reads the ground-level photographs through the history of Sapporo’s settlement and traces of forgotten people. In the snow scenes and residential views near the end of the book, he argues, distance and far views that Matsue had previously suppressed return, bringing place-specific and generational memory into the work.*33

JP-34 includes Hiroshima City, Miyajima, Kure, and Etajima. Nobuo Kuraishi argues that the distant elevated viewpoint can approach wounds of history still embedded in the contemporary surface from an unexpected distance.*16 The series does not isolate only objects that symbolize the atomic bombing or war. Roads, rivers, housing, and terrain are recorded with the same precision, and that shared treatment is central to the work.

cell / Moving Images / TYO-WTC

cell extracts details of people and objects from within high-resolution photographs even though they were not subjects Matsue consciously selected at the time of exposure. Matsue has explained that he collected information he noticed only after enlarging the photographs into the photobook cell.*1 A small fragment of the original image becomes a new photograph, making the series one of the clearest demonstrations that what the photographer saw at the moment of exposure and what the photograph actually recorded need not coincide.

In the moving-image works he began in 2010, long shots appear almost still while tiny details—a person, bird, or car—move within the frame. Shimizu describes them as “moving photographs” in which digital technology connects the single instant of a photograph to the continuous time of video.*21 In TYO-WTC, Matsue reverses his earlier method of traveling the world to collect surfaces. He repeatedly photographs a limited number of locations in Tokyo and New York over long periods, bringing construction, traffic, and human movement into sequences of urban change.*39 If cell excavates the interior of a single photograph, the moving works and TYO-WTC introduce differences of time into the same place.

LIM / makieta

LIM photographs cemeteries around the world as surfaces containing gravestones, plots, vegetation, and roads. TARO NASU’s exhibition text describes the work as applying the same gaze used for deserts, mountains, and cities to cemeteries, recording surfaces marked by religion and regional culture without isolating the cemetery solely as a symbol of death.*36 Here Matsue’s rules are applied to subjects already charged with meaning: sentiment is not built into the composition in advance, while the details present at the site remain equally precise.

makieta photographs urban and topographic models so that they approach the appearance of actual locations in CC. Matsue has said that he photographed urban models in Quito in 2007 and Tokyo in 2009, developing the series more fully from 2016 onward.*9 The techniques are in fact different: CC records distant subjects, while makieta requires macro photography that holds the entire surface of a model in focus, a distinction Matsue himself has emphasized.*9 In makietaCC, the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum placed the two series together and adjusted their apparent scale so that actual sites and models became difficult to distinguish from the photographs alone.*8 The series tests the problem of keeping a broad field and minute detail within one image by changing the scale of the subject itself, not simply the shooting distance.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Historical Position
sections.body_html:
Beyond New Topographics

The 1975 exhibition New Topographics: Photographs of a Man-Altered Landscape presented suburban housing, industrial zones, construction sites, and other ordinary human-modified environments with photographs that restrained dramatic light and the sublime conventions of landscape.*18 The Centre national des arts plastiques exhibition ATLAS (2012) likewise treated New Topographics as an important reference for contemporary landscape photography and included Matsue within a lineage concerned with typology, serial work, and altered land.*25

Matsue shares its visual restraint and its refusal to foreground the photographer’s emotions, but the unit of his investigation is different. New Topographics was organized around the idea of a “man-altered landscape.” Matsue places deserts, mountains, forests, cemeteries, and models under the same rules as cities and developed land. Comparing CC with Japanese landscape debates around 1970 and the unpeopled landscapes that followed New Topographics, Shimizu notes that people need not become central subjects for houses, roads, signs, distant figures, and traces of construction to remain dispersed across Matsue’s high-resolution urban fields.*22 His question extends beyond altered land: what remains in the record when surfaces, natural or artificial, are subjected to the same photographic conditions?

The 2005 German exhibition Landscape as a Metaphor was conceived against an era in which satellite technology had made almost the entire terrestrial surface measurable and recordable. It expanded landscape from images of pure nature to a medium through which industrialization, urbanization, and social change could be addressed. Matsue appeared alongside Robert Adams, Luigi Ghirri, Naoya Hatakeyama, Hiroshi Sugimoto, and others as an artist dealing with nature through classification and abstraction.*37 Given Matsue’s background in geography and satellite imagery, it is more accurate to situate him as a photographer reconsidering how landscape can be recorded in an age when the earth’s surface is already visible as maps, satellite images, and data than to treat him as a Japanese version of New Topographics.

Matsue and the Bechers

Matsue and Bernd and Hilla Becher share the long-term repetition of standardized photographic rules that makes comparison possible across a series. The Bechers recorded water towers, winding towers, blast furnaces, and other industrial structures of the same function with frontal views, black-and-white film, large-format cameras, and even light, then arranged related structures in grids. Hamburger Bahnhof identifies the isolation of a single building against a neutral sky and the tabular format of typology as central to their work.*26

Matsue also standardizes conditions, but his unit of comparison is different. The Bechers center a single structure and compare buildings that share a function. Matsue does not isolate one building; cities and terrain fill the frame, and the archive accumulates according to the name or code of where each photograph was made.*27 Nature, city, cemetery, and model are not confined to separate typologies. The Bechers made morphological differences among related industrial structures comparable. Matsue’s standardization places heterogeneous surfaces under the same conditions so that differences in density, arrangement, terrain, and architecture remain available for comparison. The productive point of comparison is therefore less a direct genealogy than the distinct purposes to which standardized photographic rules are put.

Why Break the Rules?

JP-01 SPK matters because Matsue breaks rules he had used for years within the work itself. Shimizu argues that clouds, oblique light, shadows, diagonal compositions, and ground-level views bring distance and time back into photographs that had usually suppressed them.*32 From the placement of the cemetery between nature and city, past and present, Shimizu develops his reading that “photographs are graves”: names and images are inscribed in matter and continue to remain after being detached from the people or meanings to which they once referred.*33

Near the end of the book, snow scenes and ground-level houses appear. Shimizu reads another kind of distance here—“memory,” linked to Sapporo in the 1960s and 1970s and to personal experience. He also records how local viewers who recognized a shooting location began comparing the photograph with their own memories.*34 These departures make clear that Matsue’s rules were never a doctrine for permanently excluding the meanings of place. They first suppress a narrative or perspective prepared in advance by the author; when memory and time become difficult to address within that method, the rules themselves change. Testing what photography can record, and what it leaves out, takes precedence over preserving a fixed style.

Elevated Views, Governance, and Kunimi

Looking down on land from an elevated position has generated sharply opposed readings. In his review of makietaTYO, Shimizu treats the panoramic view from above as the field of vision of a ruler, rereading CC, JP, and makieta through the military and political histories attached to aerial vision.*23 The deeper a viewer becomes absorbed in the details of CC, he argues, the easier it is to lose awareness of who is looking and from where. In makieta, the photographer’s position overlaps more explicitly with the position from which an urban model can be planned and possessed, bringing the politics of the overhead view to the foreground.

Natsuki Ikezawa, writing for JP-01 SPK, offers a very different reading. He connects the elevated view of land to the ancient practice of kunimi, reading the act of surveying the land as one of praise and blessing.*35 The same elevated view can therefore be understood as a gaze of management and surveillance or as a gaze that affirms attachment to place. Hokkaido’s history, however, cannot be reduced to a simple story of “developing nature.” Shimizu himself notes that Hokkaido was and remains part of Ainu cultural territory and cautions against explaining colonization solely as a conflict between nature and humanity.*33 Matsue’s elevated photographs do not settle the view from above as neutral observation; they leave open the question of which histories are embedded in that position.

Photographing History Under the Same Conditions

JP-34 shows that a method recording the entire surface under consistent conditions does not automatically erase a place’s history. In the photographs made in Hiroshima, Matsue does not isolate only established monuments such as the Atomic Bomb Dome. Rivers, roads, residential districts, ports, and island topography receive the same precision. Nobuo Kuraishi’s essay “The Position of Surveying—Taiji Matsue’s Photography to the Present” appears in the Taiji Matsue Handbook, and the publisher’s introduction to JP-34 explains that looking at the contemporary surface from a distant position can produce an unexpected encounter with historical wounds.*16

Here, the refusal to designate “historically important places” in advance becomes part of the method. Monuments and ordinary houses, traces of war and present-day infrastructure remain at the same resolution. Read afterward, history can therefore extend from a symbolic point to the larger question of how the contemporary city was formed. Matsue’s even photographic conditions prevent details from being discarded solely according to judgments of importance made at the moment of exposure, leaving traces available for later reading.*16

Photography in the Digital Era

In 2010, Risaku Suzuki, Ryudai Takano, Taiji Matsue, Nobuo Kuraishi, and Minoru Shimizu began the group Shashin Bunriha, or Photography Secession. Against the contraction of the film market and the spread of digital cameras, it reopened the questions “What is photography?” and “Where do photography’s possibilities lie?”*17 Matsue’s contemporaneous work with cell, moving images, digital processing of earlier negatives, and makieta can be understood as extending the unit of the photograph beyond a fixed final image toward a fragment within an image, continuous time, an earlier negative, and a model.

For Matsue, digitization did not lead primarily toward composites of scenes that never existed. He has said that he treats information recorded at the moment of exposure as the basis of the image and regards digital processing as an extension of darkroom work.*1 At the same time, he developed cell, which turns a fragment of one photograph into another image; moving works that introduce continuous time into compositions close to still photographs; and makieta, which applies the same photographic form to actual places and models. Maintaining trust in what the camera recorded, these works repeatedly ask where one photograph begins and ends, whether it must remain still, and whether its subject must be an actual site.

International Reception

Internationally, the Fruitmarket Gallery exhibition Liquid Crystal Futures introduced Matsue in 1994 alongside Naoya Hatakeyama, Ryuji Miyamoto, Toshio Shibata, and others.*28 Landscape as a Metaphor (2005) placed him within an international discussion of landscape that encompassed an earth measured by satellite technology, idealized nature, and industrialized land.*37 In 2012, the Centre national des arts plastiques exhibition ATLAS approached his work through seriality, typology, and the landscape of postindustrial society after New Topographics.*25

Matsue’s museum presence is likewise not confined to Japan. In Eye to Eye—Seeing, the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo situated his “camera eye,” directed toward cities and the workings of nature around the world, among works that examine the act of seeing.*14 SFMOMA also holds several works, including JP-22 08, and presents him within an international collection of contemporary photography.*10

Matsue’s work cannot be reduced to the repetition of a single style of elevated photography. Its trajectory links travel and encounters with land, geography and satellite imagery, trust in the camera’s mechanical record, rules that suppress horizon and shadow, high resolution, geographic indexing, deliberate departures from those rules, and a digital reconsideration of the unit of the photograph. His statement that the lens preserves information beyond the photographer’s attention connects directly to cell, which extracts new photographs from within a single image; to moving works, which add duration to a still-photographic structure; and to makieta, which even removes the requirement that the subject be an actual landscape.*1 At the center of his method is an effort to keep recorded detail available for later reading instead of making the photograph answer only to what seemed important at the moment of exposure. When memory, history, or time could no longer be addressed by that method alone, he altered the rules he had made.

takashi-homma.html.lead_html: Takashi Homma first encountered the instability of photographic meaning while working at an advertising agency and at i-D in London, where publication format, text, and use could alter the role of a photograph. He carried this question into the post-bubble suburbs of Tokyo, fashion, family albums, and architecture. Tokyo Suburbia brought the color and human-altered landscapes associated with William Eggleston and Robert Adams to Tokyo from a measured distance distinct from the strongly embodied or autobiographical urban photography of Daido Moriyama and Nobuyoshi Araki. Tokyo and My Daughter and “New Documentary” examined how photographers, custodians, author credits, and museums determine whose memory or artwork a photograph becomes; the camera-obscura projects extended that inquiry to architecture and light.
takashi-homma.html.thesis_html: Homma recorded Japan’s 1990s suburbs in restrained color while making the changing use and authorship of images—across magazines, photobooks, family albums, and museums—part of the work itself. Tokyo Suburbia placed built landscapes and consumer culture within the same frame; Tokyo and My Daughter separated photographer, custodian, and the author named on the cover; and “New Documentary” brought advertising photographs, snapshots, and artists’ works into a single exhibition. In contrast to a lineage of urban photography represented by Daido Moriyama and Nobuyoshi Araki, in which the photographer’s body or private life grounds the work, Homma made the media and institutions that classify a photograph as record, commodity, private memory, or artwork into a concrete subject of urban photography.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Advertising and i-D—Learning How Media Changes a Photograph’s Meaning

Takashi Homma studied photography at Nihon University College of Art and began working as a photographer for a Tokyo advertising agency in 1984*2. In 1991–92 he moved to London and worked for i-D, a magazine devoted to youth culture, music, and fashion. Tokyo Opera City Art Gallery describes this period as one in which he encountered photographers presenting work through a wide range of methods*24. In a magazine, clothing, headlines, typography, adjacent images, and readership all shape a photograph’s function and meaning. Homma’s commercial experience showed him that the same image could operate as an advertisement, a record of the city, or an artist’s work.

Advertising often demands a recognizable authorial signature, yet Homma avoided inscribing the photographer’s emotion heavily into the frame. Using a 4×5 camera, he aligned horizontal and vertical lines, stepped back from his subjects, and treated people, roads, houses, and signs as equivalent elements in the picture. He has explained that this position allows viewers to imagine where they themselves might be standing*21. The controlled surface leaves room for viewers to assess the scene through their own experience.

The same thinking extends to his commercial work. Homma places models, clothing, roads, signs, and architecture within a shared setting, and describes fashion photography as a document of the city and body of its time*12. The construction of a desirable commodity image and the recording of a city coexist within a single photograph.

Tokyo Suburbia and the Suburb Boom—Selections and Contradictions Identified by 藤田紅於

When Tokyo Suburbia appeared in 1998, Japanese debate focused intensely on new towns, roadside development, convenience stores, and standardized residential districts. After the 1997 Kobe child murders, newspapers, magazines, and sociological writing increasingly associated suburbia with a weakened sense of reality, fictionality, and the erosion of family and local community. 藤田紅於 compared contemporary reviews with suburban theory centered on Shinji Miyadai and traced how Tokyo Suburbia was received as visual evidence for this “suburb boom”*4.

According to 藤田, the sixty-three photographs concentrate on newer suburbs developed after the 1980s and largely omit accumulated signs of daily life such as laundry, potted plants, supermarkets, and banks. Nostalgic images of childhood also recede. Instead, the book repeatedly shows game centers, family restaurants, convenience stores, children in American and European brands, and landscapes suggestive of American film. These choices visually reinforced contemporary accounts of diminished reality, dispersed family life, and Americanization*4.

At the same time, the location list at the back returns apparently anonymous landscapes to places such as Tama, Makuhari, and Yokohama, while one photograph of adults with an infant unsettles the impression of a community composed only of children. 藤田 notes that contemporary newspaper and magazine reviews largely overlooked these contradictions and praised Tokyo Suburbia for visualizing a standard image of the suburban boom*4. The essay also warns against treating Homma’s suburban upbringing as sufficient proof of an insider’s viewpoint. The book carefully constructs the conventions of suburban discourse, then inserts place names and exceptions into them. Its critical force lies in this double movement.

Eggleston, Robert Adams, and Nobuyoshi Araki—Three Predecessors Named by Homma

Homma identifies William Eggleston, Robert Adams, and Nobuyoshi Araki as important predecessors*13. Eggleston brought color associated with advertising and family snapshots into art photography, treating ordinary objects, cars, interiors, and roadsides as events of color and composition*27. Within New Topographics, Robert Adams photographed the meeting of housing developments, roads, and plains in the American West from a quiet distance*26. From them, Homma learned that color and human-altered landscapes could be photographed as everyday environments in their own right.

Nobuyoshi Araki transformed private life into photobooks while working at an advertising agency, closely linking the photographer’s biography, titles, and publication. Homma cites Araki as one reason he became a photographer, yet in Tokyo and My Daughter he used a first-person title to prompt an autobiographical reading while mixing photographs of a friend’s daughter with snapshots made by her parents and rephotographed images*13. Homma’s concern extended from private subject matter to the power of the photobook and author credit to produce an image of the artist.

Daido Moriyama and Takuma Nakahira rendered Tokyo in the 1960s and 1970s as an urgent field of perception through the walking body, blur, grain, and print. Homma’s 4×5 photographs approach the later city from a fixed position several steps back, giving people, houses, roads, and signs comparable weight. The distinction lies in whether the photographer’s body anchors the urban image or attention shifts toward the arrangements and consumer signs that structure suburbia. These histories reached Homma by different routes. Eggleston, Robert Adams, and Araki are predecessors he named himself; Moriyama and Nakahira serve as points of comparison within Japanese urban photography.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
The 4×5 Camera—Restraining the Photographer’s Gesture, Recording Suburban Arrangement

Homma chose the 4×5 camera for more than its descriptive precision. The camera requires a tripod, careful alignment of horizontal and vertical lines, and the placement of people and architecture within the same frame*10. By stepping back, he removes facial expression from the center of psychological drama, allowing roads, houses, sky, and signs to become equal conditions of the image. He has said that this position helps viewers imagine where they themselves might stand*21.

Through the 1980s, a major current in Japanese urban photography entered the street with a small camera and registered the photographer’s speed and reaction in the frame. The 1990s suburbs Homma photographed were planned spaces of recurring intersections, houses, convenience stores, and construction sites. Proximity and quick response could intensify an individual scene; a fixed distance made the repetition of planned space more legible. The 4×5 format showed where a person stood among roads, buildings, and commercial signs.

What Homma calls an “open photograph” withholds the photographer’s emotion as a final conclusion and allows viewers to compare the arrangement in the frame with their own memories*13. His ordered 4×5 pictures still involve decisions about place, distance, weather, and people. Directing those decisions toward suburban arrangement while keeping expressive gesture out of the foreground defines his measured distance.

Magazines, Photobooks, Museums—Changing the Use of the Same Image

A defining feature of Homma’s publishing work is the repeated movement of the same image through different media, making changes in use and evaluation part of the work’s structure. A photograph used to present clothing in i-D becomes a record of the post-bubble city in Tokyo Suburbia, then material for examining the institutional division between commercial and artistic photography in “New Documentary”*6. Existing images reappear with traces of their earlier uses, weakening the expectation that each book must close around an entirely new body of work.

Homma has produced more than sixty publications and has said that he prefers thin books made for particular exhibitions or moments*20. In Japanese photography, Daido Moriyama and Nobuyoshi Araki placed magazines and photobooks at the center of production and changed photographic meaning through print. Homma brought advertising, fashion magazines, family albums, and museums—each with different systems of ownership and evaluation—into that history.

What distinguishes Homma’s work from the ordinary integration of shooting, selection, and book design is the recirculation of identical images. As a photograph moves from one medium to another, it may be treated as commodity, urban record, family memory, or artwork. Making that shift a sustained subject separates his books and exhibitions from a conventional editorial process.

Tokyo and My Daughter—Separating Photographer, Custodian, and Author Credit

In Tokyo and My Daughter, the author’s name on the cover and the first-person title suggest an autobiography following the photographer’s own child. The girl is in fact a friend’s daughter, and the book mixes photographs by Homma with snapshots by her parents and rephotographed images*6. Before establishing each photograph’s provenance, viewers use the title and author credit to construct a single family story.

In a family album, the person pressing the shutter, the family represented, the household preserving the photographs, and the album’s owner often overlap. Tokyo and My Daughter separates these roles and gathers images by different photographers under Homma’s name. Photographer, custodian, selector, title-giver, and publisher each participate in the photograph’s meaning and sense of ownership.

The work therefore shifts from a single photographer’s private confession to the mechanism by which family photographs are recognized as someone’s memories. Its subject is the division of labor among shooting, preservation, selection, naming, and publication. Different people perform these tasks, yet their combined work establishes whose story the book appears to tell.

Camera Obscura—Examining Authorship Through an Optical Apparatus

Since the 2010s, Homma has darkened hotel rooms and houses, admitted daylight through a small aperture in a window, and projected an inverted city onto walls or photosensitive material. Because the entire room functions as a camera, its architecture, the direction of the window, the weather, and long exposure times directly shape the image. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum presented the camera obscura as a central element of his recent inquiry into photographic apparatuses and photographic history in Revolution 9: Homma Takashi*23.

In The Narcissistic City, rooms in Tokyo, New York, Milan, and other cities become camera obscuras, allowing the city to leave its own image on photosensitive material through architecture*8. Nonaka-Hill describes this as using the city as an apparatus to photograph itself, with inversion, chance, and repetition as constitutive elements*7. The early 4×5 photographs and the camera-obscura works differ greatly in technique and appearance. They share a distance from the idea that the author’s instantaneous perception alone grounds expression. In the 4×5 pictures, the photographer’s gesture recedes; in the camera obscura, architecture, aperture, daylight, and exposure time divide responsibility for the image.

The available sources show that Homma developed the camera-obscura work as research into photographic history and architecture; it also casts his earlier understanding of authorship in a different light. At a time when smartphones and digital systems produce and circulate images instantly, sealing a room and waiting for light restores the duration by which light becomes an image. Homma refers to Nicéphore Niépce, Nobuo Yamanaka, and Jun’ichirō Tanizaki, using the dark chamber as an entry point into photographic history and the modern organization of vision*5.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Tokyo Suburbia, 1998—Thick Pages and an Externally Framed Suburbia

Tokyo Suburbia comprises sixty-three color photographs of residential districts, roads, commercial facilities, children, and young people. Its board-book construction, made from laminated card, gives the volume considerable physical weight, while full-bleed printing brings the reader into direct contact with the page surface. The light palette of the city meets the book’s physical heaviness, introducing bodily resistance into the act of viewing suburbia as an abstract image*4.

In 1999, the Kimura Ihei Award, followed by a 2000 exhibition at Fotomuseum Winterthur, brought Homma’s restrained color photographs wider international recognition*3. Current reassessments consider both the book’s reinforcement of 1990s suburban discourse and the ways its location list, infants, and the gazes of its figures fracture that typology*22. The coexistence of formal clarity and social selectivity remains a central issue in the book’s reception.

Tokyo and My Daughter, 1999–2010—The Family Album and the Displaced Author Credit

Tokyo and My Daughter follows a girl’s growth from 1999 alongside Tokyo streets, houses, airports, and family snapshots. She is the daughter of a friend, and the book includes images made by her parents as well as rephotographed existing photographs*13. Grain, color, and distance remain uneven within the volume, placing images preserved in the home on the same timeline as the artist’s urban photographs. The autobiographical expectation created by the words “Tokyo and My Daughter” conflicts with the actual provenance of the pictures, and that gap structures the book.

The Narcissistic City and Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji

In The Narcissistic City, rooms become large cameras that turn fragments of buildings, water towers, roads, and sky into inverted images*14. Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji refers to Katsushika Hokusai’s series and photographs a mountain endlessly repeated through tourism, World Heritage status, and daily life from camera obscuras in different locations*11. Both series record how an image changes as viewing position, architecture, and exposure time change, instead of presenting a single representative view of a famous site.

From Le Corbusier’s Windows to Portraiture and Moving Images

Looking Through: Le Corbusier Windows follows architecture across Europe and India, examining how windows determine light, view, and the position of the body*17. A joint project by the CCA and the Window Research Institute connects the shared structure of windows and camera obscuras to the histories of modern architecture and photography*19. According to the CCA, the research began with Homma’s 2002 photographs of Le Corbusier’s Petite Maison, continued in Chandigarh, and developed into an examination of the common structure of the window and the camera aperture*9. The subject expanded from recording a building’s exterior to studying how architecture itself organizes sight and view.

Portrait of J gathers portraits made since 2002, presenting public figures, friends, and children without a hierarchy of status*15. In 2022, an i-D project photographed nine young queer people on Tokyo streets and placed their portraits alongside their own words*16. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Videodiary developed near-empty Tokyo, domestic interiors, and family voices across twenty-eight videos*18. Across photobooks, magazines, moving images, and architectural research, Homma chooses image duration, sequence, and circulation according to the subject.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Praised Restraint and Critiques of “Ordinariness”

Homma’s reception formed around the bright color of Tokyo Suburbia, the distance that treats people and architecture with comparable temperature, and his movement between magazines and photobooks. In its 2000 exhibition, MU praised his ability to work inside the media while directing a critical gaze toward them; Fotomuseum Winterthur identified socioeconomic fractures beneath the work’s apparent lightness*1.

Aperture’s review of “New Documentary” noted that its discussion of deskilling—mixing amateur photographs with professional technique—sometimes repeated familiar art-historical arguments, and distinguished works in which the concept operated forcefully from those led by institutional explanation*6. The criticism clarifies that titles, editing, design, and display produce critical force only when they act concretely upon each series’ social setting. Homma’s restrained surfaces gain their strength when they serve a precise inquiry into society and media.

The Pictures Generation and Tillmans—Separating Direct Influence from Contemporary Comparison

In the late 1970s, the Pictures Generation appropriated images from magazines, film, and advertising to criticize an art system centered on original authors and originals*28. The available sources do not establish that Homma directly referred to the group. The useful comparison lies elsewhere: those artists moved mass-circulated images into art, while Homma began within commercial image production and moved his own advertising photographs, family snapshots, and urban pictures among different media.

Working at roughly the same time for publications including i-D, Wolfgang Tillmans treated photographs, photocopies, and reproductions of magazine pages as equivalent in a 1993 installation, shifting the hierarchy between printed matter and original prints*25. The sources likewise do not confirm a direct line of influence between Tillmans and Homma. Tillmans rearranged hierarchies of size, support, and mounting within the gallery; Homma traced how suburbia, family albums, and Japanese magazine culture classify images as advertisement, record, private memory, or artwork.

This distinction avoids presenting Homma as a synthesis of Euro-American currents. Eggleston, Robert Adams, and Araki are predecessors he named. The Pictures Generation and Tillmans offer comparisons for authorship and circulation developed in different regions and institutions. Homma’s specificity lies in placing advertising, magazines, suburbia, family albums, and museums within a single field of inquiry in 1990s Japan.

Making the Boundary Between Magazine Photography and Museum Art a Subject in 1990s Japan

Questions of photographic circulation and authorship predate Homma. Daido Moriyama made the printed surfaces of magazines and photobooks integral to the photograph; Nobuyoshi Araki linked private life and authorial identity across a vast publishing output; and art of the 1980s criticized authorship through the reuse of existing images. Homma’s work cannot be adequately described as a personal synthesis of these histories.

Its specificity lies in the circulation systems of 1990s Japan. In Tokyo Suburbia, a color palette and distance developed through fashion magazines were received as visual evidence for suburban discourse. In Tokyo and My Daughter, photographs preserved within a household appeared under the name of a single photographer. In “New Documentary,” magazine covers, commercial photographs, family pictures, and video entered a museum, and the exhibition made changes in their use and evaluation visible*24.

Homma’s place in photographic history depends on treating commercial assignments, private snapshots, artists’ works, and architectural research as connected stages in the changing meaning and evaluation of images. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s 2023 exhibition reorganized his early suburbia photographs, seascapes, mushrooms, Le Corbusier studies, and camera-obscura works around the acts of seeing photographs and examining the camera apparatus*23. Movement between magazines and museums had clear precedents. Homma’s particular contribution was to circulate advertising, suburban photography, family albums, and architectural research within one body of work and thereby show, in post-1990 Japan, how photographic use and authorship are assigned.

takashi-yasumura.html.lead_html: Takashi Yasumura is known for Domestic Scandals, made with a 4×5 camera in his parents’ home among furniture, artificial flowers, fruit, wallpaper, and tableware, and for 1/1, which isolates the surfaces of regional public buildings and harbors from their surroundings. By making slight adjustments, carrying focus across the frame, and reducing spatial clues, he tests the arrangements, commodities, decoration, and perspective that allow homes and buildings to appear natural.
takashi-yasumura.html.thesis_html: As quick snapshots of everyday life gained prominence in 1990s Japan, Yasumura chose the slow procedure of photographing his parents’ home and regional public facilities with a 4×5 camera. In Domestic Scandals, he moves artificial flowers, fruit, wallpaper, and furniture slightly, confusing the scale of garden, model, and object in works such as Japanese Oranges. In 1/1, walls and floors of public buildings are framed frontally, leaving the building as a whole and the clues to its use outside the image. Because he avoids models and digital composites, the strangeness comes from actual products, interiors, and architecture. His work brought misreadings of perspective, focus, and scale into everyday photography as a problem alongside personal disclosure.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Studying Photography and Finding a Stimulus in New Cosmos of Photography

Born in Shiga Prefecture in 1972, Yasumura studied photography at Nihon University College of Art and graduated in 1995. New Cosmos of Photography began in 1991, during his second year, and he repeatedly visited its exhibitions at P3 in Yotsuya. He has recalled being strongly affected by seeing award recipients create places for their work through both images and words, as well as by reading statements of intent in magazines*1.

He found it difficult to identify with the prominent photography of “my life, my everyday world” and began looking for something that only photography could do*1. His parents’ home offered a familiar space in which the lens repeatedly altered relations of size, distance, material, and use. His concern turned toward the conditions under which a three-dimensional living space becomes a flat image and everydayness begins to lose its stability.

Everyday Photography in the 1990s and Yasumura’s Different Direction

In 1990s Japan, photographs of friends, romance, the body, and the photographer’s immediate surroundings gained broad attention through compact cameras and magazine culture. New Cosmos of Photography was one of the forums where these varied approaches appeared. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum later included Yasumura with Masafumi Sanai, Takashi Homma, Kyoji Takahashi, Hanayo, and others in an exhibition on photography and society during the Heisei era*22. Yasumura also used the private space of his family home, but focused on the way its apparent everydayness disappeared in a photograph. In his statement for the 1999 award, he wrote that conventions within a family can look strange to an outsider and that photography brings the doubtful nature of the everyday into awareness*21. The series was published as Domestic Scandals*20. The 4×5 camera, tripod, extensive depth of field, and limited rearrangement allowed him to examine visual conditions one at a time.

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
Domestic Scandals—The Family Home as an Already Staged Set

Domestic Scandals was photographed with a 4×5 camera over seven years in his parents’ middle-class home. A Yossi Milo exhibition text describes traditional decoration, plastic and mass-produced goods, and Westernized household objects occupying the same rooms*19. Yasumura selected staplers, cassette players, snacks, slippers, walls, and floors and adjusted their color and form within the frame. The house appears as a setting where postwar Japanese domestic normality is assembled from commodities, habits, and imitative materials. The official work page presents the series as a continuous group of images*16. IBASHO’s publication entry records a book in which the photographs are accompanied by three essays treating the home as a stage of representation*3.

Finding Deliberate Awkwardness Through Minimal Arrangement

In an IMA interview, Yasumura contrasted the apparent naturalness of his early series Namanurui Kaze ga Fuku with the deliberate “awkwardness” he intensified in Domestic Scandals*2. He moves furniture and household objects and adjusts focus and light while leaving most of the room intact. The resulting strangeness remains tied to products chosen by the family, habits of display and cleanliness, and seasonal routines. Visible intervention weakens a simple division between natural life and artificial photography. Existing staging and photographic adjustment can be compared within the same frame.

Holding the Entire Frame in Focus and Destabilizing Depth

The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s Japanese Oranges holds the entire frame in focus, making depth and object scale difficult to determine. Tokyo Museum Collection describes household objects as appearing model-like and domestic space as revealing its fictive quality*4. Ordinary vision changes attention and focus with distance. A large-format camera and small aperture hold foreground and background with comparable intensity, and the camera’s descriptive capacity unsettles the apparent naturalness of space.

Why Use Real Rooms Instead of Models?

Yasumura’s photographs can resemble images of miniatures or elaborate sets, although most use actual rooms and objects. IBASHO Gallery presents Domestic Scandals and Nature Tracing as connected investigations of the artificiality of everyday life and the reproduction of nature*5.

A model would make unstable scale the result of a device designed entirely by the artist. Yasumura retains the actual objects and limits intervention to arrangement, camera position, focus, and light. The disturbance therefore returns to commodities, architecture, and household habits. The viewer is led to reconsider which cues of depth, size, use, and material made the space recognizable as everyday.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Japanese Oranges—The Scale of Fruit, Garden, and Model

In Japanese Oranges, citrus fruit, leaves, branches, and background share the same density, making it difficult to decide immediately whether the scene is a potted plant, a garden tree, or a model*4. The title identifies the subject while the photograph destabilizes its size and setting. The color of the fruit anchors the frame, yet the image presents nature as something cultivated, arranged, and observed within domestic life.

1/1—Public-Building Surfaces and the One-to-One Relation of Object and Image

1/1 was made over roughly eight years beginning in 2008 at regional public facilities and harbors, where Yasumura photographed walls, floors, equipment, and decoration with a 4×5 camera. In an IMA interview, he explained that he reduced the “background” inevitably recorded by the camera and made visual depth shallow through composition*2.

The title refers to a one-to-one relation between object and image and to the camera that mediates between them. MISAKO & ROSEN interprets the slash as the camera and explains how, after being photographed, an object gains a different autonomy as a plane of color or flat surface*6. With less information about a site’s function, public architecture approaches abstraction while retaining scratches and material traces. Antenne Books records the publication as containing 111 photographs made between 2008 and 2015*7.

Nature Tracing—Imitations of Nature Brought into the Home

Nature Tracing addresses artificial flowers, synthetic turf, printed plants, and arranged gardens—objects and actions through which everyday life imitates nature. The official site publishes the photographs and gathers imitated nature in domestic and public space as one series*17. The work observes how nature is reduced in scale, maintained, commodified, and brought indoors. As with the mass-produced objects in Domestic Scandals, naturalness is produced through material, arrangement, and repetition.

The Photobook Domestic Scandals and Comparison Across Pages

According to the official bibliography, Domestic Scandals was published by Osiris in 2005 with thirty-six color photographs and essays by Martin Jaeggi, Akihito Yasumi, and Shinobu Kuraishi*18. 1/1 contains 111 images across 132 pages, a comparison by Minoru Shimizu with Alfred Stieglitz’s Equivalents, and a text by Yasumura*18. Repetition in book form allows mass-produced domestic goods and public-building surfaces to be compared as visual habits within the same society. Format and sequence establish a common viewing distance across distinct spaces.

The Slowness of the 4×5 Camera and Minimal Intervention

The official site and biography show Yasumura’s sustained attention to homes, objects, and landscapes through precise color photography*8. MISAKO & ROSEN documents the continuity of his solo exhibitions and series*13, while IBASHO Gallery brings together images and collection information from Domestic Scandals through Nature Tracing*14. Yossi Milo records that Domestic Scandals was made with a 4×5 camera over seven years*19. The slow apparatus produces long observation before exposure as well as detailed images. Setting up the tripod, viewing the inverted image on the ground glass, and adjusting arrangement and focus temporarily detach the room from the flow of domestic life. Limited intervention in actual objects and camera conditions keeps the work centered on how reality changes as an image.

sections.title: Criticism and Reception
sections.body_html:
New Cosmos of Photography and Doubts About “Everydayness” Itself

New Cosmos of Photography began in 1991. As a university student, Yasumura attended exhibitions at P3 in Yotsuya and observed award recipients creating working contexts through their photographs*1. During the 1990s, the competition drew attention to varied uses of private life, the body, cities, staging, and photobooks. Yasumura also chose his parents’ home, but centered the disappearance of everydayness within photography. Preparing a 4×5 camera, moving furniture and objects, and adjusting focus, color, and distance turned a private setting into a place for testing realist description. PARCO’s 2005 exhibition and the photobook Domestic Scandals presented seven years of repetition as one public series*9. The work shared familiar subject matter with contemporary everyday photography while directing attention toward the perceptual structure that makes the everyday seem natural.

Photographic Distance Learned from Shigeo Gocho’s SELF AND OTHERS

In an IMA conversation, Yasumura described the influence of Shigeo Gocho’s SELF AND OTHERS and emphasized the importance of distance between photographer and subject even in his own photographs of things*2. Gocho approached intimate subjects without enclosing them entirely within the photographer’s emotion. Yasumura applied that distance to the family home, a setting too familiar to see easily, and to the objects within it. Camera distance and preparation make the known observable again.

Comparing Household Goods and Public Architecture with the Same 4×5 Camera

Yasumura photographs plastic, appliances, snacks, artificial flowers, wall materials, and public-facility equipment as elements that make contemporary life. Essays in the official Domestic Scandals publication treat the family home as a stage of representation and examine social changes beneath its quiet surfaces*18. Focus, color, and scale show how objects exist photographically without turning household goods into sentimental possessions or sociological specimens.

In 1/1, the same method turns toward regional public buildings. Domestic arrangements and architectural surfaces differ in character, yet the same 4×5 camera allows mass-produced goods, imitation materials, walls, and floors to be compared. Still life expands from the tabletop to the arrangement of objects that constitute homes and public institutions. shashasha’s artist and publication page situates Domestic Scandals and 1/1 within a continuing photobook practice*10.

The Family Home and Public Facilities as Different Conditions of Reality

Domestic Scandals shows plastic, artificial flowers, appliances, snacks, and simulated wood or stone accumulating the time and consumer choices of Yasumura’s parents’ home. In 1/1, he moves close to walls, floors, and equipment in public facilities, ports, and gymnasiums, leaving signs of function and the building as a whole outside the frame. Art Platform Japan records the two major publications and exhibition history since the late 1990s*11. In the first series, furniture and commodities produce domestic depth; in the second, reduced background turns walls and floors toward fields of color. Yasumura adjusts arrangements at home and removes surrounding information in public buildings while retaining the same 4×5 camera and color realism. The two series show how a sense of reality depends on depth, scale, use, material, and the amount of background. Formal consistency makes it possible to measure these conditions across domestic and public space.

Selection and Responsibility in Teaching and Jury Work

Canon’s archive records Yasumura as a New Cosmos of Photography juror for four consecutive years, from 2018 through 2021*12. In an English-language interview, he reflects on work from his award-winning series to recent projects and discusses how photographing, selecting, and forming a series produce a finished work*15. This continues his long-standing attention to selection after exposure, sequence, and print size. The work is not complete when an interesting object is found; the distance and scale at which its image will appear are also composed.

takeji-iwamiya.html.lead_html: Takeji Iwamiya photographed Sado, Kyoto, the stone Buddhas of Nara, gardens, architecture, crafts, and vernacular objects over long periods, bringing them together in photobooks such as Sado, Kyo, and Katachi. Shaped by the Tanpei Photography Club and Osaka’s postwar commercial and design culture, he approached tradition through stone, wood, paper, earth, line, plane, repetition, and interval rather than through nostalgia. The photobook became the form in which ancient architecture and anonymous everyday objects could share a spread and be compared across use, material, and visual structure.
takeji-iwamiya.html.thesis_html: In Katachi, Iwamiya developed a way of comparing Japanese form by placing details such as latticework, rope, stone, timber joints, and folded paper at a common photographic scale. The clarity he had cultivated in commercial photography and the modernism of the Tanpei Photography Club informed the way he reedited traditional subjects through sequences of photographs. Cultural-property photography often tended toward preservation and explanation; Iwamiya brought it closer to a visual method for testing the roots of Japanese culture from the standpoint of the postwar present.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Takeji Iwamiya was born in Yonago, Tottori Prefecture, in 1920 and later made Osaka the base of his work. FUJIFILM SQUARE’s profile traces his move from Yonago to Osaka and the beginning of his career in the Kansai photographic scene. *1 He joined the Tanpei Photography Club in 1940 and, after the war, pursued commercial assignments and personal projects in parallel. The Third Gallery Aya presents the path from the postwar Sado to Kyo and Katachi as a sustained investigation into the roots of Japanese culture through the forms of Kyoto and historic architecture. *2

In 1930s Kansai, the Tanpei Photography Club absorbed international modernist currents including New Objectivity, Constructivism, and Surrealism, experimenting with sharp tonal contrasts and estranged fragments. The Marukawa Collection describes the group, which included Nakaji Yasui, as an important site of experimentation away from Pictorialism. *3 An Osaka cultural archive also notes abstraction and symbolism in Iwamiya’s early work, placing him where modernism and realism intersected in postwar Kansai photography. *4

Iwamiya did not move directly from the war into traditional culture. The Third Gallery Aya chronology records his participation in Ei-Q’s Demokrato Artists Association in 1951, placing him after Tanpei within another postwar avant-garde network where printmaking, abstraction, and experimental art overlapped*2. His later turn toward older forms in Katachi therefore carried a visual language shaped by both modernism and postwar art; it was not a retreat into a premodern past.

The Tanpei Photography Club and Osaka: Modernism before Tradition

In temples, shrines, and gardens, Iwamiya foregrounded pillars and shadows, stone and sand, and the boundary between paper and wood. He avoided haze and sentimental figure arrangements as conventional signs of “old Japan.” In Mirror, held by the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum, the object is detached from a functional explanation and treated as surface and tonal density. *5 The same formal cutting appears in Sand Dune. *6 The bold cropping and contrast associated with Tanpei, together with the visual clarity required in commercial work, remained present even after his subjects shifted to temples and crafts.

This formation also extended beyond Kansai. Photo critic Kotaro Iizawa notes that Iwamiya participated in Otto Steinert’s Subjektive Fotografie 2 in 1954*21. Steinert’s “subjective photography” was an international postwar movement in Germany that drew on experimental methods associated with the Bauhaus while emphasizing the photographer’s individual vision over claims to neutral recording*22. In 1961, the exhibition Contemporary Photography 1960 included Iwamiya alongside Yasuhiro Ishimoto, Shoji Ueda, Ihei Kimura, Shomei Tomatsu, Ken Domon, Ikko Narahara, Eikoh Hosoe, and others*20. When Iwamiya later turned to historic architecture and crafts, his way of seeing had already passed through prewar Kansai modernism and international postwar experimental photography.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Why Iwamiya Wanted to “Confirm the Roots of Japanese Culture” through Photography

According to Iwamiya’s words quoted in an exhibition on Katachi, he felt an urgent need to confirm the “roots” of Japanese culture through photography. *2 His subjects therefore extended beyond nationally designated monuments to fittings, patterns, packaging, tools, stones, and the organization of gardens. Photography does not primarily explain provenance here; it tests what a contemporary eye selects as “Japanese form.” The English-language page from The Third Gallery Aya similarly describes Katachi as a search for the roots of form that moves from historic architecture to everyday objects. *7

Kyoto was not a subject he discovered once and then fixed in place. FUJIFILM SQUARE’s Kyoto: Color and Form presents his work there as an undertaking sustained for more than thirty years after his postwar encounter with the city, attending to both color and form*17. Through repeated photographing over decades, “confirming the roots” became less a search for a lost original than a way of repeatedly testing which colors and forms persisted within a changing Kyoto.

Katachi: Choosing Fragments over the Whole

Katachi favors close views of latticework, rope, vessels, paper, timber joints, surface wear, and repetition over photographs that explain an entire building. The National Diet Library catalog records the series as a publication that organizes “Japanese tradition” through sequences of forms*8. The English edition, Katachi: Classic Japanese Design, is also documented by the National Diet Library, confirming that the book circulated abroad as a way of looking at Japanese line, plane, and material through design*19. CiNii Books likewise shows that the project continued to circulate through publishing rather than existing only as a single exhibition*9.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Commercial Clarity and the Editing of the Photobook

Iwamiya established his own studio in 1955 and worked in commercial photography, an experience closely related to the visual clarity with which his later images make an object’s contours immediately legible. An English-language FUJIFILM retrospective describes him as influential in both commercial and fine-art photography in Kansai and includes color works such as Mannequins from 1954. *10 The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s Mannequin shows an urban and formal interest that cannot be explained solely through his later work on traditional culture. *11

Katachi Was Not Iwamiya’s Book Alone: Photography, Writing, and Layout

The first edition of Katachi in 1962 took shape through photography, writing, and design. The Third Gallery Aya notes that Iwamiya photographed for roughly eight years, expanding from historic architecture to classical performing arts and everyday objects, and that graphic designer Yoshio Hayakawa handled the book design*2. Shuji Takashina’s writing accompanied Iwamiya’s photographs, while latticework, rope, vessels, stone, and timber joints became linked as related “forms.” Meaning came from Iwamiya’s cropping at the moment of exposure and from editorial decisions about adjacency, page turns, and the placement of text. Objects of very different status and use were reread through visual similarity and difference.

Sado, Kyo, and Yamato no Sekibutsu: From Place to Form

In the early Sado, people’s lives, labor, and the character of the island remain strongly present; ToMuCo’s Peddling records the social time of the island. *12 In later projects such as Kyo, Yamato no Sekibutsu, and The Imperial Gardens, attention concentrates more on repetition, intervals, architectural structures, stone figures, and gardens than on explaining a place. Art Platform Japan’s collection information places Iwamiya within postwar Japanese photography as a figure connecting cultural form and modernism. *13 Canon’s exhibition Beauty of Boundaries revisited later work through the borders, depth, and divisions of gardens and architecture. *14

Iwamiya’s photographs also circulated within the international presentation of postwar Japan. During the period of high economic growth, architecture, crafts, and gardens were repeatedly repackaged in design magazines and publications aimed abroad as cultural resources of modern Japan. The National Diet Library records the English-language Katachi: Classic Japanese Design, showing that the photobook functioned beyond domestic connoisseurship as an entry point for looking at “Japanese design” in English*19. The clarity of the details made formal comparison easy, while also cutting provenance and lived use out of the frame. Both tendencies belong to the way modern printed photography selected and produced new images of “Japan.”

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photo History
sections.body_html:
Comparing Yasuhiro Ishimoto and Ken Domon: Between Modernism and Cultural-Property Photography

Iwamiya shares subjects with Ken Domon in temples and Buddhist sculpture, and with Yasuhiro Ishimoto in the treatment of architecture as geometric line and plane. Kotaro Iizawa, however, compares Iwamiya and Ishimoto in their photographs of Kyoto and argues that Iwamiya retains the dampness and sensory atmosphere of the Japanese environment where Ishimoto, trained at the New Bauhaus, tends toward stricter form*21. In Iwamiya’s work, modernist cropping and repetition coexist with the material presence of paper, wood, stone, moss, and light. Domon’s Buddhist sculpture photographs often stress historical and religious weight; Iwamiya instead places fragments of different functions and status together in a photobook, making the very coherence of “Japan” emerge through comparison.

Later retrospectives have also resisted reducing Iwamiya to Katachi alone. The volume Beauty and Form: The Work of Takeji Iwamiya brings together 421 images spanning Osaka, Sado, Katachi, Kyoto, the Imperial Gardens, the Sea of Japan, and Buddhist sculpture across Asia*18. It reedits his career across city, daily life, architecture, craft, and religious space. In this wider view, Iwamiya’s “Japan” is less a closed ethnic style than a point of departure for comparing places and materials through movement.

The “Japan” Iwamiya photographed cannot be separated from postwar cultural reconstruction. As modernization and high growth accelerated, tradition was repackaged through tourism, design, and cultural export. Iwamiya worked inside that system as a commercial photographer, yet used photographic cutting and editing to test tradition again. The Third Gallery Aya’s later presentation of Katachi as a search for the “roots of form” from historic architecture to everyday objects underscores a method that exceeds simple cultural preservation*2.

The 1950s Debate on “Tradition” and Katachi: Reselecting Japan from the Postwar Present

From the 1950s through the early 1960s, artists, architects, and designers repeatedly debated how “tradition” should be understood from the standpoint of postwar modernity. Kenji Kajiya describes the 1950s discourse on tradition as a field in which several meanings competed: something to be overcome in the course of Westernization, a root to which modern culture should return, and a source through which Japanese sensibility could be articulated*16. At the threshold between postwar reconstruction and rapid growth, tradition was both an object of preservation and a resource to be transformed into contemporary form.

The Printing Museum shows that advertising, packaging, books, and other printed matter expanded rapidly in 1950s Japan*15. During the same period, “design” became an increasingly important language of both economic production and visual culture, spanning traditional crafts and industrial products. Iwamiya was working in commercial photography as this graphic clarity spread through printed media. In Katachi, cutting, enlargement, and repetition place objects of different use and rank within the same page width, allowing line, plane, and repeated structures to be compared from one page turn to the next.

The Photobook as a Unit: Chains of Form over the Single “Masterpiece”

The meaning of Katachi emerges through the finish of individual photographs and through their sequence. Vessel rims, latticework, rope, stone, and timber joints—objects with different origins—connect through formal resemblance and difference as pages are turned. The National Diet Library catalog shows that the project was conceived as a publication organizing “Japanese tradition”*8. On the page, arcs, straight lines, meshes, and repetition can register before names or functions do. The clarity of commercial cropping and the sense of arranging photographs across a printed surface also shape this sequence. FUJIFILM’s retrospective treats both advertising and fine-art photography as part of Iwamiya’s work*10. The movement from Sado through Kyo to Katachi follows form into progressively smaller units within everyday life without abandoning lived reality*12.

Once it circulated as Katachi: Classic Japanese Design, Iwamiya’s fragmentary photographs could also be received abroad as design material for reading Japanese line, plane, and texture. The National Diet Library records the 1999 English edition as Katachi: Classic Japanese Design with Kazuya Takaoka*19. Later overseas catalog descriptions foreground the organization of many objects by material—paper, wood, bamboo, fiber, earth, metal, stone, and others*19. This later reception should not be equated with the project’s original 1960s intentions, but it shows how Iwamiya’s fragmentary images continued to function as comparative visual material for “Japanese design” beyond cultural-property illustration.

By photographing the same subject—children at play—for decades, he created sequences in which ruins, paved streets, houses, clothing, toys, and schools can be compared from one period to another. He later extended the same method to children around the world.
