sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Takeyoshi Tanuma was born in Asakusa, Tokyo, and experienced the Tokyo air raids. After photography school, he joined Sun News Photos in 1949 and learned magazine photography as an assistant to Ihei Kimura. FUJIFILM SQUARE’s profile traces his work under Kimura, assignments for magazines including Geijutsu Shincho, and his independence in 1959. *1 In an interview with Sarai, Tanuma recalls Kimura warning him that commissioned work alone would never become his own work, prompting him to photograph Tokyo’s children and streets outside his assignments. *2

After Kimura’s advice, Tanuma began returning to the streets on a timetable separate from magazine deadlines. Postwar magazine photography transmitted events quickly, then moved to the next story when an issue passed. By continuing to photograph the same city and generation outside commissioned work, Tanuma extended the temporal scale of news photography. Setagaya Art Museum’s Picturing My Tokyo 1948–1964 reedited ruins, markets, alleys, children’s play, and the urban transformations before the Tokyo Olympics as a single history of the city. *3

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
From Ihei Kimura’s Assistant to “My Own Photography”

What Tanuma inherited from Ihei Kimura was more than the technique of working quickly with a small camera. A Tokyo Polytechnic University retrospective recalls Kimura telling him, “Don’t imitate me,” reinforcing Tanuma’s need to find a subject of his own. *4 He consequently photographed ordinary contemporaries in the alleys even when no magazine had commissioned the work, alongside assignments involving public figures and events.

Why Photography? LIFE and Children as a “Mirror of Society”

As a young photographer, Tanuma was drawn less to the photograph as an isolated art object than to photojournalism that communicated society across the pages of magazines. In an interview, he recalls aspiring to the kind of reportage he saw in LIFE while still in photography school and forming a study group on reportage with his peers. *2 In another interview with the Kanto Federation of Bar Associations, he describes admiring Ihei Kimura, taking up a Leica, and beginning to photograph his own Asakusa neighborhood. *27 This starting point makes clear that his sustained attention to children cannot be explained by expressive faces alone.

Tanuma described children as a “mirror of society, a mirror of the times”*5. A single photograph can contain, along with a child’s face, the width of an alley, a house, clothing, toys, shops, roads, and surrounding adults. Details that functioned as background at the time of exposure can become evidence of historical difference decades later. By returning to the same subject over many years, Tanuma’s photographs of children moved from one-time news into an urban history in which living conditions and streets could be compared over time.

Children in Postwar Tokyo: How Tanuma Kept His Distance

When photographing children, Tanuma avoided joining their play in order to elicit smiles. In an interview with the Japan Foundation for Aging and Health, he says he tried to become like “air” or a “telephone pole”—a presence the children would cease to notice—and waited until ordinary behavior returned. *5 In photographs such as Endai Shogi, what remains is not a smile offered to the camera but the children’s own order of play and their use of the street. ToMuCo holds and publishes the 1955 work. *6

Finding “Children of the World” in Paris

While working abroad for Time-Life in the 1960s, Tanuma saw children playing in the Bois de Boulogne in Paris and, as he later recalled, clarified his lifelong subject of photographing children across national borders. *2 The JPS exhibition Hymn to Humanity placed the children and people he subsequently photographed in more than 130 countries in continuity with his photographs of postwar Japan. *7

The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s 2004 exhibition Portraits of Six Billion People states that Tanuma sought to approach the human world through children while looking across differences of culture, religion, wealth, and poverty*20. At the same time, his photobook Children of Planet Earth includes children who play, work, study, live through civil conflict, or wait for aid*21. “Children of the world” therefore did not erase difference through a simple universalism. The long-term project compares shared bodily vitality with the unequal social conditions that surround it.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
From Magazines to Photobooks: Turning News into Long-Term Record

In Tokyo Waga Zanzo, Shitamachi, Hitomukashi, and Sengo no Kodomotachi, accumulated photographs that allow urban change to be compared matter more than isolated high points. JCII’s Sengo no Kodomotachi assembled about one hundred photographs from 1949 to 1964, including kamishibai street theater, stilts, siblings, play, and family scenes, presenting such details as postwar history. *8 CiNii Books shows that the series was preserved through both exhibitions and photobooks. *9 Another volume devoted to everyday life in the 1950s retains stalls, housing, roads, and clothing that once belonged to the background but now function as clues to postwar life. *10

Musashino, Edo within Tokyo, and Postwar Tokyo: Photographing Place, Editing History Later

Tanuma’s long-term documentary work was not limited to children. Geographer Atsushi Naruse analyzes Musashino (1974) as a search for things that endure in place—natural landscape, architecture, and material remains—and Edo within Tokyo (1982) as an inquiry into continuities preserved in faces and ways of life*25. For Tanuma, who was unsettled by Tokyo’s rapid postwar transformation, photographing place also became a way to ask what persisted within a disappearing present.

In Naruse’s analysis, Postwar Tokyo (1993) cannot be treated simply as a transparent record of its original moment. Tanuma selected photographs made from the 1940s onward in the 1990s and arranged them as a postwar history; the photobook therefore preserves the past while also registering how the photographer interpreted that past decades later*25. Long-term documentary can accumulate time, but the selection made from that accumulation also constructs an image of history.

Tanuma’s work also extended well beyond children. A JCII exhibition on Romanesque culture in Catalonia presents photographs made during repeated visits in 1983–84, observing traces of religious architecture within lived landscapes over time. *14 In Children through the Seasons, festivals and annual observances foreground the physical roles children take within seasonal custom. *15

In Tanuma’s photobooks and retrospectives, photographs that were independent when made can be reread in new sequences decades later. This is another feature of long-term documentary. Street photographs from the 1950s recorded contemporary life when they first appeared, but they now also serve as historical material for the occupation, reconstruction, and the city before large-scale redevelopment. In a JCII exhibition on occupied Tokyo, Tanuma’s photographs of the “present-day city” were placed beside work by other photographers and reread as comparative evidence of roads, shops, housing, and clothing during the occupation. *18 The value of continuing to photograph in large quantity lies less in multiplying masterpieces than in creating enough density for later questions. Clothing, shop signs, roads, and the spacing of families can shift from background information in a single frame to a subject when decades of images are viewed together.

This capacity for reediting has kept Tanuma’s photographs active as historical material in the present.

UNICEF and More Than 130 Countries: A Link to International Humanitarianism

The photographs of children around the world are more than a collection of travel pictures. UNICEF Japan presents Tanuma’s long-term documentation of visits made by Goodwill Ambassador Tetsuko Kuroyanagi. *11 A 2005 UNICEF exhibition likewise used his photographs as a public medium through which Japanese audiences could see the lives of children in regions receiving support. *12 A memorial exhibition at Tokyo Polytechnic University placed photographs from Afghanistan, India, Cambodia, and elsewhere beside his images of Japanese children, making children living through play, labor, and family life comparable across differences of country and religion. *13

This attention to social conditions became even more explicit in his later editing. Crevis’s Mirai e Kakeru: Sekai no Kodomo organized about 210 photographs in chapters ranging from peaceful everyday life to “working” and “surviving”*22. By placing photographs that suggest the universality of children’s vitality beside images that register poverty, labor, and conflict, Tanuma’s humanism holds idealization and social documentation in tension.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photo History
sections.body_html:
“Hymn to Humanity” and Postwar Humanism: Universality and Difference

Tanuma is often praised as a photographer of “humanism” and a “hymn to humanity.” The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s major retrospective used Hymn to Humanity as its title and moved across postwar Tokyo, people around the world, and Musashino. *16 Crevis’s exhibition materials organize 205 works in three sections and describe the long career through a consistent interest in human beings. *17 Yet the phrase alone risks absorbing poverty, war, and the effects of development into a reassuring story of “resilient children.” Tanuma’s repeated work on the same subjects also records how housing, clothing, labor, and urban form change behind those faces.

Tanuma’s “hymn to humanity” shares concerns with international humanist photography after the 1950s, while his long-term projects retain specific social conditions within each frame. MoMA’s The Family of Man (1955) arranged 503 photographs around love, children, death, and other themes to propose common human experience and solidarity in the postwar world*26. Tanuma also approached shared human experience through children and families during this decade. His sustained series, however, leave labor, war, housing, religion, wealth, and poverty visible within the broad category of “children.” The Family of Man gathered the world into a single family metaphor; Tanuma’s repeated photographing and attention to place hold commonality and social difference together within a long record.

Tanuma’s work extends far beyond the category of a “photographer of children.” He carried the snapshot practice learned in Ihei Kimura’s magazine world from Tokyo to more than 130 countries and repeated it over decades. The Japan Foundation’s Metamorphosis of Japan after the War presented Tanuma as one of eleven photographers who recorded Japan’s transformation from the immediate postwar period toward high economic growth*23. The other participants included Ken Domon, Ihei Kimura, Hiroshi Hamaya, Tadahiko Hayashi, Yasuhiro Ishimoto, Shomei Tomatsu, Kikuji Kawada, Eikoh Hosoe, and others. FUJIFILM SQUARE’s Children in the Showa Era likewise placed Tanuma’s photographs of children alongside work by Kimura, Domon, Hamaya, Hayashi, and others, showing that children were a shared subject through which several photographers read social change before and after the war*24. Tanuma’s distinction lies in sustaining the subject from Tokyo to the world, and from one-off magazine assignments to a record broad enough to be compared and reedited across half a century.

A JCII exhibition on occupied Tokyo placed Tanuma beside contemporary press photographers and treated the images as testimony to urban history as well as personal memory*18. FUJIFILM’s English-language exhibition likewise presented his photographs of Tokyo’s reconstruction and high-growth period through the bodies of children and the changing street*19. After his apprenticeship with Ihei Kimura, Tanuma turned the speed of street photography into repeated documentation across decades. Children were a shared subject in his generation, but his sustained movement from Tokyo to the world and the volume of material later available for historical reediting give his work its particular outline.

Photographs of Postwar Children: Alleys, Housing, and Labor as Social History

Tanuma’s photographs of children can invite a humanist reading centered on facial expression, yet a long record makes the edges of the frame equally historical: bare feet or shoes, paved or unpaved alleys, temporary postwar walls or new construction, handmade toys or manufactured goods. Because Tanuma repeated the same broad subject—children at play—these details become legible as changes over time. Setagaya Art Museum’s 1948–64 exhibition and JCII’s postwar collection both organize his Tokyo photographs alongside the city’s reconstruction. *8 Tanuma’s method of keeping his distance until children forgot his presence also served more than the production of “natural” smiles. It preserved the social worlds children made among themselves instead of expressions performed for adults. *5 Once extended worldwide, the same approach risked romanticizing children as “all the same,” yet clothing, labor, family structure, schools, refugee camps, and other conditions remain visible as differences. Tokyo Polytechnic University’s Children of Japan, Children of the World places both groups together precisely at this intersection of commonality and difference. *13 In Tanuma’s long-term work, the child is simultaneously a figure of shared humanity and a sensitive register of historical conditions.

takuma-nakahira.html.lead_html: Takuma Nakahira was a photographer and critic who worked simultaneously in photography and criticism from the late 1960s, photographing the city at night, roads, waterfronts, plants, and islands. After using the grain, camera shake, and soft focus associated with PROVOKE to unsettle the relation between photographs and language, he went on to criticize the way that look itself became fixed as a recognizable 'Nakahira style.' In his 1973 book Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?, he reconsidered photography through differences among things, enumeration, and the position of the viewing body, seeking to reduce the tendency to gather objects under the photographer’s emotions or symbols. From Circulation and Overflow to the Amami and Tokara islands and his post-illness color photographs, he kept changing the forms of shooting, printing, photobooks, magazines, and wall installation as he examined throughout his life the terms on which photographs come into contact with the world.
takuma-nakahira.html.thesis_html: The coarse grain, camera shake, and soft focus of PROVOKE gave Nakahira a forceful and immediately recognizable authorial image. As the look was widely imitated, it increasingly functioned as a sign by which viewers could identify the photographer before attending to the subject. Nakahira refused to preserve that signature style. In Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? (1973), he proposed photographs that enumerate the differences among individual things while testing where the photographer’s body stands in relation to them*11. In Circulation, shooting, developing, and installation formed a daily cycle; in Overflow, forty-eight color photographs of manholes, subways, buildings, roads, signs, and a shark spread across a wall*2. His work consistently gives priority to testing whether a method can register differences among subjects and the photographer’s own position. The form changes sharply from PROVOKE to Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?, Overflow, the island photographs, and the color work after his illness, while the question remains the same: under what terms can a photograph meet the world?

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Reading Photographic History as an Editor

Nakahira studied Spanish at Tokyo University of Foreign Studies and joined the editorial staff of Gendai no Me after graduating in 1963, where he encountered the work of Shomei Tomatsu. He left the magazine in 1965 and began working as a photographer and critic; in 1968 he also took part in editing the exhibition A Century of Japanese Photography*2. SFMOMA notes that researching the history of Japanese photography for this exhibition strengthened his decision to concentrate on photography and led into the founding of PROVOKE that same year*16. Preparing the exhibition required extensive research into photographs from the late Edo period through the prewar years, old photography magazines, and documentary images whose makers were unidentified, along with debates over how roughly a century of Japanese photography should be presented as history*38. Just after beginning his career as a photographer, Nakahira was therefore rereading, from the editor’s desk, the ways photographs had operated across art, newspapers and magazines, state records, and wartime propaganda.

The National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo’s 2024 retrospective and catalog reconstructed this period as an editor through his post-illness work using photographs, magazines, manuscripts, and exhibition materials*30. Toshi Fūkei Zukan: Magazine Work 1964–1982 assembles a large body of photographs originally published in magazines and confirms how long the magazine page remained one of Nakahira’s principal sites of production*31.

The exhibition A Century of Japanese Photography opened in 1968, when Japan was publicly celebrating the achievements of high economic growth while the Vietnam War, pollution, student movements, and conflict over the U.S.–Japan Security Treaty unsettled society. Recent scholarship argues that the exhibition recovered anonymous documentary images and wartime photography as a way to reconsider Japanese modernization and photographers’ responsibility within it*39. The experience of assembling images made for different uses and by different or unknown makers, instead of treating photographic history as a sequence of masterpieces, gave Nakahira a concrete basis for later questioning the relations among photography, language, and institutions.

In A Century of Japanese Photography, Nakahira experienced how news, art, propaganda, and anonymous records could be selected and arranged into a single photographic history. PROVOKE, launched later that same year, made the very act of explaining the contemporary city through established photographic language a subject of criticism. Editing photographs of the past into a historical account and creating new pages responsive to the present city overlapped within a short span of time. Criticism and photography became the two main lines of his work.

Writing Criticism and Making Photographs

Nakahira had hoped to become a poet and was deeply engaged with political thought. He became wary of the power of political and artistic language to compress particular places and things into general concepts such as “city,” “nature,” or “revolution,” and later discussed the gap between the word “tree” and a single tree standing at a specific place and time*8. Photography allowed him to enter bodily into light, distance, surfaces, and surrounding circumstances and to test contact with a subject before it was classified in words. This expectation became a major reason for making photographs.

Mitsuzukeru Hate ni Hi ga...: Critical Writings 1965–1977 gathers essays whose questions continually shift, including “What Does It Mean to Be Contemporary?,” “Escape from the Image,” “The Illusion Called the Documentary,” and “Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?”*32. Nakahira used writing to articulate the limits of photography, tested those limits by shooting, then examined the results in the next piece of criticism. Through this back-and-forth movement, the photographs never settled into illustrations of a theory; making them also revised the theory itself.

The English-language selection edited by Daniel Abbe and Franz Prichard presents Nakahira's writings as thought moving across film, television, literature, politics, and urban experience, placing photography within this wider field*35. For Nakahira, the problem of photography extended through the entire process of who sees what, how it is explained in language, and through which medium it enters society. Those questions linked his criticism and his image-making.

PROVOKE and the Crisis of the City

In 1968, Nakahira, Koji Taki, Yutaka Takanashi, and Takahiko Okada founded PROVOKE; Daido Moriyama joined with the second issue. Its subtitle, “Provocative Materials for Thought,” proposed photographs as materials capable of setting thought in motion without submitting them to an already established explanation*20. International scholarship now treats the magazine as part of the contact zone among protest movements, avant-garde art, criticism, and publishing design in Japan of the late 1960s and 1970s, extending beyond the idea of a photographers’ group*33.

Research by the Art Institute of Chicago also places PROVOKE at a turning point in the relation between photography and language in postwar Japan*4. Tristan Ignas-Menzies further examines the magazine as a collective practice of realism carried out by several photographers and critics across its pages, with less emphasis on each maker’s individual style*24. Yasufumi Nakamori’s study of postwar Japanese photography offers a broader international frame for the photobooks, cities, politics, and avant-garde art of the same period*27.

Coarse grain, camera shake, soft focus, and extreme contrasts of light and dark slowed the impulse to attach immediate meanings to signs, roads, and faces. Nakahira was working in an era when newspapers, magazines, and television organized events into images for audiences, and he was concerned with the risk that organized images could be accepted as reality itself. Rei Masuda, curator of the 2024 retrospective, explains that are-bure-boke eventually became a style that could be readily imitated and congealed into another media language, helping drive Nakahira toward Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?*36.

In PROVOKE, paper stock, halftone dots, full-bleed printing, and the collision of images across a spread also shaped meaning. Gyewon Kim analyzes urban signs and printed lettering together with the paper, ink, and pages of the magazine as parts of a single media environment*26. Nakahira’s later shifts among shooting methods, photobooks, same-day installation, and wall display grew from the recognition that a photograph continues to acquire new readings through printing and placement after the shutter is released.

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
Landscape Theory: Roads, Waterfronts, and Urban Power

Nakahira repeatedly criticized the stance of a photographer who views the world from a protected position outside it. In a 1969 essay, he questioned photographers who assigned meaning to Okinawa, war, or student movements while leaving their own position hidden*37. He approached the politics of photography through both the choice of subject and the photographer’s location, emphasizing where the photographer stood and how the photographer’s body was implicated in the situation.

This thinking led into landscape theory. Roads, underpasses, reclaimed land, waterfronts, and expressways make transport networks, land development, and the plans of government and capital physically visible. A photograph of a demonstration shows people protesting. A photograph of a road or landfill can register the systems that organize movement and land use even on an ordinary day when no protest is taking place. Nakahira widened his attention from the central actors in an event to the spaces and infrastructure that keep society operating every day*17.

During the same period, the All-Japan Students’ Photo Association was producing collective documentary projects in Minamata, Yokkaichi, Ashio, and elsewhere by combining victims, land, historical documents, and statistics*29. Nakahira’s empty roads and waterfronts approached the same changes in industrial society through a different entry point. His emphasis fell on reading, through spaces without protagonists, the forms by which systems organize everyday life.

In the 1972 essay “The Illusion Called the Documentary,” written against the background of televised coverage of the United Red Army incident and the reversion of Okinawa, Nakahira examined how moving images deliver reality while also organizing the viewer’s position and the order in which events are understood*7. Yuriko Furuhata studies the image politics of this period through the relation between television, which repeatedly made events present to viewers, and avant-garde practices that read configurations of power in everyday landscapes*28. Nakahira’s photography and writing treated the politics of the subject and the mechanisms through which images circulate in society as parts of the same problem.

In “The Illusion Called the Documentary,” Nakahira focused on both the capacity of images to record events and the process by which those images are received as “reality” within the formats of television and magazines*7. Landscape theory carried the same question into roads and waterfronts, bringing transport, development, and land use—systems that organize society in ordinary time—into the frame.

Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?: Looking at Things One by One

The 1973 essay collection Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? occupies a central place in Nakahira’s work. The phrase “illustrated botanical dictionary” gave him a way to think of photography through the structure of a reference book that looks at and places things one entry at a time. Plants, buildings, roads, animals, and commodities could remain different things instead of being quickly gathered under the photographer’s emotions or turned into symbols of an era. Masashi Kohara describes the essay as Nakahira’s self-critique of the poetic imagery that had defined his earlier work and as a declaration in favor of photographs that clarify “things as things”*40.

Daniel Abbe and Franz Prichard's guide to Nakahira's major writings places the “botanical dictionary” within a long line of thought about language, realism, and the body*19. The failures of the PROVOKE period become material for the 1973 essay, which begins the work of reconsidering the terms of photography one by one.

The success of are-bure-boke itself was part of the problem. When night streets, people, roads, and animals were all enveloped in deep blacks, coarse grain, and blur, the impression of “a Nakahira photograph” could arrive before the differences among the subjects. The early look had helped him loosen the explanatory conventions of reportage; repetition and imitation turned it into a new convention. Nakahira then shifted attention toward the shape, color, surface, and location of individual things, reducing the dominance of the photographer’s emotional signature*11.

The word “dictionary” carries a sense of enumeration and classification. In a reference book, each plant sits beside other entries so their differences can be compared. Nakahira adapted this structure to photography in order to weaken the impulse to gather the world into a single narrative. Value no longer rested solely on the finished intensity of one image expressing the photographer’s feelings; it also emerged from the differences produced as separate things continued to appear side by side*11.

Names and classifications in language also stand between photographs and things. A botanical dictionary names its entries, and viewers likewise recognize subjects through words such as “tree,” “road,” or “commodity.” Nakahira wanted photography to receive the color, scars, distance, light, and surrounding space that remain after language has gathered an object under a single word. He sought to return to the photographic surface the individuality lost when one tree is subsumed under the concept “tree.” This tension lies at the root of Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?*10.

Enumeration and Juxtaposition: Why a “Dictionary”?

The structure of the “dictionary” concerns arrangement as much as shooting. Nakahira considered an enumerative form in which entries stand in parallel, moving away from compositions that make one image the representative work and subordinate the surrounding photographs to its explanation. Franz Prichard argues that the photographs and texts gathered in Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? retain the structure of fragments published over time in magazines, allowing parts to remain parts instead of resolving them into a single theme*18.

This idea was already anticipated by Circulation in 1971. Nakahira photographed large numbers of subjects encountered in Paris during the day, developed them at night, and added the prints to the wall the next day. The gallery accumulated the quantity of a day’s movement and encounters, emphasizing the expanding sequence over any single photograph*8. Because each day’s shooting fed directly into the next day’s installation, editing proceeded through the time spent walking through the city as well as through selection after the fact.

Prichard reads this repetition and enumeration as a way of following the circulation of an urban media environment without summarizing it under one meaning*18. The enumeration of Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? similarly restrains the desire to choose one photograph to stand for the world: subject A is followed by B, then C. The number of entries in the world begins to outpace the photographer’s explanation.

The Photographer’s Body and the Response of Things

While thinking through the “botanical dictionary,” Nakahira also became acutely conscious of the photographer’s body. In writing from 1973, he argued that seeing cannot be separated from the body and that the viewer is also exposed to the gaze of others. Daniel Abbe reads this as evidence that Nakahira located the politics of vision in the relation between a situated body and a place, instead of in the fantasy of an all-seeing observer*37.

When a camera is raised, the photographer occupies a place in front of the subject. Moving closer changes its scale; crouching shifts the horizon; turning the camera vertically cuts away surrounding information; the time of the exposure changes the light. These bodily decisions remain in the photograph even when the photographer tries to restrain personal emotion. Nakahira conceived objectivity as a demanding effort to receive the specificity of the subject while remaining conscious of one’s own position*23.

Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? holds together two demands: preserving differences among things by restraining the photographer’s emotional imprint, and recognizing that the photographer’s bodily decisions inevitably remain in the image. Nakahira left this tension open and carried it into later color work, wall installations, and photography on the islands. Each change of place and medium became another test of the relation between the specificity of the subject and the photographer’s position.

SFMOMA’s essay “The Man Who Became a Camera” likewise reads Nakahira through the relation between body and camera, emphasizing the pressure the world exerts on the photographer through movement and shooting*14. His demand to see a thing as a thing becomes more concrete when it includes this receptivity of the body.

Atget, Evans, and the Description of Things

By the mid-1970s, Nakahira had come to value the photographs of Eugène Atget and Walker Evans highly. Rei Masuda notes that in a 1976 “duel on photography” with Kishin Shinoyama, Nakahira connected the effort to photograph the social world extensively with Atget and Evans*36. Their descriptions of streets, buildings, interiors, commodities, and people without turning every subject into a large drama resonated with his effort to look at the world one entry at a time.

International criticism surrounding the 2025 English-language selection notes that Nakahira responded strongly to the quiet descriptive force of Evans’s photographs in Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, and that he read Atget’s photographs as images in which the city entered from the other side through an “empty eye”*21. In these examples, he sought to slow the conversion of a subject into the photographer’s symbol and to increase the information that could enter the photograph from the subject itself.

During the same years, the nouveau roman and Mono-ha were also giving increased attention to things, surfaces, arrangement, and perception, loosening the priority of psychological characterization and authorial narrative. Neil Matheson examines the relation between the nouveau roman and Japanese photography through urban alienation and the look directed toward material things*3. Philip Charrier’s study of Koji Taki’s image theory likewise traces structuralist thinking about photographs as signs and structures around PROVOKE*25. Evidence for direct lines of influence remains limited, but around 1970 the question of turning from authorial interiority toward things was being pursued across several fields, and Nakahira’s thinking developed within that critical environment.

Experiments, 1973–77

The years after Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? were a period of testing new methods of shooting and editing. Research for the 2024 retrospective confirmed that Nakahira continued taking photographs during a period he described as a slump and experimented with ways of presenting them while combining new work with earlier images*36. A gap remained between theoretical declaration and actual shooting, and the attempts to work through it form a central part of his production from 1973 to 1977.

Nakahira’s self-criticism extended beyond words. SFMOMA’s biography records that around 1973 he burned negatives and prints of his early work*16. Choosing continued photography over the preservation of images already gaining recognition as signature works gives Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? the weight of a concrete decision as well as a change in photographic thinking.

From 1973 to 1977, several demands remained active at once: weakening the authorial image, preserving differences among things, acknowledging the photographer’s bodily position, and dealing with the meanings already attached to advertising and signs. Nakahira continued testing these terms through shooting, magazine publication, photobooks, and exhibitions instead of settling on one finished formula. Overflow became a major attempt to give these questions form through forty-eight color photographs and the simultaneity of a wall installation*41.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
For a Language to Come

For a Language to Come (1970), Nakahira’s first photobook, sequences night roads, underpasses, windows, people, animals, and signs in coarse-grained black and white. Its 192 images were arranged across glossy spreads; deep blacks, blown highlights, flash reflections, and full-bleed printing draw attention to both the subject and the printed surface*5. Jelena Stojković analyzes the material of the city and the paper and ink of the photobook as two aspects of the same problem of surfaces*17.

At the Paris Youth Biennale in 1969, Nakahira presented La nuit*16. SFMOMA’s La nuit 1 shows the night city, dense blacks, and artificial light that characterize this early vision*6. For a Language to Come carried that nocturnal photography into the sequence of photobook pages, paper, ink, and spreads.

The book gives its reader no orderly explanation of the city. Turning the pages brings repeated encounters with dark roads, figures, light, and letters. The roughness of the photographs conveys urban speed and instability while also disturbing the expectation that the printed page will transport information smoothly. For Nakahira, the photobook became a site where images collide and even the tempo of reading can be altered*26.

This visual intensity quickly became influential and reproducible as a style. Nakahira treated that success as a new problem, and in Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? reconsidered the poetic charge of the images and the authorial persona attached to them. For a Language to Come thus became both a major work and the starting point for his criticism of his own signature imagery*36.

Circulation

At the 1971 Paris Youth Biennale, Nakahira photographed the city each day, developed the film at night, and added prints to the gallery wall the following day. At roughly two hundred exposures a day, shooting, movement, darkroom labor, and installation became continuous, and the wall expanded throughout the exhibition*8. The work was generated from the time he spent in Paris instead of arriving as a finished set of photographs transported from Japan.

SFMOMA now holds individual prints from Circulation: Date, Place, Events, but in the original work each photograph functioned as one element in a wall that grew day by day*9. Distinguishing the present-day individual print from the 1971 installation clarifies why the work gives such weight to process.

This method exposed the photographer’s body directly to traffic, pedestrians, commodities, signs, and weather. Daniel Abbe analyzes Circulation as a circuit in which the photographer’s body moves through the flows of the city and returns the received images to the exhibition space within the same day*23. Nakahira’s criticism of the “eye” that imagines itself outside the world took concrete form here as walking and working time.

The combinations in the gallery also changed according to where a visitor stood. A single directional sequence, like the order of pages in a book, weakened as yesterday’s images and today’s images became simultaneously visible. Circulation can be read as an early enactment of the enumeration Nakahira later developed in Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?, here materialized as an urban quantity that shooting and installation could barely keep pace with*18.

Overflow and Color

Overflow, shown in the 1974 exhibition Fifteen Photographers Today, arranged forty-eight color photographs of manholes, subways, buildings, roads, signs, a shark, and other subjects across a wall roughly six meters wide*12. SFMOMA’s research places the work among the experiments Nakahira pursued after the publication of Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? as he moved beyond the PROVOKE period*41.

Color served a specific function beyond visual renewal. Subjects that could easily be absorbed into a common look by strong black-and-white contrast could retain differences in sign colors, painted surfaces, commodities, plants, and the skin of a fish. Color became concrete information as Nakahira extended the concern with differences among things from Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? to urban artifacts and living bodies.

Across the wall, all forty-eight photographs entered the field of vision together and weakened attention to a single representative image. There was no guarantee that viewers would read from left to right: up close they could inspect one surface, while from a distance signs of the city approached as a swarm. Enumeration, first considered through the photobook, expanded into a relation between the viewer’s body and exhibition space*2.

The city itself was already emitting meanings through advertising, product names, signs, and architectural color. Even with the photographer’s emotional imprint restrained, the subjects retained meanings assigned by urban systems—brand names, signage, functions, and use. Overflow makes visible across the wall a city already saturated with signs before the photographer adds an interpretation. The work brings Nakahira’s effort to approach things directly into contact with the reality of a mediated city*17.

Amami, Tokara, and the Question of Boundaries

In Okinawa in 1973 and in Amami and Tokara from 1974 to 1978, Nakahira shifted his field of work away from Tokyo’s roads and waterfronts to the boundary zones between mainland Japan and the southwestern islands. The photobook Okinawa, Amami, Tokara 1974–1978 includes coasts, settlements, plants, people, and roads, accumulating differences in surface and everyday life from place to place instead of compressing the islands into a single image of the tropical south*34.

Here the enumeration of Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? expands into geography and politics. Places that can appear as a single category—“Okinawa” or “the southern islands”—when named from Tokyo have different histories, transport networks, settlements, and vegetation from island to island. By walking across multiple islands and continuing to photograph particular places, Nakahira approached differences that broad mainland categories leave out. SFMOMA’s research bibliography identifies Nobuo Kuraishi’s study of “borders” in Amami and Tokara as a major source for this work*22.

Nakahira held anti-imperialist political commitments. In the island photographs, he made the act of seeing from a particular point a photographic problem: from where, and whose land, is being viewed? Sea, roads, houses, plants, and people accumulate across the pictures, and the photographer’s position is renewed with each exposure*37.

A New Gaze After His Illness

In 1977, Nakahira collapsed from acute alcohol poisoning and suffered severe damage to memory and language. He resumed photographing and continued with A New Gaze in 1983, Adieu à X in 1989, and color photographs of Yokohama in the 2000s*13. The post-illness work repeatedly shows roadside plants, signs, buildings, animals, and people encountered while walking, often in lucid color and vertical frames.

His 2004 color work also includes a series titled Documentary, and SFMOMA holds a work from that year*15. The word “Documentary” reappears more than three decades after the 1972 essay, now within the daily act of walking around Yokohama and repeatedly photographing plants, buildings, signs, and people.

Sources that directly establish how Nakahira himself understood the continuity between his pre- and post-illness theories are limited. The Yokohama Museum of Art describes his pursuit of direct encounters with subjects as continuing after the illness*13. Rei Masuda also points to visual echoes between the post-illness color and vertical photographs and the direction outlined by “botanical dictionary” thinking in the 1970s*36. Claims of continuity are therefore best kept within what repeated features in the works and surviving statements can support.

After the illness, photography again took shape as a repeated activity of everyday life: walking, finding, approaching, framing, and exposing, day after day. The connection with the task in Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?—looking at things one entry at a time—is strongest at this level of action directed toward subjects. The surviving evidence supports the link most clearly here and stops short of establishing one unbroken theory across the two periods.

sections.title: Criticism and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Critiquing the Success of PROVOKE

Nakahira’s place in photographic history lies in both the intensity of are-bure-boke and the process by which he turned that success into an object of self-criticism. He treated the recognition, imitation, and eventual hardening of his own visual language into a readily identifiable style as a problem of photography itself. He criticized the PROVOKE look, moved toward enumeration in Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?, tested color and wall installation in Overflow, examined place island by island in Amami and Tokara, and after his illness returned repeatedly to walking and photographing.

His consistency lies in repeatedly examining the relation between the world and the photographer. The viewer’s body, distance from a subject, printing, photobooks, magazines, walls, and the signs of the city all became terms that one body of work could expose for reconsideration in the next. In a system where a successful look can become a photographer’s brand, Nakahira’s continued criticism of his own signature style has had lasting significance*36.

This attitude made available to later photographers a critical model of making work while questioning the method that produces it. Nakahira joined photography and thinking about photography in a structure where each continually revised the other, bringing the roles of photographer and critic into one sustained body of work.

Three Questions in Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?

Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? has generated several lines of interpretation. Philip Charrier reads critically the persistence in Nakahira of a postwar realist desire for the camera as a machine that might restrain authorial subjectivity and approach reality more directly*11. Franz Prichard emphasizes the enumeration of photographs and texts as fragments, treating it as a way to track the urban media environment without totalizing it*18. Daniel Abbe, drawing on Nakahira’s own writing about a body exposed within the act of seeing, stresses the politics of a situated gaze*37.

These readings reveal different layers of the same text. One concerns realism: how concretely can a photograph record a thing? A second concerns editing: how can multiple fragments be arranged without making one image the center? A third concerns the fact that the photographer’s body and political position remain in the photograph. The force of Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? comes from carrying these unresolved tensions into the work that followed.

When the English-language selection of Nakahira’s writings was introduced in the Spanish-speaking press in 2026, particular attention was given to his reconsideration of the relation between the “eye” and its subject through Evans and Atget, and to his understanding of seeing as participation in the world*21. International readers increasingly approach Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? as a concentrated treatment of authorship, objectivity, embodiment, and enumeration—questions that remain active in contemporary photography.

Reassessment and International Scholarship

For many years outside Japan, the coarse black-and-white work associated with PROVOKE circulated as Nakahira’s representative image. The Yokohama Museum of Art’s 2003 retrospective assembled roughly eight hundred photographs, magazines, and archival materials, presenting the early work, Magazine Work, Circulation, Overflow, and the post-illness photographs as a single production history*13. The National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo’s 2024 retrospective reexamined magazine pages and materials from the mid-1970s, giving much closer attention to the activity surrounding Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?*36.

The National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo titled its 2024 exhibition Burn—Overflow and presented the early black-and-white work, Circulation, experiments around Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?, Overflow, the islands, and the post-illness period together with extensive documentary material*1. The exhibition substantially enlarged an image of Nakahira that had often centered on PROVOKE by bringing the photography and criticism of the mid-1970s and later into view.

In 2025, At the Limits of the Gaze, the first substantial English-language selection of Nakahira’s writings, made his criticism across photography, film, journalism, literature, politics, and television broadly accessible to English-language readers*35. Recent scholarship increasingly asks why Nakahira changed methods, how the viewing body relates to its subjects, and how a photograph’s function changes across magazines, photobooks, and exhibitions, alongside the visual contrast between are-bure-boke and his later color work*30.

talbot.html.lead_html: Talbot invented the calotype, establishing the negative-positive principle that made photography reproducible from a single exposure. The Pencil of Nature (1844–46) was the first commercially published photographically illustrated book, demonstrating photography as record, art, and reproductive medium simultaneously.
talbot.html.thesis_html: Talbot invented the calotype, a negative–positive process, and introduced the principle of photographic reproducibility into the history of the medium. Where the daguerreotype was a unique, unrepeatable object, Talbot's process allowed any number of positive prints from a single negative, laying the foundation for the reproductive logic that would later underpin twentieth-century magazines, newspapers, books, and advertising. With “The Pencil of Nature” (1844–46) he realized the first commercially published, photographically illustrated book, showing that photography could function at once as record, art, and reproduction. His strict management of patents ironically slowed the spread of his methods, yet in conceptual and technical reach his contribution extends across twentieth-century photographic culture.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
William Henry Fox Talbot was born in 1800 at Melbury Sampford, Dorset. He studied Latin, Greek, mathematics, and natural science at Cambridge and later produced work across linguistics, botany, and astronomy — a nineteenth-century polymath whose photography was only one strand of a broad scientific practice*1.

The turning point came in October 1833 at Lake Como, on his honeymoon. Trying to sketch with a camera lucida, he was frustrated by what he saw as his own inability to draw. He later wrote that once he looked away from the device, "only a faint and imperfect trace" was left on the paper. That frustration prompted the question of whether the camera's projected image might be fixed chemically, and he began experiments on his return*2.

In the summer of 1835 he placed small cameras around Lacock Abbey, recording the buildings on sensitized paper. His wife called the boxes "mousetrap cameras." The Latticed Window (c.1835), a fragment barely 2.5 × 2.5 cm, is the oldest surviving Talbot image from this period*3.

When news of Daguerre's success arrived in January 1839, Talbot hastened to publicize his own method. The calotype process, patented in 1841 under that name, used paper negatives and allowed multiple positive prints from a single exposure — the first practical negative-positive photography. The Pencil of Nature, published in installments from 1844 to 1846, was the first commercially produced book illustrated with photographs, demonstrating photography as record, art, and reproduced medium across its twenty-four plates*4.

Talbot's strict patent enforcement significantly slowed British photography relative to France. He also devoted much of his later life to cuneiform decipherment. He died in 1877*5.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The difference between calotype and daguerreotype is not simply a matter of technical quality. The daguerreotype aimed at a faithful, non-reproducible record on a singular object; the calotype combined paper's grainy, soft texture with the capacity to make multiple copies*6. Talbot's process is the origin of the modern photographic concept in which "photographs are reproduced."

The material character of the paper negative — the way the paper's grain merges with the image — was both a visual limitation and the source of the painterly quality that Hill and Adamson discovered. For the first plate of The Pencil of Nature — Lacock Abbey's latticed window — Talbot wrote one of the earliest theoretical and philosophical texts about photography, raising for the first time what a photograph fundamentally is*7.

The negative-positive principle established by Talbot became the foundation for all subsequent photographic reproduction: film photography, halftone printing, photogravure, and eventually digital image capture. In this respect Talbot's contribution is more conceptual and technical than it is aesthetic, and its full significance emerged over the following century*8.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Talbot's patent policy became one of photography's early ironies: the inventor of a reproducible medium inhibited the medium's reproduction. British commercial photography was measurably slower to develop than its French counterpart through the 1840s*9. After 1852 Talbot relaxed some restrictions and allowed amateur use without fee.

The core of Talbot's legacy is the negative. That concept — one exposure, many prints — underpinned the entire photographic economy of the twentieth century: magazines, newspapers, books, and advertising. The Metropolitan Museum names him as co-inventor of photography alongside Daguerre*10, and the V&A holds one of the world's largest Talbot collections alongside the in situ holdings at Lacock Abbey*11.

Lacock Abbey (Wiltshire) is preserved by the National Trust; the rooms and darkroom where Talbot worked are open to visitors. The Fox Talbot Museum opened in 1975 and holds original prints and experimental notebooks*12. In recent years, Talbot's photogenic drawings of plant specimens have begun to attract art-historical attention in their own right, as objects that sit between scientific record and aesthetic form*13.

the-atlas-group-walid-raad.html.lead_html: The Atlas Group is a long-term project that Walid Raad began presenting in the late 1990s under the name of a fictional research foundation. Raad made and collected photographs, videos, notebooks, newspaper materials, and data tables, classifying them as documents received from invented historians and donors. The real elements include Raad himself, existing press materials, the artworks he produced, exhibitions, lectures, and the website. The foundation’s institutional history, several of its contributors, and parts of the documents’ provenance were invented. Through “Missing Lebanese Wars,” “The Bachar Tapes,” and “My Neck Is Thinner Than a Hair,” the project shows how histories of war are assembled from images, authors’ names, dates, classifications, narrators, and collecting institutions.
the-atlas-group-walid-raad.html.thesis_html: Discussions of war photography often centered on whether individual images or testimonies were true. To address whose documents the memories of civil war become, and how they enter public history, Raad created the fictional research foundation The Atlas Group. By assuming the roles of author, donor, custodian, and lecturer, he shifted the question from the authenticity of a photograph to the archives and institutions that establish a fact.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
How The Atlas Group Works

Walid Raad conceived The Atlas Group and presented it as a research foundation*6. The photographs, videos, notebooks, exhibitions, lectures, and website produced by Raad are real. The foundation’s institutional history, several donors and researchers, and parts of the provenance assigned to its documents were invented. In exhibitions, photographs and notebooks carrying file numbers appear on walls and in cases; in lectures, Raad explains their origins as a representative of the foundation. A single artist performs the roles of author, custodian, classifier, and interpreter, exposing every stage through which an archive is constituted.*1*4

Raad began using The Atlas Group name publicly in the late 1990s, while the project itself assigns the foundation an operating period of 1989 to 2004.*4. Accounts of its founding date and cofounders changed across presentations, and the biographies of its invented researchers and donors were revised. Through exhibitions, a website, lectures, and archival boxes, the imaginary foundation gradually acquired the outward behavior of an actual research institution.*7. Allowing the organization’s own history to change demonstrated how chronologies and institutional narratives support trust in documents.

Why a Fictional Foundation Was Necessary

The Lebanese Civil War, which lasted from 1975 to 1990, involved multiple political factions, religious communities, foreign armies, and militias. Even after the ceasefire, no shared account of its causes and responsibilities took hold easily. Reconstruction prioritized the physical rebuilding of Beirut, while memories of the war remained divided among political groups, families, exiles, and news organizations. Raad has explained that he collected existing documents and photographs while also imagining “the worlds in which those documents existed”*7. This idea led to a foundation that placed real and invented materials within the same system of classification.

Raad sought to address the events of the war together with the procedures through which fragmentary photographs and testimonies become public history. A work presented under an individual artist’s name identifies its maker, but it cannot reproduce all the authority added through donation, classification, preservation, exhibition, and scholarly presentation. A fictional foundation could attribute conflicting accounts to different contributors, place real and invented materials in the same formats, and allow Raad to explain them in the role of a researcher. The foundation allowed Raad to hold conflicting memories of the civil war within one project and to stage the institutional processes through which history acquires credibility.*18*8

sections.title: How Documents Become Facts
sections.body_html:
“Different Kinds of Facts”

Raad has said that his work begins with facts, and that facts possess historical, emotional, and aesthetic dimensions.A MoMA audio guide presents this statement as a key to understanding The Atlas Group’s method *2. Chronologies and statistics can record the date and location of an explosion and the number of deaths. Emotional memory also preserves the sensation of seeing a red car and anticipating a bomb, the excessive intensity of color, or a body repeating the same gesture. Fictional documents preserve verifiable information and emotional traces as distinct layers, widening the forms through which wartime experience can be conveyed.

Giving Documents a Provenance

Seen without their captions, The Atlas Group’s photographs can resemble newspaper clippings, family snapshots, police records, or research notes. Names such as Dr. Fadl Fakhouri and Souheil Bachar, along with notebook numbers, donation dates, and classification codes, give the materials a provenance. KADIST describes Raad’s manipulation of vernacular photographs and archival documents as an examination of the boundaries between document and fiction, history and memory, discourse and experience*5. In a MoMA audio guide, Raad describes combining old family slides with photographs of assassinations gathered from Lebanese photographic archives, treating images he made and images he collected as materials within the same process*3. The invented author functions as a character within the narrative and as a means of exposing the institutional habit of establishing value by asking whose document it is.

Lecture-Performance

Raad paired wall displays with lecture-performances, showing slides and explaining the origins of files in the manner of a researcher or foundation representative. The narration adopts the measured tone of an academic presentation, while contradictions in dates and relationships gradually emerge. Aperture argues that the lecture itself becomes an artistic form that produces the credibility of the documents in real time*13. The audience compares images, captions, and the speaker’s demeanor, while testing its own inclination to trust a professional mode of address. In a conversation with John Menick, Raad discusses in detail how the work asks viewers to assess both the lecturer’s authority and the credibility of the story*17*14.

Experiences That Escape Classification

The Atlas Group follows the process through which materials receive authors’ names, dates, classification numbers, and donation records, are arranged in orderly sequences, and come to be read as historical evidence. Classification turns fragments into searchable history, while organizing sensation and contradiction into a coherent account. By introducing invented contributors and shifting provenances, Raad placed the understanding produced by archival order beside the experiences that order excludes.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Medium
sections.body_html:
Missing Lebanese Wars

“Missing Lebanese Wars” uses notebooks, clippings, photographs, and annotations to construct the invented story of Lebanese historians who attended the racetrack and wagered on the exact moment the winning horse crossed the finish line. Museo Reina Sofía presents the work as a parallel between faith in photography’s “decisive moment” and the historian’s act of determining when an event begins and ends*20. The racetrack finish photograph makes concrete the question of who selects a war’s beginning, turning points, and end, and which records preserve those decisions.

My Neck Is Thinner Than a Hair

This project is framed as an investigation of car bombs used during the Lebanese wars through the relations among wreckage at blast sites, engines, newspaper photographs, photographers, and the publications in which the images appeared. The official archive describes the work as a study of 3,641 car-bomb incidents*10. By tracing engines thrown far from the explosion and the positions from which press cameras photographed them, the work follows the path through which evidence of violence is produced across the site, the newspaper, and the archive.

The Bachar Tapes

In “The Bachar Tapes,” the testimony of the fictional Lebanese hostage Souheil Bachar is inserted into the history of Western hostages held in Lebanon during the 1980s. The National Gallery of Canada describes the work as an inquiry into which experiences enter international news through the translation, editing, and delay of video testimony*11. By adding a witness who did not exist, the work makes visible how established hostage narratives were edited around particular nationalities, languages, and forms of masculinity. SFMOMA’s artist record also identifies the video as a major work in which photography, testimony, and translation intersect*9.

Comparison with the Arab Image Foundation

During the same period in Beirut, the Arab Image Foundation collected and preserved historic and studio photographs, providing a physical repository for vulnerable regional photographic cultures. A conversation in Bidoun places this real archive beside The Atlas Group: the former preserves material objects and researches their provenance, while the latter uses fictional donors and classifications to question the authority of preservation itself*7. Raad affirms the value of preservation while treating the assignment of preserved objects to particular narratives as a separate artistic problem.

sections.title: Criticism, Reception, and Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Fiction and Historical Responsibility

The Atlas Group can be criticized for relativizing real suffering by mixing invented people and events into the history of an actual war. In a conversation with The Brooklyn Rail, Raad states that he made the project’s images and stories and attributed them to fictional figures, while asking that the method not be reduced to a simple test of truth or falsity *15. A risk remains when only audiences familiar with museum conventions can recognize the device: Lebanese history may then be consumed as a conceptual game. The work’s ethical tension lies in keeping this danger visible and extending the question to who has the right to use fiction. An ICA Boston retrospective presented Raad’s movement between fact and invention together with this ethical unease*12.

Post-Documentary

Photographic history already contained debates over documentary evidence and artistic practices that criticized archival classification and institutional authority. Raad connected those debates to memories of the Lebanese Civil War and combined a fictional foundation, changing provenances, and lecture-performances within a single structure*18. A single invented photograph addresses only the image itself. Ownership, storage, narration, and public acceptance require a larger structure. Through the foundation, Raad created authors, donors, classifiers, a collecting institution, and a lecturer, reconstructing the entire process through which facts gain social credibility. Teaching materials from Art Resources Transfer likewise describe his movement among the roles of archivist, historian, teacher, performer, and artist in order to examine the power and limits of documents to communicate history*16. The Atlas Group’s significance within photographic history lies in shifting the question from “Is this photograph authentic?” to “What makes this photograph credible as a historical fact?”*11*19.

Real and Invented Materials

The real elements are Walid Raad himself; the photographs, videos, and notebooks he produced; existing newspaper photographs and broadcast materials; exhibitions; lectures; and the official website. Invented elements include the institutional history of an independent foundation, contributors such as Dr. Fadl Fakhouri and Souheil Bachar, researchers’ biographies, and parts of the documents’ provenance. Individual files combine the two. “My Neck Is Thinner Than a Hair,” for example, uses actual press materials and field research, reediting them as the foundation’s research files. The construction asks viewers to read the content of an image together with the credibility conferred by an author’s name, a date, a classification number, and a museum display.*1

thomas-demand.html.lead_html: Thomas Demand (born in Germany in 1964) works with realities that have already been framed through someone else’s viewpoint—news photographs, documentary images, personal snapshots, and architectural models. He reconstructs them at life size in paper and cardboard, then presents them as photographs.*7 Around 1993, photography shifted from a means of documenting his sculptures to the final work itself, and his subjects expanded from places he knew firsthand to history and politics encountered through other people’s images.*5 In building the models, he must infer depth and dimensions absent from the source image, while deciding which figures, texts, and signs of use to retain. Photographing the model again closes that inquiry back into a single viewpoint and returns it to circulation in the same one-image format as news and documentary photography.*30 Through works including 《Raum》, 《Poll》, 《Presidency》, 《Yellowcake》, 《Control Room》, and 《Dailies》, Demand has examined how photographs do more than lodge events in memory: they also participate in the production of political authority and factual accounts.
thomas-demand.html.thesis_html: From the late 1970s through the 1980s, Jeff Wall restaged events he had witnessed using actors.*26 James Casebere photographed tabletop models, giving seemingly plausible spaces an atmosphere of anxiety and surveillance.*25 Demand took specific news and documentary photographs that many viewers had seen in place of the actual site and rebuilt them as life-size objects, using his hands and body to construct spaces he had never experienced from another person’s single viewpoint.*5 By inferring what the source image withheld and turning the model back into a photograph, he extended constructed photography beyond invented scenes to the process by which news and documentary images become stand-ins for events through selection, omission, and repetition.*40
