sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Social Anthropology and Photography — Starting with What Is Visible, Then Researching What Is Not

Ribas studied social anthropology at the University of Barcelona and later documentary photography. The University of Brighton describes his work as an investigation of cities, geography, and history through photography, archives, and text*1 Fotografia a Catalunya likewise identifies both social anthropology and photographic training as foundations of his work*2 Oral Memories records that he completed a degree in social anthropology at the University of Barcelona in 1990 and studied documentary photography at Newport School of Art, Media and Design in the United Kingdom in 1993*20 MACBA’s artist profile traces a continuity from Sundays through Nitrate in which present-day views of places are connected to historical and political research*22 In a TANK interview, Ribas summarized his concern as how to move “from an object to its history”*23That sequence explains why photography is useful to him. The camera can first fix the present condition of a fence, extraction site, or vacant lot in concrete detail. Why the object is there, who owns it, and which institutions or transactions produced it remain outside the image. Ribas therefore uses photography as the entry point to an investigation that follows causes invisible in the frame through documents, maps, and archives. Anthropology and photography do not duplicate the same information; they divide the work between a visible present and histories that cannot be photographed directly.

Sundays — Reading Post-Olympic Barcelona from Its Margins and Leisure Spaces

Made from 1994 to 1997, Sundays is an early major series showing families and friends spending their Sunday leisure time on vacant lots, in industrial zones, and along roadsides in Barcelona. Banco de España identifies both spaces outside the city’s official public realm and the ways people use them as central concerns in Ribas’s work*3 In the collection work Untitled, Bellvitge, suburban ground and improvised leisure carry equal visual weight, making uses unplanned by urban development visible*4Ribas photographed vacant land used for picnics and walks on the city’s margins after the 1992 Olympics, recording the gap between redevelopment plans and actual land use. MACBA holds Sundays as a 1994–97 series and specifically notes the picnics, walks, rest, and play that took place on vacant lots and in industrial areas at the urban edge*18.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Sanctuary and Concrete Geographies — Photographing Structures Left after an Event

MACBA’s Nitrate exhibition framed the movement from Sundays through Sanctuary and Concrete Geographies as an expansion from the study of urban margins toward questions of territory and exclusion*5 Concrete Geographies photographs fences in Ceuta and Melilla, scarred ground, and structures that restrict access. The University of Brighton records the work as research into territory, movement, and exclusion through the border fences of Spanish North Africa*9Even without people in the frame, the height of a fence, a severed road, or damaged ground preserves policy in physical form. Instead of photographing the drama of border crossing, Ribas made the infrastructure that repeatedly produces that drama the subject of a series. In the 2008 Nòmades, after roughly sixty Roma families were expelled from a vacant lot in Barcelona, he photographed ground torn up by heavy machinery and cracks in concrete as a thirty-six-image series*21By not photographing the eviction itself and instead tracing the event through physical marks left afterward, Nòmades makes the underlying question of Concrete Geographies especially concrete.

Ownership and Contracts Do Not Appear in a Photograph — Putting Documents on Equal Footing

In Ribas’s exhibitions, documents and writing do not function simply as captions that make the photographs easier to understand. Research documentation for Concrete Geographies shows photographic grids, texts, and archival material combined so that the border landscape is not reduced to a single meaning*8 When Ribas described his interest to TANK as moving “from an object to its history,” he was pointing to the fact that the laws, ownership structures, and administrative decisions behind a fence or a patch of ground cannot be seen in the photograph itself*23Nitrate makes the same problem even more explicit. Alongside photographs of extraction sites in the desert, Ribas places corporate material and records of finance and ownership to follow the route by which nitrate extracted in Chile became assets in Britain. The exhibition asks viewers to compare two distinct forms of evidence: a present visible in photographs and causes preserved in documents.

Nitrate — Following Capital from the Atacama to London

Nitrate is a long-term project that follows nitrate extraction in Chile’s Atacama Desert and the movement of capital into British companies, financial markets, and estates through photographs, documents, commodities, and maps. The University of Brighton’s Traces of Nitrate describes a collaborative investigation of how the mineral moved from extraction site to commodity, share value, and British asset*6 In World of Matter’s Sites of Capital, financial spaces in London and traces of ownership far from the mines are treated as part of the same material history*10 Acción Cultural Española describes the exhibition as combining photographs, polyptychs, texts, and moving images while also examining photography’s own capacity to record*24Instead of asking desert photographs alone to stand as symbols of colonialism, Ribas traces where nitrate traveled and what forms of property it became, shifting attention from the appearance of a landscape to the verification of a route.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The Photobook Nitrate — Editing Research into a Sequence for Reading

The photobook Nitrate was conceived less as a record of an exhibition than as a research medium in which images and historical documents are read through page sequence. The University of Brighton bibliography records it as a publication containing texts by several researchers, underscoring its collaborative character beyond the format of a single photographer’s monograph*7 The Van Abbemuseum library likewise situates the book around the relationship among nitrate extraction, colonial economies, and photography*11After looking at photographs of the desert or buildings, readers can consult research texts in the same volume to establish facts about ownership and the movement of capital. Conversely, the present condition of extraction sites and buildings—information that research prose cannot substitute for—is available in the photographs. The editing assigns distinct functions to the two kinds of material. The ICP Library also holds Ribas’s 1998 publication IMAGO, showing that he circulated photography in book form before his later large-scale research projects*16.

Nitrate at MACBA — Turning the Exhibition into a Documentary Apparatus

At MACBA, Sanctuary, Concrete Geographies, and Nitrate occupied the same exhibition space, requiring viewers to move among photographs, archives, moving images, and historical records. MACBA’s publication record includes essays by Carles Guerra, Louise Purbrick, and others, showing that the interpretation of the work was opened to collaboration with researchers*12 The Photographers’ Gallery likewise presents Nitrate as photographic research connecting extraction sites, financial capital, and colonial history*13 Acción Cultural Española explains that photography in the exhibition serves as a tool for rereading history while its own limits as a recording medium are examined in turn*24Finished photographs are installed alongside documents and moving images, allowing viewers to compare different forms of evidence within the same space.

It Would Never Be Quite the Same Again — Linking Distant Events in Chile and Britain through Photographs and Documents

It Would Never Be Quite the Same Again is a 2015 project derived from Nitrate that connects acts of resistance, destruction, and memorialization in distant parts of Chile and Britain through photographs, artist texts, and reproductions of primary documents. ProjecteSD describes a body of work beginning with South American landscape photographs made by Mabel Loomis Todd in 1907 and connecting several events, including the destruction of a statue of Margaret Thatcher, as “distant echoes” of explosions in the Atacama Desert*14 World of Matter’s nitrate-related material likewise moves among multiple sites rather than confining images of minerals, landscape, labor, and capital to a single region*15 The same method appears in Invisible Structures. SOURCE describes the series as photographing terrain that initially appears to be untouched jungle but is identified through excavation and historical records as part of a buried city marginalized by established accounts*25When excavation records are placed alongside a site that the present-day photograph alone would read simply as “jungle,” its history as an urban ruin becomes legible. Across projects, Ribas uses other sources to identify pasts that photographs by themselves cannot establish.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Photographing the Sites and Records That Produced an Event

Dramatic actions by politicians, police, or workers rarely appear in Ribas’s photographs. An Apollo review of Nitrate notes that although the exhibition addresses colonialism, migration, and labor exploitation, it is built from photographs, moving images, and archival documents and maintains a tension between documentary evidence and aesthetically composed landscape*17 The Photographers’ Gallery also presents Nitrate as a long-term investigation of Chile’s mineral history beginning with photographs of nitrate works around 1900*13The political force of these works does not depend on assigning an abstract significance to their visual quiet. The causes under investigation are often no longer present at the site. Ribas photographs the landscape as it exists now, brings in records preserved elsewhere, and makes the two available for comparison within the same exhibition.

From the Vacant Lots of Sundays to the Mining and Financial Networks of Nitrate

Sundays began as a response to the corporate image of Barcelona produced around the 1992 Olympics, photographing vacant spaces left between redevelopment projects as local people used them for picnics, conversation, and play*19 David Campany identifies as central to the series the fact that urban planning and real-estate intentions cannot fully determine behavior, and that undesignated land can support forms of social life not anticipated by those plans*19 In the later Nitrate, the field expands from vacant land to mines, ports, financial districts, and estates, shifting attention from the use of one place to movements of commodities and capital across several sites*22Even as the method becomes more elaborate, one principle remains consistent: the appearance of a landscape is never asked to stand in for a complete social explanation. Sundays photographs the difference between the planned city and its actual use; Nitrate uses documents to follow the gap between an extraction site and the destinations of the wealth produced there.

yang-fudong.html.lead_html: Yang Fudong has portrayed the hesitation of young people and intellectuals living through China’s rapid transformation in works including An Estranged Paradise, Seven Intellectuals in a Bamboo Forest, and The General’s Smile, using black-and-white 35mm film, staged photography, and multichannel video. He brings memories of classical literature, literati painting, 1930s Chinese cinema, and European film into contact with contemporary bodies. Sparse exposition gives way to fragments, pauses, repetition, and displaced gazes, through which historical transition is felt. His work treats still and moving images as parts of a continuous temporality, giving the photographic instant a sense of what came before and what may follow.
yang-fudong.html.thesis_html: From the late 1990s through the 2000s, photography and moving image brought the lived time of urbanization into an international reception of Chinese contemporary art that had largely centered on painting. Yang Fudong used the large-format photographic triptych The First Intellectual, black-and-white 35mm film, and multiscreen video as a single visual language. Ancient literati, memories of Republican-era cinema, and post-reform youth overlap in scenes whose conclusions remain suspended. His subject is the silence, repetition, and waiting of people who defer judgment between inherited ideals and new forms of urban life. Yang’s distinction lies in fixing historical figures and contemporary youth in monumental still photographs as well as films, building a temporal structure in both media that prompts viewers to imagine events before and after the image and several historical periods at once.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
From Painting at the China Academy of Art to Cinema as a Medium of Time

Yang Fudong studied oil painting at the China Academy of Art in Hangzhou and moved to Shanghai in the mid-1990s. His training remains visible in the placement of figures, the handling of light and empty space, and the proportions between landscape and body. Yet he pursued the duration in which images appear and disappear, moving beyond the self-contained composition of a painting. Marian Goodman Gallery describes Yang as an artist with a background in painting who uses film, photography, and installation to address individual emotions and experiences in relation to history, society, and politics*1. He began shooting his first feature, An Estranged Paradise, in 1997. After interruptions caused by a lack of funding, he completed it in 2002. MoMA Post notes that Yang called it a “small intellectual film” about an educated social group and that it addressed loss and alienation among a younger generation*2.

In late-1990s China, market reform and urban development accelerated the pace of daily life while contemporary art connected rapidly to international exhibitions. Yang minimizes direct explanations through construction sites or commodities. Old houses, lakes, mist, hotels, bamboo groves, fashionably dressed youth, uniforms, and banquets appear in black-and-white images where the boundaries between periods become unstable. This slowed duration gives form to subjects who cannot fully grasp the meaning of change and seek an image of themselves between inherited culture and new urban life.

International Reception after Documenta 11 and His Distance from a Singular “Story of China”

An Estranged Paradise was completed with support from Okwui Enwezor and screened at Documenta 11 in 2002. HIAP recounts Enwezor’s role in supporting the production and the work’s path to Documenta 11*3. This international appearance made Yang visible as an artist of a transforming China, while his works translate social circumstances into gestures, silence, and sustained views of landscape. Museo Esteban Vicente describes his cinematic world as poised between dream and reality, centered on the identity, desire, and solitude of intellectuals in contemporary China*4.

In Yang’s treatment of modernity, old and new occupy the same present. Ancient legends, Republican-era cinema, socialist uniforms, and the fashions of the global city coexist on screen. Anachronism becomes a sign that contemporary subjects wear several pasts at once. In a recent M+ interview about Sparrow on the Sea, Yang explained that props from earlier works such as An Estranged Paradise and Seven Intellectuals in a Bamboo Forest returned to his mind, describing memory as something that repeats across projects*5.

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Seven Intellectuals in a Bamboo Forest — Translating Ancient Reclusion into the Gestures of Contemporary Youth

Seven Intellectuals in a Bamboo Forest (2003–2007) reworks the legend of seven Wei-Jin literati said to have withdrawn from politics to exchange poetry, music, wine, and philosophy in a bamboo grove. Contemporary young men and women perform the figures across a five-part film. M+ identifies the nearly five-hour cycle as a major work and explains that it brings into the present an ancient ideal realm repeatedly pictured in poetry, music, and literati painting*6. In the first part, seven figures in urban clothing walk through the mountains. Later parts move through rural areas, the seashore, the city, labor, and pleasure. Seeking a community, they continue to move among mountain, countryside, coast, and city without finding a stable place of belonging.

The classical past becomes a measure for the gestures of contemporary youth. The legend of literati who withdrew from politics overlaps with young people after reform and opening who pause among social participation, success, freedom, and solitude. Marian Goodman Gallery describes the five-part reenactment of ancient intellectuals by contemporary youth as a work about tensions between traditional values and contemporary society*7. Walking, smoking, silence, and glances that fail to meet stretch the time before decisive action. Repeated gestures take precedence over narrative causality, and historical transition appears as the bodily sensation of stopping before a path has been chosen.

How Black-and-White 35mm Film Unsettles the Distance between Present and Memory

Yang’s black-and-white imagery does more than style the present as nostalgia. Grain, strong backlighting, deep blacks, and slow camera movement bring contemporary scenes close to memories of old cinema while layering several cinematic periods in a single frame. Orientations notes that Yang chose 35mm film over digital formats to give his images a tactile quality*8. Film makes the present appear as though it has already entered memory, destabilizing its temporal location.

In his photographs, too, figures are caught in mid-action or with their gazes misaligned. The still image may resemble a publicity still, yet it points toward an event continuing beyond the frame. Tate collects and presents Yang’s films, photographs, and installations as parts of the same body of work*9. His photographs function as independent works by showing only a portion of time and prompting the viewer to imagine what surrounds it, even when they share a world with his films.

Staging and Improvisation — Finding the Image on Location Instead of Executing a Finished Script

Yang’s films appear meticulously composed, but the production process places considerable weight on discovering a scene on location instead of reproducing a fixed script. He has said that he begins with an indistinct idea and finds the scene through the relation among place, actors, and camera*10. A conversation published by ShanghART similarly discusses the figures, locations, and contemporaneity of Seven Intellectuals in a Bamboo Forest as a process that opens the legend to present experience instead of explaining it*11.

Improvisation allows chance to enter a prepared scene. Costume, location, light, and camera are selected in advance, while pauses among actors, glances, wind, weather, and deviations in movement remain. As staging and actuality move against each other, gestures escape the roles assigned to the performers. Yang photographs the distance between contemporary actors and the historical figures they enact. That distance gives form to intellectuals who know inherited ideals but are still seeking their place in present life.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
An Estranged Paradise — Hangzhou’s Landscape and the “Small Intellectual”

An Estranged Paradise (1997–2002) is a feature film set in Hangzhou, following a young intellectual, Zhuzi, as he drifts among physical illness, love, urban life, and landscape. MoMA Post places the work within the loss and alienation experienced by China’s young educated classes in the 1990s and relates it to independent Chinese cinema of the period*2. West Lake is a canonical ideal landscape in Chinese painting and literature. In Yang’s film, mist, rain, interiors, and the surface of the lake correspond to the protagonist’s malaise and sustain a world whose outlines have yet to settle.

The title’s “estranged paradise” describes the distance that opens between the protagonist and a landscape that remains before him, saturated with cultural memory. The five-year production history also joins the China of the late 1990s, when filming began, to the early 2000s, when the work appeared. Its screening at Documenta 11 connected this personal, slowly paced film to an international exhibition concerned with multiple modernities in a postcolonial world. EMMA later exhibited Part I of Seven Intellectuals in a Bamboo Forest, presenting it as a central work that transfers the classical image of the literatus to contemporary youth*12.

The General’s Smile — Banquet, Authority, and the Theater of Life

The General’s Smile (2009) unfolds a banquet surrounding an elderly general across multiple screens, bringing authority, memory, aging, and celebration into one setting. In Yang’s first solo exhibition in Japan, the Hara Museum presented it as a major moving-image installation that approached the universality of life through a banquet honoring a senior military officer*13. Toasts, music, dancing, silence, and the old man’s expressions repeat in place of a clear plot. The multiple screens show the same event simultaneously from different angles, dispersing the central figure’s authority into the surrounding durations.

Each time viewers move among the screens, their point of view and the order of events change. Unlike the fixed seat of a cinema, the installation gives viewers control over sequence and length of attention. Yang’s multichannel works turn film from a container for narrative into an environment in the gallery, asking viewers to compare moments as they would images in a photographic series. ACMI’s Yang Fudong: Filmscapes connected his work to Chinese painting and film noir, presenting a moving-image practice that constructs a single scene through multiple viewpoints and fragments*14.

The First Intellectual — Producing Before and After within the Still Image

The photographic work The First Intellectual (2000) is a triptych showing a wounded, bleeding young man in a suit holding a brick on a deserted urban street. ShanghART records each panel as a color chromogenic print measuring 193 by 127 centimeters*19. The attacker and the brick’s intended target remain outside the frame, and the causal sequence stays incomplete even across all three panels. Anger and helplessness repeat through different postures.

The work clarifies the difference between a photograph that looks like a cinematic scene and a still extracted from a film. Three stationary images generate an imagined sequence before and after them, requiring the viewer to construct an event beyond the frame. The monumental prints make the young man larger than life. The type of the intellectual who has lost his place during social transition appears as a specific wounded body marked by hesitation. A ShanghART critical text reads him as a contemporary intellectual uncertain whether to locate the source of the problem in himself or in society*17.

Ms. Huang at M. Last Night (2006), an independent digital print produced for Parkett, is held by MoMA as a work in the Department of Drawings and Prints*20. In Yang’s work, photographs may emerge as by-products of a film or develop as independent images from related stages and figures. This movement between media changes the still image from evidence that completes an event into a scene that suspends the historical and narrative belonging of its figures.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Does Visual Beauty Weaken Social Critique?

Yang’s refined cinematography, costumes, actors, and landscapes often lead museums and film festivals to describe his work as “poetic” or “dreamlike.” Its beauty can be criticized for obscuring China’s political and economic transformations by absorbing them into universal melancholy. Yet Yang marks an era through subjects who waver without choosing a clear position. An ART iT interview traces his movement between reality and dream, individual and society, and tradition and the contemporary through the artist’s own words*15.

The beauty of Yang’s images is both a polished surface and one of the means through which classical culture, film, advertising, and fashion teach subjects to imagine themselves. Figures remain physically apart within carefully composed scenes; their gazes drift and actions stop midway. The attraction of the image and the interruption of narrative express the distance between an ideal life and lived reality. An exhibition text from Kunsthall 3,14 describes Yang’s work as a cinematic space where historical memory intersects with contemporary psychological states*16.

The Cinematic Turn in Chinese Contemporary Art

From the 1990s through the 2000s, video, photography, and performance became important media for describing new experience in Chinese contemporary art, challenging an international reception centered on painting. Yang used the vocabulary of film history to represent modernization through youthful expressions, silence, landscape, and waiting. A ShanghART critical text discusses An Estranged Paradise and Seven Intellectuals in a Bamboo Forest through the figures of the “small intellectual” and the contemporary Chinese intellectual*17.

Wang Qingsong compresses social institutions into monumental single-frame allegories, while Yang extends the time of figures who pause before choosing their roles. Both use staging. Wang’s photographs render social structure visible; Yang examines the process by which that structure becomes delay and hesitation within a subject. This difference broadened staged photography and moving image in China from political allegory toward forms of time, memory, and feeling.

Place in Photographic History — Building the Same Unfinished Time into Still and Moving Images

Cinematic stills and staged photographs that suggest stories existed before Yang. His distinct place in photographic history lies in bringing classical Chinese literati, the visual language of Republican-era film, and post-reform youth into the same unresolved duration. In The First Intellectual, an unsettled event repeats across three images; in Seven Intellectuals in a Bamboo Forest, the ideal of community remains suspended across a five-hour film. Whether the image is still or sustained, its figures occupy a historical interval.

By working across Documenta 11, the Venice Biennale, museum multiscreen installations, and editioned photographs, Yang established a body of work in Chinese contemporary art that treats photography and film as equal media, extending the same figures and sense of time at different lengths. MoMA’s collection of his films and independent prints within the same body of holdings reflects this reception*18. His work does not stand for Chinese moving-image art as a whole. It added the duration of people living with deferred judgment as a shared subject of photography and film, alongside methods that presented social change through emblematic events or urban landscapes.

yasumasa-morimura.html.lead_html: Yasumasa Morimura inserts his own body into masterpieces, film stars, and historical photographs. In doing so, he turns photography from an act of resemblance into a site where the authority of images, gender, race, and the memory of postwar Japan are performed again. Through disguise, sets, quotation, and deliberate dissonance, his work asks how viewers come to trust history and the self through images.
yasumasa-morimura.html.thesis_html: Morimura’s contribution to photography lies in recasting self-portraiture. Instead of presenting the artist’s bare face, he used his own body to perform figures that had already been given value within art history, cinema, and news photography. Morimura has said that art education in postwar Japan was organized around Euro-American values, and that students had more opportunities to study Van Gogh, Monet, and Renoir than Japanese art history. *27 Against this background, performing Van Gogh or Manet was neither a simple act of admiration for Western art nor an outside rejection of it. By placing his Japanese male face and body inside the “art to be seen” that had been given to him through reproductions and education, he brought the desire to assimilate and the unease of not fully belonging into the same image. Morimura also connects self-portraiture to the media history of mirrors, photography, cinema, television, and the internet. He used the self-portrait less as confession than as a way to examine how images of each period make the “self.” *20 As the Getty Museum’s text on photographic reenactment suggests, Morimura’s reenactments also bring questions of gender, race, and cultural identity into view. *8

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html: Morimura’s method begins with Portrait (Van Gogh) of 1985. ShugoArts describes the work after this point as a sustained series of self-portraits in which Morimura becomes “something” or “someone,” incorporating research, dioramas, sets, costumes, and makeup into the production process. *1 This form grew out of the art education and visual culture of postwar Japan in which Morimura came of age. In a lecture, Morimura stated that art education in Japan had been Westernized since the Meiji period and became even more deeply shaped by Euro-American values after the defeat in World War II. As a student, he said, he mainly studied Van Gogh, Monet, and Renoir, with few opportunities to encounter Japanese art history. *27 Hara Museum also presents his education in postwar Osaka, born under Allied occupation and amid a void where prewar teachings had been pushed aside and Western values entered, as an important background to Ego Obscura. *7 Even with this historical background, the 1985 starting point did not appear as a fully formed critique of art history. In a 2016 interview, Morimura said that he did not yet know Western art history in depth, and that he had received Van Gogh through reproductions and the popular image of “the man of fire.” *20 In another interview, he explained that he identified the young, suffering Van Gogh with his own discomfort, and that when he saw Van Gogh’s self-portrait, it felt like seeing himself in a mirror. *22 This experience led toward a form in which the self is seen through an already known image of another person. In an ARTLOGUE interview, Morimura also recalled that a large color self-portrait appeared suddenly in 1985 and became the beginning of his current style. *21 The National Museum of Art, Osaka places Portrait (Van Gogh), first shown at Gallery 16 in Kyoto in 1985, as an early key work that opened Morimura’s self-portraiture toward art history. *2 In 1988, he took part in the Aperto section of the Venice Biennale and, with Portrait (Futago), based on Manet’s Olympia, placed a familiar masterpiece of Western art and the body of a Japanese man in the same image. *4 At the same time, artists associated with the Pictures Generation in Europe and the United States were using advertising, cinema, and existing photographs to examine photography as a medium that produces shared social patterns instead of simply transmitting reality. *23 Morimura did not repeat that movement in Japan as it stood. He built a method that transferred the figures he had received through reproductions of Western art, Hollywood cinema, and news photographs into his own body through costume, makeup, sets, and performance. Hara Museum’s retrospective text explains that he has reenacted painting, cinema, and historical moments, constructing his work as a meta-commentary that crosses time, race, and gender. *7 For that reason, it is not enough to summarize Morimura as an artist who “dressed as masterpieces.” His photographs need to be read as work that shows what shifts inside the photographic image when postwar Japanese culture receives Western art, Hollywood cinema, and news photographs, and then performs them again through the artist’s own body.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Making the Body a Site of Quotation

Morimura’s self-portraits are not disguises made to conceal his bare face. They are acts of rebuilding, through his own body, faces and poses remembered from reproductions, cinema, and news photographs. ShugoArts describes his work as self-portraiture that involves careful research, dioramas and sets, costumes, and makeup. *1 Photography here is not a medium that merely records a completed disguise. It fixes the body, costume, makeup, background, lighting, and print into a single image, making visible the gap between the source image and Morimura’s own body. If the likeness were complete, it would approach replication. If it were too distant, it would fail as quotation. Morimura’s photographs hold that intermediate dissonance, showing how deeply masterpieces, films, and historical photographs have been remembered as familiar types. Self-portraiture is thereby shifted from a form that directly reveals the artist’s interiority to one that rereads shared figures through the body.

Portrait (Van Gogh) and the Entry into Masterpieces

Portrait (Van Gogh) is one of the early works that most clearly shows Morimura’s method. The National Museum of Art, Osaka registers the work as a photograph from 1985, providing a concrete point of departure for his early self-portraiture. *3 The subject here is not the historical Van Gogh himself, but the image of Van Gogh widely shared through art books, exhibitions, reproductions, and explanatory texts. Morimura later said that, at the time of making the work, he did not know Van Gogh in depth and remembered him through reproductions and the phrase “the man of fire.” *20 At the same time, he also said that when he saw Van Gogh’s self-portrait, it felt as if he were looking at himself in a mirror. *22 Portrait (Van Gogh) therefore presents less an accurate recreation of Van Gogh than a transfer of the “Van Gogh-ness” Morimura had received into his own face and body. It brings to the surface the knowledge and stories through which the figure of the artist has been believed. In place of a photograph that proves the authenticity of the self, it begins a photography that thinks about the self through another face.

Portrait (Futago) and the Assumptions of Looking at a Masterpiece

Portrait (Futago) directs Morimura’s method toward art history, sex, and race with particular clarity. Mori Art Museum describes the work as based on Manet’s Olympia and notes that Morimura performs both the “white prostitute” and the “black maid” through the body of a Japanese man. *4 Viewers who know Manet’s Olympia read the nude woman, the maid, the frontal gaze, and the difference in skin color through their knowledge of art history. When Morimura appears as a Japanese man performing both roles at once, the divisions that had seemed settled within the masterpiece become unstable. This substitution is not a simple critique of Manet. It is a way of exposing, within the image, the habits of knowledge and looking that viewers bring to the act of seeing a masterpiece. SFMOMA’s collection entry presents the work as a chromogenic print from 1988, also confirming its place in an international photographic collection. *5 In this sense, Portrait (Futago) can be read less as a parody of Manet than as a work that rearranges the premises for looking at a masterpiece inside a single body.

The “I” Extending to Actresses, Kahlo, and Historical Photographs

Morimura’s self-portraiture is not directed only toward Western painting. The National Museum of Art, Osaka’s retrospective text presents his transformations into protagonists of masterpieces, film actresses, and historical figures as Morimura’s “my art history.” *2 An inner dialogue with Frida Kahlo (Flower wreath and tears), held by NGV, reconstructs the emblematic modern self-image of Frida Kahlo through Morimura’s own body. *6 Here, the “I” does not remain enclosed within the artist’s private interior. It emerges through another face, another costume, another pain, and another mythology. The force of Morimura’s photographs lies in the way they refuse to fix the object of disguise as either homage or satire. He neither simply takes the subject nor fully assimilates into it. He preserves a distance between the subject and himself, and within that distance he shows how unstable gender, nationality, and cultural memory can be.

Photographic Reenactment and the Likeness That Never Fully Matches

The Getty Museum’s text for Photo Reenactment explains that since the early 1980s, Morimura has reenacted famous paintings and cast himself within them. *8 The same text adds that his works do more than reproduce their sources: they include homage, satire, and anachronistic elements while raising questions of gender, race, and cultural identity. *8 As this description suggests, Morimura’s reenactments are not attempts to return faithfully to the source image. They are ways of testing how the authority of the source image has been maintained, by which bodies, in which periods, and through what forms of performance. Photographic reenactment can seem to bring the past into the present. In Morimura’s case, however, the past never returns unchanged. The texture of the face, the placement of the body, the excess of the costume, and the artificiality of the set remain somewhere in the image as a mismatch. That mismatch makes visible the roles and desires behind images that have been placed at the center of art history.

Postwar Japan’s Reception of the West and the Position of the Self

Morimura’s work cannot be understood as a view of Western art history from the outside. It is grounded in an experience of learning, becoming familiar with, and feeling distance from Euro-American culture within postwar Japan. In a lecture, Morimura stated that under the American occupation after the war, Westernization extended across lifestyle, political thought, eating habits, and art education. At school, oil painting and Western art were given as the standard of “art” more often than nihonga or Japanese art history. *27 ShugoArts’s text for My Chronicle 1985–2018 also places the background of his work in a self born in the Showa era and the twentieth century, noting Japan’s encounter with Western civilization since the Meiji period and the strong influence of American culture after the defeat in World War II. *16 Seen from this angle, Morimura’s performances of Van Gogh, Manet, or Velázquez are not simply attempts to approach Western art. They place his body inside Western images he had received from childhood as “art,” photographing both the self that had become familiar with those images and the self that appears as something out of place within them. In the same lecture, Morimura explained that his self-portraits place the Japanese face and body he possesses into figures from Western art history, bringing Japanese and Western elements into the same space while keeping their differences from being completely blended. *27 As Artizon Museum’s Jam Session reread modern Japanese painting, including Aoki Shigeru’s A Gift of the Sea, through Morimura’s method, this question does not end with Western art. It also turns toward modern Japanese art and museum collections. *9 Morimura’s photographs do not simply line up East and West as opposing terms. They show the dissonance that arises when a body formed within postwar Japan’s close reception of Euro-American culture is placed inside those images.

Self-Portraiture as Place, Improvisation, and Process

Morimura’s self-portraiture is made through more than the reconstruction of finished masterpieces. ShugoArts’s text for My Chronicle 1985–2018 presents his trajectory from early Polaroid-like on-site works to the art history and actress series. *16 What matters here is that self-portraiture does not remain confined to the studio. It develops into a wider form that includes place, travel, exhibition, documentation, and process. For Morimura, the “I” is not a fixed subject. It is a provisional position remade again and again before places, images, and histories. In his photographs, even though the artist’s face appears repeatedly, the identity of the author does not become stronger. As the same face continues to enter different roles, the self appears as an accumulation of quotation and performance, not as a single core.

sections.title: Key Works, Method, and Medium
sections.body_html:
Portrait (Van Gogh), 1985

Portrait (Van Gogh) is an early work in which Morimura clarified his method of inserting his own body into Western art history. The National Museum of Art, Osaka registers the work as a photograph from 1985 and identifies its materials as C-print and offset print. *3 The work is an attempt to recreate a masterpiece through photography, and at the same time to transform the painter’s self-portrait into the photographer’s own performance. In a painted self-portrait, the painter is both the subject who depicts and the object depicted. In Morimura’s case, that doubleness is layered with the performance of becoming another person, the documentary fixity of the photograph, and the viewer’s sense of recognition.

Portrait (Futago), 1988 and 1989

Portrait (Futago) is one of the representative works in which Morimura’s intervention into art history appears most sharply. Mori Art Museum holds the work as a 1989 piece and describes it as based on Manet’s Olympia, with Morimura performing the two roles in the image. *4 SFMOMA’s collection page, meanwhile, registers a 1988 Portrait (Futago) as a chromogenic print, confirming that the same subject has circulated internationally through multiple versions and collections. *5 In this work, questions of who is looked at, who is placed in a role of service, and who is treated as a subject of art history are layered within one body. Morimura’s photographs exceed the category of “disguise photography” because these overlapping roles destabilize the viewer’s position as well.

An inner dialogue with Frida Kahlo, 2001

An inner dialogue with Frida Kahlo (Flower wreath and tears) shows how Morimura’s self-portraiture extended beyond Western masterpieces to modern images of female authorship and pain. The National Museum of Art, Osaka’s retrospective text describes the “Frida in Me (Flower Wreath)” series as works that celebrate the love and death in Frida Kahlo’s life from Morimura’s own perspective. *2 NGV’s collection entry also presents the work as a color photograph from 2001, confirming the reception of Morimura’s transformation into Kahlo within an international collection. *6 Here, Morimura does not simply borrow Kahlo’s pain or self-image. He passes the strong image of Kahlo as an artist through his own body, showing how the “I” multiplies and wavers when it wears another face.

From Photography to Video, Performance, and the Museum

Morimura’s method extends beyond individual photographs into video, performance, exhibition structure, and dialogue with museums. Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art’s Morimura Yasumasa: My Self-Portraits as a Theater of Labyrinths introduces him as a pioneer of self-portraiture and explains that his transformations into masterpieces, historical figures, and film actresses make visible multiple identities, including gender and race. *10 Hara Museum’s Ego Obscura was structured as a retrospective that included photographs alongside video, lecture-performance, and references to modern Japanese history. *7 This expansion shows that Morimura’s photography is not completed within a single image. For him, photography is a medium that preserves the disguised body and, at the same time, a central device for creating a theatrical field that includes exhibition space, language, history, and the viewer.

sections.title: Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Photographic Quotation and Appropriation Through the Body

Morimura can be read alongside appropriation and the Pictures Generation from the 1980s onward. Yet if his work is grouped too quickly under the “use of existing images,” his method becomes harder to see. In a 2018 interview, Morimura said that since 1985 he had used artificial eyes, makeup, and sets in an attempt to go beyond classifications such as male and female, East and West. *12 The Metropolitan Museum of Art explains that Cindy Sherman, Richard Prince, Sherrie Levine, and others used film scenes, advertising photographs, and masterpieces of modern photography to examine codes of representation. *23 Levine’s After Walker Evans, in which she rephotographed Walker Evans’s photographs from a catalogue, is also described by the Centre Pompidou as a work that questions authorship, originality, and authenticity. *24 Morimura, by contrast, does more than rephotograph a source image as another photograph. He takes on the figure inside the image as his own role. The center of quotation shifts from photographic reproduction itself to the body, skin, gender, costume, and the position of the gaze.

The comparison with Sherman becomes clearer when this difference is kept in view. MoMA explains that although Sherman is her own model, Untitled Film Stills are not considered self-portraits; instead, she places herself in dialogue with stereotypes of femininity. *18 M+’s two-person exhibition, by contrast, presents Morimura and Sherman as artists who both use masquerade to explore relations among identity, mass media, and history, while remaking images from masterpieces, cinema, and popular culture from their own cultural backgrounds. *17 The Art Newspaper also notes that the two were not aware of each other from the beginning of their careers, and that Morimura later learned about Sherman through a Japanese magazine. *19 Their relation is therefore better understood as a parallel development rather than a single line of influence from the late 1970s through the 1980s, when photography began to address identity through performance, cinema, and reproduced images.

Morimura has also been read in relation to Duchamp’s use of aliases and disguise. MEM’s exhibition text introduces the Doublonage series Morimura made in the 1980s, based on Duchamp’s Chocolate Grinder and Fresh Widow. *25 QAGOMA’s commentary also reads Doublonnage (Marcel) as a work in which Morimura takes up the pose of Duchamp’s female alter ego Rrose Sélavy, as photographed by Man Ray, connecting it to reversals of gender roles and tensions between Eastern and Western images. *26 In this light, Morimura’s photographs are not simply imitations of masterpieces. They can be placed as attempts to rearrange, through the body, who becomes the author, who becomes the model, and who is positioned as the viewer within existing images.

Institutional Reception and International Reassessment

Morimura’s works have been received through museums, galleries, international exhibitions, and photographic collections. MoMA’s artist page registers Morimura as a Japanese artist and presents Ambiguous Beauty (Aimai-no-bi) as part of its collection. *13 NGV’s artist page identifies him as a Japanese artist born in Osaka and shows, through multiple collection works, that his work has entered international museum collections. *14 In Japan, institutions including The National Museum of Art, Osaka, Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art, Hara Museum, and Artizon Museum have reread Morimura’s self-portraiture as a dialogue with art history, cinema, modern Japan, and institutional collections. Luhring Augustine’s CV lists his solo exhibitions, international exhibitions, and major collections, confirming the institutional reception of his work across photography, art, and performance. *11 This breadth of reception helps explain why Morimura’s work is referenced within both Japanese contemporary art and discussions of photography after postmodernism.

What Morimura Changed in Photographic History

Morimura matters in photographic history because he changed self-portraiture from a form that “photographs me” into one that shows which historical image the “I” takes on and where it slips out of that role. The Getty Museum’s exhibition on photographic reenactment places Morimura among artists who revisit art history and identity through photography. *8 Japan Society’s catalogue introduction for Ego Obscura also presents more than thirty years of his work as a reassessment within global contemporary art. *15 Morimura’s photographs do not record reality, nor do they simply express the artist’s interior life. By placing his own body inside figures from masterpieces, film stars, and news photographs, they show how photography makes history believable, how it produces subjects, and how it organizes the viewer’s desires. His work can therefore be positioned as an expansion of the act of photographing into looking, performing, quoting, and questioning.

yasuzo-nojima.html.lead_html: Photographer who united the material quality of pictorialist printing with modern portrait expression, opening new possibilities for portraiture in Japanese modern photography. He is positioned in the transition from pictorialism to Japanese photographic modernism, bringing bodily and facial presence alive through photography.
yasuzo-nojima.html.thesis_html: Nojima joined the painterly texture of the print with a modern grasp of the human figure, raising the bodily and facial presence of the sitter as photography. In the transition from Pictorialism to a distinctly Japanese photographic modernism, his work is regarded as having opened up photographic portraiture in Japan.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Yasuzo Nojima was born in Saitama in 1889, taught himself photography, and developed his practice centred on portrait and nude photography through the 1910s and 1920s. *1 His exchange with Shinzo Fukuhara overlapped with the activities of the Sha-shin Geijutsu-sha, and he was deeply involved in the formative period of Japan's photographic art institutions. *2 Comparison with Stieglitz appears in materials at the National Film Archive of Japan (Tokyo), functioning as a reference line for thinking about the contemporaneous artistic development of photography in Japan and the United States. *3

Nojima was also active in publishing photobooks, which were made with a conscious attention to design in their covers and layout. *4 Shashasha (a specialist photobook shop and online store) stocks multiple Nojima photobooks, attesting to contemporary availability. *5 He died in 1964 and has continued to be discussed in exhibitions and research on the history of modern Japanese photography. *6

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
From pictorialism to modern portraiture

Nojima's expression is positioned in the transition from pictorialism's soft printing to modern portraiture. *7 His figure photographs and nudes are not simply about beautification; they push the presence of body and face through the material tonal quality of the photograph. The quality and gradation of the bromoil print has a painterly character, but the approach to the subject is more direct, not dissolving the person into atmosphere but bringing them up on the picture plane with strong actual presence. *8

The Shoto Museum leaflet PDF provides concrete notes on Nojima's techniques and the structure of his works, serving as an important resource for confirming the relationship between the texture of the bromoil print and composition. *9 The Iwate University research paper PDF analyses Nojima's photographic expression in academic terms, demonstrating a contemporary approach to the question of transition from pictorialism to Japanese modernism. *10

The materiality of photography and the presence of the body

What distinguishes Nojima's photography from other pictorialist photographers is that the material character of the print and the actual presence of the subject are strongly bound together. *11 The depth of the painterly tone and the direct approach to face and body coexist, evaluated not as simply "beautiful photography" but as "photography in which presence appears." The work records in ToMuCo for "Nojima Yasuzo-shi" function as materials for confirming the technique and print characteristics of individual works. *12

Comparison with Stieglitz serves as a symbolic reference line but is treated not as direct influence but as context for understanding how photography underwent artistic development contemporaneously in Japan and the United States. *13 CiNii Research holds multiple research articles on Nojima, and scholarly re-evaluation continues. *14

Later positioning and connection to Japanese modernism

Nojima's photography differs from the experimental modernism of later figures such as Nakaji Yasui or Iwata Nakayama, who foregrounded extreme angles and photomontage. *15 Yet through his distance from the subject, the depth of the print's material quality and the isolated presence of the figure, he showed a path by which photography could maintain material beauty while moving away from painting. This can be read as one example of the process through which modern Japanese photography, rather than directly imitating Western avant-garde, searched for its own language. *16

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Nojima has been re-evaluated through exhibitions, photobook reprints and research articles in the history of modern Japanese photography. *17 International materials are limited, but the British Museum's photobook materials serve as an important point of reference for the contexts of photobooks, portraiture and printing techniques. *18 NDL Search holds extensive related bibliographic materials. *19 Works and related records can also be confirmed at ICP and ToMuCo. Positioning him as a turning point from pictorialism to Japanese modernism makes the significance of his work within photographic history clear. *20 Nojima's portraits and nudes are important primary materials for thinking about how the "modern figure" was formed in Japanese modern photography, and research continues on both the printing techniques employed and the approach to the subject.

yokoyama-matsusaburo.html.lead_html: Yokoyama Matsusaburō worked across photography, photo-oil painting, lithography, and cultural heritage documentation, playing a central role in the visual record-keeping of the early Meiji state. His photographs of Edo Castle and the Jinshin Survey have been designated Important Cultural Properties of Japan.
yokoyama-matsusaburo.html.thesis_html: Yokoyama Matsusaburo combined photography with oil painting, lithographic printing, and cultural-heritage survey, connecting photography to the formation of the Meiji state's visual administrative order rather than limiting it to portrait-making alone. Through his participation in the Jinshin Survey he helped pioneer the first systematic government-led effort to document shrines, temples, and cultural assets across Japan, opening a channel through which photography functioned as a foundation of national knowledge. His contributions to the Vienna World's Exposition and his experiments with photolithography embody the process by which photography became embedded in both outward self-representation and print culture. The ongoing recognition of the related photographic materials as Important Cultural Properties shows that his recording practice continues to be evaluated as one of the founding moments of Japanese photographic history.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Yokoyama Matsusaburo was born in 1838 on Etorofu Island and studied photography in the final years of the Edo period. He is said to have learned photographic technique under Shimooka Renjo.*1 In the early Meiji period he was involved in photographing Edo Castle (later the Imperial Palace) during the transition from the shogunate to the new government, and those photographs are now among the materials held as Important Cultural Properties by the Tokyo National Museum.*2 He participated as an art photography specialist in the Jinshin Survey of 1872 — a government-led project to investigate shrines, temples, and cultural properties across the country — and made substantial contributions to cultural property documentation.*3 He was also responsible for photographing works submitted to the Vienna World Exposition (1873), connecting him to the Meiji state's external self-representation.*4 In addition to photography he worked in photo-oil painting (a technique combining oil painting with photography) and lithography, and he died in 1884.*5

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Cross-media expression: photography, oil painting, and lithography

What stands out in Yokoyama Matsusaburo's practice is that he did not treat photography as a single isolated medium but worked across it in combination with oil painting, lithography, and cultural property documentation. The Edo-Tokyo Museum's description of him as "the Leonardo da Vinci of Japan" is an exaggerated tagline, but his photo-oil painting and cross-media activities do confirm that he was not a practitioner confined to one field.*6 Photo-oil painting was an experiment in adding pictorial value and color to the reproductive capacity of photography, and it shows how photography in the Meiji period was connected to "art" and "education" as well as to "documentation." A J-STAGE paper on photo-oil painting discusses the practice and its historical context in detail.*7 The Art Platform Japan artist database presents Yokoyama's activities in a cross-domain framework and shows his positioning within the contexts of domestic art, cultural property, and photographic history.*8

National surveys and cultural property documentation

More important than reading Yokoyama's work as individual artistic output is recognizing that his practice was integrated into the visual record-keeping systems of the early Meiji state. The Tokyo National Museum holds the photographs connected to the Jinshin Survey as Important Cultural Properties, indicating that the survey in which Yokoyama participated was one of the institutional starting points for cultural property documentation in Japan.*9 The museum's page on "The Jinshin Survey" explains that this investigation was one of the earliest government-organized attempts to document temples, shrines, and cultural properties systematically across the country, with photography as its central means.*10 The cultural property designation records held in the Agency for Cultural Affairs database show that materials related to Yokoyama received a fresh designation as Important Cultural Properties in 2023, confirming the high level of current evaluation.*11 The Nikko Scenic Views Photographs in the Cultural Heritage Online database can be consulted individually as photographs connected to the Jinshin Survey.*12

Multi-media practitioner

What best conveys Yokoyama's distinctive character is the item recorded by the Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties concerning the discovery of his photographic plates. The rediscovery of the original plates confirmed the material evidence of his practice and expanded the foundation for research.*13 Works records published by the Tokyo Museum Collection show that the photographs he left are held in multiple institutions and remain the subject of ongoing research and exhibition.*14 The "Photographs Taken for the Austrian Vienna Exhibition" held in the DNP Image Archive can be consulted as a work that provides the concrete context of participation in the Vienna World Exposition.*15 The CiNii Research record "Yokoyama Matsusaburo and the Nikko Photographs" is a published academic research record showing that individual scholarly studies of his photographs continue.*16

Critical reception

The historical significance of Yokoyama Matsusaburo lies in prompting consideration of early Japanese photography not simply as technological adoption but in connection with the record-keeping systems, cultural property surveys, expositions, education, and printing technologies of the nation-building period. The Art Platform Japan artist information organizes his positioning within the domestic contexts of art and photographic history, and a certain degree of record also exists in international databases.*8 The Kyoto National Museum Bulletin article "The Achievements of Ninagawa Noritane and Art Photographer Yokoyama Matsusaburo" is positioned as a representative earlier study that addresses his role in the context of the Jinshin Survey in a specialist manner.*17 The Tokyo Metropolitan Museum of Photography's exhibition work list for "Early Photographic History of the Kanto Region" also positions Yokoyama as an important figure in the photographic history of the early Meiji period.*18 KAKEN research output report (19K00934) makes available the findings of a Grant-in-Aid research project that includes archival investigation related to Yokoyama Matsusaburo, indicating the context of ongoing academic research.*19

yoshino-oishi.html.lead_html: Yoshino Oishi has spent decades photographing people who live with the aftermath of war in Vietnam, Cambodia, Auschwitz, Afghanistan, Kosovo, Hiroshima, Nagasaki, Okinawa, and elsewhere. In series including Mukoku no Tami, Yoru to Kiri wa Ima, Vietnam Rin to, and Senka no Kioku, she first listens to a person’s experience, then photographs the face and everyday life that carry that memory in the present. Her photobooks place testimony beside faces and lives photographed years later. That combination is central to her work.
yoshino-oishi.html.thesis_html: Oishi’s contribution to war photography lies in tracing experiences that remain in bodies and everyday life years and even decades after war. By listening to people, returning to the same places, and bringing present-day portraits into contact with memories of the past, she reveals the gap between the time of news—often closed by the declaration that a war has “ended”—and the time in which survivors continue to live. Where she did not witness the fighting herself, she chose to hear people’s experiences before making their portraits, then combined those images with testimony and later visits.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Yoshino Oishi was born in Tokyo in 1944 and graduated from the Department of Photography at Nihon University College of Art. Art Platform Japan records her birth date as May 28, 1944, and her birthplace as Tokyo.*21 Her student years coincided with the Vietnam War. The distance between having been born in a country that had waged war and having no firsthand memory of war herself remained at the root of her later reporting.

Canon’s profile records that a visit to Vietnam during her student years made a strong impression on Oishi and that, after graduation, she became a documentary photographer who traveled independently to report from different regions. *3 In an interview with Sarai, Oishi explains that she goes to places of war because she wants to know, and that the camera is the means through which she can pass on what she has learned. *4 For Oishi, photography became a way to listen first, then show readers elsewhere how a person is living in the present after the experiences they have described.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
“Can I Remain Unaware?”: A Postwar Generation’s Starting Point

Oishi’s attention to life after war comes from her concern with injuries that persist after the news declares an event over. An interview in the quarterly Michi summarizes her position with the phrase “the war is not over”: once she has learned about the present lives of people harmed by war, she feels compelled to communicate what she has learned. *5 Publication materials for Senka no Kioku likewise move across Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Afghanistan, Kosovo, Sudan, the Holocaust, Hiroshima, Nagasaki, and Okinawa through the continuing time of war’s aftereffects. *6

Listening before Photographing: The Camera as an Entry into Conversation

Oishi’s portraits grow from direct conversation with people whose wartime experiences she has not witnessed herself. She has said that she asks where they were and what they were doing during the war, explains why she wants to photograph them, and only then raises the camera. *4 This makes captions and testimony as important to the photobook as facial expression. The photographed person supplies the memory; the photograph holds the person who carries it in the present.

Later assessments also describe this sequence of listening before photographing as a condition of Oishi’s images. Rikkyo University characterizes her photographs of Hiroshima, Nagasaki, Okinawa, and the Tokyo air raids as the “result of dialogue” with the people she photographed*22. The photograph takes responsibility for the present expression that remains after that dialogue, while the testimony preserves what the face alone cannot state. The two are therefore difficult to separate.

Vietnam Rin to: Twenty Years of Looking at a War That Did Not End

Oishi returned repeatedly to Vietnam beginning in 1981, photographing people affected by Agent Orange, war orphans, women who had lost family members, and others living in postwar society. Vietnam Rin to received the 20th Domon Ken Award in 2001; Mainichi’s list of past recipients confirms the award and its edition. *7 The National Art Center, Tokyo’s Art Commons record describes the work as a twenty-year documentary, begun in 1981, on ordinary people. *8

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Mukoku no Tami and Yoru to Kiri wa Ima: Aftereffects across Regions

Mukoku no Tami photographs people in different parts of Asia, while Yoru to Kiri wa Ima turns to survivors of Nazi concentration camps. Across both projects, Oishi returns from the generic category of “victim” to particular faces, names, and lives. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s Monk, made in 1981, belongs to Mukoku no Tami. *9 Baby, from the same series, dates to 1979. *10 Carolina, also in the museum’s collection, belongs to Yoru to Kiri wa Ima and was made in 1988 as a portrait of a survivor. *11

Photographing Hiroshima and Nagasaki Away from the Day of the Bombing

In Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Oishi concentrates on people and places carrying the experience of the atomic bombings decades later. Her approach leaves reconstruction of August 1945 aside in favor of present-day lives and surviving traces. Fujiwara Shoten’s author biography lists the 1995 photobook HIROSHIMA: Hanseiki no Shozo among her major publications*12. Canon’s exhibition on Nagasaki combined the words and faces of people who had been children or young adults at the time of the bombing with photographs of surviving sites, presenting memory seventy-four years later*13.

The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s 2019 exhibition Senka no Kioku presented roughly forty years of Oishi’s work in three groups: the Mekong region, ethnic and religious conflicts, and the lingering traces of the Asia-Pacific War*14. Crevis’s photobook of the same name contains 160 photographs and edits multiple regions through the shared duration of life after war*6.

Color and black-and-white vary across Oishi’s work rather than forming one fixed stylistic signature. Early projects in Papua and Mukoku no Tami include both, and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s collection records a color photograph from 1979. *1 She used the two according to place and publication medium while keeping present-day facial expression and living environment at the center of the image. Senka no Kioku, by contrast, edits 160 black-and-white photographs from across a long career, allowing differences of region and decade to be compared along one temporal axis. *6 The book keeps wars with different political causes distinct by preserving testimony and portraits region by region, while its sequence allows injuries that persist after formal endings to be compared.

Photograph, Testimony, and Caption: Bringing Time before and after the Shutter into the Work

Photography critic Kotaro Iizawa has described Oishi’s method as bringing the time “before and after” the shutter release into the photograph*27. Her repeated photographs of Viet and Duc from 1982 to 2009 accumulate time outside the portrait itself: listening before the photograph, a life that continues after it, and changes visible on later visits. As Iizawa also notes, captions are crucial. Their text becomes another layer of record, linking a past that cannot appear in the frame to the expression photographed in the present.

Oishi usually photographs years after the combat itself, in places where people who experienced it continue to live. Because the camera cannot photograph a past event directly, listening before the portrait and words within the photobook become parts of the work. Oishi’s repeated emphasis in the Sarai interview on “listening before photographing” belongs to this method*4. The twenty-year duration of Vietnam Rin to is tied to the same problem: one portrait cannot show the full time of an aftermath*8. By returning to the same places and photographing people she has met before, the series accumulates both locations where wounds remain and locations where life has changed. In Hiroshima and Nagasaki as well, she photographs the aged faces and words of hibakusha and the surviving traces of the cities in the present, rather than repeating images from the day of the bombings*13. Repeated visits and captions bridge the distance between the present expression a photograph can hold and the past that testimony must tell.

Speaking at Sophia University on human security and peacebuilding, Oishi argued that psychological wounds from war do not necessarily disappear with time and can intensify years later as recurring nightmares. She cited Agent Orange in Vietnam, unexploded ordnance in Laos, and memories of mass killing in Cambodia*24. This understanding makes it necessary for her work to return to people ten and twenty years later instead of restricting photography to the period immediately after an event. The National Diet Library’s record for her photobook Senso wa Owatte mo Owaranai describes it as a work drawn from forty years of photography and focused on the wounds left by Japan’s wars*25.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photo History
sections.body_html:
Comparing Yoshito Matsushige, Ken Domon, and Hiromi Tsuchida: Positions on Photographing the Aftermath

Before Oishi, Japanese photography already included major works concerned with people living through and after war, not just images of combat or explosion. Yoshito Matsushige photographed Hiroshima on August 6, 1945. Faced with the injured, he was unable to release the shutter for more than thirty minutes, yet he ultimately made five photographs. The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum describes those images as “witnesses to history” from the day of the atomic bombing. *18 For Matsushige, firsthand presence at the event and the ethical difficulty of photographing became conditions of the record itself.

Oishi’s own starting point also predates her work on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Her documentary photography had already entered people’s daily lives in places such as New Guinea. Kiyosato Museum of Photographic Arts included New Guinea: Mother and Child in a Taro Field (1973) in an exhibition section on postwar Japanese photography, alongside works by Daido Moriyama, Mitsuaki Iwago, and others*26. Before she concentrated on the aftereffects of war, her work was therefore grounded in documentary encounters that placed people in relation to the environments in which they lived.

Ken Domon’s 1958 photobook Hiroshima grew from work made in the city in 1957 and addressed the long-term consequences of the atomic bombing through photographs of hibakusha, hospitals, orphanages, and people unable to pay for medical treatment. *19 Oishi cannot therefore be credited with first turning Japanese photography toward war’s aftereffects. Beginning in the 1970s, Hiromi Tsuchida also photographed hibakusha, the city, and surviving objects systematically in Hiroshima 1945–1979; the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum holds his 1976 portrait of manga artist Keiji Nakazawa, among other works. *20

Oishi’s distinct position lies in repeatedly crossing among different wars and regions—Hiroshima, Nagasaki, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Afghanistan, and the Holocaust—through the shared problem of time lived after war. When she has not witnessed the fighting herself, photography alone cannot establish the past event. Listening before photographing, returning later, and incorporating captions and testimony therefore become parts of the work. Matsushige witnessed Hiroshima on the day of the bombing; Domon photographed the lives of hibakusha in the 1950s; Tsuchida systematized survivors, the city, and objects. Oishi instead returned again and again to Vietnam, Cambodia, Hiroshima, Nagasaki, Auschwitz, and elsewhere, accumulating testimony and present-day portraits of survivors through one long-term documentary method.

An international comparison can be made with W. Eugene Smith and Aileen M. Smith’s Minamata project. The National Museum of Modern Art, Kyoto describes W. Eugene Smith as a leading figure in the LIFE photo essay and identifies the period beginning in 1971, when the Smiths lived in Minamata and documented pollution and its victims over time, as a major phase of his work*2. The Smiths lived within one affected community and communicated the continuing damage through photographs and text. Oishi moved repeatedly among Vietnam, Cambodia, Hiroshima, Nagasaki, Holocaust sites, and other regions, following the persistence of “after war” through the testimony of individual survivors.

The Tension between Humanism and Testimonial Photography

Oishi’s photographs often emphasize the dignity of people who have been harmed. That humanist emphasis carries a risk: if suffering is resolved into an image of people who live with composure and dignity, the political causes and specific histories of violence can recede. Oishi’s answer has been to listen to the people she photographs, return to their places, and sustain relationships over time. Canon’s materials for a 2008 exhibition show that, alongside her work around the world, she also photographed regional traditions in Japan, including Kurokawa Noh, over long periods. *3 The Japan Professional Photographers Society’s record of her honorary membership confirms her long institutional position across both photojournalism and photographic culture. *15

Oishi herself also situates this work within the history of photojournalism. A profile published by the Japan Professional Photographers Society lists her current research interests as “changes and trends in photojournalism” and “people in war and peace as seen through photojournalism”*23. Her long-term reporting is therefore also a method for photographing aftereffects and everyday life that fall out of a news cycle structured to move to the next event after combat or ceasefire.

Oishi’s long projects operate on a time scale different from news organized around the conclusion of an event. Crevis’s exhibition introduction stresses that she followed victims of war for roughly forty years and directed her lens toward memories held by people whose voices often went unheard*16. Nagoya City Library’s bibliographic record for Senka no Kioku likewise describes the book of 160 black-and-white photographs as a collection on victims of war*17. Instead of asking one decisive photograph to stand for a war, she met some people repeatedly and joined their testimony to their present bodies, making the passage toward forgetting itself part of what the record must address.

yto-barrada.html.lead_html: Yto Barrada photographed vacant lots, advertisements, sleeping figures, and gazes directed toward the port in Tangier, bringing them together in A Life Full of Holes: The Strait Project. Instead of framing migration through the dramatic moment of crossing, she followed the traces left across the city by enforced immobility, making photography an indirect record of border politics.This page also considers why her work brings film, publishing, archives, and local cultural institutions into the same field of activity.
yto-barrada.html.thesis_html: By the late 1990s, photographs of migration often pictured boats, checkpoints, and people crossing borders to convey the danger of passage. Such images could leave out the prolonged waiting before and after a journey, housing development, unemployment, and knowledge of border routes shared across a city. Barrada photographed sleeping figures, unfinished buildings, traffic signs, and transplanted plants in Tangier as a series, showing the border as a system that distributes time, housing, and work differently between those who can travel and those who cannot. In founding the Cinémathèque de Tanger, she complemented the international circulation of local images with an institution for preserving and screening films where they were made.
