sections.title: Historical Background
sections.body_html:
Tangier and the Schengen Regime—When the Strait Shaped Everyday Urban Life

Barrada was born in Paris and raised in Morocco and France. She studied history and political science at the Sorbonne before studying photography at the International Center of Photography in New York.*13A Life Full of Holes: The Strait Project, begun in 1998, emerged as the expanding Schengen regime imposed tighter controls on travel to Europe and Tangier became a place of waiting for people unable to reach a North that seemed close at hand.*2MoMA describes the series as a record of the physical, psychological, and political effects of the Strait of Gibraltar on the city.*1Tangier retains the memory of its colonial-era status as an international zone. In the 2000s, new housing spread into former grazing land alongside the construction of port and industrial facilities. Barrada photographed windowless apartment blocks and waste from garment factories to show how border policy takes form in urban planning, employment, and housing.*20

From Political Science to Photography—Reading the Traces Institutions Leave in Daily Life

Political science explains the structures of law and international relations. In Tangier, Barrada observed how those structures shape the course of a day, the design of housing, the availability of work, and the way streets are read. By placing road signs, sleeping bodies, vacant lots, and closed windows within the same series, she translated border control from an abstract policy into recurring details of urban life. The MASS MoCA guide describes her work as responding to dominant narratives through close attention and indirect inference.*3Barrada’s own statements do not assign a separate purpose to every low vantage point or area of empty space. Within the images, however, subdued color and open space keep the information from resolving into a single event and give viewers time to compare several traces.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
The Strait Project—Photographing the Border Beyond the Ferry Terminal

Boats, checkpoints, and rescues in press photographs communicate the immediate dangers of borders. They often leave out the unemployment, family time, unfinished housing, and shared knowledge of alternative routes that precede an attempted crossing. The Strait Project includes ferries, roads leading to the port, a school overlooking the strait, people sleeping in public gardens, unfinished buildings, and images made for tourists.*5Seen as a series, these elements shift the border from a single point at sea to a system that distributes urban time, housing, and work over the long term. Jeu de Paume presented the project as an inquiry into passage between South and North, the Maghreb and Europe.*10The logo of a bus company served as both transport signage and a source of practical border knowledge, allowing young people to assess where they might hide beneath a vehicle and how stringent the security would be.*20The series draws its critical force from recording shared practical knowledge and the duration of waiting without reducing migrants to symbols of dangerous passage.

Vacancy, Peripheral Views, and Sleep—Time Outside the Decisive Moment

Barrada’s images repeatedly return to roadside walls, shuttered windows, tilted advertisements, neglected parks, and periods without work. An early interview with openDemocracy describes how the photographs linked the desire to migrate with changes in the city.*9When these scenes appear alongside photographs of the port and sea, waiting becomes visible as a duration that exceeds the news cycle. Empty spaces and stillness create intervals through which institutional effects can be read across several places and times.

Plants, Urban Planning, and Colonial History—Natural History as Evidence of the Border

Beginning with Iris Tingitana, Barrada has worked with native plants of Tangier, imported species, public gardens, fossils, and dyes.The classification and transplantation of plants also record colonial rule, tourist development, land ownership, and imported systems of value.The Guggenheim exhibition Riffs presented the works that followed The Strait Project, including projects on botany and education, as continuations of questions arising from the impasses of a postcolonial city.*2Jameel Arts Centre likewise describes her work as rooted in Tangier while moving across culture, landscape, economics, and politics.*15

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
A Life Full of Holes—How the Photobook Turns Fragments into an Urban Structure

The series takes its title from the autobiography of the Moroccan storyteller Driss ben Hamed Charhadi, recorded by Paul Bowles.*11Individual photographs remain sparing in explanation, but in the photobook, the recurring ports, roads, people, signs, sea, and architecture reveal how the desire for movement and urban redevelopment arise from the same pressures. Witte de With presented the Strait project, ongoing since 1998, through both exhibition and publication.*11The photobook does not force these local fragments into a single conclusion. The distance between pages allows readers to reconstruct a political geography.

Cinémathèque de Tanger—Building a Local Infrastructure for Preservation and Screening

International exhibitions carry images of Tangier abroad. Preserving films, providing access to earlier works, and developing new audiences within the city required a local infrastructure for screening and collection. In 2006, Barrada and her collaborators restored the former Cinéma Rif and founded the Cinémathèque de Tanger. In a Walker Art Center conversation, Barrada and Bouchra Khalili describe the institution as an artistic intervention in urban space.*7Photography carries the city’s traces to international audiences; the cinema builds a local repository for film history and opportunities to see films. A BFI interview links the restoration of the cinema with Beau Geste, a film responding to redevelopment, as two parts of the same effort to preserve Tangier’s memory.*8The institution adds a continuing responsibility to preserve and share images where they were made to an art centered on the city.

From Photography to Film, Textiles, and Sculpture—Extending Observation into Material Research

Her later work in film, textiles, dyeing, sculpture, and publishing extends the observational methods of the early photographs into material research.Pace describes her projects with plant dyes and the educational space The Mothership as investigations into the ways history and material persist in present-day life.*12World of Interiors reported that her Tangier dye workshop and garden serve at once as a site for production, research, and local knowledge.*18The method of reading traces on urban surfaces continues in the colors of cloth, the cultivation of plants, and the reuse of architecture.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
From the Decisive Moment of Crossing to the Border Accumulating in the City

From the late 1990s through the 2000s, migration and borders appeared frequently in press photography and international exhibitions. Barrada made series from streets, signs, gardens, and sleeping bodies to show how institutions turn human time into waiting and land into provisional construction. In its 2024 retrospective, ICP read more than two decades of her photography through the phrase “part-time abstractionist,” emphasizing the ways ordinary objects and urban forms carry history.*5SFMOMA presents photographs of the school overlooking the strait and public gardens as works that examine how reality is constructed at the margins of globalization.*6Her place in photographic history rests on shifting the focus of border imagery from the instant of passage to the effects that accumulate across a city.

Politics and Play, Critique and Institution—How Barrada’s Position Has Been Assessed

Barrada’s work has often been discussed through the pairing of politics and play, documentary evidence and handwork. Sculpture Magazine describes a body of work that uses found objects and pedagogical devices to draw out the multiple histories carried by things.*17An ArtReview interview shows how making, learning, and sharing give her institutional critique a constructive form.*16At MoMA PS1, Le Grand Soir turned monumental blocks that recall Tangier’s walls and structures of power into a setting through which visitors could move and play.*4Historically, Barrada has joined peripheral observation, archival work, public institutions, and material research in a continuing cultural project that extends beyond photography used chiefly to explain a political issue.A Vogue article on Barrada’s two 2024 New York exhibitions discusses both her view of walls as structures of power and Le Grand Soir as a work visitors could climb, sit on, and use for play.*19Because historical research appears through a work’s form, color, and use instead of becoming a lesson, politics enters through the viewer’s bodily encounter as well as through the presentation of knowledge.

Bouchra Khalili, Zineb Sedira, and Barrada—Who Speaks for a Place, and Through Which Institutions?

Among her contemporaries who addressed migration, diaspora, and postcolonial memory,Bouchra Khalili centers moving people’s own voices and maps in her films, while Zineb Sedira develops histories through her family’s multiple languages and memories that cross the sea.Barrada reads the terms of movement through streets, architecture, plants, and cinemas, while individual testimony remains less prominent. The Peabody Museum describes her as an artist who registers the effects of global trade and exchange through personal, everyday moments.*14The Cinémathèque de Tanger and The Mothership create infrastructures for producing and preserving images and knowledge in Tangier alongside the international circulation of her work through museums. Her commitment to sustained cultural stewardship in the place she photographs also distinguishes her position in photographic history.The asymmetry between photographer and community nevertheless remains.Any assessment must account for the tension between the international art-market circulation of her work and her support for film culture in Tangier.Conversations about the Cinémathèque de Tanger describe the institution as an ongoing intervention in the city.*7

yuki-onodera.html.lead_html: Yuki Onodera changes the apparatus of exposure and the processes of the darkroom from one series to the next: second-hand clothes suspended against the sky, a glass marble placed inside a camera, and a stereo camera whose two lenses photograph separate locations. Through Portrait of Second-hand Clothes, How to Make a Pearl, and Roma – Roma, she has questioned the assumption that photography simply records reality, working through light, the camera, movement, and the manual labor of the print.
yuki-onodera.html.thesis_html: Onodera does not let a photograph end with the choice of subject and the instant of exposure. She places foreign objects inside cameras, uses two lenses in separate locations, then cuts, makes photograms, and hand-colors the print after exposure. Chance that cannot be fully determined by the photographer’s intention enters the same work as optics, chemistry, and manual labor. What she has pursued is the strangeness originally inherent in an optical apparatus that turns the world into a flat image*20. Even after photography and contemporary art drew closer in the 1990s, she continued to keep the camera, film, photographic paper, and darkroom processes at the center of the work.

sections.title: Background & Era
sections.body_html: Yuki Onodera studied fashion at Kuwasawa Design School and worked as an accessory designer for an apparel company. Uneasy with commercial fashion, which was shaped by markets and trends, she looked for another means of expression and began using her father’s camera, which was readily available to her. She later recalled that she initially thought she could use the camera like a paintbrush. But after walking the streets taking pictures, developing the film herself, and making black-and-white prints, she reached an impasse: it felt as though she was merely “looking for subjects”*17. She then turned to constructed photography. Here, the term refers to a method in which the photographer prepares objects or a situation before making the photograph, instead of finding a subject and photographing it on the spot. Onodera photographed objects she had made herself, including abstract forms created by melting and coloring plastic, and has said that she was also aware of currents in American constructed photography*17. The aim was to stop searching endlessly for subjects and create the starting point for a photograph herself. She received an Excellence Award in the first New Cosmos of Photography competition for You Are Running. I’m Waiting with Ears Like Dumbo’s*12. Her early works layer disparate images such as window frames, boxlike spaces, and circular forms, showing that she was already looking for alternatives to simply selecting a subject from what lay before her*1. In 1993, her first solo exhibition, which she organized and installed herself, and a collaborative book with a poet attracted attention. The attention did not lead to further opportunities to show the work, and she moved her base to Paris that same year*1. Onodera has said that she felt a need to work outside Japan and chose Europe over the more commercially oriented United States because of its cultural diversity. Within Europe, she chose Paris, which she regarded as a geographic and cultural crossroads*16. After moving, she encountered many artists in France who worked across both photography and contemporary art, and saw photography being used actively as a new medium within contemporary art*17. In another interview, she recalled that her work became more conceptual in this environment and that scale also became important*19. She made Portrait of Second-hand Clothes in 1994, and the following year presented Down—comprising Liquid and Glass, Portrait of Second-hand Clothes, and Birds—at three venues in Tokyo, which brought her wider recognition in Japan*8. At a time when the relationship between photography and contemporary art was changing, Onodera developed an approach that treated the structure of the camera, the darkroom, and the scale of the print as parts of a single production process. She later reflected that the sense of suspension in works from this period may have reflected her own way of living without fixing herself to one place or affiliation, and that instability felt more natural to her*24. In Liquid and Glass, Portrait of Second-hand Clothes, and Birds, made after her move to Paris, subjects repeatedly appear detached from the ground.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Why Photography? Photography’s Original Strangeness

Onodera’s reason for continuing with photography lies in her interest in the mechanism of photography itself. In a 2013 text, she notes that her works are often described as “strange” or “mysterious.” She writes that she does not set out to make strange works; what appears strange arises from a complicated sense of resistance in the way she approaches and handles photography. Images now circulate in enormous quantities, and making and viewing photographs have become ordinary activities. Onodera looks back to a much earlier experience: how strange it must have been, soon after photography’s invention, to use an optical instrument to fix the world onto a flat surface and then see one’s own likeness as a photograph. She identifies the search for this original “strangeness” as one reason she remains committed to photography*20. Later works continue that inquiry. She places a marble inside a camera or uses two lenses in separate places, testing familiar photographic mechanisms instead of accepting them as given.

From Looking for Subjects to Designing How to Photograph

After her initial impasse, the center of her work shifted from what to photograph to the conditions under which a photograph would be made. Each series uses a different apparatus. In Camera, two cameras face one another*3. In How to Make a Pearl, she places a marble inside the camera; in Roma – Roma, she uses the two lenses of a stereo camera in separate locations. Onodera has explained that her ideas do not come directly from works of art or films. She thinks for long periods about things that continue to occupy her in everyday life, and a work begins when she discovers a connection with something else*9. Her account of looking at an old stereo camera and wondering what would happen if its two lenses were exposed in different places, an idea that led to Roma – Roma, clearly shows this process. Because each series uses a different apparatus and procedure, the appearance of the images also changes substantially. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum describes Onodera’s work as a process close to sculpture, with alteration and construction beginning before the shutter is released*13. A photograph is made through choosing an apparatus, modifying the camera, and deciding how to develop and print the image. The moment of exposure is one part of that process.

Working with Photography’s Constraints to Expand Its Possibilities

Onodera accepts photography’s lack of freedom as a condition of making work. She has said that a painter begins with a blank canvas, while a photographer cannot escape the meanings already attached to a subject or its connection to reality; for her, the interest of photography lies in picking something out from within those limits*17. A camera does not move with the freedom of a paintbrush, and the photographer’s intention cannot fully determine the image. Onodera has explored what photography can do by changing the relationships among subject, apparatus, light, chance, and darkroom work. Discussing contemporary art, she has said that she feels comfortable at the boundary between fields: the art world sees her work as “photography,” while the photography world sees it as “contemporary art.” For her, that position holds many possibilities*9. She also notes that photography circles can give form greater weight than content, while presenting a work only as contemporary art can make photography seem like one material among many. She keeps some distance from both fields without fixing herself in either one. She calls her work photography because it draws heavily on photographic history, the structure of the camera, printing techniques, and the circumstances surrounding photography*9. Looking at photography from the side of contemporary art gave her another vantage point from which to consider photographic history and technique.

Rethinking How the Camera Is Used

In 2017, Michael Lucken read the marble in How to Make a Pearl as a foreign object that prevents the camera from operating normally. He saw the same attitude in Camera, Roma – Roma, and Look Out the Window, and noted that Onodera calls such methods “anti-photography”*21. For Lucken, “anti-photography” names a way of redirecting the medium’s operations. Two lenses are used in separate places. An object is placed inside the light-tight camera body. Photographic paper receives another exposure after the picture has been taken. She departs from standard camera and darkroom procedures to draw out different operations. Lucken also points out that the act of photographing itself becomes part of the work. In 2002, Hideki Maeda based his discussion of Onodera on the difference between the perception of a camera, which has neither a body nor practical aims, and human perception. He argues that many photographers try to bring machine vision closer to human sight, while Onodera expands the possibility that the camera might see in a different way from a human being*26. In How to Make a Pearl, the glass sphere produces another light inside the dark chamber; in Camera, one camera looks at another. From this perspective, her interventions move away from the habit of treating the camera as a substitute for one’s own eye.

Looking at Bodily Movement—Dance, Film, and Muybridge

Her interest in the body is deeply connected to her encounters with dance and film. Onodera resists a simple account in which her background in fashion led directly to her treatment of the body, and has said that she was influenced by dance and film, especially the work of William Forsythe and Pina Bausch in the 1980s and 1990s*16. When watching films, she also found herself looking at how characters stood and walked, not simply following the story. This interest extends from the invisible body in Portrait of Second-hand Clothes to the later Muybridge’s Twist. In Muybridge’s Twist, the sequential photographs of Eadweard Muybridge served as a direct point of departure. Onodera collaged multiple fragments of bodies in an attempt to bring successive choreography into a single still image*16. The dance of Forsythe and Bausch deepened her attention to bodily movement, while Muybridge’s sequences provided the specific starting point for Muybridge’s Twist. These different references converge on a continuing interest in how a photograph can hold the body and movement.

The Body at Work Beyond Exposure

In 2021, Lin Ye argued that because the camera as a black box can make the photographer’s body difficult to see within production, Onodera adds numerous actions outside the moment of exposure. She constructs subjects, researches places and travels, makes collages, colors prints one by one, and cuts paper. Ye places these actions within a process of testing and revising ideas through the body, rather than treating them as decorative finishing touches*22. In Roma – Roma, memories of movement between two places return through hand-coloring; in Eleventh Finger, photographs made without using the viewfinder, with a camera held at chest level continue into the cutting of paper in the darkroom. Results partly produced by the apparatus are carried forward through later handwork. The work extends beyond the shutter into movement, memory, and darkroom labor.

Accepting Chance, Finishing by Hand

Onodera’s works combine carefully specified procedures with results that even the artist cannot fully predict. In How to Make a Pearl, the marble disrupts light inside the camera. In Roma – Roma, the order of exposure determines how the two places are paired. In Eleventh Finger, a photogram made with cut paper is layered over the face of a person photographed without using the viewfinder*6. The mechanism is established, but the exact image is not decided in advance. This opening allows unexpected images to appear. After exposure, however, Onodera personally makes large gelatin silver prints, coarsens the grain, applies oil paint, and cuts paper. In a recent interview, she also said that she values some kind of circuit connecting the work and her body, and that she wants an image to appear as a material object, not remain something seen only on a screen*16. Images that emerge through chance are shaped into works through manual decisions about scale, grain, color, and surface. She leaves some choices to the apparatus, then takes the results into the darkroom and into handwork. The two processes remain visible within the same work.

Leaving Meaning Open, Making the Method Specific

Onodera does not determine a work’s meaning in words before making it and then use photography to explain that meaning. She has said that technical ideas, words, images, and concepts mix together in her mind and may connect with another idea years later*9. In another interview, she explained that making a future work too clear from the outset weakens it; she moves from an ambiguous state toward elements that gradually begin to acquire an outline*17. As she researches camera structures, routes of movement, and darkroom techniques, ideas become specific procedures. The final image remains open. In the stereo camera of Roma – Roma and the marble in How to Make a Pearl, an idea takes the form of a concrete apparatus or procedure, while the image that results still contains something unpredictable. This method leaves parts of the finished picture that cannot be fully resolved by a single explanation.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods & Media
sections.body_html:
Portrait of Second-hand Clothes—From Large Histories to One Garment at a Time

The 1994 series Portrait of Second-hand Clothes began when Onodera, after moving to Paris, wanted to make work concerned with people. She has said that after working with constructed photography, she wanted to move closer to human beings and chose clothing instead of actual people*16. The garments came from Christian Boltanski’s exhibition Dispersion, where visitors could take second-hand clothes home. Boltanski used a vast accumulation of clothing to convey the scale of tragedy; Onodera spread out and photographed garments one by one, seeking the small histories of individuals submerged within larger history*16. At the window of her Montmartre home, she held each garment upright with wire, adjusted the shoulders and hems, and waited for the right conditions in the sky and clouds. She later said that she avoided placing the clothing on the floor and presenting it as an object because she wanted to photograph the invisible body associated with it*16. The fifty-two garments show neither owners’ names nor faces, yet each assumes a different posture. The brightness of the sky defines the contour while the inside of the fabric sinks into darkness, allowing each garment to register as something that once touched a body without adding a narrative about the person. SFMOMA holds several works from the series*15. In 2017, Michael Lucken drew attention to the difference between Boltanski’s accumulation of clothing and Onodera’s decision to raise garments one by one into the air. He reads this distinction as an invitation to reconsider, garment by garment, a former owner, a generic body, and the culture of clothing*21.

Transvest—Bringing the Outside World Inside the Body

In Transvest, begun in 2002, Onodera fills the outlines of figures cut from newspapers and magazines with existing images of streetlights, architecture, microscopic photographs, and other subjects, then photographs them in strong backlight. From a distance, each figure appears as a single black body. Up close, images from different places and scales remain visible inside it, producing a body that contains the outside world. Dana Friis-Hansen identifies a tension between presence and absence across Onodera’s work and argues that in Transvest, both the visible silhouette and the harder-to-see interior shape the work*29. The Chinese photography critic Gu Zheng reads Portrait of Second-hand Clothes as a container in which clothing remembers the absent body; in Transvest, the body itself becomes a container for the world*30. Seen together, the two series show how Onodera’s treatment of the body has moved away from photographing faces and addressed, by different means, what remains after a body disappears and the external images that enter the body.

How to Make a Pearl—Introducing a Foreign Object into the Camera

The 2000–01 series How to Make a Pearl grew from Onodera’s curiosity about the interior of a box camera she found at a flea market. An idea about marbles connected with something she had heard about how pearls form, leading to a method of placing a small glass sphere inside the camera*1. Onodera photographed crowds on city streets in daylight, but the glass sphere collected and diffused light inside the camera’s dark interior. The people sank into darkness, while a white sphere appeared to float above them*14. She then used chemical processing to make the grain extremely coarse and enlarged the images into gelatin silver prints more than two meters high. Exhibition materials from the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum explain that the enlarged grain itself becomes material in the picture, bringing the crowd out of the darkness*10. The title refers to the way a pearl forms when a foreign object enters a shell. A small object inside the camera produces an image that the naked eye could not see, through both the optical apparatus and chemical processing. The transformation of light inside the camera determines the structure of the picture. In 2013, Onodera described the series as a work that directs attention to the existence of the camera itself at the same time as the crowd outside it*20.

Roma – Roma—Setting Aside the Choice of Place

In the 2004 series Roma – Roma, the photographer’s habit of choosing places and selecting individual pictures becomes the subject of the work. Onodera covered one lens of a stereo camera and made 108 exposures in Roma, Sweden. She then rewound the film and used the opposite lens to photograph Roma, Spain, on the same roll. The order of exposure determined the pairings between the two places. She made no selection among the 108 completed pairs and hand-colored every black-and-white photograph with oil paint*2. Onodera has explained that she deliberately set aside the usual practice of traveling to a place because it interested her as a photographer, and devised a method focused on “movement” itself*17. By assigning one lens to one place and the other lens to another, the structure of the apparatus and the sequence of travel determine the combinations more than the photographer’s preference. Choices are reduced during exposure; afterward, every image is printed and colored by hand. Judgment is distributed across the entire process instead of being concentrated at the moment of the shutter. In her 2013 text, Onodera explains that Roma – Roma set aside the photographic habit of recording a place. By retaining only the place names, she attempted to remove the photographer from the center of the work*20.Evence Verdier reads Birds, Watch Your Joints!, and Roma – Roma as works that bring movement and different times into the still image*28. In Roma – Roma, a pair of images carries more than the instant of exposure: it also holds the movement between two towns, the rewinding of the film, and the hand-coloring based on memory.

Below Orpheus—Turning Fiction into Physical Travel

The 2006 work Below Orpheus began with an unresolved disappearance at a hotel. Two and a half years later, Onodera stayed in the same room and photographed it. Using a seventeenth-century legend as a further clue, she then traveled to the point on the opposite side of the earth from the place of disappearance*27. Here, a hypothesis connecting fact and fiction determines the photographer’s route, and movement itself becomes part of the production process. In Roma – Roma, identical place names determine the route; in Below Orpheus, the connection between an incident and a legend does so. For Onodera, stories and rules can send her to places she would not normally choose, as well as shape the finished photographs.

Eleventh Finger and the Large Print—Work That Continues After Exposure

In the 2006 series Eleventh Finger, Onodera photographed people on the street without using the viewfinder, then placed paper with cutout holes on the photographic paper and made a photogram over the face area. Coarse photographic grain and the hand-cut contour of the paper remain together in a single image*6. According to Onodera’s production notes, the decision to cover faces began with questions about the image rights of people photographed without permission. Instead of using a conventional blur, she placed cut black paper over the photographic paper and made a white “shadow” through the photogram process. Her aim was to make flat white areas coexist with the rough texture of gelatin silver photography. Everything, including life-size prints up to about two meters high, was made through analog processes*25. Regarding the title, LensCulture cites Onodera’s explanation of an “unknown collaboration” between the subject’s ten fingers and the photographer’s one finger pressing the shutter*23.Gu Zheng notes that covering the face redirects a viewer’s attention, which in portrait photography usually goes first to the face, toward the posture and movement of the body*30. Onodera changes where the viewer looks first as well as how the photograph is made. Onodera’s works are often made as large gelatin silver prints: Portrait of Second-hand Clothes measures 115 centimeters square, while How to Make a Pearl reaches 210 by 150 centimeters*10. Her 2010 retrospective at the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum also centered on the way her methods change from one series to another, from camera modifications and collage to computer-based transformation*10. Scale, grain, cutting, and coloring show how the work continues after exposure, on the surface of the print and into the exhibition space.

sections.title: Critical Reception & Position
sections.body_html:
A Different Direction in the Era of “Onnanoko Shashin”

In Japan during the 1990s, self-portraits and photographs of everyday life by young women drew attention and were often grouped under the label onnanoko shashin, or “girl photography.” The J. Paul Getty Museum describes the term as reductive and controversial. Its 2015 exhibition The Younger Generation presented Onodera, Rinko Kawauchi, Chino Otsuka, Tomoko Sawada, and Lieko Shiga as five diverse practices that could not be encompassed by that label*4. Onodera also emerged in the early 1990s, as the first winner of the New Cosmos of Photography, yet from the beginning she did not center direct records of private life or self-portraiture. Her attention went to constructed images, the structure of the camera, the darkroom, and large prints. These artists shared the historical moment in which young women photographers were gaining new prominence, but their work cannot be reduced to a single style. After moving to Paris, Onodera encountered a setting in which contemporary photography was actively presented as a medium of contemporary art. She later recalled that her own work became more conceptual there and that scale became more important*19. Photographic history, camera structure, and printing techniques remained integral to the work*9. Her career intersects with both the rise of women photographers in the 1990s and the growing proximity of photography and contemporary art. Within that setting, she developed work centered on the camera’s structure, the darkroom, and materiality. In the 2005 exhibition Life Actually at the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo, Michiko Kasahara discussed How to Make a Pearl as a portrait of contemporary people and Transvest as a portrait of a complex contemporary individual*31. Even within an exhibition devoted to women artists, Onodera’s work was read in terms of crowds, anonymous bodies, and figures containing multiple images, rather than private confession or first-person everyday life.

International Criticism: Apparatus, Body, and Time

International criticism has approached Onodera’s work through different questions of apparatus, body, and time. In 2005, Evence Verdier compared her placement of a marble inside the camera in How to Make a Pearl to John Cage’s prepared piano*28. The comparison does not claim a line of influence. It explains a method of inserting a foreign object into an existing device to draw out an operation it was not designed to produce. In 2021, Lin Ye discussed the travel, fabrication, coloring, and darkroom work added beyond the exposure as actions that return the body to photographic production*22. In 2024, Yuzu Murakami connected the recurring sense of suspension in the early works with Onodera’s own stated affinity for instability*24. Although these readings differ, each shows that an initial idea is carried through the camera’s structure, the photographer’s movement, manual processes, and even the order in which viewers look.

What Connects the Different Series

The Centre Pompidou collection includes multiple works from Portrait of Second-hand Clothes and Look Out the Window*7. SFMOMA holds works from Portrait of Second-hand Clothes, How to Make a Pearl, and Look Out the Window*15. Works from different periods and made by different methods have continued to be represented in major international museum collections. The series vary greatly in appearance, but Onodera does not try to determine every element of the picture through the photographer’s judgment alone. A marble changes the light inside the camera. A stereo camera combines two places. A photogram creates another contour in the darkroom. She then works directly on the scale, grain, color, and surface of the print. The actual subject before the camera, optical changes inside the apparatus, chemical processing, and the surface of photographic paper remain in the work as physical traces. From one series to another, Onodera changes the relationships among the photographer’s intention, the subject, the apparatus, chance, and handwork. Her methods continue to change, but she consistently asks how a photograph becomes an image and where the photographer can enter that process, pursuing those questions through specific production procedures. In recent work, Onodera has not limited herself to gelatin silver photography. In the 2022 work Here, No Balloon, she overlays a digital 2.5D print on a gelatin silver print nearly two meters high that she printed herself, then collages them on canvas*32. She uses gelatin silver and digital processes according to the needs of each work and combines the necessary procedures. Her commitment to treating the image again as a physical object continues in recent work.

yurie-nagashima.html.lead_html: Yurie Nagashima has moved between self-portraiture, family photography, photobooks, and writing, repeatedly asking who photographs women’s bodies and who determines what those images mean. Her methods have shifted from the 1993 nudes made with her family to work on pregnancy, domestic life, her grandmother’s belongings, and photograms. Later, through research and writing, she examined the 1990s discourse that grouped her work under the label “girly photo.”
yurie-nagashima.html.thesis_html: Nagashima did not stop at claiming the freedom to photograph herself; she took up both the making of photographs and the language used to explain them. As an art student, she modeled in films and photographs made by male friends and felt that the women she was asked to play were types drawn from the makers’ fantasies, while she herself went unseen. She responded by moving between the front and back of the tripod, controlling both sides of the camera, and placing her family’s nude bodies in ordinary situations outside the conventions of sexual commodification. Later, she studied magazines and criticism published between 1990 and 2014 that had described her work as “girly photo,” tracing how artists with different methods were grouped together by gender and age.She had once occupied the position of the photographed subject; she took up the camera and eventually returned to the archives to examine the words that had framed her own work. The combination of image-making and scrutiny of critical language is a defining feature of Nagashima’s work.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html: Nagashima entered art school hoping to become a film director. Unable to enroll in the film program she wanted, she studied visual communication design instead. Photography was a required course, and she recalls that her work began when she acquired a used Nikon FE*1. In the summer of her second year, she left for Europe with an assignment from a teacher to “photograph Japanese people.” Realizing that she herself was Japanese, she began making self-portraits with a tripod*1. Her move into nude photography the following year grew partly from her experiences acting and modeling in films and photographs made by male friends at art school. Nagashima later recalled that the female roles she was asked to play followed types drawn from the makers’ fantasies and left her feeling that she herself was not being seen*4. After she became known as an artist, established male photographers also asked her to model, but she felt that accepting such requests would contradict her own work*4. Her resistance to the contemporary Japanese “hair nude” boom also led her to look for a way to separate the female nude from male sexual desire*1. She arrived at the idea of photographing her entire family naked while they went about ordinary activities. She has explained that she saw family as the relationship least readily associated with sex and chose to photograph everyday acts in the nude*1. In 1993, these self-portraits with her family were recognized at PARCO’s Urbanart competition, bringing Nagashima wider attention*2. Her early work was introduced through terms such as “self-nude” and was later folded retrospectively into the category of “girly photo,” which spread in the late 1990s. Nagashima has pointed to the timing of her debut and her move to the United States in 1995 to argue that she did not originally belong to a single group of that kind*1. By the mid-1990s, the sight of young women carrying cameras was itself being reported as a new cultural phenomenon. A 1996 Frieze article described the simultaneous attention given to diary-like snapshots and “girly culture,” noting that, with the emergence of Nagashima and Hiromix, young women carrying many kinds of cameras were taking to the streets*35. Age and gender often came before distinctions between the artists’ methods. Anthropologist Gabriella Lukacs argues that, during the recession following the collapse of Japan’s bubble economy, male critics read photographs of family and friends by women as a feminine effort to restore lost social bonds. The women making the photographs, meanwhile, were turning to photography in order to build working lives of their own, away from expectations that wives and mothers should sustain those relationships*27. At a time when women were trying to build careers in photography, their photographs were often treated as evidence of a supposedly feminine capacity to maintain domestic and social ties. Jane Simon and Mio Bryce, comparing Nagashima with Rinko Kawauchi, likewise examine how judgments about domestic subjects, familiar surroundings, and photographic technology fed criticism that described women photographers as “immature” or “intuitive”*28. After language study in Seattle, Nagashima entered the graduate program at the California Institute of the Arts. She has said that critique classes trained her to articulate her own work and changed her belief that photographs could communicate without explanation*1. In 2001, PASTIME PARADISE received the Kimura Ihei Award*9. Later, while pregnant and raising a child, she encountered discrimination around combining work with the roles expected of her as a mother. That experience led her back to the study of sociology and feminism*1. Her 2017 solo exhibition at the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum brought together early self-portraits and family photographs, 1990s youth culture, her years in the United States, the plant series made in Switzerland in 2007, and works concerned with women’s life courses*2. In 2020, she published “Bokura” no “onna no ko shashin” kara watashitachi no girlie photo e, based on research into photographic discourse from 1990 to 2014. The artist who had made the photographs now turned to the history of the words that had been used to explain them*3.

sections.title: The Work and Its Methods
sections.body_html:
Occupying Both Sides of the Camera

Nagashima’s self-portraits make the subject standing before the tripod and the photographer who sets the conditions and releases the shutter the same person. She has explained that photographing nudes of herself—images she would have found difficult to ask someone else to make—allowed her to decide the place, time, clothing, pose, and exact moment of exposure*4. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum holds the 1993 Self-Portrait (Family #26) as a gelatin silver print from her self-portrait series*5. Nagashima later said that this method allowed her to rearrange the conventional division between a male photographer and a female model and to assert that her body belonged to her*4. Nagashima has suggested that these photographs might be understood as records of performances: she has played roles, staged scenes, and moved between lived situations and constructed ones*4. The “self” in the frame is both evidence of a lived private life and a figure performing a role set by the photographer. Discussing the 1994 Tank Girrrl, Nagashima has said that she was trying to become Tank Girl, the popular comic-book character of the time, using a cigarette, septum piercing, eye patch, and T-shirt to play another person*29. In an interview with the British Journal of Photography, she distinguished between “Myself,” grounded in lived experience, and the staged “Self Portrait,” while stressing that both were performative*30. In the same interview, she recalled that she did not disclose every personal circumstance behind the work; photography could express her while also allowing those circumstances to remain concealed*30. Speaking to i-D in 2023, she said that playing a role during the shoots offered distance from problems in everyday life, and that the feeling of teasing men in particular was liberating*31.

Testing Habits of Looking Through Family Nudes

The family photographs were conceived to test the habit of automatically linking nudity with sex. Nagashima has explained that she considered family the relationship least readily associated with sexuality and devised scenes in which everyone would “do ordinary things while naked”*1. A known family relationship, routine gestures, and the strong sign of the nude occupy the same image, forcing the photograph to hold competing ways of reading the body. As an art student, Nagashima had modeled in works by male friends and felt that she was being made to play women drawn from the makers’ fantasies, without being seen as herself*4. In the family self-portraits, she moved back and forth across the tripod and decided the location, clothing, pose, and moment of exposure*4. The structure removed a fixed separation between photographer and photographed subject and gave her control over how nudity entered the image. “Family” in Nagashima’s work did not simply affirm blood ties. During a period of estrangement from her family of origin, she came to regard friends she had chosen as her real family, and empty white room records those friends, underground parties, and time spent at the edges of the city*29. Kazoku and empty white room show two different lived worlds: the family into which she was born and the friends she came to experience as family. Critic Jörg Colberg has compared Masahisa Fukase and Nagashima because both used the title Family and both appeared in the same frames as their relatives*33. Fukase repeatedly photographed his family from the 1970s through the 1980s using the group-portrait format of the studio where his father had long worked as a photographer. Young women who were not family members joined some of the portraits, and later images included photographs of his deceased father and niece within the group*34. Nagashima’s 1993 work was made at home. Her entire family performed ordinary actions while naked, she entered the frame herself, and a self-timer allowed her to determine the conditions of the photograph*1. Fukase returned to a fixed studio format and layered it with changes in family relationships, illness, and death. Nagashima set a scene in which the entire family was nude, altering both the sexual conventions attached to nudity and the division between photographer and model. Colberg contrasts the cynicism he finds in Fukase’s work with Nagashima’s use of the camera’s liberating potential to speak about her own family relationships*33. Nagashima has said that she did not know Fukase’s Family when making her early work, so there is no basis for describing the two as a direct line of influence*23. The shared title therefore sharpens a difference in method: Fukase repeated the conventions of the studio portrait, while Nagashima staged a nude family scene at home and controlled it herself. Each artist occupied a different position within the family image and constructed the scene in a different way.

Using Photography to Investigate What She Does Not Yet Understand

Nagashima has used photography to investigate things she does not yet understand. In a 2016 interview, she said that she chooses subjects connected to social issues and wants the work to generate discussion*23. In the same interview, she described photography as a way to examine what she cannot understand and compared memory to a box full of photographs rather than a sequence arranged in chronological order*23. For her, photographing is less a single act that resolves a question than a process of observing, recognizing, and coming to accept*23. Family, home, and the body recur across different periods, with the same subjects photographed differently as life changes.

From a Single Self-Image to the Time of a Life

Nagashima’s self-portraiture extends far beyond a handful of nude images from the 1990s. She made more than 600 photographs between 1992 and 2016, later reworking them into a slide show of about thirty minutes*4. The body in the photographs changes through youth, pregnancy, childbirth, child-rearing, and aging; photographing the same person over many years becomes a form in itself*7. Nagashima has said that changes in her body and changes in her work have moved together*8. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s official profile lists the 2004 photobook not six among her major publications, and the 2017 exhibition placed her long-term self-portraits alongside works concerned with women’s life courses*2. In the slide show and the photobooks, bodies from different periods appear in sequence. The life that unfolds cannot be contained by a single label such as “nude,” “mother,” or “young woman.”

From Her Own Body to Women’s Memories of War

After giving birth, Nagashima’s attention expanded from her own experience and that of her family to the lives of other women. In Senninbari, made in 2004 and first presented in 2005, she recreated on one of her own shirts the wartime practice in which women sewed protective thousand-stitch objects for family members leaving for military service, inviting about 660 women to add a stitch*21. At a day-care center next to her son’s nursery school, she interviewed women who remembered the war and recorded them on video. The exhibition also assembled Polaroids of the participants’ faces and hands as they sewed*21. Nagashima has explained that the September 11 attacks occurred while she was pregnant in 2001, followed by the war in Afghanistan, and that giving birth amid those events made it harder to regard war as something unrelated to her own life. Questions about her child’s future began to enter the work*21. At the Chihiro Art Museum’s Life exhibition, the work appeared in the same space as video interviews with people who had experienced the war, presenting individual handwork as a way of speaking about wartime memory*26. A body of work that began with Nagashima’s own body in self-portraiture opened, in Senninbari, toward the handwork and testimony of women who had lived through wartime. Her method shifted from appearing in the image herself to listening to and recording time experienced by others.

Examining the Name “Girly Photo”

Nagashima’s examination of the term “girly photo” grew from repeated experiences of having her body and her work explained in other people’s words. She has said that from around junior high school she felt uneasy as her body and behavior were pressed toward expectations of “femininity,” and she identifies reading Simone de Beauvoir’s The Second Sex at eighteen as her first encounter with feminism*7. As a young woman, however, Nagashima did not think of herself as a feminist. In a 2021 statement for the 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa, she recalled that the feminists she saw on television seemed to be older scholars and activists. That image did not connect with her own difficulty living as a woman or with her sense that she could not easily build solidarity or join a movement*22. Over time, she began to reread the questions that had repeatedly appeared in her work—body, family, labor, and the roles expected of her as a mother—through the language of feminism*22. Discrepancies in language had already shaped the reception of her work. In 1993, after seeing a slide show by Nan Goldin and a talk with Nobuyoshi Araki at PARCO, Nagashima asked Goldin how she built relationships intimate enough to photograph private moments between people close to her. A later critical book retold the question as a desire to photograph people having sex, a version that conflicted with Nagashima’s memory*36. A question about intimacy had been rewritten as a story about a young woman and sex. Nagashima’s early self-portraits had themselves been made in response to the way a male-dominated society looked at women’s bodies*4. The works were later discussed under the name “girly photo” and associated with technical immaturity, intuition, youth, and femininity. Nagashima objected to the way artists with different methods were grouped by gender and judged through old male/female binaries and unverified claims about their private lives*18. Reading the 2010 book “Onna no ko shashin” no jidai became a direct impetus for constructing her own response. After meeting Yuki Senda through a study group led by Chizuko Ueno, which she had attended since 2007, Nagashima entered graduate school in 2011*18. She has said that the aim of her book was less to blame individual critics than to make it possible for herself, and for others who think of themselves as “girls,” to speak without sacrificing their self-respect*18. In graduate school, she collected magazines and books published between 1990 and 2014 and used discourse analysis to examine how the repeated circulation of the same explanations produced the category “girly photo”*1. In 2014, she led an ISSP workshop in Latvia titled “Photography as a Subversive Tactic: Being the Other”*32. In the same interview, she also said that she dislikes being classified under a single name*23. In the early work, she set the conditions and made her own self-portraits. Later, she returned to the magazines, books, and criticism that had explained her work and that of her contemporaries. Both in making photographs and in examining language, she chose to verify things herself rather than leave their explanation to others.

Plants as a Way Back to Her Grandmother’s Creative Life

In the 2007 series SWISS, flowers, plants, and interior spaces moved to the center of the frame. Shortly before the residency in Switzerland, Nagashima found among her late grandmother’s belongings a large group of flower photographs made about twenty-five years earlier, along with materials for pressed flowers. She has said that this was the first time she recognized in her grandmother, who had been a housewife, a creative drive similar to her own*19. Her grandmother had continued gardening and observing plants, leaving behind photographs and pressed flowers, but this work had never been recognized as a professional artistic career and remained within the home. Nagashima took her grandmother’s flower photographs with her when she traveled to a residency in Switzerland with her young son, where she photographed local plants, the rooms in which they stayed, and their life together*19. Plants became both a new subject and a way to trace the gaze of her late grandmother and the creative work one woman had sustained inside the home. That concern later continued in past, perfect, progressive., made with her grandmother’s belongings, and in questions about the standards that separate the “professional” from the “amateur”*1. 黄色い野生の花 from SWISS is held by the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum as a 2007 chromogenic print*12. Critic Noi Sawaragi read the 2010 SWISS+ as a transformation of Nagashima’s first exhibition, Ai no Heya, arguing that the focus had shifted from photographs that showed family relationships to the question of how to photograph relationships as they come apart through death and separation*38. As Nagashima incorporated her grandmother’s photographs and pressed flowers into the work, creative activity left inside the home and the boundary between “professional” and “amateur” became subjects in their own right.

Building Relationships with Strangers Through Conversation and Exchange

From 2015 onward, Nagashima began to include in her work the process through which a relationship with someone not yet close to her takes shape. During the KIITO residency project 縫うこと、着ること、語ること。, she invited women in Kobe to contribute clothes they “wanted to throw away but could not,” listened to the stories attached to them, photographed the women wearing the garments, and gathered materials through exchanges involving her own used clothes and photographs*24. The collected clothes were turned into a large tarp in collaboration with her partner’s mother and exhibited with the photographs*24. Photographing, listening, exchanging objects, and sewing with another woman all belonged to the same work. The early family photographs used existing relationships to rearrange the roles of photographer and subject. Here, relationships with women she did not know were built through conversation and exchange, and the time required to form those relationships became part of the work.

From Spaces for Photographs to Spaces of Care

Nagashima’s use of materials beyond photography and of collaborative processes increased in the 2010s. Her concern with how viewers move through a space and in what order they encounter photographs, however, can be traced back to her first exhibition, Ai no Heya, in 1994. A room covered in red fur contained a television, a sofa, and nudes of the artist; beyond a curtain, family nudes were arranged in a dark, narrow space*20. The place and sequence in which bodies were seen mattered as much as the selection of photographs. In about home, objects made with her mother and photographs of different sizes occupied the space, while her grandmother’s flower photographs and family memories became material for considering domestic life, women’s creative work, and the boundary between professional and amateur*10. In the 2020 exhibition B&W, Nagashima showed 8×10 photograms made by placing pressed flowers inherited from her grandmother directly on photographic paper, as well as landscapes printed on wooden boards coated with photographic emulsion; she made both in the darkroom herself*11. Discussing the photograms in past, perfect, progressive., she described the use of silhouettes as a way to open photography—so often dominated by vision—to the viewer’s imagination*8. For the 2023 project ケアの学校, she opened the exhibition space as her own studio and created a place where participants could learn about “care” through talks, presentations, reading groups, a flea market, tea gatherings, and other activities*25. A space for looking at artworks became a place for talking with others, learning, and sharing time. One source for this development was the death of her dog Punk in 2021*31. Nagashima has recalled that, in a relationship with a dog involving little verbal communication, what she missed most after his death was simply his presence during ordinary time. She came to think of care as something that can consist both of heavy responsibility and of “simply being there”*31. In the exhibition, she included a photograph of the back of her head, with her hair dyed the same color as Punk and tied with a ribbon he had worn, using a personal loss as a point of entry into a conversation about care*31. A 2024 checklist from the National Museum of Western Art includes photographs, drawings on postcards, and works made with human hair, dog hair, wool, yarn, and paper*17. The spatial construction that began with Ai no Heya in 1994 later expanded to include inherited objects, handwork, and collaboration.

sections.title: Criticism and Reception
sections.body_html:
Early Attention Came with Doubts About Her Status as a Photographer

Nagashima’s early work received substantial press, but attention did not automatically amount to recognition as an artist. Writing in Studio Voice in 1995, Kotaro Iizawa declined to place Nagashima alongside Robert Frank, Nan Goldin, or Nobuyoshi Araki. He suggested that she might not yet be called a “photographer,” while praising the enthusiasm of a twenty-year-old “girl” and describing her technique as an “awkward hand”*20. Even after the PARCO award, whether she qualified as a “photographer” remained a subject of criticism. The following year, Frieze placed sixteen women photographers within a trend of diary-like snapshots and “girly culture,” discussed young women photographing themselves and their surroundings, and ended by asking whether love or narcissism lay behind the camera*35. The same article welcomed the shift of women from objects of the camera to subjects behind it while still discussing their work collectively through age and gender*35. Tokyo Art Beat has described how the 1993 family photographs drew a strong response and how the work continued to be read, often with misunderstanding, through the categories of “hair nude” and “girly photo”*6. Nagashima’s first solo exhibition at a public museum, held at the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum in 2017, brought together roughly a quarter century of work, from early nudes to plants, domestic life, and collaborative projects. In doing so, it offered a broader account of an artist who had long been reduced to a few provocative images*2. A RealTokyo review of her 2020 book argued for reconsidering the discourse around women photographers and returning evaluation to the actual viewing and discussion of the works*13. Nagashima attracted attention early, but for many years her work reached the public through names such as “hair nude” and “girly photo.” The 2017 retrospective and the 2020 book examined that distance through different means: exhibition-making and archival research.

The Same Private Life, Different Photographic Methods

In mid-1990s Tokyo, diary-like snapshot photography and “girly culture” drew attention at the same time, while the names Nan Goldin, Jack Pierson, and Wolfgang Tillmans were also becoming widely familiar in the art world*35. Nagashima and Hiromix were placed at the center of the same phenomenon, and Frieze described Hiromix as a photographer of herself and her friends*35. Nagashima’s point of departure was different: a tripod, a self-timer, and the decision to stage her entire family nude*1. Although the artists shared an attention to nearby life, Nagashima kept two questions at the center of the work: who constructed the scene, and who occupied the position of being looked at. Comparing her with Rinko Kawauchi, Jane Simon and Mio Bryce distinguish Nagashima’s “feminist politics of looking” from Kawauchi’s cumulative “poetics of looking”*28. Both turn the camera toward domestic and everyday life, but the study emphasizes the gendered problem of “looking/being looked at” in Nagashima and the visual rhythm created by accumulating fragments of daily life in Kawauchi. A difference from Nan Goldin also appears in the question Nagashima asked her in 1993. The question concerned how to build relationships intimate enough to photograph friends’ private moments, not sex itself*36. Nagashima placed herself and her family inside the frame, addressing intimacy and control over the conditions of the photograph within the same work. A 2018 comparative study placed Nagashima alongside the Chinese photographer Luo Yang, citing film, familiar surroundings, and relationships with close subjects as points of contact*37. The study notes that Nagashima repeatedly photographs herself, her family, her husband, and her son, while Luo Yang photographs friends and women with whom she feels an affinity as an extended family beyond blood ties*37. All of these artists work with nearby life, but the relation between photographer and subject differs across Nagashima’s self-performance, Hiromix’s snapshots of friends, Kawauchi’s fragments of the everyday, and Luo Yang’s portraits of friends.

From a 1990s Phenomenon to a Cross-Generational History of Photography

Recent international exhibitions have placed Nagashima beyond the 1990s category of “girly photo” and within a longer history of women photographers in Japan. Aperture’s 2024 publication I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now brought together twenty-five artists across generations and included Nagashima’s photographs and writing in a reconsideration of Japanese photographic history*14. For the 2025 presentation at Fotografie Forum Frankfurt, the pregnancy self-portrait Full-figured, yet not full-term was selected as one of the exhibition’s press images*15. In a 2024 exhibition at the National Museum of Western Art, more than twenty contemporary artists and groups, including Nagashima, responded through their work to the question of whether the museum had been a place capable of nurturing the art of the future*16. Nagashima is increasingly being revisited from two directions: the history of women photographers in Japan from the postwar period to the present, and contemporary art that moves across photography, materials, and writing*14. The family nudes remain an important point of departure. Over more than three decades, she has continued to work with three related methods: photographing herself and her family, structuring lived time through photobooks, and using archives to examine the names and explanations attached to her work.

zbigniew-libera.html.lead_html: Zbigniew Libera is a central figure in Polish Critical Art who has repurposed toys, exercise equipment, home video, and press photographs to expose how society trains bodies, gender roles, and historical memory. In LEGO Concentration Camp, he brought the pedagogical character of a mass-produced commodity into collision with Holocaust representation. In Positives, he restaged iconic images of catastrophe as cheerful scenes, examining how the act of looking at photographs is governed by images already stored in memory.
zbigniew-libera.html.thesis_html: Libera worked with the habits through which toys, exercise devices, and press photographs are accepted without question. LEGO Concentration Camp inserts the architecture of mass murder into the instructional logic of play, while Positives reenacts the compositions of historical news photographs as apparently happy scenes. He made visible how familiar objects and images repeatedly teach us to understand bodies, gender, violence, and history. The central question is not whether a photograph is true or false, but how circulated images shape memory.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Born in Poland in 1959, Libera began working under martial law in the early 1980s, amid the conflict between state censorship and the formation of independent culture. His official biography records his involvement in collaborative production and publishing outside established institutions, including Kultura Zrzuty in Łódź, the magazine Tango, and circles around Zofia Kulik and Przemysław Kwiek*1. His work did not begin along a single path as a photographer. It developed across video, magazines, objects, and photography. Within this broader field, photography became one medium for examining how social commands and established images are recorded, reproduced, and learned again.

Bodies and Records under Martial Law

Materials from 1989–91 held by the Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw show how Libera preserved underground culture, everyday life, and political transition in a personal archive*2. The artist text on Niepodległe connects his imprisonment for dissident activity with his continuing interest in the ideologies that shape social roles, gender, and education*3. In this setting, the camera became less a device for objective reporting than a companion for recording the small-scale ways in which both state and household regulate the body.

Early Video and the Training of the Body

Mystical Perseverance consists of video recordings of the repetitive movements of Regina G., an elderly bedridden woman, together with medicines, a bedside table, and a television*4. Because the footage was made without her knowledge and later exhibited, the work produces an ethical tension around the viewer’s position as well as around physical decline and medicalization*4. In How to Train Little Girls, domestic acts of teaching makeup and gesture are exposed as training in the production of femininity*5. The Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw describes these early works as uses of the camera to test the boundaries of socially permissible images*6。

Libera’s Position within Critical Art

In the 1990s, Libera became a leading figure in the movement known as Polish Critical Art. Culture.pl describes his work as an analysis of the mechanisms through which social norms enter the body via commodities, medicine, education, and images*7. The Cultural Opposition archive traces the continuity of these concerns from alternative culture in the 1980s to the “corrective devices” of the 1990s*8。

Polish Critical Art after 1989

Culture.pl defines Polish Critical Art of the 1990s as a movement concerned with the ways bodies are trained by power, medicine, education, and cultural norms, and identifies Libera, Katarzyna Kozyra, and Artur Żmijewski as key artists*22. Kozyra brought social taboos such as nudity, aging, and death to the foreground through video, photography, and performance*23. Żmijewski also worked with living bodies and group behavior, while Libera chose toys, exercise equipment, packaging, and familiar press photographs*22. He approached contemporary problems as norms taught unconsciously by everyday objects, rather than as exceptional bodies or dramatic scenes. Although his subjects shifted from underground video in the 1980s to consumer goods in the 1990s, the question of how bodies are trained remained continuous.

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
The readymade objects and familiar photographs Libera uses do not function as an intellectual game of identifying sources. Commodities and press images already shape behavior and memory. A slight alteration of their established forms is enough to reveal the commands embedded in everyday life.

“Corrective Devices” Make Everyday Commands Visible

Works from the mid-1990s such as Body Master preserve the appearance of exercise equipment and toys while exaggerating ideals of the body, masculinity, and development. Libera chose these forms because social norms enter daily life through play and self-improvement, rather than as explicit commands. Raster Gallery argues that his reversals of consumer-product formats expose how commodities educate desire and behavior*9. The Zachęta collection likewise shows how his photographs, videos, and objects consistently question socially prescribed forms of behavior*10。

LEGO Concentration Camp Questions the Innocence of Toys

LEGO Concentration Camp presents a camp through the format of LEGO boxes and construction models, placing play, education, commodities, and historical violence within the same visual language. The Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw records that the artist used bricks supplied by the company, printed “sponsored by LEGO” on the boxes, and produced one of the central controversies in Polish art of the 1990s*11. The current collection page preserves the work as an installation of seven boxes, showing that the packaging itself is central to its meaning*12。

A scholarly article from Poznań analyzes the work not only as a representation of past violence but as an exposure of contemporary education through repeatable models*24. LEGO components can be assembled according to instructions to reproduce the same finished form. By placing a camp within that system, the work does not equate Nazism with children’s play. It asks what rational rules, education, and cultural policy teach people to remember as normal order. The toy is necessary because violence can be internalized through repeatable forms of learning as well as through overt commands.

Leaving the Limits of Representation Unresolved

The work simultaneously risks trivializing the Holocaust, commodifying history through consumer culture, and turning violence into a repeatable structure through a toy. The Jewish Museum’s 2002 exhibition Mirroring Evil placed it within the ethically difficult question of how recent art uses Nazi imagery*13. A review in Frieze considered both the way the work destabilizes viewers’ moral security and the danger that shock can itself be consumed within art institutions, rather than reducing it to the force of provocation*14。

A contemporary essay situated LEGO Concentration Camp within an iconoclastic lineage that questions modes of remembrance by breaking existing representations, in contrast to monuments that directly reconstruct the Holocaust*26. A binary judgment of whether the use of a toy is appropriate cannot explain the structure of the discomfort the work produces. It unsettles both the belief that only solemn representation can safeguard memory and the belief that commodified shock can deliver historical understanding, creating a space in which viewers must examine their own responses.

Meaning after Circulation over Authorial Control

In an interview with ARTMargins, Libera argues that an artist cannot own the interpretation of a work*15. This position corresponds to his method, in which boxes, newspapers, and exhibitions move a work into new settings and alter its meaning. Another ARTMargins essay argues for reading the bodily experience of late socialism together with the mentality of consumer society after the 1990s*16。

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
In the 2000s, Libera placed greater emphasis on photography and directly addressed the ways press images form personal memory. His official biography presents Positives, Masters, and La Vue as a sustained investigation into how media produce internal images of history*1。

Positives—Restaging Images of Catastrophe as Cheerful Scenes

Positives restages widely recognized press photographs of war, disaster, and violence as calm scenes with actors arranged in similar compositions. Culture.pl explains that Libera called the original photographs “negatives” and selected images that had remained in his memory since childhood*17. Casino Luxembourg observes that the eight photographs remain incomplete without knowledge of the original images, making the viewer’s memory a second medium of the work*18。

Research from Jagiellonian University considers Positives in relation to the social functions of documentary and art photography, the manipulation of reality through images, and the formation of memory*25. The cheerful reenactments are not fakes that deny the facts of the original photographs. They depend on viewers’ ability to recall the catastrophes and thus demonstrate how historical photographs are remembered as compositional templates more than as details—templates that can be transferred to different people and places. Libera’s material was not simply the press photograph, but memory standardized to the point of quotation.

Making Print Circulation Part of the Work

Some works from Positives were published in magazines and newspapers, returning them to the same channels of circulation as the original press images. A text on Bush’s Dream argues that its kitsch reenactment makes visible the conversion of images of war into cinematic narratives of good, evil, and victory*19. The critique extends beyond alterations within the image to include headlines, page design, and stories already familiar to readers.

La Vue, Masters, and the Fabrication of Photographic History

La Vue enlarges fragments that enter the everyday field of vision, showing that seeing is structured through selection and editing. InVisible Culture discusses the series together with Positives along a continuum of mediated visual experience encompassing photography, memory, and Google Street View*20. In Masters, Libera created fictional magazine spreads that appear to introduce Polish avant-garde artists in prestigious publications, demonstrating that canons are produced through publishing and institutions as well as through the qualities of individual works*10。

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Libera cannot be defined solely as a photographer, yet his objects and videos are deeply connected to photographic history through their concern with the framing, reproduction, and circulation of existing images. The Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw’s artist page surveys this long practice, including his more recent large-format photographs*12。

Controversy Is Not the Measure of the Work

The visibility of LEGO Concentration Camp can easily overshadow Libera’s other work. Culture.pl’s retrospective account treats the early videos, the corrective devices, and the book Fotografie as parts of one investigation whose focus expanded from bodily discipline to historical memory*7. The significance of the work lies less in how often it breaks taboos than in its sustained analysis of how apparently harmless forms transmit norms.

How Press-Photograph Compositions Shape Memory

Positives reenacts compositions repeatedly encountered in newspapers and photobooks, not historical events themselves. When the placement of figures, direction of gazes, shape of hands, and cropping remain recognizable, the original catastrophe returns even after expressions and circumstances have been reversed*17. Photography is not a transparent container for memory. Repeated compositions shape how events are remembered and make experiences that fall outside those templates harder to see.

Tracing How Photographs, Toys, and Advertising Carry Commands

Libera’s work does not purify photography into an autonomous art medium. By placing toy boxes, advertisements, newspapers, exercise equipment, and video alongside one another, he traces the channels through which society’s commands enter everyday life. His later photographs also emphasize how existing images acquire authority through editing, printing, and exhibition, more than the subjects before the camera. In this sense, his work connects Polish Critical Art to a media archaeology of the routes through which images and objects circulate. Results of Selected Field Studies points in this direction by bringing existing images together with research materials and treating photographs less as evidence of fact than as documents through which institutions organize the appearance of factuality.*21。
