aya-fujioka.html.title: Aya Fujioka | Here Goes River, Snapshot Photography, and Hiroshima Today | Photo Coordinates
aya-fujioka.html.meta_description: Aya Fujioka’s Here Goes River, I Don’t Sleep, and Life Studies are examined through travel, family, New York, Hiroshima, snapshot photography, and photobook sequencing.
aya-fujioka.html.lead_html: Aya Fujioka photographs gestures and disquieting details of everyday life on her travels, in her hometown of Kure, in New York, and in Hiroshima. Through delayed selection and photobook sequencing, she turns meanings she could not grasp at the moment of exposure into finished works. Through I Don’t Sleep, Here Goes River, and Life Studies, this page considers what photographs preserve beyond the photographer’s intention, and how personal experience intersects with the memories of families and cities.
aya-fujioka.html.thesis_html: Fujioka does not separate private photographs of family from the chance encounters of street photography. In Here Goes River, she did not begin with Hiroshima’s established symbols. She recognized recurring bicycles, floodwaters, children, and the Atomic Bomb Dome among thousands of instinctive photographs made while walking through the city. By keeping her own life in Hiroshima—near her hometown—within the work, and by resisting an overly explanatory sequence, she made the city’s history visible together with the photographer’s own position within it.

sections.title: Travel, Kure, New York, and Hiroshima
sections.body_html: Aya Fujioka was born in Kure, Hiroshima Prefecture, and graduated from the Department of Photography at Nihon University College of Art in 1994*1. She has recalled that she did not enroll with a clearly defined ambition to become a photographer; she began taking pictures because she found herself in a photography program*2. Her life in Taiwan and travels through Europe and Brazil began before she had a plan for making a body of work. Photographs accumulated during those journeys were later selected in Japan and published in 2004 as Comment te dire adieu*7. In 2005, she joined a roughly 300-kilometer peace march across Belgium calling for the abolition of nuclear weapons, recording the ten-day experience in photographs and words*23. For her next book, I Don’t Sleep, she traveled between Tokyo and Kure, photographing her family home, relatives, and her mother’s body and working hands*5. In 2007, she moved to New York through the Japanese Agency for Cultural Affairs’ overseas study program for emerging artists, photographing both the city and domestic interiors for about five years*11. After returning to Japan in 2012, she began living in Hiroshima in 2013 and developed Here Goes River while walking along the city’s waterways. The Hiroshima Prefectural Art Museum describes how Fujioka photographed a city where daily life overlaps with past events, treating rivers whose direction changes with the tides as a figure for memory*8. She now works between Kyoto and Hiroshima*1. Across travel, return, and relocation, she repeatedly revisits photographs after time has passed, using them to understand experiences that were not apparent when the pictures were made.

sections.title: The Core of Her Work
sections.body_html:
Snapshot Photography — Preserving What Escapes Explanation

Street snapshots are the starting point of Fujioka’s method. She has said that as a student she repeatedly studied Henri Cartier-Bresson’s photobooks, admired his ability to seize an instant, and has continued to photograph in the street ever since*4. Her present approach does not allow the decision made at exposure to determine the photograph’s final meaning. In Hiroshima, she made an enormous number of pictures because beginning with a theory or intention made it harder to photograph; she later found that the images showed her things she had looked at but failed to notice*2. When reviewing old negatives, she also discovered that she had repeatedly photographed children and flowers, prompting her to consider her own unconscious choices and the reasons she takes photographs*13. Fujioka’s snapshots preserve people and objects that slipped outside her conscious understanding. Later selection brings those overlooked elements to the center of the work.

I Don’t Sleep — Her Mother’s Hands and the Unknown Within the Familiar

I Don’t Sleep was made from photographs of Fujioka’s family and hometown, taken while she lived in Tokyo and returned regularly to Kure. SIGMA SEIN notes that the series was photographed during visits between 2000 and 2006, and that her mother appears through her back and oblique profile, working hands, and gestures more often than through a frontal portrait*5. Fujioka has said that exhibiting the work at the Nikon Salon allowed her to see the flow of the photographs more objectively, while the photobook required repeated decisions about what to include and omit*3. In its large format, sequences of hands, hair, clothing, flowers, domestic objects, and fragments of the body hold together intimacy with family and the sudden realization that those closest to her remain unknowable. The book leaves intimacy, aging, and estrangement from her hometown unresolved instead of explaining identities and relationships like a family album. The English-language annual report Photographic Expression in Japan, published in the year of the book’s release, likewise identified the raw and strange qualities of family bodies and behavior as a defining feature, indicating an early reception that exceeded the category of intimate record*18.

Walking in Belgium — Ten Days Inside a Peace March

The 2005 series Walking in Belgium records, in photographs and words, a peace march calling for the abolition of nuclear weapons that Fujioka joined almost by chance. Over ten days and roughly 300 kilometers, she later recalled becoming so absorbed in the march and its encounters that her awareness of taking photographs began to recede*23. Fugensha presents the experience as an event that occurred about a decade before Here Goes River, placing both works within a continuing engagement with peace and war. Fujioka entered the movement without first organizing a settled position and without fully understanding what she herself was doing. The photographs and words revisit, twenty years later, what it meant to become caught up in the event rather than state a conclusion from outside it. A direct line of influence on Here Goes River cannot be established, but the series anticipates her later tendency to approach historical subjects through events on the ground and her own responses, without reducing them to symbols.

Here Goes River — Why Photograph Everyday Hiroshima?

In the Hiroshima of Here Goes River, the history of the atomic bombing already existed as a powerful set of received images. Fujioka has said that after beginning life in the city, she came to understand how difficult it was to register history through the dense layers of everyday experience. Her view of contemporary Hiroshima also included the many ceremonies and expressions organized around “peace”*6. Early in the project, the more she considered how “Hiroshima” ought to be photographed, the less able she was to take pictures, burdened by the responsibility of producing an image that would stand for history*3. She instead photographed people playing by the river, young people posing, passing bodies, seasonal light, and incidents in the street. Without deciding in advance which symbols would explain Hiroshima, she followed what caught her attention in daily life. The Atomic Bomb Dome and forms that evoked past events then appeared in parts of the frame she had not treated as central while photographing. History emerged by changing the meaning of present-day images when she returned to them later.

Hiroshima mon amour — “Seeing, Yet Not Seeing”

While developing Here Goes River, Fujioka showed editor Nozomi Himeno and designer Hisaki Matsumoto Alain Resnais’s Hiroshima mon amour, scripted by Marguerite Duras, and told them that it suggested something she wanted to do in a photobook. Relating herself to the opening exchange—“I saw it” / “You saw nothing”—she described thinking about a self who was “seeing, yet not seeing”: she lived in Hiroshima and thought she knew the city, but could not present an image and declare, “This is Hiroshima”*3. In a 2025 interview, she again said that photography becomes interesting outside logic and intention, and that images taught her about things she had looked at without noticing*2. A photograph does not merely confirm prior knowledge; it can reveal, after the fact, that the photographer’s understanding at the time was incomplete. Ambiguous photographs and scenes resistant to explanation helped keep Hiroshima from being confined to a single, legible image.

Seven Rivers and Photobook Sequencing — History Through Repetition

In Here Goes River, the seven rivers crossing Hiroshima’s delta are both locations and a model of time that does not move in one direction. Akaaka describes the book as a current whose snapshots reveal relations between history and the present, society and the individual, while moving backward and forming eddies*7. Fujioka and Himeno initially shaped a sequence with narrative in mind. Matsumoto interrupted that explanatory flow and included blurred or indeterminate photographs that were difficult to judge as conventionally “good snapshots”*3. Bicycles, children, rivers, bodies, and the Atomic Bomb Dome recur on separated pages without being assigned one-to-one meanings. The Ina Nobuo Award jury praised juxtapositions in which contemporary bicycles and floodwaters evoke archival images of the bombing and the rivers of August 6, 1945*6. Past and present are not equated. Repetition across distant pages allows the past to be recalled through contemporary scenes.

From Film to Digital — How to Select from an Overwhelming Number of Images

Here Goes River was also made while Fujioka was moving from film to digital cameras. She has described the change in equipment as a shift that transformed both how she photographed and how she presented images—changing the basic character of her process*3. Once the number of exposures became enormous, the work could no longer be determined by the finish of individual pictures alone. Decisions about what to retain and which ambiguous images to include assumed greater weight. Years of walking through Hiroshima produced photographs containing not just intended subjects but also elements that had entered the edge or background of the frame by chance. During later selection, the distance became clear between the Hiroshima she thought she understood while photographing and the city that emerged from the accumulated images.

Life Studies — New York Found Thirteen Years Later

Life Studies, published in 2025, draws on photographs made during roughly five years in New York beginning in 2007 and selected after a long interval. According to Akaaka, the book contains 168 color and black-and-white images made between streets and rooms, moving from an initial encounter with the city through the wandering of an immigrant and toward increasingly private scenes*11. Fujioka has said that the book took about thirteen years to complete. Although its basic structure emerged early, she repeatedly added and removed images and revised the text until shortly before printing*4. Her observation that photographs once made simply to relieve boredom later became important shows that the judgments formed at exposure did not determine the finished work*4. Children, interiors, shadows, objects, and minor incidents in the street take precedence over emblematic views of New York, and the period of living there unfolds through a sequence that moves from public streets toward private space.

Photography as a Record — Old Photographs and Local Memory in Oda

Fujioka’s current activities include “Oda Minzoku Kotohajime,” a community project developed with residents of Oda in Kawachi, Higashihiroshima. In photography workshops, she encouraged participants to photograph whatever interested them in familiar places—the home or garden—instead of searching far away for exceptional subjects. The project also collected old local photographs. Conversations around a single image drew out different memories from different people, including details of work, customs, and daily life that rarely survive in official local histories*2. Fujioka has said that if photographs and words are not preserved, local events may come to seem as though they never happened*2. The aim is not one image that stands for a grand history, but multiple accounts preserved through photographs before personal memories disappear. The project differs in form from Here Goes River, yet it makes explicit the same refusal to place ordinary life outside history.

Photobooks and Exhibitions — A Fixed Book, a Changing Installation

Fujioka does not repeat the same sequence in a photobook and an exhibition. She explains that installations can be adjusted according to wall height, the scale of the room, the viewing route, and how images appear in the space; this makes the exhibition an experimental form*4. In a photobook, the size of each image and the order of pages are fixed in print, and a single viewer can turn through them repeatedly. The flow developed through the exhibition of I Don’t Sleep became the basis of the book. In Here Goes River, exchanges with the designer broke apart an explanatory narrative. In Life Studies, thirteen years of selection reached a fixed form. Walls and the viewer’s movement alter relationships between photographs in an exhibition; format and page order determine the pace of looking in a book. Fujioka treats them as distinct constructions, not as two presentations of an identical sequence.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Comment te dire adieu — A Work Made from an Unplanned Journey

Comment te dire adieu gathers early photographs made while moving through Taiwan, Europe, Brazil, and other places. It received the Visual Arts Photo Award Grand Prix in 2004*1. The journey began before a photographic plan had formed, leaving many images of people, children, bodies, signs, and opaque encounters found by chance in the street instead of explanations of landmarks or local culture*2. Selection after her return foregrounded the people and scenes to which she had responded abroad rather than the itinerary itself. The method—giving greater weight to what is discovered later in a photograph than to the purpose present at exposure—continues from this early work through Life Studies.

I Don’t Sleep — Private Photographs Without Explaining the Family

Published by Akaaka in 2009, I Don’t Sleep places photographs of Fujioka’s family and family home in Kure within a large-format book. Editor Nozomi Himeno has recalled that although such private snapshots were often viewed through the discourse of onnanoko shashin (“girl photography”), Fujioka’s photographs contained both a perspective that surveyed individual scenes and the pressures surrounding women’s lives in regional Japan*3. Pages enlarging the crown of her mother’s head, working hands, her back, and domestic objects do not explain family relations. They hold together a gaze that wants to move closer and another that keeps its distance. Through scale and sequence, the book foregrounds the continuing unknowability of a familiar person more than the disclosure of private life.

Here Goes River — Encountering History in Present-Day Hiroshima

Akaaka published Here Goes River in 2017. The work received the 41st Ina Nobuo Award for fiscal year 2016, followed in 2018 by the Tadahiko Hayashi Award and the Kimura Ihei Photography Award*1. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum holds chromogenic prints from the series made between 2013 and 2017*9. The Tadahiko Hayashi Award account praises Fujioka’s restrained photographs made while walking through the city across all four seasons, in which memories of the past surface within unremarkable scenes of present-day life*10. Repeated contemporary images make history felt inside the everyday without reenacting the bombing. The sequence was recognized as a way of picturing Hiroshima in the present, distinct from earlier “Hiroshima” photography centered on the bombing’s direct traces.

Life Studies — Suspending the Judgment Made at the Time of Exposure

Published in 2025, Life Studies comprises 192 pages, 168 color and black-and-white photographs, and a long text by Fujioka*11. She did not publish the New York photographs immediately. Work in Hiroshima intervened before she selected the earlier images more than a decade later. An eggplant and domestic objects that she had photographed to relieve boredom eventually became important records of her life at the time*4. As with the early journeys, the family in Kure, and the rivers of Hiroshima, the moment of exposure does not coincide with the completion of the work. The mismatch between an image’s initial assessment and its later selection becomes one of the book’s organizing conditions.

sections.title: Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Early Work Beyond “Girl Photography”

Fujioka began working in the 1990s and has recalled being invited to speak as one of the photographers associated with onnanoko shashin, or “girl photography”*4. The experience later led her back to negatives from her student years. In the 2021 exhibition Hana no Yukue and the 2022 project New Stories, she gathered subjects she had repeated unconsciously since that period—children and flowers among them—and reconsidered why she takes photographs*13. She can be compared with contemporary women photographers such as Yurie Nagashima, Rinko Kawauchi, and Asako Narahashi. Fujioka’s work, however, is distinguished by a time scale that repeatedly returns to decades of photographs involving travel, family, regional cities, and the history of Hiroshima. Images from her student years were presented in Hana no Yukue and New Stories through categories different from those of her later works.

Whose Point of View Has Street Photography Used to Picture the City?

Street photography developed as a major form of modern photography by recording chance events and human gestures in public space without staging them. In the 1930s, Henri Cartier-Bresson photographed fleeting arrangements of moving people and urban space, and his work became closely associated with the idea of the “decisive moment”*20. In postwar Japan, photographers who had lived through occupation, rapid urbanization, and political upheaval treated the street as a site of social change. Around PROVOKE in the late 1960s, grain, blur, camera shake, and contingent framing challenged the assumption that photography could describe the world clearly and neutrally*21. The 1968 exhibition A Century of Photography had already raised public questions about photographers’ wartime responsibility and the credibility of documentary images; Takuma Nakahira and Kōji Taki, who participated in editing the exhibition, went on to launch PROVOKE*22. Cartier-Bresson, PROVOKE, and Fujioka cannot be joined as a direct line of influence. They nevertheless provide a useful comparison for tracing how street photography’s concerns expanded from seizing an instant in public space to considering the photographer’s own position and historical relationship to a place.

The “Reflexive Turn” — From Where Does Aya Fujioka Photograph Hiroshima?

Yoshiaki Kai argues that Japanese street photography after 1990 underwent a “reflexive turn,” incorporating the photographer’s own relationship to the place photographed; he cites the Hiroshima works of Aya Fujioka and Keiko Sasaoka as examples*15. “Reflexive” here means that the image addresses not just what a city looks like, but who is photographing it, from what position, and with what relation to the place. Canonical accounts of street photography have often presented anonymous passersby and fleeting incidents as scenes discovered in public space. For Fujioka, who was born in Kure and later returned to live in Hiroshima, the street is not a detached field of observation. Her private photographs of family in Kure and her street photographs of Hiroshima’s rivers and roads do not belong to separate domains. High school students dancing in front of the Atomic Bomb Dome, play along the river, and rooms crowded with household objects register the city’s present alongside the experience of return, family memory, and the distance produced by living amid Hiroshima’s history. Fujioka retains the sensation of the “instant” she admired as a student while selecting, years later, elements she did not consciously notice at exposure. Because selection continues long after the shutter is released, the work’s meaning is not completed in that instant; her relation to the place becomes visible over time*4. In Here Goes River, chance encounters in the street become a form capable of including the photographer’s own belonging and memory.

Things She Carries — Approaching War Through Life in the Present

The 2023 exhibition Things She Carries at SEIZAN Gallery in New York brought together Miné Okubo, Aya Fujioka, and Yukiko Hata. It considered how the Second World War has been represented and how its history remains within the experience of women living in the present*16. The exhibition introduced Here Goes River as a project that began as a personal record through which Fujioka sought to recover a relationship with her hometown, then turned toward photographing the contemporary city instead of a “Hiroshima” fixed as a sign of catastrophe. At an artist talk in New York, it was reported that a photograph of high school students practicing a dance in front of the Atomic Bomb Dome had been criticized on social media for dishonoring the victims’ memory*17. Fujioka explained that without the Dome the image would not carry the same meaning, and that she wanted the symbols contained in the photograph to prompt viewers to think instead of imposing a single lesson. Her report that the same image drew no backlash when shown in Tokyo demonstrates how reception changes with the location of an exhibition. In a different response, the World Socialist Web Site argued that the 2025 London exhibition hiroshima, by treating war through everyday life and personal memory, risked pushing the political and historical causes of the atomic bombing into the background*19. In Here Goes River, everyday life does not replace history. The act of photographing the present brings the work into an active dispute over what Hiroshima should preserve as memory.

Compared with Ken Domon’s Hiroshima — Where Does History Appear in a Photograph?

Ken Domon photographed Hiroshima in 1957 and published the photobook Hiroshima the following year. The Met describes the book—containing survivors, hospitals, an orphanage, people blinded by the bombing, and families rebuilding their lives—as a major work in the history of Japanese photobooks*24. Writing about Here Goes River, ARTnews JAPAN observed that Fujioka evokes the “Hiroshima” latent within quiet daily scenes, including high school students dancing in front of the Dome and elementary school pupils looking in the same direction, through a method different from Domon’s*25. Their difference cannot be reduced to direct versus indirect expression, or to a contest between an older realism and a newer approach. Domon’s photographs include hospital and family life; Fujioka’s contain the Atomic Bomb Dome as an explicit historical sign. The distinction becomes clearer when asking where the history of the bombing appears in the image. Domon centered wounded bodies and ongoing damage, demonstrating that the atomic bombing had not become past. Fujioka photographed Hiroshima more than seventy years later, when people playing by the river, dance practice, school commutes, family life, and historical signs coexist within the same urban time. Here Goes River does not make the damage invisible. It uses distance and recurrence between photographs to register the past in a period when its direct traces have become harder to distinguish from everyday life.

Awards and Reassessment — Questions That Continue Beyond Hiroshima

After Here Goes River received three awards, Fujioka presented New Stories, selected from earlier negatives; Hana no Yukue, based on photographs of flowers made over many years; and Life Studies, drawn from her New York archive. The 2023 Higashikawa Awards New Photographer Award considered several of these recent activities, including New Stories, a group exhibition addressing third-wave feminism, and Hana no Yukue*13. From 2024, I Don’t Sleep appeared in I’m So Happy You Are Here and related exhibitions reassessing Japanese women photographers from the 1950s to the present*3. In 2025, the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum included Fujioka among the contemporary artists in its thirtieth-anniversary exhibition*12. That year, The Guardian introduced Here Goes River as a series in which the weight of the past remains within the everyday life of contemporary Hiroshima*14. Reception now extends beyond Here Goes River to her early family photographs, selections from old negatives, and New York work.

yuki-tawada.html.title: Yuki Tawada | Burned and Scraped Photographs and I am in You | Photo Coordinates
yuki-tawada.html.meta_description: Yuki Tawada scrapes, burns, and layers photographs of cities, crowds, family members, and the sea, turning the photographic surface into a site of memory, healing, and ritual. Through WHITE OUT, Burnt Photographs, and I am in You, this page examines the necessity of her methods and her place in photographic history.
yuki-tawada.html.lead_html: Yuki Tawada (1978–) was born in Hamamatsu, Shizuoka Prefecture. She studied photography in the United Kingdom and at the Graduate School of Tokyo University of the Arts, linking her interests in phototherapy, folk belief, and magic realism to a process of scraping, burning, and layering prints. In WHITE OUT, Burnt Photographs, and I am in You, she adds irreversible traces to images of cities, crowds, the sea, and family, returning the photograph from a reproducible image to a singular object.
yuki-tawada.html.thesis_html: Photographs readily circulate as reproducible, flat images, but Tawada turns them into objects that cannot be restored to their former state by scraping, burning, perforating, and layering their surfaces. Her decisive shift lies in making the support itself a site of production after exposure, addressing in a single work both photography’s documentary capacity and its emotional force as a surrogate for its subject. In WHITE OUT, she erases information from crowds; in Burnt Photographs and I am in You, she connects damage by fire to procedures of memory, fear, sacrifice, and healing. Crucially, alteration does not function as decoration. It inscribes in the photograph the time of making—who touched it, where they touched it, and what they caused to disappear. Her work can be situated as a critical reclamation of photography’s materiality and singularity in an age of endlessly reproduced and generated images.

sections.title: Toward Photography as Object: Education and an Interest in Healing
sections.body_html:
Yuki Tawada’s Background and the Materiality of Photography

Yuki Tawada began studying photography in earnest after becoming drawn to the medium while visiting the University of California, Santa Barbara, as an exchange student from Tohoku University. After graduating, she majored in photography at Camberwell College of Arts, University of the Arts London, and completed both master’s and doctoral programs in Intermedia Art at the Graduate School of Tokyo University of the Arts*1. At Camberwell, her attention shifted from composing only what appeared in the image to the physical properties of the photograph and the possibility of altering its surface*12.

Tawada’s turn toward paper and surface cannot be understood solely as material experimentation. In a later official statement, she explains that she works with photography because, although publicly regarded as an objective medium, it acts deeply on personal emotion and the unconscious*2. The photographic surface became a meeting place between the depicted content and the bodily response of someone touching the image.

Her master’s thesis at Tokyo University of the Arts, A Method of Healing Memory Using Photography, examined through phototherapy how photography might contribute to psychological healing. According to the review summary of her doctoral dissertation, On the Contemporary Meaning of Magic Realism, Tawada sought to introduce aura and emotional movement into still photographs through tactile methods inspired by sympathetic magic and art therapy, thereby expressing invisible forces at work within everyday life*14. Healing here lies in reconfiguring one’s relationship to memory and fear through the process of touching a photograph, not in a finished work providing a medical benefit. Tawada has written that when she applied a hot iron to a self-portrait, she felt as though her own face were actually being burned. This indicates that a photograph is experienced both as a paper object and as a surrogate for its subject*6. This duality carries her alterations of the surface beyond formal experiment and toward acts that engage memory and emotion.

sections.title: Core of Her Work
sections.body_html:
Rematerializing the Photograph

In her official statement, Tawada explains that her aim is not simply to reproduce magical or therapeutic effects. She seeks ways to make consumed photographs speak again amid the excessive circulation of information in contemporary life*2. Articulated later, this concern runs through her work in scraping, folding, and burning since WHITE OUT. Handwork does more than add an effect to an image: it records a history in which someone touched the photograph, hesitated, made a choice, and introduced a change that cannot be reversed.

In a 2025 workshop at Fotografie Forum Frankfurt, Tawada likewise set participants the tasks of experiencing a photograph as an object, beginning a story through touch, and allowing traces to open memory and reality*11. She retains the reality recorded by the camera while leaving scratches, folds, and burns on its surface, giving memories and emotions that had no form at the moment of exposure a physical presence in the photograph. This idea translates Tawada’s concept of magic realism into a concrete working method.

The Photographers’ Gallery describes Tawada’s method as treating photographic prints like “vulnerable bodies,” and identifies her scraping, cutting, burning, and perforating as an insistence on the materiality of photography*32. This reading clarifies a defining feature of her work: image and support remain inseparable, rather than alteration functioning as painterly decoration. The sense that damage to a photograph also leaves the person or memory depicted there unable to remain unscathed connects her manipulation of the object to its psychological meaning.

WHITE OUT: Crowds and Scraping

In the major early series WHITE OUT, Tawada used erasers, needles, and sandpaper to scrape large-format prints of crowds gathered in stadiums and cities. An exhibition text from 2007 explains that she sought to capture the energy that arises once a crowd exceeds a certain size, rather than the expressions of individuals, and that by erasing the picture plane she produced a torrent of white light*7.

A crowd photograph can record faces, clothes, seats, and architecture in detail, but the fervor, anxiety, conformity, and madness generated by the group do not appear as the figure of any particular person. Instead of adding information, Tawada scraped away parts of the recorded figures and made the white beneath the ink operate like light, smoke, or an explosion. The idea described in her doctoral dissertation—introducing “movement” into a still photograph to express invisible emotional forces—is enacted here through erasure*14. Scraping does more than weaken or destroy the image. It becomes drawing in reverse: removing the faces, clothing, and other information through which the crowd is read as a collection of individuals, while adding the group’s previously formless force as a white trace.

Burnt Photographs: Fire and Photographic Matter

In Burnt Photographs, fire joined the controlled method of scraping the surface. Tawada likens her process to drawing out and releasing something like the soul of a subject trapped in a print, and calls the burned photograph a “shell” that retains a presence after the substance has departed*6.

Her subjects are not chosen at random. They include taxidermied animals, tropical plants in botanical gardens, dances performed for tourists, religious artifacts removed from temples and shrines, and people who left their places of origin for the city: things displaced from their original lands or purposes and made objects of display, performance, or observation in an urban setting. Tawada associates flowers, animals, Buddhist statues, halos, and dancing bodies with motifs once offered in sacrifice, writing that burning returns the still photograph to an organic state*6. Because photography can carry its subject into the city and fix it there as a specimen, burning opens that fixity to change once more.

Erasers and needles allow relatively fine control over the movements and forms made by the hand, whereas fire irreversibly changes not just the image but also the paper’s contours, strength, and thickness. Tawada’s feeling that her own face was actually burning when she burned a self-portrait reveals a state in which photograph and subject cannot be fully separated psychologically*6. This structure, in which an action performed on an image is felt to extend to what the image denotes, overlaps with the logic of sympathetic magic, according to which an effect passes between similar things or things once in contact*20. Burning carries the conflicting sensations of violence, sacrifice, and release; Tawada herself has described both the pleasure of breaking a taboo and, ultimately, a sense of being forgiven by the subject*6. Through the irreversibility of fire, the psychological identification of photograph and subject is borne by the damaged paper.

I am in You and Family Ritual: The Sea and Family Memory

Against the background of her intensified fear of the sea after the Great East Japan Earthquake, Tawada burned photographs of breaking waves together with her mother for I am in You. During a gallery tour, she explained that she repeatedly burned away the water’s surface while leaving the sea foam, seeking to soothe her fear of and wounds associated with the sea*19.

Here, fear of the sea is not replaced by another symbol; fire is applied to the photograph that records the sea itself. By repeatedly touching an image that points to a past reality and deciding with her mother which parts to preserve and which to remove, fear moves from an emotion enclosed in the mind to a concrete task they can undertake together. Shadow Dance and Family Ritual also use photographs and archival images from her maternal family. The roles of photographer, owner, subject, and person altering the print overlap, extending the work into a process of addressing personal memory among family members*4. Healing appears as the process of creating an order and duration in which fear and the past can be approached through photographs, more than as a result in which they disappear.

Layering, Suspending, and Hanging

Tawada does not press her burned prints flat against a wall. She layers them, holds them away from the wall with pins, and sometimes hangs them from the ceiling. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum exhibition Seeing as Though Touching approached photography as matter with a support, surface, and mode of installation, beyond its depicted content, and presented I am in You as one of its central examples*5.

A flat photograph hung on a wall readily encourages the viewer to read its image head-on. Hiroshi Uemura argues that experiencing photographs as objects requires forms of display that prompt shifts in viewpoint—walking around, peering into, or looking up at a work*10. When prints are layered away from the wall, another water surface or the wall itself appears through the burned holes, charred edges cast shadows, and the images overlap differently as the viewer moves. Missing areas do not remain mere blanks; they become spaces that transmit light, reveal another image, and set the viewer in motion.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
WHITE OUT and Missing Folklore: Crowds and the City

In WHITE OUT, Tawada stripped information from images of crowds and rendered the force generated by the group as a whole in white forms. In the subsequent Missing Folklore, erasure expanded to architecture, roads, and night views, replacing the contours and signs that identify a city with white traces*3. The Japan Times introduced the exhibition as a group of large works whose urban photographic surfaces had been scraped, blurred, and scarred*8.

Even as the subject shifts from people to the city, the underlying problem remains: outward appearances captured by the camera cannot fully express the emotions and memories that animate a place. When information identifying place names, functions, and individuals is reduced, the city changes from an explicable location into a psychological site where heat, tension, and forgetting overlap. The white scars do not replace urban reality with fantasy; they add forces that exist within reality but cannot be photographed directly.

From Shadow Dance to Ash and Ceramics

In Shadow Dance, Family Tree, and I am in You, burned family photographs and images of the sea are reassembled in multiple layers, so that missing areas, supports, and shadows form a single work. The 2024 book Her smoke rose up forever includes series addressing maternal family memory as well as a collaboration in which the ash of burned photographs was used in glazes for Fuku Fukumoto’s ceramics*15.

In her work with Fukumoto, the photograph remains fixed on a ceramic surface as ash even after it can no longer be read as an image*16. As the support shifts from print to charred paper, ash, and glaze, preservation and disappearance cease to be simple opposites. The image’s information may be lost, but the matter that constituted the photograph and the history of its making pass to another support. Tawada’s “shell” is a form for sensing presence in the matter left after the image has gone, not destruction that leaves nothing behind.

In Lachrymatory, presented at Fotogalerie Wien in 2025, participants burned personal photographs they had brought with them, and the ash was used to glaze tear vessels. The work was described as transferring personal memories into tangible form while questioning the materiality of images and the fragility of memory*21. In a French article on the Rencontres d’Arles, curator Mariko Takeuchi explained that Tawada also uses remnants of consumer photographs she has found to address invisible connections between her own family and anonymous families*22. Even after private photographs lose their original owners and contexts, their burned remains and ash become materials for creating other relationships.

In Scent of the Sky (2025), Tawada also tested a structure in which intervention by the viewer or owner becomes part of the work’s transformation, leaving its final state and moment of completion to the owner*23. The transformation of photography extends beyond the passage from paper to ash or ceramics to questions of time and ownership: who touches the work and where its completion is determined.

Post-Photography and Singularity

With Shigeo Goto and others, Tawada organized Photography Transforms: MUTANT(S) on POST/PHOTOGRAPHY, presenting photography as a medium that changes state across print, three-dimensional form, video, and digital processing*13. In an essay on the project, Keiju Kita takes Tawada’s remark, “For now, it is still possible to let the material speak,” as a starting point. Kita analyzes how THEGIRLWHOWASPLUGGEDIN reuses images made for a photobook and repeats them as matter in the exhibition space*18.

Post-photography here does not mean a time after photography has ended. It is the idea that each time an image moves among book, print, cut paper, installation, ash, and ceramics, it acquires another temporality and mode of touch. In 2025, Tawada said that in an age when AI generates images resembling reality, she treats photographs as “tangible dreams” that retain traces of the hand*12. Scraping, folding, and burning do not constitute a return to analog photography. They leave an infinitely reproducible image with the history of a particular person’s touch, judgment, and irreversible alteration.

In this respect, Tawada’s materiality differs from nostalgia for pre-digital photography. It presupposes an environment in which generated and reproduced images readily proliferate, while irreversible actions performed on their supports give each image a distinct history. The critical force of the work lies in bringing photography’s reproducibility into collision with the singular time of its making, without rejecting photography as a reproductive technology*12.

Dates and Methods of Alteration

Examples of WHITE OUT date from 2006 and employ a method of scraping inkjet prints with erasers and sandpaper*26. An exhibition record for Burnt Photographs dates to 2012, by which time burning had developed as an independent working method*27. A 2015 “burnt ink jet print” survives from I am in You, showing continuity between scraping and burning as operations that turn an image into an object bearing a singular scar*28.

In the principal sources reviewed here, “applying light” cannot be confirmed as an independent third method of alteration comparable to scraping and burning. Official records clearly identify burning as part of the artistic process*27. In exhibitions, light passes through holes and cutouts in burned prints and casts shadows on the wall, emphasizing the relationship among image, support, and exhibition space. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s Seeing as Though Touching likewise presented I am in You in a context that directed attention to supports and material textures as well as images*29.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
The Materiality of Photography Since the 2000s

Describing Tawada’s work solely as a “reaction to the digital age” would obscure its personal necessity, yet omitting its broader photographic-historical setting would also be inadequate. The International Center of Photography’s 2014 exhibition What Is a Photograph? observed that, since the 1970s, artists have reconsidered not only light, color, and composition but also the support and materiality themselves, and that practices treating photographs as “photographic objects” continued to expand after the spread of digital images*30. Tawada cannot be claimed as an artist directly influenced by this exhibition’s lineage. Her work of scraping, burning, folding, and hanging prints nonetheless clearly connects with a contemporary effort to reconsider photographs as objects as well as information.

Within Japanese photography, scholars have also argued that the medium’s materiality was reconfigured after 3.11 to address traces and memories of disaster*31. Given that I am in You arose from Tawada’s growing fear of the sea after the Great East Japan Earthquake, her burns and holes can be situated as a personal method for inscribing the distance between the image preserved in a photograph and the memory of reality into the support itself, more than as a style representative of contemporary disaster imagery.

Situating Tawada in photographic history since the 2000s requires attention to an environment in which, after digitization, photography became detached from the singular material object and was reproduced, altered, and shared as on-screen data. Principles of Contemporary Photographic Art takes as its premise the major transformation of the conventional idea of photography as “capturing truth” through the ubiquity of smartphones, social media, and digital images; it includes a “Workshop / Phototherapy” by Tawada herself*35. Issue 47 of Bijutsu Forum 21, in a special feature titled “Photography as Material / Photography as Concept,” also discusses the work of Tawada and others through the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum exhibition Seeing as Though Touching*34. Tawada’s burning and perforation can be understood as a contemporary response that asks whether photography can once again become body, material, and singular event, rather than as nostalgia opposed to the digital.

Phototherapy, Ritual, and Memory

In the healing addressed by Tawada’s master’s and doctoral dissertations, the emphasis falls on a process of changing one’s relationship to memory and fear by touching photographs, repeating actions, and working with others, more than on a completed artwork providing medical benefits to viewers. In I am in You, continuing with her mother to burn the water’s surface while leaving the foam transformed fear of the sea into a duration they could address together. The work presents no outcome in which fear has been conquered. It shows the sequence and continuity of actions constructed to approach that emotion.

Charred edges, lacelike holes, and layered shadows have a strong visual effect. This creates a risk that the technique of burning photographs or the beauty of handwork will come to the fore while questions of family history, fear, and subjects gathered in the city recede. In a 2018 exhibition review, Kotaro Iizawa wrote that although the works’ physical presence first catches the eye, behind it lies Tawada’s conviction and urgent need to apprehend reality through this method*9. Reading the work therefore requires looking beyond the shapes of its wounds to what the photograph depicts, who altered it, with whom, and to what extent.

Photographic Materiality and Magic Realism

Photography historian and anthropologist Elizabeth Edwards argues that understanding photographs solely through their depicted content overlooks their status as objects that are made, touched, stored, and damaged*17. Art historian Toshiharu Ito, noting the succession of changes to photographic supports over the medium’s short history, writes that photographic images have searched for bodies in which to reside. He situates Tawada’s handwork as an effort to awaken the magical materiality and aura inherent in photography*2. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s Seeing as Though Touching considered photography and moving images as material media that act on the viewer’s senses*5. Tawada’s work can thus be placed within discussions of photographic materiality and post-photography that have become active since the 2000s.

Work concerned with photographic materiality is not exclusive to Tawada. The 2024 international exhibition I’m So Happy You Are Here organized the work of Japanese women photographers around three axes: observations of everyday life, critiques of social roles, and experiments with and expansions of photographic form. Alongside prints, it presented installations, moving images, and photobooks as part of photographic history*24. Tawada’s work was also introduced within this movement extending photographic form beyond the flat plane.

In its description of her book, The Photographers’ Gallery Bookshop likewise characterizes scraping and burning as a practice that crosses the boundaries of photography, painting, and sculpture while pursuing the possibilities of “photography as a material medium”*25. This is an example of her reception abroad, rather than an academic positioning, but it shows that Tawada is presented as an artist who expands photographic form beyond material experimentation alone.

Tawada has extended the exposure of the support into questions of photography’s surrogacy and emotional force. She draws on the way a photograph, though received as objective evidence, acts emotionally as a surrogate for its subject, turning physical changes made to an image into actions that engage invisible forces, fear, and memory. Magic realism in her doctoral dissertation is defined less as a technique for creating fantasy detached from reality than as a process of psychological healing that makes emotions and aura operating within visible everyday life manifest through tactile traces*14.

The “aura” and magical force invoked in her official statement do not imply a literal revival of old beliefs. The terms describe a way of restoring irreplaceable histories—scratches, burns, the hand’s hesitation, and collaboration with family—to images that are reproduced and consumed in great quantities, allowing photography’s effect on emotion to be experienced anew. Tawada’s place in photographic history rests on more than her treatment of photographs as three-dimensional forms and installations beyond the flat plane. By acting on prints that bear traces of reality, she expresses what photographic objectivity struggles to capture, bringing material change, psychological healing, and rituals of folk belief together as a single working method.

The Japan Foundation’s 2025 exhibition in Hanoi introduced Tawada’s photography as an interface among “memory, myth and matter,” presenting the trajectory from her studies in biochemistry to photography, video, and sculpture as a continuous development*33. For Tawada, scientific training in handling matter and an interest in folk belief and sympathetic magic are not opposing concepts. By physically changing an image and observing how that change acts on memory and bodily sensation, she brings matter and spirit into the same working procedure.

tomoko-sawada.html.title: Tomoko Sawada | ID400, ID Photos, and Self-Portraiture | Photo Coordinates
tomoko-sawada.html.meta_description: Tomoko Sawada uses ID photos, self-portraiture, and typological repetition to examine the relation between appearance and inner self, photographic identification, Japanese women photographers since the 1990s, and her method of working without pressing the shutter herself.
tomoko-sawada.html.lead_html: Tomoko Sawada uses her own face and body to repeat portrait formats that operate in everyday social life: ID photos, omiai matchmaking portraits, school group photographs, and résumé headshots. She encountered self-portraiture in a photography class as a student, then arranged 400 different appearances within the same ID-photo format for her graduation work, ID400. Her later series extend this inquiry to marriage, school, employment, youth culture, and perceptions of nationality, examining how people form judgments from appearance and how photographs shape those judgments.
tomoko-sawada.html.thesis_html: In 1990s Japan, photographs in which young women turned the camera on themselves and their daily lives attracted widespread attention. Sawada took this contemporary interest in self-portraiture toward an examination of the photographic formats through which society identifies, classifies, and evaluates people. She builds her work around existing uses of photography—photo booths, matchmaking studios, school photographs, and résumé portraits—and repeats a single body within standardized formats. The viewer becomes aware of the criteria used to infer a person from a face, hairstyle, or clothing. Sawada also delegates the act of releasing the shutter to machines or other people, concentrating authorship in the choice of format, disguise, repetition, editing, and arrangement. By joining self-portraiture to typology and allowing the photographic standards used for identification and evaluation to operate inside the work, she shows how photography helps produce the impression of “what kind of person” someone appears to be.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Why Sawada Kept Using Self-Portraiture—Holding One Person Constant

Tomoko Sawada decided to become an artist while in junior high school under the influence of Noboru Tsubaki, then her art teacher, and later entered a two-year media-design program. In a photography class during her first year, she watched a video about Cindy Sherman and made a self-portrait for an assignment. Sawada later recalled that when she saw the finished photograph, “something fell into place” for her*23. She continued to use herself as the subject because her interest remained focused on the relation between what can be seen from the outside and what lies within—between appearance and the inner self. She has also connected this concern to the ways people classify others on the basis of appearance*23.

For Sawada, self-portraiture keeps the “same person” constant within the experiment. She has said that she has never wanted to become someone else; even in disguise she remains herself and, in her words, is multiplying or amplifying herself*5. If every image used a different subject, the differences between photographs would also reflect actual differences between bodies. By holding her own body constant and changing only hairstyle, makeup, clothing, and expression, Sawada leaves a sharper question: why does the same person appear to be someone else? Self-portraiture gives her a controlled basis for separating visual signs of appearance from the judgments through which viewers turn those signs into a person.

In her statement for ID400, Sawada wrote that photography allowed her to make herself look like a model or actress, even as the distance between the self in the photograph and the self in everyday life grew larger*4. At the graduation exhibition, Sawada was present with a shaved head, yet she has said that only about twenty percent of visitors realized that all 400 photographs depicted the same person. That response became one reason she continued to explore the relation between appearance and inner self*23. Advice from her former teacher Noboru Tsubaki to maintain a connection with society also contributed to her expanding interest in settings where people are evaluated and classified, including matchmaking, school, and job hunting*5.

“I-Photography” and Women Photographers in the 1990s—When the Self-Image Drew Attention

When Sawada began working in the 1990s, photographs in which young women turned the camera toward their own bodies and everyday lives received considerable attention in Japan. In Ich-Fotografie, Madoka Yuki considers the idea of “I-photography” (watashi shashin), a term used by Nobuyoshi Araki in the 1970s, alongside the rise of so-called “girl photography” in the 1990s. She approaches photographs of the self as a “mode of communication” in which the positions of photographer, subject, and viewer can shift*7. From this perspective, the meaning of a self-portrait is not determined solely by what it says about the self. The relations among who takes the photograph, who appears in it, and who reads the image become part of the work.

Ayelet Zohar examines Heisei-era photography through self-presentation, gender, race, and class, placing Sawada alongside contemporaneous work by Yasumasa Morimura, Yurie Nagashima, HIROMIX, Mari Katayama, and Mao Ishikawa*20. Sawada chose forms used to identify and evaluate people in social life—ID photos, matchmaking portraits, school photographs, and résumé headshots. At a moment when images of the self had become prominent in Japanese photography, her work asked both what version of the self is shown and how a photographic format prompts viewers to read someone as a particular kind of person.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
ID400—Why One Person, a Photo Booth, and Repetition Were Necessary

Her graduation work, ID400, brought together the problem of “an inner self that should remain unchanged and an appearance that can change easily” through self-portraiture, a photo booth, and 400 repetitions*2. Using herself as the subject holds the person constant while disguise changes only the outward appearance. Passing each version through the format of an ID photograph, a form intended to verify identity, brings the social function of photographic identification into conflict with the perception of one person as many different people. The repetition of 400 images shifts attention away from the virtuosity of each disguise and toward the clues viewers use to classify a person.

The function of the ID photograph also explains why photography itself is necessary to the work. In her statement, Sawada wrote that even a nonexistent person can seem to have their existence verified once they appear in an ID photograph*4. In the history of institutional portraiture, Alphonse Bertillon photographed faces under standardized conditions in the late nineteenth century and used them as information for identifying individuals*9. ID photographs are likewise used on the assumption that “this face belongs to this person.” ID400 retains that credibility while producing 400 personae from one body, bringing the photograph’s role in confirming identity into direct contact with its role in prompting assumptions from appearance.

The 2019 volume Filters + Frames describes the ID photograph as a small standardized frame that stands for an individual within an official document and places ID400 in relation to that standard. Madoka Yuki’s essay “The Official Self,” included in the volume, situates Sawada within the generation of women photographers who emerged in the 1990s while arguing that her work both uses and departs from the codes associated with that generation*24. The central issue is the capacity of a photographic frame used as an official likeness to make many different versions of the self appear equally credible, rather than the search for a single “real self” among the 400 images.

The automated photo booth keeps distance, frontality, image size, and output nearly constant while reducing variations in composition and timing introduced by a photographer. Sawada has explained that she made ID400 in black and white to remove color and make the “same format” unmistakable*26. For Recruit and MASQUERADE, she chose color to match the kinds of photographs that actually circulate in those social settings*26. The camera setup, color, and image format therefore do not remain fixed as a signature style. They are determined by the social use of photography that each series takes up. Repetition and the grid make changing appearances comparable within those standards.

Repetition and the Grid—Why 400 Images Appear to Show Different People

After making Sign (2012), Sawada said she came to recognize her work explicitly as both self-portraiture and typology*25. When images share the same scale and frontality, viewers begin to pick out differences in hairstyle, eyebrows, glasses, clothing, and expression, and to form types such as “student-like” or “office-worker-like.” The grid catalogs 400 fictional personae while making visible the viewer’s own criteria for producing those distinctions.

A “Photographer Who Does Not Press the Shutter”—Using the Automation of the Photo Booth

The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum notes that Sawada describes herself as a “photographer who does not press the shutter”*1. She uses a photo booth for ID400 and a commercial portrait studio for OMIAI♡, leaving the release of the shutter to a machine or another person. Sawada has also recalled that after she received the Kimura Ihei Award, debate arose in Japan over whether someone who did not personally take the photographs could be considered a photographer*27. Authorship is concentrated in the design of the work: choosing the portrait format, constructing each appearance, deciding the number of repetitions, and editing and arranging the images.

In a 2016 essay on photo booths and automatic portraiture, photography historian Federica Muzzarelli places ID photography and the photo booth within a history of identifying and classifying individuals through the state, police, medicine, science, and anthropology since the nineteenth century*3. A photo booth reduces the photographer’s manual intervention while repeatedly producing faces under prescribed conditions. Sawada uses that automation to detach the shooting conditions from her personal taste and retain the already familiar look of an ID photograph inside the work.

Katy Deepwell describes the photo booth as a device in which the subject positions themself within a predetermined space, focus, and format, without the intervening “eye” of a photographer adjusting composition or focus*8. This description closely matches the conditions of ID400. Sawada reduces the individual viewpoint of a camera operator while retaining control over her body, makeup, wigs, and clothing as the subject. Repeatedly placing herself within the fixed conditions of a machine creates a more rigorous comparison in which only the appearance of the “same person” changes.

Sawada kept facial expression subdued in ID400 so that differences in wigs, makeup, clothing, and other aspects of appearance would be easier to compare*27. Using the photo booth or portrait studio as it normally functions preserves social portrait standards—frontality, lighting, dimensions, and shooting procedures—within the work. Even when the shutter release is delegated, Sawada determines the format, disguise, repetition, editing, and arrangement.

OMIAI♡, School Days, and Recruit—The Faces Expected by Marriage, School, and Employment

OMIAI♡ (2001) uses the format of omiai matchmaking photographs, portraits circulated between families when considering a prospective marriage partner. Sawada went to an actual portrait studio and was photographed each time as though “a different woman had come to have her matchmaking portrait taken”*23. The studio’s conventional lighting, poses, and clothing establish a format through which appearance is read in relation to a prospective marriage partner. A work from OMIAI♡ published by the Brooklyn Museum likewise presents this format as a color studio portrait*12.

School Days (2004) presents every student and teacher through Sawada’s own body. Uniforms and the conventions of the class photograph align each figure as a member of the group, while differences in hairstyle, expression, and the way a uniform is worn are read as signs of individuality. Sawada has cited her experience attending girls’ schools in junior high and high school as one point of reference for the method of this series*15. Recruit (2006) grew from her discomfort at seeing friends dye their hair black and converge on similar clothing during the job-hunting season; she responded by repeating the résumé headshot format*13.

The background to Recruit also included contemporary dress norms that paralleled Sawada’s personal observation. A 1996 Osaka Kyoiku University study of 576 male and female university students examined perceptions and actual use of recruitment suits and reported significant differences in evaluation and use according to gender and the strength of respondents’ desire for individuality*17. Job hunting evaluates individual ability and suitability while often requiring an appearance recognizable as appropriate for recruitment. Recruit makes this tension visible through a standardized résumé photograph and repeated versions of one body.

Matchmaking, school, and employment use photographs for different purposes, yet all three series select portrait forms used when people are registered socially, demonstrate belonging, or undergo evaluation and selection. The matchmaking portrait frames someone as a prospective spouse; the class photograph as a member of a group; the résumé headshot as a job applicant. Sawada reproduces these formats and repeatedly places the same body within them, making concrete the process by which photographed appearance becomes tied to the kind of person a social setting expects to see.

cover and FACIAL SIGNATURE—Reading Fashion, Individuality, and Nationality from Appearance

cover (2002) arose from Sawada’s discomfort with negative judgments of ganguro and kogal youth based on appearance alone. The series considers how conspicuous makeup can function both as an assertion of individuality and as conformity within a peer group*14. In FACIAL SIGNATURE (2015), experiences of being mistaken in New York for Korean, Chinese, Taiwanese, and other nationalities expanded her question—“what do people look at when they judge an individual?”—toward perceptions of nationality and ethnicity*14. Seigensha likewise describes the series as extending Sawada’s concern with appearance and inner self toward nationality, race, and identification through the face*18. As her subjects expand from institutions such as school, employment, and marriage to fashion and perceptions of nationality, the work continues to focus on the impulse to infer a person’s attributes from details of appearance.

Mask and Veil—Bodily Performativity Without Playing a Role

Sawada has described her work as closer to a “veil,” beneath which Tomoko Sawada remains present, than to a “mask” through which she becomes a role*5. She has also explained that she does not imagine a character’s inner life and act the part; she changes her appearance without referring to a specific person*23. The focus is on the conditions under which “the same person” can be read as 400 different people.

In her essay for Modern Women, Yuko Hasegawa considers Japanese women artists of the 1950s–60s and those working since the 1990s through the idea of “performativity,” placing Mariko Mori, Rei Naito, and Tomoko Sawada in the later group. Here, performativity is a broad concept encompassing artistic acts, temporal elements, instructions or choreography, and structures that involve other people*21. Sawada herself says she is “not acting,” yet the repeated placement of her body within established portrait standards prompts viewers to classify what they see. This reading rests on the way body, photographic format, repetition, and viewer judgment combine as a sequence of actions, without requiring her to perform the psychology of a fictional character.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
ID400, 1998—Four Hundred Images and Grids of One Hundred

ID400 consists of a series of 400 photographs, though museum holdings and exhibitions sometimes present them in groups of one hundred. MoMA holds ID400 #101–200 as one hundred gelatin silver prints and dates the work 1998–2001*11. The display unit itself encourages viewers to move between individual ID photographs and the grid as a whole, comparing differences within a common format.

OMIAI♡, 2001—The Portrait Studio as a Social Apparatus

OMIAI♡ is a 2001 series of color studio portraits that incorporates a commercial portrait studio into the production process. A work published by the Brooklyn Museum is a chromogenic print and can be viewed on the museum’s collection page*12. Where ID400 uses an automated photo booth, OMIAI♡ makes the studio lighting, pose, backdrop, and photographer’s procedure part of the social function of the matchmaking portrait.

School Days, 2004 / Recruit, 2006—Reproducing Social Standards

SFMOMA holds School Days (2004) as a chromogenic print and publishes an image of the work online*6. Fundació Joan Miró has discussed the work in relation to clothing, the individual and the group, and women’s roles in Japanese society*10. Sawada’s official website describes Recruit (2006) as a series using the ID photographs attached to résumés*13. Across these works, Sawada changes the photographic apparatus and social use to fit the subject of each series.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Self-Presentation in Heisei-Era Photography—Gender, Race, and Class

Writing about Heisei-era photography through gender, race, class, and performativity, Ayelet Zohar places Sawada alongside Yasumasa Morimura, Yurie Nagashima, HIROMIX, Mari Katayama, and Mao Ishikawa*20. Madoka Yuki understands 1990s self-imaging as a form of communication involving photographer, subject, and viewer*7; in Sawada’s work, these positions become particularly intricate. Photographer and subject are the same person, but the shutter is delegated to a machine or studio photographer, while viewers compare and classify large numbers of images. As the work moves through marriage, employment, and perceptions of nationality, one question persists: who reads whom, and through which photographic standard?

Sherman and Yasumasa Morimura—The Difference Between Referenced Images and Photographic Formats

The immediate catalyst for Sawada’s use of self-portraiture came in the first year of her two-year program, when she saw a video about Cindy Sherman in class and made a self-portrait for an assignment*23. MoMA explains that in Untitled Film Stills Sherman did not recreate specific movies. She constructed female types familiar from 1950s and 1960s Hollywood, film noir, and B movies, and even modeled the format on publicity stills*29. Sherman’s fictional scenes feel familiar because they activate codes of femininity learned through film and media. Sawada also produces many types from one body, but ID400 suppresses setting and narrative so that faces are compared within the same ID-photo format. Sherman works with types drawn from cultural imagery; Sawada brings into the work photographic formats actually used for identification and evaluation.

Yasumasa Morimura has inserted his own body into established images from art history, cinema, and media culture. M+ has presented Morimura and Sherman together as artists who reconstruct existing images through their bodies*16. Morimura’s works are anchored in specific prior images—famous paintings, actresses, historical figures—that viewers can recognize and compare. Discussing School Days, Sawada has said that she does “not try to become someone” and does “not refer to a specific person”*23. What she cites are the shooting conventions and social uses that make ID photographs, matchmaking portraits, school photographs, and résumé headshots legible as such.

Sherman, Morimura, and Sawada all transform their own bodies, but disguise serves different functions in their work. Sherman refers to female images circulating through film and advertising; Morimura to established images from art history and popular culture. Sawada has said that she avoids imagining a character’s inner life and acting the role, instead producing differences in appearance through wigs, makeup, clothing, and facial expression*23. Placing those differences inside the fixed standards of ID or group photography makes it possible to compare how viewers infer personality and social position from appearance. Disguise becomes a method for testing how social portrait formats help construct a person.

The Bechers and Ruff—Fixed Conditions, Typology, and Identification Photography

Critic Marco Bohr compares Sawada’s repetition of herself as a single subject with Bernd and Hilla Becher and their visual typologies*28. According to The Met, the Bechers used a large-format camera and standardized shooting procedures to record industrial structures of the same type—water towers, blast furnaces, gas tanks—and arranged them in grids of four to thirty images for morphological comparison. The couple themselves called these arrangements “typologies”*30. Standardized conditions and serial arrangement reveal shared structures and differences that are harder to perceive in isolated photographs.

Placed beside the Bechers’ typologies, ID400 reverses the relation between what remains fixed and what changes. The Bechers photographed many different structures under nearly identical conditions to compare formal differences among the subjects. Sawada fixes the subject as one person and uses the photo booth to standardize distance, frontality, and scale while changing hairstyle, makeup, clothing, and expression. The differences across 400 images cannot be explained by saying that they depict different people; the act of inferring age, personality, occupation, or affiliation from small visual signs becomes the object of comparison.

Within the history of portrait photography, another important comparison is Thomas Ruff’s Porträts. The Met explains that Ruff, who studied with the Bechers, combined their typological method and the seriality of Minimalism with the apparent neutrality of mug shots and identification photographs, showing that even precise frontal records of a person do not provide access to that person’s thoughts or feelings*22. Ruff photographs many actual individuals in the same format, yet their inner lives remain unreadable. Sawada photographs one actual individual in the same format, and that person increasingly appears to be many different people. Standardized portraiture promises objective identification, while viewers continue to project psychology and social position onto the surface of the face. ID400 brings self-portraiture, identification photography, and typology together around this contradiction.

FACIAL SIGNATURE—Faces, Archives, and Surveillance After Sekula

In a 2025 essay, Noam Gal reads Sawada’s FACIAL SIGNATURE through questions raised after Allan Sekula’s “The Body and the Archive,” placing the work within a history of photographic classification, archives, surveillance, and social control extending back to Bertillon and Galton*19. In this work of 300 faces, Sawada’s experience of being taken in New York for Chinese, Korean, Singaporean, and other nationalities turns toward the gaze that attempts to determine nationality or ethnicity from a face. The title “Facial Signature” also evokes contemporary facial-recognition technologies that convert facial features into comparable data.

Gal notes that viewers repeatedly asked, “Which one of these is Sawada?” when the work was exhibited*19. Although every face is Sawada’s, the attempt to locate one “real face” repeats an archival assumption that a stable individual can be identified from an accumulation of photographs. The contradiction between one and many that begins in ID400 expands in FACIAL SIGNATURE toward racialized looking and facial-recognition technology, reframing photographic identification in relation to twenty-first-century surveillance.

Feminism and Identity—Critical Readings and the Artist’s Own Position

Because OMIAI♡ and Recruit address appearances expected of women in marriage and employment, they have repeatedly been read through gender and feminism. The Brooklyn Museum’s page for a work from OMIAI♡ places it within the Elizabeth A. Sackler Center for Feminist Art, one example of the series’ reception in relation to women’s social roles and feminist art*12. Sawada herself, however, has not presented “identity” as the stated theme of her work and does not define herself as a feminist*25.

The works begin with specific institutions and norms—marriage, employment, beauty, school, nationality—while feminism and identity operate as critical terms through which those subjects can be read. Sawada repeatedly presents the classifications and evaluations viewers make at the moment they see a facial photograph. By passing one body again and again through portrait formats used in social life, she makes photography’s dual role visible: recording a person and socially constructing an image of that person.

related_annotations./en/movements/staged-photography.html: Photography in which staging, costume, and assigned roles before exposure are central elements of production.
related_annotations./en/movements/typological-photography.ht: A method that uses repetition and comparison under consistent conditions to reveal difference and classification; an important reference for understanding the grid in ID400.
related_annotations./en/movements/feminist-photography.html: A field of photographic inquiry that reconsiders images of women, social roles, and structures of looking and being looked at.

A series that constructs school group photographs from a single body, using repetition to trace differences among uniform, group membership, and individual appearance.

alec-soth.html.title: Alec Soth | Storytelling, Road Trips, and the Photobook | Photo Coordinates
alec-soth.html.meta_description: Through Sleeping by the Mississippi, NIAGARA, and Songbook, this page examines how Alec Soth uses the 8×10 camera, road trips, lists, and photobook sequencing to turn photography’s limited ability to narrate time and causality into a method of storytelling.
alec-soth.html.lead_html: Alec Soth photographs people, motels, beds, signs, and interiors encountered across the United States, bringing them together in photobooks such as Sleeping by the Mississippi, NIAGARA, and Songbook. He combines road trips, shooting lists, an 8×10 view camera, and photobook sequencing to address things a single photograph cannot directly explain—loneliness, love, escape, and the desire for community. The limited ability of photography to narrate temporal sequence or causality becomes one of the conditions through which he constructs his work.
alec-soth.html.thesis_html: Soth brought three parts of photographic work into a single method: movement on the road, extended encounters with strangers through the 8×10 view camera, and the reordering of photographs in the photobook. In Robert Frank’s The Americans, the selection and sequencing of fragments gathered on the road shaped the photographer’s own image of America. *42 Soth applied the descriptive precision of large-format color photography associated with Stephen Shore and Joel Sternfeld to encounters with people as well. *34 He then repeated people, beds, letters, rooms, signs, and rivers within a single book, leaving room for viewers to form relationships between photographs without supplying a finished plot, as in NIAGARA. *29 This allows loneliness or love to recur across several people and places instead of being assigned as a fixed trait to one individual. Editing the photobook thus becomes part of making the work: it determines which fragments of reality are connected and which relationships remain unresolved.
