sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
From Recording to Constructed Images

Marti was born in Fribourg in 1979 and studied in the photography department at HGKZ in Zurich from 2002 to 2006.*1 Around this period he made analog snapshots of friends and his immediate surroundings, then gradually shifted toward constructing images as the recording of familiar environments no longer sustained his work. A Pro Helvetia essay notes that the photography program drew little distinction between fine-art and applied photography, requiring students to define their own positions, and traces Marti’s move from snapshots toward collage and the scanner.*12

In the early exhibition Ape, Mom, I, portraits of friends, scanned images, and fired ceramic ape skulls appeared together. Materials from Galerie Peter Kilchmann describe the combination of analog photography and the scanner, and the way darkness and dust contribute to the images’ tactile quality.*7 By this point, photography had become a central process for altering existing images and objects and transforming them into something else, extending beyond the faithful recording of his surroundings.

Connecting Photography, Ceramics, and Sculpture

Marti does not treat photography, sculpture, and ceramics as separate activities. Kunsthaus Biel discusses photograms, ceramics, wallpaper, and exchanges of works with other artists within the same body of work, identifying craft and mass production, creativity and authorship as shared concerns*4.In the photographs, reproducible images carry singular traces: scratches on a negative, dust on the scanning surface, or accidental effects of darkroom exposure. Marti treats this coexistence of repeatability and one-time physical marks as a condition shared with ceramics and installation.

At Kunstmuseum Luzern, large photograms, video, and objects were assembled within a single space, emphasizing handwork and tactility.*5 By placing light-made surfaces alongside ceramics and architectural supports, he refused to limit photography to a single framed image on the wall and underscored that reproduced images also bear traces of the hand and physical scale. The continuity of the work lies in the materials through which an image passes, across objects classified as photography or sculpture.

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Using the Scanner as a Camera

In an interview with Flash Art, Marti explains that he used the scanner as a camera, scratching negatives, drawing on them, adding tiny collages, and enlarging the results.*2 With a scanner, the distance between object and glass is almost zero, so dust, scratches, and the contact surface itself enter the image. Fotomuseum Winterthur likewise identifies scanned images, photograms, and image processing as central to Marti’s photographic work.*11

His use of the scanner works against the tendency of digital processing to remove noise, leaving dust and scratches from the contact surface in the image. Enlarging marks that would normally be erased turns the image from a smooth carrier of information into a record of contact between machine and object.An artTV presentation of his Coalmine exhibition describes the open scanner as producing deep black and functioning almost like a “digital photogram,” with the apparatus itself generating the image.*19

Connecting Digital Processes and the Darkroom

After exhausting the possibilities of the scanner, Marti moved toward photograms. In an interview with ATP Diary, he explains his interest in bringing digital and analog processes into one workflow by placing computer-generated material onto photographic paper and using an old technique for contemporary work.*15 At Parc Saint Léger, he built a darkroom inside the exhibition space and incorporated the place of production into the installation.*3

Marti uses the photogram as a contemporary working process rather than as a nostalgic “return to analog.” Digitally designed forms encounter light and material in the darkroom, introducing a process that cannot produce exactly the same result each time. Swiss Re’s collection text likewise emphasizes the combination of handwork and contemporary reproduction technologies and the inclusion of a deliberate loss of control within the work*18. Digital and analog function as successive stages through which one image moves back and forth.

Keeping Scratches, Dust, and Chance

Marti retains chance as part of the work. Scratches, dust, variations in exposure, and distortions caused by firing ceramics leave results that the artist cannot fully predetermine. Kunstverein Braunschweig describes multiple exposure, inversion, appropriation, and photograms as processes through which images become connected to time and collective memory.*1 Swiss Re notes a connection with Surrealist photograms and argues that loosening control allows unexpected results and the unconscious to enter the work.*18

This approach limits the degree to which digital tools make every element conform to intention. Marti has said that he realized many digital effects have precedents in darkroom techniques and began mixing the two.*2In the same interview, he describes allowing chance into the process so that the work does not merely repeat images he already knows.*20

Mysticism and Science Fiction

The recurring skulls, crosses, spirals, crystals, eggs, masks, science-fiction book covers, and hallucinogenic plants function as recognizable symbols whose established meanings can be redirected. In a 2009 interview with Mousse, Marti explains that he uses old and widely recognizable “archetypes” because he understands knowledge of the past as something inscribed in human beings through sensation and feeling as much as through rational knowledge*20. Because these symbols already arrive with meaning, inversion, repetition, and combination can create moments in which that meaning turns in another direction. Marti says he uses the expectation that a sign carries a fixed meaning and aims for the point at which it flips toward its opposite*20.

In the Flash Art interview, Marti explains his use of African masks bought online through several associations at once: their reception by the early twentieth-century avant-garde, their ritual and mystical implications, and their relationship to portraiture*2. Parc Saint Léger likewise connects the avant-garde traditions Marti references to histories in which art approached science, literature, and psychology in order to investigate perception and the unconscious, citing figures and movements ranging from Orphism to Wallace Berman and Terence McKenna*3.This treatment of masks belongs to Marti’s broader use of familiar images as signs whose established meanings can be reversed.*20 Skulls, crosses, swords, crystals, and masks recur because their immediate recognizability gives that reversal something to work against.

In Mousse, Marti says that he uses art-historical and historical archives as “collective memory”*20.Magazines from the 1950s and 1960s, pulp science fiction from the 1970s and 1980s, religious imagery, and ethnographic images are reworked as cultural memories already in circulation, with their original explanatory contexts left behind.In the same conversation, he describes lines and tape added to appropriated images not as “distortion,” but as abstract layers that multiply possible readings of the image.*20

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Early Work and Appropriated Images

In the 2007 exhibition Ape, Mom, I, early photographs, scanned images, and ceramic ape skulls appeared together, making his expansion from photographic images toward objects explicit.*7 In Kaleidoscope from the same period, Marti altered old science-fiction book covers and rescanned them while obscuring titles and original meanings. Collection Pictet describes this operation as opening obsolete imagery to new possibilities of meaning.*16

Heroic Dose

Heroic Dose (2011) is a greenhouse-like installation combining glass, iron, ceramic pots, and hallucinogenic plants. Migros Museum describes it as a work in which New Age culture since the 1960s collides with the forms of modernism.*6 Even as the work expands into materials beyond photography, the method of placing familiar cultural signs into new combinations continues.

Venice and the Photogram

In 2011, Marti participated in the 54th Venice Biennale, ILLUMInations. La Biennale’s historical archive records his participation.*9 He continued to expand large photograms into exhibition space; at Kunstmuseum Luzern, wall-filling images made with light were combined with ceramics and video.*5 A major development of this period was the extension of photography into the scale of the exhibition environment instead of treating it as a finished image contained within a frame.

Marti Collection and the Artist Book

In Marti Collection (2013), Marti exhibited works acquired through exchanges with other artists, disrupting the convention that a solo exhibition should consist only of new work by the named artist. Kunsthaus Biel places nonmonetary networks of exchange and questions of creativity and authorship at the center of the exhibition.*4 The 2016 publication Fabian Marti. Bilder 2005–2016 brings together more than a decade of photographic work, editing photograms and inkjet prints through technical and formal relationships.The Swiss Federal Office of Culture publication record likewise notes the organization of photograms and inkjet prints through formal relationships.*8

sections.title: Criticism and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
The History of the Photogram

Marti’s photograms have technical precedents in the camera-less photographs made in the 1920s by Man Ray andLászló Moholy-Nagy. Guggenheim Bilbao, in an exhibition devoted to “new ways of seeing” since the twentieth century, connects contemporary work to a lineage of light, abstraction, and technical experimentation.*13 Marti’s materials, however, include computer-generated forms, scanned images, and appropriated science-fiction and religious imagery, preventing the photogram from becoming a simple reenactment of a historical technique. His description in ATP Diary of “making contemporary work with an old technique” states this distance succinctly.*15

Appropriation and Authorship

Another critical axis in Marti’s work is authorship: what it means to call an image “one’s own.” As the Pro Helvetia essay title “The Curse and the Power of Appropriation” suggests, his work is bound up with borrowing, damaging, and reproducing existing images and destabilizing the meanings attached to their sources.*12 Galerie Peter Kilchmann’s artist materials likewise describe an ongoing inquiry into creativity and the role of the author through photocopiers, scanners, and preexisting images.*17 All is All (2014) placed photograms, sculpture, and wall works within the same exhibition, making explicit the combination of handwork and mechanical reproduction.*14

In Marti Collection, questions of authorship expanded from image manipulation to the ownership and exchange of artworks. Instead of forming a conventional collection by purchasing works by other artists, Marti included within the exhibition the relationships created through exchanging works*4. Appropriation therefore connects the technique of altering a source image to institutional questions about who makes, owns, and assigns value to an artwork.

Photography and Ceramics

Photography and ceramics share material results that cannot be determined by intention alone. Dust, scratches, and variations in exposure remain in photographs; pressure from the hand and distortion through firing remain in ceramics. Kunstmuseum Luzern placed monumental photograms and handmade objects in the same space as questions of human scale and tactility*5. The works are connected by the retention of chance and material traces across different media.

In an environment where digital images have been reproduced ever more smoothly since the 2000s, Marti increases scratches and dust as he uses machines and brings computer-generated material into older darkroom techniques. A Frieze review likewise discusses the coexistence of photography, sculpture, appropriation, and mystical signs within a single exhibition.*10 His position is defined by movement between digital and analog processes and by retaining the points where an image comes into contact with matter.

gabriel-orozco.html.lead_html: Gabriel Orozco is a Mexican artist whose work moves across photography, sculpture, drawing, and games, often beginning with objects encountered while walking, accidental arrangements, and brief interventions in everyday space. In Island Within an Island, Until You Find Another Yellow Schwalbe, Parachute in Iceland, and Photogravity, actions and configurations that exist only briefly on a street or during travel are carried into other places and times through photography. The public legacy of Mexican muralism, the artistic environment of Mexico City in the 1980s and 1990s, a mobile post-studio approach, and Orozco’s simultaneous distrust of and need for photography are central to understanding these works.
gabriel-orozco.html.thesis_html: What Orozco demonstrated through photography in the 1990s was a way to present short-lived interventions in public space as works constituted by the camera’s position and framing, rather than as records that merely explain an earlier event. In his practice of walking, slightly moving objects, and setting chance encounters or games in motion, the event itself disappears from the site. In Island Within an Island, the correspondence between scrap materials and the distant city exists on the photographic plane; in Until You Find Another Yellow Schwalbe, the trace of a game played across the city becomes a photographic series. Photography thus serves not only as evidence of a sculptural act but, in certain works, as the final form through which a discovered relationship can be taken away from its original site.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Muralism and Public Space

Orozco was born in Xalapa, Mexico, in 1962, the son of painter Mario Orozco Rivera. He studied at the Escuela Nacional de Artes Plásticas at UNAM and at the Círculo de Bellas Artes in Madrid. After returning to Mexico, he held the Taller de los viernes (Friday Workshop) at his home from 1987 to 1992. Museo Amparo records that Gabriel Kuri, Dr. Lakra, Damián Ortega, Abraham Cruzvillegas, and others gathered there to examine theory and works in progress on a continuing basis*1.

His father, Mario Orozco Rivera, belonged to the third generation of Mexican muralism and worked with David Alfaro Siqueiros. Orozco grew up around that environment and helped his father learn mural techniques, although he later recalled that becoming a muralist himself held little appeal*2. He has nevertheless acknowledged his origins in muralism and public art while arguing that the “monumentality” of a work cannot be measured simply by its physical dimensions*3. The small interventions he began making in public space in the early 1990s pursued another way for art to appear within the city, outside the scale and permanence of the mural or monument.

Mexico in the 1990s

Around the Friday Workshop, experimentation moved away from painting as a finished object toward ordinary things, found materials, actions, and sites. Damián Ortega later recalled a gradual shift there from painting as representation toward presenting objects themselves*4. Orozco’s work was shaped not only by the legacy of conceptual art in New York and Europe, but also by an environment in Mexico City where artists shared discussions while works were still being formed.

MoMA’s 2009 retrospective described Orozco as an artist who gained international attention in the early 1990s and worked across photography, sculpture, drawing, and installation without fixing his work within a single medium, repeatedly testing the boundary between everyday surroundings and the art object*5. Photography entered this practice as one means of incorporating actions and changing states of objects from place to place, rather than as a decision to enter the specialized field of the professional photographer.

From Walking to Photography

Orozco’s move toward photography did not begin with uncomplicated faith in the medium. Claire Grace cites his recollection that he regarded Mexican art photography and photojournalism as marked by class, racial, and sexual biases and by exploitative tendencies, and notes that he bought his first camera in 1991*6. In notes from 1992, he likewise treated photography as documentation rather than an end in itself, placing walking, looking, and discovery at the center of his work*7.

Walking remained central, but Orozco later described the camera to Art21 as an excuse to look at something and a tool for sharpening attention*8. In another interview, he compared photography to drawing “in reality” instead of using a sketchbook*9. By 2006, he stated that in some cases the photograph itself is the work and may be the only way to present an idea or experience*3. He remained wary of photography as a total substitute for the world, while using it when a temporary relationship formed at a site needed to travel into an exhibition or publication. That tension explains why photography became necessary within his broader work.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Temporary Interventions and Photography

In conceptual art and performance of the 1960s and 1970s, photographs were widely used to record actions and temporary works that would disappear. The Guggenheim places Orozco’s photographs within a later field in which they can hold a double status: documents of interventions and independent works of art*10. A study in Art Journal argues that Orozco mixes sculpture, performance, and photography in ways that disturb the simpler hierarchy of “event” and “document” inherited from earlier conceptual art*6.

In his 1992 notes, Orozco did not treat photography as the “purpose” of a work and prioritized walking and discovery*7. In a 2006 conversation, however, he explained that for some works the photograph itself is the work and the only means of presenting the experience*3. Photography therefore did not occupy a fixed position from the outset. Its role changed according to what needed to remain after an event at a site had disappeared, connecting temporary intervention with autonomous photographic work.

Small Interventions in Everyday Objects

Orozco often makes minimal changes to arrangements already present in everyday life instead of building elaborate sets. The Met describes works such as Knife on Table as part of a practice, beginning in the late 1980s, in which he used the camera to record temporary sculptures and found situations that redirect attention toward familiar surroundings*11. Fruit, cans, tables, puddles, tires, dogs, and other ordinary things briefly form structures through orientation, overlap, reflection, or the alignment of circles and lines.

Writing in Aperture, Mia Fineman discusses Orozco’s photographs as acts of pointing and argues that from the mid-1990s onward the emphasis shifted from documenting interventions toward photographs in which the act of photographing itself establishes the encounter with reality*12. Frontal views and straightforward compositions avoid foregrounding technical display, leaving the slight reordering of everyday objects as the visible event.

Scale and Photography

Orozco is often described as “anti-monumental” or as an artist of small poetic gestures, but he has rejected a simple opposition to monumentality. In a conversation with Letras Libres, he emphasized his origins in muralism and public art and argued that a small photograph such as Island Within an Island can be as monumental in gesture as a skyscraper*3. The issue is the scale at which a small intervention enters into relation with the surrounding city or landscape.

In Island Within an Island, scrap materials in the foreground are positioned so that their profile corresponds to the New York skyline in the distance. MOCA holds and presents the work as a 1993 Cibachrome photograph*13. The scrap itself has no fixed relationship to the skyscrapers. Camera position and perspective superimpose the two scales on a single plane, making a relation that does not exist in the physical objects alone.

Movement and Games

For Orozco, the city is not a fixed location for photography but a working environment in which walking produces a different route each time. In Until You Find Another Yellow Schwalbe, he rode a yellow East German scooter through Berlin without a predetermined destination and parked beside every identical model he encountered before photographing the pair. He made forty such encounters into photographs and described the city as a grid in which his own action generated chance events*14.

The subject is produced by a rule of movement instead of by waiting for a “decisive moment.” An Aperture interview likewise notes the way Orozco’s photographs turn momentary sculptures into portable images*15. Walking, rules, chance, intervention, and exposure form one continuous working process; the photograph is not documentation simply added at the end.

sections.title: Key Works, Photobooks, and Exhibitions
sections.body_html:
《Island Within an Island》

Island Within an Island (1993) brings Manhattan’s distant skyline and a small profile of arranged scrap materials in the foreground into a single image*13. The arrangement does not survive as a permanent sculpture after the photograph is made; its correspondence with the skyline emerges within the photographic frame. It is an early key work in which arranging objects and choosing the camera position are equally constitutive acts.

《Until You Find Another Yellow Schwalbe》

Until You Find Another Yellow Schwalbe (1995) consists of forty photographs made in Berlin as Orozco searched for the same yellow scooter and parked his own beside each one he found*14. The photographs are not a typology of scooters but the record of a game devised to learn the city. The sequence of encounters produces a map of Berlin different from one organized around monuments or tourist destinations.

《Parachute in Iceland》

Parachute in Iceland (South) (1995) photographs a parachute placed in the landscape as wind and terrain reshape it*16. The image does not function as a multi-view record explaining a fixed sculpture. It preserves the temporary form produced by cloth, wind, and ground. As Orozco’s sculpture approaches a situation rather than a stable object, photography carries the duration of that situation.

『Photogravity』

The Philadelphia Museum of Art’s 1999 exhibition Photogravity placed Orozco’s photographs in the same space as photographs of pre-Columbian sculpture, structuring the installation as an exchange between the properties of sculpture and photography*17. The museum explains that photographs were given supports that allowed them to stand in space while sculptures were flattened into photographic images, making the dialogue between the media the subject of the exhibition*18.

Placed in the same retrospective field as sculptures such as La DS and Empty Shoe Box, Orozco’s photographs cannot be reduced to external records of sculpture. In Photogravity, photographs were physically supported and raised into space while sculptures were translated into flat images, exchanging the positions of object, space, and image*18. The installation made explicit his treatment of photography and sculpture as media that assume different states within the same body of work rather than as separate genres.

sections.title: Criticism and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Distance from Spectacle and the Finished Art Object

In notes from 1992, Orozco recorded his aversion to spectacle and his doubts about producing finished art objects*7. The lightness of his use of street debris, ordinary objects, and temporary arrangements was therefore more than a poetic tone; it also created distance from systems in which artistic value is asserted through scale, virtuosity, rare materials, and permanence. Anna Dezeuze places Orozco and artists such as Francis Alÿs within a history of fragile, understated interventions of the 1990s, arguing that their anti-heroic smallness also belongs to the historical conditions of increasingly mobile capital and “smooth” global space*19.

Dezeuze’s argument does not directly prove Orozco’s own intention, but it situates these small street events within the institutions and circulation systems of the 1990s rather than treating them as pure accidents outside history. Questions about what can count as a portable artwork and what can enter the museum affect both his small-scale interventions and his photographs.

Between Photography and Sculpture

Criticism of Orozco’s photography has repeatedly returned to the boundary between documentation and autonomy. The Art Journal essay argues that, whereas photography in much conceptual art of the 1960s and 1970s followed an event, Orozco produces hybrids in which it is difficult to assign primary and secondary status among photograph, sculpture, and performance*6. The Hirshhorn similarly organized Directions: Gabriel Orozco: Extension of Reflection around photographs that preserve temporary sculptures or found situations while operating as works in their own right*20.

A 2002 Frieze review found greater imaginative force in Orozco’s photographs than in his more conspicuously conceptual objects, linking light, shadow, movement, and repetition to a post-Duchampian conceptual lineage*21. A 2010 review of the MoMA retrospective likewise found particular strength in small photographs such as My Hands Are My Heart and images of a sleeping dog, rather than in a monumental whale skeleton*22. Both accounts value the photograph as more than supplementary material: it compresses object-making, discovery, and camera position into a single work.

Contemporary Mexico

Orozco is often discussed internationally as a post-studio artist, but his work also grew from exchanges in Mexico City in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The Friday Workshop, which Museo Amparo describes as historically important, included Kuri, Dr. Lakra, Ortega, and Cruzvillegas, all of whom later became major figures in Mexican contemporary art*1. The group shared no finished style; its common concerns included discussions during production, ordinary objects, streets, bodies, and ways of presenting things.

Dezeuze places Orozco alongside Francis Alÿs, Thomas Hirschhorn, and Martin Creed in discussing modest and temporary interventions of the 1990s as “precarious practices” shaped by the acceleration of capitalism after the 1980s and by the legacy of dematerialization since the 1960s*19. In Orozco’s case, that international field overlaps with his upbringing around muralism and public art*2 and the Friday Workshop’s discussions of everyday things, streets, and process*1. The coexistence of large-scale public art in his background and brief street interventions in his own work helped make photography, sculpture, and walking parts of one working method.

Place in Photographic History

Orozco did not enter photographic history as a specialist photographer. He used photographs as evidence of sculpture, traces of walks, results of urban games, works completed through camera position, and prints installed in exhibition space. In the contemporary field that the Guggenheim describes as an “expanded view” of photography, this ability for a photograph to hold several roles at once exemplifies the changing boundaries between photography and other media after the 1990s*10.

His 1992 notes express distrust of photography’s tendency to cut events out of the world and place priority on walking and discovery*7. Yet he did not abandon the medium, and in 2006 explicitly stated that there are experiences for which photography may be the only means of presentation*3. His photographs occupy a limited but necessary role between the idea of photography as an all-purpose record and its reduction to secondary documentation. He uses the medium when a relation that appears and disappears at a site must become a work somewhere else. That specific need links photography to sculpture, walking, and games across his work.

gregory-crewdson.html.thesis_html: Crewdson’s key shift was to concentrate the production apparatus of cinema into the time of a still image with no before or after. He uses suburbia—a setting long associated in postwar America with home life and normalcy—and prepares houses, lawns, roads, figures, and artificial light with extraordinary precision while withholding the causes and consequences of what appears to have happened. Because these suburban spaces are so familiar, small signs of abnormality or isolation can spread across the entire frame. Large crews, elaborate lighting, and set design place many narrative clues within one image while keeping the event itself unresolved.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Why the Still Image

Crewdson studied photography at SUNY Purchase and later received his MFA from the Yale School of Art*4. He has explained that, because he is dyslexic, still images suited the way he thinks more closely than the linear progression of film or literature*17. Deeply drawn to photography’s stillness, he chose to concentrate elements of filmmaking within a single image even as cinema remained a major influence*18. The cinematic appearance of his photographs grows from this decision to use film-production techniques in order to think through the still image.

The Rise of Staged Photography

Crewdson began working in the late 1980s and 1990s, when staged scenes, quotation, and fiction had become established within museum photography without relying on photography’s presumed truthfulness. The Met’s Reality Check addresses the boundary between truth and fiction in contemporary photography and places Crewdson within this development.*5 From the late 1970s, Cindy Sherman borrowed the format of the film still to perform female characters from movies that did not exist.*21 Jeff Wall developed the “cinematographic photograph,” staging and restaging scenes to create self-contained tableaux distinct from documentary and street photography.*20 Working after these precedents, Crewdson developed an approach in which suburbia itself became a constructed photographic set.

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Freezing Cinema into a Single Image

Crewdson has described photography’s narrative capacity as limited compared with film or literature, calling the photograph “frozen and mute” in time.*16 He treats that limitation as the basis of the work, compressing information into a single moment and leaving questions in place of answers.*16 For this reason, large sets and production crews do not build a completed film-like plot. They allow a dense field of clues to occupy one image without letting any single clue determine what has happened.

Beneath the Roses involved closing roads, constructing buildings and interiors, positioning actors, and combining multiple lighting setups. Gagosian describes the series through its film-like production complexity and exacting control of detail.*1 White Cube’s exhibition materials likewise show location scouting, set construction, lighting, and post-production compositing all directed toward a single finished image.*8 The film-like production process ultimately produces a photograph with no “next shot.”

Light in Place of Narrative

In a Whitney audio guide, Crewdson states that light is central to his work and that he tries to tell the story through illumination.*16 In Twilight, artificial light falls across suburban night scenes, cars, windows, gardens, and figures, giving ordinary places a brightness slightly beyond the everyday. The Frist Art Museum describes the series as scenes in which inexplicable events enter domestic surroundings.*7 The light does not explain what has happened. It determines where attention gathers and which parts of the scene take on an unnatural importance.

In Beneath the Roses, light from windows, streetlamps, car headlights, and interiors competes within the same frame. The Whitney’s Untitled, 2004 is a representative example in which figures, architecture, and road lighting are distributed across a single tableau.*6 Lighting functions as a clue that prompts the viewer to imagine time before and after the still image; its role is narrative, not merely atmospheric.

Why Suburbia Became the Stage

American suburbia had been a photographic subject well before Crewdson. The Hofstra University Museum places Dan Weiner in the 1950s, Bill Owens in the 1960s and 1970s, and Crewdson from the 1990s onward within a cultural history of how suburban life, distinct from both city and countryside, has been represented*23. Weiner and Owens documented existing suburban life; Crewdson stages similar houses, lawns, roads, and domestic interiors for the camera, introducing fictional events into places that retain the appearance of reality.

In a 1997 BOMB conversation, Crewdson said he was interested in tensions between “the domestic and nature,” “the normal and the abnormal,” “the artificial and the real,” and “the familiar and the mysterious,” linking these oppositions to the uncanny*19. Suburban houses and lawns therefore function as familiar types associated with everyday life and domestic stability, not as neutral backgrounds for an invented strange world. White Cube also describes the figures in Beneath the Roses as embodiments of “middle-class American alienation,” treating ordinary interiors and streets as stages for unease*8.

John Garrison and Philip Krejcarek analyze Twilight as a structure in which fulfillment and erotic life are excluded from suburban and small-town domesticity, leaving the figures with a desire to escape outward*24. Their study also interprets light entering from beyond the frame as connecting the desire for an “outside” with the photographer’s gaze. Suburbia gave Crewdson a setting in which established images of home, safety, and ordinary life could occupy the same frame as isolation and desire.

A Turn Toward Smaller Productions

In Sanctuary, Crewdson photographed the Cinecittà film studios outside Rome in unpopulated black-and-white images, temporarily stepping away from large crews and suburban locations*9.Cathedral of the Pines was produced over three shoots in 2013–14 around Becket, Massachusetts, using forests and interiors to address tensions between connection and separation, intimacy and isolation.*26 Even as the production environment changed, the suspended scenes, directional light, and tension between interiors and nature remained. The figures’ actions still resist a single explanation, and the missing before and after continues to structure the image.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Twilight

Twilight, produced from about 1998 to 2002, was the series that brought broad attention to Crewdson’s cinematic staging. The Frist Art Museum presents it as a body of work in which surreal events enter ordinary suburban life*7. Holes in lawns, inexplicable light, and half-clothed bodies occupy the same frames as ordinary family life, while the figures’ actions are given no clear cause. The series established a structure in which the look of a film scene is paired with the absence of visible causes and consequences.

Beneath the Roses

Beneath the Roses, produced from roughly 2003 to 2008, combined location shooting, set construction, actors, lighting, and post-production digital processing*8. In works held by the Whitney, roads, houses, figures, and several light sources are dispersed across wide compositions so that no single element determines the narrative*6.The Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, also holds works from the series.*14 The ALBERTINA online collection likewise presents a 2004 Untitled as part of Beneath the Roses.*15

Cathedral of the Pines

Cathedral of the Pines is a 31-image series made in 2013–14 in forests and interiors around Becket. Crewdson has said that working there restored his connection to making photographs and marked a period of renewal.*26 Gagosian describes the series as placing figures in ambiguous scenes where intimacy and isolation, connection and separation intersect.*26 Photomonitor discusses the series through its relationship to pictorial tableaux and landscape painting as well as the lineage of the film still*22.

The Later Trilogy

An Eclipse of Moths uses the postindustrial streets around Pittsfield, Massachusetts, as its setting, photographing closed stores, parking lots, roads, and isolated figures. Gagosian links traces of economic decline to the isolation of the people within these scenes.*10 In the subsequent Eveningside, Crewdson shifted to black and white, composing streets and storefronts in the same region under light close to the boundary between day and night. The Taubman Museum treats Cathedral of the Pines, An Eclipse of Moths, and Eveningside as a continuous trilogy.*11

sections.title: Criticism and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
After Sherman and Wall

Cindy Sherman and Jeff Wall are important points of comparison for Crewdson’s historical position. In Untitled Film Stills, Sherman performed roles from nonexistent movies, using photography to examine how familiar images of women are constructed*21. Wall staged and restaged scenes while establishing each photograph as an independent tableau*20. Crewdson differs from both in bringing the division of labor and lighting systems of film production into suburban locations and concentrating those resources into one suspended moment.

Cinematic or Pictorial?

Crewdson is frequently described as “cinematic,” but the term alone does not explain how his pictures work. He has said that although he loves film, he cannot make a linear movie and is drawn instead to suggesting a story within one image.*18 Photomonitor discusses Cathedral of the Pines in relation to the history of pictorial tableaux and landscape painting as much as to the film still.*22 Gagosian cites references including Hopper, Hitchcock, and Lynch, yet the stopped time of the finished work remains a decisive difference from cinema.*1

Crewdson’s relationship to film lies in the structure of the photographs as much as in their references. Crewdson’s images contain a cinematic density of information, but because they withhold what comes before and after the event, more information makes causes and consequences harder to settle. Smithsonian interview material also records his long-running effort to articulate both his production process and photography’s narrative capacity*13.

The Repetition of Suburbia

Long-term assessments of Crewdson have also criticized his repeated use of the same suburbia, isolated figures, and uneasy light. Reviewing Beneath the Roses in 2005, Vince Aletti argued that the enormous production scale and cinematic artifice were becoming ends in themselves, and that recurring themes of “alienation,” “isolation,” and “existential anxiety” approached self-imitation*25. The criticism identifies technical perfection itself as a potential weakness in the work.

SITE SANTA FE placed the transformation of ordinary places into psychologically tense environments at the center of its presentation of Crewdson’s work.*3 Later, Sanctuary removed human figures; Cathedral of the Pines narrowed production to private forests and interiors; and Eveningside shifted to a postindustrial town in black and white.*12 Across these changes of setting and production scale, the missing before and after, deliberately designed light, and disjunction between figures and environments remain consistent.Crewdson has also been involved in photography education at Yale for many years and currently directs its graduate photography program.*2 Throughout the work, multiple narrative clues occupy the still image while the events before and after remain undetermined.

masashi-asada.html.lead_html: Masashi Asada is best known for the photobook Asada Family, in which he appears with his family as they play roles such as firefighters, musicians, and ramen-shop workers. Beginning with his graduation project, he extended this method from his own family to other families, making commemorative photographs through shared discussions, costumes, props, and time spent on the shoot. After the Great East Japan Earthquake, The Power of Albums documented the cleaning and return of mud-damaged photographs, treating family pictures not simply as images made at the moment of exposure, but as objects that are preserved, revisited, and returned to their owners.
masashi-asada.html.thesis_html: Asada changed family photography by moving from photographs that preserve events that happened to a family toward photographs in which the family gathers in order to make an event together for the camera. In Asada Family, the entire family discusses roles, prepares costumes and locations, and spends substantial time making each image. The photograph therefore records the fictional occupation or scenario and the fact that the four family members spent that day performing it together. In The Power of Albums, he stepped away from making new photographs and followed the work of cleaning pictures taken by others and returning them to their owners. Across these projects, Asada has treated family photography over an extended span of time: as a record of events, as a commemoration created through the act of photographing, and as a physical object that continues to exist after the shoot.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Why Photography

Asada was born in Mie Prefecture and became familiar with photography after his father gave him a camera when he was in junior high school. He later enrolled at the Japan Institute of Photography and Film. After graduating, he returned to Mie for a period without a fixed career path, and later recalled that when he asked himself what he genuinely enjoyed, photography was the only answer that came to mind*1. He subsequently worked at a photography studio in Tokyo while saving up days off to return to Mie and make the pictures that would become Asada Family*2. Speaking about Daido Moriyama, Asada has said that he admired not only the photographs but the way of life built around walking the streets, shooting, developing, and printing*3.

Family photography was already part of his home life. His father photographed family events and birthdays from the time Asada and his brother were young, and continued making an annual family photograph for New Year’s cards after they had grown up*4. Asada later observed that even one picture a year preserves changes across ten or twenty years, describing family photography as a repeated habit through which time accumulates rather than as a one-time record*4.

Why Family

The direct starting point for Asada’s work was a school assignment to express himself in a single photograph and enlarge it. While deciding what to photograph, he asked himself what he would choose if he could make only one photograph in his lifetime, and selected his family. He also wanted to appear in the image rather than remain outside it as the photographer. At the hospital where his mother worked, the four family members reenacted memories of injuries suffered in succession by his father, brother, and Asada himself*2. Using the self-timer allowed him to join the frame, and the day spent reenacting a past event became a new family photograph in its own right.

Once the family had exhausted actual memories to reenact, Asada shifted his thinking from the past to the future and began inventing roles the family might have occupied: firefighters, band members, ramen-shop workers, and others*1. He has described the time spent developing the idea, finding a location, preparing costumes, and finally making the photograph as part of what the picture enables him to remember later*5. Staging became a way to create new experiences shared by the family, not simply a device for fabricating fictional scenes.

Family Photography and Staging Before Asada

In later interviews, Asada has cited the transformations and self-staging of Cindy Sherman, Yasumasa Morimura, and Tomoko Sawada, as well as family-centered photography by Masahisa Fukase and Yurie Nagashima, as precedents he knew*2. Family and costume were therefore established subjects before his work. In Asada’s photographs, however, the entire family shares the setting, preparation, and performance. The event made for the photograph is collectively produced, unlike self-portraits in which a single artist plays multiple roles or photographs that observe a family’s private life.

In a 2009 review, Kotaro Iizawa compared the early Minna Kazoku series with Miwa Yanagi’s staged work. He described Asada’s constructed scenes as relatively loose extensions of everyday life and also detected a cynical note about contemporary images of the family beneath their lightness*6. The coexistence of the familiar format of the commemorative photograph and the artificiality of family members performing social roles has remained a recurring issue in later criticism.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Staging and Commemoration in Asada Family

Asada Family is staged, but Asada has explained that he does not resolve a scene in a single exposure. He makes multiple photographs over time, allowing his family to settle into their roles before choosing the final image*7. Expressions, mistakes, and timing change during the shoot, so the photograph contains both the predetermined role and the family’s actual responses as the event unfolds.

Asada has identified the duration of the shoot, and the ability to remember that time later through the photograph, as part of the work’s value*5. The finished picture presents a fictional scene, while the time the family spent gathering, preparing, and performing for it was a real event. Staging and commemoration therefore operate together: the act of staging itself produces a new occasion to remember.

Working Collaboratively with Families

In Minna Kazoku and Watashi no Kazoku, which extend the work beyond his own family, Asada uses family albums and older photographs as prompts, listening to which memories participants share before deciding what to photograph*7. Art Tower Mito’s participatory Watashi no Kazoku project likewise combined photographs with texts written by participants and described the shoot as a collaborative undertaking between Asada and those taking part*8. The memories and words of the people photographed enter the construction of the scene, making their contribution part of how the image acquires meaning.

Asada has said that photographs can become rigid when he proceeds only with his own ideas, and that accepting suggestions from people at the shoot can produce better results*4. He does not conceal the staging in order to simulate a “natural” family. What will be performed is decided with the participants. Their memories, wishes, and play enter directly into the making of the family photograph.

Photo Washing and Photographs That Remain

Immediately after the Great East Japan Earthquake, Asada discussed with fellow photographers what photography could do. He did not believe that entering disaster areas simply to make new pictures would provide direct assistance while housing and food were scarce, so he first went as a volunteer. There he encountered efforts to wash photographs covered in tsunami mud and return them to their owners, an experience that led to The Power of Albums*9. Working to rescue existing photographs rather than produce new ones extended his concern with family photography into the period after an image has been made.

Akaaka published the expanded edition of The Power of Albums as a record, made with editor Satoshi Fujimoto, of photograph-rescue efforts in different communities*10. At Art Tower Mito, Asada noted that albums found among the debris were often set aside separately, suggesting that printed photographs could signal even to people other than their owners that they should not be thrown away*11. The value of the photograph is located not only in the quality of an image, but also in the process by which a physical record of someone’s time survives, is searched for, and returns to its owner.

sections.title: Key Works, Photobooks, and Exhibitions
sections.body_html:
Asada Family

The photobook Asada Family was published by Akaaka in 2008 and received the 34th Kimura Ihei Photography Award the following year*12. Across scenes in which the four family members appear as firefighters, a band, racing drivers, ramen-shop workers, and other roles, the recurrence of the same people holds the series together as family photography even as the costumes and settings change. The artist’s official works list places later projects, including NEW LIFE, within a long-term engagement with changes in his family*13.

The 2021 exhibition Watashi no Kazoku brought together approximately 150 works, from his father’s annual New Year’s-card photographs and Asada’s graduation project to Asada Family, Minna Kazoku, The Power of Albums, and new work made at the exhibition site*14. This structure positioned Asada Family as a starting point within a longer trajectory that moves from domestic commemorative pictures to other families and to the preservation of photographs after disaster.

Minna Kazoku and Watashi no Kazoku

Minna Kazoku applied the method developed with Asada’s own family to other families. A 2009 review, when the series still consisted of roughly fifteen works, already identified it as the next development after Asada Family*6. In the later Watashi no Kazoku, the family is not defined only through a single group portrait; the work develops around relationships and narratives selected by the participants themselves*15.

Art Tower Mito’s Somebody’s Best Album incorporated photographs and writings by members of the public, as well as workshops centered on photography, alongside Asada’s representative works*16. By placing the viewing of art and the discussion of one’s own family pictures in the same exhibition, the project refused to confine family photography to images authored by the exhibiting artist.

The Power of Albums

The Power of Albums follows people who cleaned photographs damaged by the tsunami after the Great East Japan Earthquake and worked to return them to their owners*10. A record of a talk at the University of Tsukuba notes that Asada repeatedly observed the cleaning and return of photographs in Noda, Iwate Prefecture*17. Here, family pictures made earlier by unnamed photographers become more central than photographs authored by Asada; questions of preservation and ownership come to the foreground.

Asada Photography Studio and Exhibitions

In Asada Photography Studio Mannen, Asada assumed the fictional role of a second-generation proprietor of a local portrait studio and reenacted studio commemorative photography with his family*18. By taking the family portrait studio—an established institution of commemorative photography—as his subject, the staging of Asada Family expands from domestic play to the professional question of who makes another person’s commemorative image.

Projects including Family Photo Tree, Canon’s Watashi no Kazoku, and KAAT’s YOKOHAMA PHOTOGRAPH continued this participatory approach with people recruited from local communities and organizations*19. At KAAT, portraits were produced collaboratively around the theme of “me/us now,” extending Asada’s commemorative photography beyond families defined only by blood relations*20.

sections.title: Criticism and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Asada Family and the Roles of Family

In a review of the exhibition Family and Photography, Megumi Takashima reads the family’s performances as firefighters, politicians, heroes, and other fixed roles as a reminder that the family itself can also be performed as a social fiction*21. The cosplay in Asada Family conveys the pleasure of familial play while exposing how roles such as “father,” “mother,” “older brother,” and “younger brother” are themselves shaped by social types.

Writing about the 2016 exhibition Hobo Kazoku., Kotaro Iizawa emphasized Asada’s commitment to commemorative photography and argued that the collaboration between photographer and models opened images that would normally matter only to their participants to third-party viewers*22. A critical awareness of the family as a role and the commemorative value of time actually spent together coexist within the same staged structure.

Family Photography and Self-Portraiture

Photographing the family from within has many precedents in Japanese photographic history, including work by Masahisa Fukase and Yurie Nagashima, and Asada has acknowledged his awareness of such artists*2. His emphasis falls on creating a new event for the photograph instead of exposing or closely observing private family life. Compared with the transformations of Sherman, Morimura, and Sawada, his work also shifts attention from a single artist performing multiple identities to several people sharing one scenario and producing “family” as a group within the frame.

Early Reception and Later Development

After Asada Family received the Kimura Ihei Photography Award, some criticism questioned whether its strong premise could sustain more than one project. In a 2016 review, Iizawa explicitly recalled his early concern that Asada might prove to be a one-hit phenomenon, then noted how the work had developed through NEW LIFE, Sotsugyo Shashin no Shukudai, The Power of Albums, and other projects*22. In his 2009 review, Iizawa had likewise looked to Minna Kazoku, rather than repetition of Asada Family, as the direction in which the work could continue*6.

In the later work, critical attention shifts away from cosplay as a visual device toward Asada’s ability to apply commemorative photography to other families, local communities, portrait studios, and albums after disaster. The work expanded from repeating the formal premise of Asada Family to asking who participates in making a photograph and what happens to the resulting picture afterward.

Place in Photographic History

Asada’s contribution to family photography does not depend on a new subject or specialized photographic technology. In Asada Family, the day the family gathered, devised roles, and performed for the camera became the commemoration itself. Minna Kazoku and Watashi no Kazoku extended that method toward the memories of other people and collaborative production. The Power of Albums followed photographs years after they had been made, as they were cleaned and returned to their owners. Across these projects, he has treated family photography as something that encompasses the time spent making an image, owning it, and looking back at it.

Art Tower Mito’s Somebody’s Best Album brought Asada’s major series together with texts by participants in Watashi no Kazoku and post-disaster efforts to return photographs*16. The exhibition placed artist-made works, commemorative pictures kept in homes, and the later life of physical prints within one continuum. Asada’s work has therefore addressed not only whom a photograph depicts and how it is made, but also whose object it becomes and how it remains in the world.

rineke-dijkstra.html.lead_html: Rineke Dijkstra is a Dutch photographer known for Beach Portraits, New Mothers, Almerisa, and photographs and videos of soldiers and young clubgoers. Through frontal figures, spare backgrounds, and series that return to the same person over time, she has photographed periods when bodies and social roles are changing—adolescence, childbirth, military service, and migration. Following commercial portrait work and a 1991 self-portrait, she moved away from portraits that explain a person through character, focusing instead on moments when the self-image a sitter tries to project does not fully coincide with what appears through age, body, clothing, and institutions. Her work across photography and video occupies a central place in the history of portraiture since the 1990s, particularly in questions of how individuals take shape within social forms.
rineke-dijkstra.html.thesis_html: Dijkstra brought a crucial proposition to contemporary portraiture: a portrait can record both the self a sitter tries to present and the figure that emerges through the body and social role without fixing “who someone is” in a single image. Sander located individuals within social structures through occupation and class; Arbus examined gaps between a subject’s self-presentation and the figure produced by the photograph; Ruff blocked the expectation that psychological insight could be extracted from a precise frontal face. Goldin photographed friends and lovers from within the flow of their lives. Dijkstra chose people adapting to a new body or role—during adolescence, immediately after childbirth, upon entering military service, or through migration—and allowed them to determine their own posture and expression. Their bearing reveals individual intention alongside behaviors learned through clothing, gender, peers, occupation, and state institutions. At the same time, tense shoulders, the placement of hands, shifts in balance, and a gaze that cannot be fully staged remain visible. Against portraits that stabilize a person as a finished character or social type, Dijkstra made the incomplete fit between self-presentation, social codes, and bodily response the subject of portraiture.
