sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Meurer’s Reform of Design Education

After training as a metalworker in ornamental casting, Blossfeldt studied sculpture and modeling at the teaching institute attached to Berlin’s Museum of Decorative Arts. From 1892 to 1895 he stayed in Rome as an assistant to his teacher Moritz Meurer, taking part in the collection of plants and the production of specimens, models, and illustrations*6. In late nineteenth-century applied-art education, Meurer sought to replace the copying of historical ornament with close observation of the growth and structure of plants as a source for new design. The Berlin Museum of Decorative Arts exhibition Form Follows Flower reconstructed photographs, herbarium specimens, plaster and bronze models, and wall charts as a single teaching system, making clear that Blossfeldt’s photographs originated as one component of that apparatus*2.

Meurer’s own 1895 book Pflanzenformen discusses, chapter by chapter, the significance of natural form for applied art, methods for translating natural forms into artistic forms, the conditions for studying nature in art schools, and the design of teaching materials*14. Blossfeldt’s plant photographs belonged to this shift from copying finished ornament toward observing plant structure in order to study principles of form. Repetition and enlargement entered a teaching system before the photographs were treated as autonomous works, allowing students to examine rules and variations in form.

The practical reason for using photography follows directly from this setting. Plants grow and wilt with the seasons, and their flowering periods can be brief. Tiny buds and joints are difficult to examine from the back of a classroom, while plants gathered around the Mediterranean were unavailable in Berlin for every lesson. UdK records show that Blossfeldt used photographs enlarging plant details by roughly eighteen to forty times in his classes, and that some surviving prints still bear pinholes from being mounted on walls*26. Photography allowed a changing subject to be fixed and forms from different times and places to be compared in the same classroom.

UdK’s collection overview records 631 surviving teaching photographs by Blossfeldt, while Meurer’s plant models are cataloged as a separate group*5. The scale of this material points to a visual database intended for repeated comparison by students, a function quite different from selecting a small number of finished works. MoMA likewise describes Blossfeldt as entering photography through sculpture and applied-art education because the pedagogical problem preceded his formation as a photographer*1.

From Teaching Material to Avant-Garde Photography

From 1899 until 1930, Blossfeldt continued to teach “modeling from living plants,” while the photographs accumulated for years inside the classroom*3. A turning point came around 1925–26, when the dealer Karl Nierendorf saw the plant photographs in a school exhibition and recognized their potential as art. SK Stiftung Kultur’s exhibition chronology links the 1926 show at Galerie Nierendorf, the publication of Urformen der Kunst in 1928, and the 1929 appearances in Film und Foto and at the Bauhaus in Dessau*16.

The purpose for which the images were made did not coincide with their reception at the end of the 1920s. Blossfeldt had not set out in the 1890s to make “New Objectivity photography.” Viewers in the late 1920s connected the plain backgrounds, crisp detail, enlarged forms, and suppression of expressive gesture with the new visual culture that followed the First World War. Their origin as teaching images remained visible even after they entered the art world, and the forms produced by practical use resonated strongly with questions being asked by avant-garde photography.

The move into the art world was also more than a single moment of “discovery.” MoMA’s chronology records that Nierendorf exhibited the plant photographs alongside African sculpture in 1926 and subsequently published Urformen der Kunst*7. Today Pinakothek der Moderne presents Blossfeldt as an important figure in New Objectivity*8, while SK Stiftung Kultur foregrounds the photographs’ origins as teaching material. These differing classifications show how later institutions have repeatedly reshaped the meaning of the work.

The reception of 1928–29 extended well beyond fine-art photography. SK Stiftung Kultur’s bibliography includes contemporary reviews by Paul Westheim, Curt Glaser, and the Bauhaus journal, where the plant photographs were discussed in relation to the tasks of contemporary photography, the relation between nature and art, and design education*6. Architectural Record also reviewed Urformen der Kunst in 1929 through comparisons with architecture and ornament, showing that the book circulated almost immediately among readers of architecture and design as well as photography*20.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Magnification and Comparison

In Blossfeldt’s photographs, a bud or the base of a leaf only a few centimeters long can fill the frame. Magnification first serves a comparative purpose: it brings details that the naked eye could not examine together into a shared visual scale. UdK’s catalogue raisonné records instances in which different crops and prints were made from the same negative, indicating selective editing according to the forms needed for teaching*3. Enlargement turns hairs, joints, spirals, bilateral symmetry, and branching into distinct diagrams, separating botanical size from photographic size.

This operation unsettles the assumption that photography reproduces a subject at a faithful scale. The camera records real detail precisely, but changing scale does not preserve the way an object appears to the naked eye. Small plant organs can begin to resemble architecture because structures that exist in nature are detached from the scale of the human body. Photographic evidence and visual estrangement arise from the same operation.

Magnification was neither fixed nor uniform. MoMA titles record specific ratios—four, eight, ten, twenty-five times—showing that scale was selected according to the structure being presented in each plant*13. Describing the work as a mechanical classification under identical conditions misses the decisions involved in magnification and cropping. Blossfeldt established common conditions while still deciding which portion of each specimen would make comparison most useful.

The intended use as comparative teaching material also shaped the photographic form. Positioning plants close to frontal, simplifying the background, and enlarging stems and buds to fill the frame suppress information about setting and scale while making outlines, joints, spirals, hairs, and supporting structures easier to compare. The Art Institute of Chicago likewise describes the photographs as visual studies and teaching aids for artists, designers, and architects, linking natural patterns to the teaching of ornament*28.

Images Designed for Comparison

Plain light or dark backgrounds, frontal presentation, and central placement separate plants from their natural surroundings and make one photograph easier to compare with another. Reducing information about outdoor light, soil, surrounding foliage, and season directs attention toward differences in contour and structure. SK Stiftung Kultur has examined Blossfeldt’s cutting, fixing, staging, choice of background, and enlargement of plants, showing that the appearance of “objective plant photography” was itself produced through many photographic decisions*4.

His objectivity was produced through a series of decisions. He determined which plant to gather, which stage of growth to use, where to cut it, and how much to enlarge it, removing information that hindered comparison. The later Bechers used a related structure of standardized conditions and comparative difference, but Blossfeldt’s form arose from the needs of applied-art education*17.

For Meurer and Blossfeldt, the study of plants was not limited to botanical identification. Phyllotaxis, branching, curling, support, and joints were studied as formal principles that could be applied to architecture, craft, and ornament*2. Botanical names remained in the photograph titles, while inflorescences could appear crown-like, stems columnar, and tendrils like ornamental curves. In the classroom, similarities between natural and artificial structures were examined unit by unit, with emphasis on comparing recurring forms.

This approach also belonged to a late nineteenth-century social setting in which applied-art education sought new principles of design in response to industrialization. Reformers reduced the copying of historical styles and turned instead to structures found in nature; photography was well suited to preserving large numbers of visual examples. When later histories isolated the photographs as works of art, their relation to educational reform, models, specimens, and applied design became less prominent. Recent research in Berlin and Cologne has returned this composite working environment to the interpretation of the photographs*4.

Working collages and groups of prints clearly preserve the use of placing related forms side by side to examine their relationships. UdK’s image collections allow photographs, models, and specimens to be searched across categories*19. The Spencer Museum notes Blossfeldt’s own explanation that small forms could be shown at a “convenient scale” in order to direct students’ attention*24. Removing the background therefore served a pedagogical design function—organizing information for comparison—as well as producing the formal abstraction for which the photographs later became known.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Urformen der Kunst and the Printed Page

Urformen der Kunst (1928) reproduced 120 plant photographs in photogravure, re-editing teaching images once pinned to classroom walls into a sequence of pages*10. The book does not preserve a common actual scale: buds, stems, and leaves from different plants appear at similar sizes on the page. Its sequence detaches them from botanical scale and sets up comparisons of outline, articulation, repetition, and symmetry. In the first edition held by the National Gallery of Art, the continuity of the book itself establishes a rhythm of comparison*23.

Nierendorf’s editing and publication substantially changed the use and reception of the teaching photographs. In the classroom they functioned as illustrations; in the lavish photobook, each image could be encountered as an autonomous work linking nature, art, and technology. Editing, printing, and exhibition in the late 1920s helped create the very conditions under which the teaching images came to be viewed as “Blossfeldt photographs.”

In the photobook, repetition across pages becomes part of the method and structures the work as a whole. Alexander Schürmann discusses Urformen der Kunst as an early example of extending enumeration and repetition across the structure of an entire book*29. In the University Library of Paderborn’s digital facsimile, isolated plant images follow one another page by page, repeating contours and joints across different species at comparable picture sizes*30. Teaching images that could once be compared side by side in the classroom were transformed into a book in which comparison occurs by moving backward and forward through pages and through visual memory.

Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza notes that the paper and printing quality of Urformen der Kunst strengthened the sculptural and graphic qualities of the plants*9. Publication added page size, printing, and the isolation of each image to the reproduction of teaching material, intensifying its status as an object of viewing. Taken together, the first edition preserved by the National Gallery of Art and the Met’s holdings show that the familiar image of “Blossfeldt” was shaped by book design as well as by the camera*10.

Film und Foto and International Reception

Film und Foto (FiFo), organized by the Deutscher Werkbund in Stuttgart in 1929, was an international exhibition that later traveled to Zurich, Berlin, Vienna, Tokyo, and Osaka*15. Straight photography, advertising, press imagery, photomontage, film, and Bauhaus experimentation appeared together, and Blossfeldt was shown alongside László Moholy-Nagy, El Lissitzky, Alexander Rodchenko, Man Ray, Albert Renger-Patzsch, Edward Weston, and others*7. The photographs retained the quiet frontality of teaching images, distinct from press and advertising photography, while entering an international debate about how the camera could revise everyday vision. The National Gallery of Australia likewise describes the period from the 1920s to the 1940s through the rubric of the “New Photography,” in which clear description and new viewpoints were central currents*12.

Placing Blossfeldt straightforwardly inside New Objectivity reverses this history. FiFo encompassed New Objectivity as well as the steep angles, montage, and expanded visual possibilities associated with New Vision. Blossfeldt’s own images remain frontal and still, yet their magnification altered ordinary perception in a way that appealed to avant-garde viewers. Photographs born from a relatively conservative educational function were reinterpreted in avant-garde exhibitions and criticism; that displacement is central to their reception history.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
New Objectivity and the “New Photography”

Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity) spread through German art in the mid-1920s and was associated with clear description that restrained emotive distortion and decorative ambiguity. In photography, Albert Renger-Patzsch and August Sander are among the figures most often discussed in this connection. Neues Sehen (New Vision) and the broader “New Photography,” by contrast, also encompassed steep high and low viewpoints, montage, magnification, and film—the camera’s ability to produce forms of perception unavailable to the naked eye*12. Blossfeldt did not begin within the former movement, but by the end of the 1920s his images were being received in relation to both.

At the moment when Renger-Patzsch described machines, plants, and industrial products with high precision and Sander organized social subjects typologically, Blossfeldt’s plant photographs entered the same art environment as images of lucid description. The origins of his comparative method, however, lay in teaching material required by applied-art classes in the late nineteenth century. Grouping formally similar photographs under a single movement can obscure their different purposes. Comparable photographic forms developed from distinct needs and met in the exhibitions of the late 1920s.

The National Gallery of Australia describes New Objectivity photography as a reaction against Pictorialism that favored crisp, unobstructed depictions of reality, placing Blossfeldt’s comparisons of natural and mechanical forms alongside Renger-Patzsch*12. Fotomuseum Winterthur and recent research by SK Stiftung Kultur, meanwhile, point to a broader reception that also involved New Vision*25. Fixing Blossfeldt under the label “New Objectivity” erases the time between the beginning of his work and its later reception. His particular position becomes clearer when the teaching photographs are followed into the multiple theories of photography that absorbed them at the end of the 1920s.

Benjamin, Bataille, and Later Readings

Urformen der Kunst received numerous contemporary reviews after its publication in 1928, and SK Stiftung Kultur’s bibliography includes Walter Benjamin’s “Neues von Blumen” (“News about Flowers”) among the responses*6. Benjamin drew attention to the way enlarged plants disclosed successive similarities and transformations of form that ordinarily went unnoticed at their natural scale. Fotomuseum Winterthur likewise treats this reception as an example of photographic magnification opening vision beyond ordinary experience*25.

In the 1928 review itself, Benjamin does not treat the book’s 120 plates simply as illustrations of botanical knowledge; he focuses on the capacity of magnification to connect plant forms to another world of morphology*18. In his account, the value of the photographs lies less in explanatory text about plants than in the camera and magnification making forms available that ordinary perception has difficulty isolating. The review gives a contemporary account of why Blossfeldt’s teaching images could be reinterpreted as avant-garde photography.

The core of the series lies less in the metaphor that “plants resemble architecture” than in the camera’s ability to place forms into comparable conditions. Magnifying a bud forty times, removing its background, and placing it alone on a page detaches it from the garden and makes folds, joints, radial structures, and repetitions visible as independent forms. The camera records the subject precisely while changing the scale and setting by which people ordinarily understand it. Blossfeldt arrived at this operation through the practical demands of teaching before it was attached to an avant-garde theory.

Later histories of photography have often connected Blossfeldt to Bernd and Hilla Becher because both standardized backgrounds, repeated related subjects, and made differences legible through comparison*17. The methods are genuinely comparable, but Blossfeldt used plant form in design education while the Bechers recorded disappearing industrial structures by functional type. Their connection is best understood as a shared use of photography for classification and comparison, not as a simple ranking of precursor and successor. Similar comparative structures arose under different historical conditions.

Fondazione Prada’s 2025 exhibition Typologien extended the principle of typology from botanical classification across twentieth-century German photography, comparing Blossfeldt, Sander, the Bechers, Thomas Ruff, Thomas Struth, and others outside a chronological sequence*21. The exhibition does not establish a direct line of influence, but it shows how placing subjects under common conditions and producing difference through comparison recurred for different purposes across plants, people, industrial architecture, and contemporary images. Within that history, Blossfeldt’s plant photographs mark one point at which the principle of classification and comparison moved from applied-art education into twentieth-century photographic culture.

The same plant photographs have been read through design education, the Bauhaus, Surrealism, and later typological photography as well as New Objectivity. Whitechapel Gallery has described how their precise botanical observation generated strange associations and entered avant-garde settings that included the circle around Georges Bataille*27. Their availability to multiple movements does not stem from vagueness. The force of the form comes from isolating botanically specific subjects from their normal scale and setting, allowing education, science, art, and design to deploy them for different purposes. This history of reuse has given Blossfeldt’s photographs a critical density that persists beyond any single movement.

Benjamin emphasized the way enlarged photographs opened scales outside ordinary visual experience. The Jewish Museum’s 2026 exhibition similarly places Blossfeldt alongside Moholy-Nagy, Man Ray, and Sander in relation to Benjamin’s thinking on the future of photography*11. Bataille, by contrast, used photographs including Blumenbachia hieronymi in “The Language of Flowers” in Documents, directing attention from orderly form toward reproduction, decay, and unease*22. The same exacting plant images could support both rational design and anti-rational avant-garde criticism, preventing Blossfeldt’s reception from settling into a single movement.

edward-s-curtis.html.title: Edward S. Curtis | The North American Indian and Indigenous Representation | Photo Coordinates
edward-s-curtis.html.meta_description: Edward S. Curtis, born near Whitewater, Wisconsin, in 1868, photographed Indigenous peoples across North America and assembled photographs, texts, vocabularies, and sound recordings in the twenty-volume The North American Indian, published from 1907 to 1930. His unified visual language—platinum printing, photogravure, and the staging of clothing and scenes—circulated widely while reinforcing a colonial idea of Indigenous peoples as a “vanishing race.” The project also involved assimilation policy, patronage, Indigenous collaborators, film, and the ways communities today reinterpret the archive.
edward-s-curtis.html.lead_html: Edward S. Curtis, born near Whitewater, Wisconsin, in 1868, photographed Indigenous peoples across North America and assembled photographs, texts, vocabularies, and sound recordings in the twenty-volume The North American Indian, published from 1907 to 1930. His unified visual language—platinum printing, photogravure, and the staging of clothing and scenes—circulated widely while reinforcing a colonial idea of Indigenous peoples as a “vanishing race.” The project also involved assimilation policy, patronage, Indigenous collaborators, film, and the ways communities today reinterpret the archive.
edward-s-curtis.html.thesis_html: In The North American Indian, the publishing structure itself produced a historical image on a scale that exceeded any single photograph. Curtis brought portraits, landscapes, clothing, and ceremonies into a shared Pictorialist tonal language and connected them across twenty text volumes, twenty portfolios, roughly 2,200 plates, sound recordings, lantern slides, and film*5. A staged photograph therefore did not stand alone. Across thousands of pages, the ongoing present of assimilation policy was repeatedly reframed as a past understood to be disappearing*4. The removal of a clock from In a Piegan Lodge is one visible example of that editorial principle*8. At the same time, the project was also collaborative, involving Indigenous researchers, interpreters, cultural intermediaries, and many sitters, including Alexander B. Upshaw*24. The images retain information that exceeds Curtis’s narrative of disappearance, and the power of documentary photography to construct history has become a central subject of reassessment. Current reinterpretations restore names and community knowledge to the photographs, testing aesthetic finish, ethnographic information, colonial editing, and Indigenous participation within the same archive.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Assimilation Policy and the “Vanishing” Paradigm

After establishing a successful portrait studio in Seattle, Curtis joined the Harriman Alaska Expedition in 1899 as an official photographer at the invitation of C. Hart Merriam and George Bird Grinnell. A Smithsonian chronology records that in 1900 he traveled with Grinnell to a Sun Dance on the Blackfeet Reservation in Montana, then began photographing in the Southwest; by 1904 he had announced plans for a large-scale publication*15. This was the period in which his work expanded from the commercial portrait studio to travel with scientists and ethnographers engaged in classifying and recording societies, forming the basis for the later twenty-volume project.

Recent work by Jen Rose Smith has reconsidered this beginning through land as well as portraiture. She analyzes the scientific surveys, resource studies, and territorial classifications Curtis encountered on the 1899 Alaska expedition as part of a colonial geography in which Indigenous representation and dispossession intersected*29. This does not explain the whole later project through a single Alaskan experience. It does, however, show that the twenty-volume structure—organizing people by “tribe” and region—cannot be separated from contemporary systems for classifying land and populations.

That conception of time also shaped the choice of subjects. Schools, wage labor, railroads, markets, Euro-American clothing, and federal policy appear less often than traditional dress, horses, tipis, ceremonies, and natural landscapes. A photograph can preserve one part of reality with great precision while downplaying others through decisions about what counts as culturally representative. Curtis’s work makes concrete how preservation and exclusion can operate within the same documentary act.

The relation between ethnography and photography at the time was itself varied. Smithsonian-affiliated archives preserve extensive materials gathered by government agencies and anthropologists according to different systems for classifying language, material culture, and ceremony*15. Curtis drew on the authority of ethnography while combining it with Pictorialist aesthetics and a deluxe publication intended for wealthy subscribers. That combination gave The North American Indian an authority unlike either an administrative record or a conventional fine-art photobook.

Patronage, Publication, and the Research Network

Support from J. P. Morgan beginning in 1906 enabled Curtis to sustain decades of photography, field research, plate making, and publication*3. The North American Indian appeared between 1907 and 1930 as twenty text volumes and twenty large portfolios, ultimately incorporating roughly 2,200 images alongside vocabularies, oral accounts, music, and other research*5. Expensive paper and photogravure printing positioned the publication as an authoritative object for affluent owners, libraries, and research institutions.

Curtis was not the project’s only producer. Morgan Library research identifies Alexander B. Upshaw, George Hunt, William E. Myers, and others as interpreters, researchers, writers, and cultural advisers*9. Patrons, editors, researchers, Indigenous cultural intermediaries, and the people photographed all participated in the project under unequal relations of power. Behind the appearance of a single, unified author called “Curtis,” many people supplied knowledge and shaped decisions.

Across Smithsonian holdings, letters, field records, and variant prints survive alongside the finished volumes, allowing researchers to follow the selection process that produced the publication*7. The completed twenty volumes homogenize a “Curtis viewpoint,” while the production record separates the contributions of patronage, editing, local collaborators, and printing technologies at different moments.

The finished project required long-term editing from the outset; it was never simply an accumulation of photographic trips. Mick Gidley compares proofs, publishing plans, and textual revisions from the early volumes, showing repeated selection and rearrangement between fieldwork and final publication*27. The coherent world of The North American Indian was made through editorial decisions about which communities and regions would form a volume, which photographs would appear as text illustrations or large portfolio plates, and which forms of knowledge would remain in prose.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Staging, Printing, and the Construction of Time

Curtis’s canonical images use soft focus, low viewpoints, smoke, backlighting, simplified backgrounds, and selected traditional clothing to place people in spaces that are difficult to locate in contemporary time*6. In In a Piegan Lodge, a clock visible in the original negative was removed from the published image; the British Library version and related material preserve evidence of the alteration*22. The missing clock is a symbolic example of a wider pattern in which modern objects, institutions, and ways of life were selectively reduced, producing a consistent image of Indigenous culture before modernization.

The surfaces of platinum prints and photogravures strengthened this temporal effect. Platinum prints discussed by the National Museum of the American Indian use broad tonal ranges and matte surfaces to bind skin, feathers, smoke, and background into continuous gradations, creating quiet volume instead of abrupt local contrast*20. In the books, photogravure preserved deep blacks and subtle tonal transitions while making editioned reproduction possible*19. Staging, exposure, plate making, and printing therefore worked as one chain. The politics of the project extends from the choice of subject to the form through which a particular past was made beautiful and memorable.

This staging also belongs to the history of Pictorialism. Smithsonian American Art Museum collection records place Curtis within histories of fine-art photography as well*18. Soft focus, backlighting, smoke, and deep tonal range functioned as visual conventions through which photography acquired artistic value at the time. Their political force lies inside that aesthetic achievement: beauty itself helped make a particular historical image persuasive.

Collaboration and Indigenous Agency

Recent scholarship has also revised accounts of Curtis’s fieldwork that describe it only as a site of unilateral control by a white photographer. George Hunt, deeply knowledgeable about Kwakwaka’wakw society, worked as a cultural intermediary in research and filmmaking, while Upshaw supported research on Apsáalooke language and history*9. Sitters brought their own knowledge of clothing, ceremonies, family relations, and personal names to the encounter. These facts do not erase the project’s colonial terms, but the archive records Indigenous decisions and actions within them.

Shamoon Zamir’s The Gift of the Face reconsiders this collaboration through portraiture and time*13. An account organized only around the “vanishing race” paradigm risks collapsing the specificity of individual faces, names, and collaborations with cultural intermediaries into one explanation. Zamir retains the critique of the colonial frame while asking how portraits may also preserve evidence of social change and community self-understanding. This approach allows individual photographs to be considered alongside, and not absorbed into, a single ideological explanation.

Old Images / New Views, developed by Rutgers and the UBC Museum of Anthropology, presents Indigenous scholars, writers, and curators adding new captions and testimony to historical photographs and returning them to histories of ancestors and families*10. Once the photographer’s title and publication context cease to function as the only final meaning, the archive can reenter community memory. Critical work on Curtis increasingly asks who appears in a photograph, who supplied information, and which descriptions were added later.

Zamir’s study critiques the project’s colonial structure without fixing Indigenous participants once again as passive “subjects”*24. Upshaw’s education and research skills show that his role exceeded supplying information to a white project; he moved between multiple worlds as a modern Indigenous intellectual. Current readings of Curtis therefore depend on resisting the return of such complex biographies to generalized tribal types.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Twenty Volumes and Photogravure

The basic unit of the project is the relationship among volume, text, illustration, and portfolio. Northwestern University’s digital edition presents the prose and images according to the original structure, with portraits, dwellings, ceremonies, crafts, and landscapes arranged through the logic of each chapter*5. Large portfolio plates have greater visual autonomy than illustrations embedded in the text and more strongly assume the character of fine-art photographs. The authority of the project grew from the proximity of ethnographic explanation and Pictorialist viewing within the same publication.

The twenty volumes divide regions and communities in sequence and combine photographs with histories, daily life, religion, material culture, and linguistic material. Library of Congress cataloging records vocabularies continuing into later volumes and twenty large portfolios corresponding to the text volumes*28. Through this sequence, individual portraits are placed within geographically defined chapters and become part of a publication system classifying an overall entity called “the North American Indian.” The fusion of ethnographic taxonomy and aesthetically finished plates gave Curtis’s historical image much of its authority.

The National Museum of the American Indian preserves photogravure copper plates and proofs, keeping the production process from negative to final plate as physical evidence*12. Selection of negatives, retouching, plate making, paper, ink, and book sequence each added decisions to the image. Staging therefore continued beyond the photographic encounter into the design of the publication itself.

The Vanishing Race and Film

The Vanishing Race—Navaho, included in the first volume, places a group of riders moving away from the camera into a dark image, making the idea of disappearance explicit through both title and composition*23. By contrast, a portrait such as White Man Runs Him, Apsaroke identifies a specific person by name, providing a route from the abstract category of “Indian” back toward family and community history*14. Symbolic images and identifiable individuals coexist in the same archive, preventing the body of work from being exhausted by a single political judgment.

The 1914 film In the Land of the Head Hunters shared the impulse to preserve culture before its supposed disappearance, yet its production was not a straightforward ethnographic recording. Research published by the University of Washington Press traces collaboration with Kwakwaka’wakw performers, staged action, clothing, narrative, music, and later restoration, reconsidering the film as an intercultural production*2. The reenactment of traditional life reveals Curtis’s orientation toward the past, while the film itself depended on the knowledge and performance of the people who appeared in it.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Ethnography and Pictorialism

Curtis is difficult to place because the ethnographic quantity of information and the aesthetic unity of Pictorialism occupy the same project. For an ethnographic record, modern clothing, schools, commodities, wage labor, and the effects of policy are also crucial information. Yet the representative images give less weight to such features than to traditional dress, natural landscapes, ceremony, and the stillness of portraiture. As the Morgan Library has shown, these selections reduce the visible present of assimilation policy and locate “authentic culture” in an imagined past*9.

Aesthetic finish and politics are joined within the same formal operation. Deep photogravure tones, light, and simplified backgrounds make the photographs compelling, and that attraction helps the same historical image recur with authority. Because form itself contributes to the persuasiveness of the “vanishing race” narrative, technical criticism and colonial critique meet in the analysis of the same image.

The North American Indian also changed over the twenty-three years of its publication. Shannon Egan argues that the aesthetic and political approach of individual volumes responded to changes in American modernism and contemporary representations of Indigenous peoples*25. The overarching narrative of disappearance coexists with shifts from volume to volume and period to period, so the vast archive cannot be reduced to one unchanging style.

Recontextualizing the Archive

Museums today increasingly acknowledge the artistic value of Curtis’s photographs while making the power relations of their production explicit. The Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History places staging and stereotyping at the center of its presentation*16. The James Museum has worked with tribes and communities to add personal names and cultural context*17. Such recontextualization moves beyond the choice between “beautiful but inaccurate” and “valuable record,” allowing each image to be examined for what it records precisely and what it constructs through the photographer’s program.

Seattle Art Museum’s 2018 exhibition Double Exposure presented more than one hundred works by Curtis in the same space as contemporary Indigenous artists Marianne Nicolson, Tracy Rector, and Will Wilson*1. The exhibition did more than add corrective labels to old photographs. By placing them beside images in which present-day Indigenous artists photograph their own bodies, communities, and lands, it set contemporary self-representation against Curtis’s construction of a Native America confined to the past. The exhibition format itself became a way of testing the authority of historical photographs through image-making by later generations of the communities represented.

The dispersal of Curtis material across the Library of Congress, Smithsonian, Northwestern, the National Museum of the American Indian, the Morgan Library, and other institutions also makes it possible to compare the finished twenty volumes with their production history. Research notes, letters, copper plates, variant prints, and unpublished material allow the project to be examined beyond the author’s stated intentions*15. The scale of the surviving archive does not excuse its colonial logic. It does, however, allow later researchers and communities to test that logic, revise earlier interpretations, and reuse the material for different histories.

Contemporary work by artists including Larry McNeil and Will Wilson, as presented by the Smithsonian, responds to the visual tradition that treated Indigenous peoples as remnants of the past while referring back to historical platinum printing and portrait formats*7. The National Museum of the American Indian’s Indelible likewise places historic photographic processes in dialogue with contemporary Indigenous artists, connecting the inheritance of technique to criticism of inherited historical images*21. In these works, Curtis’s photographs no longer occupy the position of an authoritative final answer; they become images to which new portraits can respond.

The twenty volumes constructed a vast visual system that fixed Indigenous cultures in the past, yet their scale also preserved information about many people, languages, clothes, objects, and places. Researchers and communities now detach that information from the publication’s original narrative and restore names, family histories, and circumstances of making. The uses of the surviving images are not fixed by the meanings Curtis assigned them; communities and researchers continue to redirect the archive. The Curtis materials therefore preserve an ongoing history in which colonial documentation can become an object of both critique and reuse.

This recontextualization also goes beyond declaring the work “fake” and stopping there. A Library of Congress research guide presents the Curtis materials as usable through multiple lines of inquiry, including photographic history, women’s history, ethnography, and family history*11. Once alterations are made explicit, the people, clothing, objects, place names, and languages in the images can be cross-checked with other records, allowing information preserved by the photograph to be returned to community histories while the photographer’s construction remains open to criticism.

Nick Yablon analyzes the case of The Oath—Apsaroke, which in 1913 was contributed to a record project intended for “future viewers”*26. A single Curtis photograph could therefore pass among ethnography, art photography, historical record, and the institution of the time capsule, acquiring different temporal roles according to the setting in which it was used.

og.title: Edward S. Curtis | The North American Indian and Indigenous Representation | Photo Coordinates
og.description: Edward S. Curtis, born near Whitewater, Wisconsin, in 1868, photographed Indigenous peoples across North America and assembled photographs, texts, vocabularies, and sound recordings in the twenty-volume The North American Indian, published from 1907 to 1930. His unified visual language—platinum printing, photogravure, and the staging of clothing and scenes—circulated widely while reinforcing a colonial idea of Indigenous peoples as a “vanishing race.” The project also involved assimilation policy, patronage, Indigenous collaborators, film, and the ways communities today reinterpret the archive.

erich-salomon.html.title: Erich Salomon | Ermanox and Modern Photojournalism | Photo Coordinates
erich-salomon.html.meta_description: Born in Berlin in 1886, Erich Salomon used the compact Ermanox camera and available interior light from the late 1920s onward to photograph courtrooms, international conferences, diplomats, and politicians before, during, and after official events. By remaining in a room for long periods, avoiding flash, and at times concealing his camera, he turned fatigue, conversation, waiting, and negotiation into news. His work reveals the conditions under which modern photojournalism developed: advances in compact cameras, journalists’ access, relationships with subjects, permission to photograph, and the mass circulation of illustrated magazines all worked together.
erich-salomon.html.lead_html: Born in Berlin in 1886, Erich Salomon used the compact Ermanox camera and available interior light from the late 1920s onward to photograph courtrooms, international conferences, diplomats, and politicians before, during, and after official events. By remaining in a room for long periods, avoiding flash, and at times concealing his camera, he turned fatigue, conversation, waiting, and negotiation into news. His work reveals the conditions under which modern photojournalism developed: advances in compact cameras, journalists’ access, relationships with subjects, permission to photograph, and the mass circulation of illustrated magazines all worked together.
erich-salomon.html.thesis_html: In political photography of the 1920s, politicians were often pictured performing public roles at lecterns, official press events, or in formally arranged groups. Using the Ermanox and available interior light, Salomon photographed waiting, negotiation, fatigue, and conversation at conferences, bringing politics into the situations in which people in power spend time and negotiate with others. The compact camera was only one condition of this shift. Salomon’s legal education, social fluency in elite circles, ongoing relationships with politicians, and the editing and distribution systems of illustrated magazines whose circulation reached roughly two million copies were all necessary before such images could reach readers as “truth from behind the scenes.” His importance to photographic history lies in making informal political gestures newsworthy while also helping to popularize a modern photojournalistic assumption: the less aware a subject appears to be of the camera, the more truthful the image seems. Salomon’s innovation in candid photography therefore has to be considered together with the power produced by access, consent, and editorial selection.

sections.title: Illustrated Magazines and the Transformation of Political Reporting
sections.body_html:
Legal Training and the Ability to Enter Closed Spaces

Salomon studied law, entered publishing and advertising after the economic difficulties that followed World War I, and moved into photographic reporting in the late 1920s. The International Center of Photography places his doctorate in law and his rapid entry into photojournalism within the same biography.*1

That background also mattered to his choice of subjects. He repeatedly photographed international conferences, courtrooms, diplomats, and cabinet ministers—people inside institutions that a photographer could not reach simply by moving physically closer. The Berlinische Galerie archive emphasizes that from 1928 onward he became a “star reporter” by photographing scenes rarely visible inside closed political and social settings.*2

Illustrated Weeklies Turned “Behind the Scenes” Into a Commodity

In 1920s Germany, illustrated magazines expanded dramatically, publishing large numbers of photographs and making individual photojournalists recognizable to readers by name and style. Salomon’s pictures were not first conceived as autonomous art objects. They were tied to a magazine culture that used articles, headlines, and page sequences to make politicians appear more immediate and familiar.*3

The Smithsonian’s photographic history collection preserves Salomon and the Ermanox as a pairing that helps explain changes in modern picture reporting. Smaller cameras and more light-sensitive working conditions expanded the spaces of news photography from outdoor ceremonies into dark conference rooms. Smithsonian records show that Salomon initially used a conventional Contessa Nettel, then adopted the Ermanox for its advantage in low light and began using a Leica around 1932. It is therefore more accurate to see him as a working reporter who updated his equipment to suit changing locations than to claim that one compact-camera invention single-handedly created a new form of news photography.*4

The German biographical dictionary likewise distinguishes Salomon from conventional representative portraiture made with large cameras, emphasizing his entry into social situations and his tendency to photograph people in the middle of action.*5

MoMA’s chronology notes that Salomon first published a photograph in a newspaper in 1926, used the Ermanox from 1927 to 1933, secretly photographed major trials in 1928–29, and was excluded from the German press in 1933 because he was Jewish.*21 The Mother of the Defendant, 1928, is an early example of his ability to show the courtroom not only as an official legal proceeding but also as a human event that included spectators and the anxiety of family members.*22

The Expansion of the Picture Press Was as Important as the Photographer’s Innovation

During Salomon’s working years, German illustrated magazines were rapidly expanding the mass audience for photography. According to MoMA, Berliner Illustrirte Zeitung had surpassed one million copies by 1920 and exceeded two million in the 1930s, becoming a major medium for reporting politics, entertainment, sports, and society through photographs.*26 The Metropolitan Museum of Art likewise explains that competition among illustrated magazines encouraged new approaches to page design and photographic reporting.*25

In this environment, a politician’s public image was shaped by sequences of photographs, headlines, captions, and page order as much as by any single innovative image. Salomon’s “behind the scenes” pictures belonged to a media culture in which readers increasingly encountered politics through faces, habits, fatigue, and social mannerisms. His place in photographic history sits at the intersection of this personalization of politics and the mass expansion of photographic magazines.

Candid Photography and the Construction of the “Real Politician”

Salomon’s photographs are often understood too simply as being closer to “truth” because they look more natural than official portraits. Bernadette Kester’s research, however, shows that politicians were already being personalized and popularized before Salomon’s success and that magazine readers were increasingly prepared to consume the private expressions of public figures.*28

Cara Finnegan’s research on the history of political photography further argues that candid photography after the late 1920s imposed new expectations of “access, intimacy, and vitality” on politicians. Herbert Hoover adapted poorly to this new visibility, while Franklin Roosevelt actively managed how his disability appeared in photographs. As apparently unguarded photography became more widespread, politicians themselves learned to manage “looking natural” as a new kind of performance.*29

This is where the historical importance and the limits of Salomon’s method meet. By reducing the camera’s presence, he made it possible to photograph outside official ritual. Yet the success of that method also helped establish a new photojournalistic value: the belief that an expression produced without apparent awareness of the camera reveals a person’s essential character. That belief itself soon became something political publicity could manage.*29

sections.title: Ermanox, Available Light, and Waiting
sections.body_html:
Removing Flash Changed How Subjects Behaved

The Ermanox had a fast lens that allowed comparatively short exposures in dim interiors. Because Salomon could avoid powerful magnesium flash, he did not have to interrupt meetings or redirect everyone’s attention toward the camera each time he photographed. The Ermanox used plate film and was not the same type of camera as the later 35mm Leica. For Salomon, its advantage was not size alone. Its fast lens allowed him to work under existing room light without remaking the atmosphere of a meeting for the sake of photography.*6

What matters in Salomon’s photographs is less the speed of “stealing a moment” than the photographer’s willingness to remain in a room for a long time. By waiting through the period before a meeting, breaks, and late-night fatigue, he allowed stretches of time excluded from official photography to enter the frame. A Berlinische Galerie retrospective also shows that his close relationships with figures such as Gustav Stresemann and Aristide Briand helped make such pictures possible. “Candid” did not mean the absence of a relationship with the subject. Salomon could photograph the moments before and after everyone turned toward the camera because he was a familiar presence at conferences and had been permitted to remain among politicians. Access and unobtrusiveness were both necessary.*7

The News Value and Ethics of the Hidden Camera

In his 1928 courtroom work, Salomon concealed his camera in places where photography was prohibited. ICP treats these courtroom images as an early body of work that was central to the making of his reputation.*8

The Smithsonian photograph of the Johann Hein trial differs from a courtroom picture in which participants pose for the camera. The very fact that photography was forbidden became part of the value of “showing the inside.” It is also an example of how the miniaturization of photographic equipment helped modern news photography renegotiate the boundary between public information and privacy. The 1928 photographs were published in Berliner Illustrirte Zeitung, and the concealed method itself became news. The technical feat of entering a prohibited zone was directly tied to the competitive promise of the picture press: giving readers access to institutions otherwise closed to them.*9

The historical question is how photojournalism came to associate a subject’s lack of awareness of the camera with photographic truthfulness, while present-day ethical concerns remain part of that assessment.*10

Social Access as a Photographic Technique

The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s study of interwar photography describes Salomon as a legally trained member of Berlin high society and argues that both his social comportment and unobtrusive equipment made entry into political conferences possible.*27 Candid photography was therefore not a method available to anyone who happened to own a small camera. The intimacy of the frame depended on social conditions: who could enter a conference room, remain there for hours without arousing suspicion, and speak with politicians.

sections.title: From International Conferences to Ellis Island
sections.body_html:
The Time in Which Politics Happens, More Than the Politician’s “Expression”

At the League of Nations and diplomatic conferences, Salomon repeatedly photographed negotiations around tables, time spent reading documents, and conversation during breaks instead of heroic poses during speeches. MoMA’s holdings include views of the League’s observation galleries and conference participants that look laterally into the institutional setting.*11

In a Metropolitan Museum photograph of Ramsay MacDonald, Albert Einstein, and Max Planck, famous figures are not ceremonially arranged in a row; they are caught in the middle of social interaction. What becomes news is not fame alone, but how well-known people behave when sharing the same space.*12

Photographs of Anthony Eden similarly emphasize distance within the room and bodily posture, with flags and official backdrops playing a secondary role. Salomon consistently photographed political power as a situation in which people gather and spend time; official symbols no longer organize the entire image.*13

Berühmte Zeitgenossen in unbewachten Augenblicken and Ellis Island

The 1931 photobook Berühmte Zeitgenossen in unbewachten Augenblicken assembled famous contemporaries in, as the title states, “unguarded moments,” presenting Salomon’s method in book form. The Berlinische Galerie lists the volume among his major achievements. By removing individual photographs from topical articles and gathering them into a book, Salomon himself presented the “unguarded moment” as a repeatable authorial method. News pictures designed for one-time consumption in magazines became a body of work bearing the photographer’s name.*14

The Ellis Island reportage preserved by the same museum shows that Salomon’s subjects were not limited to European politicians. Photographing spaces of immigration inspection extended his work from the private moments of powerful figures to the situations of people subjected to institutional authority.*15

The Observation Gallery in the League of Nations, 1928, is one example in which political reporting encompasses the conference floor together with the surrounding spaces where people watch and wait.*23 John Kennedy, London, 1939, in the National Gallery of Art, shows that Salomon continued photographing international figures after exile and prevents his method from being reduced to a brief technological fashion of the Weimar period.*24

The Weimar Picture Press as the Larger Transformation

In contemporary German illustrated magazines, Alfred Eisenstaedt, Felix H. Man, Martin Munkácsi, Willy Ruge, and others were also changing the appearance of news through compact cameras and photographic sequences. The Met situates this generation within the broader transformation of the German picture press from text-led reporting toward increasingly visual journalism after World War I.*25

Salomon’s distinctive position within that transformation was his concentration on political conferences, diplomacy, corporate leadership, and other settings in which access itself was ordinarily restricted. Pages of Berliner Illustrirte Zeitung and a group of roughly fifty-five related items preserved at ICP show that his photographs functioned as picture reporting encountered through magazine spreads and article sequences more than as isolated works.*30

SFMOMA’s holdings include dinners at San Simeon, a U.S. Senate banking investigation, a Royal Dutch Shell board meeting, the League of Nations, and social occasions. Salomon’s movement across closed social spaces where political, financial, and cultural elites gathered made “access” itself a defining field of his photography.*31

sections.title: Exile, Archive, and the Legacy of Photojournalism
sections.body_html:
The Exclusion of a Jewish Photographer and Arrest in the Netherlands

After the Nazi seizure of power, Salomon could no longer continue working in Germany because he was Jewish and moved to the Netherlands. Following the German occupation in 1940, he and his family were arrested, and he was murdered at Auschwitz in 1944. He continued photographing after exile, but under occupation the safety of his family and the preservation of his archive became urgent concerns. According to the biography preserved by the Smithsonian, he hid negatives in several locations during the war. The surviving body of work is therefore itself an archive that passed through persecution and dispersal.*16

The Berlinische Galerie now preserves a Salomon archive of more than 10,000 items, allowing his work to be followed through negatives, prints, and documents before and after publication. The archive reconstructs the production process of magazine reporting that disappears when photographs are viewed only as individual museum objects. Because it includes negatives and related records as well as famous published images, researchers can ask how many exposures were made, what was selected, and how material moved into the magazine. It makes possible a history of photojournalism as a process of waiting, repeated exposure, editing, and publication rather than a mythology of the single “decisive” picture.*17

The Myth of the “Candid” and the Limits of Equipment

The Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Smithsonian both position Salomon as an important figure in the formation of candid photography and modern photojournalism. But owning the same Ermanox would not have enabled another photographer to make the same pictures.*18

The fact that the German Society for Photography established a press photography award in his name in 1971 shows that later journalism inherited “proximity to the scene” and an individual photographer’s mode of observation as parts of Salomon’s legacy.*19

Salomon’s place in photographic history reaches beyond the appealing idea that he made politicians look human. Access to closed institutions, techniques for minimizing the visibility of photography, editorial preference for moments when subjects seemed unaware of the camera, and mass magazine circulation converged in his work to give concrete form to a journalistic norm that continues today: the promise of showing what happens “behind the scenes.”*20

The “Unguarded Moment” as a Convention of Truth

Media-historical research argues that informal images of politicians were already appearing in magazines before Salomon and that his photographs were received in a culture whose readers were increasingly prepared to see politicians as private, human personalities.*28 It is therefore more accurate to place Salomon among the photographers who made the shift from official political portraiture toward personalized political imagery especially visible than to mythologize him as a lone inventor.

A subject’s apparent unawareness of the camera does not automatically mean that a photograph shows the “real person.” The image a reader recognizes as an unguarded self is produced through choices about who gains entry, how long the photographer waits, which exposures are selected, and how a magazine supplies headlines and page design. Salomon’s innovation did not eliminate these mediations. It placed him near the center of the process through which modern photojournalism established a new convention for making “behind the scenes” appear truthful.

og.title: Erich Salomon | Ermanox and Modern Photojournalism | Photo Coordinates
og.description: Born in Berlin in 1886, Erich Salomon used the compact Ermanox camera and available interior light from the late 1920s onward to photograph courtrooms, international conferences, diplomats, and politicians before, during, and after official events. By remaining in a room for long periods, avoiding flash, and at times concealing his camera, he turned fatigue, conversation, waiting, and negotiation into news. His work reveals the conditions under which modern photojournalism developed: advances in compact cameras, journalists’ access, relationships with subjects, permission to photograph, and the mass circulation of illustrated magazines all worked together.

frantisek-drtikol.html.title: František Drtikol | Nudes, Geometry, Light, and Spiritual Thought | Photo Coordinates
frantisek-drtikol.html.meta_description: František Drtikol, born in Příbram in Bohemia, then part of Austria-Hungary, in 1883, built his career on a Prague portrait studio while constructing photographs of the nude through geometric sets and forceful light and shadow. His work moved from early Symbolist imagery to modernist nudes in the 1920s and paper and wooden figures in the 1930s; later he shifted toward Buddhist study, translation, and painting. His career traces a method of designing body, stage, and light before exposure alongside a sustained spiritual interest that eventually carried him beyond photography.
frantisek-drtikol.html.lead_html: František Drtikol, born in Příbram in Bohemia, then part of Austria-Hungary, in 1883, built his career on a Prague portrait studio while constructing photographs of the nude through geometric sets and forceful light and shadow. His work moved from early Symbolist imagery to modernist nudes in the 1920s and paper and wooden figures in the 1930s; later he shifted toward Buddhist study, translation, and painting. His career traces a method of designing body, stage, and light before exposure alongside a sustained spiritual interest that eventually carried him beyond photography.
frantisek-drtikol.html.thesis_html: Drtikol’s geometric nudes extended the control of lighting, background, pose, and printing learned in a professional portrait studio into a method for constructing reality before exposure. He adapted studio techniques developed through commercial portraiture in Prague to personal work, and during the 1920s treated the body, arcs, ramps, ropes, and shadows as components designed together before the photograph was made*4. At a moment when New Objectivity and Bauhaus-related photography sought new views of cities, machines, and everyday objects, Drtikol built a “reality for photography” inside the studio. Modern dance allowed bodies to correspond to diagonals and curves, while hard lighting turned the cast shadow into an independent pictorial element. Around 1930 he began replacing living models with paper and wooden figures, moving toward what has been termed Photopurism and gaining still greater control over posture, balance, and repetition*14. During the same period, his interest in Buddhism and other spiritual traditions deepened, and in 1935 he largely left photography for painting, meditation, and translation*1. By designing bodies and light and constructing the scene in front of the camera, Drtikol demonstrated a modernist path in photography built through the deliberate construction of reality for the camera.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Munich and Prague Photographic Culture

After training in a local photographic studio, Drtikol studied optics, chemistry, photography, and art at a photographic school in Munich from 1901 to 1903*11. The Toledo Museum of Art notes his exposure during these years to contemporary European currents including Symbolism, Jugendstil, and Pictorialism*20. Soft focus, allegorical figures, and decorative curves remain visible in his early work. He opened a studio in Příbram in 1907 and another in Prague in 1910, building a professional foundation through portraits of politicians, artists, and intellectuals*2.

His career crossed major social changes, from the final years of Austria-Hungary through the creation of Czechoslovakia in 1918 and the later avant-garde culture of Prague. No source establishes these events as direct causes of his style, but photography itself moved rapidly from Pictorialism toward modernist forms. When Bratislava City Gallery situates Drtikol in the Czech avant-garde, it treats him as a significant transitional figure moving from Art Nouveau and Symbolism toward Cubism, Futurism, abstraction, and modern dance, because those shifts can be followed within a single career*10.

The professional life of the dancer Ervína Kupferová clarifies the culture of the body with which Drtikol’s nude photography intersected. Research by the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague records that in 1925 she registered a private school of rhythmic movement. From 1927 to 1933, she taught dance and visual training at music and theater institutions in Kharkiv, where she also headed a choreography department*21. Treating Kupferová only as Drtikol’s wife and model leaves out the parallel existence of a professional dance practice concerned with extension, flexion, and movement held in suspension. Her career does not prove that she directly determined Drtikol’s style, but it documents a concrete working environment in which photography made around 1919 and the early 1920s met new forms of bodily expression.

Commemorative material from the Museum of Decorative Arts in Prague considers Drtikol’s commercial photography, nudes, spiritual studies, and later painting within a single career*11. Bringing those fields together helps trace a continuity from the geometric nudes of the 1920s through the move away from photography.

The Portrait Studio and Constructed Photography

In the Prague portrait studio, Drtikol had to control a sitter’s posture, background, lighting, negative, and final print within limited working time. The Met records that he earned his living through portraits of prominent figures while pursuing experiments with geometric sets and strong lighting in his nude studies*4. His personal experiments were made possible by a professional environment in which studio equipment and repeatable technical procedures were readily available.

The early landscapes and Pictorialist photographs form a markedly different starting point from the hard geometry of the 1920s. A Musée d’Orsay exhibition of the early landscapes foregrounds mist, countryside, and urban views rendered in soft tonal fields*18. The move from making photography approximate a painterly atmosphere toward arranging actual light and objects before the camera is central to the formation of his modernism.

The National Gallery of Art also holds multiple works that place Drtikol within Central European modern photography*13. Commercial portraiture and personal experimentation depended on the same accumulated techniques of studio control, showing that his modernism was built on professional equipment and repeatable craft.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Body, Stage, and Light

During the 1920s, Drtikol did more than place a nude in front of a backdrop. Circles, columns, ramps, wave forms, ropes, strong shadows, and the body were arranged as equivalent elements of the picture. In The Composition, the figure and geometric forms meet as a balance of flat planes, giving compositional structure priority over the illusion of depth and determining the major relations in the image before exposure*5. The camera becomes the final step that fixes relations first conceived and then built through real light and objects.

Modern dance gave this method a particular kind of movement. Stretching, twisting, and flexion in dancers and gymnasts offered gestures different from the still body of classical sculpture and could be aligned with curves and diagonals. Bratislava City Gallery notes that Drtikol drew formal stimulus from Cubism, Futurism, Expressionism, abstraction, and modern dance while refusing to make formal experimentation the sole value of avant-garde art*10. Geometry in the studio functioned as a stage through which bodily movement and spiritual states could be rendered visually.

Light became an active compositional element. Strong arc lamps and deep shadow could turn one portion of a body into a white plane, submerge another in black, and make the cast shadow of a set element as forceful as the object itself. The Museum of Fine Arts, Houston describes the postwar shift from soft Pictorialist effects toward hard lighting and geometric staging because technique itself became part of the picture’s structure*12.

Drtikol’s work is also held in international collections including the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum*19. Across these collections, circles, wave forms, ramps, and bodies recur in changing combinations, establishing a sustained compositional principle across changing sets.

Photopurism and Spiritual Thought

Around 1930, Drtikol increasingly replaced living models with paper and wooden figures. Research at Charles University examines the artificial figures of 1929–35 as part of a phase termed “Photopurism” and studies its relation to Buddhism, Christianity, and other spiritual currents through archival sources*14. The figures worked as more than substitutes for models. They allowed minute, repeated adjustments of bodily angle, balance, and distance while greatly reducing the constraints of fatigue, facial expression, and human mobility. The long-standing practice of treating the body as a compositional element thus moved toward a subject that could be controlled even more completely.

The connection to spiritual thought cannot be explained by simply labeling the late work “Buddhist.” Religious-studies research at Masaryk University follows Drtikol from the late 1920s as a translator, intermediary, and teacher. He adapted Buddhist concepts for Czech-speaking audiences and communicated them to students and listeners*6. Because this activity continued well after he withdrew from photography, spiritual study remained a sustained part of his later life.

A 2019 Charles University study also criticizes the simple description of Drtikol as the “father of Czech Buddhism,” analyzing an eclectic system in which Buddhism, Theosophy, modernism, and later Marxism coexisted*7. The study does not map particular geometric forms, mannequins, or uses of light directly onto specific Buddhist doctrines. The historical proximity between his changing photographic form and spiritual study is well documented, but evidence for explaining any individual composition through a single doctrine remains limited.

During these years Drtikol became deeply involved in the study and translation of Buddhism, yoga, Taoism, and related traditions*6. Evidence remains too limited to identify individual poses as illustrations of specific religious concepts. What can be documented is the overlap between a period in which the body became simplified into abstract structures of ascent, balance, circle, and light and a period in which spiritual study moved closer to the center of his life. Formal simplification made it easier to work with a universalized and symbolic body instead of an individual portrait, and eventually he moved toward painting and meditation, media that no longer required photography at all.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The Composition and The Wave

The Composition is a representative example in which the female nude and black-and-white geometric forms are tightly integrated, so the body functions as a component of line, plane, and light more than as a character in a narrative*5. The body’s curves and the diagonals of the set create tension, and rhythm on the picture plane becomes stronger than spatial depth. Carbon printing and deep blacks support the abstraction materially. A living person remains the subject of the photograph even as the body operates as an abstract form within the image.

Symbolist subjects continued for a time after Drtikol began moving toward geometric nudes. An article in Fotóművészet discussing a work held by the Olomouc Museum shows how Vanitas around 1920 combines a nude and skull, and how themes such as Judith, Salome, and Cleopatra—subjects of death and desire—continued into the early 1920s*22. Over the following years, props carrying explicit allegory were gradually replaced by circles, ramps, waves, light, and shadow. Drtikol’s modernism was therefore not a sudden rejection of symbolic meaning but a gradual transformation of the stage through which meaning was attached to the body.

In The Wave, the body’s curves correspond to a wave-shaped set, bringing the decorative rhythm of 1920s Art Deco into contact with the dynamic language of modern dance. The Museum of Decorative Arts in Prague treats the 1920s as a period of particularly strong international recognition and records honors including his award at the 1925 Paris Exposition of Decorative Arts*1. The set is more than attractive background decoration: it determines posture, produces shadow, and controls the direction of movement across the entire image.

Mannequin Photographs and World of the Soul

In the later World of the Soul, living models with recognizable faces and individual identities disappear, replaced by simplified figures moving through light and geometry*15. A mannequin can hold the same pose for long periods, be adjusted by minute degrees, and allow the location of a shadow to be tested repeatedly. As the Olomouc Museum notes in discussing the flexibility of Drtikol’s figures and their suitability for composition, they functioned as concrete tools for extending control over the image*8.

In explaining the move from living models to mannequins, Stanislav Doležal, curator of a Drtikol retrospective, has emphasized that freedom from the model allowed the photographer to intervene in the figure itself down to its details*23. The change did not abandon the body; it brought to a conclusion a movement toward control over posture, contour, shadow, and position within the frame. This account makes clear how a method that began in portraiture by composing the image before exposure eventually extended to the making of the figure itself.

In 1935 Drtikol sold his studio and ended his professional activity as a photographer. The Toledo Museum cites the economic effects of the Great Depression and his growing commitment to spiritual thought among the conditions surrounding this withdrawal*20. He subsequently concentrated on painting, meditation, and the translation of Buddhist texts*6. In 1942 he donated roughly two thousand photographs, documents, books, and related materials to the Museum of Decorative Arts in Prague*11. The mannequin photographs intensify the formalization of the body developed since the 1920s and connect the increasingly spiritual and abstract direction of the images to his later movement away from photography as a medium.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Central European Modernism and the Nude

Across Europe in the 1920s and 1930s, the lucid description of objects associated with New Objectivity, the new vision of the Bauhaus, photojournalism, and photomontage expanded the field of photography. Drtikol shared hard light, geometry, diagonals, and abstraction with these developments, but his subject itself was constructed inside the studio. Instead of discovering cities or machines from unfamiliar viewpoints, he arranged people, objects, and shadows in advance and built reality into a photographable composition*9. The difference shows that modernism in photography encompassed more than one understanding of the medium.

Czech Photographic Avant-Garde, 1918–1948, edited by Vladimír Birgus, places Drtikol alongside Jaromír Funke, Jaroslav Rössler, Jindřich Štyrský, Josef Sudek, and others within a shared Czech history of photography, treating Pictorialism, the avant-garde, the “New Photography,” advertising, and Surrealism as interconnected fields*3. In this setting, Drtikol’s geometric nudes are not isolated studio experiments but one response to a period after the First World War when both the uses and formal languages of photography expanded rapidly in Czechoslovakia.

Later Czech avant-garde photographers including Jaromír Funke, Josef Sudek, and Jaroslav Rössler developed light, abstraction, the city, and the photogram in other directions. Drtikol need not be treated as their direct cause; he can be situated as part of the generation moving from Pictorialism toward geometric modernity*10. His work matters as an example of photographic modernism built through constructing a stage in front of the camera, alongside modernist approaches centered on discovering a more “objective” view of external reality.

Drtikol sought to detach the nude from clothing and occupation and treat the body as a universal form. Material from Příbram presents his own association of the nude with natural and spiritual beauty*2. The idea corresponds to a method that reduces clothing, social setting, and occupational detail in order to concentrate on the body’s line and its relation to light.

Contemporary criticism can also question what this universalization does to the history and agency of individual models, especially when the female nude becomes a formal element controlled by the photographer. The work’s formal precision and the power relation involved in controlling a model’s body are two aspects of the same photographic method. When male nudes and mannequin photographs are considered alongside the female nudes, the project appears less as an exclusive concern with female sensuality than as a broader reduction of bodies to line and symbol*16.

This constructed approach marks a different Czech avant-garde trajectory from the photograms and urban or light-based experiments of Funke and Rössler. Bratislava City Gallery treats Drtikol as an artist of extended transition because Symbolism, Art Deco, Cubism, Futurism, and dance coexist within his studio representations of the body*10.

Reassessment and the Departure from Photography

Drtikol’s photographs circulated less widely internationally after the Second World War, and research and exhibitions led by Anna Fárová and others from the 1970s onward helped drive a major reassessment. The Museum of Decorative Arts in Prague traces this research history, including a 1972 retrospective, through the extensive photographs and papers donated by Drtikol himself*1. Galerie Rudolfinum’s 1998 exhibition brought photography, painting, drawing, and spiritual thought together, helping expand the familiar image of Drtikol as simply a modernist photographer of the nude*9.

Postwar reassessment depended heavily on Fárová and later curators presenting Art Nouveau, modernism, Art Deco, and the late mannequins as parts of a continuous career. Radio Prague’s account of a retrospective records Fárová’s emphasis on Drtikol’s balancing of line, contour, figure, and light within the frame, while Doležal connects the mannequins and spiritual research of the 1930s to the same history of making*24. The international reputation of Drtikol as a “modernist nude” is therefore also a history reconstructed through Czech archives and retrospective exhibitions.

His withdrawal from photography in 1935 can likewise be understood as a change of medium. A retrospective at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando concentrates on the modernist nudes of 1923–29 while extending the biography toward his later spiritual studies*17. For Drtikol, the problem of abstracting body and light continued after painting, meditation, and translation replaced photography at the center of his life. For a period, photography had been the principal means through which he materialized inwardly conceived images; later, those functions shifted to other media and practices.

The Musée d’Orsay exhibition of early landscapes shows a starting point in which mist and countryside were rendered through soft tonal effects*18. The Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando’s survey of the 1923–29 nudes concentrates on the later move into geometric studio construction*17. Considering the two periods together places the geometric nude within a methodological transformation that developed across his long career.
